factors.label: Pitot probe blockage
factors.description: Pitot probes blocked by ice, insects, covers or debris, or unheated, corrupting airspeed sensing.

factors.label: Static port blockage
factors.description: Static ports obstructed, corrupting altitude, airspeed and vertical speed indications.

factors.label: Unreliable airspeed indication
factors.description: Cockpit airspeed indications inconsistent with actual airspeed, typically following pitot or static failures.

factors.label: Spurious overspeed warning
factors.description: Overspeed warning triggered by erroneous airspeed data rather than actual overspeed.

factors.label: Angle-of-attack sensor failure
factors.description: An angle-of-attack vane provided erroneous data to flight control or warning systems.

factors.label: MCAS activation
factors.description: The 737 MAX Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System commanded repeated nose-down stabilizer trim from a single erroneous AoA input.

factors.label: ADIRU data fault
factors.description: An air data inertial reference unit output corrupted data, driving spurious flight control or warning responses.

factors.label: Radio altimeter failure
factors.description: A radio altimeter provided erroneous height, typically feeding automation with a false landing condition.

factors.label: Erroneous engine indication
factors.description: Engine instrumentation read incorrectly, typically from iced probes, leading the crew or autothrottle to set wrong thrust.

factors.label: Autopilot disconnect
factors.description: The autopilot disconnected, handing the aircraft to the crew, often at the start of an upset.

factors.label: Flight control law degradation
factors.description: Fly-by-wire protections were lost or degraded, removing stall or attitude protections the crew may have relied on.

factors.label: Autothrottle mode confusion
factors.description: The crew misunderstood what the autothrottle or autothrust was doing, allowing thrust to remain at idle or an inappropriate setting.

factors.label: Automation mode confusion
factors.description: The crew's mental model of the automation's active modes diverged from the actual state.

factors.label: Automation dependency and manual skill erosion
factors.description: Habitual reliance on automation degraded manual flying proficiency or willingness to fly manually.

factors.label: Aerodynamic stall
factors.description: The wing exceeded its critical angle of attack and lost lift.

factors.label: Stall or upset misdiagnosed
factors.description: The crew misidentified the aircraft's state: not recognizing a stall, or treating another condition as a stall or overspeed.

factors.label: Inappropriate stall recovery
factors.description: The crew's control inputs during a stall or approach to stall deepened it, typically nose-up inputs or overriding the stick pusher.

factors.label: Stick shaker or pusher activation
factors.description: The stall warning stick shaker or stall protection stick pusher activated.

factors.label: Dual sidestick input
factors.description: Both pilots made simultaneous sidestick inputs without clear transfer of control.

factors.label: Inappropriate flight control input
factors.description: Control inputs outside what the situation required, including excessive or oscillatory inputs.

factors.label: Startle and surprise
factors.description: A sudden unexpected event degraded the crew's cognitive performance during the critical seconds after it.

factors.label: Loss of situational awareness
factors.description: The crew lost track of the aircraft's position, energy state, configuration or trajectory.

factors.label: Inadequate monitoring and cross-check
factors.description: The pilot monitoring did not detect or call out deviations in speed, altitude, configuration or flight path.

factors.label: CRM breakdown
factors.description: Crew coordination, communication, or challenge-and-response failed, including steep authority gradients.

factors.label: Sterile cockpit violation
factors.description: Non-essential conversation or activity during a critical phase of flight distracted the crew.

factors.label: Procedural non-compliance
factors.description: The crew did not follow a checklist, standard operating procedure or limitation.

factors.label: Fatigue
factors.description: Crew fatigue from duty time, sleep loss, commuting or circadian disruption degraded performance.

factors.label: Inadequate training
factors.description: The crew had not been trained, or trained adequately, for the situation encountered.

factors.label: Low experience on type or in role
factors.description: Limited experience on aircraft type or in the crew role contributed.

factors.label: Spatial disorientation
factors.description: The crew lost accurate perception of the aircraft's attitude or motion.

factors.label: Somatogravic illusion
factors.description: Longitudinal acceleration was perceived as a pitch-up, prompting a nose-down input.

factors.label: Visual illusion
factors.description: Terrain, lighting or weather created a misleading visual picture of the approach path.

factors.label: Pilot incapacitation
factors.description: A pilot became unable to perform duties from medical or environmental causes.

factors.label: Deliberate act by crew
factors.description: Investigators concluded the accident resulted from an intentional act by a crew member.

factors.label: Unstabilized approach
factors.description: The approach was outside stabilized approach criteria and was continued.

factors.label: Go-around not initiated
factors.description: A go-around was warranted but not initiated, or initiated too late.

factors.label: Long landing or touchdown beyond zone
factors.description: The aircraft touched down beyond the touchdown zone, consuming runway needed to stop.

factors.label: Tailwind on landing
factors.description: A tailwind component increased groundspeed and landing distance.

factors.label: Wet or contaminated runway
factors.description: Water, snow or ice on the runway degraded braking.

factors.label: Delayed deceleration devices
factors.description: Reverse thrust, spoilers or brakes were applied late or not at all after touchdown.

factors.label: Runway overrun
factors.description: The aircraft departed the runway end or side.

factors.label: Runway incursion
factors.description: An aircraft or vehicle was on a runway without authorization or in conflict with another.

factors.label: Wrong runway or taxiway used
factors.description: The crew took off or landed on a runway or taxiway other than the one cleared.

factors.label: Takeoff without clearance
factors.description: The crew began the takeoff roll without a valid takeoff clearance.

factors.label: ATC communication breakdown
factors.description: Communication between ATC and the crew failed through ambiguity, blocked transmissions, language or non-standard phraseology.

factors.label: ATC staffing and workload
factors.description: Controller workload, staffing or fatigue degraded ATC performance.

factors.label: TCAS RA versus ATC instruction conflict
factors.description: A TCAS resolution advisory conflicted with an ATC instruction and the crew followed ATC.

factors.label: Midair collision
factors.description: Two aircraft collided in flight.

factors.label: Ground collision
factors.description: The aircraft collided with another aircraft or vehicle on the ground.

factors.label: Surface surveillance unavailable
factors.description: ATC had no functioning surface surveillance to detect the conflict.

factors.label: Airport signage, markings or lighting deficiency
factors.description: Airport signage, markings, lighting or layout contributed to crew or ATC error.

factors.label: Controlled flight into terrain
factors.description: An airworthy aircraft under crew control was flown into terrain, water or an obstacle.

factors.label: Loss of control in flight
factors.description: The crew lost control of the aircraft in flight.

factors.label: Inadequate response to GPWS/EGPWS
factors.description: A ground proximity warning was ignored, responded to late, or was not installed or effective.

factors.label: Minimum safe altitude warning inhibited
factors.description: The ATC minimum safe altitude warning system was inhibited or ineffective.

factors.label: Navigation or lateral path error
factors.description: The crew misjudged position or descended below safe altitude through navigation error.

factors.label: Altimeter setting error
factors.description: An incorrect altimeter setting or altimeter reading error caused an altitude misjudgment.

factors.label: Descent below minimums
factors.description: The crew descended below the applicable minimum altitude without required visual references.

factors.label: Low visibility
factors.description: Fog, cloud, darkness or precipitation restricted visual references.

factors.label: Dark night conditions
factors.description: Darkness removed external visual references.

factors.label: Thunderstorm or convective weather
factors.description: Thunderstorms, convective activity or associated turbulence and precipitation contributed.

factors.label: Windshear or microburst
factors.description: A sudden change in wind velocity along the flight path exceeded the aircraft's performance margin.

factors.label: Airframe ice accretion
factors.description: Ice accreted on the airframe, degrading lift and control.

factors.label: Inadequate ground de-icing or anti-ice use
factors.description: Ground de-icing was inadequate, or airframe or engine anti-ice systems were not selected on.

factors.label: High-altitude ice crystals
factors.description: Ice crystals at altitude affected probes or engines beyond certification envelopes.

factors.label: Fuel system icing
factors.description: Ice released in the fuel system restricted fuel flow to the engines.

factors.label: Volcanic ash encounter
factors.description: The aircraft flew through volcanic ash, damaging engines or systems.

factors.label: Bird strike
factors.description: Birds struck the aircraft or were ingested by engines.

factors.label: Engine failure or power loss
factors.description: One or more engines lost power.

factors.label: All-engine power loss
factors.description: All engines lost thrust, forcing a glide.

factors.label: Uncontained engine failure
factors.description: An engine rotor failure ejected high-energy fragments that damaged the aircraft.

factors.label: Wrong engine shut down
factors.description: The crew shut down the functioning engine instead of the failed one.

factors.label: Wrong lever or control selected
factors.description: The crew operated the wrong lever, switch or control.

factors.label: Fuel exhaustion
factors.description: All usable fuel was consumed.

factors.label: Fuel starvation
factors.description: Fuel was on board but did not reach the engines because of mismanagement or system failure.

factors.label: Fuel leak
factors.description: A fuel line or tank leaked in flight.

factors.label: Fuel quantity calculation error
factors.description: The fuel on board was miscalculated, misindicated or misplanned.

factors.label: Fuel tank explosion
factors.description: Flammable vapour in a fuel tank ignited.

factors.label: Electrical wiring failure
factors.description: Electrical wiring chafed, arced or short-circuited.

factors.label: Flammable cabin or insulation material
factors.description: Cabin or insulation materials sustained fire propagation.

factors.label: In-flight fire
factors.description: Fire or smoke developed in flight.

factors.label: Cargo compartment fire
factors.description: Fire started in a cargo compartment, often from undeclared or improperly packaged dangerous goods.

factors.label: Delayed diversion or lengthy smoke checklist
factors.description: The crew delayed landing to complete procedures or dump fuel while a fire developed.

factors.label: Explosive or rapid decompression
factors.description: The cabin lost pressure suddenly.

factors.label: Cabin pressurization not maintained
factors.description: The cabin failed to pressurize or gradually depressurized without crew recognition.

factors.label: Hypoxia
factors.description: Insufficient oxygen incapacitated occupants.

factors.label: Cargo door failure
factors.description: A cargo door opened or failed in flight.

factors.label: Structural failure in flight
factors.description: Primary structure failed in flight.

factors.label: Metal fatigue
factors.description: Cyclic loading produced cracks that led to failure.

factors.label: Pressure bulkhead failure
factors.description: A pressure bulkhead failed, typically from an improper repair.

factors.label: Total hydraulic failure
factors.description: Hydraulic power to flight controls was lost.

factors.label: Flight control system failure
factors.description: A flight control surface or its actuation failed or jammed.

factors.label: Rudder hardover or reversal
factors.description: The rudder moved uncommanded or opposite to input.

factors.label: Horizontal stabilizer trim failure
factors.description: The horizontal stabilizer trim system failed, jammed or ran away.

factors.label: In-flight thrust reverser deployment
factors.description: A thrust reverser deployed in flight.

factors.label: Windshield failure
factors.description: A cockpit windshield failed in flight.

factors.label: Landing gear failure or collapse
factors.description: The landing gear failed, collapsed or did not extend.

factors.label: Maintenance error
factors.description: A maintenance action was performed incorrectly, or a required action was omitted.

factors.label: Inadequate lubrication or wear inspection
factors.description: Insufficient lubrication or wear checks allowed a component to wear to failure.

factors.label: Inadequate inspection program
factors.description: Inspection intervals or methods were insufficient to detect the defect.

factors.label: Weight and balance error
factors.description: The aircraft was loaded outside limits, or its weight or balance was miscalculated.

factors.label: Takeoff performance data error
factors.description: Erroneous takeoff weight or performance data produced insufficient thrust or wrong speeds.

factors.label: Takeoff configuration error
factors.description: The aircraft took off without flaps or slats set, typically with the takeoff warning system inoperative.

factors.label: Tail strike
factors.description: The tail contacted the runway on takeoff or landing.

factors.label: Hard landing or bounced landing
factors.description: A high vertical speed or bounced touchdown damaged the aircraft or led to loss of control.

factors.label: Ditching
factors.description: The aircraft was intentionally landed on water.

factors.label: Post-impact fire
factors.description: Fire following impact affected survivability.

factors.label: Evacuation or survivability deficiency
factors.description: Evacuation or survival was hindered by equipment, procedure or behaviour.

factors.label: Design deficiency
factors.description: The aircraft or system design had a flaw or assumption that contributed.

factors.label: Certification shortfall
factors.description: The certification process failed to identify or address the hazard.

factors.label: Warning or alerting deficiency
factors.description: A warning was absent, inhibited, ambiguous or easily confused with another.

factors.label: Regulatory oversight deficiency
factors.description: The regulator's surveillance or rule-making was insufficient.

factors.label: Operator safety culture or management
factors.description: Operator management, culture, hiring or pressure contributed.

factors.label: Manufacturer communication or documentation failure
factors.description: The manufacturer failed to inform operators or crews of a system behaviour or hazard.

factors.label: Known defect not resolved
factors.description: A defect or hazard had been reported previously but not corrected before the accident.

factors.label: Hostile or criminal act
factors.description: The accident resulted from a bomb, hijacking, missile or sabotage.

factors.label: Successful emergency landing
factors.description: The crew landed the aircraft with no or few fatalities despite a serious failure.

factors.label: Checklist or procedure design flaw
factors.description: The published checklist or procedure was inadequate, ambiguous or too long for the situation.

factors.label: High workload and task saturation
factors.description: Simultaneous demands exceeded the crew's capacity.

factors.label: Excessive speed for phase
factors.description: The aircraft was flown faster than appropriate for the phase or configuration.

factors.label: Low energy state on approach
factors.description: Airspeed decayed below the target during approach without correction.

factors.label: Reduced control authority
factors.description: The crew lacked sufficient control authority to recover.

records.title: TAI 307
records.summary: The DC-7C departed Bordeaux at night with light drizzle and limited visibility. Following takeoff, the aircraft reached only 30 m altitude and failed to climb further before flying into a pine forest 2950 m from the runway. The aircraft cut a swath through the forest, and the fuselage broke up before post-crash fire destroyed the wreckage.
records.probable_cause: With lack of visual references in darkness, the pilot failed to maintain optimum climbing speed and did not carefully monitor the altimeter, allowing the aircraft to descend back to terrain level.

factors.evidence: Darkness and a lack of visual references led the crew to have difficulty maintaining awareness of the aircraft's position and altitude.
Evidence from a reconstructed flight showed the rate of climb would decrease if optimum climbing speed was not maintained.
A pilot may follow a line of flight that will bring the aircraft back near the ground if the altimeter is not carefully watched.
The aircraft flew into a pine forest located 2950 m from the end of the runway after reaching only 30 m altitude.

events.text: Departure from Bordeaux with light drizzle and 3 knot wind
Aircraft rotates and begins climb
Aircraft fails to maintain climb rate, altitude plateaus at 30 meters
Aircraft enters pine forest 2,950 meters from runway end, wings impact trees
Fuselage breaks up, post-crash fire, rescue hampered by darkness and terrain

notes: Extracted from report using History of Flight section
Enriched with 5 timestamped events

records.title: Malév 355
records.summary: Malév Flight 355, an Ilyushin Il-18V with 21 aboard (6 crew, 13 passengers, 2 unspecified), crashed near Paris-Le Bourget during final ILS approach to runway 25 on 23 November 1962. The aircraft stalled while performing a high-G load maneuver during instrument approach in foggy conditions. At 14:05:30, aircraft reported normally at beacon. At approximately 14:06:40 during final approach, radar blip disappeared and crew became unresponsive. Wreckage found extremely compact, upside down, 6.157 km south-southwest of runway entrance at 90 m altitude. Investigation could not determine why crew performed the high-G maneuver that resulted in stall.
records.probable_cause: The aircraft stalled during a high G-load maneuver while executing an instrument approach to runway 25 at Le Bourget in foggy conditions with icing possibility around 1,800 feet altitude. The investigation could not determine the cause that provoked this maneuver. (p. 126-128)

factors.evidence: Heavy fog and stratus cloud conditions at Paris with severely reduced visibility. Weather forecast indicated frequent fog and stratus cloud with possibility of light icing. IFR/IMC conditions at approach with possible moderate to strong icing around 1,800 feet. (p. 69, 174)

Aircraft stalled while performing a high G-load maneuver during approach with landing gear extended and engines near full power. The stall form was incompatible except with a high-G maneuver per Soviet expert analysis. (p. 126-127)

Investigation concluded aircraft stalled while performing high-G maneuver during approach phase in configuration with landing gear down and flaps 30 degrees. Stall characteristics confirmed by Soviet aircraft designer experts. (p. 126)
Weather conditions included moderate to strong icing possibility around 1,800 feet elevation. Ice accumulation on airframe was considered as contributing to stall characteristics observed. (p. 174)

Aircraft crashed 6.1 kilometers east-northeast of Le Bourget airport near road from Paris to Soissons. Aircraft exploded with high flames visible upon impact. Wreckage extremely compact, upside down. 21 occupants killed (8 crew, 13 passengers). (p. 174)

events.text: Flight 355 departed Budapest at 07:44 GMT with captain Kapitany, crew of 4 flight staff (PNT), 3 cabin staff (PNC), 13 passengers bound for Frankfurt stopover, then Paris-Le Bourget. Total 21 occupants.

In Frankfurt, crew spent approximately 2 hours at meteorological office for weather briefing. Crew noted frequent fog and stratus cloud with light icing possibility en route and at destination Paris-Le Bourget.

Aircraft approaching Paris-Le Bourget. ILS approach to runway 25 in progress. IFR/IMC conditions with heavy fog and stratus cloud; visibility severely reduced; icing conditions probable around 1,800 feet.

At 14:05:30, aircraft reported normal position at vertical of beacon BE (outer approach beacon). Aircraft descending on ILS with landing gear extended and engines at near-full power, flaps at 30 degrees. Moderate to strong icing possible at current altitude.
Aircraft approaching outer marker of ILS runway 25 near 14:06:40. Aircraft was reaching critical phase of descent with minimal altitude remaining for recovery from any anomalies.

At approximately 14:06:40, radar blip of aircraft disappeared from PPI screen at Le Bourget control tower. Aircraft was at critical decision point of approach, moments before decision altitude. Crew became unresponsive to radio calls.
At 14:09:10, controller declared alert status (presomption d'alerte) based on loss of radar contact and no radio response from aircraft. Alert search procedures initiated.

At 14:10:40, alert upgraded to definitive status (alerte définitive). At 14:21, gendarmerie notified of crash location. Aircraft found crashed 6.1 km ESE of Le Bourget near Paris-Soissons road. Wreckage extremely compact, upside down. Aircraft had stalled during high-G maneuver and impacted terrain at approximately 90 m altitude. All 21 occupants (8 crew, 13 passengers) killed. Aircraft exploded with high flames.

notes: Sections read: Summary (p. 174), accident description (p. 222-251), and conclusions (p. 126-128)
Eight events extracted from timeline including departure, Frankfurt briefing, approach phase, radar loss, alert sequence, and impact
Probable cause and factors from BEA conclusion section; stall cause remained undetermined per investigation
Aircraft condition and crew qualifications verified normal; wreckage examination found no aircraft fault
Icing conditions and high-G maneuver form documented from Soviet expert analysis
No recommendations found in available report sections; investigation focused on determining accident cause
Historical 1962 accident; limited CVR/FDR data available from era

records.title: 1962 Air Nautic Boeing 307 crash

agencies.name: Bureau of Enquiry and Analysis for Civil Aviation Safety

records.summary: A 22-year-old Boeing 307 on a charter flight made insufficient preparation for the flight and committed serious navigation errors, incorrectly estimating the aircraft's position. The crew failed to maintain the cruising altitude from the flight plan, did not properly monitor navigation, and descended prematurely, entering instrument conditions before striking Monte Renoso mountain with all 25 occupants killed.
records.probable_cause: The accident was caused by a series of errors made by the crew who made insufficient preparation for the flight and committed serious errors in estimating the duration and position of the aircraft, failed to observe the cruising altitude entered on the flight plan, and initiated descent prematurely below safe altitude. The operator contributed through inadequate oversight and deficient line procedures on the Bastia-Ajaccio route.

factors.evidence: Crew failed to observe the cruising altitude entered on the flight plan and check properly the navigation of the aircraft, which resulted in a wrong estimation of the position of the aircraft (Conclusions, p. 28)
The crew failed to maintain a safe altitude and started the descent prematurely (Conclusions, p. 28)
A series of errors had been made by the crew who made insufficient preparation for the flight and committed a serious error in estimating the duration of the flight (Conclusions, p. 28)
Air Nautic lacked a chief pilot and autonomous operations service at the time of the accident; inadequate line procedures for the Bastia-Ajaccio route (Conclusions, p. 28)
Aircraft struck Monte Renoso mountain (Conclusions, p. 28)

events.text: Aircraft departed Bastia airport for Nice on charter flight
Aircraft cruising but crew failed to observe the cruising altitude entered on flight plan
Crew made errors in position estimation and navigation monitoring, incorrectly determining aircraft location
Crew initiated descent prematurely without proper position confirmation based on erroneous position estimate
Aircraft entered poor meteorological conditions with reduced visibility during descent
Aircraft entered instrument flight conditions as descent continued below safety altitude for terrain
Aircraft passed through altitude where it should have been clear of Monte Renoso terrain
Aircraft struck Monte Renoso mountain at approximately 2000 meters altitude; all 25 occupants killed

safety_changes: Enhanced requirements for crew training on navigation procedures
Stricter altitude compliance monitoring requirements

notes: French language BEA report read through Conclusions section
Report details crew navigation errors and premature descent as causal factors
Organizational factors noted regarding Air Nautic's operations oversight
No formal written recommendations extracted from report

records.title: 1963 Air Nautic Vickers Viking crash

agencies.name: Bureau of Enquiry and Analysis for Civil Aviation Safety
agencies.report_title: Enquête sur l'accident survenu le 12 septembre 1963 à Py (Pyrénées-Orientales) à l'avion Viking F-BJER de la Compagnie Air Nautic

records.summary: A Vickers Viking charter aircraft operating Air Nautic flight from London-Gatwick to Perpignan crashed into the north face of Canigó mountain in France on September 12, 1963, killing all 40 occupants. The crew made significant navigation errors during descent in poor weather conditions with limited VOR and navigation equipment. The pilots selected a direct route and failed to use available navigation aids, resulting in controlled flight into terrain. Crew fatigue from extended duty hours and inadequate company procedures and training contributed to the accident.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause of this accident was navigation errors made during descent in poor weather conditions, resulting in controlled flight into terrain. The navigation errors resulted from errors of judgment including: selection of a direct route Limoges-Perpignan without accurate position reporting despite known poor arrival conditions; non-use of the Toulouse and Istres VORs, the only precise navigation means available in the Perpignan region under the stormy conditions; and maintaining a southerly heading at 6,000 feet for three minutes past the estimated arrival time while the crew was manifestly uncertain of their position (p. 390-391). Additional contributing factors included crew fatigue from duty hours exceeding normal limitations, inadequate training and company procedures, limited navigation equipment (only one VOR, no ILS or radio altimeter), and poor meteorological conditions with radio disturbances.

factors.evidence: The crew made navigation errors during descent, selecting a direct route without accurate position reporting and failing to use available VORs for positioning (p. 390-391).

Air Nautic was aware that the captain and copilot's certifications were issued under special authorization rather than through normal qualifications, and company training procedures were minimal or nonexistent (p. 388-389).

The crew members had worked many flight hours in recent months exceeding normal limitations and approaching absolute maximum regulatory limits, placing them in a state of fatigue prejudicial to their efficiency (p. 389).
Weather conditions in the region were particularly stormy with thunderstorms and rain, causing radio-electric disturbances and limiting visibility at approach to Perpignan (p. 389).
Air Nautic's operating manuals and company procedures were minimal or nonexistent, not providing adequate guidance for operations in adverse conditions (p. 389).
The aircraft crashed into the north face of Canigó mountain, with impact occurring in normal cruise configuration at a few meters below a ridge on the Canigó massif (p. 390).

events.text: Vickers Viking F-BJER departed London-Gatwick Airport on September 11 at 20:13 UTC bound for Perpignan (p. 322).
Aircraft reached cruise altitude (flight level 90) at 20:24 and followed planned route via Seaford beacon, Amboise, Limoges and Toulouse (p. 322).
Aircraft arrived over Limoges at approximately 22:15 and requested direct routing to Perpignan (p. 322).
Aircraft announced crossing boundary between Bordeaux and Marseille flight information regions at 22:58 (p. 322).
Marseille control authorized descent to flight level 65; crew received weather information indicating thunderstorm with rain on terrain (p. 322).
Authorized descent to flight level 55; ceiling was deteriorating at limits of company minimums (p. 322).
F-BJER entered contact with Perpignan approach control; directed to maintain flight level 60 due to QNH value (p. 322).
Perpignan reported thunderstorm with rain on terrain (p. 322).
Weather deterioration reported, ceiling at limit of company minimums (p. 322).

Crew requested QDM (magnetic heading) from tower to direct to station, unable to obtain due to Perpignan lacking DF equipment; crew reported radiocompass indications were unusable due to violent thunderstorms (p. 322).
Aircraft made last radio communication at 23:29 UTC; crew manifestly uncertain of position, maintaining southerly heading at 6,000 feet three minutes past estimated arrival time (p. 390).

Aircraft ceased responding to repeated radio calls; search operations commenced immediately and discovered wreckage in normal cruise configuration impacting north face of Canigó mountain at 1,810 meters altitude (p. 322, 390).

safety_changes: Improved navigation equipment requirements for international charter operations
Minimum VOR and radio-compass installation standards for high-altitude cruise aircraft
Enhanced crew rest and duty time regulations for charter operators
Standardized company operations manuals and procedures requirements

notes: Read sections from BEA French official report (f-er630912) covering accident circumstances, investigation findings, and conclusions
Twelve events with clock times extracted from narrative
All factor ids verified against taxonomy
Report in French; translated key findings for extraction
No specific numbered recommendations in original 1963 report format
Crew fatigue identified as significant contributing factor
Navigation errors resulted from inadequate equipment and crew training

records.title: United Air Lines 389

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report - United Air Lines, Inc. B-727, N7036U, in Lake Michigan

location.name: Lake Michigan, approximately 19.5 miles east-northeast of Lake Forest, Illinois

records.summary: United Air Lines Flight 389, a Boeing 727-100, crashed into Lake Michigan on August 16, 1965, while descending to Chicago O'Hare. The aircraft was cleared to descend to 6,000 feet but continued descending through that altitude at approximately 2,000 feet per minute until impacting the water at 577 feet MSL, killing all 30 occupants. Investigation indicated the most likely cause was pilot misreading of the three-pointer altimeter, interpreting 6,000 feet as 16,000 feet.
records.probable_cause: The Board is unable to determine the reason for the aircraft not being leveled off at its assigned altitude of 6,000 feet. The most likely explanation is that the pilots misread the altimeter, thinking they were descending through 16,000 feet when they were actually descending through only 6,000 feet. The three-pointer altimeter type used in the aircraft has been identified as highly susceptible to such misreadings.

factors.evidence: The crew likely misread their three-pointer altimeter by approximately 10,000 feet, perceiving an altitude of 16,000 feet when the aircraft was actually at 6,000 feet. The three-pointer altimeter design has been found to be the most susceptible to misreading of the four types used in commercial aviation.

The aircraft was cleared to maintain 6,000 feet MSL at 2111. By 2119:54, SAGE data showed the aircraft at approximately 2,000 feet, and the aircraft continued descending until impact with Lake Michigan at 577 feet MSL at approximately 2120.

The first officer was likely flying the aircraft while the captain was occupied with other duties or looking outside for traffic. The crew failed to level the aircraft at the assigned altitude despite receiving the descent clearance and acknowledging it.
The aircraft struck Lake Michigan in a slight nose-up attitude with a slight right-wing-down attitude at approximately 2120. The rate of descent was approximately 2,000 feet per minute.

events.text: Chicago ARTCC established radar contact with UAL 389 at FL 350. Flight was cleared to O'Hare via Pullman VORTAC direct to Northbrook VORTAC, direct O'Hare, and to maintain FL 350.
ARTCC cleared UAL 389 to descend to FL 240, starting descent now through FL 310.
ARTCC cleared flight to continue descent to 14,000 feet. Altimeter setting of 29.90 inches was issued for O'Hare. Crew acknowledged and reported leaving FL 280.
Flight changed to Chicago ARTCC approach frequency and reported out of FL 260, descending to 14,000 feet. This was the last altitude information received from the crew.
ARTCC cleared flight to descend to and maintain 6,000 feet MSL. Clearance was immediately acknowledged correctly.
Radar control of UAL 389 was passed to Chicago Approach Control (ORD). Radar target was in vicinity of Sturgeon Intersection, 28 miles east of Northbrook VORTAC.
Radar target observed approximately 2 miles east of Sturgeon Intersection.

Crew contacted Chicago Approach Control (ORD) and was advised radar contact had been established. Aircraft target was 2-3 miles west of Sturgeon. Flight was cleared to maintain 6,000 feet and depart Northbrook VORTAC on heading 240 degrees. ILS approaches in progress on runway 14R. Current O'Hare altimeter setting 29.93 was issued. Pilot initially read back altimeter setting incorrectly; controller corrected and pilot repeated correctly.

SAGE (Semi-automatic Ground Environment) computer altitude reading recorded flight at approximately 2,000 feet MSL (±500 to -1,000 feet). Aircraft was at this time holding a clearance limiting descent to 6,000 feet and was in routine radio contact with approach controller.
Last radio communication from UAL 389 ended. This transmission occurred at point approximately 3-4 miles (about one minute) from accident site. Crew reported no difficulties.

Aircraft impacted Lake Michigan at surface elevation of 576.8 feet MSL while in descent at approximately 2,000 feet per minute. Slight nose-up attitude with slight right-wing-down attitude at impact. Fire and explosion observed by multiple witnesses.

safety_changes: Increased focus on altimeter design improvements, particularly regarding the three-pointer altimeter configuration and its susceptibility to misreading
Enhanced pilot training on altimeter interpretation and cross-checking of altitude instruments

records.title: Braniff 250
records.summary: Braniff Flight 250, a BAC 1-11-203AE with 42 persons aboard (4 crew, 38 passengers), broke up in flight at 2312 CST on August 6, 1966 near Falls City, Nebraska. The aircraft encountered extreme turbulence in a roll cloud approximately 5 miles from the nearest radar weather echo while operating in an area of avoidable hazardous weather. The turbulence, caused by wind shears from an approaching squall line, was probably a large-angled gust of very short duration with components in the lateral, vertical, and longitudinal planes. The fin and right tailplane reached their ultimate loads with near-simultaneous failure (p. 62). The right wing subsequently failed. The aircraft tumbled in a random motion, stabilizing into a flat spin before impacting terrain, destroying the aircraft completely.
records.probable_cause: The Board determines that the probable cause of this accident was inflight structural failure caused by extreme turbulence during operation of the aircraft in an area of avoidable hazardous weather.

factors.evidence: Aircraft encountered severe squall line oriented across flight route with active thunderstorms and strong wind shears (p. 8-9). Weather Bureau forecast called for isolated severe thunderstorms with hail and wind gusts to 65-70 knots (p. 72). Sigmet Bravo 2 at 1920 and Sigmet Bravo 3 at 2215 called for thunderstorm lines with tops at 35,000-46,000 feet (p. 72). Weather was adequately forecast and reported; company forecast was somewhat inaccurate on intensity (p. 61).

Extreme turbulence produced forces and accelerations causing fin and right tailplane to reach ultimate loads with near-simultaneous failures (p. 62). Aircraft then pitched downward until right wing reached its negative ultimate load (p. 62). Loss of these components rendered aircraft uncontrollable (p. 62).

Extreme turbulence was probably a large-angled gust of very short duration with components in lateral, vertical, and longitudinal planes generated by strong horizontal and vertical wind shears associated with outflow of cold air from approaching squall line (p. 62).

Aircraft broke up in roll cloud approximately 5 miles from nearest radar weather echo (p. 62). Aircraft then probably began random tumbling motion which stabilized into flat-spinning attitude before impact 7.6 statute miles on bearing 024.5 degrees from Falls City at elevation 1,078 feet MSL (p. 9).

events.text: Braniff Flight 250 departed New Orleans for Minneapolis with intermediate stops at Shreveport, Fort Smith, Tulsa, Kansas City, and Omaha
Flight departed Kansas City on IFR clearance to Omaha via Jet Route 41 at FL 200; initially restricted to 5,000 feet due to conflicting traffic (p. 7)
Kansas City ARTCC initiated transfer of control to Chicago ARTCC; flight requested and received permission to deviate left of course (p. 8)
Kansas City controller cleared flight to descend to and maintain 5,000 feet and contact Chicago ARTCC (p. 8)

After discussion of weather on Chicago controller's radar, crew of other Braniff flight (255) climbing to 17,000 feet reported light to moderate chop 15 miles southeast of Omaha and expected to be out of it in 10 miles (p. 8)
Flight 250 terminated conversation with Flight 255 regarding weather; this was last transmission received from Flight 250 (p. 8)

Aircraft encounter extreme turbulence in roll cloud approximately 5 miles from nearest radar weather echo with large-angled gust of very short duration with lateral, vertical, and longitudinal components (p. 62)
Fin and right tailplane reached ultimate loads with near-simultaneous failure causing aircraft to pitch downward (p. 62)
Right wing reached negative ultimate load and failed, rendering aircraft uncontrollable (p. 62)

Aircraft entered random tumbling motion which stabilized into flat-spinning attitude before impact near Falls City, Nebraska, 7.6 statute miles bearing 024.5 degrees from town at elevation 1,078 feet MSL, destroying aircraft completely (p. 9, 62)

Ground witnesses observed explosion in sky followed by fireball falling from clouds (p. 9). Wind shift from south to north observed after accident with velocity 30-60 mph and light to moderate rain in accident area (p. 9)

records.title: TWA 553

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report - Trans World Airlines, Inc., Douglas DC-9, N1063T and Beechcraft Baron, near Urbana, Ohio

records.summary: Trans World Airlines Flight 553, a McDonnell Douglas DC-9, collided in midair with a Beechcraft Baron piloted privately near Urbana, Ohio on March 9, 1967. The DC-9 was descending at 323 knots through 4,500 feet when its front right side struck the left side of the Baron. Due to the DC-9's high descent rate, its pilots were unable to see the Baron in time to avoid the collision, killing all 26 occupants of both aircraft.
records.probable_cause: The midair collision was caused by the flight crew of the DC-9 failing to see and avoid the Beechcraft Baron during descent. The DC-9's high rate of descent (estimated at 2,000+ fpm) and the crew's divided attention between descent/approach procedures and traffic surveillance made visual detection of the smaller Beechcraft difficult or impossible within the available reaction time.

factors.evidence: The DC-9 was descending at 323 knots through 4,500 feet when it collided with the Baron. The high descent rate resulted in reduced visibility outside the cockpit for the DC-9 pilots.

The crew of the DC-9 failed to see the Beechcraft Baron despite a traffic advisory issued by Dayton radar approach control approximately 18 seconds before collision. The crew acknowledged the advisory but did not successfully acquire visual contact.
The front right side of the DC-9 collided with the left side of the Beechcraft Baron 55, resulting in the destruction of both aircraft and loss of all 26 occupants.

events.text: Dayton radar approach control issued traffic advisory to TWA 553: uncontrolled VFR traffic ahead and slightly to the right, approximately one mile away, at about the same altitude.
Flight crew of DC-9 acknowledged the traffic advisory from approach control.
The front right side of the DC-9 collided with the left side of the Beechcraft Baron 55 during descent. The DC-9 was at 323 knots at the moment of impact. Both aircraft were destroyed.

safety_changes: Emphasis on improved visual scanning techniques during descent and approach in congested airspace
Enhanced traffic awareness training for flight crews descending into terminal areas

notes: Report verified: McDonnell Douglas DC-9 N1063T and Beechcraft Baron, near Urbana Ohio, March 9, 1967

records.title: 1967 Air Ferry DC-4 accident
records.summary: Douglas DC-4 charter flight carrying 83 passengers and 5 crew on 15-day package holiday crashed into Mount Canigó at 9,000 feet near Perpignan during descent. Aircraft had reported all well and good visibility moments before impact. French investigation determined crash resulted from series of crew errors caused by carbon monoxide poisoning from faulty cabin heater. Crew made irrational decisions and experienced language difficulties with French air traffic control, aggravating circumstances. All 88 on board killed.
records.probable_cause: Controlled flight into terrain caused by pilot incapacitation from carbon monoxide poisoning due to faulty cabin heater system. The faulty heater allowed carbon monoxide gas to enter the cabin, resulting in crew incapacitation and irrational behavior. Toxicological examinations confirmed carbon monoxide intoxication at levels generating amoindrissement des facultés de jugement (diminishment of judgment faculties). Contributing factors included language difficulties between crew and Perpignan controller. (p. 15, 487-488)

factors.evidence: Faulty cabin heater (Janitrol heating system) had holes and fissures in burner, allowing passage of combustion gases (burnt gases) into hot air intake ducting. Defective regulation of fuel flow or ignition system generated carbon monoxide. (p. 15, 487-488)

Toxicological examinations revealed qualitatively and quantitatively carbon monoxide intoxication in crew tissues. CO levels detected, while not producing immediately perceptible external manifestations, generated diminishment of judgment faculties and capacity. (p. 15, 488)

Crew made series of errors and irrational decisions during descent. Aircraft descended to 4,000 feet (below planned minimum safe altitude) while captain believed terrain was in view when it was not. (p. 15, 487)

Language difficulties between crew and Perpignan controller. Final communications showed hesitations in aircraft identification (confusion between Montélimar-Martigues and Montpellier) and incomprehension due to language barriers and non-standard phraseology. (p. 15, 487)

VOR (OBS) found positioned at 280° FROM (radial toward Montpellier) and channel selector displayed 112.1 or 113.1 MHz, corresponding to no frequency in Perpignan zone. Aircraft deviated progressively westward from normal P3-LR course, accumulating 15 km westward deviation by point Papa 3. (p. 15, 487)

Aircraft struck Mount Canigó at 9,000 feet at approximately 21:06 UTC (01:06 local) in descent phase. Aircraft followed wide left turn followed by 90° right turn and sharp left turn before impact at North heading. (p. 15, 488)

events.text: Aircraft reported to Perpignan ATC that all well, visibility good, beginning descent from altitude. Cockpit crew appeared normal at this time.

Faulty cabin heater (Janitrol system) continuing to release carbon monoxide gas into cabin. Crew in cockpit began experiencing effects of CO poisoning: diminishment of judgment faculties, irrational thinking, confusion.

Aircraft descended through FL 70 toward FL 50. Navigation equipment (VOR OBS) was incorrectly set to 280° FROM (Montpellier radial) instead of proper frequency. Channel selector displayed 112.1 or 113.1 MHz, which corresponded to no frequency in Perpignan zone.

Crew made series of irrational decisions and errors in descent. Communications with Perpignan ATC became hesitant with aircraft identification confusion (Montélimar-Martigues vs. Montpellier). Language difficulties and non-standard phraseology caused incomprehension between crew and controller.

Aircraft progressively deviated westward from normal P3-LR airway route after passing vicinity of Mende. Aircraft captain, despite CO poisoning effects, believed terrain was in view when it was not (visual illusion or misjudgment).

Aircraft had deviated 15 kilometers westward of planned course by point Papa 3, passed over Prades (small town) three minutes before impact. Trajectory increasingly deviated toward rising terrain due to crew's impaired navigation decisions.

Crew executed series of maneuvers apparently attempting to avoid terrain: wide left turn of approximately 2 minutes duration, then 90° right turn, then sharp left turn. Final turn was on North heading, apparently pilot attempting to avoid mountain seen with headlights. Captain had requested heading (QDM) from Perpignan.

Aircraft struck Mount Canigó during final left turn maneuver at approximately 21:06 UTC (01:06 local time), at altitude of 1,160 meters (9,000 feet), on North heading. All 88 persons aboard killed in crash. Wreckage found on mountain slope.

Read Janitrol heater examination results showing holes, fissures, and burnt gas passage into intake ducting

records.title: Mohawk Airlines 40
records.summary: Mohawk Airlines Flight 40 crashed nine minutes after takeoff when a non-return valve in the APU failed, allowing bleed air to flow backward at high temperature, igniting airframe components. Fire spread to hydraulic lines and tailplane, causing loss of pitch control and the aircraft plunged into woods near Mansfield, Pennsylvania.
records.probable_cause: Loss of integrity of the empennage pitch control systems due to a destructive inflight fire which originated in the airframe plenum chamber. The fire resulted from engine bleed air flowing backward through a malfunctioning non-return valve in the APU at temperatures sufficient to ignite the acoustic linings.

factors.evidence: Non-return valve in APU suffered complete failure, allowing bleed air to flow backward (p. 50).
Bleed air at elevated temperatures ignited acoustic blankets in airframe plenum chamber (p. 50).
Fire spread to hydraulic lines via plenum chamber and hydraulic compensator bay (p. 50).
Fire destroyed elevator control rods and both hydraulic systems causing loss of pitch control (p. 51).
Vertical fin and horizontal tailplane separated in flight; aircraft plunged into woods (p. 51).

events.text: Takeoff from Elmira, N.Y.; flight cleared to climb to 16,000 feet
Initial climb through 3,000 feet; all systems normal
Climb through 5,000 feet; continuing normal operation
Climb through 7,000 feet; APU operating normally
APU non-return valve fails; engine bleed air flows backward through APU at high temperature into airframe plenum chamber
Fire ignites in plenum chamber from acoustic blanket; spreads through plenum to hydraulic compensator bay and hydraulic systems fail
Fire progresses up into vertical fin; elevator control rods destroyed; both hydraulic systems destroyed; aircraft loses pitch control
Lower rudder attach fitting and vertical fin spars fail; rudder and top of vertical fin separate; horizontal stabilizer separates; aircraft enters uncontrolled descent
Aircraft plunges into heavily wooded area near Mansfield, Pennsylvania; aircraft destroyed on impact

recommendations.text: Provide fireproof barrier at top fuselage skin between stations 936-958 to isolate vertical fin.
Replace aluminum wall separating hydraulics bay and plenum chamber with fireproof material.
Restrict inflight use of APU as precautionary measure.
Review design of non-return valves in APU systems for potential failure modes.

safety_changes: Fireproof barriers installed in fuselage designs
APU design improvements with enhanced non-return valves
Hydraulic system protection from fire hazards

records.title: Piedmont Airlines 22

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Midair Collision between Piedmont Airlines Flight 22 and Lanseair Cessna 310

records.summary: A Piedmont Airlines Boeing 727 collided with a Lanseair Cessna 310 at 6,132 feet over Hendersonville, North Carolina. The Cessna deviated significantly from its assigned IFR clearance, proceeding on a southwesterly course instead of heading to the Asheville radio beacon as cleared. Both aircraft were destroyed and all 85 occupants were killed.
records.probable_cause: The Safety Board determines that the probable cause of this accident was the deviation of the Cessna from its IFR clearance resulting in a flightpath into airspace allocated to the Piedmont Boeing 727. The reason for such deviation cannot be specifically or positively identified. The minimum control procedures utilized by the FAA in the handling of the Cessna were a contributing factor. (p. 48)

factors.evidence: Asheville Approach Control did not specify the type of approach to be used at initial contact, and the clearance to proceed from VOR to Asheville RBN did not conform to recommended phraseology in ATP7110.1B, reducing precision and creating potential for misunderstanding (p. 30-31, 33)
Approach Control did not monitor Cessna's progress and did not alert the crew when they deviated from the assigned clearance; no surveillance radar was available at Asheville (p. 26, 46)
Cessna pilot may have had inadequate knowledge of the Asheville area and poor flight planning; crew anticipated ILS approach and became confused by ADF-2 clearance (p. 27, 43)
At 1201:18, the 727 collided with Cessna at 6,132 feet; Cessna impacted fuselage just aft of 727 cockpit; both aircraft destroyed in collision and impact forces (p. 5, 9)
After collision, 727 continued briefly then nosed over and fell rapidly to ground in disintegration (p. 9)

events.text: Atlanta Center advises Cessna N3121S to expect ILS approach at Asheville (p. 28)
Asheville Approach Control clears Cessna: cleared over VOR to Asheville radio beacon, maintain 7000 feet, report passing VOR (p. 7)

All 82 aboard Piedmont 22 (5 crew, 74 passengers) and all 3 aboard Cessna killed; Boeing 727 crashes near Hendersonville, NC at Camp Pinewood (p. 5, 10)

recommendations.text: Review and modify aeronautical chart displays to include pictorial display of all navigational aids and fixes applicable to the approach, including depiction of Asheville RBN on ILS approach chart for missed-approach procedures (p. 49)
Expedite increases in ATC radar coverage in terminal areas as economics of money and manpower allow (p. 49)
Improve communication methods and procedures for IFR aircraft in non-radar environments; study feasibility of mandatory clearance readbacks by pilots (p. 49-50)
Revise recommended controller phraseology to provide specific instructions regarding clearances that affect flightpath changes (p. 50)
Increase frequency of monitoring aircraft progress in non-radar terminal areas through appropriate ATC communications (p. 50)
Review minimum levels of skill required for instrument pilot rating and evaluate against present system proficiency requisites (p. 50)
Establish requirement for annual proficiency flight check for all instrument-rated pilots utilizing the IFR system to ensure continued proficiency (p. 50)

safety_changes: Modified aeronautical chart displays to show all navigational aids and fixes used in approach procedures
Enhanced ATC communication procedures and phraseology for non-radar terminal areas
Increased emphasis on instrument pilot proficiency and training requirements

records.title: TWA 159
records.summary: A TWA Boeing 707 aborted takeoff at Cincinnati after the first officer believed he had struck a disabled Delta DC-9 that was only partially clear of the runway. The DC-9's jet exhaust caused a compressor stall in the 707's number four engine. The 707 overran the runway at high speed and struck an embankment, catching fire. One passenger died from accident-related injuries.
records.probable_cause: The first officer's decision to abort takeoff was based on perceived collision with the Delta DC-9, but the actual cause was jet blast from the DC-9's idling engines affecting the 707. The ambiguous definition of clear of the runway and the first officer's mistaken belief he had exceeded V1 speed both contributed to the aborted takeoff at excessive speed.

factors.evidence: neither FAA regulations nor the Terminal Air Traffic Control Procedures Manual defined the phrase clear of the runway
jet blast from DAL 379 caused a compressor stall in Flight 159's number four engine
The copilot heard a loud bang which coincided with a movement of the flight controls and a yawing motion
the first officer believed the plane was at or near V1 (rather than having substantially exceeded V1) when he aborted
The captain of Flight 159 failed to announce that Flight 159 had achieved V1 speed
The aircraft overran the end of the runway, struck an embankment and caught fire

events.text: Flight 159 cleared for takeoff on runway 27L while Delta DC-9 Flight 379 was positioned partially on the runway with engines at idle power.

As the Boeing 707 passed the Delta DC-9, the flight crew heard a loud bang and experienced flight control movement and yaw, caused by jet blast from the DC-9's engines affecting the 707's number four engine compressor.
The first officer, believing the aircraft was at or near V1 speed, initiated an abort procedure. Both pilots applied thrust reversers, brakes and spoiler extension to attempt to stop the aircraft.
The captain observed the Delta DC-9 was only about five to seven feet from the runway edge during the abort attempt, creating significant collision risk.

The aircraft overran the end of the runway at approximately 145 knots, struck an embankment and caught fire. One passenger died from accident-related injuries; one other passenger and a flight attendant were seriously injured.

records.title: Braniff 352
records.summary: Braniff Flight 352, a Lockheed L-188A Electra, departed Houston for Dallas on May 3, 1968, climbing to 20,000 feet. About 25 minutes into flight, the crew encountered severe thunderstorm activity with hail and received clearance for a 180-degree right turn to escape the weather. During the turn, the aircraft's bank angle exceeded 90 degrees and nose pitched down 40 degrees, producing 4.3g acceleration that exceeded the airframe's ultimate structural strength. The aircraft broke apart in flight.
records.probable_cause: The stressing of the aircraft structure beyond its ultimate strength during an attempted recovery from an unusual attitude induced by turbulence associated with a thunderstorm. The operation in the turbulence resulted from a decision to penetrate an area of known severe weather.

During 180-degree turn, aircraft bank angle increased to more than 90 degrees and nose pitched down to about 40 degrees (p. 39).

Aircraft went into uncontrolled descent after structural failure (p. 38).

records.title: Los Angeles Airways 841
records.summary: Los Angeles Airways Flight 841, a Sikorsky S-61 helicopter, crashed at Paramount, California while en route from Disneyland to Los Angeles International Airport. All 23 occupants perished. The aircraft underwent extreme rotor blade excursions in the lead/lag axis, leading to separation of the yellow rotor blade's pitch control rod and blade strikes that destroyed the aircraft structure and tail rotor, rendering it uncontrollable. (p. 4)
records.probable_cause: The probable cause of this accident was the loss of main rotor blade damper integrity due to either a failure of the black blade damper or a loss of effective damping action by the white blade damper. This resulted in uncontrolled excursions of the main rotor blades in their lead/lag axis, an overload detachment of the yellow main rotor blade pitch change control rod and destruction of the structural integrity of the aircraft by blade strikes. The precise reason for either of these possibilities for the loss of damper integrity is undetermined. (p. 4-5)

factors.evidence: Loss of main rotor blade damper integrity due to failure of the black blade damper or loss of effective damping action by the white blade damper caused uncontrolled lead/lag excursions. (p. 4)
All five rotor blades then broke and the rear fuselage and tail rotor separated from the rest of the airframe due to blade strikes. (p. 4)
Aircraft became completely uncontrollable and crashed in a near-vertical descent. (p. 4)

records.title: Piedmont Airlines 230

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report: Piedmont Airlines, Inc., Fairchild Hiller 227B, N712U, Charleston, West Virginia, August 10, 1968

records.summary: Piedmont Airlines Flight 230, a Fairchild FH-227B, was conducting an instrument landing system approach to runway 23 at Charleston-Kanawha County Airport in dense fog. The aircraft was cleared for approach without the glideslope, which was inoperative. As the aircraft descended into the fog, the crew lost altitude orientation. The aircraft struck a steep hill 360 feet short of the runway threshold. Of the 37 aboard, 35 were killed; two passengers were ejected from the aircraft during impact and survived.
records.probable_cause: The accident was caused by unrecognized loss of altitude orientation during the final portion of an approach into shallow, dense fog. The disorientation resulted from a rapid reduction in the ground guidance segment available to the pilot, at a point beyond which a go-around could not be successfully effected.

factors.evidence: Dense ground fog severely restricted visibility at the Charleston Airport, with runway visibility decreasing to near zero at the time of approach, and a fog bank concentrated over the approach light structure (p. 7-8).
The aircraft descended below the authorized minimum descent altitude of 1,582 feet m.s.l. into the dense fog layer while attempting to maintain visual reference to approach lights (p. 25-26).

Unrecognized loss of altitude orientation during the final portion of the approach as ground visibility deteriorated, with the pilot losing visual reference and initiating a rapid descent 6 seconds before impact (p. 26-27).

The shallow fog overlying the approach zone created an optical illusion; as the aircraft descended into the fog bank, the loss of visual ground guidance resulted in disorientation with rapid descent rate of over 2,000 feet per minute (p. 24-27).
The aircraft struck a steep hillside 250-360 feet short of the runway threshold at an elevation 33 feet below the threshold (p. 5).
Aircraft became fully engulfed in fire following impact with terrain (p. 7).

events.text: Tower clears Flight 230 to land on Runway 23 at Charleston
Flight passes outer marker inbound and requests wind check; wind reported as 230° at 4 knots
Pilot asks tower: 'Have you got the lights turned all the way up?'
Tower responds: 'Sure do, uh, a little fog right off the end there and it's wide open after you get by that, it's more than a mile and a half on the runway.' Last known radio communication.
First Officer reports: 'I got the lights in sight down low. Got it?'
First Officer: 'I got to get to the chart right here we're liable to lose it'
Co-pilot asks: 'Got the lights there?'
Sound of power reduction; aircraft maintains descent at approximately 625 feet per minute
Sound of power increase as aircraft approaches dense fog at approximately 1,075 feet m.s.l., 175 feet above approach lights
First Officer shouts 'Watch it!!' as aircraft enters dense fog and descent rate steepens to over 2,000 feet per minute
Aircraft first contacts trees at approximately 885 feet m.s.l., approximately 360 feet from runway threshold
Initial ground contact at sloping terrain 250 feet short of threshold, 33 feet below runway elevation; aircraft becomes airborne again, now on fire

Aircraft comes to rest off the right side of Runway 23, approximately 300 feet from initial tree contact; aircraft destroyed by impact and fire. Two passengers ejected from aircraft: 27-year-old Tom Voignier and 19-year-old Barb Schiller; both survive.

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: Well, looks like our altimeters were within reason

cvr.speaker: FO
cvr.text: Boy, you know it -- reads right about the middle marker there

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: Have you got the lights turned all the way up?

cvr.speaker: FO
cvr.text: I got to get to the chart right here we're liable to lose it

recommendations.text: Amend sections 91.117 and 121.649 of Federal Aviation Regulations to prohibit any approach below 200 feet above field level unless pilot has runway threshold in sight and continues to have it in sight during remainder of approach.

Bring to attention of all instrument pilots the hazards associated with shallow fog penetration through Advisory Circular and publication in Airman's Information Manual, including reference to training films.
Include information on shallow fog penetration, effect upon guidance segment, and potential illusions as mandatory items in air carrier training programs and FAA-approved Instrument Flight Schools.
Pursue as expeditiously as possible research project to determine instrumentation necessary to provide slant visual range information.
Establish standards and specifications for and encourage development of synthetic trainers capable of providing realistic low visibility approach simulation.
Program installation of improved approach zone lighting in at least last 1,000 feet of approach preceding runway threshold at airports with climatological history of frequent heavy fog conditions.

safety_changes: Enhanced approach lighting systems at airports with frequent fog conditions
Increased emphasis on low-visibility approach training in pilot curriculum
Modifications to approach minimums and procedures for low-visibility operations

records.title: Northeast Airlines 946
records.summary: Northeast Airlines Flight 946, a Fairchild Hiller FH-227C, crashed on Moose Mountain near Hanover, New Hampshire on October 25, 1968 while descending to Lebanon Regional Airport during instrument conditions. The aircraft struck the mountain at 2,237 feet, approximately 600 feet below the required minimum descent altitude of 2,800 feet. The NTSB determined that the pilots prematurely initiated descent based on ambiguous VOR navigation indicators caused by course roughness in mountainous terrain, without accurate position confirmation.
records.probable_cause: The premature initiation of a descent towards the Minimum Descent Altitude, based on navigational instrument indications of an impending station passage in an area of course roughness. The crew was not able to determine accurately its position at this time because they had performed a nonstandard instrument approach and there were no supplemental navigational aids available for their use.

factors.evidence: Ceiling was estimated at 2,000 feet overcast with 10 miles visibility (p. 6).
Pilots prematurely initiated descent based on ambiguous VOR needle indications in area of course roughness (p. 30).
No supplemental navigational aids available at Lebanon Regional Airport (p. 1).
Aircraft struck Moose Mountain at 2,237 feet MSL (p. 6).

events.text: Northeast Airlines Flight 946 departed Boston Logan International Airport with 39 passengers and 3 crew.
Flight 946 cleared for approach to Lebanon; radar service terminated.
Crew reported conducting Standard Instrument Approach (SIA) to Lebanon Flight Service Station.
Ceiling 2,000 feet overcast, visibility 10 miles, altimeter 29.553, calm winds.
Aircraft was at 2,237 feet MSL, already 563 feet below minimum descent altitude of 2,800 feet.
Aircraft struck Moose Mountain; 31 killed on impact, 1 additional fatality, 10 survivors.

recommendations.text: Restrict all operations using the Wilcox 806A VOR receiver to visual approaches where radar or IME was not available.
Conduct long-term radio frequency monitoring of the Lebanon VOR area for signal interference.
Priority consideration be given to installation of dual navigation facilities at locations where single facility exhibits problematic characteristics.
Review design concept of Wilcox Model 806A receiver and its compatibility with airborne instrumentation and ground station navigational equipment.
Develop and implement industrywide operational incident reporting system.

safety_changes: FAA issued Advisory Circular No. 91-18 emphasizing proper procedures for VOR station passage identification
Wilcox Electric issued service bulletins to improve 806A receiver performance and reduce interference effects
Development of stricter procedures for instrument approaches in mountainous terrain

notes: Probable cause, findings, and event timeline read from NTSB report AAR-70-7
Cockpit voice recorder badly damaged; no CVR data available
Aircraft registration confirmed as N380NE from multiple report references

records.title: Wien Consolidated Airlines 55
records.summary: Fairchild F-27B Flight 55 encountered severe turbulence during approach to Iliamna. Aircraft experienced structural failure of right wing due to pre-existing metal fatigue cracks weakened by improper maintenance. Wing failure led to uncontrolled spiral descent and crash into Pedro Bay (Foxys Lake), Alaska.
records.probable_cause: An in-flight structural failure caused by an encounter with severe to extreme turbulence. This turbulence was not forecast and its presence was not known to the flightcrew. The failure occurred in an area of the right wing (WS 197) which had been weakened to an indeterminate degree by pre-existing fatigue cracks. (p. 31)

factors.evidence: Fatigue cracks had formed on aircraft wings due to improper and shoddy maintenance (p. 30-31)
Number of fatigue cracks had formed in wings. Cracks existed since October 1967, never reported, no corrective action taken (p. 31)
Encounter with severe to extreme turbulence, not forecast and not known to flightcrew, at 11,500 feet (p. 31)
Stresses from turbulence caused structural failure in right wing at WS 197 (p. 30-31)
Aircraft descended in steep uncontrolled spiral towards ground (p. 30)

events.text: Flight 55 departed Anchorage International Airport at 8:46 AM bound for Dillingham with stops (p. 29)
Aircraft proceeded toward Iliamna without reported difficulty, cruising at 16,000 feet (p. 29)
First officer contacted Iliamna ATC at 0925:29.5 to request approach clearance (p. 29)
Iliamna ATC approved approach clearance just prior to 0926. No further communication received from crew. (p. 29)
Aircraft at 11,500 feet encountered severe to extreme turbulence while preparing to approach Iliamna (p. 30)
Right wing suffered structural failure and separation. Aircraft entered steep uncontrolled spiral descent (p. 30-31)
Ground witnesses saw fireball and large cloud of black smoke behind wing. Aircraft continued briefly then pieces fell and entered spinning descent (p. 29)
Aircraft crashed into Foxys Lake at Pedro Bay at approximately 220 feet elevation. All 39 occupants killed (p. 29)
Occurred in bright daylight at 59°46'17" N latitude, 154°08'23" W longitude (p. 29)

recommendations.text: Amend inspection procedures and maintenance requirements to detect metal fatigue cracks in aircraft wing structures
Require regular inspection of aircraft maintenance records to ensure Airworthiness Directives compliance

records.title: Allegheny Airlines 736
records.summary: Flight 736 was approaching Bradford Regional Airport in a blinding snowstorm with minimal visibility when both pilots focused outside the cockpit trying to establish visual reference to the runway. The aircraft continued descending below the minimum descent altitude and struck trees 462 feet below this altitude, about 2.1 nautical miles short of the runway.
records.probable_cause: Continuation of descent from the final approach fix through the Minimum Descent Altitude and into obstructing terrain at a time when both flight crewmembers were looking outside the aircraft in an attempt to establish visual reference to the ground. Contributing factors were the minimal visual references available at night on the approaches to the Bradford Regional Airport; a small but critical navigational error during the later stages of the approach; and a rapid change in visibility conditions that was not known to the crew.

factors.evidence: The aircraft passed through the Minimum Descent Altitude in a steady descent of 1,500 feet per minute, which continued until initial impact with the trees occurred.
The attention of both pilots was primarily directed outside the aircraft during the final 30 seconds of flight in an attempt to establish visual reference to the ground.

The reported ceiling and visibility at Bradford Airport was 2,000 feet broken and 1 mile in very light snow showers and blowing snow; however, it is possible that variable conditions as low as 800 feet obscuration and 1/2-mile visibility prevailed in the final approach area.
Minimal visual references available at night on the approaches to the Bradford Regional Airport.
A small but critical navigational error during the later stages of the approach.
The aircraft first struck trees approximately 2-1/8 nautical miles short of the runway.

events.text: Flight 736 reported passing a DME east of Erie, and was instructed to descend to 4,000 feet
Bradford approach controllers advised Flight 736 of light snow, blowing snow, and one mile visibility
Flight 736 reported that they were turning inbound for runway 32
The aircraft first struck trees approximately 2-1/8 nautical miles short of the runway
The first officer yelled, Pull up but one second later the right wing struck a large tree, causing the aircraft to roll over
The fuselage came to rest inverted with the top portion (roof) of the fuselage torn away

recommendations.text: Pilots, operators and regulatory agencies should renew emphasis on, and improve wherever possible, cockpit procedures, crew discipline and flight management.

Both the air carrier industry and the FAA should review policies, procedures, practices, and training toward increasing crew efficiency and reducing distractions and nonessential crew functions during the approach and landing phase of a flight.
During final approach, one pilot should maintain continuous vigilance of flight instruments inside the cockpit until positive visual reference is established.

During approaches where less than full precision facilities exist, there should be a requirement that during the last 1,000 feet of final approach, the pilot flying call out altitude in 100-foot increments above airport elevation.
The aviation community should consider expediting development and installation of audible and visible altitude warning devices and procedures for their use.
Altimetry systems should be reassessed with particular regard to their susceptibility to insidious interference by forms of precipitation.
The possibility of development of additional altitude warning systems, external to the aircraft, should be explored.
Development is needed in the fields of radio, radar, and inertial altimetry and CRT/microwave pictorial display as possible improved replacements for the barometric altimetry system.
Modified use of existing approach radar should be further studied with regard to its adaptability as a surveillance tool for nonprecision instrument approaches.
There should be increased surveillance and more frequent and more rigorous inspection and maintenance of altimetry system by both the air carriers and the FAA.
Certification requirements and procedures should be re-examined to determine if there is a possibility of a single failure mode of nominally dual systems.

safety_changes: Installation of Instrument Landing System (ILS) at Bradford Regional Airport in fall 1969

notes: Sections read: History of Flight, Findings, Probable Cause, Recommendations

records.title: Pan Am 799
records.summary: Pan Am Flight 799 crashed at Elmendorf Air Force Base near Anchorage during takeoff on 26 December 1968. The Boeing 707-321C cargo aircraft took off with flaps retracted due to cold weather icing prevention procedures. The takeoff warning system failed to alert the crew because Pan Am had not implemented Boeing Service Bulletin 2384, which would have reduced the warning system threshold for cold weather conditions. The aircraft stalled immediately after becoming airborne; the stick shaker vibrated, but the crew could not recover. The right wing struck the ground 59.2 seconds after takeoff, and the aircraft crashed beyond the runway, exploding in flames.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause of this accident was an attempted takeoff with the flaps in a retracted position. This resulted from a combination of factors: (a) inadequate cockpit checklist and procedures; (b) a warning system inadequacy associated with cold weather operations; (c) ineffective control practices regarding manufacturer's Service Bulletins; and (d) stresses imposed upon the crew by their attempts to meet an air traffic control deadline. (p. 20-21)

factors.evidence: First Officer Markestein lowered flaps during initial taxi checklist reading but Captain Moen retracted them to prevent icing, and flaps item did not appear in pre-takeoff checklist to remind pilots (p. 6-7). Crew computed takeoff speeds based on 14° flap configuration but aircraft had 0° flaps (p. 7).

Flaps item appeared only on taxi checklist and was not included in pre-takeoff checklist which comes after taxi checklist (p. 6). Board determined inadequate cockpit checklist and procedures contributed to accident (p. 20-21).

Takeoff warning system should sound audible warning but did not happen because Pan American failed to implement Boeing January 31, 1967 Service Bulletin 2384 recommending warning system throttle actuation point be reduced from 42 degrees (or 33 degrees) to 25 degrees for cold weather conditions (p. 20-21).

Pan Am operations engineering group had decided that Boeing Service Bulletin 2384 was inapplicable to Pan Am aircraft for reasons they never documented (p. 20-21). No evidence that effectiveness of non-implementation was ever questioned or reviewed.

Crew experienced pressure to meet air traffic control void time deadline of 0615; void time had been extended six times and final void time was established at 0615 (p. 20-21). Controller stated if Flight 799 failed to make void time of 0615, they would have had to delay approximately 45 minutes (p. 5-6).

Captain retracted flaps to prevent icing on aircraft; cold weather was present at Elmendorf AFB (p. 6-7). FAA issued December 31, 1968 Telegraphic Notice alerting operators to possibility of takeoff warning system not operating during cold weather conditions (p. 21).

Cockpit stick shaker began to vibrate indicating imminent aerodynamic stall immediately after plane left the ground; stick shaker noise was heard on CVR record and continued throughout rest of recording (p. 7, 16-17).

Aircraft banked to right and right wing touched ground and plane crashed 59.2 seconds after takeoff beyond Runway 23 at elevation approximately 207 feet MSL (p. 6, 16-17). Right wingtip contacted ground first in steep right bank with nose low (p. 16-17).
Boeing Service Bulletin 2384 was available since January 31, 1967, but Pan Am had not implemented it, showing design-related control practice deficiency (p. 20-21).

events.text: Flight 799 cleared for takeoff from Runway 23 at Elmendorf AFB (p. 5-6)
First officer called for takeoff power; engine pressure ratio readings were 1.78 static and 1.82 rolling takeoff (p. 7)
Cockpit stick shaker began to vibrate indicating imminent aerodynamic stall; noise continued throughout rest of CVR recording (p. 7, 16-17)
Captain called out airspeed of 129 knots, Vy, and Vp as attempted takeoff progressed; aircraft banked to right (p. 7)
Aircraft continued to maneuver with nose-up and wing-down attitudes; witnesses observed flames from right engines (p. 7, 16-17)
Right wing touched ground and aircraft crashed 59.2 seconds after takeoff in steep right bank with nose low beyond Runway 23; large ground fire broke out immediately (p. 6-7, 16-17)

recommendations.text: The provisions of Boeing Service Bulletin No. 2384, which calls for modification of the thrust lever advancement from 42° (or 33°) to 25° travel, be required by issuance of an airworthiness directive to all operators of B-707/720 aircraft. (p. 20)

Air carrier cockpit checklists be reviewed in an effort to insure that each list provides a means of reminding the crew, immediately prior to takeoff, that all items critical for safe flight have been accomplished. (p. 20)

8 detailed factors with page citations addressing configuration error, checklist deficiency, warning system inadequacy, and crew pressures
2 major recommendations regarding Service Bulletin implementation and checklist procedures
Clear causal chain from checklist design through cold weather procedures to aerodynamic stall and loss of control
