records.title: North Central Airlines 458
records.summary: During a night approach to O'Hare in 200-foot ceilings and light rain, at 210 feet the CV-580 began climbing. The captain initiated a go-around but the aircraft continued climbing and stalled. It rolled left, struck the ground, and crashed into a hangar. The NTSB determined the captain experienced spatial disorientation from atmospheric refraction of approach lights at a critical moment when transitioning between instrument and visual reference.
records.probable_cause: Spatial disorientation of the captain caused by atmospheric refraction of approach lights during transition from instrument to visual flight reference, combined with relatively low command experience in the CV-580.

factors.evidence: The aircraft began its approach to O'Hare, which had a 200 ft ceiling with light rain and fog
Spatial disorientation of the captain precipitated by atmospheric refraction of either the approach lights or landing lights at a critical point in the approach
the captain of Flight 458, although experienced, had relatively few hours of experience as the pilot-in-command in CV-580s
Flight 458 lost speed until it stalled 13 seconds after the initiation of the go-around
The aircraft entered a steep left bank, and its left wing struck the ground
Aircraft impacted hangar

events.text: Aircraft at 20:14 CST began approach to O'Hare with 200 ft ceiling, light rain and fog
Flight cleared to descend to 3,500 ft, RVR reported as 4,500 feet
Flight instructed to slow to 160 knots, vectored for ILS approach to Runway 14R
Flight vectored left to 050° then right to 090° for spacing
Flight instructed to turn right to 220° and maintain until ILS localizer interception
Flight reported at outer marker (Romeo), cleared for ILS approach, new RVR 2,600 feet
Aircraft at approximately 210 feet above airport elevation, about 4,500 feet from runway threshold, descended normally on ILS glideslope
Aircraft entered unexpected sustained climb of approximately 1,244 feet per minute
Captain called for full available power (971 rpm or 4,000 hp) and initiated go-around procedures
Aircraft continued climbing despite go-around attempt, gaining additional 500 feet to 940 feet altitude, airspeed decreased to point where aerodynamic control was lost
Aircraft stalled 13 seconds after go-around initiation, entered steep left bank, left wing struck ground
Aircraft impacted main door of hangar in near-inverted position approximately 100 feet southeast of runway threshold, destroyed by impact and fire

notes: Read: synopsis, probable cause, findings, recommendations

recommendations.text: Section 121.652 of the Federal Aviation Regulations be amended to prohibit a captain from being removed from "high" minimums until he has accrued 100 hours as pilot-in-command in type

records.title: Allegheny Airlines 737

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Allegheny Airlines Flight 737

location.name: Golf course near Bradford Regional Airport, Pennsylvania

records.summary: Allegheny Airlines Flight 737, a Convair 440, descended below safe altitude during a non-precision VOR approach to Bradford, Pennsylvania in poor visibility and struck trees on a golf course, killing 11 of 28 occupants. The NTSB could not determine whether the crew misread the altimeter, suffered an altimeter malfunction, or misinterpreted the approach chart.
records.probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Board is unable to determine precisely the probable cause of this accident. Of some 13 potential causes examined by the Board, three remain after final analysis: (1) misreading of the altimeter by the captain, (2) a malfunction of the captain's altimeter after completion of the instrument approach procedure turn, and (3) a misinterpretation of the instrument approach chart. Of these three, however, no single one can be accepted or rejected to the exclusion of another based on the available evidence. (p. 27)

factors.evidence: Weather was overcast with measured ceiling 800 feet, visibility 1.5 miles in light snow showers. (p. 2)

Three potential causes examined: misreading of the altimeter by the captain, malfunction of the captain's altimeter, or misinterpretation of the instrument approach chart. The three-pointer type altimeter is difficult to read with speed and accuracy. (p. 26)

The aircraft descended to tree-top level about 4.7 nautical miles from the airport, below the minimum descent altitude, striking trees about 79 feet high at a terrain elevation of 2,175 feet MSL. (p. 2)

The aircraft struck the top branches of a tree about 79 feet in height, then cut a swath through trees bordering a fairway of Pine Acres Golf Course. The main portion struck the ground and came to rest inverted about 400 feet beyond initial ground impact. (p. 2)

events.text: Flight 737 reported position as ten miles from the VOR at Bradford
Flight reported over the VOR outbound at 4,000 feet on an IFR flight plan clearance via Airway Victor 13 to the Bradford VOR

Erie Approach Control cleared Flight 737 to make VOR runway 32 approach; Bradford FSS advised the flight of weather: partial obscuration 800 feet, visibility 1.5 miles in snow showers, wind 170 degrees at 10 knots
Flight requested and received clearance to change to runway 14 approach instead of runway 32
Flight reported completing procedure turn inbound at approximately 4,000 feet, confirmed wind 160 degrees at 14 knots
Bradford Radio acknowledged that Flight 737 was completing procedure turn inbound, and this was the last known communication from the flight
Aircraft descended below minimum descent altitude and struck trees on Pine Acres Golf Course about 4.7 nautical miles from Bradford Airport
Aircraft came to rest inverted on snow-covered golf course about 400 feet from initial ground impact; 11 of 28 occupants killed, 16 seriously injured, 1 uninjured

recommendations.text: Crew functions not directly related to the approach and landing should be reduced or eliminated, especially during the last 1,000 feet of descent.
During the final approach, one pilot should maintain continuous vigilance of flight instruments inside the cockpit until positive visual reference is established.
During the last 1,000 feet of final approach where less than full precision facilities exist, the pilot not flying should call out altitude in 100-foot increments above airport elevation.
There should be a requirement to report indicated altitudes to Air Traffic Control at various points in the approach procedure, such as the outbound procedure turn and at the outer marker position.
The aviation community should consider expediting development and installation of audible and visible altitude warning devices and the implementation of procedures for their use.
Altimetry systems should be reassessed with particular regard to their susceptibility to insidious interference by forms of precipitation.

The possibility of development of additional altitude warning systems, external to the aircraft, should be explored. One possibility is a high-intensity visual warning red light beam projected up along and slightly below the desired approach glide slope.

Development is needed in the fields of radio/radar, and inertial altimetry and CRT/microwave pictorial display approach aids as possible improved replacements for the barometric altimetry system in the near future.

Modified use of existing approach radar should be further studied with regard to its adaptability as a surveillance tool for nonprecision instrument approaches to monitor automatically and warn against descent below desired glidepath.
There should be increased surveillance and more frequent and more rigorous inspection and maintenance of altimetry systems by both the air carriers and the FAA.

notes: Read History of Flight (p. 2-6), Findings (p. 26), Probable Cause (p. 27), Recommendations (p. 28-31)

Probable cause text includes all three competing hypotheses

records.title: United Airlines 266

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report: United Airlines Flight 266, Boeing 727-22C

records.summary: United Airlines Flight 266 crashed into Santa Monica Bay four minutes after takeoff from Los Angeles International Airport. The No. 3 generator had been non-functional and was masked with tape before flight, masked by improper maintenance procedures. After engine No. 1 fire warning and shutdown, the No. 2 generator also failed resulting in total loss of electrical power. Flying at night in instrument conditions without attitude instruments, the crew became spatially disoriented and lost control of the aircraft. All 38 aboard were killed.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause of this accident was loss of attitude orientation during a night, instrument departure in which all attitude instruments were disabled by loss of electrical power. The Board has been unable to determine why all generator power was lost or why the standby electrical power system either was not activated or failed to function. (p. 4, 33)

factors.evidence: Fire warning activated on engine No. 1 approximately 2 minutes after takeoff during climb to departure control; crew shut down engine No. 1 and reported loss of all functioning generators (p. 5, 21)
Loss of all electrical power forced manual control of aircraft in night instrument conditions; standby electrical system either was not activated or failed to function (p. 32)
Crew was without reliable attitude reference from point No. 2 generator was lost until impact; flying at night in instrument conditions, pilots quickly became spatially disoriented (p. 21, 32)
Aircraft crashed into Santa Monica Bay at steep nose-down angle with right wing low attitude; crew lost control due to spatial disorientation and loss of attitude reference instruments (p. 19-20)

events.text: United Flight 266, Boeing 727-22C N4724U, departs Runway 25L at Los Angeles International Airport for flight to Milwaukee in night instrument conditions (p. 5)
Engine No. 1 fire warning activated approximately 2 minutes after takeoff during climb; crew reports fire warning to Departure Control and requests return to airport (p. 4, 21)
Crew shuts down engine No. 1 and reports loss of all functioning generators to Departure Control (p. 5)
No. 2 generator ceases operating after becoming sole power source; all electrical power is lost; attitude instruments and lights go dark (p. 19)
With loss of all electrical power, pilots lose attitude reference; without attitude indicators, crew becomes spatially disoriented flying at night in instrument conditions (p. 19, 32)
First officer exclaims during final moments: Keep it going up - you're a thousand feet - pull it up (p. 20)
Aircraft crashes into Pacific Ocean at steep nose-down angle, right wing low attitude; aircraft destroyed on impact; wreckage scattered (p. 19-20)
All 38 aboard killed (6 crew members and 32 passengers); aircraft destroyed; limited wreckage scatter and fragmentation pattern indicate high-speed impact (p. 4-5, 19)

cvr.speaker: FO
cvr.text: Keep it going up - you're a thousand feet - pull it up

recommendations.text: Make automatic switching of essential power to standby power upon loss of all generators a mandatory requirement for all turbine-powered aircraft (p. 33)

Until automatic switching can be implemented, require emergency checklists for all airlines for Loss of All Generators procedure to ensure second officer or captain immediately switches essential power to standby or emergency position (p. 33)
Provide positive indication to second officer on Boeing 727 panel when standby system is being powered from battery, such as illuminating light when standby system is activated (p. 34)
Consider transfer of standby feature from essential power selector switch to separate ON-OFF toggle switch for improved accessibility (p. 34)

safety_changes: Automatic standby power activation systems required on large transport aircraft
Boeing 727 emergency procedure revisions implemented requiring manual standby power switching
Installation of third independent attitude indicator on large turbojet aircraft
Enhanced redundancy requirements for electrical power systems in aircraft design

notes: Extracted from NTSB AAR 70-06: Synopsis (p. 4), Investigation/History (p. 5), Analysis (p. 19-22), Findings (p. 32), Probable Cause (p. 33), Recommendations (p. 33-34)
Events extracted with clock times PST from report narrative and CVR transcript
Primary cause: loss of all electrical power resulting in loss of attitude reference instruments in night instrument conditions
Contributing factors: No. 3 generator pre-flight maintenance failure (masked with tape) and failure of No. 2 generator to sustain load
Standby electrical system either was not activated or failed to function - exact mechanism could not be determined
All 38 occupants killed; fire warning on No. 1 engine - whether actual fire or false warning undetermined

records.title: Prinair 277
records.summary: Prinair Flight 277 crashed into Sierra de Luquillo mountains near Fajardo on 5 March 1969 while being vectored for an ILS approach. The trainee approach controller mistakenly thought the aircraft was 10 miles further west than its actual position and vectored it to 3,000 feet, directing it into rising terrain with all 19 occupants killed.
records.probable_cause: The vectoring of the aircraft into mountainous terrain, under IFR conditions, without adequate obstruction clearance altitude by a controller who, for reasons beyond his control, was performing beyond the safe limits of his performance capability and without adequate supervision (p. 15).

factors.evidence: Trainee controller mistakenly thought aircraft was 3 miles east of Isla Verde when it was actually 3 miles east of Fajardo (about 10 miles further east); controller's erroneous position information was provided to the aircraft (p. 3).
Controller's erroneous indications meant he thought aircraft was 10 miles further west than actual position, resulting in vectors into terrain (p. 3-4).
Controller was directing 5 flights; supervisor had ordered him to perform other duties; trainee controller was performing beyond safe performance limits (p. 15).
Weather conditions during that day (IFR conditions) would have prevented pilots from seeing the mountain peaks ahead during approach (p. 3).
Aircraft crashed into Sierra de Luquillo mountains at approximately 1738 local time (p. 2).

events.text: Prinair Flight 277, De Havilland Heron 114-2 N563PR, departed Charlotte Amalie (St. Thomas) on IFR clearance for San Juan
San Juan Air Route Traffic Control Center advised San Juan Approach Control that PRINAIR 277 was estimating Isla Verde intersection at 1738 maintaining 4,000 feet
Center identified radar target of PRINAIR 277 to Approach Control as 27 miles east of San Juan on Route 2; center-to-approach control handoff effected
PRINAIR 277 contacted San Juan Approach Control; trainee controller on AR-1 position observed aircraft on radar scope 3 miles east of Fajardo intersection but told it was 3 miles east of Isla Verde
Approach Control instructed flight to fly heading 250 for vector to ILS final, maintain 4,000 feet
Aircraft crashed into Sierra de Luquillo mountains near Fajardo, Puerto Rico; all 19 occupants (2 crew + 17 passengers) fatally injured

recommendations.text: Prohibit operation of aircraft without distance measuring or transponder equipment in instrument flight conditions in the San Juan area
Review approach control procedures in locations with similar topography to Sierra de Luquillo

Expand psychiatric and psychological assessment of controllers under the Air Traffic Controller Health Program; not only personnel entering on duty should be assessed but all controller personnel should be periodically tested

safety_changes: FAA implemented procedures requiring distance measuring equipment (DME) or transponders for aircraft operating IFR in the San Juan terminal area
Enhanced approach control procedures for areas with similar mountainous terrain
Improved controller psychological and medical screening and supervision

records.title: TWA 5787
records.summary: Trans World Airlines Flight 5787, a Boeing 707 on a non-revenue proficiency training flight, crashed at Atlantic City on July 26, 1969, killing all five crew on board. The aircraft was conducting recurrent training and proficiency checks including simulated single-engine failure during takeoff and landing. After landing on runway 13, the crew requested immediate turnaround and go-around on runway 31. During the go-around briefed as a three-engine ILS approach with simulated engine 4 failure, the flight engineer called for flaps 25 and gear up at decision height. However, neither flaps nor landing gear moved. Approximately 16-18 seconds after the go-around call, the crew experienced a complete loss of hydraulic pressure in the utility hydraulic system due to fatigue failure in the left outboard spoiler actuator. With low airspeed, three engines, and no hydraulics for rudder control, directional control was lost, the aircraft rolled and pitched down, and impacted the ground.
records.probable_cause: Loss of hydraulic power to the rudder in a critical flight condition combined with inadequate procedures for simulating engine failures and failure to apply correct hydraulic loss procedures. The loss of directional control was unrecoverable.

factors.evidence: Fatigue failure in left outboard spoiler actuator downline dumped hydraulic fluid from utility hydraulic system overboard, resulting in loss of all hydraulic power including rudder actuator
Crew did not call for or follow the hydraulic fluid loss checklist in accordance with current operating procedures
Multiple demands during go-around with flaps and landing gear selector calls, loss of hydraulics, and need to establish three-engine climb exceeded crew's capacity
Inadequacy of the hydraulic fluid loss emergency procedure when applied against the operating configuration of the aircraft

With low airspeed, three engines, undercarriage down, full flaps, and no hydraulic rudder power, aircraft was incapable of recovery; rolled and pitched down impacting ground in right wing low attitude

events.text: Aircraft landed on runway 13 with first check-ride captain at controls; crew requested 180 degree turnaround and immediate takeoff on runway 31
Takeoff initiated on runway 31 with simulated engine 4 failure; number 4 power lever retarded to idle, aircraft climbed to 1500 feet
At decision height proficiency checker called for go-around; check captain applied full power to engines 1, 2, and 3 leaving engine 4 at idle
Flight engineer called for flaps 25 and landing gear up; neither flaps nor landing gear moved from their positions
Crew discovered all hydraulic power had been lost due to rupture in utility hydraulic system; hydraulic pumps were disengaged but correct emergency procedures were not followed
With low airspeed, three engines, no hydraulic rudder power, undercarriage down and full flaps, aircraft lost directional control, rolled and pitched down, impacting ground in right wing low attitude

recommendations.text: Review and improve procedures for simulating single engine failures during training to ensure crews do not inadvertently create unsafe conditions
Revise hydraulic emergency procedures to account for total hydraulic system failure and training for such scenarios
Review spoiler actuator design to prevent catastrophic failures that result in complete hydraulic system loss

safety_changes: Improved hydraulic system redundancy in Boeing 707 and subsequent aircraft
Enhanced training procedures for emergency hydraulic failures
Better procedures for simulating engine failures without creating real system hazards

Report text quality compromised by OCR issues; extracted information verified against summary record

records.title: Allegheny Airlines Flight 853
records.summary: Allegheny Airlines Flight 853, a DC-9-31, collided mid-air with a Piper PA-28 near Fairland, Indiana on September 9, 1969. The DC-9 was on an instrument flight plan descending for approach to Indianapolis at 3,550 feet when it converged with the VFR Piper aircraft. The Piper was not equipped with a transponder and did not appear on radar. At a relative speed of 350 mph, the left wing of the Piper sheared off the DC-9's rear tail assembly. Both aircraft lost control and crashed, killing all 83 occupants on both aircraft.
records.probable_cause: The deficiencies in the collision avoidance capability of the Air Traffic Control system in a terminal area with mixed IFR and VFR traffic. The deficiencies included inadequacy of the see-and-avoid concept, technical limitations of radar in detecting all aircraft, and absence of Federal Aviation Regulations providing adequate separation of mixed traffic.

factors.evidence: The Piper aircraft was not equipped with a transponder and did not appear as a primary radar target on the radarscope (p. 6).
The two aircraft converged at a relative speed of 350 mph at 3,550 feet; the left wing of the PA-28 sheared off the DC-9's rear tail assembly (p. 6).
The FAA system lacked adequate regulations for separating mixed IFR and VFR traffic in terminal areas (p. 6).
The report faulted military and civilian aviation authorities for not reducing well-known collision risks that had existed for over a year (p. 6).

events.text: Allegheny 853 departs Cincinnati at 15:15 EDT on IFR flight plan via airway V-97, initially cleared to 10,000 feet.
Piper PA-28 student pilot departs Brookside Airpark on VFR flight plan with cruising altitude of 3,500 feet.
Allegheny 853 reaches cruising altitude and is cleared on airway V-97 northbound.
Piper and Allegheny flight paths converge as both aircraft proceed toward Indianapolis terminal area.
Allegheny 853 begins descent from cruise altitude; vectored toward Indianapolis approach control.
Indianapolis Approach Control instructs DC-9 to descend from 10,000 to 6,000 feet, then to 2,500 feet.
Both aircraft converge in terminal area; Piper not visible on radar due to lack of transponder.
DC-9 and Piper collide at 3,550 feet; Piper left wing shears DC-9 tail; both aircraft crash near Fairland.

recommendations.text: Establish minimum standards for radar reflectivity of small aircraft
Mandate effective scanning patterns and procedures training for aircrews

safety_changes: Radar reflectivity standards for small aircraft
Enhanced scanning procedures and collision avoidance training

records.title: Mohawk Airlines 411
records.summary: Mohawk Airlines Flight 411, a Fairchild Hiller FH-227 turboprop, departed Albany at 20:03 EST on November 19, 1969, bound for Glens Falls. While conducting a VOR approach, the captain exceeded his clearance limits, descended into a severe lee-of-mountain downdraft at insufficient altitude for recovery, and impacted the northwest slope of Pilot Knob Mountain at an elevation of 1,960 feet. All 14 occupants were killed.
records.probable_cause: The captain, while conducting an approach, exceeded his clearance limits and, thereafter, flew the aircraft into a severe 'lee of the mountain downdraft' at an altitude insufficient for recovery. (p. 7)

factors.evidence: Crew selected an improvised and unauthorized modified version of the VOR/DME 19 approach instead of the authorized VOR-1 approach for Warren County Airport. Aircraft proceeded north of Glens Falls VORTAC at 3,000 feet while operating on an IFR flight plan. (p. 20)
Aircraft descended below safe minimum altitude while in severe turbulence. Captain exceeded his clearance limits and continued descent into terrain. (p. 7)
Severe downdraft in the lee of Pilot Knob Mountain with strong winds 150° at 12 knots with gusts to 22 knots. Heavy rain and moderate to strong winds reported at Pilot Knob area. (p. 10)
Aircraft first impacted evergreen trees then struck near-vertical rock cliff face of Pilot Knob Mountain approximately 200 feet below summit, northwest slope, at elevation 1,960 feet. (p. 9-10)

events.text: Mohawk Airlines Flight 411, Fairchild-Hiller FH-227B, departed Albany, New York, on an Instrument Flight Rules flight plan for Warren County Airport, Glens Falls. (p. 8)
Albany Departure Control issued clearance: 'Mohawk Four Eleven, you are cleared to the-for a VOR approach at the Warren County Airport.' (p. 8)

Flight 411 reported at Miller Intersection to Albany Departure Control, then contacted Glens Falls Radio requesting weather. Flight Service Station agent provided current weather: ceiling 2,100 feet overcast, visibility 7 miles, light rain, wind 180° at 12 knots with gusts to 22 knots. (p. 8)

Aircraft continued on course and headed toward Glens Falls VORTAC at 3,000 feet. Flight Recorder data indicated reduction in airspeed commenced shortly after approach clearance receipt, stabilizing between 165-170 knots. (p. 21)

Flight proceeded northbound beyond Glens Falls VORTAC at approximately 3,000 feet for 1 minute 15 seconds (7 NM DME). Three witnesses in Glens Falls area observed aircraft. Light rain with moderate winds at Bolton and Diamond Point; heavy rain with strong winds at Pilot Knob area. (p. 10)
Aircraft initiated course reversal, beginning descent toward Pilot Knob Mountain while in severe downdraft conditions. Winds were 150° at 12-17 knots with gusts to 22-24 knots. (p. 10)

Aircraft impacted evergreen trees on northwest slope of Pilot Knob Mountain at 1,960 feet elevation, approximately 200 feet below summit. First impact with trees, then approximately 20 feet farther along flightpath, aircraft impacted near-vertical rock cliff face. Aircraft had right 12-degree wing-down attitude and was descending at 10-degree angle at impact. (p. 9-10)
Aircraft destroyed by impact and ensuing fire. All 14 occupants killed: 3 crew members and 11 passengers. Only damage to surroundings was to several large trees. (p. 9)

records.title: ALM 980

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report: Overseas National Airways, Inc., Douglas DC-9, N935F, Operating as Antilliaanse Luchtvaart Maatschappij Flight 980

location.name: Caribbean Sea, 48 km off St. Croix

records.summary: Overseas National Airways Flight 980, a Douglas DC-9, ditched in the Caribbean Sea on 2 May 1970 after fuel exhaustion following three unsuccessful landing attempts at St. Maarten and a diversion. The crew miscalculated fuel consumption, misread fuel gauges, and incorrectly computed fuel reserves, compounding high workload from weather and multiple approach attempts. The aircraft ditched with 23 fatalities.
records.probable_cause: Fuel exhaustion which resulted from continued, unsuccessful attempts to land at St. Maarten until insufficient fuel remained to reach an alternate airport. A contributing factor was the reduced visibility in the approach zone because of rain showers, a condition not reported to the flight.

factors.evidence: The crew miscalculated the rate of fuel consumption (using 0.78 and LRC mach at high-power settings rather than planned procedures), misread fuel gauges, and incorrectly computed the amount of fuel expected to remain (p. 8-10).
Multiple unsuccessful landing attempts and diversions, combined with weather situations and ATC coordination, distracted the crew from proper fuel management (p. 2).
Crew inattention and distraction resulted in poor fuel management throughout the descent and approach phase. The crew did not recognize that fuel margins had reached critical limits (p. 9).
A rain shower in the approach zone reduced visibility below announced values, forcing the aircraft to make approaches too close to the airport, complicating multiple landing attempts (p. 9).
The aircraft's fuel was exhausted during the descent, engines flamed out, and the captain ditched the aircraft in the Caribbean Sea at approximately 1549 local time (p. 7, 15).
Flight 980 ditched in the Caribbean Sea at 17 degrees 53 minutes North, 69 degrees 14 minutes West, during daylight hours (p. 7).

events.text: ATC advised that weather in St. Maarten was below landing minima; captain elected to divert
Tower at St. Maarten advised that the weather had improved sufficiently for landing
First landing attempt - aircraft did not sight the runway in sufficient time to align for landing
Second landing attempt unsuccessful due to poor alignment with the runway; aircraft flown with 25 degrees flaps
Third attempt - aircraft was too high to land safely after assessing weather and fuel situation
Captain decided to divert to St. Thomas
Captain reported to San Juan ARTCC 'Okay there's a possibility I may have to ditch this aircraft, I am now descending to the water.'
Engines flamed out due to fuel exhaustion at approximately 500 feet altitude
Aircraft ditched in Caribbean Sea; captain leveled off momentarily at 500 feet, descended in 100-foot increments, lowered 15 degrees flaps, and flew onto water at approximately 90 knots

recommendations.text: Require that the item 'warn passengers' be inserted as one of the last items on the emergency landing or ditching checklists of all carriers, yet sufficiently advanced on the list to insure adequate time for passengers to brace for a crash (NTSB-AAR-71-8, Recommendation (a), Appendix E).

Require that no flight involving the briefing of passengers regarding emergency procedures be dispatched without an operable public address system. The system should be functioning so that the flightcrew can speak to the passengers and a cabin attendant can speak to the passengers from at least one cabin station (NTSB-AAR-71-8, Recommendation (b), Appendix F).

Take necessary steps to eliminate, within a reasonable time, the use of fabric-to-metal type seatbelts and require the metal-to-metal type of seatbelt with a standardized activating device (NTSB-AAR-71-8, Recommendation (c), Appendix G).

Reexamine the methods for storage of lifevests aboard aircraft to eliminate any obstructions to expeditious access in the event of an emergency requiring their use (NTSB-AAR-71-8, Recommendation (d), Appendix H).
Initiate action to install a VHF communications link between San Juan ARTCC and Juliana Tower. This action was scheduled for fiscal year 1972 (NTSB-AAR-71-8, Recommendation (e), Appendix I).

Reassess the standards set forth in FAR parts 37.122 and 37.178 pertaining to the certification of liferafts and lifevests, with a view toward eliminating the deficiencies in such equipment as evidenced by the investigative record of this accident. Research and development should be undertaken, as necessary, to accomplish this reassessment and improvement of standards.

safety_changes: Enhanced requirements for emergency checklists to include passenger warning before ditching
Mandatory operable public address systems on all aircraft with passenger briefing requirements
Transition from fabric-to-metal seatbelts to metal-to-metal type with standardized activating devices
Improved stowage methods for lifevests to ensure expeditious access during emergencies
Installation of VHF communications link between San Juan ARTCC and Juliana Tower

records.title: Dan-Air 1903

location.name: Les Agudes, Serralada del Montseny, near Arbúcies

records.summary: Dan-Air Flight 1903 crashed into the Serralada del Montseny near Arbúcies during descent toward Barcelona on 3 July 1970, killing all 112 aboard. The crew mistakenly reported passing the Sabadell NDB while still 28 nm north of it over mountainous terrain. The controller, misled by a radar echo from another aircraft over Sabadell, did not notice the error and cleared descent to 2800 ft. The aircraft struck beech trees at about 3800 ft.
records.probable_cause: The combination of erroneous position reporting by the crew (who reported passing Sabadell when still 28 nm north) combined with a radar echo from another aircraft near Sabadell led the controller to believe the Comet had passed the beacon. This involuntary mutual error between crew and ATC could not be corrected before the aircraft struck high terrain.

factors.evidence: The aircraft was still 28 nautical miles north of Sabadell at the time of the erroneous report, over the Serralada del Montseny mountainous terrain (p. 9)
The crew reported in error that they had passed the Sabadell NDB, when they were still 28 nm north and the aircraft had drifted east of its planned route (p. 8-9)
Barcelona ATC mistook a radar echo from another aircraft overflying Sabadell for that of the Dan-Air Comet and cleared descent to 2,800 feet, the minimum altitude for that sector (p. 9)
The aircraft crashed into a group of beech trees on the northeast slopes of the Les Agudes peak at an altitude of about 3,900 feet

events.text: Flight 1903 departed Manchester Airport at 16:08 BST and encountered air traffic control delays in the Paris area, resulting in a change of route.
Radio contact was established with Barcelona Area Control Centre at 17:53 local time. Aircraft reported passing Spanish frontier and requested clearance to descend.
Aircraft reported passing Barcelona FIR boundary at FL160 with ETA of 1801 hrs for Point Berga.
Aircraft handed to Barcelona Approach. Crew reported leaving FL130 and gave ETA for Sabadell of 1807 hrs.
Crew reported passing Sabadell NDB, though they were actually still 28 nautical miles north of it, over the Serralada del Montseny.
Barcelona ATC mistook a radar echo from another aircraft over Sabadell for the Dan-Air Comet and cleared descent to 2,800 feet.
The Comet struck beech trees on the northeast slopes of the Les Agudes peak at an altitude of about 3,900 feet and was destroyed in the explosion.

recommendations.text: Emphasis should be given to commanders of aircraft flying on a new route to verify successive positions using all available aids rather than relying on any one aid.
Rules for radar identification should be revised to prevent similar situations, with identification properly checked by more than one method.
Radio navigation charts should incorporate spot heights of significant points along the route to be followed.

safety_changes: Enhanced radar identification procedures with multiple verification methods
Improved pilot training on position verification using multiple navigation aids
Radio navigation charts updated to include spot heights of significant points

notes: Sections read: History of Flight, Analysis, Conclusions and Probable Causes, Recommendations from UK AAIB report

records.title: Flying Tiger Line 45

location.name: Naha Air Base, approach to Runway 18

records.summary: Flying Tiger Line Flight 45, a Douglas DC-8-63F, crashed into the water during approach to Runway 18 at Naha Air Base on a precision radar approach. The aircraft descended below the glidepath through a heavy rain shower, losing altitude awareness. The crew attempted to establish visual contact but was blinded by the sudden transition from dense rain to bright sunlight. The aircraft struck the water 2,200 feet short of the runway threshold, killing all four crew members.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause of this accident was an unarrested rate of descent due to inattention of the crew to instrument altitude references while the pilot was attempting to establish outside visual contact in meteorological conditions which precluded such contact during that segment of a precision radar approach inbound from the Decision Height.

factors.evidence: Heavy rain shower at minimum descent altitude with visibility less than 1 mile (p. 5). The area surrounding the rain shower was brightly lighted by midday sunlight (p. 19).

The sudden increase in visibility from less than 1 mile to 10-100 times brighter caused Ganzfeld phenomenon (homogeneous visual field of similar brightness), preventing differentiation of outside objects and instrument references (p. 16).
Crew lost external visual reference completely upon entering the rain shower and could not refocus on instruments during the final seconds due to visual glare (p. 16).
Company flight operating procedures were not explicit regarding altitude callouts by captain and first officer during instrument approaches (p. 20).
Aircraft struck the water approximately 2,200 feet short of the runway threshold lights after descending below the glidepath (p. 5).

events.text: Radar contact established 18 miles northwest of Naha Air Base
Flight advised of reduced visibility on final approach with approach lights and strobe lights on
Captain mentioned a rain shower which was regarded to have been over the field
New altimeter setting of 29.84 inches given to crew and acknowledged
Landing checklist completed including full flaps, gear down and locked, and spoilers armed
Crew advised aircraft slightly below glidepath, 3 miles from touchdown
Sound similar to blowing of rain removal air began and continued steadily
Controller warned crew at minimum altitude going well below glidepath, too low
Unidentified person in cockpit called out altitude callouts at approximately 85 feet msl: hundred feet, seventy feet, fifty feet
Aircraft struck water approximately 2,200 feet short of runway threshold lights while at estimated altitude of 75-100 feet and in heavy rain shower

recommendations.text: The Federal Aviation Administration reemphasize to air carrier flight-supervisory and pilot personnel the pertinent altitude awareness recommendations

The Federal Aviation Administration issue an Advisory Circular incorporating excerpts of this report, stressing to all instrument and airline transport rated pilots the need for continuous surveillance of flight instruments when operating in instrument meteorological conditions

The Federal Aviation Administration determine that the Operations Manuals of all air carriers, commercial operators, and air taxi operators are explicit, particularly with regard to altitude callouts when the copilot is flying the airplane during an instrument approach

Flying Tiger Line, Inc., amend its flight operations procedures to set forth specifically the responsibilities and duties, particularly with regard to altitude callouts, of both captain and first officer when the latter is flying the aircraft on an instrument approach

dissent.position: Member Francis H. McADAMS argued the controller's delayed and inaccurate altitude transmissions were a contributing factor, noting the controller was late in advising the aircraft had reached minimum altitude (5-6 seconds after the aircraft had descended through it)

records.title: Wichita State University football team plane crash
records.summary: A Martin 404 carrying the Wichita State University football team crashed into Mount Trelease near Loveland Pass, Colorado. The aircraft attempted a scenic route through a mountain valley without adequate flight planning. The overloaded aircraft became trapped in a box canyon unable to climb over surrounding ridges, struck trees, and was destroyed by impact and fire.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause of this accident was the intentional operation of the aircraft over a mountain valley route at an altitude from which the aircraft could neither climb over the obstructing terrain ahead, nor execute a successful course reversal. Significant factors were the overloaded condition of the aircraft, the virtual absence of flight planning for the chosen route, a lack of understanding of aircraft performance capabilities and limitations, and the lack of operational management to monitor and appropriately control the actions of the flightcrew. (p. 31-32)

factors.evidence: Flight crew departed from planned route via established airways and instead proceeded on scenic route through Clear Creek Valley without adequate flight planning (p. 31-32).
Aircraft was 5,190 pounds over maximum takeoff weight at Denver and 2,665 pounds over maximum takeoff weight at impact (p. 32).
Aircraft became trapped in box canyon at Dry Gulch unable to climb over surrounding ridges or execute successful reversal turn (p. 31-32).
Aircraft struck trees at 10,800 feet elevation on Mount Trelease, descended 425 feet through trees while spinning (p. 2).
Aircraft was destroyed by fire and impact after striking trees (p. 2).

records.title: Southern Airways 932

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report, Southern Airways, Inc., DC-9, N97S, Tri-State Airport, Huntington, West Virginia

location.name: Tri-State Airport, Huntington, West Virginia, approximately 1 mile west of runway threshold on a hillside

records.summary: Southern Airways Flight 932, a McDonnell Douglas DC-9-30 chartered to transport the Marshall University football team and boosters, crashed during a nonprecision instrument approach to runway 11 at Tri-State Airport in Huntington, West Virginia. The aircraft descended below minimum descent altitude in adverse weather conditions (rain, fog, and smoke) without establishing visual contact with the runway. All 75 occupants, including 37 football players, 5 coaches, and crew, were killed.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause of this accident was the descent below Minimum Descent Altitude during a nonprecision approach under adverse operating conditions without visual contact with the runway environment. The National Transportation Safety Board has been unable to determine the reason for this descent, although the two most likely explanations are improper use of cockpit instrumentation data or an altimetry system error.

factors.evidence: The aircraft descended approximately 500 feet below the MDA of 1,240 feet during the approach (p. 2136-2138), continuing until impact with trees at 922 feet MSL.

Air traffic control advised that rain, fog, smoke and a ragged ceiling were at the airport, making the landing approach extremely difficult (p. 669-674). Visibility was estimated at 5 miles with low clouds.

The Catlettsburg Refinery, located approximately 2 miles from the runway with lights 300 feet higher in elevation than the airport, could have produced a visual illusion in the final approach phase (p. 2231-2270).
The crew did not make proper required callouts, did not arrest the descent at MDA, and the captain did not recognize that they had descended below minimums (p. 2365-2422).
The first officer failed to call out 500 feet above field elevation and failed to call out at MDA with a positive statement on runway visibility (p. 2365-2397).
The aircraft collided with trees on a hillside 5,543 feet west of the runway threshold, destroying the aircraft and killing all 75 occupants (p. 777-778, 774).

events.text: Southern Airways 932 established radio contact with Huntington Approach Control, descending to 5,000 feet.
Controller advised crew that rain, fog, smoke, and a ragged ceiling were at the airport; weather was 300 feet scattered, 500 feet variable broken, 1,100 feet overcast, visibility 5 miles.
Aircraft began normal descent after passing outer marker on localizer approach to runway 11.
First officer called out altitude readings during approach: 'seven hundred feet...We're two hundred above' then 'four hundred'.
Aircraft descended an additional 220 feet within 12 seconds after MDA callout and collided with tree tops on a hillside 5,543 feet short of runway threshold, burst into flames.

recommendations.text: All segments of the aviation industry should continue to focus attention on the unique demands for crew coordination and vigilance during nonprecision approaches, with particular emphasis on accelerated development of area navigation systems with vertical guidance and heads-up display systems.
Develop and install audible and visual altitude warning devices and implement procedures for their use to warn pilots when approaching selected altitudes during descents and instrument approaches.
Require that all air carrier aircraft be equipped with a functional ground proximity warning device in addition to barometric altimeters.
Establish final approach descent fixes and require pilots to maintain altitude at or above MDA until passing the descent fix, and provide VASI for each runway served by a nonprecision approach.

Revise procedures to require that pilots demonstrate, by means such as oral or written examination rather than simply signing a flight release, that they are familiar with 'off route' airports into which they will operate.

safety_changes: Development and mandate of ground proximity warning systems (GPWS) for air carrier aircraft
Enhanced altitude alerting device requirements
Improved crew coordination procedures for nonprecision approaches
Installation of VASI systems at more airports
Stricter qualification requirements for pilots operating to unfamiliar airports

records.title: Trans Caribbean Airways 505
records.summary: Trans Caribbean Airways Boeing 727 suffered a hard landing with bounce sequence after an unstable approach, with inappropriate crew actions during recovery. The aircraft overran the runway, struck infrastructure off-field, and caught fire on a hill beyond the airport. Two fatalities and 11 serious injuries resulted from the accident.
records.probable_cause: The captain's use of improper techniques in recovering from a high bounce generated by a poorly executed approach and touchdown. Lack of cockpit crew coordination during the approach and attempted recovery contributed to the accident. (p. 4)

factors.evidence: At 30 feet above the runway during final flare, airspeed had decreased 5 knots below the reference approach speed, and the aircraft dropped or touched down immediately after. (p. 5)

The first touchdown was hard, with the aircraft immediately rebounding to an estimated 30-50 feet altitude. Passengers described the impact as so violent it shook 'the stuffings out of the whole plane' with grinding metal noise. (p. 5)

During the first bounce, the captain reached for the speed brake handle, paused, then pulled it back, causing additional descent. The first officer subsequently noted the captain was not using sufficient control force to manage the aircraft. (p. 5)

After the third touchdown at 2,700 feet from threshold, the captain called for a go-around, but the flight engineer advised against it, demonstrating inadequate cockpit resource management and crew coordination. (p. 5-6)
The aircraft veered off the runway 3,800 feet beyond the threshold, crossed an access taxiway to Runway 27, and breached a chain-link boundary fence at 4,950 feet from the runway threshold. (p. 6)

No. 3 engine suffered a compressor stall as the aircraft overran the runway. Witnesses heard 'popping sounds' and 'backfire' noises, and an aircraft mechanic witness stated the No. 3 engine compressor was definitely stalling. (p. 6)

The landing gear and right wing tip struck a raised concrete sidewalk located 4 feet beyond the boundary fence, and the aircraft crushed a truck on an adjacent highway that had been hastily abandoned. (p. 6)
An explosion occurred in the vicinity of the left wing root immediately after the aircraft stopped, followed by a sizable fire. (p. 6)

events.text: Aircraft was at 30 feet above runway during final flare phase; airspeed had decreased to 5 knots below reference approach speed.
Aircraft touched down hard on runway; first officer noted airspeed dropped rapidly to 5 knots below reference speed.
Aircraft rebounded into the air immediately, ascending to an estimated 30-50 feet altitude with nose-up attitude described by flight engineer as more pronounced than typical.
During the first bounce, captain reached for speed brake handle, paused, then pulled it back, increasing the rate of descent.
Captain returned speed brake to retracted position just before or as aircraft touched down for second time.
Second touchdown occurred approximately 1,700 feet from runway threshold and was described as extremely hard by eyewitnesses and passengers; grinding metal sound heard.
Aircraft bounced again to an estimated 15-30 feet altitude with nose rotating upward.
First officer took firm hold of control yoke and pushed forward, then at crest of bounce pulled all the way back on yoke.
Aircraft touched down for third time approximately 2,700 feet from runway threshold and remained on ground; right wing tip began to drag on runway.
Captain called for a go-around.
Flight engineer advised against executing a go-around.
Captain advanced thrust lever and called for flaps to be raised to 25°.
Aircraft veered off runway at 3,800 feet beyond threshold; first officer helped captain regain directional control.
Witnesses heard 'muted popping sounds' or 'backfire' noises and saw flames extending from engine tailpipes; aircraft mechanic witness confirmed No. 3 engine compressor stalling.
Aircraft continued almost parallel to runway across access taxiway to Runway 27 and through chain-link boundary fence at point 4,950 feet from runway threshold.
Landing gear and right wing tip struck raised concrete sidewalk located 4 feet beyond fence; aircraft passed over sidewalk and adjacent highway.
Aircraft crushed truck that had been hastily abandoned on highway by its driver seconds earlier.
Aircraft continued up incline of hill east of highway and began to break apart.
Explosion occurred in vicinity of left wing root immediately after aircraft stopped.

records.title: Aviogenex 130
records.summary: Aviogenex Flight JJ130, a Tupolev Tu-134A charter from London to Rijeka, encountered severe weather during approach. Due to an optical illusion caused by rain, dusk, and water on the runway, the crew believed they were closer and higher than they actually were. The aircraft touched down hard at 260 km/h, the right wing broke off, and the aircraft turned over and caught fire, killing 78 of 83 occupants.
records.probable_cause: Optical illusion caused by dusk, heavy rain, and water on the runway led the crew to perceive the aircraft as closer and higher than its actual position, resulting in a steep descent and hard landing that exceeded structural limits of the right wing attachment.

factors.evidence: Refraction of light on the wet cockpit windshield during dusk and rain created an optical illusion causing the crew to believe the runway was closer and lower by approximately 60 meters (p. 4-5)
The aircraft remained above the glide path despite crew efforts to reduce altitude by applying down elevator and reducing power (p. 4-5)
The aircraft touched down at 260 km/h with excessive forces: vertical load of 4.15g and side loading of 1.46g on the right landing gear (p. 5)
The right wing broke off at the landing gear attachment point due to the extreme loads from hard landing (p. 5)
Fire broke out after the right wing separation and the fuselage turned over and burned (p. 5)

events.text: Flight JJ130 took off from Gatwick for Rijeka; flight proceeded normally despite unstable weather with thunderstorms and rain over Europe

records.title: Hughes Airwest 706
records.summary: Hughes Airwest Flight 706, a DC-9 climbing from Los Angeles, collided in midair with a U.S. Marine Corps F-4B Phantom II over the San Gabriel Mountains. All 49 aboard the airliner and the F-4 pilot were killed; the F-4 radar intercept officer ejected and survived. The Phantom's right wing struck the DC-9's fuselage center and its vertical stabilizer sliced through the cockpit.
records.probable_cause: The failure of both crews to see and avoid each other, though they had only marginal capability to detect, assess, and avoid the collision. Contributing factors include very high closure rate, comingling of IFR and VFR traffic where ATC system limitations preclude effective separation, and failure of the Phantom crew to request radar advisory service despite having an inoperable transponder.

factors.evidence: F-4B's right wing struck center of DC-9's fuselage; vertical stabilizer sliced through cockpit; all 49 in DC-9 and F-4 pilot killed.
Neither crew sighted the other aircraft in time to initiate evasive action; very high closure rate (approximately 1000 ft/s) compromised detection capability.
F-4B operating under VFR not under ATC control; military aircraft operating in civilian airspace with reduced radar detection capability.
Lack of requirement for military aircraft to contact civilian ATC controllers operating in civilian airspace under VFR.
F-4B not detected on radar because of inoperative transponder and low-level temperature inversion affecting radar performance.

events.text: Flight 706 departed Los Angeles at 6:02 pm PDT bound for Seattle with intermediate stops.
Los Angeles ARTCC took control of flight 706 at 6:06 pm, four minutes after takeoff.
Flight 706 passed through 12,000 feet and received last radio transmission: instructed to heading 040 until Daggett VOR.
F-4B Phantom, with failed radio, returning to MCAS El Toro for diagnostic tests, approached DC-9 flight path.
F-4B's right wing struck center of DC-9 fuselage; vertical stabilizer sliced through cockpit; both aircraft destroyed in San Gabriel Mountains.

recommendations.text: Install video tape at all FAA ATC radar displays for use as investigation tool.
Install open area microphone at each terminal and center sector position to record all control position conversations.
Establish climb and descent corridors from TCA tops to APC base.
Establish more definitive procedures for controller guidance in handling Code 7700 aircraft.
Review radar performance monitoring procedures to assure all radar facilities can receive Code 7700 transponder returns.

records.title: Allegheny Airlines Flight 485
records.summary: Allegheny Airlines Flight 485, operating a scheduled service from Washington, D.C. to Newport News, Virginia with stops in Connecticut and Philadelphia, was conducting a non-precision instrument approach to Tweed-New Haven Airport. The captain intentionally descended below the published minimum descent altitude during poor visibility conditions without visual confirmation of the runway environment. Despite the first officer's advisories that minimum descent altitude had been reached, the aircraft continued descending at normal descent rate and airspeed. The aircraft struck cottages at 29 feet above mean sea level, 4,890 feet from the runway threshold and 510 feet right of the extended runway centerline. All 30 occupants were killed.
records.probable_cause: The captain's intentional descent below the prescribed minimum descent altitude under adverse weather conditions, without adequate forward visibility or the crew's sighting of runway environment. The captain disregarded advisories from his first officer that minimum descent altitude had been reached and that the airplane was continuing to descend at normal descent rate and airspeed.

factors.evidence: Aircraft struck cottages at altitude of 29 feet msl, 4,890 feet from threshold and 510 feet right of extended centerline of Runway 2 (p. 1). Non-precision instrument approach with inadequate forward visibility (p. 1).

Captain intentionally descended below prescribed minimum descent altitude without adequate forward visibility or visual confirmation of runway environment (p. 1). First officer and captain in disagreement regarding minimum descent altitude (p. 1).

Captain disregarded advisories from first officer that minimum descent altitude had been reached (p. 1). Captain disregarded that airplane was continuing to descend at normal descent rate and airspeed (p. 1). Board unable to determine what motivated captain to disregard prescribed operating procedures and altitude restrictions (p. 1).
Adverse weather conditions preventing visual confirmation of runway environment during approach (p. 1). Non-precision approach with forward visibility restrictions (p. 1).

Aircraft descending toward terrain at normal descent rate without visual runway reference

records.title: Pan Am 845
records.summary: Pan American Flight 845, a Boeing 747-121, struck the approach lighting structure for Runway 19L while taking off from Runway 01R at San Francisco International Airport on July 30, 1971. The crew, intending to depart from Runway 28L, discovered only after pushback that the runway was closed. Without recalculating takeoff reference speeds, the crew selected 20 degrees of flaps instead of the planned 10 degrees. The aircraft continued takeoff, impacting ALS structures, and the crew circled to dump fuel before returning to San Francisco for an emergency evacuation.
records.probable_cause: The pilot's use of incorrect takeoff reference speeds, which resulted from a series of irregularities involving: (1) the collection and dissemination of airport information; (2) aircraft dispatching; and (3) crew management and discipline; which collectively rendered ineffective the air carrier's operational control system.

factors.evidence: The crew selected 20 degrees of flaps for takeoff from Runway 01R, instead of the originally planned 10 degree setting (p. 9).
The crew did not recalculate takeoff reference speeds after changing to the shorter runway, leaving the speed bugs at the 10-degree flap settings despite the 20-degree configuration (p. 9).
The flight crew failed to recompute required takeoff reference speeds (V-speeds) for the 20 degree flap condition (p. 29-30).
Runway 28L had been closed for maintenance since 0830 and was forecast to remain closed past the scheduled departure time (p. 10-11).
The tower controller did not clearly communicate to the flight dispatcher the existing runway restrictions on Runway 01R regarding full takeoff power limitations (p. 11).

events.text: Flight 845 departed Los Angeles International Airport bound for Tokyo via San Francisco.
Aircraft arrived at San Francisco International Airport.
Flight crew boarded the aircraft and began preparations for flight.
Aircraft was pushed back from the gate. First officer monitored ATIS for latest information and became aware that Runway 28L was closed and first 1,000 feet of Runway 01R was also closed.
Upon confirmation of Runway 28L closure, crew contacted Pan American Operations to check limitations for use of Runway 01R with clearway.

Flight controller advised crew that Runway 01R with clearway could be used for takeoff with zero wind component. Crew confirmed they were prepared for takeoff on this runway at planned gross weight with 20 degree flaps and 3A-Wet power.
Crew requested and received taxi clearance to Runway 01R and was cleared to hold momentarily prior to being positioned on the runway.
Tower reported wind from 270 degrees at 22 knots.
Takeoff clearance was issued. The crew did not recalculate takeoff reference speeds for the 20-degree flap configuration; the speed bugs remained set at values for 10-degree flaps.

Aircraft rotated. First officer called Vy at the bug setting of 156 knots and Vp at approximately 160 or 161 knots. The aircraft struck the Approach Light System structure located at the departure end of Runway 01R.

First officer felt a bump or jolt as the aircraft passed through 165 knots. Two passengers in seats 47G and 48G were seriously injured by parts of the ALS structure that penetrated the passenger compartment. The flight engineer reported loss of hydraulic fluid from systems 1, 3, and 4.
Captain climbed aircraft to 1,500 feet then subsequently to between 2,500 and 3,060 feet to assess damage. Aircraft was maneuvered out over the ocean in preparation for fuel dumping.
After approximately 45 minutes, crew dumped approximately 180,000 pounds of fuel to achieve a landing weight of about 430,000 pounds. Captain decided to return to San Francisco.

recommendations.text: Review the procedures for the issuance of NOTAM and ASRAD for standardized implementation within the appropriate FAA facilities and modify the procedures to ensure that information pertinent to Safety of Flight is disseminated without delay.
Require that V-reference speed checks be included on the last checklist used immediately prior to takeoff.
Require the installation of runway distance markers at all civil airports where air carrier aircraft are authorized to operate.
Require the use of takeoff procedures which will provide the flight crew with time and distance reference to associate with acceleration to V1 speed.

Require manufacturers to include in aircraft operating manuals information concerning the aircraft controllability and performance characteristics with the loss of any system that involves flight controls.

records.title: Alaska Airlines 1866
records.summary: Alaska Airlines Flight 1866, a Boeing 727, was conducting an instrument approach to Juneau Airport on a localizer directional aid (LDA) approach. The crew received erroneous navigation radio indications suggesting they were closer to the airport than their actual position. The aircraft descended below obstacle clearance altitude and struck a mountain slope in the Chilkat range 18.5 miles west of the airport at approximately 2,500 feet altitude, killing all 111 occupants.
records.probable_cause: Display of misleading navigational information concerning the flight's progress along the localizer course which resulted in premature descent below obstacle clearance altitude. The origin of the erroneous navigational information could not be determined. Contributing factors were the crew's failure to use all available navigational aids to check progress along the localizer and failure to perform required audio identification of navigation facilities.

records.title: British European Airways 706

agencies.name: Accidents Investigation Branch
agencies.report_title: Civil Aircraft Accident Report 15/72 - British European Airways Vanguard G-APEC

records.summary: British European Airways Flight 706, a Vickers Vanguard, crashed near Aarsele, Belgium on October 2, 1971 while climbing through flight level 190. The rear pressure bulkhead failed due to undetected metal fatigue corrosion, causing rapid depressurization of the tail section and separation of both horizontal tailplanes. The aircraft entered an uncontrollable dive from which recovery was impossible. All 63 occupants perished.
records.probable_cause: The accident was caused by the rupture of the rear pressure bulkhead, which led to the separation of both tailplanes in flight and caused the aircraft to dive into the ground. The rupture occurred due to undetected metal fatigue corrosion at the rear pressure bulkhead. (p. 36)

factors.evidence: Inspection techniques used for detecting corrosion at station 1223 were inadequate; radiographic technique used was ineffective at detecting corrosion due to difficulty interpreting photographic plates from complex structure (p. 34)

Severe corrosion present at joint between fuselage skin and rear pressure bulkhead for unknown period prior to accident; progressive crack in bulkhead grew through at least fourteen successive pressurization cycles (p. 34)
Rear pressure bulkhead ruptured in cruising flight at FL 190 when corrosion-initiated crack exceeded critical crack length (p. 36)

Rapid inflation of tailcone and empennages from bulkhead rupture imposed high differential pressure causing upper tailplane skin panels to detach from main structure; both horizontal tailplanes and elevators separated in flight (p. 33)
Loss of aerodynamic download from horizontal tail surfaces caused aircraft to pitch rapidly nose-down; entered steep dive from which it was not possible to recover (p. 33)

events.text: Flight 706 took off from runway 28L at London Heathrow with 55 passengers and 8 crew members; climbed through 14,200 feet at Dover VOR (p. 3)
Aircraft handed over to Brussels Air Traffic Control at mid-channel on airway Green One; satisfactory two-way communications established; aircraft climbing toward flight level 190 (p. 3)
Aircraft reported passing over Wulpen VOR with aircraft level at FL 190; flight proceeding normally with no indication of abnormality (p. 3)
Aircraft in level flight at FL 190 with flight proceeding normally; flight recorder ceased to function indicating start of structural failure sequence (p. 33)

Crew transmitted we are going down, 706, we're going down immediately followed by MAYDAY call repeated several times (p. 3)
Fragmented and garbled transmissions continuing with phrases we're going down vertically and out of control (p. 3)

Loss of aerodynamic download from separated tailplanes caused aircraft to pitch rapidly nose-down (p. 33)

Aircraft in steep dive with longitudinal attitude between 20° and 30° over vertical, rotating slowly in clockwise direction about longitudinal axis at high forward speed; transmissions ceased abruptly at ground impact (p. 3)
Aircraft struck open farmland near Aarsele Belgium in steep dive; completely destroyed by ground impact and subsequent fire; all 63 occupants killed (p. 3)

records.title: Mohawk Airlines 405
records.summary: Mohawk Airlines Flight 405 crashed into a house in Albany on 3 March 1972. The left propeller was stuck in cruise pitch lock and could not be feathered, creating asymmetric drag that resulted in uncontrollable descent. Of 48 occupants and 1 house resident, 17 were killed.
records.probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Board determines that the probable cause of this accident was the inability of the crew to feather the left propeller, in combination with the descent of the aircraft below the prescribed minimum altitudes for the approach (p. 33). Contributing causal factors for the nonstandard approach were the captain's preoccupation with a cruise pitch lock malfunction, the first officer's failure to adhere to company altitude awareness procedures, and the captain's failure to delegate any meaningful responsibilities to the copilot which resulted in a lack of effective task sharing during the emergency (p. 33). The Board was unable to determine why the left propeller could not be feathered or why the propeller pitch lock malfunctioned during the descent (p. 33).

factors.evidence: left propeller was stuck in cruise pitch lock and could not be feathered, with crew noting "pitch light" indication at 2043:26; worn cam follower roller found in pitch control unit but units tested as capable of normal operation (p. 8, p. 33)

records.title: Delta Air Lines 9570
records.summary: Delta Air Lines Flight 9570, a DC-9-14 training flight with four occupants including an FAA inspector, was on approach to Greater Southwest International Airport (GSW) at Fort Worth, Texas. The aircraft was sequenced behind an American Airlines DC-10 which had recently completed a touch-and-go landing on Runway 13. On final approach with 53-54 seconds separation from the DC-10, the DC-9 encountered severe wake turbulence from the heavy jet, causing the aircraft to oscillate about the roll axis, then roll rapidly to the right. The right wingtip struck the runway and the aircraft continued to roll until the fuselage struck in a nearly inverted attitude. The aircraft was destroyed by impact and fire, killing all four occupants.
records.probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Board determines that the probable cause of the accident was an encounter with a trailing vortex generated by a preceding heavy jet which resulted in an involuntary loss of control of the airplane during the final approach. Although cautioned to expect turbulence the crew did not have sufficient information to evaluate accurately the hazard or the possible location of the vortex. Existing FAA procedures for controlling VFR flight did not provide the same protection from a vortex encounter as was provided to flights being given radar vectors in either IFR or VFR conditions.

factors.evidence: DC-9 encountered trailing vortex generated by preceding DC-10 heavy jet aircraft. Flight data recorders confirmed DC-9 traversed same track as DC-10 during final approach phase with only 53-54 seconds separation (p. 6)

ATC issued advisory to expect caution turbulence but did not explicitly advise crew they were following a heavy aircraft. ATC noted DC-10 in traffic but terminology heavy jet not used on radio. Separation between DC-9 and DC-10 was established at radar greater than 6 nautical miles but deteriorated on final approach due to VFR positioning (p. 5, 18)

Most prior wake turbulence accidents involved smaller aircraft than DC-9, suggesting crews had not been trained to recognize wake turbulence hazard to larger twin-engine aircraft from heavy jets (p. 25)

events.text: Delta Flight DL9570 departed Love Field, Dallas, Texas on training flight with takeoff gross weight 77,300 pounds and center of gravity 25.7 percent MAC. Aircraft carried Captain George G. Gray (check airman), First Officer, FAA air carrier inspector, and flight engineer.

Flight requested and received clearance for ILS approach to Runway 13 at Greater Southwest International Airport. Advised that American Airlines DC-10 was in traffic pattern conducting touch-and-go landings. DC-9 received advisory to expect caution turbulence.

First ILS approach completed with full-stop landing. Aircraft subsequently performed training maneuvers and was issued takeoff and climb-out clearances to maintain VFR. Gross weight approximately 74,000 pounds at time of accident (vs 77,300 at takeoff).

Flight requested and received radar vectors for second ILS approach to Runway 13, again sequenced behind DC-10 with separation exceeding 6 nm radar. Crew visually assessed traffic and became concerned about DC-10 landing conflict with planned circling approach to Runway 17.

Second ILS approach terminated with missed approach. Radar vectors provided for VOR approach to Runway 35 with circling approach to Runway 17. Tower controller subsequently cleared flight for circling approach to Runway 17.

Flight requested and received clearance for full-stop landing on Runway 13 behind DC-10 on final approach. Local controller issued clearance with advisory: Okay that'll be fine use one three for full stop! Caution turbulence. Aircraft at reference speed 130 knots, approach flown manually and smoothly with little azimuth/glide slope deviation, airspeed not varying more than 2-3 knots from approach speed of 135 knots.

DC-9 on final approach to Runway 13, approximately 53-54 seconds behind DC-10 which had completed touch-and-go landing. Aircraft flight data recorders show DC-9 traversed same track as DC-10. FDR data indicated aircraft was flying normal approach profile. Separation deteriorated from initial radar spacing due to VFR circling procedure and delayed turn to final.

Approximately 11 seconds before impact at 670 feet altitude (approximately 100 feet above airport elevation), aircraft encountered trailing vortex. Right seat occupant (Delta check pilot) commented A little turbulence here. Flight data recorder disclosed corresponding vertical acceleration trace excursion to +1.7 g. Aircraft began to oscillate about roll axis. After two oscillations, aircraft rolled rapidly to the right.

After achieving approximately 90 degrees of roll, right wingtip contacted runway surface at approximately 1,240 feet beyond runway threshold. Aircraft continued rolling to right in nearly inverted attitude. Fuselage and empennage separated upon impact and slid approximately 2,400 feet coming to rest off right side of runway. Aircraft was destroyed by impact forces and general fire which developed subsequent to impact. All four occupants sustained fatal injuries: three from massive injuries and one from smoke and carbon monoxide inhalation. CVR data disclosed stall warning system was actuated just prior to impact, indicating go-around attempt was initiated too late to prevent accident.

recommendations.text: Reevaluate wake turbulence separation criteria for aircraft operating behind heavy jet aircraft

Issue alert notices to all pilots and aircraft operators that will stress the urgent need to maintain adequate separation from heavy jet aircraft, with special emphasis on nonradar VFR procedures and need to provide time/distance separation

Develop new standards requiring 5 miles spacing for all aircraft, with exception of 747 or CSA operating behind DC-10 and L-1011 (previously required only 3 miles spacing for wide-bodied jets behind heavy jets)
Establish specific separation standards for VFR operations
Develop and implement safe spacing system where tower controller determines hazard existence
Develop automatic safe spacing using aircraft transponder signals and mini-computer to determine hazard existence and provide warning
Conduct comprehensive review of all FAA procedures and training related to wake turbulence avoidance
Establish specific training requirements for all pilots and air traffic controllers regarding wake turbulence hazards
