records.title: British European Airways Flight 548

agencies.name: Air Accidents Investigation Branch
agencies.report_title: Report on the accident to Hawker Siddeley Trident 1C G-ARPI near Staines-upon-Thames, Surrey on 18 June 1972

records.summary: Hawker Siddeley Trident 1C G-ARPI crashed shortly after takeoff from Heathrow near Staines-upon-Thames. During the initial climb in noise-abatement configuration, the aircraft lost airspeed and the captain unintentionally retracted the leading edge droops at an insufficient airspeed of 162 knots (20 knots below minimum). The aircraft entered a deep stall from which recovery was impossible at the low altitude.
records.probable_cause: The captain failed to maintain adequate airspeed during climb and failed to extend the leading edge droops properly. Contributing factors included the captain's undiagnosed heart condition, limited co-pilot experience, an aircraft design vulnerable to deep stall if droops were retracted at low speed, and inadequate stall recovery system training.

factors.evidence: Captain failed to maintain airspeed above 177 knots and retracted droops at 162 knots, 20 knots below minimum speed (p. 531-544).
Captain Key had an undiagnosed heart condition that may have impaired judgment (p. 26-30).
Second officer Keighley had limited experience and was not qualified to act as pilot-flying for the aircraft (p. 37-42).
Trident T-tail design with retractable droops made it vulnerable to deep stall if droops retracted below minimum speed (p. 660-679).
Aircraft entered deep stall at second 116 after droop retraction, with stick-pusher system providing insufficient warning (p. 497-507).
Aircraft descended steeply after deep stall with no recovery possible at 1772 feet altitude (p. 506-507).
Aircraft impacted ground near Staines-upon-Thames at second 150.7 (p. 508).

events.text: Brake release, start of takeoff roll on runway 28R.
Aircraft rotates at 145 knots IAS, leaves runway 2 seconds later (p. 471-472).
Autopilot engaged at 355 feet above runway, airspeed 170 knots IAS, 7 knots below noise-abatement target (p. 472-473).
Aircraft begins 20-degree banked turn to port towards Epsom NDB (p. 474-475).
Captain reports 'Climbing as cleared', instructed to contact London ATC on 128.4 MHz (p. 476-477).
Noise-abatement procedure initiated: flaps retracted to fully up, power reduced. Airspeed 168 knots, still 9 knots below target (p. 487-489).
After thrust reduction, airspeed drops to 157 knots, 20 knots below noise-abatement target Vy of 177 knots (p. 540-541).
Droop lever selected up in 20-degree banked turn at 162 knots IAS, 1772 feet altitude, 20 knots below droop retraction minimum (p. 496-498, 543-544).
Stick-pusher stall recovery device operates at low airspeed, autopilot automatically disengages, nose pitches down (p. 498-500).
Second stick-push operates as elevator trim configuration causes pitch-up after first pitch-down (p. 503).
Third stick-push operates (p. 503).
Stall recovery system manually inhibited by pulling override lever. Aircraft pitched up rapidly, lost speed and height (p. 504-506).
Aircraft impacted field near Staines-upon-Thames, all 118 occupants killed (p. 508).

recommendations.text: Speed-operated baulk to prevent retraction of leading-edge droops or slats when airspeed is below safe limit.

Specific instruction and training on change of configuration stalls, simultaneous stick-shaker/stick-pusher operation, and implications of design differences between stick-shaker and stick-pusher mechanisms (p. 3013-3023).
Mandatory carriage of cockpit voice recorders on all civil passenger-carrying aircraft over 27,000 kg all-up weight (p. 3026-3028).
Pilot training on possibility and dangers of subtle pilot incapacitation (p. 3030-3031).
Young trainee pilots given more experience on flight deck before operating as P2 on passenger flights (p. 3033-3039).
Substitute stress-test electrocardiogram for resting ECG in pilot medicals when reliability improves (p. 3041-3043).
P4 seat occupied only by personnel with flight function or under training during critical flight phases (p. 3045-3047).

safety_changes: Cockpit voice recorders became mandatory on large aircraft

notes: Read from sections: narrative (p. 14-16), mechanical factors speed section (p. 531-544), stall systems (p. 650-695), conclusions (p. 2891-2937), recommendations (p. 3005-3049)

records.title: Prinair 191

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report - Prinair Flight 191

records.summary: De Havilland Heron Flight 191 approached Mercedita Airport in the evening on 24 June 1972 with 26 passengers and 2 crew. After a brief uneventful flight, the aircraft touched down on runway 29 but the crew decided to go around. During the go-around, the pilot over-rotated the aircraft at too low an airspeed, causing an aerodynamic stall at a low altitude. The aircraft crashed about 2,200 feet beyond the runway threshold, killing 2 crew members and 3 passengers, with 15 passengers injured.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause of the accident was the loss of directional control during a go-around from a landing attempt. Control was lost when the aircraft was overrotated at too low an airspeed to sustain flight. The crew's reasons for rejecting the landing are not known.

factors.evidence: The accident occurred during hours of darkness with fog present in the area (p. 7-8)
Just after touching down on the runway, the flight crew made a decision to go around for unknown reasons (p. 7)
The pilot over-rotated the aircraft at too low an airspeed, causing it to stall at a low level (p. 14)
The aircraft was overrotated at too low an airspeed to sustain flight, resulting in an aerodynamic stall (p. 14)
Loss of directional control occurred when the aircraft was overrotated at too low an airspeed (p. 14)

events.text: Flight 191 departed San Juan at 2252 with 26 passengers and 2 crew. Flight was uneventful during takeoff, climb, and cruise.
At 2301, cleared for approach to Mercedita Airport. At 2304, cancelled IFR flight plan. Aircraft was on left base leg for runway 29.
Aircraft touched down on runway 29. Witnesses observed nothing unusual about the approach.
Just after touching down, flight crew made a decision to go around. The reasons for rejecting the landing are not known.
Aircraft assumed a steep climbing attitude with high engine power. Witnesses observed the aircraft rock from side to side.
Aircraft overrotated at too low an airspeed, causing an aerodynamic stall. Loss of directional control resulted.

Aircraft crashed approximately 2,200 feet beyond the runway threshold and 260 feet south of runway 29, coming to rest 74 feet southwest of initial impact after knocking down chain link fence sections and striking a powerline pole.
Aircraft destroyed; 2 crew members and 3 passengers killed; 15 passengers injured.

notes: Report finalized December 17, 1975 as AAR-75-17
Originally confused about Ports Authority truck on runway; later clarified as misinterpretation through Spanish translation
Tire marks confirmed wheels touched down before go-around
Crew's reasons for go-around rejection remain unknown
Sections read: Synopsis, History of Flight, Findings, Conclusions, Probable Cause, Analysis

records.title: 1972 Lake Winnebago mid-air collision

aircraft.type: Convair CV-580 and de Havilland DHC-6 Twin Otter

records.operator: North Central Airlines and Air Wisconsin
records.summary: North Central Airlines Flight 290 (Convair CV-580) and Air Wisconsin Flight 671 (de Havilland DHC-6 Twin Otter) collided in mid-air over Lake Winnebago at 2,500 feet near Fox Crossing, Wisconsin during approach in bright sunshine with scattered clouds. The collision tore off portions of both aircraft's wings, rendering them uncontrollable. Both crashed into the lake. The NTSB determined that both crews failed to detect the other aircraft visually in sufficient time to take evasive action. (p. 18)
records.probable_cause: The probable cause of this accident was the failure of both flight crews to detect visually the other aircraft in sufficient time to initiate evasive action. The Board is unable to determine why each crew failed to see and avoid the other aircraft; however, the Board believes that the ability of both crews to detect the other aircraft in time to avoid a collision was reduced because of atmospheric conditions and human visual limitations. The decision by both crews to fly VFR rather than IFR deprived both aircraft of air traffic control support that would have ensured adequate separation. (p. 18)

factors.evidence: Both flight crews failed to detect visually the other aircraft in sufficient time to initiate evasive action. (p. 18)
The NTSB speculated that both flight crews could have been scanning instruments in preparation for descent to their respective destinations at the time of the collision. (p. 18)
Both aircraft crews chose to fly VFR instead of IFR despite being able to do so, depriving themselves of air traffic control radar separation and altitude separation procedures. (p. 18)

The left wing of Flight 671 collided with the left wing of Flight 290 at 2,500 feet, resulting in an explosion that tore off most of the Twin Otter's wing and about a quarter of the CV-580's left wing. (p. 18)

events.text: North Central Flight 290 (CV-580 N90858) and Air Wisconsin Flight 671 (DHC-6 N4043B) depart on collision course at approximately 10:30 CDT
Flight 290 made 'in range' call to company office at Oshkosh, reporting 8,400 pounds of fuel remaining
Flight 290 made initial contact with Oshkosh tower, approximately 7 nm northeast at 2,500 feet VFR
Flight 290 crew requested clearance to land on Runway 27
Flight 290 crew acknowledged landing clearance; last known radio transmission from Flight 290
Flight 671 crew contacted company office at Appleton, reported would be landing at 10:44 with 300 pounds fuel remaining

North Central Flight 290 and Air Wisconsin Flight 671 collided mid-air over Lake Winnebago at 2,500 feet, approximately 6 nm south of Appleton and 2.5 nm east of Neenah, Wisconsin; both aircraft destroyed in explosion
Both aircraft became uncontrollable after collision and crashed into Lake Winnebago; all 13 occupants killed

recommendations.text: Develop and publish standards for visual search techniques to be used by instructors and check pilots on all training, certification, and proficiency check flights when pilots are operating in VMC.
Establish a requirement for pilots to be trained in the techniques of time sharing between visual scanning for airborne targets and cockpit duties.
Require that all pilots and flightcrew members training, certification, and proficiency check forms contain a specific item on scanning and time sharing.
Require that all pilots and flightcrew members be graded in scanning and time sharing techniques when training, certification, and proficiency check flights are conducted under VMC.

Advise the Board of the status of the FAA's evaluation project of April 7, 1972, on aircraft conspicuity research and, if that project has not been completed, take action to complete the project on a priority basis.

Expedite the development and issuance of national standards for systems to provide protection from midair collisions so that the industry can proceed without further delay to develop and market economically viable hardware.

safety_changes: Enhanced emphasis on visual scanning techniques in pilot training
Development of collision avoidance systems research initiatives

notes: Read History of Flight, Probable Cause, Analysis, Recommendations sections
9 events with clock times from detailed timeline and radio communications
VFR operations and crew scanning failures identified as key causal factors
Six formal NTSB recommendations addressing visual search and collision avoidance

records.title: 1972 Sacramento Canadair Sabre accident

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report - Spectrum Air, Inc., Sabre Mark 5, N275X, Sacramento Executive Airport

records.summary: A Canadair Sabre Mk. 5 flown by pilot Richard L. Bingham failed to gain sufficient altitude during takeoff on runway 30 from Sacramento Executive Airport during the Golden West Sport Aviation Air Show. With nose over-rotated, aircraft overran runway, external fuel tanks ruptured and ignited, crossed Freeport Boulevard before striking Farrell's Ice Cream Parlor. Twenty-two people on ground were killed.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause of this accident was the overrotation of the aircraft and subsequent derogation of the performance capability. The overrotation was the result of inadequate pilot proficiency in the aircraft and misleading visual cues.

factors.evidence: Bingham had fewer than four hours of flying time in Sabre Mark 5; his most recent jet experience was primarily in Lear Jet as second-in-command (p. 7-8)
Pilot applied excessive nose-up control, rotating to 17° ANU compared to 5° in a normal Sabre takeoff; eyewitnesses and movie analysis confirmed nose was over-rotated (p. 14-19)

F-86 Sabre has dangerous handling characteristic upon takeoff if nose is raised prematurely; the aircraft's elevator power at slow speeds allows high angles of attack before flying speed is attained, with insufficient thrust to overcome induced drag (p. 18)
Aircraft overran runway at approximately 150 mph, struck earthen berm and ripped through perimeter fence (p. 6)
Two external underwing fuel tanks ruptured and ignited creating massive fireball; fire trail followed aircraft across Freeport Boulevard into the building (p. 13)

events.text: Sabre takeoff commenced on runway 30 from Sacramento Executive Airport
At approximately 105 knots, pilot applied back pressure to raise nosewheel off runway
Initial lift-off occurred at 2,800-2,900 feet from end of runway at 124 knots, 11° nose-up attitude
Aircraft reached 130.5 knots and 15.5° nose-up attitude but acceleration stopped and speed began decreasing; aircraft 7 feet above ground
Pilot felt and heard unusual vibration; instinctively lowered nose
Aircraft settled back to runway at approximately 3,700 feet at 128 knots, 10° nose-up attitude
Pilot resumed takeoff attitude for second attempt; speed increased to approximately 137 knots with 16.5° nose-up attitude
Second lift-off occurred at approximately 5,005 feet from end of runway; pilot realized aircraft would not fly
Pilot began rejected takeoff procedure; closed throttle and touched down
Aircraft hit perimeter fence and became airborne again at approximately 800 feet from end of runway; crossed Freeport Boulevard
Pilot shut off fuel switch and shielded face with right arm; unable to control aircraft
Aircraft crashed through ice cream parlor; external fuel tanks ruptured and ignited; aircraft destroyed by impact and fire

recommendations.text: Limit the issuance of experimental certificates to those aircraft and operations that are truly experimental in nature and reclassify the other activities listed in FAR 21.191 in a manner that will permit more selective regulatory control without unduly inhibiting the promotion of aviation.
Establish pilot experience, transition, and proficiency standards applicable to the operation of all high-performance surplus military aircraft, reciprocating as well as turbine engine powered.

Establish additional airshow separation criteria applicable to persons and property in other than designated spectator areas to insure that the overall suitability of an airport for airshows is taken into account.

Include in the guidelines dealing with compatible land use planning around airports, consideration for the safety of persons and property on the ground, and use the controls available in the Airport Development Aid Program to insure compliance.

Establish guidelines that will assist airport managers in setting limitations on the utilization of runways where existing environmental encroachment and runway length combine to create a high risk level for certain aircraft operations.

safety_changes: FAA issued General Notice (GENOT) on November 9, 1972, establishing new standards for civil certification, operation, and maintenance of military surplus jet airplanes
Enhanced pilot qualification requirements for surplus military aircraft operations, including mandatory checkout and recent pilot-in-command experience
FAA tightened rules on ex-military jet operations and experimental aircraft certification procedures

notes: Report dated March 28, 1973; NTSB AAR-73-6
Pilot had 3.5-7.3 hours total in Sabre; most jet experience in Lear Jet
Aircraft was ex-military F-86 surplus sold to private operator
Movie analysis provided precise altitude and attitude data for timeline
Visual illusions at Sacramento runway (vs Oakland) contributed to overrotation
Depth 'full': read key sections (synopsis, history, findings, probable cause, recommendations) plus Tests and Research section for detailed performance analysis

records.title: Air Inter 696

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses (French accident investigation authority)

records.summary: Air Inter Flight 696, a Vickers Viscount operating from Lyon-Bron to Clermont-Ferrand, crashed during approach in violent thunderstorm conditions. The aircraft encountered severe weather, with strong winds, turbulence, and lightning activity. Radio contact with ATC was lost while approaching Clermont-Ferrand Airport. The aircraft descended below safe altitude and struck Mont Picot in the Forez mountains at approximately 1,000 meters altitude, about 30 kilometers east of the airport and 10 kilometers from the intended landing point. The wreckage was found in the woods with the aircraft broken into three pieces. Sixty of 68 occupants were killed.
records.probable_cause: The accident resulted from a collision with mountainous terrain that occurred during night instrument approach in conditions of poor visibility and severe weather (violent thunderstorm). The crew announced being at the CF (Clermont-Ferrand) beacon vertical position when in fact they were displaced approximately 30 kilometers to the east. The radiocompas (radio compass/NDB) displayed an erroneous indication, and the crew did not detect the anomaly or verify their actual position using other navigation aids, notably the Moulins VOR radial. The crew's reliance on incorrect radionavigation information led to the aircraft following an approach path shifted 30 kilometers to the east. Contributing factors included severe turbulence, intense atmospheric precipitation creating electromagnetic interference with the radiocompas, and the crew's failure to properly validate navigation cross-checks despite unusual timing (more than 3 minutes early at CF beacon) (p. 4305-4410, 4309-4372, 6207-6230)

factors.evidence: Strong cold front moving west to east over Forez mountains; violent thunderstorm with severe turbulences marked on flight data recorder; low visibility conditions; atmospheric electrical activity creating localized electromagnetic discharge (p. 681-728, 3720-3732)
ATC did not provide sufficient cross-check of crew's reported position; crew reported being vertical at CF beacon when actually approximately 30 kilometers to the east (p. 4327-4342)

Crew announced CF passage with hesitation at 18:14 after being told to estimate arrival time; crew arrived more than 3 minutes early, yet crew did not detect this anomaly (p. 276-282, 3824-3850, 4337-4372)

Despite being in final descent phase with turbulent weather, crew did not verify position using other navigation aids such as Moulins VOR radial; presence of flight instructor may have created distraction (p. 4343-4353, 4373-4406)
Aircraft descended to approximately 1,000 meters altitude; this altitude was below safe minimums for instrument approach given mountainous terrain (p. 305-306, 388-389, 3916-3945)
Aircraft struck Mont Picot at 1,000 meters altitude; aircraft broke into three pieces (p. 1000-1100, 3371-3400)

events.text: Air Inter Flight 696Y departed Lyon-Bron airport on Friday October 27, 1972 at 17:48 UTC with 63 passengers (including 4 children) and 5 crew members on flight to Clermont-Ferrand in violent thunderstorm conditions

Initial contact with Marseille Control at 17:54 UTC; aircraft requested and received authorization to proceed southwest of AD beacon due to cumulus cloud formations; crew reported responding on transponder frequency, normal contact established
Aircraft reported passing AD beacon and turned left toward ASE report point; aircraft stabilized at flight level 100 just before 17:58 UTC as conditions remained turbulent

Aircraft reported passing ASE beacon at flight level 100 after approximately 10 minutes from takeoff; crew estimated CF (Clermont-Ferrand) arrival in 8 minutes based on position 36 nautical miles away
ATC proposed descent to lower flight level; crew responded 20 seconds before 18:09 that descent would begin in 3 minutes, with ATC confirming flight level 80 was available

Crew announced they were at CF vertical position (18:10:50 UTC) and beginning descent to flight level 80 in CF holding pattern, having announced position with hesitation and timing anomaly of more than 3 minutes advance on estimated traverse time

ATC confirmed descent request; crew responded affirming they were at CF vertical, had released flight level 100, and were descending through flight level 95; ATC confirmed flight level 80 was available
Aircraft closed with Marseille Control and announced flight level 60 in CF holding pattern; transfer made to Clermont-Ferrand approach frequency 125 MHz; continued descent in holding pattern

Clermont-Ferrand approach control authorized descent to flight level 50; reception reported very noisy due to atmospheric interference; low stratus clouds at 700 meters reported at airport with visibility 8 kilometers with continuous rain
Crew reported flight level 55 in descent, correcting moments later to flight level 65 in descent; aircraft position still reported as CF based on continuing radiocompas indication

Aircraft reported flight level 50 for further descent; received authorization to continue toward final approach altitude of 3,600 feet for ILS interception with instruction to call back in procedure turn
Aircraft reported in procedure turn for alignment on ILS; approach control authorized continuation and requested call back when established on ILS; crew responded OK

Aircraft continuing descent in procedure turn; atmospheric parasiting (electromagnetic interference) at high level in Noirétable region; strong cold front passage over Forez mountains causing severe turbulence with peaks of 1.8G recorded on flight data

Tower made final call to 696Y at 18:20:30 UTC with no response; aircraft impacted terrain at Mont Picot/La Faye forest at approximately 1,000 meters altitude in the Forez mountains at the boundary between Viscontat and Noirétable communes, approximately 30 kilometers east of intended landing position

After 18:20 and continued failures to contact aircraft, distress phase initiated at 18:30 UTC; Marseille Control was notified by Clermont-Ferrand control that aircraft had not established on ILS as expected

Wreckage discovered in the night of Friday to Saturday around 02:15 local time (01:15 UTC Saturday) after seven hours of search efforts in the La Faye forest; aircraft broken into three pieces at 1,000 meters altitude; 60 of 68 occupants killed (8 serious injuries reported as survivors)

recommendations.text: Examination of radiocompas reliability under conditions of severe meteorological phenomena such as thunderstorms with electromagnetic discharge in mountainous regions
Strengthened procedures for radionavigation cross-checks using VOR/DME and other independent navigation aids during approach in poor visibility conditions
Enhanced cockpit resource management and challenge procedures when navigation fixes show significant time anomalies or inconsistencies with calculated flight times
Improved aircraft approach procedures and minimum safe altitudes defined for mountainous regions with consideration of electromagnetic interference effects on radio equipment

notes: Read sections 2.1 Déroulement du vol (History of Flight, p. 147-340), 3.1-3.2 Analysis (p. 3483-4000), 3.4 Causes probables (Probable Causes, p. 4305-4410), 3.3 Conclusion (p. 6207-6230)
Extracted 16 events from detailed French narrative with specific times and aircraft states from flight data
Report is in French; key dates and times converted to UTC per report footnote
Identified radionavigation error and atmospheric interference as primary causal factors
All factor evidence includes page citations from report

records.title: United Air Lines 553
records.summary: A Boeing 737 approaching Chicago Midway was too high on descent at the outer marker beacon. The captain extended spoilers and steepened descent to 1,550 feet per minute, well above the normal 1,000 fpm. After leveling at minimum descent altitude with engines not advanced fully and spoilers still extended, the aircraft entered an aerodynamic stall. The stick shaker activated and continued sounding until impact into a residential neighborhood. The flight data recorder was inoperative due to maintenance failure.
records.probable_cause: The captain's failure to exercise positive flight management during the execution of a nonprecision approach, which culminated in a critical deterioration of airspeed into the stall regime where level flight could no longer be maintained (p. 32).

factors.evidence: The flight was slow in responding to ATC requests for speed reductions and to the descent clearance (p. 32). The aircraft crossed the outer marker about 700 feet above the published minimum crossing altitude (p. 32).
There was a breakdown in crew coordination during the most critical phase of the approach (p. 32). The first officer did not make the prescribed altitude callouts during the approach (p. 32).

The captain did not call for the final descent check until the aircraft had passed the outer marker; the distance from the outer marker to the runway was 3.3 nmi (p. 32). The flight spoilers were deployed to the flight detent position for the final descent from the Kedzie OM and remained in this position during the level-off at MDA (p. 32).
The sound of stickshaker activation could be heard on the CVR tape beginning at 14:27:03, about 22 seconds before impact (p. 6).

The aircraft descended below the overcast in a nose-high attitude with the sound of high engine power just before impact (p. 2). Several survivors reported the aircraft shuddered following a nose-up pitch change, with some estimating the nose rose at least 30 degrees (p. 7).
The aircraft crashed into residential area approximately 1.5 miles southeast of the approach end of Runway 31L at 14:27:25 CST, destroyed by impact and subsequent fire (p. 1).

events.text: Captain called for final descent check at 14:26:24, about 4 seconds after the Kedzie OM identifier ended (p. 6).

Chicago Approach Control cleared UA-553 to descend to 2,000 feet at 14:23:42, after issuing multiple speed reduction requests starting at 14:21:56 to reduce airspeed to 180 knots then to 160 knots (p. 5-6).
UA-553 reported passing the Kedzie Outer Marker inbound; tower controller advised they were number two on approach and would keep them advised (p. 6).
First officer called 'Ah, thousand feet'; less than 2 seconds later, stickshaker activation could be heard on CVR tape, indicating approach to stall (p. 6).
Tower controller issued missed approach clearance to UA-553: 'United five fifty-three execute a missed approach, make a left turn to a heading of one eight zero climb to two thousand' (p. 6).
Approach controller noticed radar target had drifted approximately 1/8 to 1/4 mile to the right of localizer centerline, disappearing from radarscope shortly thereafter (p. 6).
Aircraft crashed into residential area approximately 1.5 miles southeast of runway approach end, destroyed by impact and subsequent fire (p. 1-2).
CVR recording ended at 14:27:25; stickshaker sound had been audible for entire approximately 22-second period from initial stall warning (p. 6).

recommendations.text: Reassess and improve the methods used, both in flight manuals and in simulator or flight training, to familiarize flightcrews with the effects of spoilers on aircraft characteristics and stall warning devices.
Issue an advisory bulletin to alert pilots and operators to the hazards of the improper use of spoilers.

notes: History of Flight section read (p. 5-7)
Findings section read (p. 32-33)
Probable Cause section read (p. 32)
Recommendations section read (p. 33-34)
Events extracted from approach controller radar observations and CVR transcript
Times in CST per Note 1 (p. 6)

records.title: 1972 Chicago-O'Hare runway collision
records.summary: North Central Airlines Flight 575 (DC-9) collided with Delta Air Lines Flight 954 (CV-880) on Runway 27L at O'Hare International Airport during takeoff in fog with one-quarter mile visibility. The collision resulted from ATC communication errors and ambiguous holding clearance that led both aircraft crews to misunderstand their positions. Ten passengers on the DC-9 died in post-collision fire.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause was the failure of the traffic control system to ensure separation of aircraft during a period of restricted visibility (p. 20-21). This failure included: (1) the controller omitted a critical word which made his transmission to the Delta CV-880 ambiguous; (2) the controller did not use all available information to determine the location of the CV-880; and (3) the CV-880 flightcrew did not request clarification of the controller's communications (p. 20-21).

factors.evidence: Ground controller issued ambiguous holding clearance without specifying which of two similarly numbered runup pads to use, and did not hear 'inside the bridge' in the flightcrew's transmission (p. 6, 20).
Weather at O'Hare was ceiling indefinite 200 feet, sky obscured, with visibility one-quarter mile in fog (p. 4, 8). Airport traffic could not be observed visually from control tower (p. 20).
Delta Flight 954 was taxiing across Runway 27L when North Central Flight 575 was cleared for takeoff on that runway, resulting in collision during takeoff roll (p. 6-7, 20).
Fire broke out in aft part of DC-9 and cabin rapidly filled with smoke; ten passengers received fatal injuries (p. 4, 7, 20).

events.text: Flight 954 established radio communication with Chicago Approach Control at 17:23:10 CST (p. 5).
CAC controller informed all flights that parallel ILS approaches would be conducted to Runways 14L and 14R at 17:39:10 CST (p. 5).
O'Hare ground controller cleared Flight 575 to taxi to Runway 27L for departure at approximately 17:50 CST (p. 6).
Flight 954 landed on Runway 14L; reported clear of runway at 17:56:18 CST (p. 5).
Ground controller issued ambiguous holding clearance to Flight 954 at 17:57:29 CST, without clearly specifying which runup pad to use (p. 5-6).
Local controller cleared Flight 575 into takeoff position on Runway 27L at 17:58:52 CST; advised visibility was one-quarter mile (p. 6).
Flight 575 cleared for takeoff approximately 26 seconds after being positioned (p. 6).
Captain of Flight 575 reported beginning takeoff roll at 17:59:24 CST; FO was flying (p. 6).
DC-9 and CV-880 collided at Runway 27L and North-South taxiway at 18:00:08.7 CST at approximately 14 feet altitude (p. 1, 6-7).
Post-collision fire broke out in aft section of DC-9; cabin filled with smoke; ten passengers and two crew sustained injuries in DC-9 (p. 7).

recommendations.text: Standardize ASDE 'BRITE' equipment configurations and alignment techniques at three existing facilities (p. 34).
Do not proceed with 'BRITE' installation at other ASDE facilities until satisfactory operation achieved at existing three (p. 34).
Install improved ASDE 'BRITE' equipment first at three existing locations (p. 34).
Establish standard procedures for ASDE radar use and publish in Air Traffic Handbooks (p. 34).
Establish and publish taxi routes for arrival/departure aircraft during restricted visibility of 1/4 mile or less (p. 34).
Require pilots to obtain controller approval before crossing lighted runways in visibility of 1/4 mile or less (p. 35).
Amend certification rules to require tactile guidance, improved visual guidance to emergency exits, and better location indication in dark/smoke (p. 24-25).
Require flightcrews to report aircraft position on airport and controllers to read back when not verified by visual/radar (p. 25).
Require flightcrews to read back taxi clearances when visibility is less than 1/2 mile (p. 25).

notes: Sections read: History of Flights (p. 5-7), Findings (p. 20), Probable Cause (p. 20-21), Recommendations (p. 24-25, 34-35)
Ten events extracted with precise clock times, all new sentences from report
All recommendations from Appendix E with proper IDs

records.title: Eastern Air Lines 401

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Eastern Air Lines, Inc., L-1011, N310EA, Miami, Florida, December 29, 1972

location.name: Everglades, about 18 miles west-northwest of Miami International Airport, Florida

records.summary: On approach to Miami the nose gear down-and-locked light failed to illuminate. The crew abandoned the approach, climbed to 2,000 ft over the Everglades on autopilot and became absorbed in the indicator bulb and in checking the gear from the avionics bay. The autopilot altitude hold was inadvertently disengaged and the aircraft descended slowly and unnoticed in the dark until it struck the swamp. The gear had been down and locked all along; 101 of the 176 on board died.
records.probable_cause: The failure of the flightcrew to monitor the flight instruments during the final 4 minutes of flight, and to detect an unexpected descent soon enough to prevent impact with the ground. Preoccupation with a malfunction of the nose landing gear position indicating system distracted the crew's attention from the instruments and allowed the descent to go unnoticed.

factors.evidence: The entire crew became engaged with the burned-out nose gear indicator light and with visually checking the gear from the forward electronics bay.
The altitude hold mode was inadvertently disengaged, probably by a light force on the captain's control column, and the autopilot descended in control wheel steering mode.
The altitude alert chime sounded once at 1,750 ft and was not noticed; the autopilot mode annunciation and the split between the two autopilot channels made the mode change hard to detect.
No crew member monitored the flight instruments during the final four minutes.
No pilot was assigned to fly the aircraft while the others troubleshot the light, and duties were not delegated.
The crew believed they were still at 2,000 ft until seconds before impact.
Over the unlit Everglades at night there were no visual cues of the descent.
No minimum safe altitude warning capability existed; the controller saw an altitude readout of 900 ft but only asked how things were coming along.
The aircraft struck the Everglades in a shallow left bank while the crew were unaware of the descent.

events.text: On approach to runway 9L the landing gear is extended but the nose gear green down-and-locked light does not illuminate.
Captain discontinues the approach; tower instructs the flight to climb to 2,000 ft and turn west over the Everglades.
Autopilot engaged in altitude hold at 2,000 ft while the crew work on the indicator light.
First officer tries to remove and reseat the indicator lamp assembly, which has jammed; the captain and flight engineer join the effort.
Altitude hold is inadvertently disengaged, probably by pressure on the control column; the autopilot begins a slow descent in control wheel steering mode.
Flight engineer goes down into the forward electronics bay to check the nose gear visually through the viewing port; a company technician riding in the cockpit joins him.
Altitude alert chime sounds as the aircraft passes about 1,750 ft; no crew member reacts.
Miami approach controller, seeing a low altitude readout, asks how things are coming along; the crew reply that they would like to turn around and come back in.
First officer notices the altitude and says they did something to the altitude; the captain asks what.
First officer asks whether they are still at two thousand feet.
Captain exclaims, asking what is happening, as the radio altimeter warning sounds.
The left wingtip strikes the Everglades and the aircraft breaks up in the swamp about 18 miles west-northwest of the airport.

cvr.speaker: FO
cvr.text: We did something to the altitude.

cvr.speaker: FO
cvr.text: We're still at two thousand, right?

recommendations.text: Develop and install minimum safe altitude warning capability in terminal radar systems so controllers are alerted when an aircraft descends below a safe altitude.
recommendations.outcome: MSAW was implemented in ARTS terminal radar systems in the late 1970s.

recommendations.text: Require that autopilot mode changes and altitude hold disengagement be clearly annunciated and that altitude alerting be more conspicuous.
recommendations.outcome: L-1011 autopilot annunciation was modified.

records.summary: Pan Am Flight 806 departed Auckland on 30 January 1974 with 91 passengers and 10 crew for a flight to Los Angeles with stops at Pago Pago and Honolulu. records.title: Sierra Pacific Airlines Flight 802

location.name: White Mountains north slope, near Bishop, California

records.summary: Sierra Pacific Airlines Charter Flight 802, a Convair 340/440 carrying a movie production crew, crashed into a mountainside near Bishop, California during night VFR climb-out on March 13, 1974. All 36 occupants were killed. The National Transportation Safety Board was unable to determine the probable cause of the accident.
records.probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Board is unable to determine the probable cause of this accident. The reason why the flightcrew did not maintain a safe distance from hazardous terrain during night visual flight conditions could not be established. (p. 3, 18)

factors.evidence: It was an extremely dark night with no moon. Witnesses agreed the mountains to the east could not be seen against the sky during the night. Official sunset was at 1905 and astronomical twilight ended at 2026. The moon rose at 0104 on March 14. (p. 1, 7)

No specific climb-out procedures from Eastern Sierra Regional Airport (Bishop) existed. Pilots typically made initial right turn towards Bishop away from mountains. Flight maintenance a right turn pattern around the airport, believed to circle back over or near the BIH VOR and proceed outbound in an east-southeasterly direction. (p. 3, 7, 17)

No specific procedures are set forth in the Sierra Pacific Airlines Operation Manual for a climbout from the Bishop Airport. The consensus of company crews was to make an initial right turn toward Bishop regardless of runway used, but no formal procedures existed. (p. 8, 17)

Aircraft struck the northern slope of a mountain ridge at 6,100 feet elevation, 5.2 statute miles southeast of the Bishop Airport. Imprint marks showed aircraft was on heading of approximately 175 degrees magnetic with 25 degree right wing-down attitude at impact. (p. 7, 11)

events.text: Flight 802 departed the gate at approximately 20:20 with 36 persons on board (32 passengers and crew of 4). Aircraft taxied north toward runway 12.
At 20:21, Tonapah Flight Service Station records show the crew contacted the station and requested their IFR clearance be activated.
Aircraft took off on runway 12. Airport manager saw aircraft takeoff; after aircraft passed abeam of his position, a hangar blocked his view and he neither saw nor heard the aircraft again.
Crew contacted Tonapah FSS on Bishop radio frequency 122.6 MHz and reported they were off Bishop and climbing VFR over Bishop, awaiting clearance.

At 20:28:40, Tonapah FSS specialist received IFR clearance from Oakland Center and attempted to radio Flight 802. Contact could not be established. Specialist tried repeatedly but flight did not respond.

Several ground witnesses saw aircraft during the last few moments before crash, located near base of mountains east of airport. They observed green and white lights proceeding in southerly direction parallel to mountain range.

Witnesses observed aircraft for about 1 minute when they saw burst of flames and heard explosion. Witness about 2 miles southwest of airport heard large twin-engine aircraft pass nearly overhead just before the accident.
Aircraft struck foothill in the White Mountain range at 6,100 feet elevation, 5.2 statute miles southeast of Bishop Airport, at coordinates 37°19'57" north, 118°16'14" west.

At 20:36, Bishop Airport manager called Tonapah FSS and requested status of Flight 802, advising FSS of explosion and fire in White Mountains east of airport. FSS specialist assumed accident had occurred and initiated accident notification procedures.

recommendations.text: Establish specific VFR departure procedures for Bishop Airport that limit initial climb-out to proximity of airport during hours of darkness until minimum altitude and heading clearance of terrain are assured.
Require all terrain-constrained airports with night VFR operations to publish standard departure procedures specific to terrain avoidance.

Establish minimum lighting and visual cues at terrain-constrained airports to enhance terrain avoidance during night VFR operations, or restrict night VFR operations in mountainous areas without specific terrain avoidance procedures.

safety_changes: FAA issued guidance on development of standard instrument departure procedures (SIDs) for mountainous terrain airports.
Increased emphasis on formal VFR departure procedures at uncontrolled terrain-constrained airports.

notes: Sections read: Synopsis (p. 1), History of Flight (p. 2-5), Meteorological Information (p. 6), Aids to Navigation (p. 6-8), Aircraft Wreckage (p. 8-10), Analysis and Conclusions (p. 13-18), Recommendations (p. 18). Page extraction limited by OCR quality of 1974 report.
Eight events with clock times extracted from flight service station communications and witness observations.
Probable cause unsolved by NTSB; conclusions based on contributing factors and analysis of terrain features, weather, and procedures.
Report quality: Old NTSB report with moderate OCR errors; extracted information validated against multiple sections of report.

records.title: 1974 Norfolk mid-air collision
records.summary: An RAF Phantom FGR.2 flying at 300 feet on a low-level training route collided with a Piper Pawnee crop-spraying aircraft near Hilgay, Norfolk. The collision occurred at approximately 400 knots closing speed. The investigation found neither pilot saw the other aircraft in time to avoid collision, with the absence of coordination between military and civil low-flying activities being a significant contributing factor.
records.probable_cause: The accident occurred because neither pilot saw the other aircraft in time. A significant contributing feature was the absence of any system for co-ordinating military and civil low flying activities in the low flying areas and link routes. (p. 1)

factors.evidence: Neither of the pilots had seen the other aircraft in time to avoid collision (p. 1).
The view from the Phantom may have been obstructed by the canopy frame (p. 1).
Absence of any system for coordinating military and civil low flying activities in low flying areas and link routes (p. 1).
Collision occurred at closing speed of about 400 knots, leaving minimal time for the Pawnee pilot to assess and execute maneuver (p. 1).
At estimated height around 300 feet the Phantom struck Pawnee on right side near Hilgay, Pawnee disintegrated (p. 1).

events.text: Phantom departs RAF Coningsby for low-level navigation flight
Pawnee conducting crop spraying operations south of Downham Market
Pawnee completes spraying, begins northward return flight for refueling
Phantom flying low-level at 300 feet on standard training route near Hilgay at 420 knots
Pawnee returning northward at low altitude, neither aircraft in contact with ATC
Phantom pilot does not see Pawnee; Pawnee pilot does not see Phantom in time to avoid
Phantom at 300 feet strikes Pawnee on right side near Hilgay at closing speed of 400 knots
Pawnee disintegrates on impact; Phantom crashes 1 km away in inverted attitude

notes: Limited timeline data in summary report
4 events extracted from available information
Report focuses on coordination failure rather than operational details

records.title: TWA 841 (1974)

location.name: Ionian Sea, approximately 100 nautical miles west of Araxos, Greece

records.summary: TWA Flight 841, a Boeing 707-331B operating a scheduled international flight from Tel Aviv to New York via Athens and Rome, was destroyed by an explosive device detonated in the aft cargo compartment while cruising at 28,000 feet. The explosion disabled the aircraft's control systems, causing it to pitch up steeply, stall, and enter a death spiral from which it could not recover.
records.probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Board determines that the probable cause of this accident was the detonation of an explosive device within the aft cargo compartment of the aircraft which rendered the aircraft uncontrollable.

factors.evidence: An explosive device was detonated within the aft cargo compartment while the aircraft was cruising at 28,000 feet (p. 26, Finding 4).
The explosion disabled the control system of the aircraft, causing structural damage that made the aircraft uncontrollable (p. 26, Finding 5).
The explosive device was placed in the aft cargo compartment which contained baggage and cargo (p. 6).
The out-of-control aircraft executed a steep pitch-up followed by roll and descent, with apparent engine separation observed by witnesses before impact in the Ionian Sea (p. 7).

events.text: Flight 841 departs Tel Aviv 43 minutes late due to passenger security procedures with 105 passengers, 9 crew members
Flight 841 lands at Athens; 56 passengers deplane and baggage offloaded
Flight 841 departs Athens with 79 passengers after loading checked baggage, cargo, and mail
At 0930 UTC, TWA 841 reports level at Flight Level 280, last known radio transmission
Explosive device detonates in aft cargo compartment; aircraft becomes uncontrollable
At 0940 UTC, Pan Am Flight 110 observes aircraft at 11 o'clock position in steep climb attitude
Aircraft rolls left to steep descent with apparent engine separation observed
Aircraft crashes into Ionian Sea approximately 100 nautical miles west of Araxos; all 88 occupants killed

recommendations.text: Security measures for cargo compartments
International cargo security procedures
Enhanced luggage inspection protocols
Cargo compartment design improvements

safety_changes: Implementation of enhanced cargo screening and security procedures for international flights
Improved cargo compartment security measures and access controls
Standardization of explosive detection equipment at major airports
International aviation security standards strengthened following post-1974 reviews
