records.title: Eastern Air Lines 212

location.name: Cornfield near Charlotte Douglas International Airport, Charlotte, North Carolina

records.summary: Eastern Air Lines Flight 212, a DC-9-31 operating a scheduled flight from Charleston to Chicago via Charlotte, crashed in a cornfield 3.3 statute miles short of the runway threshold while attempting to land at Charlotte. The crew became distracted by non-operational conversation during the approach and lost altitude awareness, descending far below safe altitudes despite terrain warning alerts and altitude alert tones.
records.probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Board determines that the probable cause of the accident was the flight crew's lack of altitude awareness at critical points during the approach due to poor cockpit discipline in that the crew did not follow prescribed procedures.

factors.evidence: The crew's nearly total lack of altitude awareness during approach, despite multiple altitude alert tones and terrain warning system activation at 1,000 feet above ground (p. 19).
The pilot monitoring did not detect or call out the excessive descent rate, and required altitude callouts were not made at critical points (p. 20).

The aircraft descended through the final approach fix altitude of 1,800 feet more than 2 miles before the fix was reached, eventually crossing at only 1,350 feet, which was 450 feet below prescribed altitude (p. 20).
The aircraft struck small trees and then impacted a cornfield about 100 feet below airport elevation, broke up, and burst into flames (p. 8).

events.text: Flight 212 departed Charleston with 78 passengers and 4 crew members
ATIS information recorded on CVR indicating weather at Charlotte
Atlanta ARTCC clears flight to descend to 8,000 feet; autopilot disconnect recorded
Crew engaged in non-operational discussion and conversation on several non-operational subjects from 0723:23 through approach
Altitude alert tone sounds, aircraft approaching 3,000 feet
Terrain warning alert activated at 1,000 feet above ground (0732:41), aural warning sounded but was silenced
Second altitude alert at 2,750 feet (0731:54)
Captain identifies Carowinds Tower as approach landmark, becomes fixated on visual acquisition
Initial impact with trees and cornfield; aircraft destroyed by impact and fire (0733:58)

recommendations.text: Initiate ways and means to improve professional standards among pilots
Continue emphasis on improving professional conduct and cockpit discipline

safety_changes: Establishment of Sterile Cockpit Rule requiring flight crews to limit non-essential conversation below 10,000 feet
Enhanced emphasis on altitude awareness and callout procedures
Standardization of terrain warning system utilization and response procedures

notes: Sections read: History of Flight (lines 836-1600), Findings (lines 4169-4300), Probable Cause (lines 4312-4325), Recommendations (lines 4357-4370)
Events constructed from CVR timeline and FDR data in History of Flight section
Recommendations extracted from NTSB safety recommendation letters dated October 8, 1974

records.title: Northwest Airlines 6231

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Northwest Airlines, Inc., Boeing 727-251, N274US, Near Thiells, New York, December 1, 1974

route.from_name: New York John F. Kennedy International

location.name: Harriman State Park near Thiells and Stony Point, Rockland County, New York

records.summary: On an evening ferry flight from JFK to Buffalo with only three crew aboard, the 727 climbed in cloud and icing with the pitot heat switched off. The pitot probes iced over, so the airspeed and Mach indications rose with altitude; the crew, believing the airplane was accelerating, reduced power and raised the nose until an overspeed warning sounded at 24,800 feet. They pulled up further, the airplane stalled, and the stick shaker and buffet were misread as Mach buffet. The airplane entered a spiral dive and struck the ground about 83 seconds later.
records.probable_cause: The loss of control of the aircraft because the flightcrew failed to recognize and correct the aircraft's high-angle-of-attack, low-speed stall and its descending spiral. The stall was precipitated by the flightcrew's improper reaction to erroneous airspeed and Mach indications which had resulted from a blockage of the pitot heads by atmospheric icing. Contrary to standard operational procedures, the flightcrew had not activated the pitot head heaters.

factors.evidence: The pitot heads iced over during the climb in cloud because the pitot heat switches had not been turned on.
Contrary to standard operating procedures the crew did not activate the pitot head heaters before takeoff; the checklist item was missed.
The airplane climbed through cloud in icing conditions, which produced the ice that blocked the unheated pitot heads.
With the pitot heads blocked and static ports open the indicated airspeed and Mach increased with altitude, reaching more than 400 knots indicated while the airplane was actually slowing.
The overspeed warning sounded at 24,800 feet as the erroneous indications passed the limit speed, confirming the crew's belief that the airplane was too fast.
The crew interpreted the stick shaker and pre-stall buffet as Mach buffet and continued to pitch up and reduce power.
The stick shaker activated as the airplane approached the stall but was misread by the crew.
The crew did not cross-check the implausible combination of high indicated airspeed, high pitch attitude, reduced power and a climb rate the airplane could not have sustained.
The report found crews were not adequately trained to recognize erroneous airspeed indications or the stall characteristics of the 727 at high altitude.
There was no warning to alert the crew that pitot heat was off; the NTSB recommended a pitot heat off indication.
The flight was at night in cloud, so the crew had no external visual references to contradict the instruments.
The airplane stalled at 24,800 feet in a nose-high, low-speed condition.
The airplane entered a descending spiral from which the crew did not recover, striking the ground in Harriman State Park.

events.text: The empty 727 departs JFK on a ferry flight to Buffalo with the captain, first officer and flight engineer aboard; the pitot heat switches are off.
The airplane climbs through cloud in icing conditions at night; ice begins to accumulate in the unheated pitot heads.
Passing about 16,000 feet the pitot heads are blocked; from here the indicated airspeed and Mach rise as the airplane climbs, although true airspeed is falling.
Believing the airplane is accelerating, the crew raise the nose and reduce power; the rate of climb increases to well above normal and the crew remark on the apparently excellent performance.
Indicated airspeed passes 340 knots and continues rising as the airplane climbs through 23,000 feet at a high pitch attitude and decreasing true airspeed.
The overspeed warning (clacker) sounds at about 24,800 feet with the airspeed indicators reading about 405 knots; the crew pull the nose up further to slow down.
The stick shaker activates and the airplane buffets; the crew interpret the buffet as Mach buffet consistent with the overspeed warning.
The airplane stalls at 24,800 feet in a nose-high attitude and rolls off into a descending spiral to the right.
The crew attempt to recover, still treating the situation as an overspeed; the captain calls to pull up as the descent rate exceeds 15,000 feet per minute.
In the spiral dive the airplane experiences high load factors and the horizontal stabilizer and elevator structure are overstressed.
The airplane strikes wooded terrain in Harriman State Park near Thiells, about 83 seconds after the stall began, and is destroyed; all three crew die.

recommendations.text: Require a warning or indication in the cockpit of transport airplanes when pitot heat is not on, or require pitot heat to be on automatically whenever the airplane is in flight.
recommendations.outcome: Later transport-category designs include pitot heat off caution lights or automatic probe heating.

recommendations.text: Require that air carrier training programs include recognition of and response to erroneous airspeed and Mach indications, using attitude, power and altitude cross-checks.
recommendations.outcome: Unreliable airspeed procedures were added to airline manuals and training.

recommendations.text: Ensure crews are trained to distinguish stall buffet and stick shaker warning from Mach buffet, and emphasize stall recognition and recovery at high altitude.
Review checklist design so that pitot heat and other critical anti-ice items are checked before takeoff in a way that is not easily omitted.

safety_changes: Boeing 727 operators revised checklists and flight manuals to emphasize pitot heat and added guidance on recognizing erroneous airspeed indications.
Pitot heat off warning annunciations became standard on subsequent transport airplane designs.
Unreliable airspeed and pitch-and-power procedures became a standard element of airline training, later reinforced by the Birgenair 301, Aeroperú 603 and Air France 447 accidents.

notes: Local date 1974-12-01 is used; in UTC the accident occurred on 1974-12-02.

t0 is set to the overspeed warning at about 19:24:42 EST because the onset of the erroneous climb cannot be pinned to an instant; that clock time and the 83-second duration of the descent are as recalled from the report and should be verified.

Altitudes at which the pitot heads blocked (about 16,000 feet) and of the stall (24,800 feet) and the maximum indicated airspeed (about 405 knots) are as recalled from the report; intermediate values are approximate.
No CVR excerpts are quoted; the crew's remarks are paraphrased as crew speech events.
Aircraft MSN and exact JT8D variant are omitted because they are not recalled with confidence; the report is not available online as a deep link so the NTSB home page is cited.

records.title: TWA Flight 514

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report—Trans World Airlines, Inc. Boeing 727-231, N54328

records.summary: TWA Flight 514, a Boeing 727 diverted from Washington National Airport to Dulles due to high crosswinds, was vectored for a VOR/DME approach to runway 12. At 1104 EST, while 44 nautical miles from the airport, the crew was cleared for the approach without altitude restrictions. The captain misinterpreted the clearance and descended to 1,800 feet, the final approach fix altitude, before the aircraft reached the intermediate approach fix at Round Hill. The aircraft impacted Mount Weather at 1,670 feet elevation at 11:09:22 EST, killing all 92 occupants.
records.probable_cause: The crew's decision to descend to 1,800 feet before the aircraft had reached the approach segment where that minimum altitude applied. The crew's decision to descend was a result of inadequacies and lack of clarity in the air traffic control procedures which led to a misunderstanding on the part of the pilots and of the controllers regarding each other's responsibilities during operations in terminal areas under instrument meteorological conditions. Nevertheless, the examination of the plan view of the approach chart should have disclosed to the captain that a minimum altitude of 1,800 feet was not a safe altitude.

factors.evidence: Crew descended to 1,800 feet before reaching Round Hill intersection where this altitude was authorized (p. 2-4).
Controller issued approach clearance at 44 nm without altitude restrictions; terminology 'cleared for approach' was ambiguous (p. 25-28).
Flight was not classified as radar arrival despite receiving radar service, so altitude restrictions not provided per 7110.8C procedures (p. 27).
Approach chart profile view did not depict intermediate fix Round Hill or its minimum altitudes, only showing 6 DME fix and final approach fix (p. 13).
Aircraft impacted west slope of Mount Weather at 1,670 feet elevation at approximately 230 knots (p. 4).

events.text: Flight reported level at 7,000 feet; cleared for VOR/DME approach to runway 12
Captain reviewed field elevation, minimum descent altitude of 1,800 feet, and final approach fix; announced 1,800 feet was 'the bottom'
First officer commented on altitude fluctuations and bouncing instrument panel
Captain noted minimum altitude to Round Hill was 3,400 feet but discussed with crew that flight was authorized to descend to 1,800 feet
Altitude alert horn sounded at 1,800 feet; captain stated 'I had ground contact a minute ago'
Altitude alert sounded again; first officer mentioned power and captain noted high sink rate
Radio altimeter warning horn sounded (500 feet above terrain)
Captain commanded 'Get some power on'
Aircraft impacted west slope of Mount Weather at 1,670 feet elevation, heading 120 degrees magnetic, approximately 230 knots

cvr.speaker: PF
cvr.text: I hate the altitude jumping around

cvr.speaker: PM
cvr.text: According to this dumb sheet it says thirty-four hundred to Round Hill --- is our minimum altitude

cvr.speaker: PM
cvr.text: I had ground contact a minute ago

recommendations.text: Issue a notice to all operators of air carrier aircraft in terminal areas to ensure that pilots understand the meaning of 'cleared for approach' and that altitude restrictions will be provided
Develop and implement a standardized lexicon of air traffic control words and phrases to be used by all controllers and pilots in the National Airspace System
Establish procedures requiring controllers to provide altitude restrictions when issuing approach clearances to aircraft operating on unpublished routes
Modify approach charts to depict all minimum altitudes associated with approach procedures on both plan and profile views
Mandate installation of ground proximity warning systems on all air carrier aircraft by December 1975

dissent.position: The flight was a radar arrival and should have received altitude protection from ATC. The failure of the controller to issue altitude restrictions in accordance with 7110.8C paragraph 1360, combined with the captain's failure to adhere to minimum sector altitude, was the probable cause.

safety_changes: Ground Proximity Warning System (GPWS) mandated on all air carrier aircraft by December 1975
FAA revised 14 CFR 91 regarding pilot responsibilities after receiving clearance for nonprecision approach
FAA established Aviation Safety Reporting Program for incident identification
FAA revised air traffic control procedures to provide altitude restrictions during nonprecision instrument approaches
ARTS III altitude deviation warning system installed at terminal radar facilities

notes: Read sections: synopsis (p. 1-2), history of flight (p. 3-5), analysis and conclusions (p. 25-40), probable cause and findings (p. 25-40), recommendations (p. 41-42)
Full CVR transcript analyzed; altitude alerts and crew decision-making clearly documented
Detailed timeline constructed from FDR data and CVR correlations
Two NTSB members formally dissented on probable cause analysis
This accident led to major changes in ATC procedures and CFIT prevention systems

records.title: Golden West Airlines Flight 261

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report: Golden West Airlines, Inc., De Havilland DHC-6, N6383 and CessnAir Aviation, Inc., Cessna 150, N11421, Whittier, California, January 9, 1975

aircraft.type: de Havilland Canada DHC-6 Twin Otter

records.operator: Golden West Airlines (Twin Otter); CessnAir Aviation (Cessna 150)
records.summary: Golden West Airlines Flight 261 (De Havilland Twin Otter N6383) and a Cessna 150 (N11421) collided in flight near Whittier, California on January 9, 1975. The Twin Otter carried 10 passengers and 2 crew; the Cessna carried an instructor and student pilot. Both aircraft were destroyed, with 14 fatalities. Neither flight crew saw the other aircraft in sufficient time to avoid the collision.
records.probable_cause: The failure of both flightcrews to see the other aircraft in sufficient time to initiate evasive action. The ability of both crews to detect the other aircraft in time to avoid a collision was reduced because of the position of the sun (9 degrees above the western horizon), the closure angle of the aircraft, and the necessity for the Twin Otter's flightcrew to acquire visual contact with radar-reported traffic directly in front of them.

factors.evidence: The sun was positioned 9 degrees above the western horizon at azimuth 236 degrees (south of west), directly between the Twin Otter pilots and the Cessna, making it difficult or impossible to see the Cessna against the backdrop of the setting sun (p. 14).
The Twin Otter pilots were attempting to sight a reported helicopter traffic directly in front of them, which limited their visual search to a narrow sector ahead of the aircraft (p. 14).

Ground witnesses stated that neither aircraft made any abrupt evasive maneuvers prior to the collision, indicating neither flightcrew saw the other aircraft in sufficient time to attempt evasive action (p. 11).

The Cessna 150, not equipped with a transponder, was not observed on approach control radar because its track was tangential to the radar antenna, causing its return to be cancelled by the moving target indicator (MTI) circuitry. Flight test confirmed no primary return on controller's display (p. 13).

The Cessna struck the left side of the Twin Otter at an approximate 90-degree angle just back of the large plane's cockpit, causing a midair breakup with separation of a wing from the Twin Otter's fuselage (p. 11).

events.text: Golden West Airlines Flight 261 (Twin Otter N6383) departed Ontario International Airport on VFR flight plan to Los Angeles with 10 passengers and 2 crew
Twin Otter contacted LAX arrival radar, reported over Rose Hills, 23 nmi east of airport
Arrival controller advised Twin Otter of traffic 5.5 nmi in front, climbing from 1500 to 3000 ft (police helicopter on VFR flight)
Twin Otter crew acknowledged: "Two sixty one, we'll do it."
Controller transmitted advisory that helicopter was now at their 1130 position, 3 miles northbound. No response from Twin Otter.
Midair collision: Cessna 150 N11421 struck the left side of Twin Otter N6383 at approximately 90-degree angle at 2,200 ft, near Whittier. Both aircraft broke up in the air.

Both aircraft destroyed by collision and subsequent ground impact, with wreckage scattered over 8 to 10 city block area in Whittier. Falling debris caused substantial damage to houses and lawns but no injuries to persons on the ground.

notes: Sections read: Synopsis (p. 4), History of Flight (p. 5-10), Aircraft Information (p. 7), Meteorological Information (p. 7), Analysis and Conclusions (p. 12-15), Findings and Probable Cause (p. 15)
Collision geometry study showed aircraft on collision course with 174 knot closing speed
Sun position 9° above horizon, 236° azimuth (south of west), directly between Twin Otter pilots and Cessna
Cessna positioned 57° right of Twin Otter, outside normal scan pattern
Cessna not equipped with transponder, causing radar detection failure due to tangential effect
Twin Otter crew distracted by helicopter traffic advisory immediately before collision
No CVR transcript available in public report
No recommendations issued in this report

records.title: Eastern Air Lines 66
records.summary: Eastern Air Lines Flight 66 descended through a strong thunderstorm on ILS approach to JFK runway 22L. The aircraft encountered severe wind shear with downdrafts causing high descent rate. Despite warnings of severe wind shear from preceding aircraft, the crew relied on visual references in heavy rain rather than instruments, and did not recognize dangerous descent rate until impact was inevitable. Aircraft struck non-frangible approach light towers 2400 feet from runway threshold, caught fire and came to rest on Rockaway Boulevard. Of 124 aboard, 113 died.
records.probable_cause: The aircraft's encounter with adverse winds associated with a very strong thunderstorm located astride the ILS localizer course, which resulted in a high descent rate into the nonfrangible approach light towers. The flightcrew's delayed recognition and correction of the high descent rate were probably associated with their reliance upon visual cues rather than on flight instrument references. However, the adverse winds might have been too severe for a successful approach and landing even had they relied upon and responded rapidly to the indications of the flight instruments. Contributing to the accident was the continued use of runway 22L when it should have become evident to both air traffic control personnel and the flightcrew that a severe weather hazard existed along the approach path. (p. 39-40)

factors.evidence: Between 500 and 400 feet, the headwind diminished about 5 knots; at 400 feet, the downdraft increased to about 21 fps, and the headwind decreased about 15 knots within 4 seconds. (p. 41)
A very strong thunderstorm was located along the localizer course near the middle marker when Eastern 66 approached the airport. (p. 41)

Flightcrew probably did not recognize the deviation below the normal approach path until a high descent rate had developed because of their reliance on visual references which were obscured by heavy rain and low visibility. (p. 41)

At 400 feet the captain stated he had the approach lights in sight and directed the first officer to remain on instrument references; however, first officer probably began transitioning to visual references he would need to complete the approach. (p. 41)

Captain was aware of Eastern 902's wind shear report but continued approach; neither pilots nor air traffic control took action to discontinue approaches to runway 22L or change landing runway despite thunderstorm hazards visible on approach path. (p. 42)
Aircraft struck approach light towers approximately 2400 feet from runway threshold in heavy rain. Impact was recorded on CVR at 16:05:11.4. (p. 4-5)

events.text: Eastern 66 contacted Kennedy approach control and was sequenced into pattern for runway 22L.
Southgate arrival controller broadcast that weather had changed to IFR with 2 miles visibility, very light rain showers and haze.

Flying Tiger Line Flight 161 captain reported to local controller: severe wind shear on final approach, highly recommending runway change to northwest. Controller did not respond appropriately to warning. (p. 5)

Eastern Air Lines Flight 902 reported to final vector controller severe wind shear pulling aircraft right and down with 1,500 feet per minute rate of descent at 250 feet altitude, requiring takeoff power and go-around. (p. 5)
Captain of Eastern 66 heard Eastern 902's wind shear report but decided to continue approach. First officer at 16:02:50 said 'Gonna keep a pretty healthy margin on this one.' (p. 6-7)
Eastern 66 contacted Kennedy tower local controller who cleared flight to land at 16:03:44. Captain asked about braking action.

While penetrating thunderstorm between 600 and 500 feet, aircraft encountered increased headwind of about 15 knots and downdraft of about 16 feet per second. Between 500 and 400 feet, headwind diminished 5 knots but downdraft increased to 21 fps and headwind decreased 15 knots in 4 seconds. (p. 41)

At 400 feet captain stated approach lights were in sight and directed first officer to remain on instruments; however, first officer was transitioning to visual references needed to complete landing. Aircraft began to descend rapidly below glideslope due to downdraft and decreased headwind. (p. 41)

Aircraft struck first approach light tower about 1,200 feet southwest of middle marker, then struck several more towers. Aircraft caught fire and came to rest on Rockaway Boulevard. Impact recorded on CVR at 16:05:11.4. Both flight attendants reported aircraft rolled left with engine power increase, then rolled upright and rocked back and forth before impact.

recommendations.text: Conduct a research program to define and classify the level of flight hazard of thunderstorms using specific criteria for the severity of a thunderstorm and the magnitude of change of the wind speed components measured as a function of distance along an airplane's departure or approach flight track and establish operational limitations based upon these criteria. (p. 43)

Expedite the program to develop and install equipment which would facilitate the detection and classification, by severity, of thunderstorms within 5 nautical miles of the departure of threshold ends of active runways at airports having precision instrument approaches. (p. 43)

Install equipment capable of detecting variations in the speed of the longitudinal, lateral, and vertical components of the winds as they exist along the projected takeoff and approach flightpaths within 1 nautical mile of the ends of active runways which serve air carrier aircraft. (p. 43)

Require inclusion of the wind shear penetration capability of an airplane as an operational limitation in the airplane's operations manual, and require that pilots apply this limitation as a criterion for the initiation of a takeoff from, or an approach to, an airport where equipment is available to measure the severity of a thunderstorm or the magnitude of change in wind velocity. (p. 43)

As an interim action, install equipment capable of measuring and transmitting to tower operators the speed and direction of the surface wind in the immediate vicinity of all runway ends and install lighted windsocks near to the side of the runway, approximately 1,000 feet from the ends, at airports serving air carrier operations. (p. 43)

Develop and institute procedures whereby approach controllers, tower controllers, and pilots are provided timely information regarding the existence of thunderstorm activity near to departure or approach flightpaths. (p. 44)
Revise appropriate air traffic control procedures to specify that the location and severity of thunderstorms be considered in the criteria for selecting active runways. (p. 44)
Modify or expand air traffic controller training programs to include information concerning the effect that winds produced by thunderstorms can have on an airplane's flightpath control. (p. 44)

Modify initial and recurrent pilot training programs and tests to require that pilots demonstrate their knowledge of the low-level wind conditions associated with mature thunderstorms and of the potential effects these winds might have on an airplane's performance. (p. 44)

Expedite the program to develop, in cooperation with appropriate Government agencies and industry, typical models of environmental winds associated with mature thunderstorms which can be used for demonstration purposes in pilot training simulators. (p. 44)

Place greater emphasis on the hazards of low-level flight through thunderstorms and on the effects of wind shear encounter in the Accident Prevention Program for the benefit of general aviation pilots. (p. 44)

Expedite the research to develop equipment and procedures which would permit a pilot to transition from instrument to visual references without degradation of vertical guidance during the final segment of an instrument approach. (p. 44)
Expedite the research to develop an airborne detection device which will alert a pilot to the need for rapid corrective measures as an airplane encounters a wind shear condition. (p. 44)
Expedite the development of a program leading to the production of accurate and timely forecasts of wind shear in the terminal area. (p. 45)

notes: Read History of Flight section (p. 4-8) with detailed timeline and wind shear reports
Read Findings section (p. 41-42) with 22 numbered findings including specific wind shear measurements
Read Probable Cause section (p. 39-40)
Read Recommendations section (p. 43-45) with 14 numbered recommendations
Extracted 8+ events with specific clock times and meteorological data from report
Wind shear measurements quantified: 15 knot headwind increase, 21 fps downdraft, 15 knot headwind loss in 4 seconds

records.title: Wien Air Alaska Flight 99
records.summary: Wien Air Alaska Flight 99, a Fairchild F-27B, conducted multiple missed approaches to Gambell in fog and instrument conditions on August 30, 1975. During the final approach attempt following several go-arounds, the aircraft descended below minimum safe altitude and struck Sevuokuk Mountain near Gambell, killing the captain, first officer, and eight passengers. The NTSB determined the accident was caused by improper IFR operation and failure to adhere to prescribed instrument approach procedures.
records.probable_cause: Improper IFR operation and failure to adhere to instrument approach procedures. The airplane collided with a mountain on a missed approach to landing after multiple missed approaches. The crew descended below safe altitude in instrument conditions when the prescribed procedure required them to maintain 2,800 feet minimum altitude until establishing visual contact.

factors.evidence: Fog was prevalent in Gambell area; ceiling estimated 400 feet (p. 4).
Crew failed to adhere to instrument approach procedures after multiple missed approaches (p. 5).
Aircraft impacted Sevuokuk Mountain at 424 feet elevation (p. 6).

events.text: Wien Air Alaska Flight 99 departed Savoonga for Gambell with fog prevalent in area.
Crew discussed strategies to land at Gambell despite fog and unsafe weather conditions.
After several missed approaches, crew flew north over Gambell community and turned east.
Aircraft turned south after passing north of Gambell, passed over Troutman Lake and continued southbound.
Plane impacted Sevuokuk Mountain at 424 feet elevation; broke apart and caught fire with 10 fatalities.

recommendations.text: Develop operational procedures for precision approaches in low visibility conditions in remote areas
Enhance pilot training requirements for instrument approaches in marginal weather

safety_changes: Enhanced pilot training on strict adherence to instrument approach procedures
Implementation of minimum altitude enforcement procedures for remote field approaches

notes: NTSB report AAR-76-1 examined multiple missed approach procedures
Fog conditions prevented visual contact throughout approach
32 occupants with 22 survivors

records.title: Overseas National Airways 032

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report

records.summary: During takeoff roll at approximately 100 knots, a large flock of gulls rose from the runway directly in front of the DC-10. Bird ingestion into the right engine caused an uncontained engine failure that ruptured landing gear tires, disabled the number 2 hydraulic system, and partially disabled spoilers and landing gear brakes. The crew initiated a rejected takeoff but the aircraft did not decelerate normally, veered left toward a taxiway, and ran off the runway. The aircraft was destroyed by intense post-crash fire with all 139 occupants surviving.
records.probable_cause: Bird ingestion into right engine resulting in uncontained engine failure that ruptured landing gear tires and disabled hydraulic system, combined with wet runway reducing braking effectiveness, contributing to runway excursion. The disintegration and subsequent fire in the No. 3 engine when it ingested a large number of sea gulls was the primary cause. Following the disintegration, the aircraft failed to decelerate effectively because: (1) The No. 3 hydraulic system was inoperative, which caused the loss of the No. 2 brake system and braking torque was reduced 50 percent; (2) the No. 3 engine thrust reverser was inoperative; (3) at least three tires disintegrated; (4) the No. 3 system spoiler panels on each wing could not deploy; and (5) the runway surface was wet. The bird-control program at John F. Kennedy Airport did not effectively control the bird hazard on the airport, and the Federal Aviation Administration and the General Electric Company failed to consider the effects of rotor imbalance on the abradable epoxy shroud material when the engine was tested for certification. (p. 2247-2270)

factors.evidence: During takeoff roll at about 100 knots, a flock of approximately 100 sea gulls rose from the runway and separated then grouped in front of the aircraft; crew heard one to three explosions or bangs as birds struck the aircraft (p. 704-715)

Bird strikes damaged the fan blades in the No. 3 engine causing rotor imbalance; damage to the fan assembly resulted in fan-booster stage blades rubbing on epoxy microballoon shroud material; pulverized material entered the HPC area, ignited, and caused the compressor case to separate; fire erupted in the right wing and pylon simultaneously with the breakup of No. 3 engine (p. 2159-2185)

The No. 3 hydraulic system was inoperative following the engine failure, which caused loss of the No. 2 brake system (powered by No. 3 hydraulic) with braking torque reduced 50 percent, and the No. 3 system spoiler panels on each wing could not deploy (p. 2254-2260, 738-740)
The runway surface was wet, reducing braking effectiveness and contributing to the inability to decelerate normally (p. 2261)
At least three tires on the landing gear disintegrated due to the uncontained engine failure, further impairing deceleration (p. 2258-2259)

The FAA and General Electric Company failed to consider the effects of rotor imbalance on the abradable epoxy shroud material during certification; two factory development engines with modified rub shroud material retained structural integrity when subjected to 122,000 gram-inches of rotor imbalance (p. 2177-2179, 2234-2237)

Despite rejected takeoff procedures with thrust reversers and heavy braking, the aircraft could not be stopped on runway 13R; it veered left and left the paved surface before entering taxiway Z, coming to rest about 135 feet right of the taxiway centerline (p. 800-809, 979-980)

Fire erupted in the right wing and pylon simultaneously with the engine breakup; massive quantities of fuel were released into the fire when the right wing fuel tank was fractured; intense post-crash fire destroyed the aircraft (p. 2184-2185, 2200-2207)

events.text: ONA Flight 032, DC-10-30 (N1032F), departed gate at JFK on ferry flight to Jeddah with intermediate stop at Frankfurt; IFR computer-stored flight plan with captain, first officer, flight engineer, and observer on flight deck (p. 672-674)
Flight 032 entered runway 13R (14,572 feet long, 150 feet wide) and started takeoff roll; first portion of takeoff roll was normal and aircraft accelerated as expected (p. 700-701)

As DC-10 accelerated on ground at around 100 knots, a flock of approximately 100 sea gulls rose from the runway, separated, and then grouped directly in front of the aircraft; captain alerted crew to watch the EGT (exhaust gas temperature) (p. 704-710)

Crew heard birds strike the aircraft and recalled one to three explosions or bangs; captain immediately began procedures to reject takeoff with thrust levers to idle, thrust reversal of engines, and application of heavy braking (p. 712-716, 718-719)

Master warning and master caution lights appeared; as engines went into reverse thrust, flight engineer stated they had lost No. 3 engine; Nos. 1 and 2 engines attained normal reverse thrust (p. 720-726)
Flight engineer noticed No. 2 brake system pressure had dropped to zero (No. 3 hydraulic system failure); No. 1 brake system pressure remained normal with 3,000 lbs (p. 727-732)

Fire-warning light illuminated on captain's glare shield; fire lights on fire handle and fuel control lever illuminated for No. 3 engine; first officer and flight engineer attempted to shut down No. 3 engine (p. 742-749)

Aircraft seemed to decelerate effectively initially but rate of deceleration decreased; crew believed aircraft could be guided onto taxiway Z without striking blast fence; however during turn aircraft left paved surface before entering taxiway (p. 800-804)

Aircraft proceeded northeast and stopped on shoulder of taxiway Z at approximately 40 knots; cockpit was shaken violently as aircraft rolled to stop; crew believed right gear had collapsed and did not initially know aircraft was on fire (p. 805-813)
Right wing was ablaze; first officer opened right front cockpit window and saw fire on right wing; cockpit door was opened and black smoke could be seen in cabin (p. 823-826)

Flight engineer pulled fire handles for Nos. 1 and 2 engines; captain closed engine fuel shutoff levers for these engines before leaving cockpit; three flight crew members exited through right front cockpit window down escape rope; observer and all passengers evacuated (p. 815-829)

recommendations.text: Require immediate retest of the General Electric CF6 engine to demonstrate its compliance with the complete bird ingestion criteria of AC 33-1A.
Require that any engine modifications necessary to comply with the bird ingestion criteria of AC 33-1A be incorporated into all newly manufactured CF6 engines.
Require that any engine modifications necessary to comply with the bird ingestion criteria of AC 33-1A be incorporated into all CF6 engines in service.
Until the CF6 engine is modified, require that a bird patrol sweep runways at all airports which have recognized bird problems and are served by CF6-powered aircraft.
Advise all operators, domestic and foreign, of CF6 engines of the catastrophic consequences of foreign objects damage and the need for appropriate caution to avoid such damage.

Amend 14 CFR 33.77 to increase the maximum number of birds in the various size categories required to be ingested into turbine engines with large inlets, consistent with birds ingested during service experience of these engines.

safety_changes: Improved bird control programs at major airports
Enhanced engine certification requirements for bird ingestion
Revised aircraft design standards for hydraulic redundancy

notes: Report sections read: History of Flight, Findings, Probable Cause, Recommendations, Wreckage and Impact Information, Meteorological Information
Multiple events with detailed narrative extracted from OCR text with specific actions and timings
CVR tape was severely burned and not usable; FDR data usable up to 168 knots indicated airspeed
Ten distinct events documented with actor types and factor associations
Six numbered FAA safety recommendations issued (A-76-59 through A-76-64)
Largest commercial airliner destroyed by bird strike at time of accident
All 139 occupants survived despite aircraft destruction

records.title: Graham Hill plane crash

agencies.name: Air Accidents Investigation Branch
agencies.report_title: Report on the accident at Arkley golf course, Arkley, Hertfordshire, on 29 November 1975

location.name: Arkley Golf Course, Arkley, Barnet, London

records.summary: Piper PA-23-250D Aztec N6645Y crashed near Arkley, London, on 29 November 1975 at 21:29 GMT during a visual contact approach to Elstree Airfield in thick fog with visibility of 800-1000 metres. The aircraft was 3 nautical miles from Elstree when it struck trees at 458 feet elevation and crashed. The pilot had descended prematurely, likely mistaking ground lights in the fog and underestimating his distance from the airfield.
records.probable_cause: The pilot descended the aircraft prematurely due to misidentification of ground features and lights in thick fog, likely mistaking the lights of Barnet for Boreham Wood and believing he was closer to Elstree aerodrome than he actually was.

factors.evidence: Thick fog prevailed at the accident site with visibility of 50-100 metres; Elstree visibility reported as 800 metres during approach (p. 2-3).
Accident occurred at 21:29 hrs during a nighttime approach, removing external visual references and making ground lights more prominent (p. 2).
The pilot likely mistook lights of Barnet for Boreham Wood and the dark Arkley Golf Course for the unlit area next to Elstree airfield, believing himself closer to landing than actually was (p. 11).
Aircraft descended to 458 feet amsl in fog without sufficient visual references to identify terrain features; cloud base was reported as 300 feet agl (p. 3).
Aircraft struck tree tops at 458 feet elevation 3 nautical miles east of Elstree airfield and descended further, colliding with trees and ground with all six occupants killed instantly (p. 2).

events.text: Aircraft departed Le Castellet aerodrome with IFR flight plan filed for Elstree with Luton alternate
Contacted London Air Traffic Control Centre; weather report for Elstree obtained: visibility 2000 metres, cloud base 300 feet agl (p. 2)
Descended to 4000 feet; informed visibility at Elstree had decreased to 800 metres (p. 2)
Aircraft reached 1500 feet on approach to Elstree; 4 nautical miles east of runway; pilot given discretion for further descent (p. 2)
Pilot believed he was in contact with Elstree tower and called 'finals'; radar showed aircraft 2.75 nm from Elstree (p. 2)
Aircraft struck trees at 458 feet elevation on Arkley Golf Course, 3 nm east of Elstree; caught fire and was completely destroyed; all six occupants killed instantly (p. 2)

recommendations.text: Consideration should be given to the publication of recommended aerodrome operating minima for non-public transport flights at all airfields in the United Kingdom where it is reasonably practicable to do so

notes: Read key sections: synopsis (p. 1-2), aircraft and pilot information (p. 3-8), analysis including premature descent hypothesis (p. 10-11), and findings/recommendations (p. 13-14)
Report uncertain about exact cause but probability of premature descent due to visual misidentification is strong
Pilot's ratings had expired; aircraft was unregistered but properly maintained

records.title: Alaska Airlines 60
records.summary: Flight 60 departed Juneau and established an ILS approach to Ketchikan under low cloud ceilings and low visibility due to light snow and fog. The captain abandoned the precision approach for a visual approach at 1000 ft altitude. The aircraft touched down long at 145 knots alongside a tailwind of 3 knots on the wet runway with poor braking. The captain initiated a go-around but the thrust reverser mechanism failed to fully disengage, preventing full takeoff thrust. The aircraft overran the runway and struck an antenna array support in a ravine.
records.probable_cause: Captain Burke's faulty judgement to initiate a go-around after committing to a landing following an excessively long and fast approach, combined with the thrust reverser failure. The captain's unprofessional decision to abandon the precision approach contributed.

factors.evidence: low cloud ceilings and low visibility conditions due to light snow and fog (p. 5)
high and fast approach with visual contact made at 1000 ft and distance of about 2 mi (p. 5-6)
touched down about 1,500 feet beyond the runway threshold at a speed of 145 kn (p. 6-7)
alongside a tailwind of 3 kn at the time of landing (p. 6)
braking actions were poor due to the runway being wet at the time of landing (p. 6-7)
thrust reverser mechanism failed to fully disengage during go-around (p. 6-8)
aircraft overran the runway and struck antenna array support 700 ft beyond runway end (p. 6-7)
1 fatality from crash and post-crash fire (p. 7)

events.text: Anchorage ARTCC cleared Flight 60 for an approach to runway 11 at Ketchikan International Airport (p. 5)

Flight 60 reported out of 10,000 feet and contacted Ketchikan FSS; received weather report showing ceiling 800 feet obscured, visibility 2 miles with light snow and fog, and was advised that braking action on runway 11 was poor (p. 5)

Near the 1.7-mile DME fix, as the flight descended through 4,000 feet and acquired visual contact with the ground and water near Guard Island, the captain decided to abandon the ILS approach and continue visually, establishing his own visual glide slope at approximately 1,000 feet altitude (p. 5-6)
Visual contact with approach lights was established approximately 2 miles from the runway threshold, and the airport became visible shortly thereafter (p. 5)

Aircraft touched down approximately 1,500 feet past the runway 11 threshold at an excessive speed with a tailwind of 3 knots on a wet runway; the captain did not see the yellow 1,000-foot markers or the runway clearly (p. 6-7)
Captain deployed ground spoilers, reversed the engines, and applied wheel brakes; discovering that braking action was poor, he decided to execute a go-around (p. 6)
The thrust reverser mechanism did not disengage fully, preventing the captain from obtaining full takeoff thrust; attempts to reach idle and re-apply reverse thrust were unsuccessful (p. 6)

Realizing the aircraft could not be stopped on the runway, the captain turned right, raised the nose, and passed over a gully and service road beyond the runway departure end; the aircraft came to rest in a ravine 700 feet past the departure end of runway 11 and 125 feet right of centerline, destroyed by impact and ground fire (p. 6-7)

notes: Extracted from NTSB AAR-76-20; 8 events from history of flight section with expanded descriptions from report text; all factor ids from taxonomy; recommendations extracted from Safety Recommendations section
auto-repair: cvr was null

recommendations.text: Establish a procedure to require air carrier management to establish and implement a system that would provide a method for continual assessment of the pilot-in-command's performance in executing management's operational control responsibility

Implement a program within existing professional standards committees to provide an expeditious means for peer groups monitoring and disciplining pilots who may display any unprofessional or hazardous traits
Initiate a movement among the pilots associations to form new professional standards committees and to regenerate old ones to monitor ranks for unprofessional performance and alert pilots
Develop an air carrier pilot program similar to the General Aviation Accident Prevention Program that will emphasize the dangers of unprofessional performance in all phases of flight

Inspect more frequently the crash/fire/rescue capabilities of certificated airports, especially those in Alaska, to assure adequate training of personnel, maintenance and operational readiness of CFR equipment
Initiate a program for those airports which have no full-time CFR crew, especially those in Alaska, to properly train and equip the personnel that must respond to an aircraft fire

Amend 14 CFR 139 to require that airport personnel who are not professional firefighters but who, because of their supervisory status, must direct CFR operations at airports, be qualified to perform this task
Amend 14 CFR 67 to require that all applicants for first- and second-class medical certificates be administered periodically an audiometric hearing test

records.title: American Airlines 625
records.summary: American Airlines Flight 625, a Boeing 727-195, made an unstable approach to Cyril E. King Airport with maximum flap never applied. The aircraft floated due to wind conditions, touched down 2,300 feet down a 4,658-foot runway, and the captain rejected the landing too late. Engines responded slowly to go-around thrust commands. The aircraft overran the runway and struck a Shell gas station, killing 37 of 88 occupants.
records.probable_cause: The captain's failure to apply maximum flap setting during the approach in order to achieve the prescribed landing distance, failure to recognize the significance of the excessive speed and float characteristics of the aircraft, failure to execute a timely go-around when confronted with an unstable approach, and his subsequent panic in applying full brakes and reversers immediately before the impact. The captain's actions were compounded by his failure to use reverse thrust effectively during the landing roll. (p. 36-37)

factors.evidence: Aircraft approached with maximum flap setting of 40 degrees never applied, which meant aircraft speed was 10 knots higher than VREF. (p. 13)
Aircraft floated due to turbulent winds in the area, resulting in excessive ground speed on approach. (p. 13-14)
Captain did not have awareness that when he touched down 2,300 feet down the 4,658-foot runway, he did not have enough distance for a safe landing or go-around. (p. 14-15)
Pilot did not initiate go-around at a safe point; attempted go-around with only 700 feet remaining. After 5 seconds waiting for power, pilot panicked and applied full brakes. (p. 15)
Pilot forgot to apply reverse engine thrust until immediately before impact, severely reducing available stopping distance. (p. 15)
Aircraft ran off end of runway at high speed and struck Shell gas station located near the runway threshold. (p. 16)

events.text: American Airlines Flight 625 cleared for approach to runway 1 at Cyril E. King Airport
Aircraft in approach descent at excessive speed with maximum flap setting of 40 degrees never applied
Aircraft affected by turbulent wind conditions causing floating during descent; ground effect reduced effective landing distance
Aircraft touched down 2,300 feet down the 4,658-foot runway, with only approximately 2,358 feet remaining for stop
Captain applied full throttle to engines in go-around attempt 3 seconds after touchdown
After waiting 5 seconds for engine response, captain panicked and applied full wheel brakes and reversers
Aircraft overran runway end at high speed, approximately 160 knots, and struck Shell gas station
Aircraft came to rest against Shell gas station with fuselage extensively damaged; 37 of 88 occupants killed in post-crash fire

recommendations.text: Standardized procedures should require that landing calculations be made available to both pilots and reviewed before approach.
Approach stability criteria should be reviewed and procedures developed for mandatory go-around when approach becomes unstable.
Training programs should include specific procedures for recognition and response to unstable approaches and adequate go-around procedures.
Reverse thrust should be armed and ready prior to landing to allow immediate deployment when needed.

notes: Read History of Flight, Findings, Probable Cause (p. 36-37), and Recommendations sections
8 events with clock times and detailed crew actions
Probable cause emphasizes captain's failure to apply flaps and delayed go-around decision
4 safety-focused recommendations extracted from report

records.title: Air Manila 702
records.summary: Air Manila Flight 702, a Lockheed L-188A Electra, crashed during takeoff from NAS Agana, Guam. Seconds after lifting off, the No. 3 engine propeller feathered. The captain continued the takeoff despite not yet reaching VR speed, when company policy required immediate abort. The aircraft reached only 75-100 feet altitude, lost climb capability after flaps were retracted too low, struck rising terrain and crashed, killing all 46 on board plus one person on the ground.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause of this accident was the loss of climb capability after the crew retracted the flaps at too low an altitude to clear the rising terrain. The flaps were retracted after the No. 3 propeller feathered as the aircraft lifted off the runway. Contributing to the accident was the captain's decision to continue the takeoff after an engine failed before reaching rotation speed. (p. 21)

factors.evidence: Seconds after lifting off from the runway, the No. 3 propeller feathered during or just after liftoff. (p. 6)
The captain continued the takeoff after an engine failed before reaching rotation speed, when there was adequate runway available to have aborted. (p. 20)
The crew retracted landing gear and flaps before the aircraft reached the apex of the climb at an altitude where the flaps-up climb performance was insufficient. (p. 21)

Aircraft was not accelerated to a speed at which a climb could be maintained in a flaps-up configuration; aircraft rotated to a nose-high attitude with resultant loss of airspeed and lateral stability. (p. 21)
Aircraft struck terrain in tail-low attitude, dragged across ground for 220 feet, crossed a highway striking an automobile, and burst into flames. (p. 6)

events.text: Air Manila Flight 702 initiated rolling takeoff from runway 6L at Naval Air Station Agana.
Aircraft lifted off between 6,600 and 8,000 feet down runway, with liftoff estimated at 7,500-foot point. Most witnesses stated attitude at liftoff was normal.
No. 3 propeller feathered during or just after liftoff, as aircraft was beginning initial climb phase. Witness heard definite change in propeller sound from high rpm to low rpm and back to high rpm.
Captain continued takeoff after engine failure despite not yet having reached VR speed, when adequate runway was available for abort and company policy required immediate abort.
Crew retracted landing gear and flaps before aircraft reached apex of climb at altitude of approximately 75-100 feet, before airspeed was adequate for flaps-up climb configuration.
Aircraft was not accelerated to speed at which climb could be maintained in flaps-up configuration. Aircraft yawed to the right, then rotated to nose-high attitude.
Aircraft in tail-low attitude began descending toward terrain. Slow acceleration had resulted in excessive runway usage for takeoff, and aircraft reached only 75-100 feet altitude.

Aircraft struck rising terrain approximately 4,300 feet beyond end of runway 6L. Aft fuselage dragged along ground for 220 feet in right-wing-down attitude, then crashed through chain-link perimeter fence, crossed highway striking automobile (driver killed), and burst into flames in vacant area 4,900 feet from runway end.

Read Conclusions and Findings section (p. 20-21) with 19 numbered findings
Read Probable Cause section (p. 21)
Extracted detailed event sequence with clock times and aircraft state from narrative

records.title: Japan Air Lines Cargo Flight 1045
records.summary: Japan Air Lines Cargo Flight 1045 crashed during initial climb after takeoff from Anchorage on January 13, 1977. The captain was severely intoxicated with a blood alcohol level of 0.29. Airframe icing was present on engine inlet guide vanes and cowlings. The aircraft stalled shortly after reaching V2 speed during climb, with the crew making inappropriate control inputs that aggravated the stall. All five crew members perished.
records.probable_cause: The accident was caused by a stall resulting from pilot control inputs that were aggravated by airframe icing, while the pilot was operating under the influence of alcohol with a blood alcohol level of 0.29. Contributing to the accident was the failure of the other crew members to prevent the intoxicated captain from attempting the flight.

factors.evidence: Captain was severely intoxicated with blood alcohol level of 0.29; toxicological studies indicate the captain's ability to function was impaired; captain manifested symptoms of alcohol impairment including mental confusion, dizziness, impaired balance, and slurred speech (p. 19)
Ice present on inlet guide vanes, engine cowlings and engine bullet noses; ice on airfoil could have reduced angle of attack needed for stall (p. 18-19)

Failure of other flightcrew members (first and second officers) to prevent the captain from attempting the flight; no evidence they took action to prevent flight from proceeding; captain's intoxication was apparent to crew members (p. 19-20)
Aircraft stalled almost immediately after reaching V2 speed during initial climb; rotation to higher-than-normal pitch attitude (~15-18 degrees) combined with airframe icing (p. 18)
Witness saw flight climb to approximately 100 feet above ground, veer to left, and then slide out of air; aircraft descended at 3,000 fpm before impact (p. 19)

events.text: Intoxicated captain boarded aircraft; crew car driver noted captain appeared in good condition externally but showed signs of impairment (mental confusion, dizziness, staggering gait)
Crew began prestart checklists; CVR data showed captain making wrong runway assignments and showing mental confusion
Aircraft departed runway 24L; takeoff appeared normal until aircraft slowed acceleration from VR to V2 speed
Aircraft stalled almost immediately after reaching V2 speed; witness saw flight climb to approximately 100 feet above ground, veer left, and slide out of air
Japan Air Lines Cargo Flight 1045 crashed near Anchorage International Airport shortly after takeoff with all five crew members killed

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: Captain made statements indicating mental confusion and disorientation regarding location on airport and runway assignment

recommendations.text: Develop an air carrier pilot program similar to the General Aviation Accident Prevention Program that emphasizes the dangers of unprofessional performance and provides means for peer group monitoring and disciplining of pilots displaying unprofessional traits (p. 20)
Implement a program to provide means for peer group monitoring and disciplining any air carrier pilot who may display any unprofessional traits, particularly alcohol impairment (p. 20)

safety_changes: Enhanced pre-flight alcohol screening and testing procedures for air carrier pilots
Strengthened crew resource management training emphasizing second-in-command authority to challenge pilot actions when safety is at risk
Improved procedures for monitoring pilot fitness for duty before flights

notes: NTSB report AAR78-07 read in full including Analysis section and Safety Board conclusions
Sections read: History of Flight, Investigation details, Aircraft and systems analysis, Crew information, Weather analysis, Analysis section with probable cause determination
Captain's blood alcohol level of 0.29 was definitively established through toxicological testing
Clear documentation of pilot incapacitation symptoms: mental confusion, dizziness, slurred speech, staggering gait, loss of spatial orientation
Crew resource management failure critical factor - other crew members failed to challenge captain despite obvious impairment
Airframe icing present and contributing to stall susceptibility
Analysis discusses broader implications for crew coordination and second-in-command authority
No formal numbered recommendations in traditional format; Board statements about needed actions identified

records.title: Tenerife runway collision (KLM 4805 / Pan Am 1736)

agencies.name: Comisión de Investigación de Accidentes e Incidentes de Aviación Civil
agencies.report_title: Report on the collision between KLM Boeing 747 PH-BUF and Pan Am Boeing 747 N736PA at Los Rodeos Airport, Tenerife, on 27 March 1977

records.summary: Both 747s had diverted to Los Rodeos after a bomb explosion closed Las Palmas. In fog, with no ground radar, the KLM aircraft backtracked runway 30 and turned for departure while the Pan Am 747 was still taxiing along the same runway looking for its exit. The KLM captain began the takeoff roll without a takeoff clearance; a simultaneous radio transmission from Pan Am and the tower blocked the warning that Pan Am was still on the runway. The KLM aircraft struck the Pan Am 747 at about 140 kt; all 248 on the KLM aircraft and 335 of the 396 on the Pan Am aircraft were killed.
records.probable_cause: The fundamental cause was that the KLM captain took off without clearance, did not obey the tower's 'stand by for takeoff' instruction, did not interrupt takeoff on learning that the Pan Am aircraft was still on the runway, and in reply to the flight engineer's query as to whether the Pan Am aircraft had left the runway, replied emphatically in the affirmative. Contributing factors were the fog reducing visibility below the minimum for the airport to see the runway, the simultaneous radio transmissions that made the Pan Am position report inaudible in the KLM cockpit, the use of non-standard phraseology by the KLM co-pilot and the tower, the Pan Am aircraft's failure to leave the runway at the third taxiway as instructed, and the pressure on the KLM crew from duty-time limits.

factors.evidence: The KLM captain advanced the throttles and began the takeoff roll after receiving only the route clearance, before any takeoff clearance had been issued.

Non-standard phraseology ('we are now at takeoff', 'OK... stand by for takeoff') and a simultaneous transmission from Pan Am blocked the tower's instruction and Pan Am's report that it was still on the runway.
Fog reduced visibility on the runway to about 300 m, so neither crew nor the tower could see the other aircraft.
The KLM flight engineer's question whether Pan Am was clear of the runway was dismissed by the captain, and the first officer did not challenge the takeoff.
Los Rodeos had no ground surveillance radar, so the tower could not monitor the positions of the two aircraft on the runway.
The airport was congested with diverted aircraft, taxiway lighting was unserviceable, and the taxiway exits were poorly identified in the fog.
The KLM captain was under pressure from strict Dutch duty-time regulations that threatened the crew's ability to complete the return flight.
The Pan Am crew missed the third taxiway exit they had been instructed to take and continued along the runway toward the fourth.
A small tower staff was handling many diverted aircraft in poor visibility on a single frequency.
The Pan Am 747 was still backtracking on the active runway when the KLM aircraft began its takeoff.
The KLM 747, having rotated early and struck its tail on the runway, hit the Pan Am fuselage at about 140 kt and crashed back onto the runway in flames.
Both aircraft were destroyed by fire; all 248 on the KLM aircraft died and only 61 of the Pan Am occupants survived.

events.text: A bomb explosion at Las Palmas closes the airport; KLM 4805 and Pan Am 1736 are among many aircraft diverted to Los Rodeos, which becomes congested.
Las Palmas reopens; the KLM captain decides to refuel fully at Tenerife, delaying departure and blocking the Pan Am aircraft on the apron. Duty-time limits concern the KLM crew.
Tower instructs KLM to backtrack runway 30 and make a 180 degree turn at the end; fog is rolling across the airfield and visibility is falling.
Pan Am is instructed to backtrack the runway and leave it at the third taxiway; the crew are unsure which exit is the third and continue past it.
KLM completes its turn at the end of runway 30 and lines up; the captain begins to advance the throttles and the first officer says they do not yet have ATC clearance.
Tower issues the route clearance (not a takeoff clearance); the KLM first officer reads it back ending with 'we are now at takeoff'.
The KLM captain releases the brakes and begins the takeoff roll without clearance.

Tower replies 'OK... stand by for takeoff, I will call you'; simultaneously Pan Am transmits 'we are still taxiing down the runway'. The two transmissions overlap and only a squeal is heard in the KLM cockpit.
KLM flight engineer asks whether Pan Am is clear of the runway; the captain replies emphatically yes and continues the takeoff.
Pan Am crew see the KLM landing lights approaching through the fog and apply full power to turn off the runway to the left.
KLM captain sees Pan Am and rotates early, striking the tail on the runway for 20 m in an attempt to clear it.
The KLM 747, just airborne at about 140 kt, strikes the upper fuselage of the Pan Am 747 with its fuselage and engines and crashes onto the runway 150 m beyond, exploding in flames.
Fire destroys both aircraft; 583 people die and 61 on the Pan Am aircraft survive. The tower, unable to see the runway, learns of the collision only when the fire is reported.

recommendations.text: Place great emphasis on the importance of exact compliance with instructions and clearances, use standard aeronautical phraseology, and avoid the word 'takeoff' in any ATC clearance other than a takeoff clearance.
recommendations.outcome: ICAO standardised phraseology; 'takeoff' is used only in takeoff clearances and cancellations, and read-back requirements were strengthened.

recommendations.text: Install ground radar at Los Rodeos and other airports where conditions of low visibility and traffic density justify it, and improve taxiway lighting and signage.
recommendations.outcome: Tenerife South airport opened in 1978, relieving Los Rodeos; ground surveillance radar later installed.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the members of a flight crew, whatever their rank, are trained and encouraged to challenge a captain's decision when they have doubts about safety.
recommendations.outcome: The accident became a foundation case for crew resource management training worldwide.

dissent.position: The Netherlands Aviation Safety Board, while accepting the sequence of events, disagreed with the weight given to the KLM captain's actions as the fundamental cause. It emphasised that the mutual misunderstanding created by the ambiguous route clearance, the non-standard phraseology used by the tower, and the simultaneous transmissions that blocked critical messages were of equal importance, and that the KLM crew genuinely believed they had received takeoff clearance.
dissent.topic: probable cause and allocation of responsibility

safety_changes: ICAO standard phraseology reforms: 'takeoff' reserved for takeoff clearances, mandatory read-backs, use of 'departure' for route clearances.
Crew resource management training introduced across the airline industry.
Ground surveillance radar and improved low-visibility taxi procedures at major airports; opening of Tenerife South airport.

notes: The record's aircraft is the KLM 747-206B PH-BUF; the Pan Am aircraft was Boeing 747-121 N736PA. Occupants (644) and fatalities (583) combine both aircraft: KLM 248/248, Pan Am 335 of 396. Serious injuries approximate.

Clock strings are local time; seconds around the collision (about 17:06:50) are approximate reconstructions from the published CVR times and may differ by a few seconds. Earlier times are approximate.
The Spanish report date and title are approximate; Dutch comments were published as an appendix to the Spanish report.

records.title: Southern Airways 242
records.summary: Southern Airways Flight 242 suffered total loss of thrust from both engines while descending through a severe thunderstorm with embedded cells between 17,000 and 14,000 feet near Rome, Georgia. The crew penetrated the storm despite radar indications of severe activity, based on misinterpretation of weather radar attenuation. The aircraft encountered massive amounts of rain and hail that broke the windshield and caused both Pratt & Whitney JT8D-7A engines to ingest water and hail, resulting in compressor stalling and flameout. The crew successfully glided the aircraft unpowered to a forced emergency landing on Georgia State Route 381, where it struck vehicles and a building.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause of this accident was the total and unique loss of thrust from both engines while the aircraft was penetrating an area of severe thunderstorms. The loss of thrust was caused by the ingestion of massive amounts of water and hail which in combination with thrust lever movement induced severe stalling in and major damage to the engine compressors. Major contributing factors included the failure of the company's dispatching system to provide the flightcrew with up-to-date severe weather information pertaining to the aircraft's intended route of flight, the captain's reliance on airborne weather radar for penetration of thunderstorm areas, and limitations in the Federal Aviation Administration's air traffic control system which precluded the timely dissemination of real-time hazardous weather information to the flightcrew. (p. 42)

factors.evidence: Aircraft descended from cruising altitude of 17,000 ft through a severe thunderstorm cell with massive rain and hail near Rome, Georgia. At 1606:53 (14,000 ft), sound of heavy hail or rain was recorded on CVR, continuing through 1607:57 when CVR ceased for 36 sec. (p. 3-5)
The hail was so intense that it broke the aircraft's windshield during the encounter with the storm. Multiple CVR transmissions reference crew inability to see through weather. (p. 3)

The crew were apparently misled by the radar's attenuation effect, and they proceeded toward what they believed was a low-intensity area, when in fact it was the peak convective activity point. Captain initially decided storms were too severe to penetrate, then shortly after decided to penetrate based on radar interpretation. (p. 41-42, Findings 14-17)

Ingestion of massive amounts of water and hail into both Pratt & Whitney JT8D-7A engines caused compressor stalling. Severe compressor stalls produced overpressure surge deflecting sixth-stage low-pressure compressor blades forward, clashing against fifth-stage stator vanes and breaking pieces that ingested into high-pressure compressors. Continued high thrust settings caused severe overheating and engine ceased to function. Both engines went from normal operation to complete flameout within seconds. (p. 40-41, Findings 2-9)

Southern Airways' flight dispatch personnel did not monitor adequately the storm system which moved into the Rome area, and the information that the dispatch section provided to Flight 242 did not alert the flightcrew to the weather hazards along their route. NWS had identified by radar the precipitation in the Rome area as very strong and intense with indications of hail and cloud tops over 40,000 ft at least 20 min before Flight 242 departed Huntsville. (p. 41, Findings 18-19)

Captain's decision to penetrate the storm area was probably based on his interpretation of the weather radar display and his reliance on airborne weather radar for penetration of thunderstorm areas. Before departing Huntsville, the flightcrew had no information on thunderstorms immediately west of Rome VOR. (p. 41-42, Findings 12-17)

After losing both engines at 1610:05 at approximately 7,000 ft altitude, crew conducted successful forced landing glide (all engines inoperative) on Georgia State Route 381 near New Hope at 1618:36-1618:43 as recorded on CVR crash sounds. Aircraft struck trees and ground structures. (p. 5-6)

events.text: Flight 242 departed Muscle Shoals on an instrument flight rules flight plan with 81 passengers and 4 crew aboard, heading for Atlanta via Huntsville intermediate stop.
Flight 242 landed at Huntsville with no discrepancies.
Flight 242 departed Huntsville on IFR flight plan for Atlanta direct to Rome VOR, requesting 17,000 ft with an estimated 25 minutes en route.
Huntsville departure control cleared Flight 242 to climb to 17,000 ft and proceed directly to Rome VOR.
Huntsville controller advised heavy precipitation was 5 nmi ahead; crew reported they were already in rain and conditions did not look heavier than what they were in.
Flight 242 established communications with Memphis Air Route Traffic Control Center.
Memphis Center controller advised SIGMET was current for Tennessee, Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama vicinity and instructed Flight 242 to contact Atlanta Center.
Atlanta Center cleared Flight 242 to descend to 14,000 ft and reported weather showing up northwest of Rome.
Flight 242 reported reaching 14,000 ft; sound of heavy hail or rain was recorded on CVR at this time, indicating severe weather encounter.
Flight 242 reported to Atlanta Center: 'We just got our windshield busted' indicating hail impact on cockpit windshield.
First officer said 'Left engine won't spool' and Flight 242 reported 'Our left engine just cut out.'
First evidence of engine trouble: left engine compressor stall and power loss due to water/hail ingestion.
CVR ceased recording for 36 seconds during intense precipitation encounter; when it resumed at 1608:33, rain sounds continued for another 40 seconds.
First officer said 'My...the other engine's going too...' and at 1610:05 reported 'Standby, we lost both engines.'

Total loss of thrust from both engines while at approximately 7,000 ft altitude. Both Pratt & Whitney JT8D-7A engines ceased functioning due to compressor damage from water and hail ingestion combined with thrust lever movement.
CVR ceased operation for 2 minutes 4 seconds (engine-driven electrical power interrupted when both engine rotational speed decreased below electrical generator operating thresholds).

Flight 242 transmitted to Atlanta Approach Control 'we've lost both engines, how about giving us a vector to the nearest place, we're at 7,000 ft.' Approach Control provided vector to Dobbins Air Force Base.
Crew requested emergency descent; first officer declared emergency to crew.

Captain said 'Just don't stall this thing out' and directed 'Get your wing flaps.' First officer confirmed 'Got hydraulics' - APU was providing essential electrical power for flight control actuation.

Captain: 'I'm picking out a clear field.' First officer: 'Bill, you've got to find me a highway.' Captain: 'Let's get the next clear open field.' First officer: 'No...' This exchange shows crew search for emergency landing site.
Captain said 'See a highway over--no cars' and first officer asked 'Right there, is that straight?' Captain replied 'No.' First officer said 'We'll have to take it.'
Flight 242's last transmission: 'we're putting it on the highway, we're down to nothing' indicating decision to land on Georgia State Route 381.

Crash impact sequence recorded on CVR. Aircraft touched down on Georgia State Route 381 in unpowered glide after 28+ minutes of engine-out flight, striking trees and ground structures at elevation 1,020 ft.

recommendations.text: Expedite the development and implementation of an aviation weather subsystem for both en route and terminal area environments, which is capable of providing a real-time display of either precipitation or turbulence, or both, and which includes a multiple-intensity classification scheme. Transmit this information to pilots either via the controller as a safety advisory or via an electronic data link.

Establish a standard scale of thunderstorm intensity based on the NWS six-level scale and promote its widespread use as a common language to describe thunderstorm precipitation intensity. Additionally, indoctrinate pilots and air traffic control personnel in the use of this system.
Transmit SIGMETs more frequently on navaids so that pilots can receive more timely information about hazardous weather.

Code, according to geographic applicability, Severe Thunderstorm Bulletins and Tornado Watch Bulletins issued by the National Severe Storms Forecast Center so that they may be transmitted to appropriate air traffic control facilities by the FAA Weather Message Switching Center.

Require that each air traffic control facility depict on the map portion of its radar displays those airports immediately outside of that facility's jurisdiction to the extent that adjacent facilities depict those airports on their displays.
Formulate rules and procedures for the timely dissemination by air traffic controllers of all available severe weather information to inbound and outbound flightcrews in the terminal area.

Initiate research to determine the attenuating effects of various levels of precipitation and icing on airborne radomes of both x- and c-band radar, and disseminate to the aviation community any data derived concerning the limitations of airborne radar in precipitation.
Expedite its review of Recommendation A-73-40 with a view toward early requirement of properly designed shoulder harnesses at flight attendant stations in air carrier aircraft.

dissent.position: Disagreed with the probable cause, arguing it was merely a statement of what happened rather than why it occurred. Stated the probable cause should emphasize the captain's critical decision to penetrate rather than avoid a known area of severe weather.

safety_changes: Development of wind shear detection systems and microburst forecasting
Implementation of real-time weather information systems for pilots
Enhanced weather radar technology and interpretation training
Standard phraseology for thunderstorm intensity description

records.title: 1977 Dan-Air Boeing 707 crash

agencies.name: Air Accidents Investigation Branch
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report No. 9/78

records.summary: A Boeing 707-321C cargo aircraft operating for Dan-Air Services experienced an in-flight separation of its right horizontal stabilizer and elevator during approach to Lusaka on 14 May 1977, resulting in immediate loss of pitch control. The aircraft nose-dived from 800 feet and struck the ground 3,660 meters short of the runway threshold, killing all six occupants. Investigation revealed the stabilizer's rear spar had failed due to metal fatigue in a concealed internal location that was not detectable during routine maintenance.
records.probable_cause: The accident was caused by a loss of pitch control following the in-flight separation of the right hand horizontal stabilizer and elevator as a result of a combination of metal fatigue and inadequate failsafe design in the rear spar structure. Shortcomings in design assessment, certification and inspection procedures were contributory factors.

factors.evidence: The replacement of the horizontal stabilizer light alloy top skin by stainless steel altered the stiffness distribution of the structure, creating high fastener loadings in the rear spar top chord. The higher stiffness would result in higher skin loadings and higher fastener loads, increasing bearing stress in the chord forward flange (p. 1071-1085). Insufficient consideration had been given at the design and certification stage to stress distribution following a top chord failure outboard of the closure rib (p. 1677-1679).

The right hand stabilizer rear spar top chord failed due to long term fatigue damage. The fatigue crack had existed for about 7,200 flights, of which approximately 6,750 were made on the US register (p. 1667-1670). The crack occurred at the 11th fastener on the top chord forward flange outboard of the closure rib (p. 618-620).

Neither the inspections detailed in the approved maintenance schedule nor those recommended by the manufacturer were adequate to detect partial cracks in the horizontal stabiliser rear spar top chord (p. 1687-1690). The inspections required by Dan-Air's UK CAA approved maintenance schedule were less specific than those recommended by the manufacturer (p. 1692-1694). The fatigue crack had gone undetected due to its concealed internal location within the structure.

Following the failure of the stabilizer rear spar top chord, the structure could not sustain the flight loads and the entire right horizontal stabilizer and elevator assembly detached from the aircraft (p. 1672-1675). The stabilizer was found 200 meters back along the flight path, indicating in-flight separation prior to the nose-down pitch maneuver (p. 115-116).

The instantaneous loss of the right stabilizer download caused an immediate nose-down pitching moment. The elevator linkage was pulled to full up position, fracturing the stabilizer jack screw and allowing the entire left stabilizer to rotate to a large nose-up angle, resulting in a very rapid pitch-down (p. 1024-1043).

A very rapid pitch down resulted and the aircraft struck the ground in a 50-degree dive from approximately 800 feet, with pitch attitude at approximately 100 degrees beyond vertical. Ground impact occurred 3,660 meters from the runway threshold (p. 1041-1043, p. 122-125).

Co-pilot contacted Lusaka Approach
Cleared to descend to FL 110 at LW NDB
Levelling at FL 110 at 37 nm DME from Lusaka

Turning downwind; cleared for visual approach to runway 10 as number two
