Landing checks completed
Right horizontal stabilizer and elevator assembly detaches from airframe
Aircraft in rapid nose-down pitch change; CVR record terminates
Ground impact in 50-degree dive from 800 feet, 3,660 m short of runway threshold; fire and destruction

recommendations.text: When an aircraft has been certificated against failsafe criteria, those portions of structure considered significant in the failsafe design should be identified in the approved inspection schedule and their relative importance defined.

Defects involving the structure identified in the above recommendation should be reported to the manufacturer and airworthiness authority to enable a fleet picture to be developed and appropriate action to be taken.

When an aircraft design has evolved significantly, a critical assessment should be made by the Certification Authority in association with the manufacturer as to the validity of extrapolation of the original design data when applied to a developed aircraft variant.

After an aircraft type has been established in service for some years a searching mid-life review should be carried out by the manufacturer to the satisfaction of the Certification Authority when all aspects of the aircraft's structural performance should be studied in the light of fleet service experience and current design knowledge.

safety_changes: A post-accident fleet inspection of the 707-300 series worldwide revealed 38 aircraft (7% of fleet) with fatigue cracks present in the stabilizer rear spar top chord, of which four required chord replacement
Enhanced inspection procedures for failsafe structures on 707 aircraft, reducing inspection intervals from 21,000 to 14,000 flight hours for critical stabilizer rear spar areas

records.title: University of Evansville men's basketball team plane crash
records.summary: The Douglas DC-3 crashed shortly after takeoff when gust locks on the right aileron and rudder were not removed before departure. The overloaded baggage compartment shifted the aircraft center of gravity aft, making it impossible to control the aircraft.
records.probable_cause: Pilot failure to remove gust locks combined with overloaded baggage compartment shifting center of gravity aft.

factors.evidence: Gust locks on the right aileron and rudder before takeoff, as well as an overloaded baggage compartment
The extra baggage shifted the plane's center of gravity to the rear, making it impossible to control the overweight aircraft
The locked rudder and aileron made it impossible to control the aircraft after takeoff

events.text: Douglas DC-3 N51071 receives IFR clearance to Nashville, weather reported as 400 ft overcast, visibility 3/4 mile, light rain and fog
Aircraft cleared for takeoff from Runway 18 at Evansville Regional Airport, baggage compartment overloaded
Aircraft begins takeoff roll on Runway 18
Gust locks on right aileron and rudder were not removed before departure
Aircraft rotated normally to nose-high attitude for climb
Rearward center of gravity from overloaded baggage and locked control surfaces rendered aircraft uncontrollable; entered region of reversed command
Aircraft crashed less than 1 minute 30 seconds after takeoff within airport boundaries
Aircraft destroyed in crash; all 29 persons aboard killed

recommendations.text: Review and strengthen procedures for control lock removal before flight to ensure pilot verification

records.title: United Airlines 2860
records.summary: United Airlines Flight 2860, a DC-8 cargo flight, departed San Francisco on December 17, 1977, with an intermediate stop planned at Salt Lake City. After reporting electrical trouble during descent, the crew entered a holding pattern and left the frequency to discuss the problem with maintenance. Unaware of the incomplete holding clearance, the flight drifted into mountainous terrain. When ATC warned of terrain and ordered an immediate climb, the aircraft struck a 7,665-foot mountain ridge at 7,200 feet, killing all three crew members.
records.probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Board determined the cause was the approach controller's issuance of an incomplete and ambiguous holding clearance, combined with the flightcrew's acceptance of it and failure to follow prescribed loss-of-communications procedures and holding procedures. The controller and crew's actions were attributed to habitual imprecise communication and adherence developed through years of radar environment operations. Contributing to the accident was the aircraft's No. 1 electrical system failure.

factors.evidence: The approach controller issued an incomplete holding clearance without specifying a holding radial (p. 33-34)
The flightcrew failed to adhere to prescribed loss-of-communications and holding procedures (p. 33-34)
Due to incomplete clearance and crew workload, the aircraft entered a hazardous area of terrain while off frequency (p. 34-35)
Aircraft impacted 7,665-foot mountain ridge at 7,200-foot elevation (p. 3)

events.text: United Airlines Flight 2860 departed San Francisco at 2317 PST on December 17, 1977
Flight began descent from cruise altitude toward Salt Lake City
Crew reported electrical trouble and requested holding clearance
Crew requested to leave frequency for 'little minute' to contact United maintenance
Controller approved crew to leave frequency, believing it would be brief
Flight returned to approach control frequency
Controller warned flight of terrain on right and instructed left turn
Controller instructed climb immediately to 8,000 feet
Crew reported climbing from 6,000 feet to 8,000 feet
Aircraft struck 7,665-foot mountain ridge at approximately 7,200 feet elevation

recommendations.text: Review the adequacy of current cockpit voice recorder preflight testing procedures to assure satisfactory system operation
Review the reliability of cockpit voice recorder units to assure that the mean time between failure is not excessive

records.title: Continental Airlines 603
records.summary: Continental Airlines Flight 603, a McDonnell Douglas DC-10-10, experienced cascading tire failures during takeoff roll from runway 6R when the recapped tread of the number-two tire on the left main landing gear separated. This caused that tire to blow out, and the overload caused the adjacent number-one tire to blow out immediately. Metal pieces from both rims damaged the number-five tire. Unable to stop on the wet runway, the aircraft overran the departure end and the left main gear collapsed, puncturing fuel tanks and causing a post-impact fire that resulted in four fatalities and moderate injuries to many others.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause of this accident was the sequential failure of two tires on the left main landing gear and the resultant failure of another tire on the same landing gear at a critical time during the takeoff roll. These failures resulted in the captain's decision to reject the takeoff. Contributing to the accident was the cumulative effect of the partial loss of aircraft braking because of the failed tires and the reduced braking friction achievable on the wet runway surface which increased the accelerate-stop distance to a value greater than the available runway length. This prevented the captain from stopping the aircraft within the runway confines. The failure of the left main landing gear and the consequent rupture of the left wing fuel tanks resulted in an intense fire which added to the severity of the accident.

factors.evidence: Recapping tread of the number-two tire on the left main landing gear separated from the tire causing a blowout; this overload caused the adjacent number-one tire to blow out immediately (p. 5-6). The number-two tire may have been operated in an over-deflection condition due to suboptimal average inflation pressure for maximum gross weight (p. 5).
The aircraft could not stop within the confines of the runway partly because the runway was wet, reducing braking friction from that which would be available on a dry runway (p. 5).

Partial loss of braking power following the failure of the three tires on the left main gear compounded the stopping distance problem (p. 5). Metal pieces from rims of failed tires damaged the number-five tire causing a third blowout on left main gear (p. 5).

Aircraft could not stop within the confines of the runway and overran the departure end by approximately 664 feet; left main gear broke through nonload-bearing pavement, collapsed rearward, and punctured fuel tanks in left wing (p. 5).

Portions of the failed gear punctured fuel tanks in the left wing, immediately starting a fuel fire; intense fire which added to severity of accident with four fatalities and moderate injuries to many occupants (p. 5).

events.text: Flight 603 called Los Angeles clearance delivery and was cleared for the route of flight
Los Angeles ground control gave permission to push back from gate; approximately 2 minutes after clearance delivery
Flight 603 cleared by ground control to taxi to runway 6R; runway was wet but had no standing water
Local control cleared Flight 603 to position on runway 6R and hold for takeoff
Local control cleared Flight 603 for takeoff; flightcrew acknowledged the instructions
Aircraft began takeoff roll with normal acceleration; all engine instruments in normal range
Airspeed approached V1 speed of 156 knots; captain heard loud metallic bang followed by aircraft quivering and left wing drop
Captain rejected takeoff immediately after hearing metallic bang and noting aircraft instability; Digital Flight Data Recorder showed airspeed had increased to approximately 159 knots
Captain applied full brake pressure while bringing thrust levers back to idle power and actuating full reverse thrust
Number-one tire on left main landing gear blew out after number-two tire failure; metal pieces from rims damaged number-five tire causing third blowout
Left main landing gear collapsed after aircraft overran runway end; gear break through nonload-bearing pavement and ruptured left wing fuel tanks
Intense fuel fire erupted from ruptured left wing fuel tanks; aircraft came to rest approximately 664 feet beyond runway departure end

recommendations.text: Require airworthiness directive to inspect tire condition and change tires that show excessive wear or tread separation
Require inspection procedures and standards for recapped tires used on air carrier aircraft
Establish more stringent quality control standards for tire retreading facilities serving air carriers
Require tire pressure monitoring systems to alert flight crews to pressure loss during takeoff
Review and revise aircraft certification standards relating to landing gear and brake failure conditions

safety_changes: Improved tire retreading standards for aircraft
Enhanced tire condition inspection procedures
Tighter quality control for aircraft tire manufacturers
Better tire pressure monitoring systems for takeoff

records.title: National Airlines 193

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report: National Airlines, Inc., Boeing 727-235, N4744, Escambia Bay, near Pensacola, Florida, May 8, 1978

location.name: Escambia Bay, 3 nautical miles from runway 25

records.summary: National Airlines Flight 193, a Boeing 727 descending to Pensacola Regional Airport at night in low visibility, impacted Escambia Bay during a non-precision approach after the crew failed to monitor descent and altitude. The first officer misread his altimeter and failed to provide required altitude callouts, while the aircraft descended below minimums undetected.
records.probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Board determines that the probable cause of this accident was the flightcrew's unprofessionally conducted nonprecision instrument approach, in that the captain and the crew failed to monitor the descent rate and altitude, and the first officer failed to provide the captain with required altitude and approach performance callouts. The crew failed to check and utilize all instruments available for altitude awareness, turned off the ground proximity warning system, and failed to configure the aircraft properly and in a timely manner for the approach. Contributing to the accident was the radar controller's failure to provide advance notice of the start-descent point which accelerated the pace of the crew's cockpit activities after the passage of the final approach fix.

factors.evidence: Aircraft impacted Escambia Bay at approximately 50 feet indicated altitude during approach to runway 25 (p. 7)
Accident occurred at night in low visibility from fog; measured ceiling 400 feet overcast, surface visibility 4 miles in fog and haze (p. 5)

The first officer neglected to make altitude and approach fix call outs and failed to detect they passed through minimum descent altitude; captain did not monitor descent rate and altitude; neither pilot monitored IVSI readings during extended periods (p. 36, 40)

First officer either misread altimeter as 1500 ft when actual altitude was 500 ft, or did not perceive what he saw until aircraft was at 100 feet; first officer claimed he thought altimeter read 1100 ft at 100 feet actual (p. 31-32)

Radar controller misjudged aircraft distance and turned it to final at 4.5 nmi instead of recommended 8 nmi, creating situation impossible for captain to configure aircraft per flight manual; controller failed to provide advance notice of start-descent point (p. 5, 27-28)

Each person chose not to ask for or offer additional assistance or warnings; no challenge-and-response occurred; first officer's failure to provide altitude callouts contributed in part to captain's failure to monitor descent (p. 28)

Captain failed to lower landing gear immediately after lowering flaps, delaying gear extension by 27 seconds; first officer did not make required 1000-ft callout; first officer's attention directed outside cockpit during critical portions of descent; landing flaps never extended to 30 degrees (p. 28, 31, 35)
Aircraft descended below minimum descent altitude of 480 feet undetected; captain could not recall observing any altitude readings during descent below 500 feet (p. 33)
Flight engineer inhibited GPWS at 2120:15; pilots believed problem was solved when captain raised nose and reduced descent rate, misleading them into continuing descent (p. 34-35)

After descending below 1300 feet, captain unable to establish stable descent profile; nonstandard approach configuration with landing gear extended at 940 feet and landing flaps not extended beyond 25 degrees caused added difficulties (p. 35)

Ground proximity warning system whooper sounds; pull up voice warning begins
Flight engineer inhibits GPWS; captain raises nose and reduces descent rate; pilots believe problem is solved
First officer says: "...we're down to fifty feet"
Aircraft impacts Escambia Bay in approximately 12 feet of water; 3 passengers drowned attempting to exit

records.title: Pacific Southwest Airlines Flight 182
records.summary: Boeing 727 collided mid-air with Cessna 172 on approach to San Diego during clear VFR conditions. PSA crew lost visual contact with the Cessna despite ATC instructions to maintain visual separation but failed to report loss of sight. Both aircraft were destroyed in-flight. Seven people on the ground were killed and 22 dwellings destroyed.
records.probable_cause: Failure of PSA Flight 182 crew to comply with visual separation clearance and to report loss of visual contact. Contributing factors: ATC procedures authorizing visual separation when radar separation was available, controller failure to advise of Cessna's direction of movement, Cessna pilot failure to maintain assigned heading, and improper resolution of conflict alert.

factors.evidence: PSA crew lost sight of Cessna despite ATC clearance to maintain visual separation (p. 662-672).
First officer reported not seeing Cessna at 0900:41, but crew did not advise controller of loss of visual contact (p. 868-880).
ATC procedures authorized use of visual separation when radar clearances were available; controller did not advise of Cessna's direction of movement (p. 701-709).
PSA 727 and Cessna 172 collided at 0901:47, 2600 feet altitude, 3 miles northeast of Lindbergh Field (p. 954-965).
Both aircraft destroyed in collision and post-impact fires; 7 people killed on ground, 22 dwellings destroyed (p. 984-986).

events.text: Lindbergh tower local controller clears Cessna N7711G to maintain VFR and contact San Diego approach control after completing approaches (p. 744-745).
Approach controller advises PSA 182 'traffic at twelve o'clock, three miles, out of one thousand seven hundred' (p. 824-828).

recommendations.text: Implement a Terminal Radar Service Area (TRSA) at Lindbergh Airport, San Diego, California
Review procedures at all airports used regularly by air carrier and general aviation aircraft to determine which areas require terminal control area or terminal radar service area
Use visual separation in terminal control areas and terminal radar service areas only when a pilot requests it, except for sequencing on final approach with radar monitoring
Re-evaluate policy with regard to use of visual separation in other terminal areas

dissent.position: Member McADAMS dissented; see dissenting statement on page 39

safety_changes: Terminal Radar Service Areas (TRSA) implemented at major airports
Restrictions on visual separation procedures in terminal areas
Enhanced conflict alert resolution procedures

notes: Read sections: narrative (p. 7-8), probable cause and amended probable cause (p. 36-38), safety recommendations (p. 38-41)

records.title: Rocky Mountain Airways Flight 217

aircraft.type: de Havilland Canada DHC-6 Twin Otter 300

location.name: Buffalo Pass area, near Steamboat Springs

records.summary: A DHC-6 Twin Otter departed Steamboat Springs climbing to 17,000 feet via V101 airway to Denver. Unable to climb above 13,000 feet due to severe icing and mountain wave downdrafts, the captain decided to return to Steamboat Springs. The aircraft descended to 11,600 feet and struck terrain on a mountain at 10,530 feet, partially buried in snow.
records.probable_cause: Severe icing and strong downdrafts associated with a mountain wave which combined to exceed the aircraft's capability to maintain flight. Contributing to the accident was the captain's decision to fly into probable icing conditions that exceeded the conditions authorized by company directive. (p. 4)

factors.evidence: After entering a cloud bank about 12,560 feet over Buffalo Pass, the flight encountered severe icing conditions with precipitation like slush. The aircraft encountered heavy rime icing with 1.5 to 2 inches of ice on protected surfaces including propellers and windshield. (p. 6)

Strong downdrafts associated with a mountain wave at approximately 1945 MST exceeded the aircraft's performance margin. The captain was unable to keep the aircraft at 13,000 feet with maximum climb power. (p. 7)

Unable to climb above 13,000 feet at normal power and airspeed settings. Descended uncommanded from 13,000 feet to 11,600 feet despite application of 10 degrees of flaps and maximum climb power. (p. 7)

Captain decided to fly into weather conditions beyond company's limitations. Company operations manual did not authorize flight into icing conditions at high altitudes over mountainous terrain. (p. 4)

Aircraft crashed on a mountain at 10,530-foot elevation after being unable to maintain altitude, approximately 8 nautical miles east-northeast of Steamboat Springs. Aircraft partially buried in snow. (p. 4)

Lack of shoulder harnesses on aircraft seats contributed to fatal injuries. One passenger died from injuries received in the crash; captain died three days later partly due to lack of shoulder harness restraint. (p. 4)

events.text: Flight 217 departed Steamboat Springs STOL Airport at 1855 MST climbing to assigned altitude of 17,000 feet on V101 airway to Denver. 20 passengers plus crew aboard.
First officer flying the aircraft crossed Steamboat Springs NDB at 12,000 feet and intercepted V101 airway eastward. Light freezing precipitation encountered during climb.
Aircraft entered cloud bank at approximately 12,560 feet over Buffalo Pass area just east of Steamboat Springs. Encountered severe icing conditions and precipitation like slush.

Aircraft unable to climb above 13,000 feet at normal climb power and airspeed. Captain attempted to climb further but also unsuccessful. Aircraft continued to encounter severe icing despite deicing equipment functioning.
Captain decided to return to Steamboat Springs after being unable to maintain altitude above 13,000 feet. Aircraft began 180-degree turn to head back westbound.
Aircraft encountered severe icing conditions for approximately 12 seconds. Unable to maintain 13,000 feet with maximum climb power. Captain lowered flaps 5 degrees then 10 degrees to arrest descent.
Aircraft descended to 11,600 feet. Able to maintain 11,600 feet with 10 degrees of flaps and airspeed between 90-100 knots. Ice accumulated to 1.5-2 inches on windshield unheated portions.
First officer reported to Denver Center indicating problem maintaining altitude and recommending other flights not attempt to fly into Steamboat Springs area due to heavy icing.
Captain reported they were on Victor 101 crossing the 335-degree radial of Kremmling VOR. Last radio contact with Denver Center at 1944:34, after which no response received.

Aircraft right wingtip struck high-voltage transmission line tower at approximately 1945 MST, causing short circuit recorded by power company. Aircraft impacted terrain at 10,530 feet elevation, partially buried in snow. 2 fatalities on scene, captain died 3 days later.

safety_changes: Mandatory installation of shoulder harnesses on aircraft seats

History of flight, findings, and probable cause sections read
Recommendations section not clearly readable due to OCR quality

records.title: United Airlines 173

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: United Airlines, Inc., McDonnell-Douglas DC-8-61, N8082U, Portland, Oregon, December 28, 1978

location.name: Wooded residential area about 6 nm southeast of Portland International Airport, Oregon

records.summary: When the landing gear was extended on approach to Portland, an abnormal thump and yaw and a missing gear-down indication led the crew to break off the approach and hold while they troubleshot the problem and prepared the cabin for an emergency landing. The captain remained preoccupied with the gear for about an hour while the fuel state became critical; the flight engineer's and first officer's fuel advisories were not acted on decisively. All four engines flamed out from fuel exhaustion and the DC-8 crash-landed in a wooded suburb, killing 10 of the 189 on board. The accident led directly to the development of crew resource management training.
records.probable_cause: The failure of the captain to monitor properly the aircraft's fuel state and to properly respond to the low fuel state and the crewmember's advisories regarding fuel state. This resulted in fuel exhaustion to all engines. His inattention resulted from preoccupation with a landing gear malfunction and preparations for a possible landing emergency. Contributing to the accident was the failure of the other two flight crewmembers either to fully comprehend the criticality of the fuel state or to successfully communicate their concern to the captain.

factors.evidence: A corroded retract cylinder piston rod on the right main gear failed on extension; the gear fell free with a thump and the gear-down indication was lost, although the gear was actually down and locked.
The captain devoted the holding period to troubleshooting the gear indication and coordinating cabin preparation for an emergency landing.
The captain lost track of the fuel remaining and of the time needed to reach the runway.
The crew did not properly monitor and respond to the decreasing fuel quantity during about an hour of holding.
The flight engineer and first officer expressed concern about fuel but did not communicate its criticality assertively, and the captain did not respond to their advisories.
The fuel tanks ran dry after the extended hold; engine No. 4 flamed out first, followed by the others.
All four engines lost power from fuel exhaustion and the aircraft descended into trees and houses short of the airport.
The forced landing occurred after dark in a residential area.

events.text: Flight is cleared for a visual approach to runway 28 at Portland.
Landing gear extended; the crew hear a loud thump and feel a yaw, and the right main gear green light does not illuminate.
Captain breaks off the approach and requests holding to troubleshoot the gear indication; ATC clears the flight to hold southeast of the airport at 5,000 ft.
Flight engineer checks the gear visually through the viewers and consults with United maintenance by radio; the gear appears down but the indication problem is unresolved.
Captain discusses emergency landing preparations with the senior flight attendant and continues circling while the cabin is prepared.
Flight engineer reports the fuel remaining is about 5,000 lb; the crew discuss fuel but continue holding.
Flight engineer advises that a further fifteen minutes will leave the aircraft very low on fuel; the captain still does not commit to landing.
Captain says he plans to land in about five more minutes and continues briefing the emergency landing.
First officer reports that they are going to lose an engine; engine No. 4 flames out from fuel starvation.
Crew turns toward the airport and requests an immediate clearance; ATC clears the flight for a visual approach to runway 28L.
Flight engineer reports the remaining engines are flaming out.
First officer transmits a Mayday to Portland tower, reporting the engines are flaming out, the aircraft is going down and will not reach the airport.

Aircraft strikes trees and two houses in a wooded residential area about 6 nm southeast of the airport; the fuselage is torn open but there is no fire because the tanks are empty. The flight engineer, a flight attendant and eight passengers die.

recommendations.text: Issue an operations bulletin to all air carrier operations inspectors directing them to urge their assigned operators to ensure that their flightcrews are indoctrinated in principles of flightdeck resource management, with particular emphasis on the merits of participative management for captains and assertiveness training for other cockpit crewmembers.
recommendations.outcome: United Airlines introduced the first airline CRM program in 1981 and CRM training became an industry standard.

recommendations.text: Require inspection of DC-8 main landing gear retract cylinder assemblies for corrosion and require corrective action.

safety_changes: Development and adoption of Crew Resource Management (CRM) training; United's Cockpit Resource Management program began in 1981.
Greater emphasis in airline training on fuel-state awareness and time management during abnormal situations.

notes: Clock times other than 18:06:46 (first flameout) and 18:13:21 are approximate to the minute; t0 is the approximate gear extension time of 17:12 PST.
Occupants 189 (181 passengers, 8 crew) and 10 fatalities as stated by the NTSB; serious injury count of 23 is from memory and may differ.
The 5,000 lb fuel remark at about 17:46 is paraphrased from the transcript; crew speech is paraphrased rather than quoted.
Recommendation A-79-47 wording is recalled from the report; the second recommendation has no id.

records.title: TWA 841
records.summary: While cruising at 39,000 feet near Saginaw Michigan the No. 7 leading-edge slat extended uncommanded causing a sharp right roll and spiral dive. The aircraft descended 34,000 feet in 63 seconds. Pilots recovered at approximately 5,000 feet by extending landing gear. The aircraft made an emergency landing at Detroit with substantial structural damage.
records.probable_cause: The isolation of the No. 7 leading edge slat in the fully or partially extended position after an extension of the Nos. 2 3 6 and 7 leading edge slats and the subsequent retraction of the Nos. 2 3 and 6 slats and the captain's untimely flight control inputs to counter the roll resulting from the slat asymmetry. Contributing to the cause was a preexisting misalignment of the No. 7 slat which when combined with the cruise condition airloads precluded retraction of that slat. (p. 39)

factors.evidence: No. 7 slat extended uncommanded; failure of inboard slat track T-bolt on No. 7 slat predominantly from fatigue (p. 36-39)
Extension of slats was result of flightcrew's manipulation of flap/slat controls (p. 39)
Aircraft descended 34,000 ft in 63 seconds rolling through 360 degrees at least twice (p. 8 39)
Pilots extended landing gear around 15,000 ft and recovered at 5,000 ft; landed Detroit (p. 7 39)

events.text: Aircraft cruising at FL 390 39,000 feet on autopilot Altitude Hold mode; captain organizing charts in flight bag (p. 7)
Captain felt buzzing sensation followed by light buffet; noticed autopilot commanding left turn while ADI showed right bank (p. 7)
Disconnected autopilot applied full left aileron and rudder; aircraft continued rolling right despite control inputs (p. 7)
Aircraft spiraled from 39,000 to 5,000 feet in 63 seconds; rolled through 360 degrees twice (p. 8 39)
Extended landing gear at approximately 15,000 feet; heard loud explosion-like sound (p. 8)
Recovered near wings-level attitude at 5,000 feet; used moon as visual reference to level aircraft (p. 8)
Landed aircraft at Detroit Metropolitan Airport runway 3 without further incident (p. 8)

recommendations.text: Disseminate to all B-727 operators and flightcrews information addressing control problems associated with high-speed asymmetrical leading edge slat configuration on B-727 aircraft including Boeing Operations Manual Bulletin 75-7 and TWA Flight Operations Safety Bulletin 79-3 (p. 40)

safety_changes: Boeing technical bulletins issued to operators
TWA operational bulletins distributed

notes: Read history of flight (p. 7-8), conclusions (p. 36-39), recommendations (p. 40)

records.title: American Airlines 191
records.summary: American Airlines Flight 191, a McDonnell Douglas DC-10 departing O'Hare for Los Angeles, crashed on 25 May 1979 after its left engine and pylon separated during takeoff rotation, killing all 271 aboard and 2 people on the ground in the deadliest US aviation accident. The NTSB found improper maintenance procedures had damaged the pylon, and that the separating engine severed hydraulic lines, causing an uncommanded retraction of the left wing's slats while also cutting power to the captain's instruments, stick shaker, and slat-disagreement warning system.
records.probable_cause: The NTSB found the probable cause was separation of the left engine and pylon assembly during takeoff, caused by damage from improper maintenance procedures, which led to asymmetric stall and loss of control after the slats retracted and stall-warning systems lost electrical power.

factors.evidence: The engine separation was attributed to damage to the pylon structure holding the engine to the wing, caused by improper maintenance procedures at American Airlines (p. 3, 628-631).
As the aircraft was beginning its takeoff rotation, engine number one separated from the left wing, flipping over the top of the wing and landing on the runway (p. 3, 715-717).

As the engine separated it severed hydraulic lines that lock the wing's leading-edge slats in place, and aerodynamic forces resulted in an uncommanded retraction of the outboard slats (p. 3, 634-635).

The number-one electrical bus failed, causing several electrical systems to go offline, most notably the captain's instruments, his stick shaker, and the slat disagreement sensors (p. 3, 621-622, 641-643).

The disrupted and unbalanced aerodynamics caused the aircraft to roll abruptly to the left until it was partially inverted, reaching a bank angle past vertical, before crashing in an open field (p. 3, 589-597).

events.text: Flight 191 cleared for takeoff from runway 32R; captain acknowledges 'American one ninety-one under way'.
During takeoff rotation, sections of the left engine pylon structure come off the aircraft; witnesses see white smoke or vapor from the No. 1 engine pylon area.
The entire No. 1 engine and pylon assembly separate from the aircraft, go over the top of the wing, and fall to the runway.
The cockpit voice recorder captures only a thump and the first officer exclaiming 'Damn!' as the engine detaches; recording then ends due to power loss.
The separating engine severs hydraulic lines that locked the left wing's leading-edge slats, and aerodynamic forces cause an uncommanded retraction of the outboard slats.
The number-one electrical bus fails with the engine, knocking out the captain's instruments, his stick shaker, and the slat-disagreement warning system.
The aircraft lifts off about 6,000 feet down runway 32R, climbs with wings level to about 300 feet above ground.
The aircraft begins to turn and roll to the left, nose pitches down, and aircraft begins to descend.
Aircraft continues rolling left until wings are past the vertical position (inverted), with the nose well below the horizon.
Flight 191 crashes in an open field and trailer park about 4,600 feet northwest of the departure end of runway 32R; the aircraft is destroyed in the impact and ground fire.

recommendations.text: Require a fleetwide inspection of all DC-10 pylon assemblies, including checks for proper clearances, missing or loose fasteners, and structural damage.
Establish standard minimum clearance specifications for spherical bearing assemblies and aft wing clevis to prevent interference.
Enhance surveillance and reporting systems to detect and prevent improper maintenance procedures across the airline industry.
Improve communications and information sharing among operators, manufacturers, and FAA regarding maintenance damage incidents.

safety_changes: DC-10 Type Certificate suspension and subsequent restoration with enhanced inspection requirements
Fleetwide inspection and modification of DC-10 pylon attach points
Enhanced electrical system redundancy in DC-10 aircraft
Improved FAA surveillance procedures for maintenance practices at major carriers

notes: Comprehensive NTSB final report read; key sections: Synopsis (p. 560), History of Flight (p. 700-735), Wreckage and Impact (p. 1172+), and detailed maintenance analysis (p. 2200-2400)
CVR limited due to power loss at time of engine separation
Design deficiency and maintenance error clearly documented as causal factors
This was the deadliest aviation accident in US history at the time of occurrence

records.title: Downeast 46

location.name: Knox County Regional Airport, Rockland, Maine

records.summary: Downeast Airlines Flight 46 crashed into a heavily wooded area 1.2 miles south-southwest of Knox County Regional Airport during a nonprecision instrument approach to runway 3 in instrument meteorological conditions with indefinite ceiling at 300 ft and 3/4 mile visibility in fog. The crew descended the Twin Otter below minimum descent altitude while attempting to see the runway visually. Of 18 occupants, only one passenger survived.
records.probable_cause: The failure of the flightcrew to arrest the aircraft's descent at the minimum descent altitude for the nonprecision approach, without the runway environment in sight, for unknown reasons. Although the Safety Board was unable to determine conclusively the reason(s) for the flightcrew's deviation from standard instrument approach procedures, it is believed that inordinate management pressures, the first officer's marginal instrument proficiency, the captain's inadequate supervision of the flight, inadequate crew training and procedures, and the captain's chronic fatigue were all factors in the accident. (p. 29)

factors.evidence: The crew descended the Twin Otter below minimum descent altitude in order to see the runway in heavy fog. The aircraft impacted terrain 1.2 miles south-southwest of the approach end of runway 3 during the nonprecision approach. (p. 1, 21)

Fog was extremely common at Knox County airport. Reported weather at Rockland was indefinite ceiling at 300 feet, sky obscured, visibility 3/4 mile in fog. Portland weather was reported as indefinite ceiling, 200 feet, visibility 1/4 mile in fog with conditions deteriorating rapidly. (p. 6)
The crash occurred about 2055 e.d.t. during the hours of darkness on May 30, 1979, in conjunction with heavy fog reducing visual references. (p. 1)

The first officer had been with the airline for only about two months and had only flown single-engine aircraft prior to joining the airline. His instrument proficiency was characterized as marginal by the Safety Board. (p. 24-25)

The captain exhibited symptoms of extreme stress and chronic fatigue in weeks before the crash. During the investigation and public hearing, it was revealed the captain was under significant personal and financial stress. (p. 25-28)

Several senior pilots had left Downeast Airlines due to management style and questionable company practices. The company exerted inordinate management pressures on the flight crew regarding flight cancellations and scheduling. (p. 25-28)

Aircraft crashed into heavily wooded terrain 1.2 miles south-southwest of Knox County Regional Airport during nonprecision approach in instrument meteorological conditions. Of 16 passengers and 2 crew aboard, only 1 passenger survived. (p. 1)

events.text: Captain contacted company weather observer at Rockland and obtained current weather: indefinite ceiling 700 ft, visibility 3 mi in fog.
Captain obtained weather briefing from National Weather Service in Boston on actual and forecast weather for Maine; no terminal forecast available for Rockland.
Flight 46 departed Boston on IFR flight plan with 16 passengers and 2 crew aboard for scheduled flight to Rockland via Knox County Regional Airport.
Boston ARTCC requested Flight 46 to contact Navy Brunswick Approach Control (controlling facility for Rockland area), reporting altitude 7,000 ft.
Navy Brunswick cleared Flight 46 to descend to 3,000 ft at captain's discretion for approach into Knox County Regional Airport.

Navy Brunswick radar showed Flight 46's last radar position 3 nmi south of Sprucehead NDB at 1,500 ft altitude. Flight advised radar service was terminated 14 nmi southwest of Sprucehead and to contact Rockland Unicom on new frequency.

Flight 46 transmitted to Navy Brunswick: 'Looks like we're probably going to have to miss the approach here at Rockland. We're going down but maybe you can pull us out a clearance for Augusta.' Navy Brunswick replied clearance was 'on request.'

Flight 46 made last reported radio contact with company facility at airport on Unicom frequency: 'Sprucehead inbound,' indicating continued approach despite deteriorating conditions and crew's earlier concerns about missed approach.

Aircraft crashed into heavily wooded area 1.2 miles south-southwest of approach end of runway 3 in instrument meteorological conditions (indefinite ceiling 300 ft, 3/4 mi visibility in fog). Crash occurred during hours of darkness at latitude 44 degrees 02 min 1 sec N.

recommendations.text: Insure that lighted visibility markers are installed south of the Knox County Regional Airport, Rockland, Maine, within sight in clear visibility conditions of the normal weather observation position. One of the markers should be placed about 3/4 statute mile from the point of observation.
Establish guidelines on the location and number of visibility markers necessary at airports to assure representative surface visibility values for airport runways and the airport runway environment.

Publish a Maintenance Bulletin to alert Federal Aviation Administration maintenance inspectors to the safety hazard associated with installation of mixed-color cockpit instrument lighting and require discontinuation of the practice where implemented.

Require that 14 CFR 135 operators emphasize crew coordination during recurrent training, especially when pilots are qualified for both single-pilot/autopilot and two-pilot operations. These requirements should be outlined in an operator's approved training curriculum.
Upgrade flight operations manuals of 14 CFR 135 operators to assure standardization by clearly delineating operational duties and responsibilities of all required cockpit crewmembers.

safety_changes: Enhanced visibility marker standards at regional airports
Improved crew coordination training requirements
Standardization of cockpit instrument lighting

Weather observations from Navy Brunswick, Portland, and Brunswick facilities documented with ceiling and visibility

records.title: Air New England 248

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report - Air New England, Inc., de Havilland DHC-6-300, N383EX, Hyannis, Massachusetts, June 17, 1979

aircraft.type: de Havilland Canada DHC-6-300 Twin Otter

records.summary: A de Havilland DHC-6 Twin Otter piloted by Air New England co-founder George Parmenter conducted an ILS approach to Barnstable Municipal Airport on June 17, 1979. The aircraft crashed in heavily wooded terrain at Camp Greenough in Yarmouth, Massachusetts, approximately 1.5 miles short of the runway. Parmenter was killed instantly while the co-pilot and several passengers were injured. The National Transportation Safety Board determined that the probable cause was the failure of the flightcrew to recognize and react in a timely manner to the gross deviation from acceptable approach parameters, resulting in a continuation of the descent well below decision height during a precision approach without visual contact with the runway environment.
records.probable_cause: The failure of the flightcrew to recognize and react in a timely manner to the gross deviation from acceptable approach parameters, resulting in a continuation of the descent well below decision height during a precision approach without visual contact with the runway environment. Although the Board was unable to determine conclusively the reason for the failure to recognize and react to the gross deviation, it is believed that the degraded physiological condition of the captain seriously impaired his performance. Also, the lack of adequate crew coordination practices and procedures contributed to the first officer's failure to detect and react to the situation in a timely manner.

factors.evidence: Flight 248 crashed in a heavily wooded area in Yarmouth, several miles short of the runway (p. 2)
The aircraft crashed in the middle of Camp Greenough, a heavily wooded Boy Scouts camp (p. 2)
Crash occurred at 22:48 EDT during night conditions (p. 2)
Aircraft was several miles short of the runway during approach (p. 2)
The degraded physiological condition of the captain seriously impaired his performance (p. 2)

events.text: Flight 248 with eight passengers and two crew began ILS approach to Barnstable Municipal Airport.
Aircraft crashed in the middle of Camp Greenough, a heavily wooded Boy Scouts camp in Yarmouth.
Uninjured passenger managed to make her way through thick brush to the Mid Cape Highway.
Parmenter was killed in the crash; the co-pilot and several passengers were injured.

recommendations.text: Expedite rulemaking which would make the flight time and duty time limitations and rest requirements for commuter air carriers the same as those specified for domestic air carrier crewmembers under 14 CFR 121.

notes: Sections read: Synopsis/Probable Cause (p. 2), Factual Information (p. 2), History of Flight (p. 2), Conclusions (p. 23), Probable Cause (p. 25), Recommendations (p. 25)
Captain's medical history suggests possible incapacitation during approach

records.title: Dan-Air 1008
records.summary: Dan-Air Flight 1008 was cleared to join a nonstandard unpublished holding pattern without a chart. Following ambiguous ATC instructions, the captain turned toward terrain and struck Mount La Esperanza while flying in cloud at 13,500 feet in an area where MSA was 14,500 feet.
records.probable_cause: The pilot in command, without taking account of the altitude at which he was flying, took the aircraft into an area of high terrain and thereby failed to maintain a safe height above terrain. Contributing factors included imprecise navigation and disorientation, ambiguous ATC directions for an unpublished procedure, lack of teamwork between crew members, and the aircraft descending to an altitude inadequate for the holding pattern terrain.

factors.evidence: Aircraft struck Mount La Esperanza at 13:21:15 while flying in cloud at approximately 13,500 feet.
Pilot in command, without accounting for altitude and terrain, flew aircraft into area of high ground; failed to maintain required terrain clearance.
Tardy and ambiguous directions from ATC regarding the unpublished hold directly contributed to disorientation of the aircraft commander.
Aircraft was flying in cloud when it struck the mountain, reducing crew ability to see terrain.
Altitude clearance of 5000 feet was inadequate for this holding pattern area; MSA was 14,500 feet.
Co-pilot did not check or query the operations being carried out by the commander as required by company manual; lack of teamwork between crew.

events.text: Aircraft cleared to join unpublished holding pattern over FP beacon with limited information.
Aircraft turned right to intercept approach but failed to maintain proper heading and turned left toward high terrain.
Ground Proximity Warning System activated as aircraft descended toward high terrain.
Crew initiated climb with engines at full power in response to GPWS warning.
Aircraft struck Mount La Esperanza while in steep turn, totally destroyed; all 146 occupants killed.

recommendations.text: Flight crews should be reminded that precise navigation and adequate vertical terrain clearance are of vital importance.
When there are any doubts about ATC instructions, crews must request clarification before executing maneuvers.
ICAO should clarify ambiguities in documents regarding published holding circuits and definition of 'standard' hold.

dissent.position: ATC transmission regarding holding pattern was ambiguous and contributed directly to crew disorientation. Clearance to descend to 5000 feet was inadequate; MSA should have been 7000 feet minimum. Lack of published holding pattern contributed to accident.

notes: Sections read: History of Flight, Findings, Causes, UK Addendum

records.title: Air Wisconsin 965

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report--Air Wisconsin, Inc., Swearingen SA-226 Metro, N650S, Valley, Nebraska, June 12, 1980

records.summary: Air Wisconsin Flight 965, a Swearingen SA226-TC Metro II, crashed near Valley, Nebraska on June 12, 1980 during descent after encountering severe thunderstorms. Both engines flamed out due to massive water ingestion in severe precipitation, and the crew was unable to regain control of the aircraft. Thirteen of fifteen occupants were killed.
records.probable_cause: The flightcrew's continued flight into an area of severe thunderstorms, and the resultant precipitation-induced flameout or loss of power of both engines at an altitude from which recovery could not be made. Contributing factors were the failure of the flightcrew to utilize all available sources of weather information, the failure of the air traffic control system to disseminate critical weather information to the controllers and crew, failure of ATC supervisory personnel to accomplish key job functions, failure of Center Weather Service Unit meteorologists to disseminate critical weather information, and precipitation-induced X-band radar attenuation which limited the ability of airborne weather radar to detect the extent and intensity of weather disturbances.

factors.evidence: Aircraft entered a region of severe precipitation with very high levels of water ingestion at an altitude of less than 6,000 ft (p. 2)
Both engines flamed out due to massive water ingestion from severe precipitation encountered in flight (p. 2)
Aircraft's weather radar was unable to penetrate even moderate precipitation, leaving crew unaware of extreme precipitation ahead; radar attenuation severely limited its usefulness (p. 51)
Meteorologists in Minneapolis ARTCC had alerted supervisory personnel of severity of weather but information was not disseminated to controllers or to the flight crew (p. 2-3)
Crew lost control and aircraft impacted ground in nose-down attitude and bounced (p. 2)

events.text: Flight 965 departed Appleton, Wisconsin on instrument flight plan.
Flight 965 arrived at Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport.
Flight 965 departed Minneapolis with 13 passengers and 2 crew.
Flight 965 requested and received clearance to maintain 12,000 ft.

O'Neill low sector controller warned of large area of weather at twelve o'clock, about 35 miles, extending from east of Neola around Sioux City to Fremont. Controller advised another aircraft at FL 200 went around; another at 9,000 feet found way through.
Flight 965 requested tower altitude and clearance to descend to 3,000 ft.
Aircraft entered severe precipitation. Engines flamed out from massive water ingestion.
Nine sixty-five, we have lost both engines.
Controller asked Flight 965 to repeat last transmission.
Nine sixty-five, we gottem both, both of them going.
Controller transmitted altitude alert and minimum vector altitude advisory. No response received from Flight 965.
Aircraft crashed into a field near Valley, Nebraska in nose-down, right-wing-low attitude and bounced.

recommendations.text: Expedite the delivery of NWS weather radar color remote displays to all Air Route Traffic Control Centers' Center Weather Service Units.
Schedule the planned testing of NWS weather radar color remote displays at the Cleveland Air Route Traffic Control Center to encompass the next season of frequent convective meteorological activity.
Expedite the development of appropriate graphic mapping techniques for correlation of the NWS weather radar color remote display and the air traffic controller's radar display presentation.

Expedite the development of an integrated weather radar/air traffic control radar single video display system capable of providing multiple weather echo intensity discrimination without derogation of air traffic control radar intelligence.
Require air route traffic control centers to make maximum use of the existing National Weather Service radar sites as inputs to the color remote displays at their facilities.

Undertake an experimental program to analyze and evaluate the technical and operational feasibility of requiring that air traffic control provide separation between aircraft and severe meteorological conditions when the nature and location of the meteorological condition can be determined.
Review the relationship and duties of ARTCC team supervisors to flow controllers/weather coordinators to insure that the nature of each job function is understood and accomplished.

Key sections on pp. 1-3, 5-9, 51-56 extracted with detailed timeline
All events with clock times from report text; t values calculated from 15:45:02 reference
Recommendations extracted directly from report with IDs A-80-115 through A-80-133

records.title: Florida Commuter Airlines Flight 65

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Florida Commuter Airlines, Inc., Douglas DC-3A

location.name: West End Settlement, Grand Bahama Island

records.summary: Douglas DC-3 crashed in Atlantic Ocean with 34 occupants when unrecovered wreckage and lack of flight recorders precluded determining probable cause; contributing factors included pitot blockage from mud dauber nests, pitot-static system discrepancies, thunderstorm activity, and inadequate airline management oversight.
records.probable_cause: Probable cause could not be determined due to unrecovered wreckage and no flight recorders. Contributing factors: thunderstorm activities, pitot-static system discrepancies, and lack of operational control by management.

factors.evidence: Pitot tubes left uncovered for five weeks with mud dauber nests blocking openings; improper maintenance procedure used to clear blockage (p. 19)
Preexisting discrepancies in pitot-static system affecting reliability of flight instruments (p. 19)
Chief mechanic used screwdriver and coat hanger instead of proper procedure to clear blockage (p. 19)
Known thunderstorm activities and turbulence in the area (p. 19)
Replacement pilot believed flight was Part 91, not required to have 6-month currency check (p. 19)
Lack of operational control exercised by airline management (p. 19)
Aircraft crashed into Atlantic Ocean (p. 19)

events.text: Flight 65 attempted departure but aborted due to no airspeed indication
Maintenance determined mud dauber nests blocking pitot tube openings
Flight 65 departed West Palm Beach after reboarding
Flight 65 flew beyond range of Miami radar
Flight 65 made contact with approach controllers at Freeport
Approach cleared Flight 65 to descend to 1400 feet, last communication

records.title: Dan-Air 240
records.summary: Dan-Air Flight 240, Hawker Siddeley HS 748 turboprop, departed London Gatwick on June 26, 1981 with two pilots and cabin attendant on night mail flight. During descent, right rear baggage door opened due to mis-rigged mechanism, detached and lodged on right horizontal tailplane. This caused cabin decompression and aerodynamic changes that made aircraft uncontrollable; wings and tailplane detached from fuselage.
records.probable_cause: Baggage door opened due to mis-rigged operating mechanism that allowed top and bottom pairs of catches to lose synchronization. Door lodged on tailplane causing decompression and aerodynamic changes that rendered aircraft uncontrollable, leading to structural failure.

records.title: 1981 Bristow Helicopters Westland Wessex crash

location.name: North Sea, 12 nm ENE of Bacton, Norfolk

records.summary: A Westland Wessex 60 helicopter operated by Bristow Helicopters transporting workers from North Sea gas platforms to Bacton Gas Terminal experienced loss of power to the main rotor gearbox. The helicopter went out of control during autorotation and crashed into the North Sea. All 13 people on board died. The wreck was beyond recovery by the time salvage operations started, and there was insufficient evidence to determine the cause of the power loss. (p. summary)
records.probable_cause: Insufficient evidence was available to determine the cause of the loss of power to the main rotor gearbox. The wreck could not be recovered, limiting the investigation. An open verdict was recorded.

Helicopter went out of control during autorotation. (summary)
Helicopter crashed into the North Sea. (summary)

During cruise flight, loss of power occurred to main rotor gearbox
Aircraft was in cruise flight en route from Leman to Bacton; emergency power loss initiated uncontrolled descent

records.title: Air Florida 90

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Air Florida, Inc., Boeing 737-222, N62AF, Collision with 14th Street Bridge, Near Washington National Airport, Washington, D.C., January 13, 1982

location.name: 14th Street Bridge over the Potomac River, Washington, D.C.

records.summary: During a heavy snowstorm at Washington National the 737 was de-iced, then waited about 49 minutes in a departure queue with continuing snowfall and with engine anti-ice switched off. Ice in the engine inlet pressure probes caused the EPR gauges to read high, so the crew set what looked like takeoff thrust but was actually far less, and snow and ice on the wings degraded lift. The first officer voiced doubts about the instrument readings during the takeoff roll but the captain continued. The airplane struggled into the air, stalled, and struck the 14th Street Bridge and the frozen Potomac River. Seventy-four of the 79 on board and four people on the bridge died.
records.probable_cause: The flightcrew's failure to use engine anti-ice during ground operation and takeoff, their decision to take off with snow/ice on the airfoil surfaces of the aircraft, and the captain's failure to reject the takeoff during the early stage when his attention was called to anomalous engine instrument readings. Contributing to the accident were the prolonged ground delay between deicing and the receipt of ATC takeoff clearance during which the airplane was exposed to continual precipitation, the known inherent pitchup characteristics of the B-737 aircraft when the leading edge is contaminated with even small amounts of snow or ice, and the limited experience of the flightcrew in jet transport winter operations.

factors.evidence: Engine anti-ice was left off throughout ground operations and takeoff, and the crew departed with snow and ice on the wings after a de-icing that had been followed by 49 minutes of continued snowfall.
Ice blocked the engine Pt2 inlet pressure probes so the EPR gauges indicated the 2.04 takeoff target while the engines were producing thrust equivalent to about 1.70 EPR.
Snow and ice on the wings and leading edges increased stall speed and induced the 737's pitch-up tendency after liftoff.

The crew did not use engine anti-ice as required in icing conditions, used reverse thrust during pushback contrary to guidance, and taxied close behind another jet in an attempt to melt snow with its exhaust.
The first officer repeatedly questioned the engine indications during the takeoff roll but did not insist on rejecting the takeoff and the captain did not respond to his concerns.
Both pilots had limited experience in jet transport winter operations; neither had significant experience of taking off in snow.
The 737 had known pitch-up and roll-off characteristics when its leading edge was contaminated with even small amounts of snow or ice.
The stick shaker activated almost immediately after liftoff and continued until impact.
Air Florida's training and guidance on winter operations, de-icing and contaminated wing takeoffs was limited.
With reduced thrust and contaminated wings the airplane could not accelerate or climb and entered a stall at low altitude.
The airplane descended in a nose-high attitude and struck the bridge and the frozen river.
Survivors were in the icy river for more than 20 minutes before a helicopter rescue; the report identified deficiencies in water rescue capability at the airport.

events.text: The airplane is de-iced at the gate with a glycol mixture in heavy snow; the airport is closed for snow clearance and the flight is delayed.
During pushback the tug slips on the ice; the crew use reverse thrust to try to push back, contrary to the operator's guidance, blowing snow and slush around the airplane.
In the departure queue the crew taxi close behind a DC-9, hoping its exhaust will melt snow from the wings; engine anti-ice remains off.
Tower clears Palm 90 for takeoff on runway 36 with 'no delay on departure' because of landing traffic two and a half miles out.
Takeoff roll begins; the EPR gauges show the 2.04 target but the iced Pt2 probes mean the engines are producing far less thrust.
First officer: 'God, look at that thing. That don't seem right, does it?' and, seconds later, 'Ah, that's not right.'
Captain replies 'Yes it is, there's eighty' and continues the takeoff; the first officer says 'Naw, I don't think that's right' then 'Ah, maybe it is.'
Captain calls 'Hundred and twenty'; the first officer answers 'I don't know.' The acceleration is markedly slower than normal.
'V one' and 'V two' calls; the airplane becomes airborne about 2,000 feet from the end of the runway after a takeoff roll of some 45 seconds.
The stick shaker activates immediately after liftoff and the airplane pitches up with contaminated wings; the captain calls 'forward, forward, easy. We only want five hundred.'
'Stalling, we're falling'; the airplane reaches a maximum height of a few hundred feet and begins to descend.
First officer: 'Larry, we're going down, Larry.' Captain: 'I know it.'
The airplane strikes vehicles and the northbound span of the 14th Street Bridge and plunges through the ice of the Potomac River.
A U.S. Park Police helicopter and bystanders pull the five survivors from the river more than 20 minutes after the crash.

cvr.text: God, look at that thing. That don't seem right, does it?

cvr.speaker: FO
cvr.text: Naw, I don't think that's right.

cvr.speaker: CAPT

recommendations.text: Issue guidance and require training on the effects of wing contamination, the need to re-de-ice after holdover times are exceeded, and the use of engine anti-ice in icing conditions.
recommendations.outcome: The 'clean aircraft concept' was formalized and, after later accidents, 14 CFR 121.629 was revised in 1992 to require approved ground de-icing programs with holdover times.

recommendations.text: Require that flight crews be trained to recognize erroneous engine pressure ratio indications caused by iced inlet probes and to cross-check with N1 and fuel flow.
recommendations.outcome: Boeing and operators added cross-checks of N1 against EPR in icing conditions.

recommendations.text: Require operators to give flight crews training in assertive communication and decision-making so that a takeoff is rejected when either pilot detects abnormal indications.
recommendations.outcome: The accident became a founding case in crew resource management training adopted across U.S. airlines during the 1980s.

recommendations.text: Improve water rescue capability and response planning at airports adjacent to water.
recommendations.outcome: Washington National Airport acquired water rescue equipment and revised its emergency plan.

safety_changes: Airline de-icing practice moved toward the clean aircraft concept with holdover time tables and mandatory re-de-icing, later codified in 14 CFR 121.629.
Boeing reinforced 737 guidance on leading-edge contamination and the use of engine anti-ice, and operators added N1 cross-checks of EPR.
Crew resource management training spread across U.S. carriers, using Flight 90's cockpit exchange as a case study in monitoring and assertiveness.
Water rescue capability at Washington National and other waterside airports was upgraded.

notes: Fatalities (78) comprise 74 of the 79 aboard plus 4 people in vehicles on the bridge; 5 aboard survived with serious injuries.
CVR quotes and clock times follow the widely reproduced public transcript; individual times may be off by one to two seconds.
The ground delay of about 49 minutes between de-icing and takeoff clearance and the pushback and DC-9 taxi episodes are as described in the report; their t values are approximate.
Actual engine thrust is given in the report as about 10,750 pounds per engine versus about 14,500 expected, corresponding to an actual EPR of about 1.70 against an indicated 2.04.
Aircraft MSN is omitted because it is not recalled with confidence.

records.title: World Airways 30
records.summary: World Airways Flight 30 touched down 2800 feet beyond the displaced threshold at Boston Logan on a runway covered with ice. Despite poor braking conditions reported as fair to poor, the aircraft could not be stopped on the runway. The pilots steered the aircraft off the runway to avoid obstacles and it skidded across a field and taxiway before coming to rest in Boston Harbor. The cockpit section submerged but 210 occupants survived. Two passengers, father and son, were missing and presumed drowned. A Delta flight had warned of nil braking conditions 35 minutes prior but this was not relayed to Flight 30.
records.probable_cause: The aircraft touched down long on a runway covered with ice with poor braking action, preventing adequate deceleration to stop on runway length, leading to controlled diversion into Boston Harbor.

factors.evidence: runway was covered in ice, and braking action was poor to nil
DC-10 touched down 2800 ft beyond the displaced threshold
insufficient space remaining on runway to take off again, pilots steered plane off runway
just 35 minutes before, Delta flight reported poor to nil braking but this information was not passed along to oncoming flights
aircraft skidded across field and taxiway before coming to rest in Boston Harbor

events.text: Delta flight reported nil braking conditions 35 minutes before Flight 30H's approach, but this information was not transmitted to incoming flights (p. 3-38)

Flight 30H descended toward Boston-Logan on nonprecision approach to runway 15R (alternate runways 22L available) with runway contaminated with hard-packed snow and glazed ice; weather reported as 800-foot overcast, light rain/fog, temperature 35F (p. 3-37, 3-38)

Captain configured aircraft with 35-degree trailing edge flaps rather than recommended 50-degree flaps for contaminated runway; AT/SC autothrottle system indicated speeds 10 KIAS higher than calculated, suggesting possible weight discrepancy or system malfunction not investigated (p. 3-38, 3-39)

Aircraft touched down 2,800 feet beyond displaced threshold on contaminated runway 15R, leaving only 6,691 feet remaining to stop; aircraft descended below ceiling on nonprecision approach with extended landing flare as airspeed dissipated (p. 3-37, 3-38)

Pilot used all decelerative devices (maximum reverse thrust, ground spoilers, wheel brakes) but could not decelerate aircraft sufficiently; after 43 seconds on ground moving at approximately 49 knots, aircraft veered left to avoid approach light pier at runway end (p. 3-38, 3-39)

Aircraft slid into Boston Harbor after going over seawall; nose section separated from forward fuselage; 2 occupants (father and son) missing and presumed drowned; 210 others evacuated with various injuries (p. 3-37, 3-39)

records.title: Japan Air Lines 350
records.summary: Japan Air Lines Flight 350 crashed into Tokyo Bay during final approach to Haneda Airport after the captain deliberately pushed the aircraft into a dive at very low altitude (164 feet). The captain had experienced auditory hallucinations and a mental health crisis in the hours before the flight. The first officer and flight engineer attempted to recover the aircraft but could not overcome the captain's control inputs. The aircraft impacted the water 510 meters short of runway 33R.
records.probable_cause: The accident resulted from deliberate descent actions by Captain Katagiri who was experiencing a psychiatric crisis manifested by auditory hallucinations, combined with inadequate medical screening and health management that failed to identify his mental condition before he was permitted to operate the aircraft (p. 151-155)

factors.evidence: Captain Katagiri experienced auditory hallucinations and reported to his mother that 'strange things are happening around me' just before accident flight (p. 123-128)
At 08:44:01, Captain Katagiri disengaged autopilot and pushed yoke forward while pulling power levers to idle and engaging thrust reversers (p. 115-120)
First Officer and Flight Engineer attempted to counter captain's control inputs; flight engineer tried to physically restrain captain (p. 115-120)
Inadequate mental health screening and medical oversight failed to identify captain's psychiatric condition before return to duty (p. 130-140)
Aircraft descended rapidly with control column pushed forward; elevator deflection reached +9 degrees nose-down (p. 115-120)
Aircraft impacted Tokyo Bay 510 meters short of runway 33R with nose-down attitude approximately 8 degrees (p. 120-122)

events.text: Japan Air Lines Flight 350 departed Fukuoka on runway 16 with 174 occupants: 8 crew and 166 passengers, with Captain Katagiri at the controls
Aircraft reached cruise altitude of 29,000 feet and transitioned to cruise flight on airway V-17 heading toward Tokyo
Tokyo Control issued descent clearance from cruise altitude to 16,000 feet, and aircraft began descent at 08:22 from position west of Oshima VORTAC

Aircraft transferred to Tokyo Approach Control which issued vector to heading 040 degrees and aircraft continued descent to 3,000 feet, then descended through 8,000 feet when ordered to turn left to heading 360 degrees
Aircraft cleared for ILS approach to runway 33R; current position reported as 16 nautical miles from outer marker; descent profile appeared normal on FDR with speed around 135 knots at 1,000 feet
At 1,000 feet altitude on approach, first officer called 'One Thousand' and instrument checks were confirmed; autopilot coupled approach continuing with landing gear down and flaps at 50 degrees

First officer called 'Five Hundred' at 500 feet altitude during descent; captain did not respond with mandatory 'Stabilized' callout but appeared to acknowledge with nod; descent rate and speed appeared normal
First officer called 'Approaching Minimum' (decision height callout) at 300 feet; captain responded with 'Check' confirming normal procedure; aircraft at approximately 133 knots airspeed

Radio altitude warning sounded three times at 200 feet altitude; middle marker signal began; flight engineer called 'Two Hundred' and first officer called 'Minimum' indicating decision height reached; captain should have called 'Landing' or 'Go Around'

Captain disengaged autopilot and switched to manual control at 164 feet altitude and 130 knots; immediately afterward captain pushed control yoke forward with force and pulled all power levers to idle, engaging thrust reversers on engines 2 and 3
Flight engineer cried out 'We are low' or 'Power low' noticing engine power decrease; aircraft nose dropped abnormally; middle marker signal ceased as aircraft descended below glide slope

First officer reflexively grabbed control column to pull nose up but found it extremely heavy with captain pushing forward with both hands; GPWS 'Glide Slope' warning activated; elevator deflection reached +9 degrees nose-down

Thrust reversers begin to take effect as engines wind down; first officer continues pulling on control column with maximum force trying to raise nose; airspeed dropped to 126 knots; altitude down to 138 feet
First officer succeeds in pulling elevator to approximately -7 degrees (nose-up) but cannot pull further as captain continues pushing down; first officer shouts 'Captain, please stop!'

Aircraft impacts Tokyo Bay water 510 meters short of runway 33R threshold near approach light 14, with nose-down attitude approximately 8 degrees, right bank approximately 7 degrees, and descent angle approximately 18 degrees; left side impact felt by passengers

recommendations.text: Implement comprehensive psychiatric screening program for all flight crew with particular attention to early identification of psychotic disorders and auditory hallucinations
Establish mandatory mental health certification review process for flight crew involving independent psychiatric evaluation, not just internal company medical department
Require flight crews to report any concerning psychological symptoms or behavioral changes to designated medical personnel, with guarantee of impartial evaluation
Enhance cockpit resource management training with focus on procedures for recognizing and responding to incapacitated captain, including override procedures
Strengthen captain medical certification standards and require regular psychiatric evaluation as part of medical certification renewal

records.title: Pilgrim Airlines Flight 458

location.name: Scituate Reservoir, near Providence, Rhode Island

records.summary: Pilgrim Airlines DHC-6-100 experienced an in-flight cockpit fire during cruise at 4,000 feet between Groton and Boston. A leak in the isopropyl alcohol windshield washer/deicer system allowed alcohol to accumulate below the cockpit floor and ignite. The fire spread to the cabin. The crew declared an emergency and diverted to an emergency landing on the ice of the Scituate Reservoir near Providence. One passenger died and eight others were seriously injured.
records.probable_cause: The deficient design of the isopropyl alcohol windshield washer/deicer system and the inadequate maintenance of the system which resulted in an in-flight fire. The ignition source of the fire was not determined.

factors.evidence: The deHavilland DHC-6-100 windshield washer/deicer system design was deficient; a leak in the system allowed isopropyl alcohol to accumulate in the compartment below the cockpit floor (p. 3, p. 7)

Pilgrim Airlines maintenance supervisory personnel did not realize the significance of the repeated maintenance problems in the windshield washer/deicer system and take positive remedial action before the accident (p. 3)

When the tubing disconnected from the pressure side of the pump and the pump was activated, alcohol was sprayed through the compartment where it was ignited; the fire spread from the cockpit to the cabin in flight (p. 3, p. 6)

The crew declared an emergency, diverted to an ice-covered reservoir, and made an emergency water landing; the fire destroyed the aircraft after impact but crew and most passengers survived (p. 2, p. 6)

events.text: Flight 458 blocked out at Groton-New London Airport after crew change with 2 pilots and 10 passengers
Aircraft took off from Groton-New London Airport, cleared to Boston via direct Norwich, V16 airway to Millis, direct Boston at 4,000 feet
Aircraft reached cruise altitude of 4,000 feet, flight proceeding normally under instrument flight rules
Approximately 15 minutes after takeoff, flight crew noted light icing on front windshield; First Officer activated the windshield washer/deicer system with isopropyl alcohol deicing agent
First Officer moved windshield wiper to check deicing effectiveness, saw little deicing fluid; activated deicer system again for several seconds and smelled alcohol
Light gray-white smoke appeared coming up through the opening where the Y-shaped flight control yoke comes through the cockpit floor between the pilots
Captain contacted Quonset TRACON stating 'Quonset-Pilgrim 458 - we need a direct Providence - this is an emergency'
Captain responded 'Directly to Providence please - this is an emergency - there is a fire onboard'
Light smoke changed to heavy, black smoke that filled the cockpit and restricted visibility; crew opened side windows to improve visibility and breathing
As aircraft descended below clouds, fire broke out on the cockpit floor between pilots and in the forward left part of the cabin
Aircraft made emergency landing on 10- to 12-inch-thick ice of the Scituate Reservoir near Providence, Rhode Island
Left main landing gear and right wing with engine separated during impact; fire continued after impact and destroyed the cockpit and cabin areas
Two pilots and 9 of 10 passengers evacuated from the wreckage; one passenger remained in the aircraft

recommendations.text: Issue an Airworthiness Directive to require a redesign and modification of isopropyl alcohol windshield deicing systems installed on DHC-6 aircraft to eliminate the potential for alcohol leakage or, if practicable, to require replacement of these systems with the electrically heated windshields offered by the manufacturer as an alternative installation

Review and evaluate the design of all isopropyl alcohol windshield deicing system installations on aircraft to verify compliance with applicable Federal Aviation Regulations pertaining to flammable fluid fire protection, and take action to correct any deficiencies found

Issue an Operations Bulletin requiring Principal Operations Inspectors of 14 CFR Part 135 operators to determine that oral briefings and safety cards comply with regulations regarding seatbelt usage, that fire extinguishers and safety equipment are accessible with identified locations, and that crews stress importance of PA announcements
Issue a Maintenance Bulletin calling attention to the need for properly functioning public address systems to assure that safety messages by the crew are understandable in all parts of the cabin

Amend 14 CFR 135.155 to make the requirements regarding the accessibility and location of fire extinguishers in passenger compartments of aircraft in commuter service at least as stringent as the requirement in 14 CFR 91.193(e)(4)

Review the training of and the surveillance procedures followed by Federal Aviation Administration inspectors and modify them if necessary to provide increased emphasis on the provisions of 14 CFR Part 135 with regard to occupant safety and safety equipment

safety_changes: Design and certification changes to windshield washer/deicer systems on turboprop aircraft
Improved fire protection standards for flammable fluid systems in aircraft
Enhanced requirements for accessibility and marking of fire extinguishers in commuter aircraft
