records.title: Pan Am 759

location.name: Kenner, Louisiana (residential area near New Orleans International Airport)

records.summary: Pan American World Airways Flight 759, a Boeing 727-235 carrying 145 persons (7 crew, 137 passengers, 1 nonrevenue jumpseat passenger), crashed in the residential area of Kenner, Louisiana, immediately after takeoff from runway 10 at New Orleans International Airport on July 9, 1982. The aircraft lifted off, climbed to 95-150 feet above ground level, then began to descend, striking trees and residential structures. Eight persons on the ground were also killed. The aircraft encountered microburst-induced wind shear producing a strong downdraft and decreasing headwind during the critical liftoff and initial climb phase.
records.probable_cause: The aircraft's encounter with microburst-induced wind shear during liftoff, which imposed a downdraft and a decreasing headwind. Contributing factors included the limited capability of then-current wind shear detection technology, the limited capability of the aircraft to climb out of wind shear with heavy loading, and inadequate wind shear training and recognition by the flightcrew. (p. 72)

factors.evidence: The aircraft's encounter with microburst-induced wind shear during the liftoff imposed a downdraft and a decreasing headwind, which prevented the aircraft from continuing to climb. The microburst produced strong downdraft with wind direction changes from 040 at 8 knots to 070 at 17 knots with peak gusts to 23 knots in approximately 3 minutes. (p. 64-82)

At the time of Flight 759's takeoff, there were showers over the east end of the airport and to the east of the airport along the airplane's intended takeoff path. The winds were gusty, variable, and swirling. Low level wind shear alerts were in effect all quadrants with a frontal system passing overhead. (p. 8)

The flightcrew would have had difficulty recognizing and reacting to the wind shear in time for the aircraft's descent to be stopped. At the time of the accident, wind shear recognition training was limited and Low Level Wind Shear Alert System (LLWSAS) technology was not widely available in commercial aviation. (p. 68-70)

The aircraft struck a line of trees at an altitude of about 50 feet and crashed into the residential area of Kenner at coordinates 29 degrees 59 min 15 sec N, 90 degrees 14 min 08 sec W, destroying six houses and substantially damaging five others. One hundred thirty-seven passengers, 7 crew members, and 8 persons on the ground were killed. (p. 9-10)

events.text: Flight 759 (Clipper 759) taxied from its gate at New Orleans International Airport with 7 crewmembers, 1 nonrevenue passenger on cockpit jumpseat, and 137 passengers (145 total) aboard. Takeoff gross weight 170,000 lbs.

Ground control advised another aircraft of low level wind shear alerts in northeast quadrants of the airport with relevant wind directions and speeds. Clipper 759's radio received this advisory while taxiing.

First officer requested wind check. Ground control replied: Wind now 070 degrees at 17, peak gusts 23, and we have low level wind shear alerts all quadrants, appears to be a frontal passing overhead right now, we're right in the middle of everything.
Captain advised first officer to let your airspeed build up on takeoff and said they would turn off the air conditioning packs for the takeoff to enable increase of EPRs on engines 1 and 3 to 1.92.
Clipper 759 informed tower that it was ready for takeoff from runway 10. Takeoff briefing completed; target EPR 1.90 engines 1 and 3, 1.92 engine 2; V1=138 KIAS, Vr=138 KIAS, V2=151 KIAS.
Local controller cleared Flight 759 for takeoff; first officer acknowledged. This was the last radio transmission received from Clipper 759.

Local controller cleared Eastern Flight 956 to land runway 10 and advised: Wind 070 at 17, heavy Boeing just landed said a ten knot wind shear at about a hundred feet on the final. This advisory was also received on Clipper 759's radio.
Clipper 759 began its takeoff from runway 10. CVR showed Vr and V2 callouts made by captain. Aircraft was at approximately 7,000 feet down the runway at liftoff point.
Aircraft lifted off runway 10, climbed in wings-level attitude to altitude of 95-150 feet above ground level in normal takeoff manner according to witnesses. Aircraft then began to descend.

Aircraft in descent approximately 2,376 feet from end of runway 10, struck line of trees at altitude of about 50 feet above ground level while still in noseup attitude (7-10 degrees by witness reports), indicating aircraft was in stall or low-speed condition.

Aircraft crashed into residential area of Kenner, Louisiana (coordinates 29 degrees 59 min 15 sec N, 90 degrees 14 min 08 sec W), destroying six houses and substantially damaging five others. Aircraft was destroyed in impact, explosion, and subsequent fire. Total 153 fatal injuries (137 passengers, 7 crew, 1 fetus, 8 on ground); 1 serious injury on ground.

recommendations.text: Expedite the installation of Low Level Wind Shear Alert System (LLWSAS) equipment at all major commercial airports, with particular emphasis on those in areas prone to thunderstorm activity and microbursts.

Develop and require specific training for airline crews on recognition and avoidance of low-altitude wind shear, including tactical maneuvers to escape wind shear encounters during takeoff and landing phases.
Evaluate and develop methods to improve aircraft performance during wind shear encounters, particularly regarding climb capability, engine response, and automation logic to assist flight crews.

Require installation of airborne wind shear detection systems on commercial transport category aircraft, to provide real-time wind shear awareness to flight crews during takeoff and landing operations.

safety_changes: Development and installation of Low Level Wind Shear Alert System (LLWSAS) at major airports
Implementation of airborne wind shear detection systems on commercial aircraft
Enhanced wind shear recognition training for airline flight crews
Improved microburst forecasting and nowcasting capabilities
Better communication of wind shear information between ATC and flight crews

records.title: Twilight Zone accident
records.summary: On 23 July 1982, a Bell UH-1B Iroquois helicopter was positioned 25 feet above ground hovering near a large mortar effect during filming of Twilight Zone: The Movie at Indian Dunes in Valencia, California. The helicopter turned 180 degrees and a mortar effect was detonated while the helicopter's tail rotor was still above it. The metal lid on top of the mortar struck the tail rotor, causing it to fail and detach. The helicopter fell and killed actor Vic Morrow and child actors Myca Dinh Le and Renee Shin-Yi Chen on the ground. Six helicopter passengers were injured.
records.probable_cause: The detonation of debris-laden high temperature special effects explosions too near to a low-flying helicopter, leading to foreign object damage to the tail rotor. Failure to establish direct communications and coordination between the helicopter pilot and the film director (p. 1-2).

factors.evidence: Metal lid on top of the mortar struck the tail-rotor, causing the rotor to fail and detach from the tail; tail rotor assembly separated and helicopter descended out of control (p. 1).

Failure to establish direct communications and coordination between Wingo, who was in command of the helicopter operation, and Landis, who was in charge of the filming operation; pilot did not maintain contact with director during maneuvering (p. 2).

Explosions were detonated with helicopter positioned too close at 25 ft altitude while tail rotor still above the mortar; helicopter turned 180 degrees to the left for next camera shot while tail rotor still above mortar effect (p. 1).
The low-flying helicopter spun out of control and fell on top of all three people; helicopter's main rotor blade struck and fatally injured three actors on the ground (p. 1).

events.text: Helicopter pilot Dorcey Wingo stationed Bell UH-1B helicopter 25 feet above ground hovering near large mortar effect during Twilight Zone: The Movie filming at Indian Dunes
Pilot maneuvered aircraft for camera positioning; turned helicopter 180 degrees to the left for next camera shot while tail rotor remained positioned above mortar explosive
Film director Landis initiated detonation of mortar effect while helicopter's tail rotor was still above it; metal lid on top of mortar struck tail rotor
Tail rotor assembly separated from helicopter; foreign object damage and delamination from heat caused tail rotor failure

Helicopter spun out of control and fell; helicopter's main rotor blades struck three people on the ground (actors Vic Morrow, Myca Dinh Le, and Renee Shin-Yi Chen); six helicopter occupants sustained injuries

recommendations.text: Restrict use of helicopters and explosive effects on motion picture sets with specific safety protocols

safety_changes: Establishment of federal safety standards for helicopter use in film and television production
Requirement for clear communications and coordination between helicopter pilots and film directors
Restrictions on explosive effects proximity to aircraft during filming operations

notes: Report extracted from NTSB Aircraft Accident Report AAR-84-14 (superseding AAR-84-02)
Abstract and probable cause from pages 1-2

No direct communications between pilot and director regarding mortar detonation

records.title: 1982 Bristow Helicopters Bell 212 crash
records.summary: Bristow Helicopters Bell 212 G-BDIL departed on a medical evacuation mission from the Treasure Finder platform on September 14, 1982 at 02:25 UTC in darkness, driving rain, and poor visibility. The helicopter searched for the Baffin Seal vessel at very low altitude over the North Sea to locate an injured crewman. The last transmission reported the helicopter five miles north of Murchison platform letting down to surface contact. The helicopter subsequently lost altitude during a right turn and crashed into the North Sea. Investigation found insufficient evidence for definitive cause but identified adverse weather, total darkness, and difficult mission profile as major contributing factors.
records.probable_cause: The investigation found insufficient evidence to determine the specific cause. The helicopter was flown at critically low altitude in darkness with driving rain and high winds, searching for a difficult target, leaving no margin for error. Loss of altitude during a low-altitude right turn proved fatal.

factors.evidence: Flight took place in complete darkness (p. 4).
Driving rain and poor visibility throughout flight (p. 4).
High winds and adverse weather conditions in North Sea (p. 4).
Aircraft crew had been recently awakened for medical evacuation mission (p. 5).
Crew operating at very low altitude while attempting to locate difficult target on dark night (p. 5).
Helicopter lost altitude during a right turn at low altitude while searching for vessel (p. 6).

events.text: Bell 212 G-BDIL lifted off from Treasure Finder platform on course for Baffin Seal location.
Co-pilot reported unable to establish marine VHF communication with vessel; requested navigational assistance from Murchison platform.
Approach control informed helicopter Baffin Seal had searchlight pointing vertically to assist location.
Co-pilot replied they could see Baffin Seal and were in radio communication.
Approach control attempted to call helicopter but received no reply.
Last transmission: Five miles north of Murchison platform letting down to surface contact.
Helicopter lost altitude during right turn at low altitude and plunged into North Sea; all 6 crew perished.

recommendations.text: Review procedures for medical evacuation missions in adverse weather conditions
Implement stricter altitude and visibility minimums for helicopter operations in North Sea

safety_changes: Enhanced weather minimums for offshore helicopter medical evacuation missions
Improved crew resource management training for high-workload low-visibility operations

notes: AAIB investigation explicitly concluded insufficient evidence for definitive cause
Category UNK reflects undetermined nature per SPEC.md
Environmental factors strongly implicated but no single root cause identified
All 6 crew perished in crash; no survivors

records.title: United Airlines 2885
records.summary: A McDonnell Douglas DC-8-54F cargo flight experienced an unstabilized takeoff from Detroit with the horizontal stabilizer incorrectly trimmed to landing configuration instead of takeoff configuration. The crew failed to follow procedural checklists to detect the error. After takeoff, the aircraft climbed to about 1,000 feet with an abnormally steep pitch attitude, then rolled right and descended rapidly into terrain (p. 3-4).
records.probable_cause: The flightcrew's failure to follow procedural checklist requirements and to detect and correct a mistrimmed stabilizer before the airplane became uncontrollable. Contributing to the accident was the captain's allowing the second officer, who was not qualified to act as a pilot, to occupy the seat of the first officer and to conduct the takeoff (p. 28).

factors.evidence: The horizontal stabilizer trim was at 7.6 units ANU at impact, which was the previous landing trim setting instead of takeoff configuration (p. 28). The flightcrew inadvertently overlooked setting the stabilizer trim for takeoff (p. 28).

The flightcrew failed to follow procedural checklist requirements to detect and correct the mistrimmed stabilizer (p. 28). Had any one of six distinct procedural requirements involving all three crewmembers been followed, the stabilizer landing trim should have been set within acceptable limits at takeoff (p. 28).

The captain allowed the second officer, who was not qualified to act as a pilot, to occupy the seat of the first officer and to conduct the takeoff (p. 3). The second officer had failed to qualify as a DC-8 first officer and subsequently lost the B-737 first officer qualification after a year on the line (p. 28).
The captain and first officer did not have the prescribed crew rest prior to the trip sequence and might have been fatigued (p. 28).

After takeoff, the aircraft's pitch attitude steepened abnormally, and it climbed to about 1,000 feet above ground level. The engines surged during the climb causing visible flames to emit from the engines (p. 28).
After reaching approximately 1,000 feet, the airplane then rolled to the right and descended rapidly to the ground (p. 3).
An explosion and fireball occurred at impact. The airplane was destroyed by impact and by the postimpact fire (p. 3).

events.text: The first officer and second officer swapped duty stations about 6.5 seconds before takeoff with the approval of the captain, with the second officer moving to the first officer seat (p. 28).
Aircraft called for clearance onto runway 21R at 02:49:58 and was cleared for takeoff at 02:50:03 (p. 4).
Takeoff roll was normal and the airplane rotated to takeoff attitude one-half to two-thirds of the way down runway 21R (p. 4).
After liftoff, the airplane's pitch attitude steepened abnormally, and the aircraft began climbing rapidly from the runway surface (p. 4).
The airplane climbed to about 1,000 feet above ground level with the engines surging during the climb, causing visible flames to emit from the engines (p. 28).
After reaching approximately 1,000 feet, the airplane rolled to the right and began descending rapidly to the ground (p. 3).
Aircraft continues rapid descent from approximately 500 feet altitude with increasing right roll (p. 3).

An explosion and fireball occurred as the aircraft impacted terrain. The airplane was destroyed by impact and postimpact fire. The flightcrew, consisting of the captain, the first officer, and the second officer, were killed (p. 3).

records.title: Reeve Aleutian Airways 8
records.summary: During cruise climb from Cold Bay to Seattle, the No. 4 propeller separated from the Lockheed L-188C Electra, struck the fuselage creating an eight-foot gash, depressurizing the cabin and jamming flight and engine controls. The crew diverted to Anchorage using unconventional control methods including autopilot and landing gear manipulation. All 15 occupants survived.
records.probable_cause: The propeller on engine No. 4 separated in flight. The exact cause of the propeller separation was not determined since the propeller fell in the ocean during the occurrence.

factors.evidence: The No. 4 propeller separated from the aircraft and struck the fuselage, creating an eight-foot gash in the lower fuselage (p. 1)
The propeller strike resulted in decompression of the cabin (p. 1)
The flight controls became jammed and the engines would not respond to throttle movement (p. 1)
The crew were only able to climb and descend by retracting and extending the landing gear with the No. 2 engine shut down (p. 1)
The aircraft was landed safely at Anchorage with no injuries to the 15 occupants despite severe damage (p. 1)

events.text: Aircraft departed Cold Bay Airport for Seattle, Washington
Aircraft climbed through FL190 toward FL250, indicating cruise climb phase
Aircrew noted unusual vibration; attempts to isolate the vibration were unsuccessful
Flight engineer went aft to observe the engines and propellers but noted nothing unusual
Flight attendant went forward to advise captain that nothing was observed
Vibration increased in intensity
No. 4 propeller separated from the aircraft and struck the fuselage, causing major damage to the lower fuselage
Cabin depressurized and flight controls became jammed; engines would not respond to throttle movement
Crew diverted to Anchorage International Airport and used autopilot for minimal control
Crew climbed and descended by retracting and extending the landing gear with No. 2 engine shut down to manipulate aircraft attitude
Aircraft landed safely at Anchorage International Airport; veered off runway into a ditch but all occupants survived
Engines were shut down to decelerate the aircraft

records.title: Air Canada 143 (Gimli Glider)
records.time_reference: CDT (local); the report gives few exact clock times, so t is relative to the first fuel-pressure warning at about 20:00 CDT

agencies.name: Canadian Aviation Safety Board (predecessor of TSB)
agencies.report_title: Final Report of the Board of Inquiry Investigating the Circumstances of an Accident Involving the Air Canada Boeing 767 Aircraft C-GAUN that Effected an Emergency Landing at Gimli, Manitoba on the 23rd Day of July, 1983 (Lockwood Board of Inquiry)

location.name: Gimli Industrial Park Airport (former RCAF Station Gimli), Manitoba

records.summary: The new Boeing 767 was dispatched from Montreal with its fuel quantity indicators blank after a maintenance circuit-breaker mix-up. The fuel load was determined by dripstick, but the litres were converted to kilograms using the pounds-per-litre factor, so the aircraft carried less than half the fuel required. Both engines flamed out over Ontario at 41,000 ft; the crew glided the airliner to a dead-stick landing on a disused runway at Gimli, Manitoba, and all 69 occupants survived.
records.probable_cause: The Board of Inquiry found that the aircraft ran out of fuel because the fuel quantity was calculated with an incorrect conversion factor after the fuel quantity indicating system had been rendered inoperative, and because the aircraft was dispatched contrary to the minimum equipment list. Underlying deficiencies included the unresolved FQIS defect, confusion over the maintenance log and MEL, Air Canada's incomplete transition to metric fuel measurement on its first metric aircraft, and the absence of a clearly assigned responsibility and training for fuel-quantity calculations without a flight engineer.

factors.evidence: The fuel quantity indicating system had a known intermittent fault in one processor channel that had not been rectified; a replacement part was not available.

A technician in Edmonton had deactivated the faulty channel by pulling and tagging a circuit breaker; in Montreal another technician reset it during troubleshooting, blanking the gauges, and did not restore the earlier configuration or clearly record what he had done.
The aircraft was dispatched with blank fuel gauges although the MEL did not permit it; the captain understood from the log and discussions that it had been flown that way and was acceptable.
Neither the flight crew nor the ground personnel had been trained to perform fuel-quantity calculations by dripstick in metric units for the 767, Air Canada's first metric aircraft.
The inquiry criticised Air Canada's corporate procedures, the ambiguity over who was responsible for fuel calculations on the two-crew 767, and the handling of the FQIS defect and MEL.

The 7,682 litres measured by dripstick were converted with a factor of 1.77 (pounds per litre) instead of 0.8 (kilograms per litre), so the crew believed they had 22,300 kg when the aircraft held roughly 10,000 kg.
The fuel was exhausted in cruise at 41,000 ft near Red Lake, Ontario, well short of Edmonton.
The left engine flamed out first, followed a few minutes later by the right; the aircraft lost all generated electrical power and most instruments, leaving the ram air turbine for hydraulics.
The crew glided the aircraft to a dead-stick landing on runway 32L at the former RCAF station at Gimli, which was in use as a motor-racing venue.

events.text: The previous day in Edmonton a technician finds the fuel quantity processor's channel 2 faulty; he deactivates it by pulling and tagging a circuit breaker so the gauges work on one channel, and logs the fault with a reference to the MEL.
In Montreal a technician troubleshooting the fault resets the circuit breaker; the fuel gauges go blank. He is called away and does not pull the breaker again or make a clear log entry.

Captain Pearson sees the blank fuel gauges and the log entry; from the log and discussions with maintenance he concludes the aircraft has been flying in this condition and is dispatchable, although the MEL does not permit it.

The fuel tanks are dripsticked: 7,682 litres. Ground crew and pilots convert to mass using 1.77, the pounds-per-litre factor, instead of 0.8 kg per litre, and compute an uplift to reach 22,300 kg. The actual total after fuelling is roughly 10,000 kg.
Departs Montreal for Ottawa with the erroneous fuel figure entered manually into the flight management computer.
After a second dripstick check in Ottawa using the same wrong factor, the aircraft departs for Edmonton with 61 passengers and 8 crew.
Cruising at 41,000 ft near Red Lake, Ontario, a warning indicates low fuel pressure at the left engine's forward boost pump; the crew initially suspect a pump failure.
A second fuel-pressure warning follows; the crew decide to divert to Winnipeg.
The left engine flames out. The crew begin a descent toward Winnipeg on one engine and declare an emergency.

The right engine flames out; the 'all engines out' condition leaves the electronic flight instruments blank. The ram air turbine deploys to provide hydraulic pressure for the flight controls; only standby instruments remain.
First Officer Quintal, using DME distance and altitude, determines the aircraft cannot reach Winnipeg and proposes the former RCAF base at Gimli, where he once served, about 12 nm away.
Captain Pearson glides the aircraft at about 220 kt toward Gimli; the landing gear is released by gravity but the nose gear fails to lock.
Finding the aircraft too high and fast on final, the captain flies a forward slip to lose altitude without gaining speed.

Touchdown on Gimli runway 32L, which is in use as a drag-racing strip with people on it; the nose gear collapses and the aircraft stops short of the spectators. All 69 evacuate; 10 sustain minor injuries.

recommendations.text: Establish clear responsibility for, and training in, fuel quantity calculations for two-crew aircraft operating in metric units, and ensure MEL restrictions on the fuel quantity indicating system are unambiguous and enforced.
recommendations.outcome: Air Canada revised its fuelling and MEL procedures and metric training.

recommendations.text: Improve the reliability and support of the 767 fuel quantity indicating system and the maintenance recording practices that led to the defect being carried unresolved.

safety_changes: Air Canada revised its fuel-loading procedures, metric conversion training and MEL handling for the 767 fleet.
The accident became a standard case study in unit-conversion error and in dispatch with inoperative fuel indication.
Boeing improved the fuel quantity processor's reliability on the 767.

notes: The formal investigation was the Lockwood Board of Inquiry (report April 1985) with Transport Canada's Aviation Safety Bureau; the agency code TSB with the CASB name is used as instructed.
Event times are approximate reconstructions; the report's exact clock times were not available, so all clock fields are null and t is relative to the first fuel-pressure warning at about 20:00 CDT.
The altitude at which the second engine failed is not stated in the record because sources differ.
The actual fuel on board figure is given as roughly 10,000 kg; some accounts cite 10,100 kg or 4,916 litres uplifted.

records.title: Air Illinois 710

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report - Air Illinois Hawker Siddeley HS 748-2A, N748LL, near Pinckneyville, Illinois, October 11, 1983

records.summary: An Air Illinois HS 748 crashed near Pinckneyville, Illinois after takeoff from Springfield. The first officer mistakenly isolated the right generator instead of the left, degrading electrical power. The crew failed to properly manage the remaining electrical load, and when the battery depleted, the aircraft lost flight instruments and navigation radios. The crew descended to 2400 feet and crashed in a hilly pasture. All 10 occupants were killed.
records.probable_cause: The captain's decision to continue the flight toward the more distant destination airport after the loss of d.c. electrical power from both airplane generators instead of returning to the nearby departure airport. The captain's decision was adversely affected by self-imposed psychological factors which led him to assess inadequately the airplane's battery endurance after the loss of generator power and the magnitude of the risks involved in continuing to the destination airport. Contributing to the accident was the airline management's failure to provide and the FAA's failure to assure an adequate company recurrent flightcrew training program which contributed to the captain's inability to assess properly the battery endurance of the airplane before making the decision to continue, and led to the inability of the captain and the first officer to cope promptly and correctly with the airplane's electrical malfunction.

factors.evidence: The captain had a habit of violating safety regulations in order to arrive on time (p. 62)
The first officer mistakenly pushed the right generator isolate button instead of the left generator isolate button without checking the gauges and warning lights (p. 62)
The first officer did not check the gauges and warning lights to confirm which generator was the problem (p. 62)
The crew shut off excess lights in the cabin but did not further reduce the electrical load on the aircraft's battery (p. 62)
The battery was depleted resulting in failure of flight instruments and radios, and the aircraft crashed (p. 62)

events.text: Flight 710 took off from Springfield Airport at 20:20 CDT.
The crew reported a slight electrical problem and would keep air traffic control advised.
The first officer mistakenly pushed the right generator isolate button instead of the left generator isolate button without checking the gauges.
The first officer reported to the captain that the left generator was totally dead.
The crew shut off excess lights in the cabin but did not further reduce the electrical load on the aircraft's battery.
At 20:52 the captain decided to descend to 2400 feet from where the aircraft slowly descended into a hilly pasture area.
The aircraft crashed in the hilly pasture near Pinckneyville with all ten on board perishing.

recommendations.text: Issue an air carrier maintenance bulletin to emphasize the need for air carrier airworthiness inspectors to require during certification and the need to conduct surveillance to verify conformity.
Issue air carrier maintenance and operations bulletins to emphasize regulatory requirements related to recording of mechanical irregularities in maintenance logs and proper surveillance.

dissent.position: While the accident report correctly identifies training and surveillance, the pilot should never have continued the flight to the destination airport but should have returned to the nearby airport upon realizing electrical d.c. power had been lost.

notes: Sections read: Synopsis (p. 4), Factual Information (p. 5), History of Flight (p. 5), Conclusions (p. 65), Findings (p. 62), Probable Cause (p. 65), Recommendations (p. 65)
Dissenting statement from Patricia A. Goldman noted

records.title: Ozark Air Lines 650
records.summary: On December 20, 1983, while landing on Runway 3 in deteriorating visibility with snow removal operations in progress, the DC-9's right wing struck a large snowsweeping vehicle called Sweeper 7, destroying it and killing its driver Douglas Stoner. The impact ripped the right wing from the aircraft causing it to spin 180 degrees. The tower had not advised the flight crew that snow removal operations were in progress.
records.probable_cause: Inadequate supervision of snow removal operations by the tower; no communications had been made between the tower and the snow plow operator after the flight was handed off to the tower controller.

factors.evidence: Neither the approach nor tower controller had advised the flight that snow removal operations were in progress (p. 2)
No communications had been made between the tower and Sweeper 7 after Flight 650 was handed off to the tower controller (p. 2)
The DC-9's right wing then struck a large snowsweeping vehicle on the runway (p. 2)
The impact ripped the right wing from the plane, destroying the snow plow (p. 2)

When Flight 650 was about 4 miles out from the airport, the Sioux Falls approach controller directed the flight to contact the airport tower

The DC-9's right wing then struck a large snowsweeping vehicle on the runway, ripping the right wing from the plane and destroying the snow plow with its driver, killing Douglas Stoner age 38
The plane spun through 180 degrees before coming to rest off the runway to the left of the centerline with leaking fuel briefly creating a fireball

records.title: Scandinavian Airlines System 901
records.summary: Scandinavian Airlines DC-10 overran Runway 04R at JFK while landing from Stockholm after a stopover in Oslo. All 177 occupants survived, though 12 were injured. The crew approached at an unusually high speed of 205 knots due to autothrottle malfunction and failure to monitor airspeed, touching down long and veering into shallow water 650 feet from the runway.
records.probable_cause: The flightcrew's disregard for prescribed procedures for monitoring and controlling airspeed during the final stages of the approach, decision to continue the landing rather than to execute a missed approach, and overreliance on the autothrottle speed control system which had a history of recent malfunctions. (p. 3)

factors.evidence: The autothrottle system had undergone recent malfunctions, and the crew relied heavily on it for speed control during final approach rather than monitoring actual airspeed. (p. 24)

During descent from 700 to 70 feet, indicated airspeed climbed to a peak of 209 knots, significantly above the desired approach speed, but the crew did not detect or respond to this excessive airspeed. (p. 24)
The captain stated 'It didn't take power off,' indicating he expected the autothrottle to manage the approach automatically, but the system failed to retard throttles at the proper time. (p. 24)
Despite the unstable approach with excessive airspeed, the crew decided to continue the landing rather than execute a missed approach. (p. 3)
The aircraft touched down approximately 4,600 feet down the 10,000-foot runway due to the high approach speed, leaving insufficient distance to stop. (p. 24)
The aircraft overran Runway 04R and came to rest in shallow water 650 feet beyond the runway after passing through and damaging the approach light structure. (p. 11)

events.text: Aircraft was approximately 2,000 feet above ground level, tracking 015° true at about 130 knots indicated airspeed with autothrottles engaged in speed mode.
Aircraft descended to 1,500 feet AGL and No. 2 autopilot ILS mode was selected; aircraft began turning toward runway heading.
Flaps began descent from 15° to 22° position; autopilot switched to glideslope capture mode; N1 began decreasing to flight idle and aircraft pitched over to begin descent.

During first 30 seconds of descent from 1,500 to 870 feet AGL, throttle position and engine N1 went to flight idle, indicated airspeed increased to 190 knots then began to decrease, and flaps started down to 35° position.
From 870 to 700 feet, throttles and engine N1 came up to about 84 percent and indicated airspeed began climbing from 189 knots; flaps reached 35° position.

For 32 seconds from 700 to 70 feet radio altitude, throttle position and N1 remained at about 84 percent while indicated airspeed continued to climb to a peak of 209 knots. As airspeed increased past 193 knots, flap limiting system began to retract flaps. Autopilot switched from command to control wheel steering mode.
Captain stated 'It didn't take power off,' indicating the autothrottle failed to retard throttles as expected.

At approximately 50 feet radio altitude, pitch began increasing, airspeed began decreasing from peak of 209 knots, flaps began to extend back to 35° setting, and autothrottles went from speed mode to retard mode.
Flaps arrived at 35° setting, airspeed had decreased to 185 knots at approximately 20 feet radio altitude, aircraft well below desired glide path for continuation of approach.
Aircraft touched down on Runway 04R at indicated airspeed of approximately 179 knots and groundspeed of 179 knots at 4,600 feet down the 10,000-foot runway.

Within 0.7 second after touchdown, spoiler handle came out of retract position, spoiler panels deployed from zero degree position, vertical acceleration peaked, and thrust reversers on engines 1 and 3 were recorded in stowed position.
Nose gear strut switch transitioned to ground position; wheel brakes still in off position; spoiler panels deployed to approximately 60 degrees.
Recorded data showed both wheel brakes activated; No. 1 thrust reverser in stowed position with N1 at flight idle on all three engines.
Aircraft came to rest in shallow water 650 feet beyond end of Runway 04R after passing through approach light structure.

recommendations.text: Apply the findings of behavioral research programs and accident/incident investigations regarding degradation of pilot performance as a result of automation to modify pilot training programs and flight procedures so as to take full advantage of the safety benefits of automation technology.

Direct air carrier principal operations inspectors to review the airspeed callout procedures of assigned air carriers and, where necessary, to require that these procedures specify the actual speed deviations (in appropriate increments, e.g., +10, +20, -10, -20, etc.) from computed reference speeds.

safety_changes: Scandinavian Airlines modified DC-10 flight procedures to require manual backup of autothrottle and emphasize airspeed as primary control reference
Increased emphasis in pilot training on automation limitations and the need for continuous airspeed monitoring

Probable cause and recommendations from pp. 3, 53-54

records.title: Vieques Air Link 901A

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report - Vieques Air Link, Inc. Flight 901A

location.name: Atlantic Ocean, approximately 1/2 mile north of runway 9 at Vieques Airport

records.summary: Vieques Air Link Flight 901A, a Britten-Norman Islander, crashed into the Atlantic Ocean shortly after takeoff from Vieques Airport on August 2, 1984. The pilot and eight passengers were killed. Investigation revealed the left engine failed due to water-contaminated fuel that had entered the airport's underground fuel storage tank following heavy rains. The pilot, inadequately trained for multi-engine operations, failed to execute proper emergency procedures after engine failure, leading to loss of control and impact with the sea.
records.probable_cause: The accident resulted from the failure of the pilot to execute the emergency engine-out procedure properly shortly after takeoff following a loss of power in the left engine because of water in the airplane's fuel system and the failure of the Puerto Rico Ports Authority to remove excess water known to be in the airport's in-ground fuel tank before conducting fueling operations. The pilot's failure to execute the engine-out procedure properly was due to his inexperience in multi-engine airplanes. Contributing to the accident were: (1) the air carrier's use of a pilot not certificated for the flight; (2) the air carrier's failure to train the pilot adequately; (3) the pilot's failure to follow proper practices to detect water in the airplane's fuel tanks; (4) the out of weight and balance condition of the airplane; (5) the FAA's incorrect application of 14 CFR Part 135 Rules to commuter air carriers; and (6) the FAA's generally inadequate surveillance of the air carrier.

factors.evidence: Left fuel tank filled with water-contaminated fuel from the airport's underground storage tank on August 2 at approximately 0740 AST. The No. 2 tank at Vieques showed 1.5 inches of water when tested at 0645 AST on the morning of the accident following heavy rains (p. 6).

No. 1 (left) engine lost power when aircraft was at approximately 200 feet during initial climb, shortly after takeoff. Physical evidence revealed conclusively that the left engine was not producing power on impact, and fresh water was found in the left engine fuel system (p. 4, 29).

Aircraft appeared to lose power when about 200 feet above the ocean, then gained about 50 feet before descending into the ocean. The left propeller was not feathered and flaps were found full down, indicating pilot did not follow prescribed emergency procedures. Aircraft rolled left abruptly and pitched down steeply, indicating loss of control when airspeed decreased below minimum control speed (p. 4, 29-30).

Pilot claimed 1,088 hours total flying time and 480 hours in the BN-2A Islander but investigation disclosed he had at most only 72 total hours, 182 of which were multi-engine experience with only 37 hours of dual instruction. He was inadequately trained in multi-engine emergency procedures (p. 8, 30).

Aircraft was estimated to be as much as 600 to 700 pounds over its certificated TOGW, and its center of gravity was as much as 5 inches aft of its 25.6 inch rearmost limit. This adverse weight and balance condition would decrease response time available for pilot to maintain control and reduce performance capabilities (p. 30).

Pilot was not qualified to fly as pilot-in-command of a commuter air carrier flight or as pilot-in-command of an extra section of a commuter air carrier flight. He was restricted to on-demand flights only per his Certificate of Proficiency (p. 8).

The Puerto Rico Ports Authority failed to remove the 1.5 inches of water from the No. 2 tank before allowing the aircraft to be fueled. Water had accumulated due to heavy rains and was known to be present at 0645 AST before the aircraft was refueled (p. 6).
FAA's generally inadequate surveillance of the air carrier and incorrect application of 14 CFR Part 135 Rules to commuter air carriers contributed to the accident (p. 4).

events.text: Pilot reported for duty at Vieques Airport for the day's operations

Ramp inspector drained the gasoline pump filter and tested the fuel storage tanks for water. No. 2 tank indicated 1.5 inches of water, which was higher than the previous day and the highest in recent recorded history
Pilot flew aircraft N589SA to Fajardo, Puerto Rico, with nine passengers stowed and returned to Vieques at 0736

After deplaning passengers in Vieques, pilot taxied N589SA to the gas pump where 30 U.S. gallons of 103/130 octane low lead fuel were added to each wing tank from the contaminated No. 2 tank. Pilot did not drain fuel tank sumps and no witness saw pilot check for water or drain the sumps

Flight 901A departed from the ramp at Vieques with eight passengers aboard, all of whom had reserved seats and purchased tickets for Flight 901. Pilot contacted UNICOM as he taxied out to the takeoff end of runway 9

Aircraft appeared to climb out normally after takeoff. As aircraft turned left in a crosswind departure pattern at approximately 200 feet altitude, it appeared to lose power in the left engine due to water in the fuel system
Aircraft gained approximately 50 feet of altitude while in a nose-high attitude as pilot may have attempted recovery, then engines appeared to develop more power momentarily

With left propeller not feathered and flaps found full down (at 25 degrees takeoff configuration), pilot did not execute prescribed emergency engine-out procedures including feathering propeller, allowing airspeed to increase to best single-engine rate of climb speed of 65 KIAS, and retracting takeoff flaps

Aircraft rolled abruptly to the left and pitched down steeply, indicating loss of directional control when airspeed decreased below minimum control speed (Vmc) of 39 KIAS. Aircraft crashed into the Atlantic Ocean approximately 1/2 mile north of runway 9. Wreckage sank in approximately 18 feet of water

recommendations.text: Issue an Airworthiness Directive applicable to Pilatus Britten-Norman BN-2, BN-2A, BN-2B, BN-2T, and BN-2A Mk I model airplanes requiring the incorporation of Britten Norman modification NB/M/350 to provide increased protection from fuel contamination

Amend the FAA's operations specifications applicable to Vieques Air Link, Inc., and other U.S. operators of Pilatus Britten-Norman BN-2, BN-2A, BN-2B, BN-2T, and BN-2A Mk III model airplanes engaged in commuter/air taxi operations, to require that preflight checks for fuel contamination be made before the first flight of the day and after each refueling operation in strict accordance with the manufacturer's instructions

Require Pilatus Britten-Norman to install a device to measure airplane attitude, e.g., a small bubble-level, on all BN-2, BN-2A, BN-2B, BN-2T, and BN-2A Mk III model airplanes delivered in the United States in order to provide a ready means for ensuring the airplane is level during preflight checks for fuel contamination. Concurrently, require Britten Norman to develop a service kit or modification instructions to retrofit existing BN-2, BN-2A, BN-2B, BN-2T, and BN-2A Mk II mode airplanes with a similar device

Require Pilatus Britten-Norman to prepare and disseminate a Safety Advisory relating to water in the fuel to all operators of BN-2, BN-2A, BN-2B, BN-2T, and BN-2A Mk III model airplanes. The advisory should outline the circumstances relating to the Vieques Air Link accident of August 2, 1984, and the criticality of proper preflight fuel tank drainage procedures, and should urge operators to incorporate Britten Norman Modification NB/M/380 in their airplanes

records.title: 1984 San Luis Obispo mid-air collision

aircraft.type: Beechcraft C-99 Commuter and Rockwell Commander 112

location.name: 8 nm west-northwest of San Luis Obispo County Airport

records.summary: Wings West Airlines Flight 628 (Beechcraft C-99) collided head-on at 3,400 feet with a Rockwell Commander 112 during initial climb near San Luis Obispo, California. Both aircraft were destroyed and all 17 occupants perished. The NTSB determined that both flight crews' decisions to operate under VFR instead of IFR prevented air traffic control from detecting and preventing the collision threat.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause of this accident was the failure of the pilots of both aircraft to follow the recommended communications and traffic advisory practices for uncontrolled airports contained in the Airman's Information Manual to alert each other to their presence and to enhance the controller's ability to provide timely traffic advisories. Underlying the accident were the physiological limitations of human vision and reaction time. Also underlying the accident was the short time available to the controller to detect and appraise radar data and to issue a safety advisory. Contributing to the accident was the Wings West Airlines policy which required its pilots to tune one radio to the company frequency at all times. (p. 4-5)

factors.evidence: Flight 628 pilots failed to monitor local aviation radio transmissions, monitoring the appropriate frequency for only the first 5 miles of flight. (p. 4-5)
Both aircraft crews chose to fly VFR instead of IFR despite being in controlled airspace, depriving themselves of air traffic control radar separation. (p. 4)
Both flight crews failed to detect the other aircraft visually in sufficient time to initiate evasive action. (p. 4)

Despite clear skies, the Beechcraft pilots would have noticed the Commander only about 10 seconds before collision, and Commander pilots saw the Beechcraft 6-8 seconds before impact. Given physiological limitations of human vision and the rapid closure rate of head-on approach, detection was marginal. (p. 6)
Flight 628 collided head-on with Commander N112SM at altitude 3,400 feet near San Luis Obispo at 11:17:38 PDT. (p. 4)

events.text: Wings West Flight 628 (Beechcraft C-99 N6399U) pushed back from gate at San Luis Obispo County Airport with 13 passengers and 2 crew
Los Angeles ARTCC radar controller answered Flight 628 after delay due to congestion on frequency
Flight 628 reported climbing through 2,700 feet, IFR to San Francisco
Controller assigned discrete transponder code 6721 to Flight 628
Flight 628 took off from runway 29 at San Luis Obispo County Airport bound for San Francisco
Controller reported Flight 628 in radar contact 6 miles northwest of San Luis Obispo airport and requested altitude
Los Angeles ARTCC cleared Flight 628 to San Francisco as filed, climb and maintain 7,000 feet
Flight 628 acknowledged clearance by reading back to controller; seconds later controller lost radar contact
Wings West Flight 628 collided head-on with Rockwell Commander N112SM at 3,400 feet near San Luis Obispo; both aircraft destroyed

recommendations.text: Issue an Air Carrier Operations Bulletin directing the Principal Operations Inspectors of Wings West and Imperial Airlines to require that the airlines amend their operating procedures so that their flights contact Los Angeles Center prior to departure from San Luis Obispo County Airport and obtain either an IFR clearance or a discrete transponder code if departing VFR.

Require that the instrument approach chart for the localizer approach to runway 11 at San Luis Obispo County Airport and the Crepe One Departure Chart include a cautionary note with appropriate communication frequencies advising VFR flights on practice instrument approaches and departures to contact Los Angeles Center for traffic advisories.
Disseminate the contents of this safety recommendation letter to fixed based operators in the general vicinity of the San Luis Obispo County Airport.

records.title: PBA 1039
records.summary: PBA Flight 1039 received takeoff clearance and began the takeoff roll from Runway 31. Thirty seconds after takeoff, witnesses saw the aircraft in a steep descent. The horizontal stabilizer, elevators, tail cone, and ventral fin separated from the aircraft in flight. Investigation found fractures in hinge brackets from overstress and multiple potential causes including elevator control system or trim system malfunction.
records.probable_cause: Malfunction of either the elevator control system or the elevator trim system, which resulted in an airplane pitch control problem. The reaction of the flight crew to correct the pitch control problem overstressed the left elevator control rod, which resulted in asymmetrical elevator deflection and overstress failure of the horizontal stabilizer attachment structure. The Safety Board was not able to determine the precise problem with the pitch control system (p. 6-7)

factors.evidence: Malfunction of either elevator control system or elevator trim system resulted in pitch control problem; left elevator control rod overstressed (p. 6-7)
Aircraft design lacked fail-safe elevator control systems susceptible to overstress separation; EMB-110 had history of elevator control problems with one disconnected rod and broken trim tabs (p. 15)
Lack of cockpit voice recorder and flight data recorder hampered investigation; maintenance records showed last inspection September 20, 1984 complying with AD 82-27-69 found no defects (p. 15)
Horizontal stabilizer and elevators separated from aircraft in flight; male lugs of forward attachment fitting fractured in shear and tension overstress at bulkhead No. 33 (p. 10-11)
Structural failure resulted in asymmetrical elevator deflection and loss of control, causing steep descent (p. 6-7)
EMB-110 crashed approximately 7800 feet beyond end of runway 31 and 85 feet to northeast of centerline (p. 6)
Aircraft caught fire after ground impact (p. 6)

records.title: Galaxy Airlines 203
records.summary: Galaxy Airlines Flight 203, a Lockheed L-188 Electra, experienced severe vibrations shortly after takeoff from Reno. The pilots mistakenly attributed the vibrations to a faulty engine and reduced power to all four engines simultaneously. This caused loss of lift and induced an aerodynamic stall. The aircraft crashed nose-high onto Reno Field approximately 1.5 miles from the runway end.
records.probable_cause: The captain's failure to control and the copilot's failure to monitor the flight path and airspeed of the aircraft. This breakdown in crew coordination followed the onset of unexpected vibration shortly after takeoff. Contributing to the accident was the failure of ground handlers to properly close an air start access door, which led to the vibration.

factors.evidence: Ground crew failed to properly close air start access door before aircraft was taxied from service ramp (p. 2, Finding 10).
Aircraft stalled from insufficient engine power to maintain flight at too low altitude to effect recovery (p. 2, Finding 13).
Captain reacted to vibration by reducing power in all four engines, indicating belief vibration was caused by powerplants or propellers (p. 2, Finding 14).
Flightcrew did not complete required checklists prior to flight (p. 2, Finding 6).
Aircraft crashed at 105 knots in nose-high condition 1.5 miles short of runway end (p. 2).

events.text: Aircraft took off from Reno and immediately experienced significant vibrations due to open air start access door
Pilots reduced power to all four engines, misinterpreting vibrations as faulty engine
Airspeed decreased as aircraft lost thrust; aerodynamic stall developed in nose-high attitude
Aircraft crashed onto Reno Field at 105 knots in nose-high condition 1.5 miles short of runway end

Instruct Principal Operations Inspectors to verify operators' maintenance and service competence at transient locations

records.title: China Airlines 006
records.summary: China Airlines Flight 006, a Boeing 747SP, lost thrust in the No. 4 engine at 41,000 feet over the Pacific. During an engine restart attempt, the autopilot masked the approaching loss of control. As airspeed decreased, the autopilot reached maximum aileron trim while the aircraft began to roll. The captain disconnected the autopilot and recovered from a 31,500-foot dive experiencing g-forces as high as 5g. The aircraft diverted to San Francisco with substantial structural damage.
records.probable_cause: The captain's preoccupation with an inflight malfunction and his failure to monitor properly the airplane's flight instruments which resulted in his losing control of the airplane. Contributing to the accident was the captain's over-reliance on the autopilot after the loss of thrust on the No. 4 engine.

factors.evidence: The No. 4 engine lost thrust at 41,000 feet while cruising west of reporting point Redoo (p. 5).
The flight engineer did not close the required bleed valve during the restart attempt at 41,000 feet, which exceeded the maximum engine restart altitude of 30,000 feet (p. 5-6).
The captain over-relied on the autopilot after engine loss, and the autopilot effectively masked the approaching onset of loss of control by maintaining altitude hold while airspeed decreased (p. 7).
During engine restart, airspeed began decreasing as the Performance Management System retarded throttles to maintain Mach number (p. 5-6).

The autopilot slowly applied more aileron to keep wings level until maximum 23 degree aileron limit was reached. As speed decreased, the aircraft rolled right despite maximum left roll input from autopilot (p. 6-7).
By the time the captain disconnected the autopilot, the aircraft had rolled over and plunged 31,500 feet while experiencing g-forces as high as 5g before recovery (p. 7).

events.text: China Airlines Flight 006 departed Taipei at 06:22 PST (16:22 Taipei local time) with 251 passengers and 23 crewmembers en route to Los Angeles via Pacific routing.

Aircraft was cruising at FL 410 (41,000 feet) west of reporting point Redoo, about 300 nm northwest of San Francisco, at 0.85 Mach and 254 KIAS. Autopilot was in Performance Management System (PMS) mode providing pitch and altitude guidance.
Aircraft encountered light clear air turbulence. Airspeed began fluctuating between 0.84 Mach (251 KIAS) and 0.88 Mach (264 KIAS).

At approximately 10:10, as Mach number increased to 0.88 M, PMS retarded throttles and engine thrust decreased to about 1.0 EPR. Flight engineer observed that No. 4 engine instruments did not indicate corresponding acceleration when PMS moved throttles forward. Engines 1, 2, and 3 responded normally.

Flight engineer moved No. 4 throttle forward and aft manually but saw no response on engine instruments. Flight engineer reported to captain that No. 4 engine had flamed out and noted that No. 4 generator control breaker open light was lit (p. 5-6).

Captain directed flight engineer to attempt engine restart at 41,000 feet (exceeding maximum restart altitude of 30,000 feet). Flight engineer placed No. 2 ignition switch to flight start, putting both ignition systems in continuous ignition, but restart attempt was unsuccessful.

First officer called Oakland ARTCC requesting lower altitude but did not declare emergency or mention engine failure. Oakland ARTCC cleared descent to FL 240 at 10:15:01, but flight did not acknowledge (p. 6).

Captain switched autopilot from PMS to OFF mode when airspeed dropped below 240 KIAS, transitioning to pitch attitude hold. Captain rotated nose-down to arrest airspeed loss but airspeed continued decreasing.
Captain disengaged autopilot to lower nose faster. First officer observed airplane banking right slightly. Captain disengaged autopilot and airplane rolled further right.

As airplane continued banking right, attitude director indicators (ADIs) rotated rapidly. Airplane's three remaining engines lost thrust simultaneously. Indicated airspeed increased rapidly and exceeded Vmo (maximum operating speed).
Captain pulled control column back hard, trying to arrest overspeed and regain control during steep bank in clouds. Airspeed decreased to 80-100 KIAS momentarily, then increased again beyond Vmo.

Captain, assisted by first officer, continued pulling back on control column. Airplane decelerated. Captain lowered nose smoothly and airplane began accelerating slowly. At 11,000 feet, aircraft emerged from clouds and captain could see horizon.

As aircraft descended through 10,000 feet, engines 1, 2, and 3 restarted but No. 4 engine did not. Flight engineer placed No. 4 ignition switch in ground start position and engine started in accordance with checklist procedures.
After airplane stabilized at 9,500 feet, Oakland ARTCC was contacted and Flight 006 reported 'flameout, ah, we have emergency...we are niner thousand feet' (p. 7).

records.title: Delta Air Lines 191

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Delta Air Lines, Inc., Lockheed L-1011-385-1, N726DA, Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport, Texas, August 2, 1985

location.name: Short of runway 17L, Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport, Texas

records.summary: On approach to runway 17L at DFW the L-1011 flew into a rapidly developing thunderstorm cell on the final approach course and encountered a microburst. The aircraft struck the ground in a field north of the runway, hit a car on Highway 114 killing its driver, and struck water tanks on the airport, breaking up and catching fire. Of the 163 on board, 136 died, plus one person on the ground.
records.probable_cause: The flightcrew's decision to initiate and continue the approach into a cumulonimbus cloud which they observed to contain visible lightning; the lack of specific guidelines, procedures, and training for avoiding and escaping from low-altitude wind shear; and the lack of definitive, real-time wind shear hazard information. This resulted in the aircraft's encounter at low altitude with a microburst-induced, severe wind shear from a rapidly developing thunderstorm located on the final approach course.

factors.evidence: A thunderstorm cell developed rapidly on the final approach course to runway 17L and the crew observed lightning in it before continuing the approach.
The aircraft encountered a microburst with a strong headwind-to-tailwind shear and downdraft at low altitude.
The crew continued the approach into the cumulonimbus rather than abandoning it; a go-around was commanded only after the aircraft was already sinking rapidly.
The NTSB cited the lack of specific guidelines, procedures and training for avoiding and escaping low-altitude wind shear.
No definitive, real-time wind shear hazard information was available; the airport low-level wind shear alert system did not alert before the encounter.
The lack of industry-wide wind shear guidance and detection requirements was a cited factor.
Thrust was reduced during the initial airspeed increase in the headwind and the nose was lowered as airspeed decayed, consistent with training of the time, which increased the sink rate.
The downdraft and tailwind produced a sink rate that could not be arrested before ground contact.
The aircraft broke up on striking water tanks and the wreckage was consumed by fire.

events.text: Aircraft is vectored for the ILS approach to runway 17L; a rain shower and rapidly building cell lie north of the airport on the final approach course.
First officer points out lightning coming out of the cloud ahead; the captain asks where and is told it is right ahead of them.
Aircraft enters heavy rain beneath the cell on final approach.
Airspeed increases in the microburst outflow headwind; captain tells the first officer to watch his speed and thrust is reduced.
Captain warns that the airspeed will be lost all of a sudden as the aircraft passes through the downdraft into the tailwind.
Captain calls for thrust to be pushed way up as airspeed decays and the sink rate increases.
Aircraft descends below the glideslope with a high sink rate in the downdraft and tailwind.
GPWS 'whoop whoop pull up' warning sounds.
Captain calls TOGA; full go-around thrust is applied but the aircraft is still descending.
Main landing gear strikes a plowed field about 6,300 ft north of the runway 17L threshold; the aircraft bounces.
Aircraft crosses Highway 114 and strikes a car, killing the driver, and hits a light pole.
Aircraft strikes two water tanks on the airport, breaks up and is engulfed in fire; the tail section separates and most survivors are in the rear.

recommendations.text: Expedite development and installation of terminal Doppler weather radar and improved low-level wind shear alert systems at airports prone to microbursts.
recommendations.outcome: Terminal Doppler Weather Radar was developed and installed at major US airports.

recommendations.text: Develop and require wind shear avoidance and escape training and procedures for air carrier flightcrews, including simulator training in microburst encounters.
recommendations.outcome: FAA Windshear Training Aid published in 1987; wind shear training became mandatory.

recommendations.text: Require airborne wind shear detection and warning systems on transport category aircraft.
recommendations.outcome: Airborne reactive and later predictive wind shear systems were mandated for air carrier aircraft.

FAA Windshear Training Aid and mandatory wind shear escape training for airline pilots.
Requirement for airborne wind shear warning and, later, predictive wind shear radar on transport aircraft.

records.title: Japan Airlines 123

agencies.name: Aircraft Accident Investigation Commission
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Investigation Report, Japan Air Lines Co., Ltd., Boeing 747 SR-100, JA8119, Gunma Prefecture, Japan, August 12, 1985

location.name: Ridge near Mount Osutaka, Ueno village, Gunma Prefecture

records.summary: Twelve minutes after leaving Haneda for Osaka, the 747SR's aft pressure bulkhead ruptured as it climbed through about 24,000 ft. The escaping cabin air blew off most of the vertical fin and severed all four hydraulic systems, leaving the crew without flight controls. They kept the aircraft airborne for 32 minutes using engine thrust before it struck a mountain ridge in Gunma Prefecture. Of the 524 people on board, 520 died; four survived.
records.probable_cause: The AAIC concluded that the bulkhead failed because a repair carried out by Boeing after a 1978 tailstrike had been performed improperly: a splice plate was fitted in a way that left only a single row of rivets carrying the load across the joint, greatly reducing the fatigue strength. Fatigue cracks propagated from the rivet holes over the following 12,318 flights and were not detected by Japan Airlines' inspections. The rupture of the bulkhead caused the loss of the vertical fin and of all hydraulic systems, making the aircraft uncontrollable.

factors.evidence: The 1978 repair of the aft pressure bulkhead by a Boeing team used a splice plate cut in two, so that only one row of rivets carried the load across the joint, contrary to the repair instructions.
The improper repair was not detected when the work was accepted, and subsequent inspections by Japan Airlines did not find the fatigue cracks growing in the bulkhead.
Multi-site fatigue cracks propagated from the rivet holes along the repaired joint over about 12,300 pressurisation cycles until the remaining structure could not hold cabin pressure.
The aft pressure bulkhead ruptured at 18:24:35 as the aircraft climbed through about 24,000 ft.
The cabin decompressed rapidly, with mist in the cabin and oxygen masks deployed.
The pressure released into the unpressurised tail blew off most of the vertical fin and damaged the tail cone and APU.
All four hydraulic systems, whose lines ran through the fin area, were severed and lost pressure.
With no hydraulic pressure the crew had no control over the ailerons, elevators, rudder or stabiliser and could influence the flight path only with engine thrust, flaps and landing gear.

The routing of all hydraulic systems through the same area of the tail allowed a single structural event to disable every system; Boeing subsequently modified the 747 with hydraulic fuses and a fin-base bulkhead.
The aircraft flew in phugoid and Dutch-roll oscillations for 32 minutes before descending into mountainous terrain.

events.text: 2 June 1978: JA8119 suffers a tailstrike on landing at Osaka that damages the aft pressure bulkhead.

Boeing repairs the bulkhead. The splice plate specified in the repair is fitted as two pieces, so only a single row of rivets carries the load across the joint. The discrepancy is not detected on inspection.
Departs Haneda for Osaka with 509 passengers and 15 crew; the aircraft has flown 12,318 flights since the repair.
Climbing through about 24,000 ft over Sagami Bay, the aft pressure bulkhead ruptures with a loud bang; the cabin decompresses.
Escaping cabin air blows off most of the vertical fin and severs all four hydraulic systems; the aircraft begins to oscillate in pitch and yaw.
Captain orders squawk 7700; the crew declare an emergency to Tokyo Control.
Crew request an immediate return to Haneda; Tokyo Control approves.
The flight engineer reports that hydraulic pressure is lost on all systems.
Crew inform Tokyo Control that the aircraft is uncontrollable; they attempt to steer using differential thrust as the aircraft wanders over the Izu peninsula and turns north.
The landing gear is lowered by the alternate (gravity) system in an attempt to damp the oscillations and slow the aircraft.
The captain remarks that the situation may be hopeless as the aircraft continues in phugoid oscillations over the mountains west of Tokyo.
The aircraft descends rapidly toward the mountains of Gunma Prefecture; the crew apply maximum power and call for the nose to be raised; GPWS sounds.
The aircraft strikes trees and a ridge near Mount Osutaka at about 5,100 ft, breaks up and burns; 520 of the 524 on board are killed, 4 survive.

recommendations.text: Improve the quality control and inspection of major structural repairs, and the inspection procedures for pressure bulkheads, so that improper repairs and fatigue cracking are detected.
recommendations.outcome: Airworthiness directives required detailed inspections of 747 aft pressure bulkheads; JAL revised its inspection program.

recommendations.text: Modify the 747 so that a failure of the aft pressure bulkhead cannot cause the loss of the vertical fin and of all hydraulic systems.
recommendations.outcome: Boeing installed hydraulic fuses and a bulkhead at the base of the fin and improved the tail-cone venting on the 747 fleet.

safety_changes: Boeing modified the 747 with hydraulic fuses and structural changes to protect the fin and hydraulic systems from a bulkhead failure.
Airworthiness directives required detailed inspections of 747 aft pressure bulkheads and of major structural repairs.
Japan Airlines overhauled its maintenance quality control and inspection procedures; the accident remains the deadliest single-aircraft accident in history.

records.title: British Airtours 28M

agencies.name: Air Accidents Investigation Branch
agencies.report_title: Report on the accident to Boeing 737-236 series 1, G-BGJL at Manchester International Airport on 22 August 1985

location.name: Runway 24 / taxiway link D, Manchester International Airport

records.summary: During the takeoff roll on runway 24 at Manchester the left engine's No.9 combustor can failed; a section of the can was ejected forward and struck an underwing fuel tank access panel, releasing fuel that ignited. The crew rejected the takeoff and turned off the runway, positioning the aircraft so that a light wind carried the fire onto the fuselage. Fire penetrated the cabin during evacuation and 55 occupants died, mainly from smoke and toxic gases.
records.probable_cause: The cause of the accident was an uncontained failure of the left engine, initiated by a failure of the No.9 combustor can which had been the subject of a repair. A section of the combustor can was ejected forward and struck the underwing fuel tank access panel, rupturing it and releasing fuel which ignited. The major cause of the fatalities was the rapid incapacitation of occupants by toxic gases and smoke from the burning cabin, aggravated by evacuation difficulties, the aircraft having been stopped with the wind carrying the fire onto the fuselage, and the loss of time before exits were opened.

factors.evidence: The No.9 combustor can had been weld-repaired in a manner that did not restore its fatigue resistance, and the subsequent inspection regime did not catch the propagating crack.
The JT8D combustor can cracking problem was known to the manufacturer and operators, but the airworthiness response did not prevent recurrence.
The combustor can failed at about 125 kt during the takeoff roll, producing a thud heard by the crew who believed it to be a tyre burst.
The forward section of the can was ejected through the combustion casing and struck the wing fuel tank access panel.
The underwing fuel tank access panels were not designed to resist impact from ejected engine debris and the cabin materials produced dense toxic smoke.
Fuel escaped from the ruptured access panel and pooled on the runway, igniting against the hot engine.
A ground fire developed during the rejected takeoff (no impact), was carried onto the fuselage by the wind after the aircraft turned off the runway, and burned through the rear cabin.
The cabin furnishings burned rapidly and produced toxic smoke and gases that incapacitated occupants within minutes.
The right forward door was delayed by a jammed slide, the overwing exit was obstructed by seat pitch, and passengers were slow to leave due to the narrow bulkhead gap and smoke.
The crew stopped the aircraft with the wind blowing the fire onto the fuselage and there was a delay before the evacuation was ordered while the cause of the emergency was being assessed.

events.text: Flight KT28M cleared for takeoff on runway 24 with 131 passengers and 6 crew for a charter flight to Corfu.
About 36 seconds into the takeoff roll at about 125 kt a thud is heard as the No.9 combustor can of the left engine fails; a section is ejected forward and strikes the wing fuel tank access panel.
Commander, believing a tyre has burst, calls stop and rejects the takeoff using reverse thrust and light braking.
Tower informs the crew that there is a lot of fire on the left side; the crew request the fire services.
Fire warning for the left engine; the crew carry out the engine fire drill.
Commander turns right off the runway onto taxiway link D, placing the fire on the upwind side; a 7 kt wind carries flames onto the rear fuselage.
Aircraft stops; fire penetrates the rear fuselage and the cabin fills with thick black smoke within seconds.
Commander orders evacuation via the starboard side; the right forward door slide initially jams and the door is delayed about 25 seconds.
Passengers crowd the narrow gap beside the forward galley bulkhead; the right overwing exit is opened by a passenger after a struggle with the hatch.
Airport fire service arrives and applies foam; the fire has already breached the cabin and the rear of the aircraft is burning fiercely.
Last survivors leave the aircraft; 55 occupants die, 48 of them from the effects of toxic gases and smoke, and the aircraft is destroyed by fire.

recommendations.text: Require the fitting of floor-level emergency lighting and smoke hoods or other respiratory protection for passengers, and review cabin material flammability and toxicity standards.
recommendations.outcome: Floor proximity lighting and fire-blocking seat covers were mandated; smoke hoods were not.

recommendations.text: Review the minimum access gap beside galley bulkheads and the spacing of seats adjacent to overwing exits to improve evacuation flow.
recommendations.outcome: Regulations on exit access and minimum bulkhead gaps were introduced.

recommendations.text: Review the JT8D combustor can repair schemes and inspection intervals and make fuel tank access panels resistant to impact from ejected engine debris.
Provide guidance to flight crews on positioning the aircraft relative to wind after a ground fire and on ordering an immediate evacuation when a fire is reported.

safety_changes: Floor-level emergency lighting, fire-blocking seat materials and improved cabin material toxicity standards.
Minimum access gap requirements beside overwing exits and galley bulkheads.
Revised guidance on rejected takeoff and evacuation decision making, including stopping on the runway and evacuation drills for cabin crew.
Research programme into passenger smoke hoods and cabin water spray systems.

notes: post_impact_fire is used for a ground fire that started during the rejected takeoff; there was no impact.
Event seconds are approximate; the report gives the failure at about 125 kt roughly 36 s into the roll.
Recommendation numbers omitted; the report contained 31 recommendations.

records.title: Bar Harbor Airlines 1808
records.summary: Bar Harbor Airlines Flight 1808, a Beechcraft Model 99, departed Logan International Airport in Boston for Bangor, Maine, with planned stops in Augusta and Waterville, including an unscheduled flag stop in Auburn/Lewiston. At 22:00 EDT, weather at Auburn consisted of a 300-foot obscured indefinite ceiling, 1-mile visibility, and light drizzle. A Portland controller advised the flight it was drifting east of the ILS approach course and instructed a heading of 340 degrees. The aircraft flew through the approach course, requiring a 60-degree right turn less than 1 nautical mile from the outer marker. The aircraft did not begin descent until after passing Lewiston, already above the glide slope, causing the crew to rush the descent and approach with a steep descent profile. The aircraft crashed into trees 4,007 feet from the runway end and 440 feet to the right of centerline. All eight people on board were killed.
records.probable_cause: The captain's continuation of an unstabilized approach which resulted in a descent below glideslope. Contributing to the unstabilized approach was the radar controller's issuance and the captain's acceptance of a nonstandard air traffic control radar vector resulting in an excessive intercept with the localizer (p. 59)

factors.evidence: Controller advised large 60-degree course correction less than 1 nautical mile from outer marker with poor judgment (p. 10)
Crew continued unstabilized approach instead of executing missed approach despite large late course correction (p. 10-11)
Crew descended below published decision height without required visual references (p. 11)
actual altimeter settings on captain's and first officer's altimeters could not be determined due to fire and impact damage, may have contributed to altitude misjudgment
1 mile visibility, light drizzle, 300 foot obscured indefinite ceiling at night Auburn-Lewiston (p. 8)
night approach in low visibility condition
aircraft flew into trees 4,007 feet from runway end and 440 feet right of centerline
