recommendations.text: Establish for aircraft used in commercial operation the maximum cockpit noise levels which will permit adequate direct voice communication between flight crewmembers under all operating conditions.

Require the installation and use of crew interphone systems in the cockpits of those aircraft in which noise levels reach or exceed the maximum level established for adequate direct voice communication between flight crewmembers under all operating conditions.

Require that all multiengine, turbine-powered, fixed-wing aircraft certificated to carry six or more passengers manufactured on or after a specified date be prewired to accept a cockpit voice recorder and flight data recorder.

Require that general aviation cockpit voice recorders and flight data recorders be installed when commercially available as standard equipment in all multiengine, turbine-powered fixed-wing aircraft and rotorcraft certificated to carry six or more passengers.

Require that general aviation cockpit voice recorders be installed as soon as commercially available in all multiengine, turbine-powered aircraft certificated to carry six or more passengers and required to have two pilots.

records.title: Midwest Express Airlines 105
records.summary: Midwest Express Airlines Flight 105, a McDonnell Douglas DC-9-14, departed Milwaukee on September 6, 1985. At 450 feet during initial climb, the right engine experienced a catastrophic failure due to rupture of a removable sleeve spacer in the high-pressure compressor. The crew failed to properly control the aircraft during the emergency, resulting in an accelerated stall, loss of control, and crash into a field southwest of the airport. All 31 occupants were killed.
records.probable_cause: The flightcrew's improper use of flight controls in response to the catastrophic failure of the right engine during a critical phase of flight, which led to an accelerated stall and loss of control of the airplane. Contributing to the loss of control was a lack of crew coordination in response to the emergency. The right engine failed from the rupture of the 9th to 10th stage removable sleeve spacer in the high pressure compressor because of the spacer's vulnerability to cracks. (p. 74)

factors.evidence: Removable sleeve spacer suffered metal fatigue with fatigue crack in knife edge of 9th to 10th stage spacer. Crack had propagated to a length which should have allowed detection at the occasion of the last high pressure compressor overhaul in 1981. (p. 73)
Right engine failed abruptly and completely due to uncontained failure of the 8th to 10th stage high pressure compressor spacer during initial climb at 450 feet above ground level. (p. 73)

The crew response to the right engine failure was not coordinated. Neither pilot verbally identified the emergency condition or made the emergency callouts required by FAA-approved Midwest Express procedures. (p. 73)

The rudder was incorrectly deflected to the right 4 to 5 seconds after the right engine failure. Captain initially responded correctly by deflecting rudder to the left but appeared unaware of exact nature of emergency. (p. 73)
An accelerated stall occurred 10 seconds after the failure of the right engine. Airplane rolled to the right until wings were in near vertical approximately right 90 degree banked turn. (p. 1)
During accelerated stall, control was lost and the airplane crashed into an open field. Aircraft was destroyed by impact forces and post-crash fire. (p. 1)
Flight 105 crashed into an open field at the edge of a wooded area about 1,686 feet southwest of the departure end of runway 19R. (p. 1)

events.text: Clearance for takeoff on runway 19R at General Billy Mitchell Field, Milwaukee, Wisconsin acknowledged. (p. 1)
Flight 105 became airborne, carrying 27 passengers and 4 crew members, climbing from runway 19R. (p. 1)

Right engine catastrophic failure occurred at approximately 450 feet above ground level. Loud 'clunk' noise recorded on CVR indicating uncontained failure of 8th to 10th stage high pressure compressor spacer. (p. 1)
Captain asked first officer: 'What do you got there?' indicating delayed recognition of emergency condition. (p. 1)
Stickshaker activated and continued until end of CVR recording, indicating aerodynamic stall condition developing. (p. 1)

Flight 105 crashed into an open field at edge of wooded area approximately 1,686 feet southwest of runway 19R departure end. Aircraft rolled to right until wings were in near vertical right 90-degree banked turn during accelerated stall. (p. 1)
Aircraft destroyed by impact forces and post-crash fire. All 31 occupants, including captain, first officer, two flight attendants, and 27 passengers, were fatally injured. (p. 1)

recommendations.text: Issue an Airworthiness Directive to require the installation of the one-piece, integral sleeve spacer at all six locations in the high-pressure compressor rotor of Pratt & Whitney JT8D-series engines not so equipped. The installation should be made as soon as practical but no later than the next opportunity wherein the engine is available in a maintenance facility where a partial or complete disassembly of the compressor can be accomplished.

Notify appropriate foreign civil aviation authorities and foreign operators of airplanes equipped with Pratt & Whitney JT8D-series engines of the failures associated with the removable sleeve spacers installed in the high-pressure compressor rotor and of the actions which should be taken to minimize or eliminate the failures.

Issue a Telegraphic Airworthiness Directive and amend the airworthiness directive proposed in the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking published at 51 FR 37696, Docket No. 85-ANA-46, to require that the one-time, on-wing eddy current inspection specified in the proposed airworthiness directive be repeated at 1,000-cycle intervals until stage 7-8, 8-9, and 9-10 removable sleeve spacers between the high-pressure compressor are replaced with integral sleeve spacers.

Issue an air carrier operations bulletin directing Principal Operations Inspectors to review their respective air carrier's flightcrew training programs to ensure the existence of new coordination procedures that, notwithstanding a policy endorsing nonessential conversation during an emergency condition, require any crewmember who observes a potential or actual emergency situation to verbally call it to the captain's attention.

Issue an air carrier operations bulletin directing Principal Operations Inspectors to review their respective air carrier's simulator training programs to verify that engine failures in the posttakeoff climb are frequently given with particular emphasis on the use of engine and flight instruments as the primary source of information for airplane control and on the need for deliberate actions based upon flight and engine instrument analysis rather than hasty action based upon kinesthetic cues.

Require Principal Operations Inspectors of 14 CFR 121 certificate holders to have training and experience commensurate with the air carrier involved, including a comparable type rating (e.g., turbojet powered transport category) in the category and class of aircraft to be used by the certificate holder.

dissent.position: The probable cause of the accident was the catastrophic failure of a high pressure compressor spacer in the right engine during a critical phase of flight, together with the flightcrew's improper use of the flight controls that resulted in an accelerated stall and loss of control of the airplane. Contributing to the cause of the accident was a training program which inadequately prepared the flightcrew to diagnose and respond to an engine-out situation in the climb-out phase of flight, a lack of crew coordination in response to the emergency, and the inadequate inspection of the compressor spacer at the engine repair facility.

safety_changes: Installation of integral sleeve spacers in JT8D engines to eliminate fatigue crack vulnerability
Enhanced pilot training for engine failure recognition and response in the critical takeoff and initial climb phase

records.title: Henson Airlines 1517

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Henson Airlines Flight 1517 Beech B99

records.summary: Henson Airlines Flight 1517, a Beech 99 with 14 aboard (12 passengers, 2 crew), crashed into Hall Mountain near Grottoes, Virginia on September 23, 1985 during approach to Shenandoah Valley Regional Airport. The crew used an incorrect VOR navigational facility and failed to adequately monitor flight instruments. The aircraft descended into terrain at 2,400 feet elevation while the crew believed they were on a proper approach path.
records.probable_cause: Navigational error by the flight crew resulting from use of an incorrect navigational facility and failure to adequately monitor the flight instruments. Contributing factors included nonstandardized navigational radio systems, intracockpit communication difficulties due to high cockpit noise, inadequate training, pilot inexperience, and inadequate Federal Aviation Administration surveillance.

factors.evidence: At 10:14 am, Captain Burns told the Air Traffic Controller that he believed the plane was too far west of his course (p. 1)
Failure to adequately monitor the flight instruments during the approach (p. 1)
Inadequate training of the pilots by the airline (p. 1)
The first officer's limited multiengine and instrument flying experience and pilots' limited experience in their positions in the Beech 99 (p. 1)
Intracockpit communication difficulties associated with high ambient noise levels in the airplane (p. 1)
Inadequate surveillance of the airline by the Federal Aviation Administration which failed to detect the deficiencies (p. 1)
Flight 1517 struck the southwest face of Hall Mountain at an elevation of 2,400 ft (p. 1)

Flight 1517 departed BWI on filed IFR flight plan: BWI direct to LDN VORTAC, direct to SHD, cruising altitude 6,000 feet

records.title: 1985 Teterboro collision

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report: Midair Collision of Nabisco Brands, Inc., Dassault Falcon, DASO, N784B and Air Pegasus Corporation Piper Archer, PA28-181, N1977H

location.name: Fairview/Cliffside Park, New Jersey, over Teterboro Airport

records.summary: A Dassault Falcon 50 and Piper Cherokee collided mid-air over Teterboro Airport near 1,500 feet altitude at approximately 22:24 EST. The Falcon was cleared for a standard instrument approach and turned to downwind leg to runway 19. Both aircraft fell into residential areas of Fairview and Cliffside Park, causing fires and destroying buildings. The NTSB found a breakdown in ATC coordination and controller failure to follow procedures, preventing the crew from seeing and avoiding the other aircraft in darkness.
records.probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Board determines that the probable cause of the accident was a breakdown in air traffic control coordination which resulted in an air traffic conflict and the inability of the DA50 flightcrew to 'see and avoid' the other aircraft due to (1) an erroneous and inadequate traffic advisory and (2) the physiological limitations of human vision and reaction time at night. Air traffic control management contributed to the accident by failing to insure that controllers were following prescribed procedures and by failing to recognize and correct operational deficiencies.

factors.evidence: Dassault Falcon 50 and Piper Cherokee collided mid-air at approximately 1,500 feet altitude (p. 60)
Local controller gave misleading traffic advisories concerning the direction of the transiting PA28 (p. 60)
DA50 flightcrew loss of situational awareness and probably misidentified the PA28 (p. 61)
Limitations to vision at night contributed to difficulty in resolving collision course geometry (p. 61)
Breakdown in coordination among FAA air traffic controllers and congested radio frequency (p. 61)
TEB control tower coordinator and clearance delivery controller failed to follow prescribed procedures (p. 60)

events.text: Dassault Falcon 50 cleared for standard instrument approach to Teterboro
Falcon turned left to position on downwind leg to runway 19
Piper Cherokee flying westbound over airport at approximately 1,500 feet in VFR conditions
Dassault Falcon 50 and Piper Cherokee collided mid-air at approximately 1,500 feet altitude
Both aircraft fell into residential areas of Fairview and Cliffside Park causing fires

recommendations.text: Issue a General Notice to all facilities to require briefing on importance of conducting complete position relief briefing prior to assuming duties
Require the implementation of traffic advisories that will help pilots to avoid collision hazards when the target is in close proximity to the hearing pilot's position
Reassess the adequacy of current minimum safe altitude rules and procedures
Direct the Teterboro control tower to establish and enforce mandatory procedures requiring the radar controller to ensure that every inbound or outbound aircraft is advised of known traffic
Require air traffic controllers and supervisors at Teterboro to receive training emphasizing the importance of operating procedures
Revise FAA Order 7210.3 to clarify responsibilities and procedures for radar and local controllers

Event times estimated based on controller communications and radar data
ATC coordination failure with misleading traffic advisories as key factor

records.title: Arrow Air 1285R

agencies.name: Transportation Safety Board of Canada
agencies.report_title: Aviation Occurrence Report - Arrow Air Inc. Flight MF1285R

location.name: Near Gander International Airport, approximately 2,975 feet beyond runway 22 departure end

records.summary: Arrow Air Flight MF1285R, a Douglas DC-8-63, crashed shortly after takeoff from Gander, Newfoundland on December 12, 1985. The aircraft had accumulated ice contamination on the wings' leading edges and upper surfaces during the approach and ground stop at Gander in freezing precipitation conditions. The aircraft was not de-iced prior to takeoff, and the ice buildup degraded aerodynamic efficiency while increasing drag, resulting in an aerodynamic stall at low altitude from which recovery was not possible. All 256 occupants were killed in the impact and resulting fire.
records.probable_cause: The most probable cause of the stall was ice contamination on the leading edge and upper surface of the wing. The Board believes that the weight of evidence supports the conclusion that, shortly after lift-off, the aircraft experienced an increase in drag and reduction in lift which resulted in a stall at low altitude from which recovery was not possible. Other possible factors such as a loss of thrust from the number four engine and inappropriate take-off reference speeds may have compounded the effects of the contamination.

factors.evidence: During the approach to Gander, existing meteorological conditions were conducive to ice accretion on the leading edge of the wing (p. 93-94). While the aircraft was on the ground at Gander, the aircraft was exposed to freezing and frozen precipitation capable of producing roughening on the wing upper surface, with wing surface temperatures conducive to formation of frost (p. 93-94). The aircraft stalled at a higher than normal airspeed after leaving ground effect, and the performance was consistent with reduced aerodynamic efficiency and high drag associated with wing ice contamination (p. 94).

The aircraft was not de-iced prior to take-off despite exposure to freezing and frozen precipitation (p. 95). Despite existing regulations and promotional material concerning clean wing procedures, numerous aircraft occurrences including this DC-8 accident confirm that leading edge and wing surface contamination due to ice and snow can degrade aircraft performance during takeoff to the point where there is little to no margin of safety (p. 97-98).

Within a few seconds of lift-off, the aircraft experienced stall buffet evidenced by extreme oscillations in altitude measurements and vertical acceleration readings reaching 1.30G and as low as 0.77G (p. 24). The aircraft struck downsloping terrain near the top of a wooded hillside approximately 2,975 feet beyond the departure end of runway 22, broke up and was destroyed by impact forces and severe fuel-fed fire, killing all 256 occupants (p. 2, 25).

The take-off weight at Gander calculated by the crew was approximately 14,000 pounds less than the actual take-off weight of the aircraft (p. 93). The take-off reference speeds used by the crew were applicable to a take-off weight at least 14,000 pounds less than actual, and may have been applicable to a take-off weight as much as 35,000 pounds less (p. 93). Although the use of actual passenger weights was required by Arrow Air's Operations Manual, the crew used a standard average weight which did not accurately reflect the actual weight of passengers carried (p. 93). The maximum design zero fuel weight of 230,000 pounds was exceeded on each of the MFO rotation flights in December 1985 (p. 93).

A non-functioning cockpit area microphone went undetected for an indeterminate number of flights, and no steps on standard checklists tested its functionality, preventing crucial cockpit communications from being recorded during the accident (p. 99). No evidence was found to indicate that specific inspections required following a 1981 Casablanca accident had been carried out, and life-limited repairs were not replaced in accordance with Douglas Aircraft Company recommendations (p. 9).

Although a heavy maintenance check was accomplished after June 1984, replacement of trailing edge repairs which were nearing their life-limits had not occurred (p. 9). The cockpit voice recorder relied on functional testing by flight crews to detect unserviceabilities, but inconsistent testing procedures meant unserviceabilities could remain undetected through multiple flights (p. 99).

events.text: Arrow Air Flight MF1285R departed Cairo, Egypt on international charter flight to Fort Campbell, Kentucky with planned stops at Cologne and Gander. Eight crew members and 248 passengers were on board, all members of 101st Airborne Division returning from peacekeeping duties in the Sinai Desert.
Aircraft arrived at Cologne, Germany for planned technical stop. A complete crew change took place.
Aircraft departed Cologne for Gander with the replacement crew.

Aircraft arrived at Gander International Airport under overcast conditions with light freezing drizzle and snow. Passengers were deplaned, aircraft was refueled, trash and waste water removed, catering supplies boarded. The flight engineer conducted an external inspection of portions of the aircraft while meteorological conditions with freezing precipitation were favorable for ice formation on wing leading edges.

Passengers reboarded the aircraft at Gander. The aircraft remained exposed to freezing and frozen precipitation conditions on the ground for approximately 15 minutes after passengers completed boarding, allowing ice contamination to form and develop on the wing leading edges and upper surfaces.

Following engine start-up, the aircraft was taxied via taxiway D and runway 13 to runway 22 for departure. No de-icing procedure was performed despite the aircraft having been exposed to freezing and frozen precipitation while on the ground.

Take-off on runway 22 commenced from the intersection of runway 13. Takeoff roll began at 10:15:06 local time. The aircraft accelerated down the runway with first officer at the controls. Take-off reference speeds used by the crew were calculated based on incorrectly determined weight (approximately 14,000 to 35,000 pounds less than actual).

Rotation of the aircraft occurred 51 seconds after commencement of take-off roll at approximately 167 knots indicated airspeed. Aircraft lifted off from the runway having covered approximately 8,000 feet. Vertical acceleration reached peak value of 1.26G during initial climb.

Peak indicated airspeed of 172 knots was achieved 53 seconds after commencement of takeoff roll. Aircraft heading began to deviate to the right at approximately this time. As maximum recorded airspeed was reached, altitude measurements on flight data recorder started to oscillate in extreme manner due to stall buffet.

Aircraft crossed the end of runway 22 approximately 57 seconds after start of takeoff roll at very low altitude. Aircraft continued over the Trans-Canada Highway which is located 900 feet beyond the runway departure end at a very low altitude. Witnesses observed the aircraft in a right bank as it crossed the highway with pitch angle increasing, but aircraft continued to descend.

Airspeed continued to decrease following the peak of 172 knots. Vertical acceleration oscillated between values as high as 1.30G and as low as 0.77G, with final values almost entirely below 1.0G level, reaching minimum of 0.72G before impact. The aircraft struck downsloping terrain near the top of a wooded hillside at coordinates 48°54'40"N, 54°34'35"W, approximately 2,975 feet beyond the departure end of runway 22 and 720 feet to the right of the extended runway centerline.

Aircraft broke up upon impact and was destroyed by impact forces and severe fuel-fed fire at the accident site. The aircraft had impacted in a seven-degree right bank, nine-degree pitch, and 10-degree yaw right attitude on a descending 12-degree flight path angle. All 256 occupants on board sustained fatal injuries from impact and fire.

recommendations.text: Review company documentation for Canadian air carriers to confirm the adequacy of provisions for the use of actual weights (versus standard average weights) and that the associated load calculation forms reflect the basis for the load determinations.
Re-emphasize to each carrier the need to use actual weights for passengers, if the passenger load is likely to deviate from standard weights.
Consider issuing parallel recommendations to CASB 86-01 and 86-02 above, requiring similar action for American-registered air carriers.
Initiate a national safety campaign to ensure that all pilots are aware of the potential consequences of attempting take-off with even minor amounts of contamination on the wings.

Require all Canadian operators of McDonnell-Douglas DC-8 aircraft, and such other aircraft types which the Department deems appropriate, to establish detailed procedures for detecting ice on the wings prior to take-off.
Review the procedures currently in place with respect to functional checks of cockpit voice recorders with a view to ensuring that the serviceability of the equipment is being tested adequately.
Consider seeking parallel action in the United States to that outlined for Canada in CASB 88-09.

Consider recommending a change in U.S. Federal Aviation Regulations such that the flight-time, duty-time, and crew-rest provisions of FAR Part 121 would apply to all operations of Part 121 air carriers, including non-revenue flights.

safety_changes: Enhanced emphasis on clean wing procedures and verification before takeoff
Improved pilot training on effects of minor wing contamination on aircraft performance
Enhanced procedures for detecting upper wing ice prior to takeoff for DC-8 aircraft
Mandatory functional testing of cockpit voice recorders before flight
Stricter weight and balance procedures using actual weights instead of standard averages
FAA Master Minimum Equipment List revised to require serviceable flight data recorders and cockpit voice recorders on all aircraft types including DC-8

notes: History of Flight section read from TSB report (p. 1, 7-8): departure times, arrival at Gander, ground operations sequence
Meteorological Information section read (p. 16-17): freezing precipitation and icing conditions at Gander
Flight Data Recorder readout read (p. 23-24): rotation timing at 51 seconds, peak airspeed 172 KIAS at 53 seconds, vertical acceleration values, heading deviation

Safety Action section read (p. 97-101): weight and balance issues, clean wing campaign, ice detection procedures, cockpit voice recorder testing, crew fatigue

records.title: Grand Canyon Airlines 6

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Grand Canyon Airlines, Inc., and Helitech Inc., Midair Collision over Grand Canyon National Park

aircraft.type: de Havilland Canada DHC-6 Twin Otter

location.name: Tonto Plateau, Grand Canyon National Park

records.summary: Grand Canyon Airlines Flight 6, a DHC-6 Twin Otter with 20 aboard (18 passengers, 2 crew), collided with a Helitech Bell 206 helicopter (5 aboard) over Grand Canyon National Park on June 18, 1986. The collision occurred at 6,500 feet at approximately 0933 MST. The helicopter's main rotor struck the Twin Otter's nose landing gear and tail, tearing off the rotor and separating the Twin Otter's tail. Both aircraft crashed.
records.probable_cause: The flight crews of both aircraft failed to see and avoid each other for undetermined reasons. Contributing to the accident was the failure of the Federal Aviation Administration to exercise its oversight responsibility over flight operations in the Grand Canyon airspace and the actions of the National Park Service to influence the selection of routes by Grand Canyon scenic air tour operators. Also contributing to the accident was the modification and configuration of the routes of the rotary-wing operators resulting in their intersecting with the routes of Grand Canyon Airlines near Crystal Rapids.

factors.evidence: The crews of the two aircraft failed to see and avoid each other despite operating in visual meteorological conditions (p. 7)
The limited number of scenic points of interest in the Grand Canyon concentrated flights over these points, increasing the risk of collision (p. 7)
The FAA did not modify the regulations necessary to allow them to properly oversee Grand Canyon scenic air tour flight operations (p. 30)
At approximately 0933, at an altitude of approximately 6,500 feet, the Bell 206 and DHC-6 collided, with the helicopter on the left of the Twin Otter (p. 8)

events.text: Grand Canyon Airlines Flight 6 (DHC-6 Twin Otter N76GC, call sign Canyon 6) took off from runway 21 of Grand Canyon Airport for a scheduled 50-minute sightseeing flight with 18 passengers and 2 crew members
Helitech Flight 2 (Bell 206B Jet Ranger N6TC, call sign Tech 2) took off from its heliport in Tusayan, Arizona for an on-demand 30-minute sightseeing flight with 4 passengers and 1 crew member
Both aircraft operated in uncontrolled airspace under visual flight rules, making voluntary position reports on frequency 122.75 MHz over scenic landmarks
A pilot south of Mencius Temple heard Bell 206B report 'west of Mencius at 6400 feet, southbound' and had previously heard Canyon 6 report passing Havasupai Point
A pilot passing Havasupai Point eastbound at 7,100 feet reported seeing a 'mushroom-topped' column of smoke about 1,000 feet high and vaporous clouds rising from Tonto Plateau
At 6,500 feet altitude over Tonto Plateau, the Bell 206 collided with the DHC-6; the helicopter's main rotor struck the Twin Otter's nose landing gear and tail
The helicopter's main rotor was torn off and the Twin Otter's tail separated from the fuselage, with both aircraft losing controllability
Whitewater rafters 3 miles from the accident site saw both aircraft emerge from smoke, the helicopter falling west and the DHC-6 falling east; they heard ground impact sounds and saw black smoke
Both aircraft impacted terrain; all 25 occupants (20 on DHC-6 and 5 on Bell 206) were killed in the collision and crash

recommendations.text: Apply to revenue air tour flights the same flight and duty time limitations that apply to operations conducted under 14 CFR 135.265
Require pilots of revenue air tour flights to use a public address system, intercom, or similar system while narrating air tour flights
Require all revenue air tour flights, regardless of the distance flown, to be subject to the regulatory provisions of 14 CFR Part 135, and not 14 CFR Part 91

safety_changes: FAA implemented Part 135 flight and duty time limitations on scenic air tour operations
Requirement for air tour pilots to use public address or intercom systems while narrating
All scenic air tour flights brought under 14 CFR Part 135 regulatory framework

Key sections: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY (pp. 5-7), CONCLUSIONS and Probable Cause (pp. 29-31)

records.title: Aeroméxico 498
records.summary: Aeroméxico Flight 498 collided with a Piper PA-28 Cherokee that entered the Los Angeles Terminal Control Area without clearance. The Piper was not equipped with a Mode C transponder and was not visible to either crew or ATC radar. The DC-9 crashed in a residential neighborhood in Cerritos, killing 64 on the aircraft, 3 in the Piper, and 15 on the ground.
records.probable_cause: The limitations of the air traffic control system to provide collision protection, through both ATC procedures and automated redundancy. Contributing factors were the inadvertent and unauthorized entry of the PA-28 into the Los Angeles Terminal Control Area and the limitations of the 'see and avoid' concept to ensure traffic separation.

factors.evidence: Piper collided nearly perpendicular with DC-9, shearing top of Piper cockpit and damaging DC-9's tail surfaces; DC-9 crashed in Cerritos.
Neither pilot sighted the other aircraft; neither appeared to attempt evasive maneuvers.
Piper not equipped with Mode C transponder; LAX radar not equipped with automatic warning systems.
ATC was distracted by another unauthorized private aircraft (Grumman AA-5B Tiger) entering the Terminal Control Area.
Piper pilot entered the Los Angeles Terminal Control Area without required clearance; entry was inadvertent, not due to physiological disablement.

events.text: DC-9 Flight 498 begins descent into Los Angeles with 58 passengers and 6 crew.
Piper PA-28 collided nearly perpendicular with DC-9's upper left side of horizontal stabilizer support.
Collision sheared top of Piper's cockpit and severely damaged DC-9's tail surfaces including horizontal stabilizer, rudder, and vertical stabilizer.
DC-9 with damaged tail surfaces over-banked to right and entered steep dive; crashed in residential area of Cerritos.

recommendations.text: Expedite development, operational evaluation, and final certification of Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System (TCAS)
Amend 14 CFR Parts 121 and 135 to require TCAS installation in certificated air carrier aircraft
Implement procedures to track, identify, and take enforcement action against pilots who intrude into ARSAs without ATC communications

notes: Sections read: Findings, Probable Cause, Recommendations

records.title: 1986 Mozambican Tupolev Tu-134 crash

agencies.name: South African Civil Aviation Authority
agencies.report_title: Board of Inquiry Report - Tupolev TU-134A Aircraft C9-CAA

records.summary: A Tupolev Tu-134A carrying President Samora Machel and 43 others departed Mbala, Zambia on October 19, 1986 for Maputo. The navigator inadvertently tuned the primary VOR receiver to Matsapa Airport frequency in Swaziland instead of Maputo, diverting the aircraft 37° off course. The crew failed to monitor the second VOR receiver or cross-check their position. Despite ground proximity warnings, the captain continued descending below minimum safe altitude in darkness and clouds without visual reference to the ground, resulting in controlled flight into terrain near Mbuzini in South Africa.
records.probable_cause: The cause of the accident was that the flight crew failed to follow procedural requirements for an instrument let-down approach, but continued to descend under visual flight rules in darkness and some cloud, i.e. without having visual contact with the ground, below minimum safe altitude and minimum assigned altitude, and in addition ignored the GPWS alarm. (p. 109)

factors.evidence: Crew set first VOR receiver to Matsapa frequency instead of Maputo frequency, causing 37° deviation off course; navigator unaware of the error and continued to follow Matsapa beacon (p. 108)

Poor design of VOR frequency display with no back-lighting, unusually close frequencies between Matsapa and Maputo, and similar appearance of displayed numerals made frequency selection error more likely (p. 108)
Second VOR receiver correctly set to Maputo but apparently not being used or monitored by crew; no cross-checking by challenge and answer system took place (p. 107)
Required procedures and callouts during final let-down and approach were not followed; breakdown in crew discipline and coordination; crew did not file required flight plan (p. 108)
GPWS alarm sounded at 19:21:02 at height of 796m and remained active for 32 seconds; captain cursed but continued descent, ignoring the warning (p. 25)
Aircraft impacted terrain at Mbuzini at 19:21:39 in darkness at high descent rate of 480 feet per minute; 34 of 44 occupants killed including President Samora Machel (p. 26)

events.text: Tupolev Tu-134A C9-CAA departed Mbala Airport with crew of 9 and 35 passengers; computed fuel mass of 10,384 kg for non-stop flight to Maputo (p. 21-22)
Aircraft reported overhead Lusaka at 17:44; cleared to FL 370; handed over to Harare FIR at 17:53 at FIR boundary (p. 22)
Aircraft made contact with Maputo Information and reported position as Kurla at FL 350; stated endurance as 4 hours and persons on board as 48 (actual: 3h 45m endurance, 44 persons) (p. 22)
Aircraft initiated descent from FL 350; instructed by AFIS to report at 3,000 feet or runway lights in sight (p. 22)
Captain observed reserve fuel warning light did not light up during initial descent; navigator reported distance remaining as 120 km (p. 22)

Turn to right commenced from 184°M to 221°M initiated by navigator via autopilot Doppler navigation mode; turn based on VOR signal but was actually Matsapa VOR, diverting aircraft 37° off course (p. 23)
Navigator replied to captain's question about turn: VOR indicates that way; turn completed at 19:11:39 from altitude 19,167 feet to 17,217 feet with 10-15° bank angle (p. 23)
Navigator reported distance as 60 km; reserve fuel warning light illuminated for 25 seconds at 19:12:26 indicating 2,400 kg fuel remaining (p. 23)
Aircraft reached 3,000 feet and informed controller that it was maintaining that altitude; in fact, DFDR showed aircraft continued to descend (p. 24)
Aircraft was cleared for ILS approach to runway 23 with QNH of 1017; radio operator acknowledged but stated ILS was out of service; controller cleared for visual approach to runway 05 instead (p. 24)
Radio operator requested controller check runway lights; aircraft continued to descend below minimums (p. 24)
Ground proximity warning system alarm sounded at height of 796 m (2,611 feet) above ground and remained on for 32 seconds; captain cursed but descent was continued at 480 feet per minute (p. 25)

Aircraft impacted terrain at Mbuzini near Komatipoort in darkness; all aircraft systems functioning normally immediately before impact; destroyed by ground impact; 34 fatalities including President Samora Machel (p. 26)

agencies.name: Air Accidents Investigation Branch
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report: Boeing Vertol 234 LR, G-BWFC

location.name: 2.5 nautical miles east of Sumburgh Airport, Shetland Isles

records.summary: A Boeing-Vertol 234LR helicopter departing the Brent oilfield with 44 passengers and 2 crew experienced catastrophic failure of the forward transmission bevel ring gear while on approach to Sumburgh Airport. Loss of rotor synchronization caused the rotor blades to collide, the aft rotor assembly to detach, and the aircraft to crash into the sea from 150 feet, killing 44 occupants.
records.probable_cause: The immediate cause of the accident was the failure of the modified spiral bevel ring gear in the forward transmission which allowed the twin rotors to collide when synchronisation was lost. Underlying causes were the inadequacy of the hitherto accepted aircraft industry standard of test programme carried out by the manufacturers and the insufficiently stringent inspection programmes required by the FAA and the CAA (p. 41).

factors.evidence: The modified bevel ring gear was redesigned to increase clamping force by introducing larger diameter bolts installed at higher torque (p. 24). The manufacturer and airworthiness authorities failed to perceive that the change in the design of the bolted joint might lead to it performing in a radically different way to that previously experienced (p. 39).

The hitherto accepted aircraft industry standard of test performed on an aft transmission was inadequate to expose the behaviour of the modified joint in the forward transmission (p. 40). The in-service inspection programme based on aft transmission test results was not adequate to reveal the impending failure of the forward bolted joint (p. 40).

The ring gear failure stemmed from corrosion fatigue which was initiated by the unpredicted wear and corrosion characteristics of the bolted joint attaching the gear to its shaft (p. 39). The radial crack progressed by fatigue until the remaining section available to transfer meshing loads circumferentially failed in overload (p. 31). Modified spiral bevel ring gears consistently suffered wear and corrosion which gave rise to conditions in which fatigue could readily initiate in the bolted joint flange (p. 40).

The spiral bevel ring gear in the forward transmission fractured and synchronisation between the rotors was lost (p. 40). The tip of an aft rotor blade struck the root end of a forward rotor blade and the resultant forces tore the complete aft rotor assembly from the aircraft (p. 40).
The helicopter was largely broken up by the clashing rotor blades in mid air and fell towards the sea from a height of 150 feet (p. 3).
The aircraft struck the sea in a tail down attitude with considerable force, broke up and sank (p. 1).

Coastguard helicopter crew noticed two inflated liferafts floating in sea east of Sumburgh Airport; two survivors were spotted and winched aboard the rescue helicopter (p. 12)

records.title: Skywest Airlines 1834

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Midair Collision of SkyWest Airlines Swearingen Metro II and Mooney M20, Kearns, Utah

records.summary: SkyWest Airlines Flight 1834, a Metro II on final approach to Salt Lake City, collided with a Mooney M20 that had intruded into the Salt Lake City Airport Radar Service Area from Salt Lake City Municipal Airport. The Mooney was operating without a mode-C transponder and without proper clearance into controlled airspace. Both aircraft were destroyed and all 10 occupants were killed.
records.probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Board determines that the probable cause of this accident was lack of navigational vigilance by the Mooney instructor pilot which led to the unauthorized intrusion into the Salt Lake City airport radar service area. Contributing to the accident were the absence of a mode-C transponder on the Mooney airplane and the limitations of the air traffic control system to provide collision protection under the circumstances of this accident. (p. 26)

factors.evidence: Mooney departed SLC Municipal Airport traffic pattern and intruded into Salt Lake City ARSA without proper clearance at 1251:58 (p. 20-21)
Final approach controller did not observe Mooney radar target and failed to issue traffic advisories; Mooney target was without mode-C altitude reporting (p. 21, 26)
Flight instructor in Mooney did not maintain sufficient navigational vigilance to ensure aircraft remained clear of ARSA; controller did not track non-mode-C intruders (p. 26-27)
Metro II collided with Mooney at approximately 7,000 feet MSL in visual meteorological conditions; pilot made evasive maneuver but collision was unavoidable (p. 18-19, 26)
After collision, Metro II aircraft slid through chain-link fence stopping in middle of suburban street; wreckage scattered over one-mile square area (p. 19)

events.text: SkyWest Flight 1834 departs Pocatello for SLC; flight is 30 minutes late; handed off from Center to SLC TRACON Bear Sector (p. 5)
Bear Sector controller issues heading 100° to SkyWest 1834; advises to expect vectors for visual approach to runway 34L (p. 5)
SkyWest 1834 given frequency change to TRACON Final controller; continues receipt of descent clearances and vectors (p. 5)
Final controller advises SkyWest 1834 of traffic 10 o'clock 4 miles at 6,000 feet; crew reports traffic in sight (p. 5)
Final controller transmits: traffic 10-11 o'clock, 3 miles; SkyWest 1834 does not acknowledge (p. 5)
Metro II collides with Mooney M20 at approximately 7,000 feet MSL; radar targets merge on final controller scope; expletive recorded on ATC frequency (p. 5-6, 20)
Metro II aircraft slides through chain-link fence and stops in middle of suburban street in Kearns area; wreckage scattered over one-mile-square area with body parts in trees (p. 19)
All 8 aboard Metro II (2 pilots, 6 passengers) and all 2 aboard Mooney killed; both aircraft destroyed in collision and impact (p. 19)

recommendations.text: Expedite the development, operational evaluation, and final certification of the Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System for installation and use in certificated air carrier aircraft (p. 27)

Amend 14 CFR Parts 121 and 135 to require the installation and use of Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System equipment in certificated air carrier aircraft when it becomes available for operational use (p. 27)
Implement procedures to track, identify, and take appropriate enforcement action against pilots who intrude into Airport Radar Areas without the required Air Traffic Control communications (p. 27-28)

Require transponder equipment with mode-C altitude reporting for operations around all Terminal Control Areas and within an Airport Radar Service Area after a specified date compatible with implementation of TCAS requirements for air carrier aircraft (p. 28)

Take expedited action to add visual flight rules conflict alert (mode-C intruder) logic to Automated Radar Terminal System systems as an interim measure to the ultimate implementation of the Advanced Automation System (p. 28)
Incorporate formal training on the dangers of the low-workload environment at all levels of air traffic controller training (p. 29)

Establish an ad hoc task force including controller and human performance expertise to evaluate the extent to which radar air traffic controllers are dependent on FDB radar symbology to carry out their duties and to make appropriate improvements in initial and recurrent radar training (p. 29)

Review and revise as necessary the Air Traffic Control Academy and facility terminal radar training programs to include 'real world' aspects, such as visual flight rules intruders, into the radar training facility and the electronic target generator scenarios (p. 29)

safety_changes: Implementation of TCAS (Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System) on air carrier aircraft
Expanded Mode-C transponder requirements for aircraft operating in Terminal Control Areas and Airport Radar Service Areas
Enhanced ATC training to include VFR intruder scenarios and low-workload environment management

records.summary: Northwest Airlink Flight 2268, a CASA C-212 turboprop, was cleared for a visual approach to Runway 21R at Detroit Metropolitan Airport at 14:30. At 60-70 feet above ground, the aircraft banked left and then rolled right, striking the ramp area and flipping over.
records.probable_cause: The captain's inability to control the airplane in an attempt to recover from an asymmetric power condition at low speed following his intentional use of beta mode to descend and slow the airplane rapidly on final approach.

records.title: American Eagle 5452
records.summary: An American Eagle CASA C-212 Aviocar crashed on 8 May 1987 on approach to Eugenio María de Hostos Airport in Mayagüez, Puerto Rico. The aircraft made an unstable, steep descent and touched down 600 feet short of the runway. Both pilots were killed but all four passengers survived with only minor injuries. The crash resulted from maintenance defects and inadequate inspection procedures by Executive Air Charter.
records.probable_cause: The aircraft likely had one engine slip to idle during approach, causing asymmetrical thrust and loss of speed. Executive Air Charter failed to perform scheduled maintenance and inspections in conformance with its approved maintenance program, and required inspections were not conducted in accordance with proper maintenance practices.

factors.evidence: Scheduled maintenance and inspections of the airplane were not performed in conformance with its approved maintenance program (p. 2, 7)
The right engine propeller and fuel flow settings were improper, likely causing one engine to slip to idle during approach, causing asymmetrical thrust and loss of speed (p. 5, 10-15)

The captain had flown an unstable approach, descending steeply and too close to the runway. Witnesses reported the airplane seemed too fast, overshot the extended centerline, and made a violent turn (p. 5-6, 42)
The plane's flaps were found to be in the up (retracted) position at impact, which is improper for approach and landing (p. 9)
plane crashed 600 feet short of the runway

events.text: The captain arrived 15 minutes late at 0600 local time while the first officer arrived on time at 0545 for flight 5452 scheduled departure at 0615 local time.
Flight 5452 departed San Juan at 0620 local time with four passengers and two crewmembers aboard the CASA C-212-CC, registration N432CA, on a visual flight rules flight plan.

While in the vicinity of Mayaguez, the captain cancelled the visual flight rules flight plan and proceeded to make a visual approach to runway 9 without making the customary in-range call to operations.
Witnesses who observed the airplane on its downwind leg reported it appeared normal, though one witness said it seemed too fast and appeared to overshoot the extended centerline on the base leg.

A crop duster pilot reported everything appeared normal until the airplane was about 1,000 feet from the runway and 100 feet above ground, when he heard a sound similar to reverse pitch being applied.

The airplane yawed to the right followed by a roll to the left, then rolled back to the right as the right wing tip struck the ground 643 feet short of the runway threshold and 67 feet right of centerline.
The airplane traveled about 100 feet after initial ground impact, with the nose striking a chain-link fence and ditch before pivoting about 180 degrees and coming to rest upright.

The right wing separated about midspan and the cockpit was demolished up to the forward cabin bulkhead. Postcrash fire destroyed portions of the airframe. Both pilots were killed but all four passengers survived with minor injuries.

Expedite the rulemaking action to require installation of an artificial stall warning system on the CASA C-212 airplanes.
Correct any deficiencies in compliance with Title 14 CFR 25.813 regarding the installation of passenger seats adjacent to Type II and III exits in CASA C-212 airplanes with 19 seats or less.

Remedy the deficiencies in compliance with Title 14 CFR 25.809, .811, and .813 of the supplemental type certificate for the CASA C-212-CC main door regarding accessibility to door controls during emergency conditions.
Require in accordance with Title 14 CFR 25.785(c) adequate head clearance between passenger seats and bulkheads/partitions installed in CASA C-212 airplanes.
Inspect flightcrew restraints in CASA C-212 airplanes to verify the adequacy of operation, convenience, and comfort based on anthropomorphic criteria, and take appropriate remedial action.

Require fire-blocking materials on all passenger and crew seats on Title 14 CFR Part 21 and Special Federal Aviation Regulations No. 41 and Title 14 CFR Part 23 commuter category airplanes operated under Title 14 CFR Part 135.

Conduct a special surveillance inspection of approved Hartzell Propeller overhaul facilities and of other propeller manufacturer overhaul facilities to determine that proper quality control organization and procedures are in place and are being followed.

Alert all principal operations and maintenance inspectors to emphasize in their surveillance of operators of turbopropeller airplanes the need to adhere to prescribed manufacturer instructions in maintaining flight idle blade angles and to emphasize to operators the criticalness of maintaining them properly.
Reissue to operations and maintenance inspectors Federal Aviation Administration Notice N8320.301 of September 17, 1984, prompted by Safety Board Recommendation A-84-15.

Complete as soon as possible and make the findings available to the Safety Board the report on the in-house review of the bilateral aircraft type certification program and the corrective actions taken or contemplated as a result of the review.
Amend Title 14 CFR 23.207 and 25.207 to require a stall warning device and eliminate the use of inherent aerodynamic qualities (aerodynamic buffeting) as a stall warning.
Amend Title 14 CFR Parts 121 and 135 to require a stall warning device on those airplanes that currently use inherent aerodynamic qualities (aerodynamic buffeting) as a stall warning.

Require the aircraft evaluation group during the type certification process of turbopropeller airplanes to review carefully the design of propeller pitch controls in order to identify and establish appropriate flightcrew training guidelines and to emphasize the proper use of these controls to prevent inadvertent operation in the beta mode in flight where prohibited by the airplane manufacturer.

Require the principal operations inspectors for operators of turbopropeller airplanes to review carefully flightcrew training programs to verify that appropriate information is provided by the operators on the proper use of propeller pitch controls to prevent inadvertent operation in the beta mode in flight.

Amend Title 14 CFR 25.1155 and 23.1155 to provide for a positive means to prevent inadvertent operation of the propellers at blade pitch settings below the flight regime in those airplanes where such operation of the propellers is prohibited.

records.title: Vuelo 103 de Ryan Air Service
records.summary: A Beechcraft 1900C operated by Ryan Air Services crashed during approach to Homer Airport on November 23, 1987. The aircraft was overloaded with approximately 600 pounds more cargo than requested, displacing the center of gravity to an excessively aft position. During the landing approach, when flaps were extended, the aircraft lost control and descended steeply, striking a fence before coming to rest on its belly.
records.probable_cause: The failure of the flightcrew to properly supervise the loading of the airplane which resulted in the center of gravity being displaced to such an aft location that airplane control was lost when the flaps were lowered for landing.

factors.evidence: The aircraft was loaded with approximately 1,800 pounds of cargo in the aft compartment, exceeding the allowable limit by 600 to 750 pounds
Up to 3/8 inch of rime ice was found on the leading edges but had minimal effect on controllability under normal loading
When flaps were extended for landing, the aircraft pitched up and rolled, striking terrain in a steep descent

records.title: Air Littoral Flight 1919

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses
agencies.report_title: Accident d'un Brasilia EMB 120 immatriculé F-GEGH, survenu le 21 décembre 1987 à Eysines (Gironde)

records.summary: Air Littoral Flight 1919, an EMB 120 Brasilia en route from Brussels to Bordeaux, conducted an ILS approach during foggy weather. Poor crew coordination and inadequate altitude monitoring resulted in the aircraft descending below the safe approach path. The aircraft struck trees in a forest 5,100 meters short of the runway threshold, killing all 16 occupants.
records.probable_cause: The accident resulted directly from poor trajectory management. The crew failed to coordinate effectively during the critical final approach phase, with neither pilot maintaining adequate vigilance over altitude and ILS compliance. When cloud base height improved to 160 feet, the crew made an optimistic decision to attempt a direct approach from an unfavorable position (too close, too high, too fast) without adequate preparation. The crew continued descending below decision height (220 feet) despite insufficient visual references and regulations requiring a go-around when cloud base fell below 150 feet. An untimely exchange of pilot duties immediately before the outer marker compounded the coordination breakdown, leaving the crew confused about the approach strategy.

factors.evidence: Dense fog with cloud base of 100-130 feet at arrival. Visibility 200 meters (p. 8)

Poor coordination between the two pilots. Exchange of duties exactly at the outer marker created confusion about approach strategy. The non-flying pilot provided inadequate assistance during the critical descent phase. (p. 14-15)

Neither pilot maintained adequate vigilance over altitude during approach. Altitude and ILS compliance were not properly monitored. The crew failed to recognize they were well below the glide slope. (p. 13-15)
The aircraft was positioned too close to the airport, too high, and too fast (265 knots) when the crew decided to attempt the direct approach. The approach parameters were unsatisfactory. (p. 15)

Aircraft descended below the required decision height (220 feet) and below the safe approach trajectory. Cloud base dropped to 130 feet, below the 150-foot minimum required by regulation, but crew continued descent. (p. 13-15)

When conditions deteriorated and cloud base fell below minimums at the outer marker, regulations and procedures required an immediate go-around. The crew did not execute this procedure despite clear indications. (p. 15)

The final approach phase involved a rapid sequence of complex actions: weather monitoring, radio communications transfers, altitude and speed management, approach briefing changes, and pilot duties exchange. The workload was high and compressed into the critical final approach period. (p. 14-15)
Aircraft impacted trees at 5,100 meters before the runway threshold at Eysines in the Pinsan forest. (p. 8, 11)

events.text: Aircraft departs Brussels for Bordeaux with 16 occupants (2 pilots, 1 flight attendant, 13 passengers). Flight conditions forecast as marginal at Bordeaux with dense fog.
Captain inquires about Bordeaux weather conditions again.
Approach control directs aircraft to waiting beacon BE, descend to FL 50.
Approach reports cloud base height 160 feet, sufficient for ILS approach.
Controller reports updated cloud base height 130 feet, below the 150-foot minimum required for approach.
Captain takes control from first officer with brief instruction 'Remets-moi l'ILS chez moi' (Put the ILS on my display) and acknowledges 'O.K.', indicating duties exchange is complete.
Captain orders 'Deux cents neuds, volets vers 15, le train sur sortie' (200 knots, flaps 15, gear down) to prepare for landing.
Captain queries 'Bon, où est l'axe 2?' (Where is runway 2?), showing concern about runway alignment.
Captain asks 'On passe combien là?' (How much altitude are we at?), indicating insufficient altitude surveillance during the critical final moments.

Aircraft strikes trees on approach to Bordeaux, descending at high rate with insufficient altitude and with crew still attempting to gain control. Impact occurs 5,100 meters short of runway threshold. Immediate post-impact fire destroys the aircraft.

recommendations.text: That regulations regarding minimum cloud base heights be revised. The regulation that prohibited approach attempts below 100 feet (later 130 feet) created an incentive for crews to plan descents for holding patterns rather than approaches, and when conditions improved slightly, made crews commit to marginal approaches without adequate preparation.
recommendations.outcome: Regulation modified on 17 November 1988 to eliminate visibility vertical (sky not obscured) as a minimum requirement for ILS approaches, allowing approaches when only ceiling minima are met.

recommendations.text: That precise terminology be used in safety-critical domains. The cloudbase meter provides a cloud height value that does not correspond to true cloud base during fog conditions and can create false sense of security.

That crew training emphasize decision-making during marginal weather approaches and teach pilots to recognize when an approach is becoming unstable. Training should include go-around procedures and decision height management.

That pilot training on the Embraer EMB 120 include specific preparation for high-workload terminal procedures. The aircraft's performance characteristics can lead to excessive speed retention and require active energy management during instrument approaches.

safety_changes: French regulation on minimum cloud base for ILS approaches modified (17 November 1988) to eliminate visibility vertical requirement
Enhanced emphasis on crew resource management training in regional carrier operations
Improved terminal aerodrome forecast (TAF) terminology and dissemination to crews

records.title: Trans-Colorado Airlines 2286
records.summary: The crew chose a direct non-precision approach to runway 20 instead of an ILS approach that would have added ten minutes, motivated by time savings. The first officer flew a rapid descent of 3,000 feet per minute, more than three times the intended rate. The aircraft struck terrain approximately five miles from the airport while descending. Tests revealed the captain had used cocaine 12 to 18 hours before the flight, which likely degraded his piloting skills.

records.title: Nürnberger Flugdienst 108
records.summary: Swearingen Metroliner III Flight 108 was struck by lightning during approach to Düsseldorf on February 8, 1988. The lightning strike caused complete electrical system failure, including loss of all flight instruments and autopilot. Spatially disoriented, the pilots descended uncontrollably and the aircraft disintegrated in midair after approximately 2 minutes of predominantly uncontrolled flight.
records.probable_cause: The crew continued flight into an area where electrical discharges were expected despite possibility of deviation. Complete electrical power failure resulted from lightning strike during instrument flight conditions, causing loss of cockpit and instrument lighting and rendering flap and stabilizer trim inoperable. The aircraft subsequently entered predominantly uncontrolled flight and was structurally overloaded and broke apart in midair.

factors.evidence: Aircraft struck by lightning inside thunderstorm, causing entire electrical system to fail (p. 7-8)
Pilots became disoriented without flight instruments and entered high-speed descent (p. 8, 50)
After approximately 2 minutes of predominantly uncontrolled flight, trailing edge flap failed due to overloading (p. 50)
Aircraft disintegrated in midair after trailing edge flap failure caused unrecoverable spiral (p. 50)

events.text: Flight 108 initiated descent from 14,000 feet after 24 minutes of climb from Hannover
Düsseldorf director cleared Flight 108 for ILS approach to runway 24 and warned that preceding aircraft experienced lightning strike on 6 miles final
Crew reached localizer at 2,900 feet and observed on weather radar that thunderstorm activity was directly ahead
Aircraft entered thunderstorm. Lightning strike at 07:55:08 caused complete electrical system failure, including all flight instruments and lighting
Without flight instruments, pilots became disoriented and entered high-speed descent
After approximately 2 minutes of predominantly uncontrolled flight, aircraft disintegrated in midair near Kettwig. All 21 occupants killed.

recommendations.text: Equip aircraft with independent gyroscopic horizon powered by sources independent of normal electrical system for all aircraft operating in commercial air transport
Provide guidance in flight manual regarding behavior in and near thunderstorms and procedure for restoring power after total electrical failure
Modify Battery-Bus-Relay to make failure extremely unlikely or modify electrical system to allow generator reconnection with open relay

safety_changes: Airlines now required to avoid thunderstorms more strictly

records.title: AVAir 3378
records.summary: AVAir Flight 3378 departed Raleigh-Durham at 21:25 on an IFR flight to Richmond in low ceiling, low visibility conditions. Shortly after takeoff during initial climb to 300 feet, the aircraft executed an excessive rate of turn instead of maintaining standard climb profile. The first officer was flying while the captain communicated with ATC. The aircraft descended in a 45-degree turn and struck a reservoir, impacting with water then continuing onto land.
records.probable_cause: The failure of flight crew to maintain a proper flightpath. Contributing factors were the ineffective management and supervision of flight crew training and operations and inappropriate FAA surveillance of AVAir.

factors.evidence: Ceiling 100 feet AGL, visibility 2400 feet RVR, fog condition (p. 2)
Improper instrument scanning and visual/aural perception by copilot/second pilot; pilot in command with inadequate monitoring (p. 2, Finding #5, #9, #13)

Company records showed instances of substandard performance by first officer; inadequate surveillance of operation and training by company/operator management; inadequate FAA surveillance (p. 1, Finding #6, #7, #73, #74)
Aircraft in 45-degree descending turn during initial climb; inadvertent descent by copilot (p. 1, Finding #1, #14)
Aircraft struck water in reservoir and continued onto land (p. 1)

records.title: Aloha Airlines 243

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report--Aloha Airlines, Flight 243

records.summary: The Boeing 737-200 suffered an explosive decompression in flight when a large section of the fuselage roof tore off at 24,000 feet. The damage resulted from metal fatigue and crevice corrosion in the lap joint along the upper fuselage. Flight attendant Clarabelle Lansing was ejected from the aircraft. The crew successfully diverted and landed at Kahului Airport with 94 survivors.
records.probable_cause: The failure of the Aloha Airlines maintenance program to detect the presence of significant disbonding and fatigue damage which ultimately led to failure of the lap joint at S-10L and the separation of the fuselage upper lobe. Contributing to the accident were the failure of Aloha Airlines management to supervise properly its maintenance force; the failure of the FAA to evaluate properly the Aloha Airlines maintenance program and to assess the airline's inspection and quality control deficiencies; the failure of the FAA to require Airworthiness Directive 87-21-08 inspection of all the lap joints proposed by Boeing Alert Service Bulletin SB 737-53A1039; and, the lack of a complete terminating action after the discovery of early production difficulties in the B-737 cold bond lap joint which resulted in low bond durability, corrosion, and premature fatigue cracking.

factors.evidence: Multiple-site fatigue cracking of the skin adjacent to rivet holes along lap joint upper rivet row initiated from knife edges associated with countersunk lap joint rivet holes; the knife edge concentrated stresses transferred through rivets because of lap joint disbonding (p. 72).

Failure of Aloha Airlines maintenance program to detect significant disbonding and fatigue damage in the lap joint at S-10L; the aircraft was 19 years old with 89,680 flight cycles in a coastal saltwater environment prone to corrosion (p. 72).

Fuselage examinations were scheduled during the night and not performed as required by company procedures, making carrying out an adequate inspection more difficult; Aloha Airlines management failed to recognize the human performance factors of inspection (p. 72-73).

Entire top half of the aircraft skin extending from just behind the cockpit to the fore-wing area separated; a major portion of the upper crown skin and structure of section 43 separated in flight causing an explosive decompression of the cabin (p. 12).
Section on left side of roof ruptured with whooshing sound at 24,000 feet cruising altitude (p. 8).

events.text: Flight 243 reached normal cruising altitude of 24,000 feet
Section on the left side of roof ruptured with whooshing sound; cockpit door broke away exposing blue sky
Captain Schornstheimer took over controls and performed immediate emergency descent, extending speed brakes and descending at 280-290 knots with rate of descent of 4,100 feet per minute
Honolulu ARTCC controller attempting to communicate with flight 243, observing emergency code 7700 transponder return about 23 nautical miles south-southeast of Kahului Airport
First officer switched radio to Maui Tower frequency and informed tower of rapid decompression, declaring an emergency and stating need for emergency equipment
Emergency coordination began between Honolulu Center and Maui Approach Control; Honolulu advised Maui that 7700 transponder return could be an Aloha 737
Local controller requested flight 243 to change to Maui Approach Control frequency 119.5 MHz; request acknowledged but flight continued transmitting on local controller frequency
First officer informed local controller: We're going to need assistance. We cannot communicate with the flight attendants. We'll need assistance for the passengers when we land
First officer advised tower: We won't have a nose gear; manual nose gear extension was selected but green indicator light did not illuminate
Crew advised tower: We'll need all the equipment you've got; discovered No. 1 (left) engine had failed during power maneuver for approach
Flight 243 landed on runway 02 at Maui's Kahului Airport with normal touchdown and landing rollout; used No. 2 engine thrust reverser and brakes to stop; emergency evacuation accomplished on runway

recommendations.text: Provide specific guidance and proper engineering support to Principal Maintenance Inspectors to evaluate modifications of airline maintenance programs and operations specifications which propose segmenting major maintenance inspections.

Identify operators whose airplane use differs significantly from the flight cycle versus flight time relationship upon which the Maintenance Planning Document was predicated, and verify that their maintenance programs provide timely detection of both cycle and time related deficiencies.

Revise the regulations governing the certification of aviation maintenance technician schools and the licensing of airframe and powerplant mechanics to require that the curriculum and testing requirements include modern aviation industry technology.

Require formal certification and recurrent training of aviation maintenance inspectors performing nondestructive inspection functions. Formal training should include apprenticeship and periodic skill demonstration.

Require operators to provide specific training programs for maintenance and inspection personnel about the conditions under which visual inspections must be conducted and periodically test personnel on their ability to detect defined defects.

Develop a continuing inspection program for those B-737 airplanes that have incorporated lap joint terminating action to detect any fatigue cracking that may develop in the middle or lower rows of fuselage lap joint fastener holes and define the types of inspections, inspection intervals, and corrective actions needed for continuing airworthiness.
Develop a model program for a comprehensive corrosion control program to be included in each operator's approved maintenance program.

Issue an Airworthiness Directive for B-737 airplanes equipped with carbon steel engine control cables to periodically inspect the cables for evidence of corrosion and if there is such evidence, to accomplish the actions set forth in Boeing Service Letter 737-SL-76-2-A.

Require that air carrier maintenance departments use the engineering services available from the manufacturer or other sources to periodically evaluate their maintenance practices including structural repair, compliance with airworthiness directives and service bulletins, performance of inspection and quality assurance sections and overall effectiveness of continuing airworthiness programs.

Revise the National Aviation Safety Inspection Program objectives to require that inspectors evaluate not only the paperwork trail, but also the actual condition of the fleet airplanes undergoing maintenance and on the operational ramp.
Require National Aviation Safety Inspection Program teams to indicate related systemic deficiencies within an operators maintenance activity when less than satisfactory fleet condition is identified.
Evaluate the quality of FAA surveillance provided by the principal inspectors as part of the National Aviation Safety Inspection Program.
Integrate the National Aviation Safety Inspection Program team leader in the closeout of the team findings.

Enhance the stature and performance of the principal inspectors through formal management training and guidance, greater encouragement and backing by headquarters, improved accountability for the quality of the surveillance, and additional headquarters assistance in standardizing surveillance activities.

Require that all turbojet transport category airplanes certificated in the future receive full scale structural fatigue testing to a minimum of two times the projected economic service life. Also require that all currently certificated turbojet transport category airplanes that have not been fatigue tested to two lifetimes, be subjected to such testing. As a result of this testing and subsequent inspection and analysis, require manufacturers to identify structure susceptible to multiple site damage and adopt inspection programs appropriate for the detection of such damage.

Discontinue classification of fuselage skin as "malfunction evident" or "damage obvious" on supplemental structural inspection documents. In addition, review all the remaining structurally significant items in the damage obvious category for possible inclusion in the Supplementary Inspection Program.

Issue an Air Carrier Operations Bulletin for all air carrier flight training departments to review the accident scenario and reiterate the need to assess airplane airworthiness as stated in the operators manual before taking action that may cause further damage or breakup of a damaged airframe.

Revise the maintenance program to recognize the high-time high cycles nature of the fleet operations and initiate maintenance inspection and overhaul concepts based on realistic and acceptable calendar and flight cycle intervals.
Initiate a corrosion prevention and control program designed to afford maximum protection from the effects of harsh operating environments.

Revise and upgrade the technical division manpower and organization to provide the necessary Management, quality assurance, engineering, technical training and production personnel to maintain a high level of airworthiness of the fleet.

Assist member air carriers to establish maintenance department engineering services to evaluate maintenance practices including structural repair, compliance with airworthiness directives and service bulletins, performance of inspection and quality assurance sections, and overall effectiveness of continuing airworthiness programs.
