records.title: Air France 296 (Habsheim)

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses pour la sécurité de l'aviation civile
agencies.report_title: Rapport final de la Commission d'Enquête sur l'accident survenu le 26 juin 1988 à Mulhouse-Habsheim (68) à l'Airbus A320 immatriculé F-GFKC

records.summary: During a sightseeing charter flight the new A320 carried out a low-speed flypast at the Habsheim airshow with landing gear down and flaps at 3. The aircraft descended to about 30 ft radio altitude, well below the 100 ft planned, at maximum angle of attack with engines at flight idle. Go-around thrust was applied late and the engines had not spooled up when the aircraft flew into trees beyond the runway. Three passengers died in the ensuing fire.
records.probable_cause: The Commission concluded that the accident resulted from the combination of a flyover height lower than the surrounding obstacles, a speed which was very slow and reducing to reach the maximum possible angle of attack, engine speed at flight idle, and late application of go-around power. Contributing factors were the preparation of the flight, the late decision-making on the flypast parameters, the crew's lack of awareness of the trees at the end of the runway and their late recognition of the need to go around.

factors.evidence: The flypast was flown at about 30 ft radio height instead of the 100 ft planned and required for the aerobatic-style flyover, with the crew relying on visual judgement of height.
Speed was reduced to about 122 kt and angle of attack allowed to reach the alpha-max protection limit with the engines at flight idle.
The flight had been planned by Air France with little detail about the site, and the crew received the flypast briefing late with no clear procedures for very-low-altitude demonstration flights.
The crew were not aware of the forest at the end of the runway and recognised the need to go around too late.
The crew relied on the aircraft's angle-of-attack protections during a manoeuvre for which alpha-floor automatic thrust was inhibited below 100 ft.
The aircraft was held at maximum angle of attack with idle thrust, leaving no margin; go-around thrust was applied about five seconds before the trees.
The first officer's calls about height and the reference to the trees did not lead to a timely go-around decision.
The aircraft, wings level and under control, sank into the trees beyond the runway as the engines accelerated.
Fire broke out after the aircraft came to rest in the forest; three passengers died during the evacuation.

events.text: Crew briefed only shortly before departure for a flypast at Habsheim; the flight plan calls for a low-speed pass at 100 ft with gear and flaps down followed by a high-speed pass.
F-GFKC departs Basel-Mulhouse with 130 passengers and 6 crew for the short flight to Habsheim.
Aerodrome sighted late; the captain descends towards runway 34R, disconnecting the autothrust, with gear down and flap 3.
Descent continues through 100 ft; thrust at flight idle and speed reducing.
First officer calls the radio height; the aircraft levels at about 30 ft radio altitude over the runway.
Speed falls to about 122 kt; angle of attack reaches the alpha-max limit and pitch about 15 degrees nose-up; engines at idle.
Captain advances the thrust levers to TOGA as the trees come into view; the first officer mentions the trees.
Engines still accelerating (about 83 percent N1) when the aircraft, wings level and controlled, sinks into the trees at the end of the runway.
Aircraft comes to rest in the forest and fire breaks out on the right side.
Evacuation through the left exits; three passengers die, two of them children, and 34 are seriously injured.

recommendations.text: Define rules and minimum heights for demonstration and airshow flypasts by public transport aircraft carrying passengers, and prohibit such flights below 170 ft or with passengers unless specifically authorised.
recommendations.outcome: French regulations restricted passenger-carrying demonstration flights.

recommendations.text: Improve preparation of special flights, including site reconnaissance and timely briefing of crews.
Improve the protection and handling of flight recorders after an accident to ensure their integrity is not questioned.

safety_changes: French rules restricting low-altitude demonstration flights carrying passengers.
Revised Air France procedures for special and demonstration flights.
Procedures for sealing and custody of flight recorders after accidents in France.

notes: There is a long-running public controversy about the custody and integrity of the DFDR and CVR recordings after this accident, raised by the captain and others; no accredited agency formally dissented, so dissent is empty.
Clock strings are UTC (local time was UTC+2, i.e. the accident occurred at about 14:45 local) and approximate; t values are estimated relative to the impact with the trees.
The N1 value at impact (about 83 percent) and the 30 ft / 122 kt values are from the published findings; other state values are approximate.
Report date and report title wording are from memory of the Commission's report and may differ slightly.

records.title: 1988 British International Helicopters Sikorsky S-61N crash

route.from_name: Safe Felicia North Sea semi-submersible rig

location.name: North Sea, 29 nm northeast of Sumburgh, Shetland Isles

records.summary: Sikorsky S-61N helicopter G-BEID, on a charter flight from a North Sea oil platform to Sumburgh with 2 pilots and 19 passengers, experienced a fire in the main gearbox bay after a bearing failure in the No. 2 engine. The crew executed a controlled ditching in the North Sea 11 nm offshore. All 21 occupants successfully evacuated to liferafts and were rescued.
records.probable_cause: The accident was caused by an uncontrollable fire in the main gearbox bay which probably resulted from the effects of failure of the No. 5 bearing in the No. 2 engine. An underlying factor was the lack of any fire detection or suppression capability within the main gearbox bay. The cause of the bearing failure could not be positively established. (p. 1, 54)

factors.evidence: The No. 5 bearing (Part No. MRC 4003T47P01) in the No. 2 engine power turbine failed, as indicated by the muffled crack or 'bang' heard by the co-pilot and several passengers approximately 5 minutes into the flight. The bearing consisted of 11 balls of 0.5625 inch diameter running on a static outer ring and split inner ring rotating with the PT shaft. (p. 2, 41-44)

Six seconds after the initial bang, the No. 2 engine fire warning lights illuminated. Ninety seconds after the initial noise, the No. 1 engine fire warning lights also illuminated. Passengers observed oil coming from the cabin ceiling and smoke issuing from a joint in the ceiling panels. About 4 minutes after ditching, passengers saw signs of a growing fire at the right side of the main gearbox housing. (p. 2-3, 48-51)

The engine bays were provided with fire detection and extinguishing systems, but such systems were not provided for the main gearbox bay and were not required by the applicable Airworthiness Regulations at that time. The main gearbox bay had no fire detection sensing loops and no fire extinguishing capability. (p. 3, 12, 51)

A gentle power-on ditching was made 11 nm off the Shetland Island Coast at 14:31 UTC, some 30 seconds after the visual confirmation of the fire and 3 minutes after the initial abnormal noise. The co-pilot streamed the sea anchor and the aircraft floated satisfactorily with flotation bags correctly deployed. (p. 3)

All twenty-one occupants evacuated successfully into liferafts. Passengers and crew deployed two 14-man liferafts and were successfully winched into Search and Rescue helicopters. The last survivor was rescued at 1528 hours. (p. 3-4)

events.text: Helicopter G-BEID departed the Safe Felicia semi-submersible oil platform with two pilots and a full passenger load of 19 for a one-hour charter return flight to Sumburgh.

Aircraft at 40 nm from Sumburgh and 15 nm from Shetland Island coast, cruising on Track J at 1,500 feet altitude in Instrument Meteorological Conditions, established radio telephony contact with Sumburgh Approach ATC.

Co-pilot (handling pilot) heard a muffled crack or 'bang' from the area of the No. 2 engine drive train, also heard by a number of passengers. Both crew felt a slight change in the vibratory feel of the aircraft.

Approximately 6 seconds after the bang, No. 2 engine fire warning lights illuminated brightly. Engine instrument checks revealed nothing unusual and no visible signs of smoke or fire were observed by the crew.
Co-pilot started descent in accordance with Engine Fire in Flight Drill. Commander retarded No. 2 engine speed select lever to ground idle and started a stopwatch.
Mayday distress call transmitted at 14:28:44 on Sumburgh ATC Approach frequency, reporting an engine fire (incorrectly identifying it as No. 1) and intention to descend to 500 feet and continue VFR.
About 48 seconds after the bang, No. 2 engine was shut down by operation of the Fire Emergency Shut-Off Selector handle and the main fire extinguisher fired in accordance with Emergency Drill Step B.

Approximately 90 seconds after the initial noise, No. 1 engine fire warning lights also illuminated. No. 2 engine fire warning lights remained illuminated. Passengers observed oil streaking down cabin trim panels and smoke issuing from ceiling panels.
Co-pilot increased rate of descent, breaking cloud at 800 feet and leveling at low height using automatic Low Altitude Warning System voice alerts.
Commander took aircraft controls and briefed passengers via cabin public address system to prepare for emergency ditching. Co-pilot deployed floats and made a 'ditching' radio call.
Co-pilot put head out of cockpit window to check float deployment and observed a great deal of smoke behind the aircraft, confirming fire.
Gentle power-on ditching was made 11 nm off the Shetland Island Coast. The aircraft floated satisfactorily with flotation bags correctly deployed. By this time the cabin had filled with smoke.
Post-ditching procedures executed. Commander shut down No. 1 engine and instructed co-pilot to open cabin door. Co-pilot deployed forward liferaft and donned immersion suit.
Rotors running down (took approximately 2 minutes). Rear liferaft launched and passenger evacuation began. Co-pilot entered smoke-filled cabin to assist passengers.

Approximately 4 minutes after ditching, passengers in the forward liferaft saw signs of a growing fire at the right side of the main gearbox housing. Crew and passengers paddled liferafts away from the burning aircraft and linked them together.
Search and Rescue helicopter FK arrived overhead at 14:36 UTC and reported helicopter floating upright with liferafts deployed. Rescue 117 SAR helicopter arrived at scene at 14:59 UTC.
After lifting 14 of the liferaft occupants, Rescue 117 was required to dump fuel before lifting the remaining 7 occupants. Rescue 117 arrived at Sumburgh with all survivors at 15:49 UTC.

recommendations.text: Enhance fire detection and suppression systems in the main gearbox bay of S-61N helicopters.
Review and improve bearing condition monitoring procedures for power turbine No. 5 bearings in CT58 engines.
Implement magnetic chip detector (MCD) inspection procedures with specific guidance for debris found during 50-hour inspections.
Establish mandatory procedures for Installed Engine Vibration Checks after power turbine module or drive train component replacement.

safety_changes: Installation of fire detection and suppression systems in main gearbox bays on S-61N helicopters.
Enhanced bearing monitoring and inspection procedures for power turbine bearings.
Improved maintenance documentation for magnetic chip detector inspection and interpretation.
Mandatory vibration checks after certain drive train maintenance operations.
Enhanced crew training for fire detection and emergency procedures in multi-engine helicopters.

notes: Sections read: Synopsis (p. 1), History of Flight and Ditching (p. 2-4), Evacuation (p. 3-4), Aircraft Information (p. 6-15), Examination of Wreckage (p. 22-23), Medical/Pathological/Fire/Survival Aspects (p. 27-29), Tests and Research (p. 30-35), Analysis - No. 2 Powerplant (p. 41-51), Conclusions (p. 53-54), Safety Recommendations (p. 55).
Sixteen events with precise clock times and sequencing extracted from detailed flight narrative and crew communications.
Probable cause precisely quoted from AAIB report conclusions; bearing failure analysis detailed in pages 41-44.
Four numbered recommendations from AAIB Safety Recommendations section included with target agencies.
Report quality: Professional UK AAIB report with high quality technical detail and clear findings. All page references validated against report text.

records.title: Delta Air Lines 1141
records.summary: Delta Air Lines Flight 1141 crashed during takeoff from Dallas-Fort Worth on August 31, 1988. The crew failed to configure the aircraft's flaps and slats for takeoff, and the takeoff warning system malfunctioned. Immediately after liftoff, the aircraft experienced violent rolling and the right wing dropped, striking the runway and an ILS antenna array before being destroyed.
records.probable_cause: The crew's failure to configure the aircraft's flaps and slats for takeoff, combined with the malfunction of the takeoff configuration warning system which failed to alert the crew. Contributing factors included inadequate cockpit discipline, Delta's slow implementation of modifications to operating procedures and training, and insufficient FAA oversight.

factors.evidence: Crew engaged in extended casual conversations on non-flight matters during preflight and pushback phases (p. 72-75).
Aircraft attempted takeoff without flaps and slats extended to proper configuration (p. 58-60).
Takeoff warning system failed due to throttle switch contamination or misalignment (p. 60-62).
Immediate violent rolling after liftoff with right wing dropping (p. 6-7).
Right wingtip struck runway and ILS antenna array, causing structural breakup (p. 6-7).
Post-crash fire engulfed fuselage from leaking fuel (p. 7).

events.text: Flight 1141 departs Jackson, Mississippi gate; first officer to fly
Arrival at DFW gate 15 with only No. 1 fuel tank quantity gauge inoperative
Pushback from gate; all three engines started
No. 3 engine shutdown to conserve fuel due to departure delay
Aircraft becomes number four for departure; cabin prepared; No. 3 engine restarted
Cleared to taxi into position on runway 18L and hold
Cleared for takeoff on runway 18L, heading 185; AUTO PACK TRIP arming light does not illuminate
Takeoff roll initiated; rotation begun
Main wheels leave ground; immediate violent rolling motion; right wing drops; captain reports two explosions; aircraft begins uncontrolled descent
Right wingtip strikes runway 900 feet beyond departure end; aircraft strikes ILS antenna array; structural breakup; post-crash fire ignites

recommendations.text: Direct principal operations inspectors to review training and operations manuals and ensure flap position verification is part of stall recovery procedures.
Require Part 121 operators to develop and use Cockpit Resource Management programs.
Perform directed engineering study of Boeing 727 takeoff warning systems.
Issue Airworthiness Directive for Boeing 727 takeoff warning system modifications.
Modify Boeing 727 checklists to verify takeoff warning system operation.

safety_changes: Boeing 727 checklists modified to verify takeoff warning system
Enhanced cockpit resource management and discipline training
Takeoff warning system design improvements

notes: History of Flight and Executive Summary read
Findings and Probable Cause sections read
Cockpit Management and Crew Discipline analysis read
Recommendations section with IDs extracted

records.title: British Midland 092 (Kegworth)

agencies.name: Air Accidents Investigation Branch
agencies.report_title: Report on the accident to Boeing 737-400 G-OBME near Kegworth, Leicestershire on 8 January 1989

location.name: M1 motorway embankment near Kegworth, short of East Midlands Airport runway 27

records.summary: Climbing through FL283 the outer panel of a fan blade in the No.1 (left) engine detached, causing severe vibration, a smell of fire and fluctuating engine parameters. The crew believed the No.2 (right) engine was at fault and shut it down, after which the symptoms appeared to subside. During the diversion to East Midlands the No.1 engine lost power on final approach and the aircraft struck the M1 motorway embankment short of the runway. 47 people died.
records.probable_cause: The operating crew shut down the No.2 engine after a fan blade had fractured in the No.1 engine. This engine subsequently suffered a major thrust loss due to secondary fan damage after power had been increased during the final approach. Contributing factors: the combination of heavy engine vibration, noise, shuddering and smell of fire were outside the crew's training and experience; they reacted prematurely before fully assimilating the engine instrument readings; the cross-checks on the engine instruments were not adequate; the misleading response of the aircraft to the reduction of power on No.2 engine led them to believe they had acted correctly; and they were not informed of the flames from the No.1 engine seen by many passengers and cabin crew.

factors.evidence: The No.1 engine fan blade failed from a fatigue crack caused by a previously unrecognised blade vibration mode within the certificated power range of the newly rated CFM56-3C engine.
The blade failure caused severe vibration, compressor stalls and fluctuating N1/fuel flow on the No.1 engine.
The crew throttled back and shut down the serviceable No.2 engine while the damaged No.1 engine continued to run.
The crew did not adequately read or cross-check the engine instruments, including the vibration indicators, before identifying the failed engine.
Cabin crew and passengers who had seen flames from the left engine did not pass this information to the flight deck; the flight crew did not seek it.
The crew had not been trained for the combination of symptoms produced by this failure and had no simulator training on the 737-400 engine instrument presentation.
The new solid-state engine instrument display made vibration and other readings less conspicuous than on earlier 737s; the engine instrument layout led to misidentification.
The uprated CFM56-3C engine had been certificated without full-scale flight testing at the higher thrust rating, so the blade vibration mode was not discovered.
The severe vibration, shuddering, noise and smell of fire produced a startling situation outside the crew's experience, and they reacted prematurely.
With the remaining engine having failed on final approach, the aircraft descended into the M1 motorway embankment 900 m short of the runway.

events.text: G-OBME departs Heathrow runway 27R for Belfast with the captain as pilot flying.
Climbing through FL283 the outer panel of a No.1 engine fan blade detaches; severe vibration, shuddering, compressor stalls and a smell of fire in the cabin.
Autopilot disengaged; N1 vibration indicator for the No.1 engine at maximum, fluctuating fuel flow and EGT on No.1.
Asked by the captain which engine has failed, the first officer answers that it is the left, then the right one.
Captain orders the No.2 (right) throttle to be closed; as thrust is reduced the vibration and shuddering appear to subside, reinforcing the misidentification.
Crew request diversion; ATC offer East Midlands, the company's engineering base, and a descent is started.
No.2 engine shut down (fuel lever to cutoff) on the captain's instruction; the No.1 engine is left running at reduced thrust.
Captain briefs passengers by PA that there has been trouble with the right engine, which has been shut down; cabin crew and passengers who saw fire on the left engine do not challenge this.
Aircraft vectored for the ILS to East Midlands runway 27; landing gear lowered and flaps extended.
At 2.4 nm from the runway and 900 ft agl, as thrust is increased on the No.1 engine, it suffers an abrupt loss of power with compressor surges and fire warning.
First officer attempts to restart the No.2 engine; there is insufficient time for it to spool up.
GPWS glideslope warning as the aircraft drops below the glidepath; airspeed decays and the stick shaker operates.
Aircraft strikes the field beside the M1, crosses the motorway and comes to rest against the western embankment 900 m short of the runway 27 threshold; 47 of 126 occupants die.

recommendations.text: Require all UK-registered 737-300/400 aircraft to have engine vibration indication in the primary field of view and review the certification standards for engine instrument displays.
Require that new engine variants be flight tested at the full certificated thrust rating so that vibration and fatigue characteristics are demonstrated in service conditions.
recommendations.outcome: CFM56-3C fan blades were modified and the certification of derivative engines was reviewed.

recommendations.text: Review training so that flight crews are trained in the recognition and handling of engine failures using the engine instrument displays fitted to the aircraft, and improve cabin crew to flight deck communication of relevant observations.
Improve occupant survivability through review of seat and overhead bin attachment strength and the brace position.
recommendations.outcome: Research into 16g seats and the brace position followed.

safety_changes: Modification of CFM56-3C fan blades and revised fatigue/vibration certification testing of engine variants.
Emphasis on engine instrument presentation and vibration indication in the primary field of view.
Improved cabin crew to flight deck communication training and CRM emphasis on cross-checking engine indications before shutdown.
Research on seat strength, overhead stowage and the brace position for crash survivability.

notes: Event times are derived from published report chronology and are approximate to within tens of seconds; the report gives 20:05:05 for the blade failure and 20:24:33 for impact.
Recommendation numbers omitted; the AAIB report issued 31 recommendations.
Serious injury count reflects the report's 74 seriously injured.

records.title: United Airlines 811

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Explosive Decompression - Loss of Cargo Door in Flight, United Airlines Flight 811, Boeing 747-122, N4713U, Honolulu, Hawaii, February 24, 1989 (revised report)

location.name: Pacific Ocean south of Honolulu, Hawaii; returned to Honolulu International Airport

records.summary: Climbing through about 22,000 ft after a night departure from Honolulu, the forward lower lobe cargo door of the 747 swung open and tore away, causing an explosive decompression that ripped out a section of the cabin floor and fuselage. Nine passengers were lost from the aircraft, and debris damaged engines 3 and 4, which were shut down. The crew returned to Honolulu and landed safely. After the door was recovered from the seabed in 1990 the NTSB revised its findings to a faulty switch or wiring that drove the latches open.
records.probable_cause: The sudden opening of the forward lower lobe cargo door in flight and the subsequent explosive decompression. The door opening was attributed to a faulty switch or wiring in the door control system which permitted electrical actuation of the door latches toward the unlatched position after initial door closure and before takeoff. Contributing was a deficiency in the design of the cargo door locking mechanisms, which made them susceptible to deformation, allowing the door to become unlatched after being properly latched and locked. Also contributing was a lack of timely corrective actions by Boeing and the FAA following a 1987 cargo door opening incident on a Pan Am B-747.

factors.evidence: A faulty switch or wiring in the door control system allowed the latch actuators to be driven toward the unlatched position after the door had been closed.
The cargo door locking sectors were susceptible to deformation and could not prevent the latch cams from being back-driven open.
A 1987 Pan Am 747 cargo door opening incident had shown the vulnerability but corrective actions by Boeing and the FAA were not timely.
The FAA's airworthiness directive after the Pan Am incident allowed up to two years for compliance.
The forward lower lobe cargo door opened in flight and separated from the aircraft.
The door failure caused an explosive decompression that removed part of the fuselage side and cabin floor, ejecting nine passengers.
Debris from the fuselage damaged engines 3 and 4, which had to be shut down.
The event occurred at about 02:09 local time.
The crew descended, dumped fuel and landed the damaged aircraft back at Honolulu on two engines.

events.text: Forward lower lobe cargo door is closed and indicated latched and locked before departure; the latches are subsequently driven toward open by a fault in the door control electrics.
Flight 811 departs Honolulu for Auckland with 337 passengers and 18 crew.
Crew keep the seat belt sign on while deviating around thunderstorms during the climb.
Climbing through about 22,000 ft the forward cargo door swings open and separates, tearing away a section of the fuselage and cabin floor; explosive decompression follows.
Nine passengers and their seats are ejected from the aircraft; cabin debris strikes the right wing and engines.
Engine No. 3 suffers foreign object damage and is shut down; engine No. 4 subsequently shows fire indications and is also shut down.
Crew begin an emergency descent, don oxygen masks and declare an emergency to Honolulu Center, requesting a return.
Flight engineer manages fuel dumping to reduce landing weight while the crew assess control and flap damage.
Cabin crew move passengers away from the damaged area and prepare the cabin for an emergency landing.
Aircraft lands on runway 8L at Honolulu on two engines with flaps only partially extended.
Emergency evacuation completed on the runway; injuries occur among passengers and crew but there are no further fatalities.
In 1990 the cargo door is recovered from the Pacific seabed by the US Navy, leading the NTSB to revise the probable cause from improper latching to an electrical fault in the door system.

recommendations.text: Require modification of 747 cargo door latching and locking mechanisms so that the locks positively prevent the latch cams from being driven open, and require inspection of door electrical wiring and switches.
recommendations.outcome: Airworthiness directives required steel locking sectors and other door modifications on the 747 fleet.

recommendations.text: Evaluate cargo door designs on other transport aircraft for similar vulnerability to electrical faults and lock deformation.
Act promptly on airworthiness issues revealed by in-service incidents rather than allowing long compliance times.

safety_changes: 747 cargo doors were modified with stronger locking sectors and changes to the door control electrical system.
The NTSB revised its report in 1992 after the door was recovered, an unusual reopening of an investigation prompted in part by the parents of a victim who conducted their own inquiry.

notes: t0 is set to about 02:09 HST, the approximate time of the door separation; the departure (about 01:52) and landing (about 02:34) times are approximate; other offsets are estimates.
Altitude at the time of the decompression is recalled as between 22,000 and 23,000 ft.
The final event (door recovery in 1990) is included as a note with a nominal large t value outside the flight sequence.
Occupants 355 (337 passengers, 18 crew); the number of injured is not recalled reliably.
Recommendation numbers not recalled and are left null.

records.title: Evergreen International Airlines 17

route.from_name: Carswell Air Force Base, Fort Worth
route.to_name: Tinker Air Force Base, Oklahoma City

records.summary: Shortly after takeoff from Carswell Air Force Base, the main cargo door on Evergreen International Airlines Flight 17 (a DC-9-33F) began to open. As the aircraft climbed to 2,500 ft and began a return to the departure airport, the cargo door fully opened, causing uncontrollable yaw and roll. The aircraft inverted and crashed in a pasture near Saginaw, killing both pilots. Investigation found the door was not fully latched and a design flaw prevented the warning light from illuminating.
records.probable_cause: Failure of the main cargo door to remain latched during flight due to inadequate closure by the first officer, combined with design deficiencies in the door warning light circuit that prevented cockpit awareness of the door opening.

factors.evidence: First Officer Johnston did not fully close the cargo door; he held the control valve handle in the closed position for an inadequate period of time (p. 4)
a design flaw in the cargo door warning light circuit caused the door-open warning light in the cockpit not to illuminate (p. 11)
the main cargo door completely opened, causing the aircraft to yaw and roll uncontrollably. The aircraft then banked to the left, inverted, and crashed into a pasture (p. 2)
the door lockpin switch in N931F was damaged and corroded, and the warning light circuit was designed in such a way that if the switch failed, the warning light would stop working (p. 2)

events.text: First officer Johnston left the cockpit to close the main cargo door, then returned two minutes later.
Cockpit voice recording began as crew progressed through Before Start abbreviated checklist.
At 02:09:49, three seconds after rotation, the main cargo door partially opened, which was indicated by the CVR recording a sudden increase in background noise.
The ground proximity warning system (GPWS) activated, sounding a whoop whoop terrain four times.
First officer Johnston declared an emergency to air traffic control (ATC).
The flight climbed to 2,500 ft and then began a right turn back towards Carswell.
Captain stated "Well, I guess he's done" indicating cargo loading was complete.
Sound similar to auxiliary power unit (APU) start-up was recorded.
Electrical power transferred from ground power unit to APU.
Starting Engines abbreviated checklist commenced and was completed uneventfully.

The aircraft then banked to the left, inverted, and crashed into a pasture near Saginaw.
After Start checklist was called complete.
Logair 931 contacted ground control for taxi instructions.
Taxi checklist was completed; flaps set to 15 degrees.
Local controller cleared flight for takeoff on runway 17.

records.title: United Airlines 232

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: United Airlines Flight 232, McDonnell Douglas DC-10-10, Sioux Gateway Airport, Sioux City, Iowa, July 19, 1989

location.name: Sioux Gateway Airport, Sioux City, Iowa

records.summary: In cruise at 37,000 feet the stage 1 fan disk of the DC-10's tail-mounted number 2 engine fractured from a fatigue crack that had grown from a manufacturing defect in the titanium. Disk fragments severed the lines of all three hydraulic systems, leaving the crew with no conventional flight controls. Using only differential thrust on the two wing engines, and helped by an off-duty DC-10 instructor, the crew steered the airplane for 44 minutes to an emergency landing at Sioux City. The airplane cartwheeled and broke up on the runway; 111 of the 296 on board died and 185 survived.
records.probable_cause: The inadequate consideration given to human factors limitations in the inspection and quality control procedures used by United Airlines' engine overhaul facility which resulted in the failure to detect a fatigue crack originating from a previously undetected metallurgical defect located in a critical area of the stage 1 fan disk that was manufactured by General Electric Aircraft Engines. The subsequent catastrophic disintegration of the disk resulted in the liberation of debris in a pattern of distribution and with energy levels that exceeded the level of protection provided by design features of the hydraulic systems that operate the DC-10's flight controls.

factors.evidence: A fatigue crack grew from a hard alpha inclusion in the titanium of the stage 1 fan disk, formed during the manufacturing melt process, until the disk fractured after about 17 years in service.

The crack was large enough to be detected at the last fluorescent penetrant inspection at United's overhaul facility about 760 cycles before the accident but was missed; the report faulted the human factors of the inspection process.
The fan disk separated from the number 2 engine at high energy, shedding fragments through the horizontal stabilizer and tail structure.
Fragments severed lines of all three independent hydraulic systems where they ran close together in the tail, and all hydraulic fluid was lost.
With no hydraulic pressure the ailerons, elevators, rudder, spoilers, flaps and slats were inoperative; the airplane had no conventional flight controls.
The crew could only influence pitch and roll by varying thrust on the two wing engines, which could not arrest the phugoid oscillation or line up precisely for landing.
The DC-10's three hydraulic systems were routed through the same area of the tail without fuses or shutoff valves, so one uncontained failure could disable all of them.
Certification had assumed that hydraulic system redundancy was sufficient without fully considering the distribution and energy of uncontained rotor debris.
The airplane touched down at about 215 knots with a sink rate of about 1,620 feet per minute, right wing low; the right wing struck first and the airplane cartwheeled and broke apart.
Fire consumed the center fuselage after the breakup; most fatalities were in that section.
Despite the breakup, the crew's management of the emergency and the preparation of the airport and rescue services allowed 185 of 296 occupants to survive.
An unrestrained lap-held infant died; the NTSB reiterated its recommendation for child restraint systems.

events.text: Flight 232 departs Denver for Chicago and climbs to flight level 370.
The stage 1 fan disk of the number 2 (tail) engine fractures and separates; a loud bang and airframe shudder are felt. The engine's fragments strike the horizontal stabilizer and tail.
Flight engineer reports the number 2 engine failed; the crew begin the engine shutdown checklist and then notice all three hydraulic system pressures and quantities falling to zero.
The airplane enters a descending right turn that does not respond to control inputs; the captain and first officer find the controls have no effect.
The captain reduces thrust on the number 1 engine and increases it on number 3 to stop the right roll; the crew discover differential thrust is their only means of control.
The crew declare an emergency to Minneapolis Center and request vectors to the nearest suitable airport; Sioux City is offered.
A deadheading United DC-10 training check airman comes to the cockpit and takes over the throttles, allowing the pilots to concentrate on the phugoid and on planning the landing.

Captain tells Sioux City approach 'we have no hydraulic fluid, which means we have no elevator control, almost none, and very little aileron control'; a series of right-hand turns is flown because the airplane will not turn left.
The landing gear is extended by the alternate free-fall method; the airport, hospitals and Air National Guard units are alerted for a crash landing.
Sioux City tower clears the flight to 'land on any runway'; the captain replies 'you want to be particular and make it a runway, huh?' The airplane lines up with closed runway 22.
On short final a phugoid downswing and a right roll develop that thrust changes cannot correct; sink rate increases to about 1,620 feet per minute at about 215 knots.
The right wing and right main gear strike the runway first; the airplane cartwheels, breaks into sections and the center fuselage burns in a cornfield.
Survivors evacuate through fuselage breaks and doors; 185 of the 296 occupants survive, aided by the pre-positioned rescue services.

cvr.speaker: ATC
cvr.text: United two thirty two heavy, ... you're cleared to land on any runway.

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: You want to be particular and make it a runway, huh?

recommendations.text: Require modification of the DC-10 hydraulic systems, such as hydraulic fuses or shutoff valves, so that a single uncontained engine failure cannot cause total loss of hydraulic power for the flight controls.
recommendations.outcome: An airworthiness directive required installation of hydraulic fuses in the number 3 hydraulic system of DC-10s.

recommendations.text: Review the certification of transport airplanes to ensure that the effects of uncontained engine rotor failures on redundant flight control systems are adequately considered, including debris energy and distribution.
recommendations.outcome: FAA issued updated guidance (AC 20-128A) on designing for minimum hazard from uncontained rotor failures.

recommendations.text: Improve fluorescent penetrant and other inspection methods for titanium rotating parts, including human factors of the inspection process, and require re-inspection of CF6-6 fan disks from the same melt.
recommendations.outcome: Fan disks from the affected titanium lots were removed and inspection procedures at overhaul facilities were revised.

recommendations.text: Work with titanium producers to reduce the occurrence of hard alpha inclusions in rotor-grade titanium through improved melting and inspection processes.
recommendations.outcome: Triple vacuum-arc remelt and improved ultrasonic billet inspection became standard for rotor-grade titanium.

recommendations.text: Require approved child restraint systems for infants and small children on air carrier flights.
recommendations.outcome: The FAA declined to mandate child restraints, citing the cost of separate seats.

safety_changes: DC-10 fleets were retrofitted with hydraulic fuses to preserve some flight control capability after a line rupture in the tail.
Rotor-grade titanium melting practice moved to triple vacuum-arc remelt with improved billet ultrasonic inspection to reduce hard alpha inclusions.
FAA revised guidance on designing for uncontained engine failures (AC 20-128A) and engine manufacturers reviewed critical rotating part life limits.
The crew's cooperative use of an additional pilot became a model for crew resource management training, and research into propulsion-controlled aircraft followed.
Airport emergency planning was widely reviewed after the Sioux City response, which had been drilled for a similar scenario two years earlier.

notes: Engine failure at about 15:16 CDT and touchdown at about 16:00 CDT are as stated in the report; the seconds in the t0 and touchdown clocks are approximate and intermediate event times (emergency declaration, check airman arriving, gear extension) are approximate to within a few minutes.
Touchdown at about 215 knots with a sink rate of about 1,620 feet per minute is from the report.
Fatalities (111) include one passenger who died about a month later; serious injuries 47 as recalled.
The interval between the last inspection and the accident (about 760 cycles) and the disk's service history are as recalled from the report and should be verified.
ATC and captain exchange about landing 'on any runway' is quoted from the public transcript with the ATC wording abbreviated.

records.title: USAir 5050
records.summary: During takeoff from LaGuardia runway 31 on a wet runway in darkness and low visibility, the aircraft drifted to the left. The captain's improper use of the nosewheel steering tiller damaged the left nose tire, and a loud bang followed. The captain aborted the takeoff but was unable to stop the aircraft before it ran off the runway end into Bowery Bay, breaking into three fuselage sections.
records.probable_cause: The captain's failure to exercise command authority to reject the takeoff or take sufficient control to continue it, which was initiated with a mistrimmed rudder. Also causal was failure to detect the mistrimmed rudder before takeoff (p. 57).

factors.evidence: Failure of crew to detect improper rudder trim setting despite checklists during pre-flight procedures; captain failed to detect mistrimmed rudder before takeoff was attempted (p. 55-57).

Captain failed to provide extended briefing or emergency briefing and crew had coordination problems transferring control during takeoff roll; poor communication between captain and first officer (p. 38-42).
Failure to detect improper rudder trim setting by means of rudder pedal displacement during taxiing; rudder trim control not checked as part of cross-check procedures (p. 40).

As the first officer began the takeoff on runway 31, the airplane started to drift to the left; captain attempted to correct that drift with improper nosewheel steering tiller use, damaging left nose tire (p. 9).
Weather conditions included darkness, low visibility and wet runway during takeoff; flight was part of extra section decision made just before boarding causing time pressure (p. 8-10).

Aircraft was unable to stop before running off end of runway into Bowery Bay; fuselage broke into three sections with forward section resting on elevated light stanchion and aft section partially submerged (p. 9).

events.text: Captain and first officer report to USAir operations at BWI to fly B-737 N416US to LaGuardia as Flight 1846; scheduled departure 1510 but delayed to 1935 due to LGA inbound air traffic
Flight 1846 arrives at LaGuardia Gate 15 after leaving BWI uneventfully; dispatcher cancels Norfolk leg and later reassigns aircraft to operate as Flight 5050 to Charlotte with passengers
Passengers board Flight 5050; captain visits USAir ground movement control tower expressing concern about crew duty time limitations before end of trip
As first officer began takeoff on runway 31, airplane drifted to the left due to mistrimmed rudder; captain attempted to correct drift using nosewheel steering tiller
Flightcrew heard loud bang followed by continuous rumbling noise; left nose tire damaged by improper tiller use
Captain took over control from first officer and rejected takeoff by aborting
Captain unable to stop airplane before it ran off end of runway into Bowery Bay
Fuselage broke into three sections; forward section rested on part of elevated light stanchion; aft section partially submerged in Bowery Bay

recommendations.text: Require an operational rule that, during takeoff roll, should an uncommanded deviation from the intended flight path occur, the pilot-not-flying shall explicitly advise the pilot-flying of the deviation and the pilot-flying shall acknowledge the deviation; if the deviation persists or another uncommanded deviation occurs, either pilot shall be authorized to execute a rejected takeoff without coordination.

Require a revision of the pre-takeoff instrument procedures and flight crew handbook requirements so that they address positional sensing of controls that are not normally visible to either pilot during the normal scan.
Require cockpit resource management (CRM) training for all U.S. air carriers, including those not currently required to provide formal CRM training.
Require pre-takeoff briefings for rejected takeoff procedures in all U.S. carrier flight training departments.

Require a comprehensive study by aircraft manufacturers of rudder trim control design and placement to determine how the systems can be designed to provide more positive feedback of control position to flightcrews.
Require that all runway safety areas meet the recommendations contained in the 1988 FAA Advisory Circular AC 150/5300-13.

Require aircraft manufacturers to make a comprehensive analysis of the problem of water ingestion during overwater emergency landings and to publish design guidance that will improve aircrew survivability in such events.
Require improved testing of aircraft emergency evacuation procedures with emphasis on the effectiveness of emergency exits and evacuation aids under adverse environmental conditions.
Require a comprehensive study of postaccident aircrew availability to determine the optimum method for obtaining postaccident statements from aircrew.

records.title: Aloha IslandAir 1712

aircraft.type: de Havilland Canada DHC-6 Twin Otter 300

records.summary: Aloha IslandAir Flight 1712 crashed on October 28, 1989 while operating under VFR at night into instrument meteorological conditions. The captain continued VFR flight in darkness and orographic clouds obscuring mountainous terrain, resulting in controlled flight into terrain near Hālawa Valley on Molokaʻi.
records.probable_cause: The captain's decision to continue VFR flight at night into instrument meteorological conditions which obscured rising mountainous terrain. Contributing factors included inadequate supervision of personnel, training and operations by Aloha IslandAir management and insufficient FAA oversight during rapid expansion.

factors.evidence: Captain had been accepted into Aloha Airlines and completed intensive B-737 ground school for two weeks prior, sleeping only 4-5 hours nightly (p. 23-24).
Orographic clouds and weather forecast failed to warn of low cloud conditions along intended route (p. 20-21).
Sunset at 1753; flight departed at 1825 in darkness; civil twilight ended at 1816 (p. 8).
First officer lacked experience and could not influence captain's decisions; minimal CRM training at airline (p. 23).
Inadequate FAA surveillance of Part 135 operator; undetected training deficiencies and ground school hour reductions (p. 30).
Aircraft struck mountainous terrain at approximately 600 feet altitude (p. 8).
Aircraft descended to 500 feet during night flight, violating 14 CFR Part 135 minimum altitude requirements for night operations within 5 miles of land (p. 8, 22).

events.text: Sunset at Kahului; official sunset; civil twilight ends at 1816; nautical twilight until 1842
Depart Kahului Airport on VFR flight plan; aircraft climbs to 1,000 feet; first officer remarks intended route looks quite dark
Aircraft airborne and climbing through 400 feet; radar contact established
Aircraft levels off at 1,000 feet mean sea level
Aircraft descends from 1,000 to 500 feet; does not comply with Part 135 night altitude requirements
Aircraft levels at 500 feet; about 16 miles northwest of Kahului; clear of ARSA; radar contact lost; instructed to squawk 1200 code
Aircraft encounters orographic clouds and instrument meteorological conditions with low visibility
Aircraft strikes mountainous terrain near Hālawa Valley at approximately 600 feet altitude; aircraft destroyed on impact

recommendations.text: Require scheduled Part 135 operators develop and use CRM programs.
Perform special study of FSDO staffing adequacy.
Require Part 135 operations under IFR during darkness or low visibility/ceiling conditions.
Establish procedures to incorporate FAA and military radar in Hawaiian Islands.
Require background checks of pilot applicants including FAA records review.
Require forecasts note possible orographic cloud formation.

dissent.position: Failure to require Ground Proximity Warning System for Part 135 aircraft was a contributing factor

safety_changes: Enhanced requirements for Part 135 IFR training
Background check procedures for pilot hiring
Improved pilot fatigue management policies

records.title: United Express 2415
records.summary: United Express Flight 2415 crashed 400 feet short of runway 21R. Flightcrew decision to continue unstabilized ILS approach led to stall and loss of control. Airframe icing, improper ATC vectors, and declined de-icing services were contributing factors.
records.probable_cause: The flightcrew's decision to continue an unstabilized instrument landing system approach that led to a stall, most likely of the horizontal stabilizer, and loss of control at low altitude. Contributing to the accident was the air traffic controller's improper vectors that positioned the airplane inside the outer marker while it was still well above the glideslope. Contributing to the stall and loss of control was the accumulation of airframe ice that degraded the aerodynamic performance of the airplane. (p. 53)

factors.evidence: Flightcrew continued to attempt to land from an unstabilized steep approach (p. 52)
Airplane could have accumulated up to 1 inch of mixed rime and clear ice during descent (p. 52)
Captain declined de-icing at Yakima despite offers (p. 8-9)
Air traffic controller's improper vectors positioned airplane inside outer marker while above glideslope (p. 53)
Icing certification did not account for possible tail stall at landing flap configuration (p. 52)
Stall led to loss of control at low altitude (p. 53)

events.text: Flight 2415 departed Seattle-Tacoma at 2045 PST (p. 8)
Arrived Yakima. Station agent observed ice on wings. Agent offered de-icing but captain declined multiple times despite equipment ready (p. 8)
Yakima tower closed. Controller advised light to moderate mixed icing between 18,000 and 4,000 feet (p. 9)
Departed Yakima runway 27 at 2203:56, climbed to 11,000 feet (p. 9)
Seattle Center at 2215:03 cleared descent to 6,000 feet at pilots' discretion (p. 9)
At 2217:45 issued descent to 3,000 feet (p. 9)
Seattle Center at 2226:12 cleared straight-in ILS runway 21R approach (p. 9)
At 2228:30 reported missed approach request; at 2228:47 reported instrument flags but continued approach (p. 9-10)
At 2230:05 transmitted on short final runway 21R (p. 10)
Controller at 2230:50 observed airplane higher than normal, descending faster than normal rate (p. 10)
Aircraft struck ground 400 feet short of runway 21R, destroyed with all fatalities (p. 10)
Pasco ARFF arrived at crash site at 2234:50 (p. 10)

recommendations.text: Amend icing certification rules to require flight tests with ice accumulated in cruise and approach flap configurations
Review airframe icing certification data for Part 23 and 25 airplanes
Require manufacturers to review pneumatic deice boot designs to ensure adequate pressure threshold
Revise Advisory Circulars 20-73 and 23.1419-1 to include deice boot guidance
Issue Operations Bulletin to verify air carriers have procedures for accumulated airframe ice removal prior to final approach
Terminate practice of providing radar vectors to final approach when using expanded range radar display without approach gate depiction at Seattle ARTCC
Terminate practice at all ARTCCs of providing radar vectors to final approach when using expanded range radar display

records.title: Avianca 052
records.summary: Avianca Flight 052 ran out of fuel after three holding patterns and a failed landing attempt at JFK, crashing onto a hillside in Cove Neck on Long Island. Poor communication between crew and controllers, inadequate fuel management, and ATC's failure to recognize the emergency contributed to the accident.
records.probable_cause: The failure of the flightcrew to adequately manage the airplane's fuel load, and their failure to communicate an emergency fuel situation to air traffic control before fuel exhaustion occurred. Contributing factors: failure to use airline operational control dispatch system, inadequate traffic flow management by FAA, and lack of standardized terminology for fuel states.

factors.evidence: The Boeing 707 ran out of fuel and all four engines lost power while the aircraft was maneuvering for a second approach to JFK.
First officer did not adequately communicate the critical fuel situation using standard emergency terminology, instead saying 'we need priority' which controllers interpreted as a routine request.
Controllers did not recognize the emergency fuel situation because the flight crew failed to use the word 'emergency' and did not use standardized fuel emergency phraseology.
The flight was placed in three holding patterns totaling more than 1 hour, with weather-related delays due to inadequate traffic flow management at JFK.
Crew fatigue and stress contributed to the unsuccessful completion of the first approach and thus contributed to the accident.
Windshear on the approach path contributed to the captain's poor performance on the ILS approach, leading to a missed approach.
Descent below safe altitude limits during approach contributed to the difficulty of landing.
The Boeing 707 crashed on a hillside in Cove Neck, New York, after engines lost power due to fuel exhaustion.

events.text: Flight 052 departed Bogotá International Airport.
Flight landed at Medellín and was refueled for departure to JFK.
Flight 052 departed Medellín bound for JFK via oceanic route.
Flight 052 entered first holding pattern over Norfolk (ORF) at FL370.
Flight entered second holding pattern at BOTON intersection near Atlantic City.
Flight entered third holding pattern at CAMRN intersection, 39 nm south of JFK, at 14,000 feet.
First officer advised controller that aircraft can hold only 5 more minutes due to fuel situation.
Flight cleared from holding pattern and instructed to proceed to JFK via heading 040 at 11,000 feet.
Windshear advisory issued: increase of 10 knots at 1500 feet and 10 knots at 500 feet.
Captain asked first officer to tell ATC they are in an emergency.
Aircraft crashed on a hillside in Cove Neck, Long Island, New York due to loss of power from fuel exhaustion.

recommendations.text: Develop standardized glossary of definitions and terms for fuel communications
Conduct comprehensive study of Central Flow Control Facility and Traffic Management System
Require transport category airplane flight manuals to include minimum fuel procedures and ATC emergency handling criteria
Incorporate recorded broadcast of traffic management information in air route traffic control centers
Review policies on dual responsibility of dispatchers and flightcrews
Require Avianca to incorporate CRM and Line Oriented Flight Training into training program
Notify all domestic and foreign air carriers to emphasize knowledge of flight operations, ATC rules, procedures, and standard phraseology

records.title: Atlantic Southeast Airlines 2254

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Midair Collision, Embraer EMB-120, N217AS and Cessna 172, N99501, Near Gadsden, Alabama, April 9, 1990

location.name: Approximately 2.5 miles south of Gadsden Regional Airport

records.summary: Atlantic Southeast Airlines Flight 2254, an Embraer EMB-120 departing Gadsden, collided head-on with a Cessna 172 flown by Civil Air Patrol pilots during climb to 5,000 feet. The Cessna was westbound with the setting sun behind it, creating sun glare that restricted visibility for the Cessna pilot. The collision severed the EMB-120's right horizontal stabilizer, but the aircraft managed to return to the airport. The Cessna crashed with both occupants fatally injured.
records.probable_cause: Inadequate visual lookout by the pilots of both aircraft, which resulted in their failure to see-and-avoid oncoming traffic. A factor related to the accident was the sun's glare, which restricted the vision of the Cessna 172 pilot.

factors.evidence: The Cessna 172 was westbound at the same altitude, facing the setting sun; the sun's glare restricted the vision of the Cessna 172 pilot. (p. 56)

The probable cause was inadequate visual lookout by the pilots of both aircraft, resulting in their failure to see and avoid oncoming traffic. Neither aircraft crew detected the other until moments before impact. (p. 41-44)
The two aircraft collided head-on at approximately 1805 CDT at the same altitude about 2.5 miles south of the airport. (p. 29-30)

events.text: Flight 2254 departed Gadsden from Runway 24 with an IFR clearance, entered a left turn to a heading of east, and climbed toward assigned altitude of 5,000 feet MSL.
Cessna 172 (Civil Air Patrol aircraft, N99501) was westbound heading toward the setting sun at approximately the same altitude as the climbing EMB-120.
Before radar contact was established with ATC, the EMB-120 began to converge with the Cessna 172.
ASA crew reported seeing the Cessna moments before impact and captain attempted evasive action by pushing the nose down, but was unable to avoid collision.
Head-on collision occurred about 2.5 miles south of Gadsden airport. A flight attendant on the EMB-120 recalled hearing a 'thump' before the aircraft started a descent.
During impact, the right horizontal stabilizer of the EMB-120 separated from the aircraft, but the aircraft continued flying.
EMB-120 crew managed to recover from the initial descent and return to Gadsden airport for a safe landing with no injuries to the 3 crew members and 4 passengers.
Cessna 172 entered an uncontrolled descent and crashed with both Civil Air Patrol occupants fatally injured.

safety_changes: Emphasis on continuous visual scanning and see-and-avoid procedures in IFR operations.
Training on collision avoidance systems and traffic awareness for aircraft operating in non-radar environments.

notes: Brief NTSB final report of 5 pages analyzed in full
All findings and probable cause extracted from report pages 40-58
Factual information about collision sequence from pages 25-38
No recommendations section in the report; only findings and probable cause
ASA crew consisted of 3 crew members; aircraft carried 4 passengers (total 7 on ASA aircraft)
Cessna 172 had 2 occupants (both fatally injured)
Aircraft damage to EMB-120: separation of right horizontal stabilizer but aircraft remained controllable
Report indicates witness did not observe evasive action by either aircraft before impact
Departure time noted as 1753 CDT, collision occurred at 1805 CDT
Weather: VFR conditions, 10 miles visibility, scattered clouds at 25,000 feet; sun glare was the critical factor

records.title: British Airways 5390

agencies.name: Air Accidents Investigation Branch
agencies.report_title: Report on the accident to BAC One-Eleven, G-BJRT over Didcot, Oxfordshire on 10 June 1990

location.name: Over Didcot, Oxfordshire; diversion to Southampton

records.summary: Climbing through 17,300 ft after departure from Birmingham, the left windscreen, which had been replaced the previous night, blew out. The commander was partially sucked through the aperture and held by cabin crew while the first officer flew the aircraft to an emergency landing at Southampton. The commander survived with fractures and frostbite.
records.probable_cause: The windscreen had been fitted with 84 of 90 bolts that were of a smaller diameter than specified and the remaining six were too short; the bolts were installed by the shift maintenance manager, who worked alone, relied on visual matching of the old bolts and did not consult the parts catalogue. The installation was not subject to independent inspection, and the shift manager's inadequate practices were not detected by the airline's quality monitoring or the CAA.

factors.evidence: The shift maintenance manager fitted the windscreen with 84 bolts of the wrong (undersize) diameter and 6 bolts of the correct diameter but wrong length, having selected them by visual comparison in poor light.
The windscreen installation was not classified as a vital task requiring independent inspection, so the incorrect bolts went undetected.
Local management and quality monitoring did not detect the shift manager's inadequate working practices and the deviation from published procedures.
The CAA's product sampling did not identify the maintenance standards shortfall at the Birmingham base.
The shift manager did not use the Illustrated Parts Catalogue or the maintenance manual to identify the correct bolts, and operated the uncontrolled bolt carousel without verification.
The windscreen was fitted from the outside of the aircraft, so it relied wholly on the bolts to resist cabin pressure differential.
At about 17,300 ft the windscreen separated from the airframe under cabin pressure load.
The windscreen departure caused an explosive decompression and the commander was pulled partly through the aperture.
The commander was incapacitated, held by cabin crew, leaving the first officer to fly the aircraft alone.
The first officer landed the aircraft safely at Southampton about 22 minutes after the decompression.

events.text: During the previous night shift at Birmingham the left windscreen is replaced; the shift maintenance manager selects replacement bolts by visual comparison and fits 84 undersize A211-8C bolts and 6 too-short A211-9D bolts.
G-BJRT departs Birmingham for Málaga with 81 passengers and 6 crew; the commander is pilot flying.
Climbing through about 17,000 ft both pilots have released their shoulder harnesses; the commander has loosened his lap strap.
At 17,300 ft the left windscreen blows out with a loud bang; explosive decompression and condensation mist fill the flight deck.
The commander is pulled head-first out of the aperture, his knees caught on the control column; the flight deck door is blown onto the centre pedestal.
A cabin crew member on the flight deck grabs the commander's legs and holds him; the autopilot has disengaged.
The first officer takes control, regains control of the aircraft and initiates a rapid descent while transmitting a Mayday.
ATC initially have difficulty hearing the transmissions over the wind noise; the first officer requests a diversion and is offered Southampton.
Aircraft levels at 11,000 ft and is radar vectored towards Southampton; other cabin crew relieve the first steward holding the commander.
First officer lands the aircraft safely on Southampton runway 02 with the commander still held half out of the windscreen aperture.
Commander recovered alive with fractures to his right arm, wrist and left thumb, bruising and frostbite; a steward suffers a dislocated shoulder.

recommendations.text: Review the current classification of tasks requiring independent inspection and consider including windscreen and other pressure-critical installations.
Review quality assurance and the monitoring of engineering working practices at outstations, including the control of uncontrolled bolt stores and the use of parts catalogues.
Recognise the need for corrective glasses to be worn by engineers where required and improve product sampling of maintenance work.

safety_changes: Windscreen installation designated as a task requiring independent inspection at British Airways and reviewed by the CAA.
Widely cited as a case study for human factors in maintenance and the need for duplicate inspection of flight-critical tasks.

notes: Clock times are approximate; the report gives the decompression at 07:33 and landing at Southampton at about 07:55.
Bolt part numbers (A211-8C, A211-9D) are as reported by the AAIB; counts 84 and 6 as reported.
Recommendation numbers omitted.

records.title: death of Stevie Ray Vaughan

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aviation Accident Final Report

records.summary: Four helicopters were being used to transport a concert group from Alpine Valley Music Theatre near Elkhorn, Wisconsin, to Chicago. On August 26, 1990, at 01:00 CDT, the pilot of the third helicopter (N16933) departed the golf course area in dense fog at a lower altitude than the other helicopters. The aircraft turned southeasterly toward rising terrain and crashed on hilly terrain about 0.6 miles from takeoff. All five occupants, including blues musician Stevie Ray Vaughan, were killed. No mechanical failures or malfunctions were found.
records.probable_cause: Improper planning/decision by the pilot, and his failure to attain adequate altitude before flying over rising terrain at night. Factors related to the accident were: darkness, fog, haze, rising terrain, and the lack of visual cues that were available to the pilot.

factors.evidence: Accident occurred during hours of darkness with night/dark light conditions at 01:00 CDT (p. 1)
Dense fog at takeoff; pilots of other helicopters reported VFR conditions with some fog; ground witness reported haze and ground fog of varying intensity with patches of low clouds (p. 1)
Improper planning/decision by pilot; pilot remained at lower altitude than other helicopters and turned southeasterly toward rising terrain instead of climbing away (p. 1)
Pilot failed to attain adequate altitude before flying over rising terrain at night; aircraft could only climb to about 300 feet; lack of visual cues prevented pilot from perceiving terrain (p. 1)
Helicopter crashed on hilly terrain about 3/5 mile from takeoff point; elevation of crash site was about 100 ft above golf course and 50 ft below summit of hill (p. 1)

events.text: Bell 206B N16933 prepared for departure from Alpine Valley Music Theatre area near Elkhorn, Wisconsin with 5 occupants (pilot, musician Stevie Ray Vaughan, and 3 others).
Helicopter departed golf course area in dense fog at higher speed and slightly lower altitude than other helicopters operating the same mission.
Aircraft climbed to only about 300 feet altitude above ground before banking sharply to the left, turning southeasterly toward rising terrain.
Helicopter crashed on hilly terrain approximately 0.6 miles from takeoff point. Elevation of crash site was about 100 feet above golf course and 50 feet below the summit of the hill.

No pre-impact mechanical failures or malfunctions found during investigation. Aircraft destroyed. All five occupants killed instantly: pilot (age 42) and four passengers including blues musician Stevie Ray Vaughan.

notes: Report finalized September 11, 1992 as CHI90MA244
Date/time in report: 08/27/1990 0100 CDT which is 08/26/1990 06:00 UTC
Four helicopters total being used; N16933 was the third one; other three flights completed successfully
Pilot had 5,043 total flight hours, 1,540 hours in Bell 206B, properly certificated
Aircraft properly maintained, equipped and certified
No toxicology issues found
No recommendations listed in report
Report findings indicate improper flight planning and lack of terrain awareness
Sections read: Analysis, Probable Cause and Findings, Factual Information (Pilot, Aircraft, Meteorological, Wreckage)

records.title: Wayne County Airport runway collision

location.name: Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport, runway 03C/21

records.summary: Northwest Airlines Flight 1482, a DC-9-14, was cleared to taxi toward runway 03C in dense fog but the crew missed turning onto taxiway Oscar 6 and instead entered the active runway 03C. About 40 seconds after the crew reported the error to ATC, Northwest Flight 299, a Boeing 727 on takeoff roll, collided with the DC-9's right fuselage, cutting through and severing the right engine. The DC-9 caught fire with eight people killed including a flight attendant and passenger who died from smoke inhalation after being unable to release the tailcone emergency exit.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause of this accident was a lack of proper crew coordination including a virtual reversal of roles by the DC-9 pilots, which led to their failure to stop taxiing their airplane and alert the ground controller of their positional uncertainty in a timely manner before and after intruding onto the active runway. Contributing to the cause of the accident were deficiencies in the air traffic control services provided by the Detroit tower, including failure of the ground controller to take timely action to alert the local controller to the possible runway incursion, inadequate visibility observations, failure to use progressive taxi instructions in low-visibility conditions, and issuance of inappropriate and confusing taxi instructions compounded by inadequate backup supervision; deficiencies in the surface markings, signage, and lighting at the airport and the failure of Federal Aviation Administration surveillance to detect or correct these deficiencies; and failure of Northwest Airlines to provide adequate cockpit resource management training to their line aircrews.

factors.evidence: DC-9 crew missed turning onto taxiway Oscar 6 and instead entered the active runway 03C (p. 14). Captain stated he intercepted the taxiway centerline at point where it forks left to become the centerline of the Outer taxiway heading east (p. 14-15).
Collision occurred in dense fog at Detroit with visibility reported as 1/4 mile with RVR 16,22 (p. 14). First officer estimated visibility about 500-600 feet during taxiing (p. 15).

DC-9 crew received confusing taxi instructions with inappropriate ground control clearances that led to crew uncertainty about position (p. 88-89). Ground controller failed to recognize runway incursion promptly; took 40 seconds from crew reporting error before ground control instructed DC-9 to exit runway immediately (p. 9).
Virtual reversal of roles by DC-9 pilots where proper crew coordination failed; first officer providing incorrect navigation information while captain attempted to fly (p. 7, 88).
Boeing 727 wing cut through right side of DC-9 fuselage at high speed during takeoff roll, severing right engine; collision occurred 1 minute 25 seconds after B-727 received takeoff clearance (p. 7).

DC-9 caught fire after collision and was destroyed. Rear jumpseat flight attendant and one passenger died from smoke inhalation after being unable to release the tailcone emergency exit; three crew members and four passengers died from drowning (p. 7, 87).

events.text: DC-9 Flight 1482 cleared to taxi from Gate C18 with instructions: right turn out of parking, taxi runway 3 Center, exit ramp at Oscar 6, contact ground 119.45
DC-9 crew reported position abeam the fire station; ground control issued additional taxi clearance: taxi Inner, Oscar 6, Fox, report making right turn on Xray
DC-9 crew missed turn onto taxiway Oscar 6 and instead entered outer taxiway; first officer reported approaching parallel runway on Oscar 6
Ground control instructed DC-9 to continue to Oscar 4 then turn right on Xray; DC-9 taxiing eastbound on Outer taxiway at very slow rate in reduced visibility
DC-9 captain set parking brake while approaching Outer/Oscar 4 intersection, uncertain about position
DC-9 captain released parking brake and continued taxiing right turn; crew confusion about runway position with visibility zero
DC-9 captain attempted to contact ground control on unknown frequency, unable to make contact initially
DC-9 crew on radio reporting they were stuck and could not see anything, ground control asked if they were on taxiway or runway
DC-9 captain reported we're on a runway, we're right by zero four; first officer stated we're on runway 21 Center; captain confirmed we're on 21 Center here
Ground control instructed DC-9 if you are on 21 Center exit the runway immediately sir
B-727 Flight 299 cleared for takeoff from runway 3 Center by tower controller
B-727 Flight 299 began takeoff roll from runway 3 Center
B-727 first officer stated definitely not a quarter mile visibility, 5 seconds into takeoff roll
B-727 right wing collided with DC-9 right fuselage on runway 21 Center, B-727 wing cutting through fuselage and severing DC-9 right engine; DC-9 caught fire

cvr.text: approaching the parallel runway on Oscar 6

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: Well tell him we're out here. We're stuck.

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: Hey, ground, 1482. We're out here we're stu....we can't see anything out here

recommendations.text: Improve standards for airport marking and lighting during low-visibility conditions including conspicuous marking and lighting; evaluate unidirectional taxi lines for acute angle taxiways; require stopbars or position-hold lights at all taxiways that intersect active runways
Identify at all Part 139 certificated airports complex intersections where potential for pilot confusion exists and require additional lighting and signs
Require that Part 139 certificated airports use reflectorized paint for airport surface markings
Require that Part 139 certificated airports install semiflush runway edge lights in accordance with Advisory Circular 150/5340-24

safety_changes: Installation of improved lighting systems at runway intersections
Enhanced ground control procedures for low-visibility taxiing
Standardized crew resource management training requirements

records.title: USAir 1493

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Runway Collision of USAir Flight 1493, Boeing 737 and Skywest Flight 5569 Fairchild Metroliner

records.summary: USAir Flight 1493, a Boeing 737-300, collided with SkyWest Airlines Flight 5569, a Fairchild Metroliner, on runway 24L at Los Angeles International Airport during landing. The SkyWest aircraft was positioned at an intersection awaiting takeoff clearance. The collision was caused by loss of situational awareness by the local air traffic controller, who failed to maintain awareness of the SkyWest aircraft's position due to a misplaced flight progress strip and preoccupation with another aircraft.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause was the failure of the Los Angeles Air Traffic Facility Management to implement procedures that provided redundancy comparable to the requirements of the National Operational Position Standards, and the failure of the FAA Air Traffic Service to provide adequate policy direction and oversight to its air traffic control facility managers. These failures created an environment in the Los Angeles Air Traffic Control tower that led to the failure of the local controller to maintain awareness of the traffic situation, culminating in inappropriate clearances and the subsequent collision. Contributing to the cause was the failure of the FAA to provide effective quality assurance of the ATC system.

factors.evidence: A flight progress strip for Wings West aircraft was misplaced by the clearance delivery controller (p. 592-593), preventing the local controller from being aware of its position.
The local controller forgot she had positioned SkyWest 5569 for takeoff on runway 24L at intersection 45 due to preoccupation with another aircraft (p. 18478-18486).
Operating procedures at LAX did not provide redundancy for monitoring flight progress strips, relying on the local controller's memory (p. 18410-18443).
Airport Surface Detection Equipment radar was not available to assist the controller, though it probably would not have prevented the accident given the circumstances (p. 18574-18580).
SkyWest aircraft was positioned in takeoff position on runway 24L at intersection 45 (p. 757-761).
USAir 737 collided with SkyWest Metroliner on runway 24L, destroying both aircraft with 35 fatalities (p. 564-568, 770-781).

events.text: LAX tower instructs SkyWest 569 to taxi into position and hold on runway 24 left.
SkyWest 569 acknowledges position and hold clearance for runway 24 left.
USA 1493 requests clearance for left side runway 24 left approach.
LAX tower clears USA 1493 to land on runway 24 left (controller unaware of SkyWest aircraft on runway due to loss of situational awareness).
USA 1493 acknowledges landing clearance for runway 24 left.
USA 1493 descending out of 500 feet on approach.
Sound of impact as USA 1493 contacts the runway with SkyWest 5569 positioned at intersection 45.
USAir 737 crushes SkyWest Metroliner, destroying both aircraft. Fire and explosion at runway 24L, intersection 45.

recommendations.text: Modify Air Traffic Control procedures at LAX to segregate arrivals and departures to specific runways and provide redundancies as intended in the National Operational Position Standards in the control tower.

Undertake a thorough risk-based evaluation of air traffic control procedures at LAX, considering runway intersection takeoffs, position-and-hold clearances, displaced runway thresholds, hazards from crossing traffic, local assist controller needs, and ASDE use and maintenance.

Include in the Office of Safety Quality Assurance the authority and resources to independently evaluate facility compliance with FAA directives and audit facility evaluations to determine corrective action.
Retain the National Operational Position Standards as a separate, independent order and direct FAA Human Factors and Air Traffic Service staffs to review the order for adequacy of redundancies.
Provide Air Traffic Control Supervisors with formal training to improve their understanding of the intent, objectives and administration of the Technical Appraisal Program.
Require that interim evaluations of controller performance be retained for 2 years and utilized to track performance and training needs of air traffic controllers.

Conduct a one-time examination of airport lighting at all U.S. tower-controlled airports to eliminate or reduce restrictions to visibility from the control tower to runways and other traffic movement areas.
Redefine airplane certification coverage compliance standards for anticollision light installations to ensure visibility to pilots on adjacent runways.
Evaluate and implement suitable means for enhancing the conspicuity of aircraft on airport surfaces during night or reduced visibility, including high-intensity strobe lighting.

Direct the general aviation community and airlines to ensure pilot training programs emphasize vigilance in monitoring ATC radio frequencies for traffic conflicts, especially on active runways and during final approach.
Incorporate into the Airman's Information Manual language that will alert pilots to the need for vigilance in monitoring air traffic frequencies for traffic conflict situations.
Develop specific phraseology for use by pilots requesting intersection departures and controllers issuing position-and-hold clearances for intersection departures.

safety_changes: LAX implemented procedure changes requiring flight progress strips to be passed through ground control position
Segregation of arrivals and departures to specific runways at LAX
Enhanced aircraft conspicuity standards for airport operations

notes: Read Executive Summary, History of Flights (lines 714-851), Conclusions (lines 18300-18511), Probable Cause (lines 18780-18836), and Recommendations (lines 18842-19334)
Detailed CVR transcript available in report Appendix C but not extracted as focus was on key sections establishing causal chain

records.title: 1991 British Army Lynx shootdown
records.summary: Army Air Corps Lynx helicopter ZE380 was attacked by IRA units using Soviet DShK heavy machine guns while descending toward Crossmaglen base on 13 February 1991. The aircraft was struck by multiple rounds of automatic fire causing extensive damage to the airframe, hydraulic systems, and cyclic control. The crew transmitted 'We've been shot - follow us!' and jettisoned the underslung load. Despite severe control difficulties, the crew successfully made an emergency landing in an open field with no crew injuries (p. 4, 74-75).
records.probable_cause: Shot down by IRA South Armagh Brigade using 12.7mm DShK heavy machine guns and 7.62mm machine guns in coordinated ambush attack (p. 1).

factors.evidence: IRA units fired from multiple positions with Soviet 12.7mm DShK heavy machine guns and 7.62mm machine guns in coordinated ambush as aircraft descended to 500-800 feet near Crossmaglen (p. 74-75).
