records.title: Ryan International Airlines 590
records.summary: A McDonnell Douglas DC-9-15RC cargo flight crashed on takeoff from Cleveland Hopkins International Airport during icing conditions. The flight crew failing to deice their aircraft contributed to the accident. The captain had 10,505 flight hours including 505 hours on the DC-9, while the first officer had 3,820 flight hours including 510 hours on the DC-9. Both pilots were killed when the aircraft rolled 90 degrees to the left and entered a stall shortly after liftoff.

records.title: LAN Chile 1069
records.summary: LAN Chile Flight 1069 was cleared for a VOR A approach to Puerto Williams on runway 26, but the captain decided to perform a direct approach to runway 08. The aircraft touched down 427 meters from the runway threshold at 112 knots on a wet runway with a negative slope and little braking action. records.title: United Airlines Flight 585
records.summary: United Airlines Flight 585, a Boeing 737-291, experienced a sudden rudder hardover on final approach to Colorado Springs on March 3, 1991. Prior to the fatal accident, the rudder abruptly deflected on February 25 and again on February 27, but these incidents were not fully resolved. On March 3, the aircraft rolled over and entered an uncontrolled dive on final approach, killing all 25 aboard. The NTSB eventually determined the crash resulted from a design defect in the 737's rudder power control unit.
records.probable_cause: A loss of control of the airplane resulting from the movement of the rudder surface to its blowdown limit. The rudder surface most likely deflected in a direction opposite to that commanded by the pilots as a result of a jam of the main rudder power control unit servo valve secondary slide to the servo valve housing offset from its neutral position and overtravel of the primary slide (p. 158).

factors.evidence: The design of the 737's rudder power control unit had a flaw allowing secondary slide overtravel (p. 158).
On February 25, 1991, rudder abruptly deflected 10 degrees right; similar event occurred February 27, but not fully resolved before fatal accident (p. 139).
The aircraft experienced rudder hardover while on final approach to runway 35 (p. 139).

records.title: 1991 Merion mid-air collision
records.operator: Lycoming Air Services / Sun Company Aviation Department
records.summary: A Piper Aerostar with an inoperative nose gear indicator light requested and received a low pass from a Bell 412 helicopter to visually inspect the gear status. During this inspection maneuver, the helicopter maneuvered into a position where it could not be seen by the Aerostar pilots. The two aircraft collided over Merion Elementary School, with the helicopter's rotor blades clipping the Aerostar from underneath. Both aircraft caught fire and crashed onto school grounds, killing five occupants from both aircraft and two children on the ground.
records.probable_cause: The probable causes were the poor judgment by the Aerostar captain to permit an in-flight inspection after determining the gear was extended, the poor judgment of the Bell captain to conduct the inspection, and the failure of the Bell crew to maintain safe separation. Contributing factors were incomplete training and checking of the Aerostar crew and deficient FAA principal operations inspector oversight.

factors.evidence: Neither crew of the two aircraft adequately recognized and maintained situational awareness of the other aircraft's position (p. 23)
Helicopter's rotor blades clipped the Aerostar from underneath, severing main rotor blade of helicopter and main wing panel of airplane (p. 5)
Nose gear doors of Aerostar partially close when gear extends, obscuring most of the locking mechanism from visual inspection (p. 23)
Piper flight manual emergency procedures section lacked explicit procedures if nose gear indicator light would not illuminate (p. 23)
Neither flightcrew of either aircraft had experience flying in close proximity to another aircraft; deficiencies found in Lycoming training program (p. 23)

Advise members of the circumstances of the midair collision involving Bell N78S and Piper N3645D and of the potential dangers associated with performing in-flight inspections or other close proximity maneuvers

records.title: Atlantic Southeast Airlines 2311
records.summary: Atlantic Southeast Airlines Flight 2311, an Embraer EMB 120 Brasilia with 23 aboard (2 crew, 20 passengers, 1 flight attendant), crashed north of Brunswick, Georgia on April 5, 1991 during approach to runway 07. The NTSB investigation determined that the left propeller control unit experienced severe wear of the quill spline teeth due to the introduction of a titanium-nitrided transfer tube with harder surface characteristics. This wear allowed the left propeller to move to a near-zero blade angle, creating severe asymmetric thrust that rolled the aircraft left beyond pilot control authority. The aircraft struck trees and terrain 9,975 feet from runway 07 threshold.
records.probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Board determines that the probable cause of this accident was the loss of control in flight as a result of a malfunction of the left engine propeller control unit which allowed the propeller blade angles to go below the flight idle position. Contributing to the accident was the deficient design of the Propeller control unit by Hamilton Standard and the approval of the design by the Federal Aviation Administration. The design did not correctly evaluate the failure mode that occurred during this flight, which resulted in an uncommanded and uncorrectable movement of the blades of the airplane's left propeller below the flight idle position.

factors.evidence: Left propeller blade angle 3 degrees with PCU commanded 79.2 degrees caused asymmetric thrust (p. 21).
Left propeller control unit malfunction allowed blade angles below flight idle (p. 21-23).
Aircraft rolled left 90 degrees and struck terrain 9,975 feet from runway (p. 9-10).
Crew completed 3 round-trip flights on consecutive days before accident flight (p. 9).

records.time_reference: Thailand local time (UTC+7); clock strings approximate to the minute, t is relative to the reverser deployment at about 23:31

agencies.name: Aircraft Accident Investigation Committee
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Investigation Report, Lauda Air Luftfahrt Aktiengesellschaft, Boeing 767-300ER, Registration OE-LAV, Ban Dan Chang, Suphan Buri Province, Thailand, 26 May 1991

location.name: Phu Toei National Park, Ban Dan Chang, Suphan Buri Province

records.summary: About 16 minutes after leaving Bangkok for Vienna, the 767's left engine thrust reverser deployed in flight while the aircraft was climbing through about 24,700 ft at Mach 0.78. The reverser plume disrupted the airflow over the left wing, the aircraft rolled and pitched down, and it broke up in flight during the ensuing dive. All 223 on board died. A REV ISLN advisory light had illuminated some 20 minutes earlier, and the checklist had indicated that no action was required.
records.probable_cause: The Thai Aircraft Accident Investigation Committee determined that the probable cause was the uncommanded in-flight deployment of the left engine thrust reverser, which resulted in loss of flight path control. The specific cause of the deployment was not positively identified, but the investigation showed that the reverser could be deployed by hydraulic pressure reaching the actuator through a failure in the directional control valve or associated wiring, and that the certification assumption that an in-flight deployment was controllable was not valid at climb speed and altitude.

factors.evidence: The 767 thrust reverser system's hydraulic isolation and directional control valves could allow deployment from a single failure; Boeing subsequently added a third, independent locking system.

The design had been certificated on the assumption that an in-flight reverser deployment was controllable; Boeing's post-accident simulations showed a loss of about 25 percent of wing lift and that recovery was not possible at the accident conditions.
The REV ISLN advisory light that illuminated 20 minutes before the accident did not convey the possibility of an imminent deployment.

The quick reference handbook indicated that additional system failures might cause in-flight deployment but that normal reverser operation should be expected after landing, leading the crew to take no action.
The left engine thrust reverser deployed uncommanded during the climb at about 24,700 ft and Mach 0.78.
The aircraft rolled and pitched down into a steep dive from which the crew could not recover.
The aircraft exceeded its structural limits in the dive and broke up in flight before striking the ground.

events.text: Departs Bangkok Don Mueang for Vienna, the second leg of the flight from Hong Kong, with 213 passengers and 10 crew.
The left engine REV ISLN advisory light illuminates intermittently during the climb.

The first officer reads the quick reference handbook entry, which states that additional system failures may cause in-flight deployment and that normal reverser operation should be expected after landing; the crew conclude no action is required.
The crew discuss the light and continue the climb; the captain regards it as an advisory only.
Climbing through about 24,700 ft at Mach 0.78, the left engine thrust reverser deploys uncommanded. The first officer calls out that the reverser has deployed.
The reverser efflux disrupts airflow over the left wing; the aircraft rolls and yaws left and pitches nose-down. Autopilot disconnects.
The crew attempt to recover; the aircraft continues into a steep, accelerating dive.
The aircraft exceeds its structural limits and breaks up in flight; recorders stop.
The wreckage falls into jungle in Phu Toei National Park, Suphan Buri Province; all 223 on board are killed.

recommendations.text: Modify the 767 thrust reverser system to prevent uncommanded in-flight deployment, and review the reverser systems of other transport aircraft against the same failure modes.
recommendations.outcome: The FAA required Boeing to install an additional independent sync-lock on 767 reversers, and reverser systems on other types were reviewed and modified.

recommendations.text: Revise the certification requirements so that in-flight reverser deployment is treated as a hazardous event to be prevented rather than assumed controllable.
recommendations.outcome: FAA and JAA certification policy for thrust reversers was revised to require multiple independent locks and no reliance on controllability after deployment.

recommendations.text: Revise the REV ISLN checklist guidance and crew training so that an isolation-valve indication is treated as a warning of possible in-flight deployment.

safety_changes: Boeing 767 aircraft with PW4000 engines were restricted from using reverse thrust until an additional independent locking system was installed.
Certification requirements for thrust reverser systems were revised worldwide to require multiple independent locks and to remove the assumption that in-flight deployment is controllable.
The failure of the flight data recorder to survive the fire led to improvements in recorder crash and fire protection standards.

records.title: Continental Express 2574
records.summary: Continental Express Flight 2574, an Embraer EMB 120 Brasilia, crashed near Eagle Lake, Texas during descent while initiating landing sequence. Investigation revealed that screws had been removed from the left horizontal stabilizer during maintenance and were not replaced following a shift change, causing the stabilizer leading edge to separate in flight and resulting in a severe nose-down pitch and structural breakup, killing all 14 on board.
records.probable_cause: The failure of Continental Express maintenance and inspection personnel to adhere to proper maintenance and quality assurance procedures for the airplane's horizontal stabilizer de-ice boots led to the sudden in-flight loss of the partially secured left horizontal stabilizer leading edge. Contributing factors included failure of management to ensure compliance with approved maintenance procedures and failure of FAA surveillance to detect non-compliance (p. 50).

factors.evidence: Screws had been removed from the horizontal stabilizer leading edge during second shift maintenance but were not replaced after shift change; the bag containing the removed screws was left on the lift and not found by third shift mechanics (p. 26-27).

The failure of airline maintenance and inspection personnel to adhere to proper maintenance and quality-assurance procedures; third shift inspector did not see missing screws from top of left leading edge in dark conditions (p. 26).
The failure of FAA surveillance to detect and verify compliance with approved procedures; FAA did not conduct sufficient oversight of Continental Express maintenance practices (p. 50).
The left horizontal stabilizer leading edge separated from the airframe in flight at approximately 11,800 feet during descent (p. 20).
The airplane pitched down dramatically with a negative load factor of at least -3.375 g, rolled 160+ degrees in 1 second, and broke apart in flight (p. 20-21).

agencies.report_title: Rapport de la Commission d'Enquête sur l'accident survenu le 20 janvier 1992 près du Mont Sainte-Odile (Bas-Rhin) à l'Airbus A320 immatriculé F-GGED exploité par la compagnie Air Inter

location.name: La Bloss ridge near Mont Sainte-Odile, Vosges, Bas-Rhin

records.summary: On a night VOR/DME approach to Strasbourg runway 05, after a late change of runway and approach by ATC, the crew descended from the final approach fix at about 3,300 ft/min instead of the intended 3.3 degree flight path angle. The aircraft struck the wooded ridge of La Bloss at 2,620 ft in cloud. 87 of the 96 occupants died; the wreckage was not located for several hours.
records.probable_cause: The Commission concluded that the accident was most probably due to a very high rate of descent during the final approach, the origin of which could not be determined with certainty; the most probable hypothesis was that the crew selected a vertical speed of -3,300 ft/min when they intended a flight path angle of -3.3 degrees on the FCU, whose display of the two modes was similar. Contributing factors included the crew's high workload following the late change of approach, the absence of cross-checking of the descent, the absence of a GPWS on the aircraft, the lack of an altitude check-call culture at Air Inter, and the limited radar and MSAW coverage at Strasbourg.

factors.evidence: ATC changed the expected ILS approach to runway 23 to a VOR/DME approach to runway 05 late in the descent, requiring the crew to re-plan under time pressure.
The crew were re-briefing the approach, managing the autopilot and flying a tight circuit with little time between the approach fix and the descent.
The most probable hypothesis is that the crew set -33 on the FCU in vertical speed mode (-3,300 ft/min) while intending -3.3 degrees flight path angle.
The FCU display presented flight path angle and vertical speed in a similar two-digit format with only a small mode indication, facilitating confusion.
Neither pilot monitored the vertical speed or altitude against the approach profile during the roughly one-minute descent.
There was no callout or cross-check of altitude and descent rate between the two pilots.
The aircraft was not fitted with a GPWS; Air Inter had obtained an exemption, so no terrain warning was available to the crew.
Air Inter had chosen not to equip its fleet with GPWS and did not require altitude callouts on non-precision approaches.
Strasbourg approach radar did not provide minimum safe altitude warning to the controller.
The approach was flown at night in cloud with no visual reference to the terrain.
The aircraft was in cloud with snow showers over the Vosges during the descent.
The aircraft struck the ridge at 2,620 ft in a controlled descent with no indication that the crew saw the terrain.

events.text: Flight IT148 departs Lyon for Strasbourg with 90 passengers and 6 crew; the captain is pilot flying.
Strasbourg approach informs the crew that the ILS to runway 23 is not available for them and offers a VOR/DME approach to runway 05; the crew re-brief the approach.
ATC vectors the aircraft to intercept the final approach track, which brings it to the ANDLO final fix closer in than planned.
The crew set up the descent on the FCU; the most probable hypothesis is a -33 selection in vertical speed mode rather than -3.3 degree flight path angle.
Aircraft begins descent from about 5,000 ft after ANDLO at about 3,300 ft/min, well above the expected 800 ft/min.
Controller, without MSAW, sees nothing abnormal on the radar and clears the crew to continue; no altitude alert is available.
The aircraft passes through 3,500 ft in cloud at night still descending at high rate; no callouts are made and no GPWS is fitted.
Aircraft strikes trees on the ridge of La Bloss at 2,620 ft in level flight and breaks up; 87 of 96 occupants die.
Rescuers reach the wreckage some four hours after the accident; nine survivors are recovered.

recommendations.text: Make the carriage of a ground proximity warning system mandatory on French public transport aircraft.
recommendations.outcome: GPWS became mandatory in France and Air Inter equipped its fleet.

recommendations.text: Modify the FCU so that the vertical speed and flight path angle modes are clearly distinguishable in the display.
recommendations.outcome: Airbus modified the FCU display to show vertical speed with four digits and flight path angle with two digits and a decimal point.

recommendations.text: Extend minimum safe altitude warning coverage at French approach radar facilities and review approach procedures at Strasbourg.
Introduce systematic altitude and descent rate callouts and cross-checks during non-precision approaches.
Improve the location of accident sites through ELT performance and coordination of search and rescue.

safety_changes: GPWS made mandatory in France; Air Inter equipped its A320 fleet.
Airbus FCU display modification distinguishing V/S from FPA (four digits versus two with decimal point).
Reinforced altitude callouts and approach monitoring procedures at Air Inter and improved SAR coordination.

notes: Impact at 18:20:33 UTC (19:20 local) is from the report; intermediate times and the descent initiation clock are approximate.
The ATC runway change and radar vectoring are recorded contributors but the report attributes the descent rate primarily to the probable FCU mode confusion, which could not be proved definitively.
Report reference number omitted; recommendation ids null.

records.title: Air Transport International 805
records.summary: A Douglas DC-8 cargo flight executing a second go-around at Toledo crashed after the captain became spatially disoriented while regaining control from the first officer. During the second approach attempt the aircraft experienced GPWS glideslope warnings and unstable conditions. When captain Baker took control at 03:24, he became disoriented and commanded an unrecoverable 80-degree bank and 25-degree pitch-up. The crew's mode awareness and control coordination failed during the emergency.
records.probable_cause: The failure of the flightcrew to properly recognize or recover in a timely manner from the unusual aircraft attitude that resulted from the captain's apparent spatial disorientation, resulting from physiological factors and/or a failed attitude director indicator (p. 60).

factors.evidence: First approach unstable with captain complaining to first officer that he was flying too slow with flaps not extended; aircraft failed to capture localizer and was below glide path; crew directed to climb and maintain 3,000 feet for second approach (p. 9-10).

Aircraft managed to capture localizer during second approach but approach became destabilized again between 0324:01 and 0324:15 with GPWS sounding three glideslope warnings and three sink rate warnings (p. 10).
Flight crew interactions were not representing proper crew resource management; captain took control at 0324:17 without clear transfer, and communication deteriorated during the go-around (p. 52-57).
When captain Baker took control at 0324:46, he became spatially disoriented; CVR recorded 'what's the matter?' and 'what the [expletive] the matter here?' before loss of control (p. 10-11).
Aircraft began to bank 80 degrees and pitch up 25 degrees during go-around; crashed about 3 miles northwest of Toledo Express Airport (p. 8, 10-11).

Captain expressed alarm on CVR: '[expletives]...what's the matter?'; 22 seconds before impact captain exchanges control with first officer saying 'You got it?'
Aircraft crashed approximately 3 miles northwest of Toledo Express Airport in steep nose-up attitude with bank exceeding 80 degrees

records.title: USAir Flight 405

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report - USAir Flight 405

records.summary: USAir Flight 405, a Fokker F-28-4000, crashed during takeoff from runway 13 at LaGuardia Airport on March 22, 1992. Due to inadequate ground de-icing procedures and weather-related delays up to 35 minutes, significant ice accumulated on the wings and airframe. The flight crew was unaware of the extent of ice buildup. The aircraft lifted off but failed to gain altitude, veering off the runway into Flushing Bay. Of the 51 people on board, 27 were killed, including the captain and one cabin crew member.
records.probable_cause: The failure of the airline industry and the Federal Aviation Administration to provide flightcrews with procedures, requirements, and criteria compatible with departure delays in conditions conducive to airframe icing, and the decision by the flightcrew to take off without positive assurance that the airplane's wings were free of ice accumulation after 35 minutes of exposure to precipitation following deicing. The ice contamination on the wings resulted in an aerodynamic stall and loss of control after liftoff. Contributing to the cause were the inappropriate procedures used by, and inadequate coordination between, the flightcrew that led to a takeoff rotation at a lower than prescribed airspeed.

factors.evidence: Poor weather conditions at LaGuardia resulted in heavy ground traffic and delays up to 35 minutes (p. 10).
A large amount of ice had accumulated on the wings and airframe due to inadequate de-icing procedures and delays exceeding the deicing fluid holdover time (p. 10).

De-icing procedures at LaGuardia were found to be substandard by the investigation; the aircraft deiced at approximately 2026 but delays extended beyond the holdover time before takeoff at 2135 (p. 9-10).

The flight crew was unaware of the amount of ice that had built up after the jet was delayed during taxiing to the runway; the first officer said he did not see contamination when inspecting the wing (p. 10).

The aircraft began its takeoff rotation at too low a speed; the specified V_R for the F-28 at this weight and flap configuration was 124 knots, but the aircraft rotated about 2.2 seconds after the V_R callout (p. 10).
Approximately 4.8 seconds after nose strut extension, stick shaker began; stall warnings were recorded (p. 10).

The aircraft veered off the runway, struck visual approach slope-indicator posts and other obstructions, with the left wing scraping the asphalt for 110 feet before separating from the fuselage (p. 10).
The aircraft came to rest in Flushing Bay, just beyond the end of the runway, in a partially inverted position (p. 10).

events.text: Flight 405 departs Jacksonville at 1715 EST for Cleveland via LaGuardia stopover.
Aircraft lands at LaGuardia; ground delays due to poor weather conditions.
First deicing at approximately 2026; first deicing truck experiences mechanical problems.
Aircraft pushed away from gate; second deicing by single truck at approximately 2026-2100.
Crew inspects aircraft; first officer does not see contamination on wing; aircraft cleared for departure.
Aircraft taxies to runway 13; second deicing holdover time expired by takeoff.
Aircraft cleared for takeoff at 2134:51; takeoff roll commences.
First officer calls 'VR' at approximately 124 knots; aircraft rotates about 2.2 seconds later.
Stick shaker activates; stall warning beeps recorded; aircraft at ~600 feet altitude.
Left wing scrapes runway for 110 feet; aircraft veers off runway into Flushing Bay.

recommendations.text: If gate holds are required to limit deicing fluid holdover time, encourage ATC to initiate gate holds as soon as a deicing operation begins rather than after delays have exceeded 15 minutes.
Where deicing operations are conducted away from the departure runway, report taxi delays in conditions conducive to airframe icing in increments less than 15 minutes.

Require flight crewmembers and appropriate ground personnel responsible for inspection of transport-category airplanes for wing contamination receive specific periodic training on what contamination looks like and feels like.
Study the effects on performance of swept-wing turbojet airplanes when specific amounts of airspeed are added to the computed rotation speed during takeoffs when wing contamination is possible.
Require airlines to establish a way to inform flightcrews of the type of fluid and mixture used, the current moisture accumulation rate, and the available holdover time.
Require that all airports which might experience freezing conditions and that are certified under Title 14 CFR Part 139 establish deicing plans for approval.

safety_changes: Enhanced de-icing procedures and training for flight crews
Improved holdover time guidelines for de-icing fluids
More stringent requirements for wing contamination inspection

records.title: Trans-Air Service 671

agencies.name: Bureau of Enquiry and Analysis for Civil Aviation Safety

records.summary: A 28-year-old Boeing 707 cargo aircraft lost its right-wing engines during cruise at 32,000 feet over southeastern France. Metal fatigue in the number 3 engine pylon caused it to crack and separate, which struck and separated the number 4 engine. The crew successfully descended and performed an emergency landing at Istres Air Base. All five crew members survived despite damage from post-landing fire.
records.probable_cause: La rupture des attaches pylône du moteur n° 3, causée par une fissure de fatigue de l'attache médiane intérieure, qui n'a pas été détectée lors de l'inspection visuelle prescrite. Cette fissure n'était pas détectable par les inspections visuelles périodiques imposées par la consigne de navigabilité. La rupture a entraîné l'arrachement du moteur n° 4 lorsque le moteur n° 3 est venu le percuter. (p. 39-40)

factors.evidence: Metal fatigue crack in number 3 engine pylon median attachment bracket (p. 39-40)
Airworthiness Directive requiring periodic visual inspection of pylons was found to be ineffective in detecting hidden fatigue cracks (p. 39-40)
Separated number 3 engine struck and separated number 4 engine (p. 4)
Aircraft began to roll to the right due to loss of both right engines (p. 4)
Pilots successfully performed emergency landing on runway 15 at Istres-Le Tubé Air Base (p. 4)
Right wing caught fire during landing sequence (p. 6)

events.text: Aircraft climbing through Flight Level 320 from FL290, authorized to climb to FL330, airspeed 280 knots indicated, autopilot engaged, turbulent conditions over Drôme department
Severe turbulence and loud double bang experienced; aircraft began to roll sharply to the right (p. 4)

First Officer requested left circuit for landing on runway 15 (opposite normal direction); controller accepted (p. 5)
Controller notified crew that aircraft was on fire during final approach (p. 6)
Aircraft landed slightly left of centerline at 190 knots; touched runway after approximately 24 minutes following engine loss (p. 6)
First Officer and flight engineer assisted captain; throttles of left engines controlled; no hydraulic brakes, used backup pneumatic system (p. 6)
Main landing gear tires burst; number 2 engine reverser deployed at full power (p. 6)
Aircraft exited runway left side after 2300 meters rollout and stopped 250 meters beyond runway at approximately 90 degrees to runway axis (p. 6)
Fire and rescue services extinguished right wing fire with large capacity fire trucks (p. 6)
Crew evacuated aircraft via lateral cockpit windows using emergency ropes; two passengers exited via front left door (p. 6)

recommendations.text: Inspection of median attachments of engine pylons should be modified to permit detection of hidden cracks, or these attachments should be systematically replaced with reinforced attachments. Reinforced attachments must account for new stresses potentially induced by HUSH KIT engine noise reduction modification.
Air traffic controllers should be regularly trained to face emergency and distress situations through theoretical study of possible cases and practical exercises

records.title: GP Express 861
records.summary: GP Express Flight 861 crashed while maneuvering to land at Anniston. The crew lost situational awareness after confusion about aircraft position during descent. Despite receiving navigational guidance, they failed to use proper instrument procedures, misinterpreted navigation signals by intercepting the back course localizer while north of the airport, and descended into terrain in fog. Contributing factors included inadequate training and preparation of newly hired captain, limited first officer experience, failure to provide approach charts to both pilots, crew coordination breakdown, and intercom system problems.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause was the failure of senior management of GP Express to provide adequate training and operational support for the startup of the southern operation, which resulted in the assignment of an inadequately prepared captain with a relatively inexperienced first officer in revenue passenger service and the failure of the flightcrew to use approved instrument flight procedures, which resulted in a loss of situational awareness and terrain clearance. Contributing to the causes of the accident was GP Express' failure to provide approach charts to each pilot and to establish stabilized approach criteria. Also contributing were the inadequate crew coordination and a role reversal on the part of the captain and first officer. (p. 48)

factors.evidence: Captain hired May 31, 1992, received only 11.1 hours C99 flight training with 22 instrument approaches before assigned as captain on his first revenue revenue flight on June 8, 1992 (p. 8-9). First officer completed initial training but failed first proficiency check on April 28, 1992, requiring retesting (p. 10).

Although captain had 857 total hours, he had only 17.6 hours turbine experience and no turboprop aircraft experience prior to GP Express assignment (p. 8-9). First officer had 1,234 total hours with only 37.7 hours actual instrument conditions (p. 10-11).

At 0842:39 captain states 'way off course' during descent confusion (p. 2). At 0848:49 first officer comments 'you're going to get this much on your first day' indicating crew stress (p. 6). Crew misidentified position, believed they received radar vectors when they had not, and could not determine actual position relative to navigational aids (p. 27-29).

First officer assumed captain-directing role, providing instructions beginning at 0848:49 (p. 6, 31). Captain failed to assert concerns or demand clarification about ATC instructions or crew's actual position (p. 29-30). At 0850:53 captain suggested missed approach but first officer encouraged continuation (p. 6).

Crew failed to complete in-range checklist properly; were unaware of BOGGA initial approach fix location (p. 3, 29-30). No ILS approach briefing conducted; captain had not reviewed approach chart (p. 30). At 0849:26 first officer assumed position over BOGGA without confirmation (p. 6, 30).

Crew intercepted back course localizer while actually north of airport, turning right believing they were south (p. 31). Radar data and aircraft performance analysis show crew completed 180-degree right turn north of airport, then left turn intercepting back course localizer (p. 16).

Only one set of approach charts available in aircraft; flying pilot would review then give to non-flying pilot (p. 6). Director of operations noted some captains had to purchase own charts (p. 8-9). Charts were not available to both pilots during critical approach phase.

Area enveloped in fog and low-lying clouds at accident time with 1,500 feet ceiling and 3 miles visibility in fog and haze (p. 3, 6). Weather conditions limited ability to visually acquire airport (p. 1).

Aircraft impacted heavily wooded ridge at 0852:25 about 7.5 miles north of Anniston airport at elevation 1,800 feet MSL (p. 6). Aircraft was destroyed by impact and postcrash fire causing 3 fatalities (p. 1).

events.text: Captain and first officer report for duty at GP Express operation facility at Tuscaloosa Municipal Airport (p. 1)

Atlanta Center controller clears Flight 861 to 'descend pilot's discretion maintain five thousand'; crew acknowledges and begins descent to 5,000 feet (p. 2)
Captain questions 'does he want us to resume own navigation?' but first officer assures captain they are 'on course anyway so let's just hold it' (p. 2)

After crew discussion about aircraft heading and course, captain concludes 'then we're way off course' (p. 2). Conversation shows first officer provided inbound course as 085° which was actually outbound VOR radial, creating crew confusion (p. 2)
Atlanta Center controller terminates radar service and instructs contact with Birmingham Approach Control; first officer acknowledges and contacts Birmingham at 0843:19 (p. 2-3)

First officer acknowledges with 'possible visual and ah if we don't see it we'll let you know for the ILS' indicating intention to attempt visual first (p. 3)
Approach controller reports latest weather for Anniston: ceiling 1,500 feet, visibility 3 miles in fog and haze, 700 foot cloud layer scattered variable to broken (p. 3)

First officer states 'didn't realize that you're going to get this much on your first day did ya'; captain responds 'it's all kind of ganged up here on me a little fast' indicating workload and stress (p. 3, 6, 32)
Captain asks 'got the localizer in?'; first officer replies 'workin' on it' indicating difficulty tuning navigational radios to correct frequencies for approach (p. 3, 32)

First officer states 'there you go'; captain replies 'yup went right through it', later first officer asks 'can you go around for it?' implying aircraft passed through localizer course while significantly north of BOGGA (p. 3, 6, 31)
First officer states 'we're right over BOGGA' and instructs to 'go ahead and drop your gear, speed checks' despite no confirmation of actual position (p. 6)
Captain asks 'glideslope isn't even alive. What's the minimum altitude I can descend to 'til I'm established?'; first officer responds 'til established. Twenty two hundred' (p. 6)
First officer reports to controller 'we're out of four thousand for the localizer at this time and we're inside of BOGGA' showing continued position confusion (p. 6)
First officer states 'ah procedure turn inbound complete' but radar data shows aircraft was north of airport, intercepting back course localizer while flying away from runway (p. 6, 31)
Captain states 'ah we gotta go missed on this'; first officer encourages continuation: 'just a minute--there you go--there your gonna' shoot right through it again--there you go see' (p. 6)
First officer states 'okay we gettin' in close keep 'er goin,' followed by 'you're okay' providing continued directive coaching to captain (p. 6)
Captain asks 'what's our missed approach point now?'; first officer responds 'middle marker at 1,200 feet' (p. 6)
First officer states 'coming up' (p. 6)

Sound of impact recorded on CVR at 0852:25; aircraft impacted heavily wooded ridge approximately 7.5 miles north of Anniston airport at elevation 1,800 feet MSL; aircraft destroyed by impact and postcrash fire in fog and low-lying clouds (p. 6)

Captain responds 'okay we're on our way' then 'there's the glideslope'; first officer replies 'we can continue our descent on down. We're way high' and confirms no glideslope, requiring descent minimum of 1,100 feet (p. 6)

recommendations.text: Require that all pilots operating aircraft under 14 CFR Part 135 have access to their own set of instrument approach charts. (p. 50)

Require that scheduled air carriers operating under 14 CFR Part 135 develop and include in their flight operation manuals and training programs stabilized approach criteria. The criteria should include specific limits of localizer, glideslope, and VOR needle deflections and rates of descent, etc., near the airport, beyond which initiation of an immediate missed approach would be required. (p. 50)

Develop guidance and evaluation criteria for Principal Operations Inspectors to use to ensure that airline cockpit resource management training programs adequately address crew interaction, decision-making processes, information gathering, flightcrew communication, and leadership skills. (p. 50)

For airlines that utilize contracted flight and ground training programs, require that pilots hired directly to be captains receive additional flight instruction pertaining to the operating environment and procedures unique to the airline from an FAA-approved company check airman or instructor, rather than only from the contractor instructor. (p. 50)

Amend 14 CFR 135.243(c)(2) to require that the pilot-in-command of a commuter air carrier flight that requires two crewmembers have at least 100 hours of flight time or an equivalent level of training in commuter air carrier operations requiring two pilots. (p. 50-51)

records.title: TWA 843
records.summary: TWA Flight 843 aborted takeoff from JFK on July 30, 1992 when stick shaker stall warning activated just after rotation at 14 feet altitude and 170 knots. The first officer, startled, transferred control to the captain, who aborted the takeoff. The aircraft touched down hard, overran the runway into grass, and caught fire. All 280 passengers were evacuated within two minutes. Ten passengers and crew suffered injuries.
records.probable_cause: An angle-of-attack sensor with an intermittent fault triggered a spurious stick shaker stall warning (p. 24-28). The first officer transferred control to the captain without clear handover during the unexpected warning (p. 24-28). The captain, sensing aircraft sinking from relaxed control during the transfer, aborted the takeoff (p. 24-28). The aircraft was performing normally and could have climbed away safely (p. 28-32).

factors.evidence: The Angle of Attack sensor had been found unserviceable on nine previous occasions; it had an intermittent fault that triggered spurious stall warning (p. 25-28).
First Officer Hergert announced 'Gettin' a stall' when stick shaker activated just after rotation; the aircraft was not actually stalled (p. 24-28).
First Officer made exclamation of surprise and transferred control to captain without clear handover; both pilots may have been providing control inputs during transfer (p. 24-28).
Handover techniques clearly defined in procedures were not followed; unclear communication between captain and first officer during unexpected warning (p. 24-32).

events.text: Flight 843 pushed back from gate at JFK and taxied to runway 13R at 17:40 EDT (p. 1, 11).
Aircraft began to rotate at 158 knots and reached V1 and VR at 17:40:58 and 17:41:03 respectively (p. 12-13).
First officer rotated aircraft; aircraft became airborne, climbing to approximately 14 feet altitude (p. 12-13).
Stick shaker activated at 17:41:11 seconds as the first abnormality after rotation; aircraft was 14 feet above runway, 170 knots (p. 13, 25-28).
First Officer Hergert announced 'Gettin' a stall. You got it' at 17:41:13, transferring control of aircraft back to Captain Kinkead (p. 13).
Captain Kinkead retarded the thrust levers and aborted the takeoff just 6 seconds after rotation (p. 13).
Aircraft overran the runway after aborting, traveled 296 feet from runway 13R, crossed grass and ditch, and stopped while burning (p. 13-14).
Fire spread in aircraft; emergency evacuation of all 280 passengers and crew completed within 2 minutes; 10 passengers and crew sustained injuries (p. 1, 13-14).

cvr.speaker: FO
cvr.text: Gettin' a stall. You got it.

recommendations.text: Require airlines to establish and implement procedures for clearly establishing and maintaining control of the aircraft during all takeoffs, with particular emphasis on training for abnormal situations during takeoff and initial climb (p. 48-52).
Require airlines to establish trend monitoring programs to track component failures and intermittent malfunctions to identify components requiring replacement (p. 48-52).
Modify the location of the blast fence at JFK runway 13R to protect adjacent facilities from future takeoff accidents (p. 52-53).

records.title: Lufthansa CityLine 5634
records.summary: Lufthansa CityLine Flight 5634 departing Bremen for Paris on January 6, 1993 was cleared to land on runway 27 but diverted to runway 28 due to incident. records.title: Japan Airlines Cargo Flight 46E

location.name: Near Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport

records.summary: Japan Air Lines Cargo Flight 46E, a Boeing 747-121 wet-leased from Evergreen International Airlines, experienced severe turbulence while climbing through 2,000 feet from Anchorage. The No. 2 engine pylon detached, causing the entire engine to separate from the wing. The aircraft was substantially damaged but the experienced flight crew conducted an emergency return and successfully landed the 747 back at Anchorage without additional incident or injuries.
records.probable_cause: The lateral separation of the No. 2 engine pylon resulted from encounter with severe or possibly extreme turbulence that resulted in dynamic multi-axis lateral loadings that exceeded the ultimate lateral load-carrying capability of the pylon, which was already reduced by a fatigue crack near the forward end of the pylon's forward firewall web.

factors.evidence: A 2-inch-long fatigue crack in the forward firewall web near the front engine mount bulkhead reduced the ultimate lateral load-carrying capability of the pylon structure by about 10 percent (p. 54)
Severe turbulence was reported by other airplanes; at takeoff the local controller informed crew that another Evergreen B-747 reported severe turbulence at 2,500 feet (p. 7)

At altitude of about 2,000 feet, the airplane experienced an uncommanded left bank of approximately 50 degrees and the pylon for engine two detached, causing the whole engine to fall off the wing (p. 11)
The flight crew declared an emergency, maintained power on No. 1 engine, and successfully landed the 747 back at Anchorage on runway 6R (p. 11)

events.text: Flight 46E departed Anchorage on runway 6 right; local controller informed crew that another Evergreen B-747 reported severe turbulence at 2,500 feet while climbing out.
At about 2,000 feet altitude, airplane experienced uncommanded 50-degree left bank and airspeed fluctuated 75 knots from 245 to 170 knots; No. 2 throttle slammed aft and reverser deployed.
No. 2 engine pylon structural failure begins at fatigue crack near forward firewall web; entire No. 2 engine separates from wing.
Flight crew immediately recognized the engine emergency from instrument readings and aircraft motion; performed emergency checklist memory items for engine failure.

Flight crew declared emergency and captain initiated large radius left turn to return; used emergency/maximum power on No. 1 engine, full rudder authority, and almost full right aileron; aircraft landed safely on runway 06R.

cvr.speaker: GND-1
cvr.text: Japan Air forty six Echo heavy, runway six right, cleared for takeoff.

cvr.speaker: CREW
cvr.text: Reports of severe turbulence on climbout; aircraft encounters severe turbulence with uncommanded left bank of 50 degrees and airspeed fluctuation of 75 knots.

recommendations.text: Develop and implement a meteorological program to observe, document, and analyze potential meteorological aircraft hazards in the area of Anchorage International Airport, Anchorage, Alaska, with an emphasis on the approach and departure paths of the airport.
Amend the design load requirements of 14 CFR Part 25 to consider multiple axis loads encountered during severe turbulence.
Require the Boeing-proposed B-747 engine pylon structural modification program to include increasing the lateral-load capability of the pylon structure.
Require any future structural modifications of existing engine pylons to consider multiple axis loading.
Issue an Airworthiness Directive to require compliance with Boeing Service Bulletin 747-54-2160.

Consider the necessity and feasibility of requiring the modification of the aircraft departure routes at Anchorage International Airport during periods of moderate or severe turbulence to minimize the potential of aircraft encountering mountain-induced low level turbulence.
Use the WSR-88D doppler weather radar system at Anchorage, Alaska, to document mountain-generated wind fields in the Anchorage area and to develop in greater detail low altitude turbulence forecasts.

notes: Key sections read: executive summary, history of flight, aircraft accident data, engine/pylon examination, findings, probable cause, and recommendations
CVR transcript available in report but only brief context provided as full transcript is extensive
Report contains FDR data but detailed parameter reconstruction would require full reading of appendices
Multiple recommendations indicate systemic issues with engine pylon design and mountainous terrain wind hazards

records.title: 1993 Tennessee Fairchild Merlin crash

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aviation Accident Final Report

location.name: Meadow near Blountville, Tennessee, 5.5 miles northeast of Tri-Cities Regional Airport

records.summary: A Fairchild Merlin on approach to Tri-Cities Airport in icing conditions encountered engine failures after the pilot failed to properly engage the engine inlet anti-ice system. Both engines flamed out, the aircraft stalled during the descent, and impacted a meadow 5.5 miles northeast of the airport, destroying the aircraft and killing all four occupants.
records.probable_cause: Failure of the pilot to follow procedures concerning use of the engine inlet anti-ice system and/or continuous ignition while operating in icing conditions, which resulted in probable ice ingestion and loss of engine power; and the pilot's failure to maintain sufficient airspeed while coping with the engine problem, which resulted in a stall. Factors related to the accident were: darkness, icing conditions, and engine inlet (nacelle) ice. (p. 1)

factors.evidence: The aircraft encountered light to moderate icing conditions during descent from 16,000 to 11,000 feet, and again encountered icing reported by other aircraft at 10,000 feet on final approach. (p. 3, 4)

Engine inlet anti-ice annunciator lights were illuminated at impact, indicating the anti-ice system was not properly engaged. The pilot failed to follow the flight manual procedures which specified selecting continuous ignition and then selecting engine and propeller heat one engine at a time when icing was encountered. (p. 1, 9)

Both engines were not operating at impact and both propellers were feathered. Examination revealed no mechanical failure or malfunction of the engines or propellers. The engine manufacturer reported flameouts occurred in other TPE331 aircraft during or following operation in icing conditions, sometimes after descent into warmer air. (p. 1, 9)

The pilot failed to follow procedures concerning the use of the engine inlet anti-ice system and continuous ignition while operating in icing conditions, as specified in the Fairchild SA227TT flight manual. (p. 1)

The aircraft entered a steep spiraling descent after engine power loss. Radar data showed the aircraft slowed in a manner consistent with power reduction, then entered a steep descent and crashed. The pilot's failure to maintain sufficient airspeed resulted in a stall. (p. 1, 3)

events.text: Pilot telephoned Georgia Automated Flight Service Station, Macon, Georgia, requesting weather briefing for planned instrument flights from Fulton County Airport, Atlanta.
Atlanta Center cleared the flight to descend from 16,000 feet to 11,000 feet; pilot was advised to expect light to moderate icing during descent.
Flight cleared for takeoff from Knoxville en route to Tri-City; assigned en route altitude of 7,000 feet.

Tri-City Approach accepted the flight as a radar handoff from Knoxville Approach Control; pilot advised to expect ILS approach to Runway 23. Approach control informed another aircraft of light icing reported by another aircraft at 10,000 feet.
Aircraft encountered icing conditions on final approach; radar data showed substantial speed reduction consistent with partial loss of power.
N500AK cleared to land at Tri-City Regional Airport on runway 23.
Pilot made an unintelligible radio transmission while on final approach.
Aircraft descended out of clouds in steep spiraling descent; air traffic controller observed airplane lights descending in steep spiral.
Radio contact lost; aircraft impacted meadow 5.5 miles northeast of Tri-City Regional Airport; both propellers feathered at impact.
Post-crash fire consumed cockpit, center section and left wing; all four on board killed; aircraft destroyed by impact forces and fire.

safety_changes: Garrett Engine Division issued operating information letter (February 24, 1988) emphasizing engine inlet anti-ice system use and continuous ignition in icing conditions.
Fairchild revised SA227TT flight manual (June 24, 1988) to provide explicit procedures for engine anti-ice and continuous ignition when icing conditions are encountered.

notes: Report sections read: Analysis/Probable Cause (p. 1), Findings (p. 2), History of Flight (p. 3-4), Personnel Information (p. 4), Aircraft Information (p. 4), Meteorological Information (p. 4-5), Wreckage and Impact Information (p. 5-7), Additional Information (p. 9).
10 events extracted with clock times from narrative timeline; t values calculated relative to 21:28 EST impact time.
All factor evidence cites page numbers from OCR-extracted text.
Aircraft had 2,294 total airframe hours and was properly maintained.
Pilot was ATP-rated with 19,105 total hours and 235 hours on SA227TT type.
No formal NTSB Safety Recommendations found in this report; safety changes documented from industry responses to TPE331 engine flameouts.

records.title: China Eastern Airlines 583

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Inadvertent In-Flight Slat Deployment, China Eastern Airlines Flight 583, McDonnell Douglas MD-11, B-2171, 950 Nautical Miles South of Shemya, Alaska, April 6, 1993

location.name: 950 nautical miles south of Shemya, Aleutian Islands

records.summary: China Eastern Airlines Flight 583 experienced an inadvertent leading-edge slat deployment during cruise flight at FL330 over the North Pacific. The deployment caused a nose-up pitch tendency, followed by pilot-induced pitch oscillations that resulted in loss of 5,000 feet of altitude, severe structural damage to the cabin interior, and injuries to 157 occupants. The aircraft stabilized and diverted safely to Shemya Air Force Base.
records.probable_cause: The inadequate design of the flap/slat actuation handle by McDonnell Douglas that allowed the handle to be easily and inadvertently dislodged from the UP/RET position, thereby causing extension of the leading edge slats during cruise flight. The captain's attempt to recover from the slat extension, given the reduced longitudinal stability and light control force characteristics of the MD-11 in cruise flight, led to several violent pitch oscillations. Contributing to the violence of the pitch oscillations were the lack of specific MD-11 pilot training in recovery from high altitude upsets and the influence of the stall warning system on the captain's control responses.

factors.evidence: The flap/slat handle was inadequately designed and could be easily inadvertently dislodged from the UP/RET position during routine cockpit movements. (p. 353-359)

The captain was attempting to resolve a discrepancy with the FMC Mach number indication and was making inputs to the MCDU keypad, which is located near the slat handle, likely resulting in inadvertent handle contact. (p. 5195-5245)

Following the slat extension and nose-up pitch, the pilot pushed the control column forward with significant force, which disconnected the autopilot and caused severe nose-down elevator deflections, initiating violent oscillations. (p. 784-807)
The stall warning system activated and deactivated during the pitch oscillations, influencing the pilot's control responses and contributing to the severity of the oscillations. (p. 710, 769)
The crew lacked specific training in recovery from high-altitude upsets accompanied by stall warnings, contributing to their loss of control during the recovery attempt. (p. 375)

events.text: Aircraft cruising at FL330 (33,000 feet), 296 knots indicated airspeed, Mach 0.82, with No. 1 autopilot engaged over Pacific Ocean about 950 nm south of Shemya, Alaska.
Captain observed a secondary Mach speed indication on the airspeed indicator and attempted to correct it by momentarily engaging and disengaging autopilot speed command.
Captain made inputs to the FMC through the No. 2 MCDU keypad to attempt correction; the keypad is located near the flap/slat handle.
White SLAT light with down arrow illuminated on the PFD; angle of attack bars changed from cyan to red (stall condition); stall warning stick shaker activated; slat overspeed warning chime sounded.
Captain verified flap/slat handle was in retracted position by pushing it forward; flight engineer placed hand on handle twice to ensure it remained forward.
FDR recorded slat disagree indication; outboard ailerons began to move; aircraft was at 296 knots indicated airspeed with No. 1 autopilot engaged.
Airplane began pitching nose up despite autopilot-commanded nose-down elevator deflections; autopilot elevator commands insufficient to counteract nose-up pitch moment from slat deployment.
Stall warning system activated while pitching nose up through 7.4 degrees at 296 knots and 1.37G vertical acceleration.
Airplane reached maximum nose-up pitch attitude of 9.5 degrees; airspeed decreased to 293 knots; vertical acceleration peaked at 1.50G.
Airplane began to pitch nose down after reaching maximum nose-up attitude.
Elevators began moving in nose-up direction as nose-down pitch rate was decreasing and vertical acceleration increasing.
Captain pulled elevator control with significant force; FDR recorded rapid elevator movements in nose-down and nose-up directions followed by autopilot disengagement.
Stall warning system deactivated; No. 1 autopilot disengaged; airplane reached 5.6 degrees nose-down pitch at 286 knots and -0.29G.
Aircraft completed second pitch oscillation; another stall warning occurred during this cycle.
Aircraft completed third pitch oscillation; slat disagree indication deactivated.
Vertical acceleration oscillating divergently with peak values of +1.53G and -1.24G during the third oscillation.
Aircraft completed fourth and final major pitch oscillation; maximum nose-down pitch reached 24.3 degrees; vertical acceleration began to converge as airspeed increased through 320 knots.
FDR data became unrecoverable for undetermined reasons after fourth oscillation; aircraft reported to have descended to approximately 28,000 feet.

FDR data recovered approximately 5 seconds later showing airplane pitching nose down through 15 degrees nose-down with vertical acceleration decreasing through +2.0G and airspeed increasing through 337 knots.
Airplane began to pull out of oscillating descent with pitch attitude steadily increasing; overspeed warning recorded as airspeed increased through 348 knots.
Airspeed peaked at 364 knots before beginning to decrease; overspeed warning deactivated as airspeed decreased through 360 knots.
Pitch attitude stopped increasing at approximately 7 degrees nose-up and oscillated between 5 and 8 degrees nose-up as aircraft climbed.

No. 2 autopilot engaged approximately 30 seconds after initial slat disagree indication (94 seconds after upset began); elevator position, pitch attitude, and vertical acceleration oscillations stopped.
Aircraft continued climb and then leveled out at FL330 (per crew report); FDR indicates stabilized flight during remainder of flight.
Crew requested deviation to nearest airport because of passenger injuries.
Aircraft diverted to Shemya Air Force Base, Alaska; emergency landing made safely with minor landing-gear-related damage.

recommendations.text: Require Douglas Aircraft Company to provide data needed to upgrade MD-11 training simulators to accurately represent the aircraft's longitudinal stability and control characteristics for high altitude cruise flight; and to develop specific guidance and simulator scenarios to train pilots in optimum techniques for the recovery from high altitude upsets, including those accompanied by stall warning.
Require operators to provide specific training for the recovery from high altitude upsets, including those accompanied by stall warning.
Establish high altitude stall margins for MD-11 airplanes in order to limit the effects of high altitude pitch upsets.
Evaluate the dynamics of the MD-11 stall warning system to ensure that the 'on' and 'off' logic are consistent with providing the pilot timely information.

Conduct a thorough review of the MD-11 high altitude cruise longitudinal stability and control characteristics, stall warning margins, and stall buffet susceptibility to ensure that pilot responses to routine pitch attitude upsets do not result in hazardous pitch oscillations, structural damage, or any other condition that could lead to unsafe flight.
Require that fire-blocking materials identified as Testori 0200-316 and 0206-100 be replaced with new materials that meet the fire retardant requirements of 14 CFR 25.853.
recommendations.outcome: Fire-blocking materials were replaced with materials meeting CFR requirements.

recommendations.text: Amend 14 CFR 25.853 to include a requirement to test the fire-retardant properties of fire blocking materials after they have been subjected to in-service wear.

Conduct research upon the effects of actual in-service wear on the continued airworthiness of fire-blocking materials. Based on the findings, require periodic actual in-service tests of fire-blocking materials to verify compliance with the requirements of 14 CFR 25.853.

Inform other certification authorities of the findings regarding the deterioration of the fire-blocking materials noted in this accident investigation with the view toward replacing them, as required.
Direct principal maintenance inspectors to inform operators of the need to periodically inspect fire-blocking materials for wear and damage and to replace defective materials.

Issue an Airworthiness Directive requiring the operators of MD-11s to install an interim flap/slat handle system or device to prevent the inadvertent deployment of the wing leading edge slats, when such a system or device becomes available.
recommendations.outcome: FAA issued Airworthiness Directive 93-15-03 requiring installation of retainer assembly on flap/slat control module.

recommendations.text: Issue an Air Carrier Operations Bulletin to Principal Operations Inspectors to verify that MD-11 operators have advised flightcrews of the potential for an inadvertent in-flight slat extension if contact is made with the flap/slat handle.

Require an expeditious installation of a redesigned flap/slat actuating system, when it becomes available for retrofit, that will prevent uncommanded and inadvertent deployment of the leading edge wing slats on MD-11 airplanes.

safety_changes: FAA issued Airworthiness Directive 93-15-03 requiring installation of retainer assembly on MD-11 flap/slat control module to prevent inadvertent slat deployment.
McDonnell Douglas and FAA worked to develop training simulators better representing MD-11 high-altitude stability characteristics.
Industry emphasis on training for recovery from high-altitude upsets and stall warning system behavior.

notes: Report read: Executive Summary, History of Flight, Analysis (general and slat extension sections), and Recommendations
Factual information on crew actions, aircraft systems, and pitch oscillation sequence extracted from pages 296-807
Event timeline reconstructed from FDR data and narrative; clock times approximate for initial event; most subsequent times are relative to upset initiation
FDR data gap noted between t=120 and t=125; report indicates oscillations continued but specifics unavailable
Fire-blocking material recommendations included as they were part of the investigation even though not directly related to the upset
Aircraft suffered substantial cabin interior damage; no external structural damage
Vertical acceleration values from FDR data; attitude changes from FDR recordings

records.title: American Airlines 102

route.from_name: Daniel K. Inouye International Airport, Honolulu

records.summary: American Airlines Flight 102, a DC-10-30, experienced loss of directional control during the landing rollout at Dallas/Fort Worth on 14 April 1993. Upon landing in rain with thunderstorms in the area, shortly after touchdown on runway 17L, the pilot lost directional control as the aircraft began to weathervane and departed the right side of the runway. The aircraft dug into mud, collapsed the nose landing gear, and damaged the left engine and wing. All 202 occupants survived; 38 received injuries during evacuation.
records.probable_cause: The failure of the captain to use proper directional control techniques to maintain the airplane on the runway. (p. 107)

factors.evidence: Runway surface was wet with rain during landing; weather conditions included visibility 2.5 miles, thunderstorms, rain showers, fog, wind 140° at 11 knots per 0647:58 broadcast; special weather report at 0701 showed wind shifted to 300° at 22 knots gusting to 33 knots with heavy rain (p. 7, 17).

Failure of the captain to use proper directional control techniques to maintain the airplane on the runway during landing rollout; captain took control at 50 feet altitude when first officer announced go-around (p. 6-7, 107).

Aircraft began to weathervane and departed right side of runway; tire tracks paralleled centerline for about 1,700 feet then turned gradually right and departed runway 3,303 feet from runway threshold; aircraft crossed high-speed taxiway 3S before returning to soft soil (p. 10).

events.text: First officer said 'I'm gonna go around' at 50 feet altitude, less than 1 second after automated voice called out 'fifty feet' (p. 6).
Captain stated 'No, no, no, I got it' in response to first officer's go-around call; first officer replied 'You got the airplane' (p. 6).
Automated voice said 'thirty' feet altitude during control transfer (p. 6).
Sound of thump similar to aircraft touchdown recorded on CVR at 0659:29 (p. 7).
Sound of second thump recorded on CVR about 2 seconds after first thump (p. 7).
First officer said 'OK, hundred and twenty knots' indicating airspeed during rollout (p. 7).
Captain said 'Oh [expletive]' during landing rollout (p. 7).
First officer said 'hundred knots' then 'OK, we're off the grass' indicating aircraft had departed paved runway surface (p. 7).
First officer called 'eighty knots' airspeed (p. 7).
Sound similar to a horn sounded in the cockpit during rollout (p. 7).
Captain stated 'Emergency evacuation' (p. 7).

One of the flightcrew members made evacuation announcement on public address system, though only one flight attendant reported hearing it; at least two flight attendants initiated cabin emergency evacuation by activating evacuation signaling system without hearing cockpit call (p. 7).

Aircraft came to rest upright approximately 2,607 feet from departure end of runway 17L and about 250 feet from right edge of runway, with nose on perpendicular taxiway 31; tire tracks started 4,303 feet from runway beginning, paralleled centerline for 1,700 feet then turned right and departed runway (p. 10).

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: No, no, no, I got it.

recommendations.text: Review the pilot training recordkeeping systems of airlines operated under FAR Parts 121 and 135 to determine the quality of information contained therein, and require the airlines to maintain appropriate information on the quality of pilot performance in training and checking programs.
Amend the ATC handbook, 7110.65, Chapter 3 to require that tower controllers issue the LLWAS advisory, 'Low Level Windshear Advisories in Effect,' whether or not equipped with ATIS.

Revise ATC handbook, 7110.65, Chapter 3 to require controllers to select for display all sensors on the LLWAS when adverse weather conditions such as thunderstorms are forecast or present in the terminal area.
Require the manufacturers of rechargeable batteries to provide specific maintenance instructions and recommended care practices.
Issue an Advisory Circular that provides proper maintenance instructions to aviation battery maintenance and repair facilities.
Require all 14 CFR Part 139 airports to perform runway friction tests regularly.
Provide FAA certification and safety inspectors with the training and resources necessary to oversee airport runway friction measurement programs.
Place airport certification and safety inspectors on the special emphasis workforce list.
Monitor surface friction on all operational runways on a more frequent basis, including the buildup of rubber on all runways, and perform rubber removal operations as required.

Review the guidelines for developing, implementing, reinforcing, and assessing CRM training programs for flight crewmembers and ensure that the CRM program conforms to FAA guidance contained in Advisory Circular 120-51 A.
Examine the maintenance procedures and practices that resulted in the misconfiguring of two reverse thrust cascades on the No. 2 engine of N139AA and make appropriate changes.

notes: Deep read from comprehensive sections: Executive Summary (p. 7), History of Flight (p. 8-10), Analysis - Flightcrew Actions (p. 6-7), Probable Cause (p. 107), Recommendations (p. 108-110)
12 events extracted with clock times from CVR and FDR data; 8 new events vs summary_record showing detailed control transfer and rollout sequence
All 11 formal safety recommendations extracted with IDs A-94-24 through A-94-34 (note: A-94-30 labeled as A-93-30 in document, corrected to sequence)
Factors include contaminated runway based on weather analysis; directional control failure as initiating factor per probable cause

records.title: Japan Air System 451
records.summary: Japan Air System Flight 451, a Douglas DC-9-41 with 72 passengers and 5 crew, was landing at Hanamaki Airport on 18 April 1993 after a short flight from Nagoya when it encountered windshear on final approach. Wind suddenly changed from 240° to 320° gusting 26 to 47 knots at 300 feet altitude. The relatively inexperienced first officer, who was at the controls, failed to recognize the condition and initiate a go-around. The aircraft made a hard landing with such force that the landing gear root penetrated the wing and punctured the fuel tank, causing a fire. All 77 occupants survived and evacuated quickly, with 19 sustaining injuries.
records.probable_cause: Aircraft encountered windshear on short final approach with insufficient crew experience and late recognition of the condition, causing hard landing with estimated impact force of +6G that punctured the fuel tank and ignited fire. (p. 94-96)

factors.evidence: When the aircraft reached 300 ft the wind suddenly changed and began to sink fast causing the aircraft's warning system to announce a Sink rate warning. Wind changed from 240° to 320° gusting 26 to 47 knots. (p. 94-100)
The co-pilot who was at controls at this time was not sufficiently experienced according to the operator operational procedures for handling windshear approach situations. (p. 94-96)
Poor supervision on part of the captain and a too late recovery were considered as contributing factors. The captain did not immediately take control when windshear was encountered. (p. 94-96)
The pilots were faulted by the fact that they failed to initiate a go-around until it was too late in the descent sequence. (p. 94-96)
Aircraft impacted the runway with such force that the gear was estimated to suffer up to +6G causing it to puncture the fuel tank and cause a fire. (p. 94-96)
The landing gear root penetrated the wing and punctured the fuel tank due to excessive impact force, causing fuel leakage and fire. (p. 94-96)
Fire developed from ruptured fuel tank after hard landing impact. (p. 94-96)
All 77 occupants survived the hard landing and fire. Aircraft successfully evacuated with quick crew actions to remove shoes and orderly evacuation preventing casualties. (p. 94-96)

events.text: Aircraft (JAS 451) departed from Nagoya Airport with captain in left seat and first officer in right seat as pilot flying. (p. 49-50)
First officer confirmed winds with Hanamaki and set runway 02 for landing approach. Weather briefing indicated winds 290° 14 kt with gusts to 33 kt, variable 250-320°. (p. 49-50)
Aircraft entered final approach course at high altitude. Configuration completed with gear down, flaps 50°, auto-brake minimum, and ground spoilers armed. (p. 88-91)
Hanamaki radio transmitted winds 280° 25 kt gusting 34 kt minimum 20 kt as aircraft descended through approximately 1,400 feet on final approach. (p. 88-94)

At approximately 600 feet altitude, aircraft was passing through boundary layer crossing the cold front. Wind suddenly changed from 240° to 320° with gusts increasing to 26-47 knots at 300 feet, initiating windshear condition. (p. 94-100)
Aircraft's warning system announced 'Minimum Minimum' alarm at 460 feet (200 ft radio altitude setting), followed immediately by 'Sink rate' warning indicating excessive descent rate. (p. 94-100)

Aircraft impacted runway with estimated +6G force due to excessive descent rate from windshear encounter. Landing gear root went up into wing puncturing fuel tank and igniting fire, aircraft skidded off runway and stopped burning. (p. 94-96)

All 77 occupants evacuated successfully from burning aircraft. Crew directed passenger evacuation without shoe requirement, enabling rapid and orderly evacuation. 3 crew members sustained serious injuries, 16 passengers slightly injured. (p. 94-96)

notes: Extracted from Japanese Transportation Safety Board (JTSB) investigation report 94-6
Report is in Japanese language, sections translated from CVR and flight data recorder analysis
Timeline events extracted from pages 87-100 of original report
8 events with local times (JST) converted from report data
All 77 occupants survived due to effective evacuation procedures
Crew survival attributed to quick evacuation without stopping for shoes or belongings

records.title: Indian Airlines Flight 491

agencies.name: Directorate General of Civil Aviation
agencies.report_title: Civil Aviation Aircraft Accident Summary for the Year 1993

records.summary: Indian Airlines Flight 491, a Boeing 737-200, took off from Aurangabad Airport with 118 persons on board. The aircraft lifted off near the end of the 6,000-foot runway with inadequate rotation. Shortly after takeoff, the left landing gear and left engine struck a truck carrying cotton bales on a road adjacent to the runway at approximately 410 feet from the runway end. The impact damaged the aircraft's left landing gear, left engine thrust reverser, and control surfaces. The aircraft continued in flight but subsequently struck high-tension power lines approximately 3 km northeast of the airport and crashed, killing 55 persons.
records.probable_cause: The captain's error in initiating late rotation and following wrong rotation technique resulted in inadequate climb performance. Additionally, the airport authorities failed to regulate mobile traffic on the Beed Road during flight operations, allowing a truck to remain in the hazard zone near the runway end.

factors.evidence: Captain's false perception of takeoff technique resulted in late rotation and failure to achieve adequate liftoff altitude before the runway end (p. 1).
Pilot did not initiate rotation at appropriate airspeed or position on runway, resulting in aircraft lifting off near end of 6,000-foot runway; error in rotation technique (p. 1).
Airport authorities failed to regulate or exclude mobile traffic from Beed Road adjacent to runway during flight operations (p. 1).
Aircraft's left main landing gear and left engine thrust reverser were severed; left elevator and horizontal stabilizer damaged by collision with truck (p. 1).
Aircraft impacted high-tension electric wires approximately 3 km northeast of runway and struck ground, resulting in destruction by post-impact fire (p. 1).

events.text: Aircraft cleared for takeoff from Aurangabad runway; 118 persons on board
Pilot initiated takeoff roll
Aircraft did not lift off until near the end of 6,000-foot runway with inadequate rotation technique
Left main landing gear and left engine collided with truck carrying cotton bales at approximately 410 feet from runway end
Impact severed left main landing gear and left engine thrust reverser; damaged left elevator and horizontal stabilizer
Aircraft struck high-tension electric power lines approximately 3 km northeast of runway
Aircraft descended and struck ground; fuselage separated and burst into flames due to post-impact fire

safety_changes: Increased airport regulatory enforcement to control vehicular traffic near active runways
Enhanced NOTAMs and ground operations coordination at regional airports
