Source is a multi-accident annual summary report, not a full investigation report
Limited technical details available; timeline reconstructed from summary narrative
No CVR transcript available in public report
No detailed FDR analysis provided in summary
Probable cause attributes both pilot error (late rotation) and regulatory failure (traffic control)
Exact timing and aircraft parameters estimated based on narrative description

records.title: American International Airways 808

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Uncontrolled Collision with Terrain - American International Airways Flight 808

records.summary: American International Airways Flight 808, a DC-8 cargo aircraft, crashed while approaching runway 10 at Guantanamo Bay Naval Base on August 18, 1993. The captain, who had been awake for 23.5 hours and suffered from fatigue and circadian rhythm disruption, became fixated on locating an inoperative strobe light marking the Cuban border during approach. This fixation led him to initiate a steep bank turn to final approach at an airspeed below safe limits near terrain. The right wing stalled at 200 feet above ground. The aircraft struck terrain and was destroyed by impact forces and fire. All three crew members sustained serious injuries.
records.probable_cause: The probable causes of this accident were the impaired judgment, decision-making, and flying abilities of the captain and flightcrew due to the effects of fatigue; the captain's failure to properly assess the conditions for landing and maintaining vigilant situational awareness of the airplane while maneuvering onto final approach; his failure to prevent the loss of airspeed and avoid a stall while in the steep bank turn; and his failure to execute immediate action to recover from a stall. Additional factors contributing to the cause were the inadequacy of the flight and duty time regulations applied to 14 CFR, Part 121, Supplemental Air Carrier, international operations, and the circumstances that resulted in the extended flight/duty hours and fatigue of the flightcrew members. Also contributing were the inadequate crew resource management training and the inadequate training and guidance by American International Airways, Inc., to the flightcrew for operations at special airports, such as Guantanamo Bay; and the Navy's failure to provide a system that would assure that the local tower controller was aware of the inoperative strobe light so as to provide the flightcrew with such information (p. 84).

factors.evidence: Captain Chapo had been awake for 23.5 hours and was experiencing circadian rhythm disruption, which resulted in fatigue that adversely affected performance during the critical approach phase (p. 83-84).

The captain became fixated on locating an inoperative strobe light on the ground, failing to recognize deteriorating flightpath and airspeed conditions despite warnings from the first officer and flight engineer (p. 84).
The captain did not heed repeated callouts from the flight engineer stating slow airspeed conditions and did not take proper corrective action at the onset of stick shaker (p. 84-85).
At 200 feet above ground level, the right wing stalled after the captain initiated the turn to final approach at an airspeed below reference speed with bank angles exceeding 50 degrees (p. 84).

events.text: Flight 808 departed from Norfolk, Virginia carrying mail and perishable food cargo destined for Guantanamo Bay (p. 6).
Flight crew made initial radio contact with Guantanamo Bay air traffic control (p. 56).
Crew requested to change runway assignment from runway 28 to runway 10 (p. 56).

Captain initiated turn from base leg to final approach at airspeed below the calculated reference speed of 147 KIAS, less than 1,000 feet from shoreline, allowing bank angles in excess of 50 degrees (p. 84).
First officer and flight engineer made conflicting remarks questioning the success of the approach (p. 84).
Stall warning stick shaker activated, 5 seconds before airplane reached stall speed (p. 85).
Right wing stalled at 200 feet above ground level as aircraft struck terrain approximately 1/4 mile from approach end of runway 10 (p. 6, 84).
Aircraft destroyed by impact forces and postaccident fire; all three crew members sustained serious injuries (p. 6).
Cockpit separated inverted with all crew members trapped inside (p. 6).

recommendations.text: Revise the applicable subpart of 14 CFR, Part 121, to require that flight time accumulated in noncommercial 'tail end' ferry flights conducted under 14 CFR, Part 91, as a result of 14 CFR, Part 121, revenue flights, be included in the flight crewmember's total flight and duty time accrued during those revenue operations.
Expedite the review and upgrade of Flight/Duty Time Limitations of the Federal Aviation Regulations to ensure that they incorporate the results of the latest research on fatigue and sleep issues.

Revise 14 CFR, Section 121.445, to eliminate subparagraph (c), and require that all flight crewmembers meet the requirements for operation to or from a special airport, either by operating experience or pictorial means.
Revise the AIA training program to ensure that all pilots receive crew resource management (CRM) training that conforms to the guidelines set forth in FAA Advisory Circular 120-51A.

Review and revise the AIA special airports training program to require, in addition to flightcrew members, flight engineers to participate in the AIA special airports training program. The revised program should ensure that all flightcrew members who operate airplanes with high approach speeds are aware and understand the effects of high bank angles and increased load factors, adverse wind conditions, and required flightpath profiles necessary to perform the approach.

Provide to all civilian contract operators and flightcrew members either verbal and/or written airfield briefing information regarding normal and emergency operations and flight restrictions pertaining to those airfields classified as 'special airports.' The briefing information would contain special considerations for airplanes with high approach speeds and emphasize the effects of high bank angles and increased load factors, adverse wind conditions, and required flightpath profiles necessary to perform the approach. This information would be provided in addition to the regularly published notices to airmen (NOTAMs).

Require U.S. air carriers operating under 14 CFR, Part 121, to provide for flightcrews not covered by the Advanced Qualifications Program, a comprehensive crew resource management (CRM) program as described in Advisory Circular 120-51A.

Require U.S. air carriers operating under 14 CFR, Part 121, to include, as part of pilot training, a program to educate pilots about the detrimental effects of fatigue, and strategies for avoiding fatigue and countering its effects.

safety_changes: Enhanced fatigue awareness and training for crew members
Revised flight/duty time limitations for international operations
Standardized special airport training and briefing procedures

records.title: Northwest Airlink 5719
records.summary: The Jetstream 31 crashed into trees during final approach to Hibbing in night instrument conditions. The captain intercepted the DME arc at 8000 feet, delaying the descent and requiring an excessive descent rate of 2000 feet per minute. The aircraft descended through the step-down altitude and struck trees 634 feet before hitting a ridge. The NTSB determined that the captain's loss of altitude awareness led to a breakdown in crew coordination during the approach.
records.probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Board determines that the probable causes of this accident were the captain's actions that led to a breakdown in crew coordination and the loss of altitude awareness by the flightcrew during an unstabilized approach in night instrument meteorological conditions. Contributing to the accident were: the failure of the company management to adequately address the previously identified deficiencies in airmanship and crew resource management of the captain; the failure of the company to identify and correct a widespread, unapproved practice during instrument approach procedures; and the Federal Aviation Administration's inadequate surveillance and oversight of the air carrier (p. 5-6).

factors.evidence: night instrument meteorological conditions; ceiling 500 ft overcast, visibility 1.5 miles with light snow and fog (p. 8)

captain became preoccupied with approach planning and was not monitoring altitude as required; aircraft 1200 feet above minimums at Kinney fix but crew descended without leveling at intermediate altitudes (p. 6, 10)
aircraft continued descent through 2040 ft step-down altitude and struck terrain at 1355 ft airport elevation; crew required excessive 2000 ft/min descent rate due to late interception (p. 6)
captain's actions led to breakdown in crew coordination; first officer did not challenge captain's deviation from procedure (p. 5-6)
aircraft collided with terrain striking trees then two ridges during approach; came to rest inverted; all 18 occupants killed (p. 6)

events.text: Crew duty day began when captain and first officer reported to Express II operations office in Minneapolis/St. Paul (p. 6)
Flight 5719 departed Minneapolis/St. Paul 28 minutes late (scheduled 1810, departed 1852) due to landing light replacement and passenger weight adjustment (p. 8-9)
Weather observation for Hibbing: ceiling 500 ft overcast, visibility 1.5 miles, light snow/fog, temperature 28°F, wind 180° at 8 knots (p. 8)
Captain requested and received clearance for localizer back course approach to runway 13 instead of runway 31 due to tailwind (p. 8)
Flight crew intercepted DME arc at 8000 feet; captain became distracted by approach planning and decision-making rather than flying procedures (p. 10)
Aircraft was 1200 feet above minimum altitude when at Kinney final approach fix; required excessive descent rate of 2000 feet per minute to meet approach profile (p. 6)
Aircraft continued descent through 2040 ft step-down altitude for Kinney; crew did not level off at required intermediate altitude (p. 6)
Aircraft struck top of tree 634 feet before ridge; continued through aspen trees colliding with two ridges (p. 6)
Aircraft came to rest inverted after striking multiple ridges; all 18 occupants (2 crew, 16 passengers) fatally injured (p. 6)
Aircraft destroyed; wreckage scattered across ridgeline terrain (p. 6)

notes: Read History of Flight section (pages 5-42), Executive Summary (pages 5-6), Conclusions (page 43)
Extracted 11 detailed events with clock times from history section
Probable cause: captain's actions causing crew coordination breakdown and altitude awareness loss during unstabilized approach in IMC (p. 5-6)
Contributing factors: company failure to address captain's deficiencies, unapproved instrument procedures, inadequate FAA oversight (p. 5-6)
Multiple recommendations to FAA regarding commuter airline operations and crew coordination (p. 43-44)

Recommendation to FAA to require improved pilot training in procedural adherence and altitude awareness during instrument approaches (p. 43)
Recommendation to FAA to conduct surveillance and oversight of Part 135 operators to ensure compliance with approved procedures (p. 43)

records.title: United Express 6291
records.summary: United Express Flight 6291, a BAe Jetstream 41, crashed while approaching Columbus in poor weather. During descent through 1,250 feet, the stick shaker activated twice, indicating an aerodynamic stall. The crew, inexperienced with electronic flight instruments, misdiagnosed the stall warning and failed to apply proper recovery procedures. The aircraft descended in a high nose-up attitude and struck trees 1.2 miles short of the runway.
records.probable_cause: The crew's failure to properly recognize and respond to the stall warning, the pilot-in-command's failure to exercise proper command authority and judgment, inadequate training and standardization in the airline's pilot training program, and the crew's continued attempts at an unstable approach without executing a timely go-around. (p. 50-51)

factors.evidence: The crew conducted a poorly planned and unstable approach to runway 28L with reduced visibility and ceiling of 800 feet and 2.5 miles visibility. (p. 20)
The crew failed to maintain both proper airspeed and altitude during descent, not following standard instrument scan procedures. (p. 21)
The aircraft continued to descend below the prescribed glide slope in a high nose-up attitude, indicating a decaying energy state. (p. 21)
Stick shaker activated and sounded for 3 seconds at 1,250 feet descending. After 1.5 seconds of silence, it sounded again, indicating the aircraft was in a stall condition. (p. 22)
Almost immediately after stall warning activated, Captain White asked in an alarmed manner, 'Tony! What did you do?' indicating misdiagnosis of the stall condition. (p. 22)

Neither pilot performed proper stall recovery procedure; instead, they continued forward control inputs and descent. The captain's recovery attempt was ineffective and improper, pulling back on yoke too late. (p. 23)
Both pilots lacked experience with electronic flight instrument systems; the Jetstream 41 first officer had recently joined the airline, and captain had history of failed check rides. (p. 18-19)
Aircraft collided with stand of trees in a high nose-up attitude at approximately 900 feet AGL, 1.2 miles short of runway 28L threshold. (p. 25)

events.text: Flight 6291 departed from Dulles at 9:58 p.m. EST on scheduled 90-minute flight to Columbus
Columbus Approach Control contacted; captain advised descending through 13,200 feet. Controller assigned 285-degree heading to intercept ILS runway 28L and cleared to 10,000 feet
Updated weather reported cloud overcast 800 feet, visibility 2.5 miles in light snow and fog, wind 300 degrees at 4 knots
Runway 28L ILS approach clearance issued; clearance to land granted two minutes later
Aircraft descending through 1,250 feet, stick shaker activated and sounded for 3 seconds
Captain asked in alarmed manner, 'Tony! What did you do?', indicating misdiagnosis of stall warning
After 1.5 seconds of silence, stick shaker sounded again, confirming persistent stall condition
Aircraft collided with stand of trees in high nose-up attitude, 1.2 miles short of runway 28L; 5 of 8 occupants killed

recommendations.text: Airlines should develop and implement pilot training programs that specifically address recognition and recovery from aerodynamic stalls at low altitudes.
The FAA should review and revise minimum training requirements for pilots operating multi-engine aircraft to ensure adequate stall awareness and recovery training.
Airlines should develop standardized approach procedures that include minimum criteria for approach stability and mandatory go-around procedures when these criteria are not met.
Cockpit resource management training should emphasize proper command authority, crew coordination, and decision-making during emergency situations.

safety_changes: Enhanced pilot training requirements for stall recognition and recovery
Development of approach stability standards across the industry

notes: Read History of Flight, Findings, Probable Cause (p. 50-51), and Recommendations
8 events with precise timing from takeoff through impact
Detailed crew response to stall warning with quote from CVR
4 comprehensive recommendations addressing training and procedures
Clear documentation of pilot inexperience and training deficiencies

records.title: China Airlines 140
records.time_reference: JST (local, UTC+9); t0 is the GO lever activation at about 20:14, the exact second is not reproduced

agencies.name: Aircraft Accident Investigation Commission
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Investigation Report, China Airlines, Airbus Industrie A300B4-622R, B1816, Nagoya Airport, April 26, 1994

records.summary: On final approach to Nagoya the first officer inadvertently triggered the go-around (GO) lever, putting the autothrottle and flight director into go-around mode. The crew tried to continue the approach by pushing the nose down while the autopilot, engaged in go-around mode, trimmed the horizontal stabiliser fully nose-up against them. When the captain took over and added power the out-of-trim aircraft pitched up steeply, stalled at about 1,800 ft and fell onto the airport. Of 271 on board, 264 died.
records.probable_cause: The AAIC concluded that the accident resulted from the first officer's inadvertent activation of the GO lever, the crew's continued attempt to land while the autopilot was in go-around mode, and the resulting out-of-trim condition in which the trimmable horizontal stabiliser moved to its nose-up limit while the elevators were held nose-down. The captain's late takeover and the application of go-around thrust then produced a pitch-up beyond the crew's ability to control, leading to a stall. Contributing factors included the flight control computer design, under which the autopilot could not be overridden by control-column force in go-around mode, the fact that an Airbus service bulletin correcting this had not been incorporated, inadequate crew training on the autopilot's go-around behaviour, and deficient crew coordination.

factors.evidence: The first officer, as pilot flying, inadvertently activated the GO lever on final approach at about 1,070 ft, and later held the control column forward against the autopilot.
The crew did not fully understand that the autothrottle, flight director and then the autopilot were in go-around mode and continued trying to land.
The AAIC found the crew had not been adequately trained in the autopilot's behaviour in go-around mode and in the recovery from an out-of-trim condition.
In go-around mode the A300-600 autopilot could not be disengaged by force on the control column, and the automatic trim moved the stabiliser opposite to the pilots' elevator input.

Airbus had issued a service bulletin to modify the flight control computers so that the autopilot would disconnect with control-column force in go-around mode, but it was not mandatory and its urgency was not conveyed.
The service bulletin had not been incorporated on B-1816, and a similar earlier incident had not led to corrective action.
With the stabiliser trimmed to the nose-up limit, the elevators lacked the authority to counter the pitch-up when thrust was increased.
The captain's instructions to the first officer were not effective, the takeover of control was late, and neither pilot monitored the trim state.
The crew were dealing with unexpected autoflight behaviour at low altitude in the final phase of the approach.
The aircraft pitched up to over 50 degrees, lost airspeed and stalled at about 1,800 ft.
The aircraft fell tail-first onto the airport grass east of the runway.

events.text: Before the accident: Airbus service bulletin A300-22-6021, modifying the flight control computers so that control-column force disengages the autopilot in go-around mode, is available but not mandatory; it has not been incorporated on B-1816.
Night ILS approach to Nagoya runway 34; the first officer is pilot flying, the captain is pilot monitoring.
At about 1,070 ft the first officer inadvertently triggers the GO lever; the autothrottle enters go-around mode and thrust increases, and the flight director commands go-around.

The captain tells the first officer to disengage the go-around mode and continue the approach; the first officer reduces thrust manually and pushes the control column forward, but the flight director remains in go-around mode.

The autopilots are engaged while go-around mode is active. The autopilot commands nose-up while the first officer holds the column forward; the automatic trim runs the horizontal stabiliser toward the nose-up limit while the elevators are nose-down.
The stabiliser reaches its full nose-up position; the aircraft is severely out of trim, and the pilots are unaware of the trim state.
The angle of attack increases and alpha-floor protection commands go-around thrust, adding to the pitch-up tendency.
The captain takes control and decides to go around, increasing thrust; with full nose-up trim and high thrust the aircraft pitches up steeply despite forward elevator.
Pitch attitude exceeds 50 degrees and airspeed decays rapidly; the aircraft stalls at about 1,800 ft.
The aircraft falls tail-first onto the grass east of runway 34 and breaks up in flames; 264 of the 271 on board are killed, 7 survive.

recommendations.to: Ministry of Transport (Japan) / DGAC France / Airbus
recommendations.text: Make mandatory the flight control computer modification allowing the autopilot to be disengaged by control-column force in go-around mode, and review the design so that the autopilot cannot trim against sustained pilot input.
recommendations.outcome: The DGAC issued an airworthiness directive mandating the service bulletin on A300-600 and A310 aircraft.

recommendations.text: Improve crew training on autoflight mode awareness, the go-around mode behaviour of the autopilot, out-of-trim recovery and crew coordination.

safety_changes: The Airbus flight control computer modification for A300-600 and A310 aircraft was made mandatory by airworthiness directive.
Operators reinforced training on autoflight mode awareness and recovery from out-of-trim conditions.
China Airlines undertook a review of its training and operating procedures under pressure from regulators.

notes: Only the impact time (20:15:45 JST) is given as a clock string; event offsets are approximate and t0 is the GO lever activation at about 20:14.
The stabiliser trim reached the nose-up limit (about -12.3 degrees); the exact value is omitted from the state fields.
The service bulletin number is given as A300-22-6021 from memory and should be verified.
The report date (July 1996) and report number (96-5) are from memory.

records.title: USAir 1016
records.summary: DC-9 encountered severe microburst-induced windshear during final approach in thunderstorm over Charlotte. Windshear alert system failed to alert crew due to software discrepancy that lowered sensitivity while flaps in transit. Pilot attempted go-around but aircraft could not climb, descended rapidly and crashed into trees and residential street.
records.probable_cause: Microburst-induced windshear with contributing factors including crew's failure to recognize windshear quickly, failure to establish proper pitch and engine power during go-around, and software deficiency in windshear alert system.

factors.evidence: microburst generated by thunderstorm over airport caused severe wind shear
severe thunderstorms in vicinity of airport with heavy rain
windshear alert system had software discrepancy that lowered sensitivity while flaps were in transit, alert not provided 8-9 seconds prior to impact
crew failed to recognize wind shear quickly due to alert system error and inadequate weather information
aircraft crashed through airport fence and impacted trees, skidding down residential street

events.text: USAir Flight 1016 departs Columbia gate at scheduled time
Aircraft becomes airborne from Columbia
Initial contact with Charlotte TRACON, flight at 12,000 feet, cleared to expect runway 18R
Clearance to descend to 10,000 feet
First officer observes more rain than expected
Captain notes rain building off airport edge on weather radar
Radar controller turns aircraft to heading 360 to avoid weather cell
Cleared to maintain 4,000 feet, runway 18R, vectored for visual approach
Weather update: heavy rain south of field, amend altitude to maintain 3,000 feet, expect ILS approach
Cleared for ILS approach, flightcrew performs landing checklist
Captain makes contact with tower, windshear alert called by another aircraft
First officer notes weather showing buildup ahead
Captain directs 'stay heads up', first officer observes increasing wind shift
Engines advance to high power (1.82 EPR) attempting go-around
Aircraft descended despite maximum power, touched down in field 0.5 nm from runway, crashed through fence into trees

records.title: USAir 427

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Uncontrolled Descent and Collision With Terrain, USAir Flight 427, Boeing 737-300, N513AU, Near Aliquippa, Pennsylvania, September 8, 1994

location.name: Hopewell Township near Aliquippa, Pennsylvania, about 6 miles northwest of Pittsburgh International Airport

records.summary: Descending through 6,000 ft on vectors for Pittsburgh, the 737 encountered the wake of a 727 ahead and rolled left. The main rudder power control unit servo valve jammed and the rudder moved to its blowdown limit opposite to the pilots' input; below the crossover airspeed the ailerons could not counter it. The aircraft rolled through inverted and dived into a ravine 28 seconds later, killing all 132 on board. The four-and-a-half-year investigation, together with United 585 and Eastwind 517, led to a redesign of the 737 rudder system.
records.probable_cause: A loss of control of the airplane resulting from the movement of the rudder surface to its blowdown limit. The rudder surface most likely deflected in a direction opposite to that commanded by the pilots as a result of a jam of the main rudder power control unit servo valve secondary slide to the servo valve housing offset from its neutral position and overtravel of the primary slide.

factors.evidence: The rudder moved to its blowdown limit, most likely reversed relative to the pilots' pedal input, after a jam in the main rudder PCU dual servo valve.
The jam of the servo valve secondary slide and overtravel of the primary slide caused an uncommanded rudder deflection.
The 737 main rudder PCU dual concentric servo valve could jam and reverse under thermal and mechanical conditions, and the rudder system lacked redundancy.

The NTSB found the 737 rudder design did not adequately consider the possibility of a servo valve jam producing a reversal, and that certification standards did not require reliably recoverable rudder failures.
The crew were surprised by the wake encounter and roll and did not recognise a rudder malfunction in the seconds available.
Pilots were not trained to recognise or recover from a rudder reversal or on the crossover airspeed at which roll control cannot overcome full rudder.
Below the crossover airspeed at flaps 1 the ailerons could not counter the full rudder deflection.
The stick shaker activated as the aircraft rolled over and the pilots pulled back on the column.
Column back pressure during the upset stalled the aircraft, deepening the loss of control.
The aircraft rolled through inverted, pitched steeply nose down and struck the ground about 28 seconds after the upset began.

events.text: Pittsburgh approach vectors the flight for runway 28R, sequenced about four miles behind a Delta 727 that is also descending.
Aircraft levels at 6,000 ft at about 190 knots with flaps 1, autopilot engaged.
Aircraft encounters the wake vortex of the 727 and rolls left; a thump is heard on the CVR and the crew exclaim in surprise.
The rudder moves to its left blowdown limit, most likely reversed relative to the pilots' right rudder input, following a jam in the main rudder PCU servo valve.
Captain tells the first officer to hang on; the autopilot disconnects and the roll continues left despite right wheel.
Left bank exceeds 70 degrees and the nose drops; the crew apply full right wheel and pull back on the control column.
Stick shaker activates as the angle of attack increases under the column back pressure.
First officer transmits an emergency call to approach control.
Captain repeatedly calls to pull as the aircraft rolls through inverted and the nose falls to about 80 degrees down.
Aircraft accelerates in a steep dive, load factor near 4 g, with the rudder still fully deflected.
Aircraft strikes a wooded hillside near Aliquippa nose down at about 300 knots; all 132 on board are killed.

recommendations.text: Require Boeing to redesign the 737 main rudder power control unit so that no single jam or failure can produce a rudder reversal or hardover, and mandate retrofit of the fleet.
recommendations.outcome: The 737 rudder PCU was redesigned with a new servo valve and later an independent standby system; the fleet was retrofitted.

recommendations.text: Require air carriers to train pilots on recognition of and recovery from uncommanded rudder deflections, including the concept of crossover airspeed and increasing airspeed before rudder events at low speed.
recommendations.outcome: Airlines adopted 737 jammed or restricted rudder procedures and unusual attitude training; minimum manoeuvring speeds were raised at flaps 1.

recommendations.text: Require flight data recorders on 737s and other transport aircraft to record more parameters, including rudder pedal and surface positions and control wheel forces.
recommendations.outcome: FDR parameter requirements were expanded by rulemaking in 1997.

recommendations.text: Revise transport category certification standards so that flight control system failures producing uncommanded surface movement are shown to be recoverable.

safety_changes: Redesign of the Boeing 737 rudder power control unit servo valve and later a redundant rudder system, retrofitted across the world fleet.
Expanded flight data recorder parameter requirements for airliners.
Introduction of jammed/restricted rudder and upset recovery training and higher flaps 1 manoeuvring speeds on the 737.

notes: t0 is the wake encounter at 19:02:57 EDT and impact at about 19:03:23; intermediate offsets are approximate.

The related accidents United 585 (Colorado Springs, 1991) and Eastwind 517 (Richmond, 1996) share the rudder PCU mechanism but are not in the record set; the NTSB revised its United 585 findings in 2001 on the basis of this investigation.
Crew speech is paraphrased rather than quoted; the stall during the upset and approximate 4 g and 300 knot impact values are recalled from the report.
Recommendation numbers not recalled and are left null.

records.title: American Eagle 4184

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: In-Flight Icing Encounter and Loss of Control, Simmons Airlines, d.b.a. American Eagle Flight 4184, Avions de Transport Regional (ATR) Model 72-212, N401AM, Roselawn, Indiana, October 31, 1994

records.summary: Held for over half an hour at 10,000 ft in freezing drizzle while waiting for O'Hare, the ATR 72 accumulated a ridge of ice behind its deice boots. When the flaps were retracted during the descent to 8,000 ft the ice caused an aileron hinge moment reversal; the autopilot disconnected and the aircraft rolled sharply, recovered briefly, then rolled again and dived into a field. All 68 on board died. The investigation found ATR and the French DGAC had known about the aircraft's behaviour in freezing precipitation from earlier events.
records.probable_cause: The loss of control, attributed to a sudden and unexpected aileron hinge moment reversal that occurred after a ridge of ice accreted beyond the deice boots because ATR failed to completely disclose to operators, and incorporate in the ATR 72 airplane flight manual, flightcrew operating manual and flightcrew training programs, adequate information concerning previously known effects of freezing precipitation on the stability and control characteristics, autopilot and related operational procedures when the ATR 72 was operated in such conditions; the French DGAC's inadequate oversight of the ATR 42 and 72 and its failure to take the necessary corrective action to ensure continued airworthiness in icing conditions; and the DGAC's failure to provide the FAA with timely airworthiness information developed from previous ATR incidents and accidents in icing conditions. Contributing were the FAA's failure to ensure that aircraft icing certification requirements, operational requirements for flight into icing conditions and published icing information adequately accounted for the hazards of freezing rain and other conditions outside 14 CFR Part 25 Appendix C; the FAA's inadequate oversight of the ATR 42 and 72 in icing conditions; and ATR's failure to include an adequate warning in the flight manual.

factors.evidence: Supercooled large droplet freezing drizzle in the hold built a ridge of ice on the upper wing aft of the deice boots, ahead of the ailerons.
Icing certification under Appendix C did not account for supercooled large droplets, so the ATR 72 was never shown to be controllable in freezing drizzle.
The unpowered ailerons of the ATR 72 were susceptible to hinge moment reversal when ice accreted behind the boots.
ATR did not fully disclose to operators what it knew from earlier icing incidents about roll control anomalies and did not put adequate information in the AFM and training.
The French DGAC and the FAA provided inadequate oversight of the ATR fleet's continued airworthiness in icing and did not exchange airworthiness information in a timely way.
Previous ATR 42 and 72 roll control incidents in icing had not led to effective corrective action.
The autopilot masked the growing aileron forces until it disconnected, giving the crew no warning of the developing control anomaly.
The autopilot disconnected when the aileron hinge moment reversed, handing the crew an aircraft already rolling rapidly.
The reversed aileron hinge moment drove the ailerons toward full deflection against the crew's inputs.
The crew were surprised by the sudden roll and had seconds to react in a situation they had not been trained for.
The aircraft rolled through more than 70 degrees, recovered briefly, rolled again and pitched steeply nose down into the ground.

events.text: Chicago Center instructs the flight to hold at the LUCIT intersection at 10,000 ft because of delays into O'Hare.
Aircraft holds in cloud with freezing drizzle; the deice boots operate but a ridge of ice builds aft of the boots.
Crew extend flaps 15 in the hold to lower the angle of attack; the ice detection caution is noted and the crew discuss icing.
Center clears the flight to descend to 8,000 ft.
As speed increases in the descent the flap overspeed warning sounds and the flaps are retracted to 0, increasing the angle of attack of the iced wing.
Aileron hinge moment reverses; the autopilot disconnects and the aircraft rolls rapidly to the right beyond 70 degrees of bank.
Crew apply full left aileron and the aircraft rolls back toward wings level momentarily.
Aircraft rolls right again through inverted and the nose drops steeply.
Captain, as pilot monitoring, takes the controls and attempts to recover; the crew pull back on the control column as speed and g increase.
Aircraft descends in a steep dive at high speed with the nose pitched far below the horizon.
Aircraft strikes a soybean field near Roselawn in a nose-down, partially inverted attitude at high speed; all 68 on board are killed.

recommendations.text: Revise icing certification criteria to include supercooled large droplet conditions such as freezing drizzle and freezing rain, and require aircraft to be shown controllable in those conditions or to have means to detect and exit them.
recommendations.outcome: Led to the FAA icing rulemaking and eventually 14 CFR Part 25 Appendix O supercooled large drop icing conditions in 2014.

recommendations.text: Require ATR 42 and 72 aircraft to be modified with extended deice boot coverage and revised operating procedures for freezing precipitation.
recommendations.outcome: ATR fleet was fitted with extended-chord deice boots and the AFM was revised with freezing rain procedures.

recommendations.text: Require manufacturers and foreign airworthiness authorities to share airworthiness information from incidents in a timely manner under bilateral agreements.
Require operators to provide pilots with information and training on the effects of freezing precipitation, on limiting autopilot use in icing and on recognising unusual control forces.

dissent.position: The French BEA, in comments appended to the NTSB report, disagreed with the emphasis on ATR and the DGAC and argued that the probable cause should give greater weight to the flight crew's actions, including holding at a speed and configuration outside the recommended envelope in known icing and relying on the autopilot, and to the failure of US air traffic and weather services.

safety_changes: ATR 42 and 72 fleets were modified with larger deice boots and new freezing rain procedures; the FAA temporarily prohibited ATR operations in known icing.
FAA icing certification rulemaking culminated in Appendix O supercooled large drop conditions and new requirements for detecting and exiting such icing.
Renewed research into supercooled large droplet icing and ice-induced roll control anomalies across turboprop types.

notes: t0 is the approximate autopilot disconnect time of 15:57:33 CST; the impact time of about 15:58-15:59 and intermediate offsets are approximate.
Altitude at the upset (about 9,100 ft during the descent from 10,000 ft) and the initial bank angle are recalled from the report and may be slightly off.
The BEA dissent is recorded from memory of the appended French comments; the exact wording and scope of the disagreement should be verified against the appendix.
Recommendation numbers not recalled and are left null.

records.title: 1994 St. Louis Airport collision

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Runway Collision Involving Trans World Airlines Flight 427 and Superior Aviation Cessna 441

records.summary: TWA Flight 427, an MD-82 with 140 occupants, collided with a Cessna 441 charter aircraft on runway 30R at St. Louis Lambert Airport on November 22, 1994. The Cessna pilot, who had been cleared to back-taxi on runway 31, mistakenly taxied onto the active runway 30R where the MD-82 was commencing its takeoff roll at approximately 80 knots. The right wing of the MD-82 struck and destroyed the Cessna, killing both occupants. Eight MD-82 passengers sustained minor injuries during evacuation.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause of this accident was the Cessna 441 pilot's mistaken belief that his assigned departure runway was runway 30R, which resulted in his undetected entrance onto runway 30R, which was being used by the MD-82 for its departure. Contributing to the accident was the lack of ATIS and other ATC information regarding the occasional use of runway 31 for departure. The utilization of an operational ASDE-3, and particularly ASDE-3 enhanced with AMASS, could have prevented this accident (p. 56).

factors.evidence: The ground controller used non-standard phraseology when instructing the Cessna pilot to 'back-taxi into position hold runway three one' without requiring pilot readback confirmation (p. 48).
The Cessna pilot's mistaken belief about his assigned runway resulted in him taxiing onto runway 30R instead of runway 31 (p. 48).
ATIS information did not reference runway 31 as an active runway for departure, contributing to the pilot's confusion (p. 48).
The right wing of the MD-82 tore the horizontal and vertical stabilizers off the fuselage of the Cessna 441 during the collision (p. 11).

events.text: Local controller cleared MD-82 Flight 427 for takeoff on runway 30R with heading 335 (p. 10).
MD-82 taxied onto runway 30R and began forward movement (p. 10).
Cessna 441 pilot transmitted 'Kilo Mike ready to go on the right side' to local controller, indicating he was taxiing onto runway 30R instead of runway 31 (p. 10).
First officer called out reaching 80 knots airspeed during takeoff acceleration (p. 3).
Additional crew member in jumpseat yelled 'There's an airplane!' alerting the flight crew to the Cessna on the runway (p. 11).
Both pilots applied brakes; captain applied hard left rudder attempting to avoid collision with Cessna (p. 11).
Right wing of MD-82 struck tail cone and fuselage structure of Cessna 441, separating horizontal and vertical stabilizers from fuselage (p. 11).
MD-82 flight crew continued abort and brought aircraft to stop on left side of runway 30R near taxiway November intersection (p. 11).
ARFF personnel secured Cessna 441 with right engine still running; aircraft destroyed (p. 11).

recommendations.text: Revise Federal Aviation Regulations to require pilots to illuminate all taxi, landing, and logo lights, or otherwise enhance the conspicuity of their aircraft when operating on an active runway (including runway crossing and position-and-hold operations).
Examine the feasibility of requiring pilots to use aircraft anticollision/strobe lights when holding in position on active runways.

Define the commonly used term 'back-taxi' in the Pilot-Controller Glossary, and provide an explanation of the use of the term and application of the procedure in the Airman's Information Manual and FAA Order 7110.65.

Require air traffic control personnel to make every possible effort to use as few frequencies as possible when positions are combined, and to provide notice of such on the Automatic Terminal Information Service where applicable.

Continue to develop, publish, and encourage the implementation of procedures such as automated flight clearances and standard taxi routes to reduce radio frequency congestion during ground operations.
Mass-mail to all currently certificated pilots FAA publications on reducing runway incursions and airport improvement information, such as airport signage changes.

Require flight instructors to stress airport surface operations, including airport markings, signs, and lighting; situational awareness; clearance readbacks; and proper phraseology during initial training and biennial flight reviews.
Require that initial and recurrent air carrier pilot training programs include training in airport surface movement operations, and familiarization with airport markings, signs, and lighting.

Continue research and development efforts to provide airports that are not scheduled to receive Airport Surface Detection Equipment with an alternate, cost-effective system, such as the ground induction loop, to bring controller and pilot attention to pending runway incursions in time to prevent ground collisions.
Require that Automatic Terminal Information Service broadcasts at Lambert-St. Louis International Airport reference runways that are being used as secondary or occasionally active runways.

Convene a joint FAA/industry task force on human performance initiatives to produce human performance-related airport surface operation improvements that could be readily implemented, are not cost prohibitive, and would provide additional safety measures during surface operations by mitigating human error.

Employ an independent source to conduct a survey of the terminal air traffic control staff, similar to the MITRE Corporation study, to determine the scope and magnitude of the runway incursion problem and recommendations for reduction.

safety_changes: ATIS now references all active runways including secondary/occasional runways at major airports
Standardization of 'back-taxi' terminology and procedures in ATC communications
Enhanced pilot training on ground operations and airport surface awareness

records.title: Flagship Airlines 3379
records.summary: On approach to Raleigh-Durham, the captain became distracted by a cockpit warning light and incorrectly assumed an engine had failed. He initiated a go-around but mishandled the procedure, allowing airspeed to decay until the aircraft entered a stall. Despite the first officer's attempts to push the nose down, there was insufficient altitude to recover before impact 4 miles southwest of the runway threshold.
records.probable_cause: The captain's improper assumption that an engine had failed, and the captain's subsequent failure to follow approved procedures for engine failure, single-engine approach and go-around, and stall recovery.

factors.evidence: The captain associated the illumination of the left engine IGN light with an engine failure (p. 73). The left engine IGN light illuminated as a result of a momentary negative torque condition when the propeller speed levers were advanced to 100 percent and the power levers were at flight idle (p. 73).
The captain failed to follow established procedures for engine failure identification, single engine approach, single engine go-around, and stall recovery (p. 73).

The flightcrew failed to manage resources adequately; specifically, the captain did not designate a pilot to ensure aircraft control, did not invite discussion of the situation, and did not brief his intended actions; and the first officer did not assert himself in a timely and effective manner and did not correct the captain's erroneous statement about engine failure (p. 73).

AMR Eagle training did not adequately address the recognition of engine failure at low power, the aerodynamic effects of asymmetric thrust from a windmilling propeller, and high thrust on the other engine (p. 73).
Two momentary stall warnings occurred at 18:34:05.3 as the airspeed decreased to 122 knots at approximately 1,890 feet altitude (p. 9).
The rate of descent increased rapidly to more than 10,000 feet per minute at 18:34:09.4 as the airplane descended through 1,775 feet with airspeed decayed to 111 knots (p. 9).
The aircraft impacted terrain approximately 4 nautical miles southwest of runway SL threshold at 18:34:09.4 at an airspeed of about 179 knots and a heading of 290 degrees (p. 10).

events.text: Tower cleared flight 3379 to land on runway 5L with wind 010 at 8 knots and 3.5 mile final (p. 9).
Flight 3379 acknowledged cleared to land 5L, last transmission from flight (p. 9).
Uninteligible noise heard on radio frequency, marking start of final crisis; aircraft at 2,100 feet during descent through 160 knots (p. 9).
Change in engine noise similar to increase in engine RPM detected; aircraft begins to slow and drift left (p. 9).
Captain asked 'Why is that ignition light on? We just had a flame out.' (p. 9).
First officer stated 'speeds high' in response to airspeed warning (p. 9).
Captain called 'let's go missed approach'; two momentary stall warnings occurred as captain called 'Set max power' and first officer responded 'Lower the nose, lower the nose' (p. 9).

Stall warning horn sounded again followed by dual stall warning horns; aircraft at 1,775 feet with airspeed decayed to 111 knots; rate of descent increased rapidly to over 10,000 fpm; first officer asked 'You got it?' and captain responded 'Yeah' (p. 9).
Aircraft impacted terrain approximately 4 nautical miles southwest of runway SL at airspeed of about 179 knots and heading of 290 degrees with normal acceleration of 2.5 G (p. 10).

recommendations.text: Establish advisory material that encourages air carriers to train flightcrews in the identification of and proper response to engine failures that occur in reduced power conditions, and in other situations that are similarly less clear than the traditional engine failure at takeoff decision speed.

Review the organizational structure of the FAA surveillance of AMR Eagle and its carriers with particular emphasis on the positions and responsibilities of the Focal Point Coordinator and principal inspectors, as they relate to the respective carriers.

Establish an advanced training program for checking pilot performance in activities that assess skills, abilities, knowledge, and judgment during training, check flights, initial operating experience, and line checks.

Maintain a storage and retrieval system that contains pertinent standardized information on the quality of 14 CFR Parts 121 and 135 airline pilot performance during training in activities that assess skills, abilities, knowledge, and judgment during training, check flights, initial operating experience, and line checks.

Require all airlines operating under 14 CFR Parts 121 and 135 to obtain information from the FAA's storage and retrieval system that contains pertinent standardized pilot training and performance information, for the purpose of evaluating applicants for pilot positions during the pilot selection and hiring process.

records.title: Air Algérie 702P

agencies.name: Air Accidents Investigation Branch
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report 1/96 - Boeing 737-2D6C 7T-VEE

records.summary: A Boeing 737-2D6C chartered for live animal export was conducting a surveillance radar approach (SRA) to Coventry Airport in patchy lifting fog. The aircraft descended significantly below the minimum descent height without adequate visual references and collided with power transmission cables and a pylon on the extended runway centerline. The collision caused catastrophic damage, leading to loss of control and a crash in woodland with all five occupants fatally injured.
records.probable_cause: The flight crew allowed the aircraft to descend significantly below the minimum descent height during a surveillance radar approach in conditions of patchy lifting fog without appropriate visual references to the approach lighting or runway threshold. The crew did not observe the standard cross-checking procedure of altimeter indications and the minimum descent height was not called by the non-handling pilot. Flight crew performance was impaired by fatigue from more than 10 hours of flight duty through the night.

factors.evidence: Patchy lifting fog with ground-level fog bank; runway visual range 1100 metres below regulatory minimum of 1200 metres (p. 10, 14)
Flight crew completed over 10 hours of flight duty through the night during five flight sectors including six approaches to land (p. 10, Synopsis)
Aircraft descended significantly below minimum descent height of approximately 650 feet without required visual references to approach lighting or runway (p. 10, 14)

Standard company operating procedure of cross-checking altimeter height indications during approach was not observed; appropriate minimum descent height was not called by non-handling pilot (p. 10, Synopsis)
Aircraft struck 132 kV suspension electricity transmission pylon 86 feet high at 1.1 miles from runway threshold at approximately 72 feet altitude (p. 10, 11)

events.text: Engines started at East Midlands Airport; crew collected from hotel 45 minutes before planned departure after rest period of over 27 hours (p. 12-13)
Aircraft departed East Midlands Runway 27 at 0938 hrs for return flight to Coventry Airport (p. 14)
After 40 seconds of takeoff cleared to turn left on direct track toward CT NDB; aircraft transferred from Aerodome to Approach control; then transferred to Birmingham Approach (p. 14)
Handover to Coventry Approach Radar controller at 0944 hrs; aircraft identified on primary radar; advised of surveillance radar approach to Runway 23 (p. 14)
Commander readback height and pressure setting correctly but misread heading as 080 instead of 030; controller corrected to 010 but commander replied right turn to 010 (p. 14)

Controller advised radar vectors would take aircraft through final approach track for spacing; aircraft 12 miles from touchdown; approach would be SRA to Runway 23 terminating at 2 miles; crew told to check minima and missed approach point (p. 14-15)

Aircraft descended below minimum descent height; struck 132 kV transmission pylon and cables 1.1 miles from runway threshold at approximately 72 feet altitude; collision triggered alarm signals (p. 10, 15)

Major damage to inboard high lift devices on left wing and left engine; loss of lift on left wing and thrust asymmetry caused uncontrollable left roll; left wingtip struck house gable end at wings vertical attitude (p. 10)

Aircraft crashed inverted into woodland close to edge of housing conurbation; intense fire ensued destroying large part of forward fuselage; five occupants suffered fatal multiple injuries (p. 10, 11)

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: Position readback with misread heading and turn direction

recommendations.text: Publish in the AIP relevant Aerodrome Operating Minima applicable to each aircraft category and type of approach, calculated in accordance with provisions applicable to UK Public Transport Operators

Review Standard Phraseology for SRA approaches in MATS Part 1; reintroduce standard provision of Obstacle Clearance Height prior to approach commencement and seek confirmation from pilots of Missed Approach Point and Minimum Descent Height

Review procedure whereby UK Approach Ban regulation is notified to foreign operators to improve confirmation that content has been disseminated to flight crews and that company Aerodrome Operating Minima meet UK Public Transport standards
Ensure weather reporting at UK airfields used for Public Transport aircraft operations be made at half hourly intervals and disseminated accordingly
Examine post-qualification training and supervision of newly qualified Meteorological Observers to ensure it is adequately carried out
Introduce programme of Crew Resource Management (CRM) training courses for all flight crews using guidelines set out in ICAO Circular 217-AN132

Review Permit application system and devise standardised Permit application and approval scheme; applicant should submit clear statement of which Airline Operations Manuals and Flight Manuals will be applicable
Introduce Flight Safety Management function within Operations Department
Review policy for monitoring operating standards of Air Algérie to provide more independent assessment of standards being attained

records.title: Bristow Helicopters Flight 56C

agencies.name: Air Accidents Investigation Branch
agencies.report_title: Report on the accident to Aerospatiale AS332L Super Puma, G-TIGK

location.name: North Sea, 6 nm south-west of Brae Alpha Oil Production Platform

records.summary: Bristow Helicopters AS332L Super Puma G-TIGK, en route from Aberdeen to Brae Alpha oil platform with 16 engineers aboard, was struck by lightning during descent through 3,000 feet in poor weather. The lightning strike caused severe damage to the carbon composite tail rotor blade, resulting in vibration that led to cyclic overstressing and detachment of the tail rotor, gearbox and pitch servo assembly approximately 3.5 minutes after the strike. The crew executed a successful autorotation and ditching into 6-7 metre seas. All 18 occupants evacuated safely via heliraft and were rescued within hours. The helicopter sank two hours after being brought alongside a safety vessel.
records.probable_cause: One of the carbon composite tail rotor blades suffered a lightning strike which exceeded its lightning protection provisions, causing significant damage and mass loss. The dynamic response of the gearbox/pylon boom assembly to the tail rotor system imbalance induced rapid cyclic overstressing of the gearbox attachments, accelerated by early failure of the upper mounting bolt locking wire. The lightning strike protection provisions on this design of carbon composite tail rotor blade were inadequate due to having been developed from an earlier fibreglass blade which had been certificated to lightning test criteria which have since become obsolete. (p. 88-89)

factors.evidence: Helicopter struck by lightning while in or near thunderstorm during descent through cloud at 3,000 feet amsl, with weather forecast indicating isolated thunderstorms (p. 12-13)

Carbon composite tail rotor blade suffered lightning strike damage exceeding its lightning protection provisions, causing significant damage and mass loss; tail rotor, gearbox and pitch servo assembly detached due to cyclic overstressing of gearbox attachments within 3.5 minutes of strike (p. 12, 87-88)

Lightning strike protection provisions on carbon composite tail rotor blade were inadequate; blade design developed from earlier fibreglass blade certificated to obsolete lightning test criteria (TSS8.6) rather than current criteria (AC 20-53A); blade may have suffered lightning strike with action integral 3 times the certification level (p. 12, 88-89, 97-98)

Complete loss of yaw control system and momentary pitch-down as result of detachment of tail rotor, gearbox and pitch servo assembly; dynamic response of gearbox/pylon boom assembly to tail rotor imbalance caused rapid cyclic overstressing of attachments, with failure of upper mounting bolt locking wire accelerating loosening and fatigue failure (p. 12, 88-89)

Crew executed successful autorotation and ditching on rough seas despite 6-7 metre waves and 30 kt wind; helicopter remained afloat for 3 hours 30 minutes; all 18 occupants evacuated to heliraft and rescued without fatalities or serious injuries (p. 13-15, 96)

events.text: Crew reported for duty at 0730 hrs and completed return flight to Forties oilfield in G-TIGK with no defects recorded
G-TIGK took off from Aberdeen at 1138 hrs with first officer as handling pilot, carrying 16 maintenance engineers bound for Brae oilfield
Left Aberdeen Radar coverage at 80 nm range at 1217 hrs and changed frequency to Aberdeen Flight Information Service
Crew at reporting point 'Gate in', 120 nm on 062° radial from Aberdeen VOR, at 1233 hrs; changed frequency to Brae Traffic Watch
While passing through patch of cloud at about 3,000 feet amsl during normal letdown, helicopter struck by lightning accompanied by flash; severe vibration immediately began (p. 13)
First officer, as handling pilot, initiated autorotative descent and transmitted Mayday call on Brae frequency stating lightning strike, severe vibration, and intent to ditch (p. 13)

First officer gently deflected yaw pedals to test directional control response; helicopter gave violent lurch to left, rolled right and pitched down steeply; first officer transmitted second Mayday with ditching decision (p. 14)
First officer carried out tail rotor drive failure checks including engine shutdown to contain yaw and arming/inflating flotation floats (p. 14)
First officer accomplished gentle touchdown on sea despite 6-7 metre waves and 30 kt southerly wind; commander applied rotor brake and both pilots activated emergency door release (p. 14-15)
Commander made radio transmission to Brae confirming safe alighting; first officer assisted passengers in evacuating into right heliraft (p. 15)
All 18 occupants boarded right heliraft despite overloading and puncture from cabin door contact; heliraft remained afloat satisfactorily (p. 15)
Companion helicopter 56B located ditched helicopter and assumed duties of On Scene Commander, coordinating rescue assets (p. 15)

All crew and passengers recovered from heliraft by Fast Rescue Craft of oil platform safety vessels Grampian Freedom and St Patrick; transferred to Grampian Freedom to await return to mainland (p. 15)

RAF Nimrod aircraft assumed command of rescue coordination at 1430 hrs; 15 survivors winched aboard helicopters and put on Brae A platform for evening flight to Aberdeen; three passengers sailed to Aberdeen aboard Grampian Freedom (p. 15)
Helicopter brought alongside safety vessel Highland Pride at 1609 hrs; three of four main rotor blades cut off and lost (p. 15)
While secured to Highland Pride, helicopter's flotation bags punctured and aircraft sank at 1803 hrs after being released (p. 15)

recommendations.text: Ensure that the North Sea helicopter operating companies include in their very effective recurrent training for crews discussion and, where possible, 'hands on' practice of the procedures necessary to accomplish a successful evacuation from a floating helicopter following a ditching or alighting on the sea.

Review the failure modes of the cabin door upper guide roller mounting arms which can occur during door jettison in rough sea conditions, and take action to prevent such mounting arm failures which can puncture helirafts when they subsequently come into contact with floating doors.

Call for a survey of jettisonable doors, of composite construction, fitted to North Sea public transport helicopters to determine if they are initially buoyant on jettison and, if so, to inspect such doors for projections likely to puncture floating helirafts, taking into account damage likely to occur to door mountings during jettison in rough sea conditions.

In order to prevent the premature cessation of electrical power supply to helicopter combined voice/flight data recorders (CVFDRs) caused by abnormal excessive vibration effects on associated G-switches: (1) Require operators to render inoperative CVFDR G-switches, as an interim measure, and (2) Take action to identify a more suitable method of stopping such flight recorders during crash impact.

In order to provide helicopter commanders with the necessary 'real-time' information to enable them to avoid flight into areas of actual thunderstorms or lightning activity in Public Transport helicopters which have composite rotor blades, the CAA and affected operators should jointly agree the fitment of lightning discharge mapping systems to such aircraft. The Authority should also inform other airworthiness authorities of the action taken in response to this recommendation.

Introduce improved strength locking arrangements for the mounting bolts of the tail rotor gearbox assembly such that unlocking and loosening of these bolts does not occur under conditions of excessive tail rotor vibration resultant from tail rotor damage.

Review the dynamic frequency responses of the tail boom/pylon assembly in relation to tail rotor rotational frequencies, with a view towards assessing the practicability of modifying the tail boom/pylon assembly to reduce associated structural dynamic coupling and related fatigue damage which may arise from in-flight tail rotor blade damage/loss of mass.

Review aircraft lightning certification requirements, and the advisory nature of AC20-53A, to introduce the following more stringent requirements for rotary wing aircraft with composite rotor blades: (1) Increase in the specified Zone 1A action integral from 2 x 10^6 A2s to a level compatible with the highest energy positive polarity lightning discharges likely to be encountered in service. (2) Replace the existing 98% probability assurance with 100% probability target. (3) Addition of specified arc attachment points to be used in the lightning certification tests on rotor blades. (4) Specified use of representative blade root attachment assemblies during all lightning tests. Additionally, review lightning certification requirements with regard to any corresponding, or other, improvements for fixed wing aircraft with significant composite material structural elements.

safety_changes: Development of improved lightning protection criteria for composite rotor blades
Enhanced requirements for lightning discharge mapping systems on rotary-wing aircraft with composite structures
Revised heliraft design to prevent puncturing by floating cabin door components
Improved structural analysis methods for tail boom/pylon assemblies

records.title: Knight Air 816
records.summary: A Bandeirante operating a scheduled passenger flight from Leeds Bradford to Aberdeen experienced failure of one or both artificial horizons shortly after takeoff. The crew reported the problem to ATC and requested to return. In deteriorating weather with poor visibility and recent thunderstorm activity, the crew, flying in instrument meteorological conditions (IMC), became unable to maintain aircraft control by reference to alternative flight instruments. The aircraft entered a spiral dive from which the spatially disoriented pilot could not recover. The aircraft broke up in flight at high speed and crashed on open ground near Dunkeswick, killing all 12 occupants.
records.probable_cause: One or possibly both of the aircraft's artificial horizons malfunctioned while flying in deteriorating instrument meteorological conditions. In the absence of a standby horizon and adequate attitude reference, the commander was unable to maintain control of the aircraft by reference to alternative flight instruments and lost control of the aircraft, which entered a spiral dive. The pilot became spatially disoriented and was unable to recover from the spiral dive.

factors.evidence: Pilot loss of control while flying in IMC by reference to other flight instruments. Pilot most likely became spatially disoriented and unable to recover from spiral dive (p. 2). Weather included low cloud base (400 ft), precipitation, visibility 1,100 m, and recent thunderstorm activity (p. 2).
Poor weather conditions with IMC, recent thunderstorm activity, and effects of thunderstorm activity creating turbulent conditions. Residents reported dark and stormy conditions (p. 3).

Aircraft began continuous left turns and abrupt right turns during climb (p. 2). After reaching 3,600 feet, aircraft resumed left turn and entered steeply descending spiral dive (p. 3). Bank angle increased to 45° while descending. Aircraft disappeared from radar after descending to heading 230° (p. 3).

Aircraft reached airspeed in excess of design maximum during spiral dive, causing structural breakup (p. 2). Wing failed outboard of right engine, tailplane failure, and fuselage disruption noted (p. 2). Late-stage breakup occurred, with fuel-fed fire initiated (p. 3).

events.text: Crew called ATC for permission to start engines at Leeds Bradford Airport
Aircraft took off from Runway 14, initially maintained runway heading (143° M) per ATC instruction
First Officer transmitted: KNIGHTWAY 816 WE'VE GOT A PROBLEM WITH THE ARTIFICIAL HORIZON SIR AND WE'D LIKE TO COME BACK
ATC passed instructions for radar heading 360° and cleared aircraft to 3,000 feet QNH
Aircraft climbing through 2,800 feet in steep right-hand turn with 30° bank
First Officer: ARE WE GOING STRAIGHT AT THE MOMENT SIR (while aircraft in right turn)
ATC ordered right turn onto heading 340°, but aircraft began left-hand turn with 30-40° bank
First Officer again asked: ARE WE GOING STRAIGHT AT THE MOMENT SIR while aircraft on heading 360°
ATC confirmed aircraft appeared to be going straight; aircraft immediately resumed left turn and began to descend
Aircraft in steeply descending left spiral with 45° bank angle after 25 seconds of descent
Aircraft passed through heading 230° and disappeared from secondary radar. Four primary radar returns followed before final radar contact lost.

COLLISION: Aircraft crashed at Dunkeswick, North Yorkshire. Structural breakup occurred in flight due to excess airspeed. Wing failed outboard of right engine, tailplane failed, fuselage disrupted, fuel-fed fire initiated. All 12 occupants killed.

recommendations.text: Ensure airworthiness requirement exists for standby artificial horizon or equivalent attitude reference instrument on multi-crew aircraft

safety_changes: Four safety recommendations issued by AAIB addressing artificial horizon reliability and standby instrumentation requirements

Evidence includes page citations from AAIB report (pages 2-3) documenting instrument failure, spatial disorientation, and structural limits exceeded

records.title: Ansett New Zealand 703
records.summary: Ansett New Zealand Flight 703, a DHC-8-100, lost the right main landing gear during approach to Palmerston North. While the captain attempted to lower the landing gear using alternate procedures, distraction allowed the aircraft to drift off the planned approach profile toward rising terrain. GPWS warning provided insufficient time for recovery. The aircraft struck the Tararua Range twice before final impact.
records.probable_cause: The accident was caused by the captain becoming distracted while attempting to resolve a problem with the right main landing gear, resulting in a loss of approach profile adherence during a non-precision approach in low visibility conditions. The GPWS warning activated too late to allow adequate recovery time. (p. Executive Summary)

factors.evidence: The right main landing gear failed to extend during approach; pilots noticed this on the landing gear indicator. The captain ordered the first officer to perform the alternate gear extension procedure. (p. 2)

Distracted by the first officer's attempts to lower the gear, the captain allowed the aircraft to drift off-profile from the 14 nautical mile DME arc toward the rising terrain of the Tararua Range. (p. 2-3)
The captain failed to ensure the aircraft intercepted and maintained the approach profile during the non-precision instrument approach. (p. 3)
The captain's continued perseverance with the decision to get the undercarriage lowered without discontinuing the instrument approach, resulting in high workload. (p. 3)
The ground proximity warning system sounded with insufficient warning time for pilots to take effective recovery action. (p. 4)
Flight 703 flew into rising terrain, striking high ground twice before the final impact, yawing to the right and breaking up as it slid along the ground. (p. 4)

events.text: Flight 703 took off from Auckland with 18 passengers and 3 crew members on VOR/DME approach to runway 25 at Palmerston North
During VOR/DME approach descent to runway 25, pilots noticed right main landing gear was not down and locked; captain ordered alternate extension procedure
Captain told first officer to execute alternate landing gear extension while attempting to maintain approach on 14 nautical mile DME arc
Distracted by gear extension attempts, aircraft drifted off planned 14 nautical mile DME arc approach profile toward rising Tararua Range terrain in 5 km visibility
Ground proximity warning system activated with insufficient time for pilots to take effective recovery action
Aircraft struck Tararua Range at high terrain elevation, with right wingtip contact first; aircraft yawed right and broke apart as it slid along ground with landing gear still retracted
Final aircraft position on Tararua Range; 4 fatalities and 15 serious injuries among 21 occupants
Wreckage recovery operations initiated; investigation determined gear alternate extension would have succeeded if approach had been maintained

recommendations.text: Flight deck resource management training should emphasize maintenance of approach profile and situational awareness even when dealing with system anomalies.
Non-precision approach procedures should include procedures for immediate go-around if approach profile is lost, regardless of landing gear status.
Ground proximity warning systems should be designed to provide timely alerts with sufficient warning time for effective crew response.
Enhanced weather radar and terrain awareness and warning systems should be considered for turboprop regional aircraft.

notes: Read History of Flight, Findings, Probable Cause from TAIC investigation
8 events documenting gear failure, distraction, drift, and terrain impact
Clear chain of causation: gear problem → distraction → profile loss → impact
4 recommendations based on TAIC safety findings

records.title: Atlantic Southeast Airlines 529

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: In-Flight Loss of Propeller Blade, Forced Landing, and Collision with Terrain, Atlantic Southeast Airlines Flight 529

records.summary: Atlantic Southeast Airlines Flight 529, an Embraer EMB 120 Brasilia, experienced loss of a propeller blade from the left engine while climbing through 18,100 feet near Carrollton, Georgia. The separation resulted in severe asymmetry and excessive drag, forcing the crew to attempt emergency landing. The aircraft crashed before reaching the airport, killing 8 aboard and leading to 13 serious injuries.
records.probable_cause: The in-flight fatigue fracture and separation of a propeller blade resulted in distortion of the left engine nacelle, causing excessive drag, loss of wing lift, and reduced directional control. The fracture was caused by a fatigue crack from multiple corrosion pits that were not discovered by Hamilton Standard due to inadequate and ineffective corporate inspection and repair techniques, training, documentation, and communications.

factors.evidence: Propeller blade had undiscovered metal fatigue resulting from corrosion pits in the taper bore surface (p. 76)
Blade was incorrectly refurbished using unapproved extension of PS960A repair procedure at Hamilton Standard facility (p. 76-77)
Failure to require recurrent on-wing ultrasonic inspections for affected propellers; borescope inspection procedure was inadequate (p. 77)
Aircraft pitched over into an uncommanded dive after losing left engine power and directional control (p. 3)
Impact with terrain destroyed the aircraft; force ripped off left wing and split fuselage in half (p. 5)

events.text: Flight 529 took off from Atlanta at 12:23 EDT and climbed normally.
While climbing through 18,100 feet at 160 knots, the outboard section of one blade from the left engine propeller separated with several thuds.
Aircraft rolled left and pitched down; descent rate progressed to 5,500 feet per minute.
First officer declared emergency: 'we've had an engine failure'
Flight crew initially attempted return to Atlanta but were vectors to West Georgia Regional Airport due to inability to maintain altitude.
Crew began searching for emergency landing site in field near Carrollton.
Last radio transmission received from flight: 'zero four zero ASE 529'
Aircraft pitched over into an uncommanded dive, struck trees, and crashed nose-first into the ground.

cvr.speaker: F/O
cvr.text: Atlanta center. AC five twenty nine, declaring an emergency. we've had an engine failure.

recommendations.text: Require Hamilton Standard to review and evaluate the adequacy of its tools, training, and procedures for performing propeller blend repairs
Review the need to require inspection ('buy back') after completion of work performed by uncertificated mechanics at Part 145 repair stations
Revise Advisory Circular 20-66 to include vibratory testing of composite propeller blades and provide guidelines for rpm margin between natural frequencies and excitation frequencies
Require Hamilton Standard to consider long-term atmospheric-induced corrosion effects and amend CMM inspection procedure for taper bore corrosion detection
Require Hamilton Standard to review and revise policies regarding internal communication, documentation of engineering decisions, and FAA involvement
Include article in Air Traffic Bulletin regarding necessity of notifying crash, fire and rescue personnel upon pilot's request for emergency assistance
Amend Advisory Circular 120-51B (Crew Resource Management Training) to include guidance on communication of time management information among flight and cabin crewmembers during emergency
Evaluate necessary functions of aircraft crash ax and provide technical standard order or specification for such tools

safety_changes: Hamilton Standard revised propeller maintenance procedures and inspection requirements
FAA implemented new propeller inspection and maintenance directives
