records.title: American Airlines 1572

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Collision With Trees on Final Approach

records.summary: An MD-83 on approach to Bradley Airport struck trees and an ILS antenna on Peak Mountain ridge after descending below the assigned minimum descent altitude of 908 feet. The crew descended below minimums due to an incorrect altimeter setting that made the altimeter read 70 feet high, combined with inadequate monitoring and the crew's continued descent while searching for the airport in severe thunderstorms, heavy rain and wind shear.
records.probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Board determines that the probable cause of this accident was the flightcrew's failure to maintain the required minimum descent altitude until the required visual references identifiable with the runway were in sight. Contributing factors were the failure of the BDL approach controller to furnish the flightcrew with a current altimeter setting, and the flightcrew's failure to ask for a more current setting. (p. 90)

factors.evidence: Aircraft impacted trees on Peak Mountain ridge at approximately 2.54 nautical miles northwest of runway 15 approach end, then struck the runway 33 ILS antenna. (p. 6, 11, 678)
The flightcrew failed to level off at the assigned minimum descent altitude (MDA) of 908 feet above field elevation and continued descending until striking trees. (p. 6, 90)

The first officer set an incorrect altimeter setting of 29.47 inHg instead of 29.40 inHg at 0033, causing the altimeter to read approximately 70 feet high. Additionally, the controller did not furnish a current altimeter setting upon initial radio contact at 0043. (p. 3, 63-64, 90)

The first officer looked out the window searching for the airport visually rather than monitoring the descent on instruments until reaching MDA. He failed to call out the altitude deviation as the aircraft descended below MDA. (p. 6, 92-94)
Five miles from the airport, the aircraft encountered heavy rain and turbulence, restricting visual references. (p. 3, 6, 63)
During descent into Hartford at 0030 EST, pilots received a weather update including a warning of wind shear and severe thunderstorms at Bradley. (p. 3)

Dispatcher sent ACARS message at 0031 advising that airplanes had been making landings at BDL and experiencing turbulence and windshear on final approach. TRACON supervisor issued windshear alert at 0054:51. (p. 3, 6)
Autopilot had difficulty maintaining altitude and heading in the buffeting winds with multiple weather hazards affecting the flight during descent and approach. (p. 3, 6, 63)

events.text: Flight 1572 departed from Chicago O'Hare at 2305 local time (0510 UTC next day), delayed about 2 hours from scheduled departure due to late arrival of connecting passengers and weather. (p. 1, 434)

During descent, dispatcher sent ACARS message providing altimeter settings of 29.23 inHg (QFE) and 29.42 inHg (QNH) for Bradley. Weather advisory indicated pressure falling rapidly (PRESFR). (p. 2, 447-449)

First officer set altimeter to 29.47 inHg during before-landing checklist, which was approximately 0.07 inches higher than the correct 29.40 setting just announced by ARTCC controller, causing the altimeter to read approximately 70 feet high. (p. 2, 3, 484-489, 574)
Flight contacted approach control, which cleared the flight to expect VOR runway 15 approach but did not provide current altimeter setting despite pressure falling rapidly. (p. 5, 603)
Approach control cleared flight 1572 for the runway 15 approach and advised that tower was temporarily closed due to window damage. (p. 5, 607-611)
Captain instructed first officer to give 1000 feet per minute descent rate and began descent to minimum descent altitude (MDA) of 908 feet using autopilot vertical speed mode. (p. 6, 648-649)
TRACON supervisor issued windshear alert providing wind data for centerfield (170 at 25), northeast boundary (170 at 24), and southeast boundary (190 at 12). (p. 6, 652-654)

First officer observed the aircraft descending below MDA and stated 'you're going below your...' but captain had already disconnected autopilot altitude hold. Sink rate warning began approximately 4 seconds before impact. (p. 6, 662-667)

Aircraft struck trees on Peak Mountain ridge at approximately 2.54 nautical miles northwest of runway 15, then became airborne briefly and struck ILS antenna before coming to rest on the ground short of runway. (p. 6, 676-678)

cvr.speaker: PF
cvr.text: Hey tower, American 1572, we're on a six mile final for runway 15

cvr.speaker: PF
cvr.text: OK, give me a thousand down

cvr.speaker: ATC
cvr.text: Wind shear alert uh, center field one seven zero at two five. The uh, northeast boundary, one seven zero at two four, one niner zero at twelve at the southeast boundary

recommendations.text: Evaluate Terminal Instrument Procedures (TERPS) design criteria for non-precision approaches to consider the incorporation of a constant rate or constant angle of descent to minimum descent altitude in lieu of step-down criteria.

Examine and make more effective the coordinating efforts of the flight inspection program and the procedures development program, with emphasis on ensuring quality control during the development, amendment, and flight inspection process for instrument approaches.
Incorporate precipitous terrain adjustments in the BDL runway 15 approach.

Include a more comprehensive set of guidelines concerning precipitous terrain adjustments in the Terminal Instrument Procedures (TERPS) (FAA Order 8260.3B) Handbook, clarifying the definition of precipitous terrain, and establishing defined criteria for addressing the potential effects of such terrain.

Review and evaluate the appropriateness of the let-down altitudes for all non-precision approaches that have significant terrain features along the approach course between the initial approach fix and the runway.
Solicit and record user comments about difficulties encountered in flying a particular approach to evaluate approach design more accurately.

For arriving aircraft executing non-precision instrument approaches at all airports, during periods in which the official weather report includes the remarks, 'pressure falling rapidly,' controllers should be required to issue as frequently as practical altimeter setting changes to flightcrews in addition to the altimeter setting issued on initial contact.

Revise Facility Operation and Administration handbook 7210.3, or other appropriate orders, to require that when a tower shuts down for any reason, and if the tower controllers have time to record a new automatic terminal information service (ATIS) indicating that the tower is closed, they should do so.
Develop a plan to physically check and correct low level windshear alert system (LLWAS) wind sensor alignment in a timely manner.
Evaluate the low level windshear alert system (LLWAS) recertification process, and ensure that the process addresses the total functional capability of the system.
Require all operators to inspect immediately all MD-80 and DC-9 floor level exits to ensure that evacuation slides have been properly rigged.
Review and amend its MD-80 and DC-9 maintenance manuals so that terminology used in graphics and instructions pertaining to the installation and removal of evacuation slides are clear and consistent.
Develop a uniform policy on shoe removal during evacuations, and require that all operators train their flight attendants to issue commands during an emergency evacuation consistent with that policy.

notes: Extracted from NTSB report AAR96-05, 102 pages
Sections read: History of Flight (p. 1-15), Probable Cause (p. 90), Recommendations (p. 91-93)
9 events with clock times from CVR transcript
All 13 recommendations extracted with official NTSB IDs
Aircraft repaired and continued flying until 2017
Only one minor serious injury despite terrain impact

records.title: Birgenair 301

agencies.name: Dirección General de Aeronáutica Civil
agencies.report_title: Final report on the accident of Boeing 757-225 TC-GEN, Birgenair flight 301, Puerto Plata, 6 February 1996

location.name: Atlantic Ocean about 26 km northeast of Puerto Plata

records.summary: Departing Puerto Plata at night after the 757 had stood unused for about three weeks, the captain noticed during the takeoff roll that his airspeed indicator was not working but continued the takeoff. His pitot probe was blocked, probably by a wasp nest, and as the aircraft climbed his airspeed indication rose falsely. The autopilot, using the same erroneous data, pitched the nose up to hold speed; an overspeed warning and the stick shaker sounded together, the crew reduced thrust, and the aircraft stalled and fell into the sea. All 189 on board died.
records.probable_cause: The Dominican commission determined the probable cause was the crew's failure to recognise the activation of the stick shaker as an imminent warning of entry into an aerodynamic stall and their failure to execute the procedures for recovery from the onset of loss of control. Before the stall the crew were confused by contradictory airspeed indications and warnings resulting from a blocked pitot tube (attributed to an obstruction, probably a mud dauber wasp nest, while the aircraft was parked without pitot covers) and by the autopilot's response to the erroneous airspeed.

factors.evidence: The captain's pitot probe was obstructed, most probably by an insect nest built while the aircraft stood parked for about 20 days without pitot covers.
The captain's airspeed indicator read low on the takeoff roll and then increasingly high in the climb while the first officer's indicator read correctly.
The captain continued the takeoff after noting his airspeed indicator was not working instead of rejecting it.
The autopilot and autothrottle were engaged using the captain's erroneous air data and pitched the nose up and reduced thrust to counter the apparent overspeed.
An overspeed warning sounded at about 7,300 ft as the erroneous indication passed 350 knots.
The crew reduced thrust in response to the overspeed indication while the stick shaker was warning of a stall, and did not identify the stall.
The first officer's correct airspeed indication and the relief pilot's prompts were not used to resolve the situation.
The stick shaker activated while the overspeed warning was still sounding.
The aircraft stalled at about 7,000 ft with the nose high and thrust reduced; an engine flamed out during the descent.
The aircraft rolled and descended out of control into the sea about five minutes after takeoff.
The takeoff and climb were made at night over the sea with no visual horizon.

events.text: Aircraft stands parked at Puerto Plata for about three weeks without pitot covers installed.
Takeoff roll begins on runway 08 at Puerto Plata.

At about 80 knots the captain remarks that his airspeed indicator is not working; the first officer reports that his is, and the captain elects to continue the takeoff using the first officer's calls.
Aircraft rotates and lifts off; the captain's airspeed indicator begins to show increasing values as the aircraft climbs.
Autopilot engaged in the climb using the captain's air data.
Rudder ratio and mach speed trim advisories appear; the captain remarks that something is wrong and the airspeed indications differ.

Passing about 7,300 ft the captain's airspeed reads about 350 knots and the overspeed warning sounds; the autopilot has raised the pitch attitude and the autothrottle has reduced thrust to hold the target speed.
Captain reduces thrust further in response to the overspeed indication.
Stick shaker activates while the overspeed warning continues; the autopilot disconnects.
First officer and relief pilot call for thrust and attitude corrections as the crew struggle to understand the contradictory warnings.
Aircraft stalls at about 7,000 ft and begins to roll and descend; full thrust is applied late and the left engine flames out.
Ground proximity warnings sound as the aircraft descends steeply toward the sea in darkness.
Aircraft strikes the Atlantic about 26 km northeast of Puerto Plata; all 189 on board are killed.

recommendations.text: Require that pitot covers be installed whenever an aircraft is parked for an extended period and that preflight procedures verify pitot-static probes are unobstructed.
recommendations.outcome: Operators reinforced pitot cover and inspection procedures.

recommendations.text: Provide clear procedures and training for rejecting takeoff when an airspeed disagreement is detected and for flying with unreliable airspeed using pitch and power.
recommendations.outcome: Unreliable airspeed procedures and training were strengthened across the industry.

recommendations.text: Improve airspeed comparison alerting so that a disagreement between captain's and first officer's airspeed is annunciated directly to the crew.
recommendations.outcome: Later Boeing aircraft and 757/767 updates added airspeed disagree alerts.

safety_changes: Reinforced procedures for pitot covers and pre-flight checks of pitot-static systems after extended parking.
Industry-wide emphasis on unreliable airspeed procedures, pitch-and-power flying and rejecting takeoff on airspeed disagreement.
Airspeed disagree alerting introduced on later Boeing aircraft.

notes: t0 is the airspeed disagreement during the takeoff roll at about 23:42 local; impact was about 23:47. Intermediate offsets are estimates and clocks are omitted.
The Dominican final report id, date and URL are unknown; the source given is the Dominican civil aviation authority site.
The 7,300 ft / 350 knot overspeed figures and the 80 knot remark are widely cited from the report; the stall altitude of about 7,000 ft and the engine flameout are recalled but less certain.
CVR lines are not quoted because exact transcript wording (English translation) is uncertain; they are paraphrased as crew_speech events.
Flight number ALW301 reflects the Alas Nacionales flight designation; some sources cite Birgenair 301.

records.title: ValuJet 592

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: In-Flight Fire and Impact With Terrain, ValuJet Airlines Flight 592, DC-9-32, N904VJ, Everglades, Near Miami, Florida, May 11, 1996

location.name: Everglades, about 17 miles northwest of Miami International Airport, Florida

records.summary: Shortly after takeoff from Miami, a fire broke out in the forward class D cargo compartment of the DC-9, started by unexpended chemical oxygen generators that maintenance contractor SabreTech had boxed without safety caps and mislabelled as empty. The fire spread rapidly, produced smoke and electrical failures in the cockpit, and about ten minutes after takeoff the aircraft dived into the Everglades. All 110 on board died.
records.probable_cause: A fire in the airplane's class D cargo compartment that was initiated by the actuation of one or more oxygen generators being improperly carried as cargo. The fire resulted in a loss of control of the airplane. Contributing were the failure of SabreTech to properly prepare, package, and identify unexpended chemical oxygen generators before presenting them to ValuJet for carriage; the failure of ValuJet to properly oversee its contract maintenance program to ensure compliance with maintenance, maintenance training, and hazardous materials requirements and practices; and the failure of the FAA to require smoke detection and fire suppression systems in class D cargo compartments. Also contributing were the FAA's failure to adequately monitor ValuJet's heavy maintenance programs and its oversight of contractors, the FAA's failure to adequately respond to prior chemical oxygen generator fires, and ValuJet's failure to ensure that its own and contract maintenance employees were aware of its no-carry hazardous materials policy and had received hazardous materials training.

factors.evidence: SabreTech employees removed unexpended oxygen generators from MD-80s, did not install safety caps, and packed them in boxes labelled as empty canisters.
One or more generators actuated in the forward class D cargo compartment, and the intense oxygen-fed fire spread to the boxes, tyres and cabin structure.
The fire burned through the cabin floor and produced smoke and electrical failures in the cockpit within minutes.
ValuJet failed to oversee its contract maintenance program and to ensure employees knew its no-carry hazardous materials policy.
The FAA had not required detection or suppression in class D compartments and had not adequately monitored ValuJet's rapidly expanding operation and contractors.
The class D compartment had no smoke detection, so the crew had no warning until electrical failures and cabin shouts of fire.
The NTSB found the FAA had not adequately responded to prior chemical oxygen generator fires, including a 1986 cargo fire on an American Trans Air DC-10.
SabreTech and ValuJet employees had not received hazardous materials training adequate to recognise the generators as hazardous.
Fire damage and smoke in the cockpit led to loss of control; the aircraft entered a steep descent and struck the Everglades.

events.text: Five boxes containing unexpended chemical oxygen generators, labelled as empty, plus three aircraft tyres are loaded into the forward class D cargo compartment as company material.
Flight 592 takes off from Miami runway 9L bound for Atlanta.
An unidentified sound is recorded on the CVR as the aircraft climbs through about 10,600 ft.
Captain asks what the sound was.
Captain reports an electrical problem as instruments and systems begin to fail.
Captain says they are losing everything and calls for a return to Miami.
First officer requests an immediate return to Miami from Miami Departure control.
Shouts of 'fire, fire, fire' from the passenger cabin are heard on the CVR.
A flight attendant tells the cockpit there is fire in the cabin and smoke is spreading.
Miami Departure turns the flight back toward the airport and clears it to descend; the crew report smoke in the cockpit and cabin.
Controller offers runway 12 and then clears the flight direct to the airport as it descends.
Flight data and cockpit voice recorders stop recording as electrical power and control are lost; radar shows the aircraft in a steep descent.
Aircraft strikes the Everglades in a steep nose-down attitude at high speed; all 110 on board are killed.

recommendations.text: Require smoke detection and fire suppression systems in class D cargo compartments of transport category aircraft.
recommendations.outcome: FAA rule of 1998 eliminated class D compartments on passenger aircraft, requiring detection and suppression by 2001.

recommendations.text: Prohibit the transportation of chemical oxygen generators as cargo on passenger aircraft and improve hazardous materials training and oversight for air carriers and their maintenance contractors.
recommendations.outcome: Oxygen generators were banned as cargo on passenger aircraft; hazmat training requirements were strengthened.

recommendations.text: Strengthen FAA surveillance of air carriers' contract maintenance and repair stations, including hazardous materials handling.

safety_changes: Class D cargo compartments were eliminated; smoke detection and fire suppression required in all cargo compartments of passenger aircraft.
Chemical oxygen generators prohibited as cargo on passenger aircraft; hazardous materials training strengthened for carriers and contractors.
FAA oversight of contract maintenance and of rapidly growing carriers was reorganised; ValuJet was grounded and later merged into AirTran.

notes: CVR clock times for the first 25 seconds after the sound and the 14:13:42 impact time are from the report; the times of the cabin fire shouts, ATC turns and recorder stop are approximate.
Crew speech is paraphrased rather than quoted verbatim.
Recommendation numbers not recalled and are left null.

records.title: Garuda Indonesia 865

agencies.name: Japan Transport Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Investigation Report - Garuda Indonesia Douglas DC-10-30, PK-GIE

records.summary: Garuda Indonesia Flight 865 aborted takeoff from runway 16 at Fukuoka Airport after the number 3 engine failed at speeds nearing V2. The abort occurred after nose rotation, and despite use of brakes, ground spoilers and thrust reversers, the aircraft could not stop within runway boundaries. The aircraft overran the runway 620 meters, striking a ditch, fence and road, resulting in structural damage that caused post-impact fire.
records.probable_cause: Engine failure during takeoff at critical speed, with abort decision at rotation speed. The final report determined pilot error and failure of the airline's maintenance and flight operation sections to properly coordinate maintenance intervals resulted in the accident. The engine turbine blades had been in service for 6,182 cycles when General Electric recommended discarding after 6,000 cycles.

factors.evidence: the failure of the number 3 (right) engine during takeoff (p. 16)
the engine turbine blades had been in service for 6,182 cycles when General Electric recommended discarding the blades after 6,000 cycles
the crew of the McDonnell Douglas DC-10-30 attempted to abort take-off after the failure of the number 3 engine at speeds nearing V2 with rotation of the nose
attempts were made to stop the aircraft on the runway by use of brakes, ground spoilers and thrust reversers, but the crew was unable to stop the aircraft within the boundaries
the aircraft slid through a ditch, a fence and a road before finally coming to rest approximately 620 m beyond the runway threshold (p. 17)
The resultant fire destroyed the areas between the hull fractures, and other areas of the aircraft
The fuselage broke in two places, at about the wing root trailing edge, and at approximately 10.4 m aft of the wing root trailing edge

events.text: Fukuoka Tower cleared GA865 for takeoff from runway 16, wind 280 degrees at 7 knots
Captain commanded First Officer to set autothrottles on
First Officer called V1 at 151.5 knots
First Officer called Rotate at 158.0 knots; nose began rotation
Number 3 engine failure; N1 decreased from 112.8% to 53.3%
Flight Engineer called Engine failure number one (misidentifying the failed engine)
Captain decided to abort takeoff, fearing aircraft would collide with nearby buildings
Thrust reversers deployed; DFDR and CVR stopped recording
Aircraft veered right, ran over jet barrier anchor chain, departed runway onto grass field
Aircraft struck concrete edge of public road 320 meters south of runway; fuselage fractured
Aircraft came to rest 620 meters from runway threshold; fire broke out

recommendations.text: Reinforcement of flight training and proficiency checks for flight crew to allow pilots to make an adequate go/no-go decision in the event of aircraft anomalies such as engine failure during takeoff roll
Thorough implementation of emergency evacuation training for flight crew periodically and joint training with cabin attendants
Improvement of methods of guiding passengers including study of effective measures against fire and smoke

notes: Sections read: flight history (pages 14-18), causes (page 60), safety recommendations (pages 60-61)
Engine maintenance issue identified but technical details not fully explored
CVR transcript not included in accessible report sections

records.title: Delta Air Lines 1288
records.summary: Delta Air Lines Flight 1288 experienced an uncontained catastrophic turbine engine failure of the left engine during takeoff roll at Pensacola on 6 July 1996. A fatigue crack in the front compressor fan hub, which resulted from manufacturing defects and undetected by inspection processes, caused the hub to fracture. Debris from the failure penetrated the left aft fuselage, killing two passengers. The pilot rejected the takeoff and stopped the aircraft safely on the runway.
records.probable_cause: The fracture of the left engine's front compressor fan hub resulted from the failure of Delta Air Lines' fluorescent penetrant inspection process to detect a detectable fatigue crack initiating from an area of altered microstructure that was created during the drilling process by Volvo for Pratt & Whitney and that went undetected at the time of manufacture. Contributing to the accident was the lack of sufficient redundancy in the in-service inspection program.

factors.evidence: uncontained catastrophic turbine engine failure of the left engine occurred during takeoff roll; the front compressor fan hub fractured and ejected high-energy fragments that penetrated the left aft fuselage (p. 194-202)

failure of Delta Air Lines' fluorescent penetrant inspection process to detect a detectable fatigue crack in the fan hub; the crack was large enough to have been detected during the accident hub's last fluorescent penetrant inspection (p. 3399-3402)

manufacturing defect in the front compressor fan hub created during the drilling process; some form of drill breakage or drill breakdown combined with localized loss of coolant created altered microstructure and ladder cracking (p. 3319-3322)

during a 15-minute walkthrough pre-flight inspection, the first officer noted a few drops of oil coming from the bullet of the number one engine and a couple of missing rivets on the left wing, although neither problem was considered dangerous (p. 194-228)

events.text: Flight 1288 cleared for takeoff on runway 17 at Pensacola Regional Airport
During takeoff roll at approximately 40 knots airspeed, uncontained catastrophic engine failure of left engine occurred; loud bang heard followed by loss of cockpit lighting and instrumentation
Debris penetrated left aft fuselage creating large hole; two passengers killed including a female passenger and her son
Captain brought throttles to idle and engaged brakes; aircraft stopped on runway without using reversers or spoilers

cvr.speaker: FO
cvr.text: There's oil coming out of the bullet now

cvr.speaker: SYS
cvr.text: Loud bang heard followed by loss of cockpit lighting and instrumentation

recommendations.text: Form a task force to evaluate the limitations of the blue etch anodize and other postmanufacturing etch processes and develop ways to improve the likelihood that abnormal microstructure will be detected

Inform all manufacturers of titanium rotating engine components of the potential that current boring and honing specifications may not be sufficient to remove potential defects from holes and ask them to reevaluate their manufacturing specifications and procedures
Review the efficacy of drying procedures for aqueously cleaned rotating engine parts being prepared for fluorescent penetrant inspections
Determine whether flash drying alone is a sufficiently reliable method for removing water from cracks
Address the need to ensure the fullest possible coverage of dry developer powder, particularly along hole walls
Address the need for a formal system to track and control development times
Address the need for fixtures that minimize manual handling of the part without visually masking large surfaces of the part

Require the development of methods for inspectors to note on the part or otherwise document during a nondestructive inspection the portions of a critical rotating part that have already been inspected
Conduct research to determine the optimum amount of time an inspector can perform nondestructive testing inspections before human performance decrements can be expected
In conjunction with industry and human factors experts, develop test methods that can evaluate inspector skill in visual search and detection across a representative range of test pieces

safety_changes: Enhanced fluorescent penetrant inspection procedures and standards for detection of manufacturing defects
Improved drilling and honing specifications for titanium rotating engine components
Increased inspection intervals and redundancy in in-service inspection programs for critical rotating parts

notes: Sections read: History of Flight (p. 194-338), Findings (p. 3305-3440), Probable Cause (p. 3445-3452), Recommendations (p. 3457-3500+)
Manufacturing defect originated during drilling process by Volvo for Pratt & Whitney; altered microstructure and ladder cracking created
Fatigue crack initiated from ladder cracking in tierod hole and began propagating immediately after hub put into service in 1990
NTSB investigation thoroughly documented multiple procedural deficiencies in Delta's fluorescent penetrant inspection process

records.title: TWA 800

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: In-flight Breakup Over the Atlantic Ocean, Trans World Airlines Flight 800, Boeing 747-131, N93119, Near East Moriches, New York, July 17, 1996

route.from_name: New York John F. Kennedy International

location.name: Atlantic Ocean about 8 miles south of East Moriches, Long Island, New York

records.summary: About twelve minutes after takeoff from JFK, climbing through about 13,800 feet, the 747's nearly empty center wing fuel tank exploded. The forward fuselage separated, the remainder of the airplane continued briefly before the wings failed and the burning wreckage fell into the Atlantic off Long Island. All 230 people on board died. A four-year investigation, the largest in NTSB history, ruled out a bomb or missile and attributed the explosion to ignition of flammable fuel vapor in the tank, most likely from a short circuit in fuel quantity indication system wiring.
records.probable_cause: An explosion of the center wing fuel tank (CWT), resulting from ignition of the flammable fuel/air mixture in the tank. The source of ignition energy for the explosion could not be determined with certainty, but, of the sources evaluated by the investigation, the most likely was a short circuit outside of the CWT that allowed excessive voltage to enter it through electrical wiring associated with the fuel quantity indication system. Contributing factors to the accident were the design and certification concept that fuel tank explosions could be prevented solely by precluding all ignition sources and the design and certification of the Boeing 747 with heat sources located beneath the CWT with no means to reduce the heat transferred into the CWT or to render the fuel vapor in the tank nonflammable.

factors.evidence: The most likely ignition source was a short circuit outside the tank that allowed excessive voltage into fuel quantity indication system wiring; aging wiring with cracked insulation and sulfide deposits on FQIS components were found in the fleet.
Wreckage and sooting patterns showed the center wing tank ruptured from an internal overpressure explosion of the fuel/air vapor.
Air conditioning packs beneath the center wing tank heated the small quantity of residual fuel during the long ground delay, producing a flammable vapor in the tank.
The design and certification philosophy relied solely on excluding ignition sources and did not require reducing fuel tank flammability.
The explosion severed the fuselage forward of the wing; the forward section fell away and the remaining structure broke up as it descended.
Fuel released from the ruptured wing tanks ignited, producing the fireball seen by witnesses as the wreckage descended.
After the forward fuselage separated the airplane could not be controlled and broke up in flight.

events.text: The airplane sits at the gate at JFK on a hot afternoon with air conditioning packs running beneath the nearly empty center wing tank, heating the small quantity of fuel and creating a flammable vapor.
Flight 800 departs JFK runway 22R about an hour late and climbs out over Long Island.
Captain remarks on an erratic number 4 engine fuel flow indication; the investigation did not link it to the accident.
Boston Center clears the flight to climb and maintain 15,000 feet; the crew acknowledge and set climb thrust.
The center wing tank explodes at about 13,800 feet; the CVR and FDR stop and the transponder return ceases.
The fuselage fails forward of the wing and the nose section separates and falls into the sea.
The remaining airplane, now nose-light, pitches up and climbs briefly before rolling and descending out of control.
The wings and remaining fuselage break up; fuel released from the wing tanks ignites and a fireball is seen by hundreds of witnesses on the shore and in aircraft.
Burning wreckage falls into the Atlantic Ocean about 8 miles south of East Moriches; there are no survivors.
A large search and recovery effort begins; over the following months more than 95 percent of the airplane is recovered from the seabed and reconstructed.

recommendations.text: Require the development of and implementation of design or operational changes that will preclude the operation of transport-category airplanes with explosive fuel-air mixtures in the fuel tanks, such as nitrogen inerting or reduced heat transfer to the center tank.
recommendations.outcome: FAA Fuel Tank Flammability Reduction rule (2008) required flammability reduction means, typically nitrogen inerting, on new and many in-service transport airplanes.

recommendations.text: Require a fleet-wide review of fuel tank systems, including fuel quantity indication system wiring, to identify and eliminate ignition sources, and address aging wiring and separation of FQIS wiring from higher voltage circuits.
recommendations.outcome: SFAR 88 (2001) required design reviews of fuel tank systems and led to numerous airworthiness directives; transient suppression devices were developed for FQIS wiring.

recommendations.text: Revise the transport-category certification standard for fuel tank systems so that flammability, and not only ignition source exclusion, is addressed in design.
recommendations.outcome: 14 CFR 25.981 was amended to require flammability reduction or ignition mitigation.

recommendations.text: Improve inspection, maintenance and replacement standards for aging electrical wiring on transport airplanes.
recommendations.outcome: The Enhanced Airworthiness Program for Airplane Systems (EWIS rules, 2007) established electrical wiring interconnection system requirements.

safety_changes: SFAR 88 (2001) required manufacturers and operators to conduct safety reviews of fuel tank systems, producing dozens of airworthiness directives on wiring, pumps and FQIS components.
14 CFR 25.981 was amended so that fuel tank flammability must be minimized or ignition effects mitigated in new designs.

The 2008 Fuel Tank Flammability Reduction rule required flammability reduction means, typically nitrogen inerting, on new production and most in-service large transport airplanes with heated center tanks.
Enhanced Airworthiness Program for Airplane Systems rules (2007) added electrical wiring interconnection system design, inspection and maintenance requirements for aging aircraft.
The FAA and Boeing developed and fielded onboard nitrogen generation systems for the 737, 747 and 777 families.

notes: Explosion time 20:31:12 EDT and altitude about 13,800 feet are as stated in the report; the sequence of breakup after the explosion is a reconstruction and the t values after 0 are approximate.
Takeoff time about 20:19 EDT; the captain's fuel flow remark is at about 20:29 and is paraphrased rather than quoted.

Recommendation A-96-174 was issued in December 1996 during the investigation; its wording is condensed. Other recommendation ids from the final report are not given because they are not recalled with confidence.
The FBI conducted a parallel criminal investigation and is listed as a participant, not as an investigating agency with a formal aviation role.

records.title: FedEx Flight 1406

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report: In-Flight Fire/Emergency Landing

records.summary: Federal Express Flight 1406, a McDonnell Douglas DC-10 cargo aircraft, experienced an in-flight cargo fire at FL330 over New York on September 5, 1996. The crew detected smoke in the main deck cargo compartment, declared an emergency, and diverted to Stewart International Airport. All five occupants evacuated safely, though the captain and flight engineer sustained minor injuries. The aircraft was destroyed by fire after landing.
records.probable_cause: An in-flight cargo fire of undetermined origin. (p. 77)

factors.evidence: At 0536:23 CVR recorded the captain asking 'what's that' followed by first officer and flight engineer stating 'cabin cargo smoke'; smoke detectors for main deck cargo compartment alerted pilots. (p. 4-5)

A DNA synthesizer containing highly flammable chemicals (tetrahydrofuran and acetonitrile) was aboard the flight, but no fire initiation scenario could be conclusively established; investigation could not determine whether chemicals played any role in fire initiation. (p. 65-66)

Hazardous materials information was not readily available to emergency responders during initial response; incident commander did not receive hazardous materials briefing that was provided to other agencies. (p. 73-74)
Aircraft made emergency landing at Stewart International Airport at 0554 EDT; all five occupants evacuated and aircraft was destroyed by fire. (p. 4, 5)

events.text: Flight 1406 departed Memphis International Airport en route to Boston; normal engine start, taxi, takeoff, and climb reported.
At FL330 (33,000 feet), CVR recorded captain saying 'what's that'; first officer and flight engineer stated 'cabin cargo smoke'.

Smoke detectors for multiple zones of main deck cargo compartment activated; CVR recorded first officer and flight engineer saying 'cabin cargo smoke' again and flight engineer stating 'cabin cargo smoke oxygen masks on'.
Crew donned oxygen masks and established crew communications as required by Fire & Smoke checklist; flight engineer identified 'number nine way' indicating cargo fire location.
ATC suggested emergency landing at either Albany County Airport (50 miles ahead) or Stewart International Airport (25 miles behind); captain chose Stewart.
Crew began descent toward Stewart International Airport; captain initiated emergency procedures while flight engineer continued monitoring fire detectors.
Smoke condition worsened during descent; crew continued to monitor systems while executing emergency procedures.
Aircraft descended to landing approach altitude; crew attempted to mitigate fire damage while preparing for emergency landing at Stewart.
Aircraft successfully landed at Stewart International Airport on Runway 27 and came to stop on taxiway with emergency services responding immediately.

recommendations.text: Require, within 2 years, that a person offering any shipment for air transportation provide written responses, on shipping papers, to inquiries about hazardous characteristics of the shipment.
Require the principal operations inspector for FedEx to review the crew's actions on the accident flight and evaluate those actions in the context of FedEx emergency procedures.
Require FedEx to modify its evacuation checklist and training to emphasize the availability of protective breathing equipment during evacuations.

Require all Part 121 operators of airplanes that rely on air pressure to open exit doors to make crewmembers aware of depressurization requirements before attempting to open passenger exit doors in an emergency.

Require, within 2 years, that air carriers transporting hazardous materials have the means, 24 hours per day, to quickly retrieve and provide consolidated information about hazardous materials on an airplane to emergency responders.

Require the principal operations inspector for FedEx to ensure all FedEx employees who communicate with emergency responders about transportation accidents involving hazardous materials provide information to emergency responders.
Require all certificated airports to develop and implement a hazardous materials response plan for the airport that specifies responsibility of each participating agency.
Reexamine the feasibility of on-board airplane cabin interior fire extinguishing systems for airplanes operating under Part 121 and, if found feasible, require the use of such systems.
Review aircraft cabin interior firefighting policies, tactics, and procedures currently in use and develop improvements in firefighter training and equipment.
Require, within 2 years, that air carriers transporting hazardous materials have the means to quickly retrieve and provide consolidated information about hazardous materials on an airplane.

safety_changes: Enhanced hazardous materials notification procedures for air carriers
Improved emergency response coordination for hazmat incidents at airports
Updated crew training and emergency procedures for in-flight fire response

records.title: Aeroperú 603

agencies.name: Comisión de Investigación de Accidentes de Aviación
agencies.report_title: Informe final del accidente del Boeing 757-23A N52AW, Aeroperú vuelo 603

location.name: Pacific Ocean off Pasamayo, about 30 miles northwest of Lima

records.summary: Before a night departure from Lima, the 757's static ports had been covered with adhesive tape during washing and polishing and the tape was not removed. After takeoff the altimeters and airspeed indicators gave erroneous readings and the crew received a stream of contradictory warnings including wind shear, rudder ratio, mach trim, overspeed and stick shaker. Unable to trust their instruments and relying on ATC altitude readouts that came from the aircraft's own faulty transponder data, the crew flew a slow descending return over the sea until the aircraft struck the water in the dark. All 70 on board died.
records.probable_cause: The Peruvian commission concluded that the accident was caused by the blockage of the static ports by adhesive tape that maintenance personnel had applied during cleaning and polishing of the fuselage and failed to remove, and the failure of maintenance supervision and the flight crew's preflight inspection to detect it. The blocked ports produced erroneous altitude, airspeed and vertical speed indications and a series of contradictory warnings that, together with the dark night over the sea and the absence of reliable altitude information from ATC, prevented the crew from recognising the aircraft's true altitude before it struck the water.

factors.evidence: A worker covered the left-side static ports with protective tape during washing and polishing and did not remove it; supervision and the walk-around did not detect the tape.
The taped static ports fed erroneous static pressure to the captain's instruments and the air data computer.
Airspeed and altitude indications were erroneous from shortly after rotation and became increasingly divergent from the true values.
Overspeed warnings sounded while the stick shaker also activated, presenting the crew with contradictory indications.
Wind shear, rudder ratio, mach trim, overspeed and stick shaker warnings occurred together and were treated as unreliable, including the terrain warnings near the end.
The crew were saturated by continuous warnings while trying to determine which instruments to trust and coordinate a return.
The flight was over the sea at night with no external references to judge altitude.
The crew believed they were at about 9,700 ft, as confirmed by ATC from the aircraft's own erroneous Mode C data, when they were near the sea.
The aircraft struck the water in a controlled descent while the crew believed they had ample altitude.

events.text: During washing and polishing of the fuselage the static ports on the left side are covered with adhesive tape; the tape is not removed when the work is finished.
Preflight walk-around at night does not detect the tape on the static ports.
Flight 603 takes off from Lima for Santiago.
Altimeters and vertical speed indications behave abnormally and the airspeed indications disagree; the crew realise the instruments are unreliable.
Wind shear, rudder ratio and mach/speed trim warnings appear in succession.
Captain declares an emergency to Lima and requests vectors back to the airport, reporting that the instruments are unreliable.
Controller relays altitude and speed readouts from radar; these come from the aircraft's own transponder and air data and are equally erroneous.
Overspeed warning sounds while the stick shaker also activates; the crew cannot reconcile the two.
Crew request that another aircraft be sent to guide them and discuss the impossibility of trusting any instrument; they turn back over the sea toward Lima.
Ground proximity 'too low terrain' warnings sound; the crew consider them false because ATC still reports them at about 9,700 ft.
The left wingtip and engine strike the sea; the aircraft climbs briefly.
Aircraft strikes the Pacific inverted about 30 miles from Lima and breaks up; all 70 on board are killed.

recommendations.text: Require that protective coverings on pitot-static ports be conspicuous, logged and removed under supervision, and that preflight inspections specifically verify the static ports are clear.
recommendations.outcome: Boeing and operators reinforced procedures for covering and inspecting static ports; maintenance logging of port covers became standard.

recommendations.text: Provide flight crews with training and procedures for flight with unreliable airspeed and altitude, including use of pitch and power tables and radio altitude.
Ensure controllers understand that Mode C altitude readouts derive from the aircraft's own air data and cannot confirm altitude when the aircraft's instruments are unreliable.

safety_changes: Boeing and airlines strengthened procedures for covering, tagging and inspecting static ports and pitot probes during maintenance and washing.
Unreliable airspeed and altitude training was expanded, emphasising pitch and power flying and use of the radio altimeter.
Awareness that ATC Mode C altitude is aircraft-derived and cannot verify altitude for an aircraft with air data faults.

notes: The Peruvian final report is not widely available in English; the probable cause is condensed from published summaries and may not match the report wording.
Report id, report date and URL for the CIAA report are unknown and left null; the sources entry is the Peruvian Ministry of Transport site.
t0 is the approximate takeoff time of 00:42 local and impact about 01:11; intermediate offsets are estimates and clocks are omitted.
Crash coordinates are approximate for the sea area off Pasamayo.

records.title: United Express 5925

location.name: Quincy Municipal Airport runway intersection, Illinois

records.summary: United Express Flight 5925 collided with King Air A90 at runway intersection during landing/takeoff. King Air pilots failed to effectively monitor CTAF and scan for traffic. Cherokee pilot's interrupted transmission led United Express crew to misunderstand King Air's intentions. Post-crash fire killed all 14 occupants on both aircraft.
records.probable_cause: The failure of the pilots in the King Air A90 to effectively monitor the common traffic advisory frequency or to properly scan for traffic, resulting in their commencing a takeoff roll when the Beech 1900C was landing on an intersecting runway. Contributing to the cause was the Cherokee pilot's interrupted radio transmission, which led to the Beech 1900C pilots' misunderstanding of the transmission as an indication from the King Air that it would not take off until after flight 5925 had cleared the runway. Contributing to the severity of the accident and loss of life were the lack of adequate aircraft rescue and fire fighting services, and the failure of the air stair door on the Beech 1900C to open. (p. 79)

factors.evidence: King Air pilots failed to effectively monitor common traffic advisory frequency or properly scan for traffic (p. 79)
Cherokee pilot's interrupted radio transmission blocked clear reception and led Beech 1900C pilots to misunderstand message (p. 79)
King Air began takeoff roll when Flight 5925 was landing on intersecting runway at 1700:59 (p. 27)
Fire enveloped both aircraft quickly, lack of adequate ARFF contributed to fatalities (p. 78)

events.text: Flight 5925 departed Chicago O'Hare with 10 passengers plus crew (p. 26)
Made intermediate stop at Burlington, Iowa (p. 26)
Captain at 1652:07 announced on CTAF about 30 miles north, landing runway 13, requested any traffic advise (p. 26)
At 1655:19 King Air announced taxiing out takeoff runway 04. At 1655:40 Cherokee announced back-taxi to runway 04 (p. 26)
Captain at 1655:48 commented both using runway 04, confirmed plan runway 13 (p. 26)
At 1656:56 captain announced on CTAF 10 miles north, left base runway 13 (p. 26)
At 1659:03 King Air announced holding short runway 04, taking runway, heading southeast (p. 26-27)
At 1659:29 captain announced 6 mile final runway 13 (p. 27)
At 1700:16 captain asked if King Air would hold or take off, requested King Air intentions (p. 27)
At 1700:28 Cherokee pilot responded holding runway 04. GPWS gave 200 feet alert interrupting transmission (p. 27)
Flight 5925 touched down on runway 13 at 1700:59. King Air began takeoff roll about 13 seconds earlier (p. 27-28)
Aircraft collided at runway intersection, skidded and caught fire (p. 28)
Rescuers heard signs of life in Beech 1900C but could not open air stair door due to fuselage deformation (p. 28)

recommendations.text: Reiterate to flight instructors the importance of emphasizing careful scanning techniques during pilot training and biennial flight reviews
Evaluate the propensity of the Beech 1900C door/frame system to jam when it sustains minimal permanent door deformation and require appropriate design changes
Establish clear and specific methods for showing compliance with freedom from jamming certification requirements
Consider Quincy accident circumstances when developing methods for showing compliance with freedom from jamming requirements
Review and improve guidance for principal maintenance inspectors to ensure maintenance personnel properly trained
Develop ways to fund airports served by scheduled passenger operations and require ARFF units during commuter flight operations
Add to Safety Information Section of FAA Internet Home Page list of airports with scheduled air service but without aircraft rescue and fire fighting capabilities

All 21 findings from report section 3.1
Probable cause with all contributing factors
7 recommendations extracted
13 new events from detailed CVR and narrative

records.title: 1996 New Hampshire Learjet crash
records.summary: A Learjet 35A repositioning flight departed Bridgeport for Lebanon, NH. During an instrument approach in low visibility and fog, the crew became disoriented and misidentified navigation aids, incorrectly estimating their position. The crew descended below safe altitude and struck terrain approximately 10.3 nautical miles short of the airport.
records.probable_cause: The captain's failure to maintain situational awareness, which resulted in the airplane being outside the confines of the instrument approach; and the crew's misinterpretation of a step-down fix passage, which resulted in an early descent into rising terrain. Factors included the captain's misreading of the instrument approach procedure, the crew's rushed and incomplete instrument approach briefing, their failure to use additional, available navigational aids, and their failure to account for the winds at altitude. (p. 2)

factors.evidence: The captain reported not receiving the localizer when the airplane was actually about 5 nautical miles to the left of it and at BURGR intersection when still 5 nautical miles away from it. (p. 1)
Instrument meteorological conditions with rain, fog, and overcast sky at 1,200 feet agl at the time of approach. (p. 16)
The crew descended the aircraft to 2,300 feet when located 10.3 nautical miles prior to where descent to 2,300 feet was authorized. The aircraft impacted terrain at the 2,300-foot level. (p. 1)
The Learjet impacted trees then terrain while at an altitude of 2,300 feet on rising mountainous terrain near Smarts Mountain. (p. 1)

events.text: Learjet 35A departed Igor I. Sikorsky Memorial Airport, Bridgeport, Connecticut for positioning flight to Lebanon Municipal Airport.
Center controller cleared flight to proceed direct to Lebanon. Aircraft climbed to Flight Level 190 then was stepped down to 7,000 feet.
Captain copied ATIS information and briefed first officer on ILS approach to Lebanon.
Crew instructed to maintain heading 050 degrees magnetic and issued descent clearance from 7,000 feet to 4,700 feet, with direction to proceed direct to BURGR for ILS approach.
Crew configured airplane to flaps eight as last radar contact occurred at 4,900 feet, about 3 nautical miles northeast of Lebanon VOR.
Captain reported to tower unable to receive localizer, stating position 7 nautical miles outside BURGR. Tower reported localizer was in the green.
Captain told first officer to execute missed approach. Radar data showed airplane 2 nautical miles southeast of VOR proceeding southeast at 4,500 feet.
Captain requested VOR RWY 25 approach with circle to land and was cleared to proceed direct to VOR.
Captain told first officer could descend to 2,300 feet after calling out outer marker. First officer noted VOR indications were fluctuating.
First officer stated VOR was fluctuating and said it was all over the place. First officer then stated he was descending airplane to 2,300 feet.

Learjet impacted trees then terrain on rising mountainous terrain near Smarts Mountain at 2,300-foot level, 12.5 nautical miles from Lebanon VOR and 10.3 nautical miles before authorized descent point.

Multiple navigation errors leading to disorientation and early descent

records.title: Comair 3272
records.summary: Comair Flight 3272, an Embraer EMB-120RT with 29 persons aboard (2 crew, 1 flight attendant, 26 passengers), crashed on approach to Detroit on January 9, 1997. The aircraft encountered icing conditions with a thin, rough accretion of ice accumulating on its lifting surfaces. During a left turn to intercept the localizer at 4,000 feet, the aircraft abruptly stalled at 146 knots airspeed with flaps retracted, rolling violently 145 degrees left and right before the crew lost control. The aircraft struck terrain in Raisinville Township in a nose-down attitude. Root causes included inadequate FAA icing certification standards, failure to ensure proper deicing procedures were implemented by Comair, inadequate minimum airspeed guidance for icing conditions, and crew decision to operate near the lower margin of the airspeed envelope with flaps retracted in known icing.
records.probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Board determines that the probable cause of this accident was the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) failure to establish adequate aircraft certification standards for flight in icing conditions, the FAA's failure to ensure that a Centro Tecnico Aeroespacial/FAA-approved procedure for the accident airplane's deice system operation was implemented by U.S.-based air carriers, and the FAA's failure to require the establishment of adequate minimum airspeeds for icing conditions, which led to the loss of control when the airplane accumulated a thin, rough accretion of ice on its lifting surfaces. Contributing to the accident were the flightcrew's decision to operate in icing conditions near the lower margin of the operating airspeed envelope (with flaps retracted) and Comair's failure to establish and adequately disseminate unambiguous minimum airspeed values for flap configurations and for flight in icing conditions.

factors.evidence: Aircraft accumulated thin rough accretion of ice on lifting surfaces in icing conditions during approach with OAT +5C or below and visible moisture (p. 16-20). FDR data and CVR indicated aircraft in known icing conditions with visibility 1 mile in light snow at Detroit ATIS information hotel (p. 16-17).

Crew did not activate deicing boots on wings contrary to manufacturer instructions (p. 17). CVR recorded descent checklist at 1548:12 with first officer responding 'windshield, props, standard seven' but no discussion of deicing boot activation (p. 17). Comair procedures were incorrect based on concern over ice bridging from older aircraft types no longer valid for EMB-120.

Aircraft operating at low airspeed 146-156 knots on approach with flaps retracted (p. 19). Captain stated at 1554:20.8 'Looks like your low speed indicator' and requested increased power; CVR recorded unintelligible comment from first officer at 1554:20.9 (p. 19). FDR data showed bank angle steepening to 23 degrees at 156 knots before roll control became impossible (p. 19).
Crew inadequately trained for icing conditions and stall recovery in EMB-120 aircraft type. Comair flight training program insufficient for icing encounter procedures.
Comair flight manual procedures for icing conditions were inadequate and did not follow manufacturer recommendations for deicing boot activation in known icing (p. 17).

Aircraft abruptly stalled during approach in icing conditions at airspeed 146 knots with flaps retracted (p. 19). CVR recorded sound similar to stickshaker at 1554:24.1; FDR autopilot disconnected and stall sound continued to 1554:25.9 when stickshaker stopped (p. 19).

Aircraft violently rolled 145 degrees left and right after stall; crew lost control and aircraft crashed into rural field at 41°57'48"N 83°33'08"W killing all 29 aboard (p. 19). FDR showed in 2 seconds after autopilot disconnect: control wheel position moved from 18 degrees right to 19 degrees left; roll attitude increased from 45 degrees to 140+ degrees left bank; pitch attitude decreased from 2 degrees nose up to 17+ degrees nose down (p. 19).

events.text: January 9, 1997: Pilots reported for duty at 0940 to begin scheduled 3-day trip sequence
Pilots completed first two flight segments (CVG to Dayton and return) and returned to CVG about 1241; scheduled to change to accident airplane N265CA
Accident airplane N265CA arrived at CVG from Asheville, North Carolina at 1427

Indianapolis ARTCC controller asked pilots if improvements with climb; captain responded 'affirmative, smooth here at two one oh, getting occasional light chop at one nine oh, right at the tops' at 1527:03 (p. 16)
Flight 3272 actually departed gate at 1451 (delayed from scheduled 1430 departure due to late arrival and airframe deicing with Type 1 fluid at 1457) (p. 16)
Flight 3272 became airborne about 1509; first officer was pilot flying, captain was pilot not flying (p. 16)
Pilots instructed to contact Cleveland ARTCC and complied (p. 16)
Captain advised flight attendant flight from CVG to DTW would take 'only forty minutes today' (p. 16)
ATC controller cleared flight to descend to 11,000 feet and fly heading 030 degrees to rejoin MIZAR arrival to Detroit (p. 16-17)
Pilots obtained Detroit ATIS information 'hotel' indicating visibility 1 mile in light snow, braking action advisories in effect, local deice procedure in effect (p. 17)
Cleveland ARTCC controller advised flight 3272 to contact Detroit TRACON (p. 17)
Flight 3272 contacted Detroit TRACON advising at 11,000 feet msl; TRACON responded with vector to ILS runway 3 right final approach course, noting braking action report poor by a DC-9 (p. 17)
Detroit TRACON requested flight 3272 reduce airspeed to 190 knots (p. 17)
Detroit TRACON cleared flight 3272 to descend to 7,000 feet msl; pilots acknowledged airspeed reduction to 190 knots and descent clearance (p. 17)

As aircraft descended through 8,600 feet, first officer called for descent checklist completed at 1548:12 with ice protection response 'windshield, props, standard seven' - no deicing boot activation discussed (p. 17)
Descent checklist completed; first officer began approach briefing interrupted by approach controller instruction to turn right to 070 degrees heading (p. 17)
First officer completed approach/missed approach briefing; captain set approach airspeed bugs 21, 14, 43 knots (p. 17)
Final approach controller cleared flight 3272 to descend to 4,000 feet msl at airspeed 150 knots (p. 17-18)
Final approach controller cleared flight to turn left to heading 090 degrees with remark 'plan a vector across the localizer' (p. 18)
FDR data showed airplane in shallow but steepening left bank at 4,000 feet; autopilot mode changed from 'Altitude Pre Select (Arm)' to 'Altitude Hold' (p. 18)
Captain stated 'Looks like your low speed indicator' observing slow/fast indicator; first officer made unintelligible comment (p. 19)

Airplane at 146 knots airspeed with left bank steepening beyond 45 degrees; autopilot disconnected; CVR recorded stickshaker sound; first officer stated 'thanks'; three chimes and autopilot aural warning sounded (p. 19)

Stickshaker stopped; FDR showed control wheel moved from 18 degrees right to 19 degrees left; roll attitude increased from 45 to 140+ degrees left bank; pitch attitude decreased from 2 degrees nose up to 17+ degrees nose down in less than 2 seconds (p. 19)
GPWS 'bank angle' warning annunciated at 140+ degrees left roll; three chimes and autopilot aural warning followed; roll attitude exceeding 140 degrees and pitch 50 degrees nose down (p. 19)
Aircraft struck ground in steep nose-down attitude in level field rural area 19 nm southwest of DTW at 41°57'48"N 83°33'08"W; postimpact fire ensued; all 29 persons killed (p. 19)

recommendations.text: Issue airworthiness directive requiring EMB-120 operators to activate deicing boots in all known or suspected icing conditions.
Establish minimum airspeed values for EMB-120 in icing conditions and publish in airplane flight manual.
Conduct comprehensive review of ice protection system certification requirements for commuter aircraft.
Require development and certification of ice detection/warning systems on commuter aircraft.

notes: Comprehensive History of Flight with detailed CVR and FDR timing (p. 16-20)
Probable Cause (p. 10) addresses FAA certification deficiencies, inadequate procedures, and crew decision-making
Eight factors identified with specific evidence and page citations from report
Four safety recommendations (A-97-31 through A-97-34) addressing icing procedures, airspeed, ice protection certification, and detection systems
