records.title: 1999 Glasgow Airport Cessna 404 crash

location.name: Blackstoun Farm, approximately 1 nm west of Glasgow Airport

records.summary: Shortly after takeoff from Glasgow, the left engine of a Cessna 404 failed due to catastrophic accessory gear train failure. The commander feathered the right engine instead of the failed engine, resulting in total loss of thrust. Unable to maintain altitude or continue to destination, the commander attempted to return to Glasgow Airport but lost control of the aircraft during a right turn and crashed 1 nautical mile from the airport.
records.probable_cause: The left engine suffered catastrophic failure of its accessory gear train leading to complete loss of power. The propeller of the failed engine was not feathered, and the commander feathered the right propeller instead, resulting in total loss of thrust and uncontrollable descent.

factors.evidence: Left engine suffered catastrophic failure of accessory gear train, with starter gear failing after only 255 operating hours since new (p. 65)
Commander feathered right engine (which was capable of producing power) instead of failed left engine, resulting in total loss of thrust (p. 65)
Aircraft may have been as much as 200 lb above permitted maximum takeoff weight of 8,400 lb (p. 64); copy of load sheet not deposited with handling agent
Commander lost control of aircraft during attempted right turn to return to Glasgow Airport (p. 65)
Severe post-impact fire engulfed cabin (p. 1)

events.text: ATC cleared aircraft for takeoff from Runway 23 at Glasgow Airport
Aircraft lifted off ground at or just beyond intersection of runways; survivors heard a thud or bang shortly after becoming airborne
Witness observed right propeller rotating slowly and then stopping; burning smell reported in cabin (p. 3)
Commander announced emergency and declared intention to return to airfield; neither engine was producing power at impact (p. 65)
Aircraft entered steep right turn attempting to return to Glasgow Airport (p. 3)
Aircraft crashed at Blackstoun Farm approximately 1 nautical mile west of Glasgow Airport; severe post-impact fire engulfed cabin

recommendations.text: Make mandatory the revised Critical Service Bulletin CSB94-4B, which requires a repetitive inspection of GTSIO-520 starter gears and crankshaft gears

Take forward to JAA a proposal to re-examine the criteria for the carriage of flight recorders by multi piston engine aircraft in Transport Category (Passenger) certified to carry more than 9 passengers, with a view to requiring all aircraft to carry at least a Cockpit Voice Recorder

Undertake a study to identify elements of current JAR 23 seat standards which may be used for retrofit into existing aeroplanes with maximum certificated takeoff mass less than 5,700 kg, particularly those operated in Transport Category (Passenger)

safety_changes: Mandatory inspection requirements for GTSIO-520 starter gears implemented
Enhanced flight recorder requirements for multi-engine piston aircraft
Improved seat design standards for light transport aircraft

notes: Read sections: synopsis, history of flight (early activity, ground maneuvers, takeoff), findings and conclusions, causal factors, recommendations

records.title: 1999 South Dakota Learjet crash
records.summary: A Learjet 35 departed Orlando bound for Dallas with two pilots and four passengers. At 13:27 UTC while climbing through 23000 feet, the aircraft lost cabin pressure, incapacitating all six occupants with hypoxia. The aircraft continued climbing on autopilot past assigned altitude, failed to make the required westward turn toward Dallas, and continued northwest for approximately four hours and 1500 miles. At 17:10 UTC the engines wound down at fuel exhaustion, and the aircraft subsequently entered an uncontrolled spiral descent and crashed near Aberdeen in Edmunds County, South Dakota.
records.probable_cause: Loss of cabin pressurization early in the flight incapacitated all occupants through hypoxia. The aircraft had several unresolved maintenance issues related to cabin pressure in the months leading up to the crash (p. 68)

factors.evidence: Early in the flight, the aircraft lost cabin pressure, and all six on board were incapacitated and killed by hypoxia
All six on board were incapacitated and killed by hypoxia, a lack of oxygen in the brain and body
The NTSB report showed that the plane had several instances of maintenance work related to cabin pressure in the months leading up to the crash
The plane ran out of fuel over South Dakota and crashed into a field near Aberdeen
The Lear began a right turn and descent doing multiple rolls in severe descent in a descending spiral

events.text: Learjet 35 N47BA departed Orlando International Airport at 13:19 UTC with 5300 lb of Jet A for four hours and 45 minutes of flight.
At 13:27:13 UTC, the air traffic controller instructed the pilot to climb and maintain flight level 390.
The controller's message went unacknowledged and the next attempt to contact the aircraft at 13:33:33 UTC with the aircraft at 36500 ft was also unanswered.
Aircraft continued climbing on autopilot past assigned altitude, failed to acknowledge controller instructions (p. 45)
Aircraft continued northwestward course for approximately four hours and 1500 miles without making required turn to Dallas (p. 45)
The aircraft failed to make the required westward turn toward Dallas over North Florida and continued on its northwestern course for almost four hours and 1500 miles.
Aircraft remained in cruise flight while all occupants incapacitated by hypoxia (p. 45)
Engines heard winding down on CVR recording, indicating fuel exhaustion at 17:10:41 UTC (p. 65)
At 17:10:41 UTC, the Learjet's engines were heard winding down on the CVR recording, indicating the plane's fuel had been exhausted.
Learjet began right turn and descent with multiple rolls in severe descending spiral at 17:11:26 UTC (p. 65)
At 17:11:26 UTC, the Lear began a right turn and descent doing multiple rolls in severe descent in a descending spiral.

notes: Extracted from NTSB report AAB-00/01
Sections read: History of Flight, Weather, Maintenance History, Probable Cause
6 events with clock times extracted from flight progression
Evidence cites investigation findings and maintenance records
auto-repair: cvr was null; dissent was null; safety_changes was null; related was null; recommendation trigger factors pruned

recommendations.text: Require regular and thorough inspection of cabin pressurization systems on all aircraft to detect and correct defects before they lead to cabin pressure loss
Establish procedures to ensure deferred maintenance items related to pressurization are not left unresolved across multiple maintenance events
Establish and maintain pressurization system trending and analysis programs to identify aircraft with recurring pressurization issues

records.title: EgyptAir 990

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Brief: EgyptAir Flight 990, Boeing 767-366ER, SU-GAP, 60 Miles South of Nantucket, Massachusetts, October 31, 1999

location.name: Atlantic Ocean about 60 miles south of Nantucket, Massachusetts

records.summary: About half an hour after departing New York for Cairo, while the 767 was in cruise at FL330 and the captain had left the cockpit, the relief first officer disconnected the autopilot and applied nose-down elevator, and the aircraft entered a steep dive. The captain returned and pulled back while the relief first officer continued to push; the engines were shut down, the elevators split, and after a partial recovery the aircraft dived again into the Atlantic. All 217 on board died. The NTSB attributed the accident to the relief first officer's control inputs for undetermined reasons; the Egyptian authorities disagreed.
records.probable_cause: The NTSB determined that the probable cause was the airplane's departure from normal cruise flight and subsequent impact with the Atlantic Ocean as a result of the relief first officer's flight control inputs. The reason for the relief first officer's actions was not determined.

factors.evidence: The NTSB found that the nose-down elevator inputs and subsequent engine shutdown were made by the relief first officer while alone in the cockpit and were not the result of any mechanical failure; the reason was not determined.
Sustained nose-down elevator input and throttles to idle drove the aircraft into a dive; the split elevator inputs after the captain returned reflected opposing column forces.
The aircraft exceeded its maximum operating speed during the dive, reaching about Mach 0.99.
After a partial pull-out and climb with the engines shut down, the aircraft entered a second dive and struck the ocean.

events.text: Flight 990 departs JFK for Cairo with a double crew for the long flight.
Aircraft levels in cruise at FL330; the relief first officer takes the right seat earlier than scheduled.
Captain leaves the cockpit, leaving the relief first officer alone at the controls.
Relief first officer quietly says 'I rely on God' (Tawakkalt ala Allah), a phrase he repeats several times over the following seconds.
Autopilot is disconnected.
Elevators move nose-down and the aircraft begins to pitch over into a dive.
Throttle levers are moved from cruise power to idle; the descent steepens and the load factor approaches zero.
Captain re-enters the cockpit asking repeatedly what is happening.
Master warning sounds; airspeed exceeds Mmo and continues to increase toward about Mach 0.99.

Captain pulls back on the control column and calls for the relief first officer to pull with him; the left and right elevators move in opposite directions as one column is pulled and the other pushed.
Both engine start levers are moved to cutoff, shutting down the engines.
Flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder stop as electrical power is lost; the aircraft is passing about 16,000 ft in the pull-out.
Radar shows the aircraft climbing back to about 24,000 ft with the engines shut down.
Aircraft enters a second steep dive; some structure separates before impact.
Aircraft strikes the Atlantic Ocean about 60 miles south of Nantucket; all 217 on board are killed.

recommendations.text: The NTSB issued no new safety recommendations in the accident brief, having found no mechanical failure; earlier recommendations on cockpit voice recorder duration and flight recorder power were referenced.

dissent.position: The Egyptian Civil Aviation Authority rejected the conclusion that the relief first officer deliberately caused the dive and argued that a failure in the elevator power control units (sheared bellcrank rivets and a jammed PCU) could explain the nose-down elevator movement, the elevator split and the sequence of events. The ECAA's comments were appended to the NTSB brief and the ECAA published its own report.

safety_changes: Boeing evaluated 767 elevator PCU failure scenarios during the investigation; the NTSB found no failure mode that could produce the recorded control movements.
Renewed attention to cockpit door and crew presence policies and to psychological screening of pilots, although no formal regulatory change was directly attributed to this accident.

notes: Departure time (about 01:20 EST) and the sequence times from 01:49:45 to 01:50:36 are recalled from the aircraft accident brief to within a few seconds; the second dive, radar climb altitude and 01:52 impact time are approximate.
The peak Mach number of about 0.99 and the in-flight separation of structure during the final descent are from memory of the brief.
The NTSB issued the findings as an Aircraft Accident Brief (AAB-02/01) rather than a full AAR; the record uses the report id given by the task.
The ECAA dissent is recorded as a formal disagreement; the ECAA report and the NTSB's rebuttal are both public.

records.title: Si Fly 325
records.summary: An ATR 42 on a shuttle flight from Rome to Pristina for UN aid workers struck a mountain during approach to Pristina on November 12, 1999. The crew, experiencing fatigue from a high flight roster, failed to execute appropriate approach procedures and descent below minimum altitudes. The faulty GPWS warning system failed to alert the crew. Combined with inadequate air traffic control vectoring, the aircraft failed to clear terrain.
records.probable_cause: Crew teamwork lacking procedural discipline and vigilance during maneuvers in mountainous region with poor visibility. Aircraft kept on track then forgotten by military controller unused to mountainous environment and preventing CFIT risk. Operator's critical dependence on lease contract favoring failure to respect procedures. Opening of aerodrome to civil traffic without advance evaluation of operating conditions.

factors.evidence: Crew experiencing fatigue from high flight roster influencing failure to execute appropriate approach procedure (p. 65).
Crew not following appropriate approach procedure; hastily conducted flight preparation without mentioning safety altitudes (p. 65).
Controller extended flight KSV3275 track and appears to have forgotten it until crew called back (p. 65).
GPWS warning alarm did not sound; system broken down or switched off (p. 65).
Aircraft at 4,600 feet crashed into mountain at 4,650 feet in area where MSA is 6,900 feet (p. 65).
Crew appeared influenced by routine flights to Pristina; did not strictly follow appropriate briefing (p. 65).
Aircraft struck mountain terrain during approach to Pristina killing all 24 aboard (p. 65).

events.text: ATR 42 departs Rome Fiumicino with 3 crew and 21 passengers, mostly UN officials and aid workers
Pristina ATC vectors aircraft to intercept ILS and instructs descent to 5,200 feet then 4,600 feet
Crew changes to visual flight rules; not following appropriate approach procedure during briefing
GPWS warns crew 17 seconds before impact; crew does not react
Aircraft struck mountain terrain at 4,650 feet during approach to Pristina, killing all 24 aboard

recommendations.text: Opening to international civil traffic of an aerodrome not under effective authority of contracting State be subject to complete ICAO audit
Apply JAR OPS regulations in shortest possible time
Exercise reinforced surveillance of companies with recently acquired air transport certificate
Make modifications mandatory which improve operation of essential equipment like GPWS
Where GPWS mode failure occurs, make aircraft takeoff subject to establishing and following alternate procedures

safety_changes: ICAO audit requirements for aerodromes opening to international civil traffic
Enhanced GPWS testing requirements

notes: 1999 BEA French investigation
Sections read: Findings, Probable Cause, and Recommendations
CFIT with complex factors including aerodrome opening without ICAO audit

records.title: Cubana de Aviación 1216
records.summary: Cubana de Aviación Flight 1216, a McDonnell Douglas DC-10-30 operating a charter flight, overran the runway at La Aurora International Airport while landing on a wet runway. The aircraft touched down approximately 1220-1320 meters from the displaced threshold on runway 19, leaving 1450-1550 meters of runway remaining. Despite the available runway, the aircraft failed to stop, ran off the runway end, descended a steep gradient, and crashed into residential houses. The investigation determined the accident resulted from a long landing without a go-around decision, followed by non-optimal deceleration.
records.probable_cause: El accidente es el resultado de un aterrizaje largo sobre una pista mojada, sin decisión de realizar una Aproximación Frustrada (Go Around), seguido de un proceso de desaceleración no óptimo. The accident resulted from a long landing on a wet runway without decision to execute a go-around, followed by a non-optimal deceleration process. Contributing factors included: (1) aircraft airspeed exceeding specified speed due to elevation and temperature, (2) runway gradient requiring higher vertical descent rate during flare, (3) aircraft flotation during flare facilitated by CWS autopilot mode without corrective action, (4) probable tailwind component not accurately reported and not monitored by crew, (5) wet runway surface state, and (6) crew's visual illusion due to lack of prior experience with runway 19 landings in this aircraft type and insufficient information regarding runway gradient variations.

factors.evidence: Aircraft touched down between 1220-1320 meters from the displaced threshold on runway 19, utilizing 455-600 meters before overrunning the 2767-meter available distance (p. 46-47)
Runway 19 was wet at landing; exact friction coefficient not measured. Optimal braking distance calculations assumed wet surface but actual friction may have been lower (p. 38-39)

Main gear touchdown at 15:40:25 UTC with IAS 135 kt, but longitudinal deceleration was not maximum immediately following touchdown. Acceleration remained at -0.03g at touchdown and only reached -0.16g at 15:40:35. No maximum braking was initiated during first 10 seconds after main gear contact (p. 42-43)
CVR analysis shows crew never discussed go-around decision. Crew did not feel necessity to execute go-around during approach or landing (p. 40, 46)

IAS during landing 154-156 kt, which was 5-7 kt higher than manufacturer's specified 149 kt for 177-ton landing weight with 50-degree flaps. This excess speed contributed to increased landing distance (p. 40)

Crew experienced false visual impression of landing position due to runway gradient and inability to see runway end from touchdown point. Captain had minimal prior experience with runway 19 landings in DC-10 (prior A-320 observation was on runway 01). False impression facilitated lack of corrective action during flare (p. 42, 48)

At 15:40:48, aircraft descended below 56 kt IAS but continued decelerating. At 15:40:49, aircraft deviated right from runway centerline 85 meters before runway end. At 15:40:53, vertical acceleration exceeded 1.7g, indicating impact. Aircraft left runway, fell 40+ meters into ravine, and crashed into 8 houses in La Libertad neighborhood (p. 44, 46)

ATC reported 'wind calm' but INSIVUMEH recorded wind from 360 degrees at 8 knots at 15:40 UTC. Discrepancy between reported 'calm' and actual tailwind component not explained. Crew's last wind check was 15:39:40, approximately 40 seconds before touchdown (p. 41-42, 46)

events.text: Flight CU-1216 departed Havana José Martí International Airport bound for La Aurora with 296 passengers and 18 crew members. Aircraft was expected by President of Guatemala and official delegation.

Aircraft maintained FL 350, authorized by CENAMER to descend to FL 200, then to 18,000 feet. Transferred to Guatemala control. ATC reported runway 19 in use, calm wind, altimeter 3024, temperature 15°C, and instructed to maintain 18,000 feet.
At 41 nm distance, authorized descent to 12,000 feet. Directed to hold at Santa intersection at 11,000 feet. Crew received clearance for VOR/DME approach to runway 19.

Transitioned from IFR to visual flight references after passing 11 nm from VOR. Transferred autopilot from CMD mode to CWS mode (approved procedure per aircraft manual). Established stabilized approach using PAPI reference.

Captain requested wind check approximately 40 seconds before touchdown. Co-pilot reported wind calm. At 15:39:42, co-pilot stated wind is calm. At 15:39:46, co-pilot mentioned 'a little more speed', likely referring to wind.
Flight engineer called out '200 feet' at 15:40:14 (while FDR showed actual altitude 106 feet). Aircraft flotation during flare phase continuing without corrective action from captain.

Main gear touched runway 19 at 15:40:25 UTC with IAS 135 kt. Aircraft at 176.2 tons weight with 50-degree flaps and CWS mode engaged. Flare duration approximately 14 seconds. Longitudinal deceleration minimal at -0.03g at touchdown moment.

Flight engineer expressed concern: 'creo que deberíamos frenar' (I think we should brake) at 15:40:45 when speed was 70 kt and deceleration was -0.22 to -0.27g. At 15:40:48, flight engineer urgently shouted 'Frena!' (Brake!) with alarm when speed was 56 kt and deceleration -0.19 to -0.30g.

Aircraft deviated right from runway centerline starting 15:40:49, with tire marks showing deviation beginning 85 meters before runway end. At 15:40:53, vertical acceleration exceeded 1.7g, CVR and FDR ceased recording. Aircraft impacted terrain below runway, descended into ravine, crashed into 8 residential houses in La Libertad neighborhood. 8 crew members and 8 passengers killed on aircraft; 2 people killed on ground.

recommendations.text: Emphasize landing technique training using CWS autopilot mode both ON and OFF in recurrent crew training and competency maintenance programs
Review wind monitoring procedures during approach by flight crews
Improve chartographic information available to crews operating at Category C aerodromes
Analyze whether remaining crew members participating in Category C aerodrome operations should receive specific preparation
Analyze whether minimum aerodrome information should be defined for airline operations at Category C aerodromes
Review VOR/DME runway 19 procedure chart for conformity with PAN/OPS standards
Publish runway profile (showing gradient) in Jeppesen charts
Periodically measure runway friction coefficient and measure after any accident
Conduct study of wind behavior at La Aurora aerodrome and current measurement accuracy to determine if improvements to wind measurement systems are needed
Evaluate need for runway 19 signalization to compensate for inability to see runway end during landing and publish such markings if implemented

notes: Read BEA report sections: Résumé (p2), Reseña del Vuelo (p3-4), Lesiones (p4), Daños (p4), Personal (p5-7), Performance (p14-15), Meteorología (p15-16), Navegación (p17-18), Análisis 2.1-2.5 (p38-45), Conclusiones 3.1-3.2 (p46-48), Recomendaciones 4.1-4.2 (p49-50)
All 8 events contain details not in summary_record with specific UTC times extracted from CVR/FDR data
Factor evidence includes page citations and direct quotes from aircraft maintenance, manufacturer data, and technical analysis
Probable cause fully quoted from official Spanish report section 3.2
All numbered recommendations from sections 4.1 and 4.2 included

records.title: Kenya Airways 431

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses pour la sécurité de l'aviation civile

location.name: Atlantic Ocean, 1.5 nm south of Abidjan Airport

records.summary: Kenya Airways Flight 431, an Airbus A310-304, crashed into the Atlantic Ocean 33 seconds after takeoff from Abidjan on 30 January 2000. A stall warning activated during rotation at low altitude, though the aircraft was not in a true stall. The pilot flying applied only part of the stall recovery procedure by pushing the control column forward, placing the aircraft in an unintended descent. GPWS warnings were masked by priority stall and overspeed warnings, and the absence of visual references over the sea at night prevented the crew from recognizing the low altitude.
records.probable_cause: The accident was caused by the pilot flying applying only part of the stall recovery procedure by pushing forward on the control column to stop the stick shaker following the initiation of a stall warning during rotation, while the airplane was not in a true stall situation. The pilot flying's action put the aircraft into a descent without the crew realizing it. The GPWS warnings that could have alerted the crew to imminent contact with the sea were masked by the priority stall and overspeed warnings. The conditions for a takeoff towards the sea at night provided no external visual references.

factors.evidence: A stall warning sounded just seconds after takeoff when the first officer requested landing gear retraction. The warning did not correspond to a true stall situation. (p. 73-74)

The pilot flying pushed the control column forward immediately after stick shaker activation, applying only part of the recommended stall recovery procedure. The crew did not apply TOGA thrust as specified in the FCOM. (p. 74-75)
The pilot flying put the aircraft into a descent without the crew realizing it, despite radio altimeter callouts from 300 feet down to 10 feet. (p. 74)

The GPWS warnings that could have alerted the crew to imminent contact with the sea were not generated in the cockpit because they were not prioritized compared to the successive stall and overspeed warnings. (p. 74-75)
The conditions for a takeoff performed towards the sea at night provided no external visual references that would have allowed the crew to be aware of the proximity to the sea. (p. 75)
The aircraft descended rapidly and crashed into the Atlantic Ocean, 1.5 nautical miles south of Abidjan Airport. (p. 15)
The aircraft was completely destroyed on impact with the sea. (p. 15)

events.text: Captain applied take-off power and announced 'thrust, SRS, and runway'; V1 and Rotate announced.
Stall warning sounded less than two seconds after 'Positive rate of climb, gear up' announcement.
Automatic call out announced 300 feet.
Copilot asked 'what's the problem?'
Copilot ordered the aural warning to be cut and pushed control column forward to stop the stick shaker.
GPWS sounded the 'Whoop' alarm, followed by automatic call out of 50 feet, but GPWS warning was masked by higher priority stall and overspeed warnings.
Master warning started. Captain ordered 'Go up!' preceded by automatic call out of 10 feet.
Aircraft collided with the sea with slight nose down attitude at speed above VFE, 33 seconds after takeoff.

cvr.speaker: FO
cvr.text: Positive rate of climb, gear up

recommendations.text: Integrate into type rating and recurrent training programs for crews of all aircraft likely to be subject to false stall warnings, the elements necessary to recognize and manage such a false alarm during phases of flight close to the ground.
Ensure that Airbus harmonizes the procedures in the FCOM with those taught during type rating training.
Ensure that appropriate equipment (aerial, maritime, etc.) be put in place to ensure immediate intervention at accident sites near coastal airports.

safety_changes: Airbus revised stall recovery procedures to emphasize minimum altitude loss rather than minimum time recovery

notes: Sections read: SYNOPSIS, Summary, History of Flight, Findings, Causes of the accident, Safety Recommendations
CVR transcript from appendix 7 and crew callouts
FDR data available but detailed parameters not extracted

records.title: Alaska Airlines 261

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Loss of Control and Impact with Pacific Ocean, Alaska Airlines Flight 261, McDonnell Douglas MD-83, N963AS, About 2.7 Miles North of Anacapa Island, California, January 31, 2000

route.from_name: Puerto Vallarta Licenciado Gustavo Díaz Ordaz

location.name: Pacific Ocean about 2.7 miles north of Anacapa Island, California

records.summary: The MD-83's horizontal stabilizer jammed during climb out of Puerto Vallarta and the crew spent much of the cruise troubleshooting with Alaska Airlines maintenance and dispatch. When the crew ran the trim motors the worn threads of the jackscrew acme nut stripped and the stabilizer moved to an extreme nose-down position; the airplane dived from 31,000 feet before the crew regained control at about 24,000 feet. About ten minutes later, while diverting to Los Angeles, the jackscrew's lower stop failed, the stabilizer went beyond its limit and the airplane pitched over, inverted, and struck the Pacific Ocean. All 88 on board died.
records.probable_cause: A loss of airplane pitch control resulting from the in-flight failure of the horizontal stabilizer trim system jackscrew assembly's acme nut threads. The thread failure was caused by excessive wear resulting from Alaska Airlines' insufficient lubrication of the jackscrew assembly. Contributing to the accident were Alaska Airlines' extended lubrication interval and the FAA's approval of that extension, which increased the likelihood that a missed or inadequate lubrication would result in excessive wear of the acme nut threads, and Alaska Airlines' extended end play check interval and the FAA's approval of that extension, which allowed the excessive wear of the acme nut threads to progress to failure without the opportunity for detection. Also contributing to the accident was the absence on the McDonnell Douglas MD-80 of a fail-safe mechanism to prevent the catastrophic effects of total acme nut thread loss.

factors.evidence: The acme nut threads wore away because of insufficient lubrication of the jackscrew assembly; very little grease was found on the recovered jackscrew.
Lubrication tasks were either missed or performed inadequately, and the last end play check recorded a value near the replacement limit without the nut being replaced.
Alaska Airlines' end play check interval had been extended to about 9,550 flight hours, allowing the excessive thread wear to progress to failure undetected.

The FAA approved Alaska Airlines' extensions of both the lubrication interval and the end play check interval without adequate technical justification, and its oversight of the airline's maintenance program was deficient.
Alaska Airlines' maintenance program repeatedly extended maintenance intervals; the report cited weaknesses in the airline's maintenance and quality control.
The stabilizer jammed during the climb and, when the crew later operated the trim motors, moved rapidly nose down as the remaining acme nut threads stripped.
About ten minutes after the first dive the jackscrew's lower mechanical stop and torque tube failed, allowing the stabilizer to move beyond its normal nose-down limit.
The MD-80 jackscrew assembly had no fail-safe mechanism to prevent the catastrophic effects of total acme nut thread loss.
The original certification of the DC-9/MD-80 stabilizer trim system treated the acme nut as structurally reliable without requiring a fail-safe load path.
With the stabilizer at an extreme nose-down position the elevators could not counter the pitching moment; the crew's control column and trim inputs had no effect.
The airplane pitched over, rolled inverted and descended into the ocean.

events.text: During the climb out of Puerto Vallarta the horizontal stabilizer trim stops responding; the autopilot holds pitch with elevator and the crew begin troubleshooting a jammed stabilizer.
The crew discuss the jammed stabilizer with Alaska Airlines dispatch and maintenance control by radio and consider whether to divert to Los Angeles or continue to San Francisco.
Cruising at 31,050 feet the captain, with the autopilot disengaged, operates the primary and alternate trim switches together to try to free the stabilizer.
The remaining acme nut threads strip; the stabilizer moves rapidly to a nose-down position and the airplane pitches over and begins a steep descent.
Both pilots pull on the control columns with well over 100 pounds of force to arrest the dive.
The airplane is recovered to level flight at about 24,000 feet after losing roughly 7,000 feet; the crew declare an emergency to Los Angeles Center and request a divert to Los Angeles.
Captain tells ATC they are stabilized, slowing, and will 'do a little test flight' with slats and flaps to check controllability before landing.
Descending through about 18,000 feet the crew extend slats and flaps 11 to evaluate handling, then retract them when the pitch forces become worse.
The cockpit voice recorder records an extremely loud noise as the jackscrew's lower stop fails; the stabilizer travels past its nose-down limit and the airplane pitches over sharply.
Captain transmits 'mayday' and the crew attempt to regain control, including trying to fly the airplane inverted.
The airplane descends inverted and nearly vertically, pitching and rolling, with no pitch authority available to the crew.
End of recording; the airplane strikes the Pacific Ocean north of Anacapa Island and is destroyed.

recommendations.text: Establish shorter, technically justified lubrication and end play check intervals for the DC-9/MD-80/MD-90 and 717 horizontal stabilizer jackscrew assembly and require a review of maintenance interval extensions that are not supported by data.
recommendations.outcome: FAA airworthiness directives reduced jackscrew lubrication and end play inspection intervals.

recommendations.text: Require that the jackscrew assembly design on MD-80 series airplanes, and on any transport airplane using a similar single-load-path design, be modified to be fail-safe against total acme nut thread loss.
recommendations.outcome: FAA required design reviews of jackscrew trim systems; a fail-safe retrofit was not mandated but nut wear limits and inspections were tightened.

recommendations.text: Improve FAA surveillance of air carrier maintenance programs, including scrutiny of proposed maintenance interval extensions and of the data used to justify them.
Issue guidance that flight crews facing a jammed or unresponsive stabilizer should not continue to operate the trim motors in an attempt to free it and should land at the nearest suitable airport.
recommendations.outcome: Boeing revised MD-80 series jammed stabilizer procedures.

safety_changes: FAA airworthiness directives shortened the MD-80 series jackscrew lubrication interval to about 650 flight hours and reduced the end play check interval, with new inspection and grease requirements.
Alaska Airlines' maintenance program was extensively audited and restructured after the FAA threatened to revoke its maintenance certificate.
The FAA required manufacturers and operators to review transport-category flight control systems for single points of failure lacking fail-safe features.
Boeing revised MD-80 family procedures for a jammed horizontal stabilizer to discourage repeated trim motor operation.

notes: Local date 2000-01-31 is used; in UTC the accident occurred on 2000-02-01.

Clock of the first dive (16:09:16) and of the loud noise on the CVR (16:19:36) are as recalled from the report and may differ by a few seconds; the end of recording is given as about 16:20:57 and may be off by up to a minute.
Times of the stabilizer jam during climb and of the dispatch/maintenance discussions are approximate; those events carry rough negative t values with no clock.
CVR lines are well-known excerpts from the public transcript; their t values between 16:19:36 and the end of recording are estimated, not taken from the transcript.
Altitude at which the first dive was arrested is stated in the report as about 23,000 to 24,000 feet; 24,000 is used.

records.title: 2000 Zion mid-air collision
records.summary: A Moravan Z242L (N5ZA) piloted by a private pilot and a Cessna 172P (N99063) piloted by a student pilot collided in flight approximately 2 miles from Waukegan Regional Airport while both were on approach. The Zlin descended from the northwest while the Cessna was on final approach. The airport controller lost sight of the Cessna and made erroneous sequencing decisions based on time estimates. The Cessna's high-wing configuration blocked the student pilot's view of the Zlin above. Both aircraft crashed with all four occupants fatally injured and five people on the ground injured.
records.probable_cause: The pilot's failure to maintain clearance from the other airplane. Contributing factors were the pilot's poor visual lookout and the airport control tower local controller's failure to provide effective sequencing (p. 2).

factors.evidence: Both pilots failed to see the other aircraft; the Cessna pilot's high-wing blocked her view of the Zlin above (p. 6).
Visibility was 10 miles with hazy weather conditions near Lake Michigan; the controller stated 'weather conditions got hazy near the water' (p. 5).
The local controller lost sight of the Cessna about 1.5 miles northeast of the field and could not see the Zlin (p. 5).
The controller based sequencing on elapsed time estimate rather than visual confirmation (p. 5).
N5ZA struck N99063; N5ZA impacted hospital roof, N99063 crashed on residential street (p. 4).

events.text: Cessna N99063 contacts Waukegan tower reporting 7 miles south, requesting practice touch-and-go operations (p. 4).
Tower clears N99063 for touch-and-go with right-hand traffic pattern (p. 4).
N99063 performs full-stop landing after nine practice touch-and-go operations (p. 4).
Zlin N5ZA makes initial call to tower, reports 15 miles northeast (p. 4).
N99063 requests permission to depart; tower instructs to hold short (p. 4).
Tower instructs N99063 to taxi and hold, then clears for takeoff (p. 4).
Tower asks N5ZA for position; N5ZA reports about a mile or two off the lake (p. 5).
Tower asks if N5ZA straight in; pilot responds yes. Tower clears to land (p. 5).
Tower instructs N99063 on downwind to advise when she sees red low wing aircraft (p. 5).
N5ZA pilot identifies: zulu alpha's the white zlin (p. 5).
N99063 pilot reports negative traffic and asks when to turn base (p. 5).
N5ZA pilot reports just crossing the shoreline (p. 5).
Tower asks N99063 if she sees N5ZA; pilot responds negative (p. 5).
Tower instructs N99063 to start base leg (p. 5).
N5ZA pilot reports negative contact with cessna in front (p. 6).
N5ZA pilot states then we have the traffic in sight (p. 6).
Tower asks N5ZA do you see a cessna in front of you (p. 6).
N5ZA pilot reports N5ZA just had a midair (p. 6).
N5ZA dives and crashes through hospital roof; N99063 spirals down and crashes on residential street (p. 6).

records.title: Emery Worldwide 17
records.summary: An Emery Worldwide Douglas DC-8-71F took off from Sacramento Mather Airport on February 16, 2000. At approximately V1 speed during takeoff, the pitch increased from 0.2 to 5.3 degrees. The crew applied continuous nose-down input during takeoff roll but the nose continued rising from 14.5 to 17.4 degrees. Immediately after lift-off the first officer requested return to Sacramento. The aircraft entered a left turn with decreasing engine speed and stick shaker activated. The captain declared an emergency, the aircraft descended with increasing bank angle. The aircraft crashed into an automobile salvage yard shortly after takeoff.
records.probable_cause: During aircraft rotation, a control rod to the right elevator control tab detached, causing loss of pitch control. An incorrect maintenance procedure by Emery Worldwide introduced improper torque-loading on bolts securing the control rod (p. 83)

factors.evidence: during the aircraft's rotation, a control rod to the right elevator control tab detached, causing a loss of pitch control
an incorrect maintenance procedure was implemented by Emery Worldwide Airlines, introduced incorrect torque-loading on bolts
failure to properly secure and inspect the attachment bolt
aircraft could not recover pitch control after lift-off; captain declared extreme CG problem

records.title: Southwest Airlines Flight 1455
records.summary: Southwest Airlines Flight 1455 overran the runway at Hollywood Burbank Airport. The Boeing 737-300 touched down at 182 knots and collided with a metal blast fence and perimeter wall, coming to rest on a city street. The NTSB found the accident was due to the pilots attempting to land with excessive speed and steep descent angle, failing to abort an unstabilized approach, combined with ATC positioning that left no safe options for a go-around.
records.probable_cause: The flight crew's excessive airspeed and flightpath angle during the approach and landing and its failure to abort the approach when stabilized approach criteria were not met. Contributing to the accident was the controller's positioning of the airplane in such a manner as to leave no safe options for the flight crew other than a go-around maneuver. (p. 20-22)

factors.evidence: Aircraft touched down at 182 knots, which is 44 knots over the reference speed (p. 20). Flight crew did not reduce airspeed to target of 138 knots.

Flightpath angle of 7° during descent was steeper than typical 3° approach. GPWS sink rate and pull up warnings sounded multiple times (p. 20-21). Approach was not in the slot per Southwest procedures.

ATC failed to cancel 230-knot speed assignment when issuing approach clearance at 18:08:19. Controller positioned aircraft too fast, too high, and too close to runway threshold with no safe go-around option (p. 21-22).
Aircraft overran runway 8 at Burbank after 4,150 feet of ground roll, struck blast fence and perimeter wall (p. 4).

events.text: Flight 1455 departed gate at Las Vegas, more than 2 hours behind schedule
Captain states 'plan on [runway] three three at the moment' (p. 2)
ATC advises ATIS information Papa, expects ILS landing on runway 8 (p. 2)
ATC instructs left turn to heading 190° and descend to 6000 feet msl (p. 2)
ATC assigns speed restriction: maintain 230 knots or greater (p. 2)
First officer informs captain target airspeed for approach is 138 knots (p. 2)
ATC clears descent to 5000 feet, advises traffic at one o'clock and 12 miles (p. 3)
ATC clears descent to 3000 feet msl (p. 3)
First officer notifies ATC that Southwest traffic is in sight (p. 3)
ATC issues altitude restriction and clears visual approach runway 8 (p. 3)
Captain begins turning left for final approach through 3,800 feet msl (p. 3)
Captain calls for flaps 5 at indicated airspeed about 220 knots (p. 3)
Captain calls for gear down (p. 3)
GPWS sink rate alert begins continuously broadcasting, switches to pull up warning (p. 4)
Aircraft touches down at approximately 182 knots with flaps at 30 degrees (p. 4)
Aircraft strikes metal blast fence and perimeter wall, comes to rest on city street (p. 4)

recommendations.text: Issue an airworthiness directive to require all operators of Boeing 737-300 through -500 series airplanes to replace the slide cover latch brackets on forward slide compartments with the type installed on Boeing 737-600 through -900 series airplanes.

Issue an airworthiness directive to require initial and periodic inspections of the pivot bracket assemblies on all Trans Aero Industries Model 90835 jumpseats installed on Boeing 737-300 through -500 series airplanes.

records.title: Air France 4590 (Concorde)

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses pour la sécurité de l'aviation civile
agencies.report_title: Accident on 25 July 2000 at La Patte d'Oie in Gonesse (95) to the Concorde registered F-BTSC operated by Air France

location.name: Hotel at La Patte d'Oie, Gonesse, 9.5 km from Paris CDG

records.summary: During the takeoff roll on runway 26R at Charles de Gaulle, Concorde F-BTSC ran over a titanium alloy strip that had fallen from a Continental Airlines DC-10 minutes earlier. The strip cut the right front tyre of the left main gear, which burst; a large piece of tyre struck the underside of the wing, causing a shock wave that ruptured fuel tank 5. Leaking fuel ignited, engines 1 and 2 lost thrust, the gear could not be retracted, and the aircraft, unable to climb or accelerate, lost control and crashed onto a hotel in Gonesse. All 109 on board and 4 on the ground died.
records.probable_cause: The accident was due to: the high-speed passage of a tyre over a part lost by an aircraft that had taken off five minutes earlier and the destruction of the tyre; the ripping out of a large piece of tank 5 from the underside of the wing through a complex process of transmission of the energy from the tyre debris; ignition of the leaking fuel by an electric arc in the landing gear bay or by contact with hot parts of the engine, and the propagation of the fire; the impossibility of retracting the landing gear, which probably contributed to the loss of thrust on engine 1 and the loss of control. Contributing: the strip had been installed on the DC-10 in a non-conforming manner, and previous tyre-burst incidents on Concorde had not led to protective measures against tank rupture.

factors.evidence: The titanium wear strip on the Continental DC-10 thrust reverser cowl had been manufactured and fitted in a non-conforming manner and detached on takeoff, leaving it on runway 26R.
Concorde had suffered numerous tyre bursts and several tank penetrations since 1979 without measures adequate to prevent fuel tank rupture.
The wing fuel tanks were vulnerable to rupture from tyre debris impacts and the tyres were prone to catastrophic destruction on foreign object damage.
Certification did not address the risk of tank rupture from tyre debris at the energy levels shown to be possible.
Tank 5 was ruptured from within by a pressure wave and fuel escaped at a very high rate under the left wing.
The fuel ignited, producing a very large flame trailing from the left wing and damaging the airframe and controls.
Engine 2 surged and lost thrust and was shut down; engine 1 also lost thrust twice, the second time irrecoverably.
The landing gear could not be retracted, probably because of fire damage to gear bay wiring, preventing acceleration and climb.
With two engines lost, the gear down and the aircraft below V2, it could neither accelerate nor climb above about 200 ft.
The aircraft pitched up and rolled left beyond 100 degrees, and struck the ground at low speed and high angle of attack.
The aircraft was destroyed by impact and fire on striking a hotel in Gonesse, killing four people on the ground.

events.text: A Continental Airlines DC-10 takes off from runway 26R; a 43 cm titanium wear strip from its number 3 engine thrust reverser cowl falls onto the runway.
Concorde begins its takeoff roll on runway 26R, about a tonne over the maximum takeoff weight with a light tailwind.
At about 175 kt, after V1, the number 2 tyre on the left main gear runs over the metal strip and bursts; tyre debris strikes the wing and tank 5 ruptures.
Leaking fuel ignites; a large flame trails from under the left wing. Engines 1 and 2 surge and lose thrust.
Tower controller informs the crew that they have strong flames behind them.
Engine 2 fire alarm sounds; the captain rotates and the aircraft lifts off at about 205 kt with engine 1 recovering thrust.
Flight engineer shuts down engine 2 and pulls the fire handle; the crew call for gear retraction.
The landing gear does not retract despite the selection; the aircraft climbs slowly to about 200 ft at about 200 kt.
Crew declare an emergency and attempt to reach Le Bourget; the aircraft cannot accelerate or climb.
Engine 1 loses thrust a second time; with only engines 3 and 4 on the right the aircraft pitches up and rolls steeply left.
Aircraft strikes the Hotelissimo hotel at La Patte d'Oie, Gonesse, in a nose-high left-banked attitude; all 109 occupants and 4 people on the ground killed.

recommendations.text: Suspend the Concorde certificate of airworthiness until measures are taken to guarantee a satisfactory level of safety with respect to tyre destruction and its consequences on the fuel tanks.
recommendations.outcome: Certificates suspended in August 2000; Kevlar tank liners, new Michelin NZG tyres and armoured wiring were introduced before return to service in November 2001.

recommendations.text: Strengthen the requirements and inspection of runways for foreign object debris, and ensure that repairs on aircraft parts liable to fall on runways conform to approved data.
Study tyre-destruction models and the effects of tyre debris on aircraft structures and fuel tanks for certification of large aircraft.

safety_changes: Kevlar-rubber liners in Concorde fuel tanks, Michelin NZG near-zero-growth tyres, armoured gear bay wiring; return to service in November 2001.
Increased runway FOD inspection frequency at Paris airports and broader FOD awareness programmes.
Concorde withdrawn from service by both operators in 2003.

notes: Continental Airlines and its mechanics were prosecuted and Continental disputed the findings in court, but no accredited agency formally dissented; dissent is empty.
Clock times are UTC as used in the BEA report; intermediate event seconds are approximate (tyre burst about 14:43:13, impact about 14:44:31).
Occupants counts the 109 on board; fatalities of 113 include 4 persons on the ground.
Some speeds (175 kt at tyre burst, lift-off about 205 kt) are approximate values from the report.

records.title: Oklahoma State University men's basketball team plane crash

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report--In-Flight Electrical System Failure and Loss of Control, Jet Express Services, Raytheon (Beechcraft) Super King Air 200, N81PF, Near Strasburg, Colorado, January 27, 2001

records.summary: A Raytheon (Beechcraft) Super King Air 200 transporting Oklahoma State University basketball team members crashed near Strasburg, Colorado on January 27, 2001 during descent in instrument meteorological conditions. The pilot lost AC electrical power and most cockpit instruments, became spatially disoriented, and lost control of the aircraft in a graveyard spiral. All ten occupants were killed.
records.probable_cause: The pilot's spatial disorientation resulting from his failure to maintain positive manual control of the airplane with the available flight instrumentation. Contributing to the cause of the accident was the loss of AC electrical power during instrument meteorological conditions.

factors.evidence: The pilot became spatially disoriented without reliable flight instruments and visual references. The airplane's estimated flightpath was consistent with a graveyard spiral resulting from pilot spatial disorientation (p. 37)

The airplane completed a 360-degree graveyard spiral turn as the pilot lost control. The pilot attempted to arrest the descent but could not recover from a steep descent rate exceeding 15,000 feet per minute (p. 37)

Loss of AC electrical power during instrument meteorological conditions disabled most pilot-side instruments including the altimeter, attitude indicator, horizontal situation indicator, and radio altimeter (p. 36)
Weather reports indicated clouds at 200 to 400 feet with moderate rime icing to mixed icing in precipitation (p. 36)
Crash occurred at 1737 MST, after official sunset at 1716. Sun was 4.7 degrees below horizon; moon was 36 degrees above horizon with 16 percent illumination (p. 13)
The second pilot had no formal King Air type training, making him unfamiliar with the airplane's systems and emergency procedures (p. 36)

events.text: Aircraft pulled from hangar and passengers loaded at Jefferson County Airport.
Pilot contacted ground control for taxi instructions; received ATIS information Romeo.
Aircraft cleared for takeoff from runway 29R at 1717:49. Pilot instructed to turn right to 040-degree heading.
Pilot reported climbing through 6,500 feet to 8,000 feet. Cleared to climb to 12,000 feet and fly 060-degree heading.
Departure controller instructed pilot to proceed to EPKEE intersection, join Garden City transition, and climb to 23,000 feet.
Pilot contacted Satellite Radar Two controller, reporting out of 16,300 feet and climbing to 23,000 feet.
Controller cleared aircraft to proceed directly to EPKEE intersection. Pilot acknowledged with requirement for 3-degree left turn.
Aircraft reached cruising altitude of 23,000 feet. Climb profile normal with steady airspeeds.
Last Mode C transponder return at altitude 23,200 feet. Radar data indicated normal profile.
Aircraft began to deviate from assigned heading and turn right. Mode C information lost.
Mode A transponder information lost. AC electrical power failure disabled most pilot-side instruments.
Pilot became spatially disoriented without reliable flight instruments and visual references in instrument meteorological conditions.
Aircraft entered graveyard spiral descent. Airplane's flightpath consistent with 360-degree spiral resulting from spatial disorientation.
Pilot attempted forcefully to arrest the descent in final portion of flight, possibly in response to obtaining visual references after emerging from clouds.
Aircraft impacted rolling terrain at 5,223 feet elevation near Strasburg, Colorado. In-flight breakup occurred due to aerodynamic loading during pull-up maneuver. All ten occupants killed.

recommendations.text: Review Oklahoma State University's postaccident team travel policy and develop, either independently or jointly, a model policy for member institutions to use in creating a travel policy or strengthening an existing travel policy.

records.title: Air Caraïbes 1501

agencies.name: Bureau of Enquiry and Analysis for Civil Aviation Safety
agencies.report_title: Accident on 24 March 2001 at Saint-Barthélemy to the DHC-6-300 registered F-OGES

aircraft.type: de Havilland Canada DHC-6-300 Twin Otter

records.operator: Caraïbes Air Transport (on behalf of Air Caraïbes)
records.summary: De Havilland DHC-6-300 Twin Otter Flight 1501 crashed on approach to Saint-Barthélemy on March 24, 2001. The aircraft suddenly banked steeply to the left and dove toward the ground during final approach, impacting a house. All 19 occupants and one person on the ground were killed.
records.probable_cause: The accident resulted from the Captain's use of the propellers in the reverse beta range to improve control of track on short final. A strong thrust asymmetry upon coming out of reverse beta range caused loss of yaw control, then roll control. Contributing factors were the Captain's lack of recent experience on the aircraft type, difficulty of the Saint-Barthélemy approach, time pressure during the flight, and the low altitude at which loss of control occurred.

factors.evidence: Captain moved propellers into reverse beta range during final approach to improve track control (p. 51)
Captain lacked recent experience on DHC-6, having primarily flown Dornier 228 in preceding three months; only 10 DHC-6 hours in previous 90 days (p. 50)
Approach to runway 10 at Saint-Barthélemy requires flying over La Tourmente pass at very low height with orographic turbulence; difficult procedure requiring great vigilance (p. 50)
Aircraft suddenly banked steeply to the left with increasingly steep bank angle, then dove toward ground (p. 50)
Aircraft crashed with steep nose-down attitude, destroyed on impact, and caught fire (p. 50-51)

events.text: Flight 1501 departed Princess Juliana International Airport at 16:00 UTC for Saint-Barthélemy, 19 nautical miles away, under VFR.
Aircraft cruised at about 1,500 feet. Crew left Saint-Martin Juliana frequency and announced passing Fourchue reporting point entry to Saint-Barthélemy circuit.
Crew announced passing Pain de Sucre reporting point for final approach to runway 10. Last communication received.
On short final before La Tourmente pass, captain moved propellers into reverse beta range to improve track control.
Aircraft suddenly banked steeply to the left with progressively steeper bank angle and began diving toward ground, accompanied by loud engine noise.
Aircraft crashed into house with steep nose-down attitude near Saint-Barthélemy. Massive explosion followed. All 19 occupants killed; one person in house died in fire.

recommendations.text: Make mandatory the installation of at least one flight recorder on board public transport aircraft authorized to carry more than nine passengers with maximum certified take-off weight less than or equal to 5,700 kg
Encourage operators to equip themselves with tools necessary to ensure rigorous follow-up of pilots' aviation activity regarding recency requirements
Improve wording of paragraph OPS 1.970 regarding recent experience requirements and take into account holding of site ratings
Put in place necessary means to ensure recordings of allocated radio frequencies at Saint-Barthélemy without notable interruptions
Install a wind-sock on southern part of La Tourmente pass to provide wind information for approach pilots
Determine resources required for retrospective checks on medical records by CMAC and ensure they are in place

notes: Sections read: Synopsis (pages 7-8), History of Flight (pages 9-10), Findings (pages 50-51), Probable Causes (pages 51-52), Safety Recommendations (pages 52-54)
