records.title: Pinnacle Airlines 3701

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Crash of Pinnacle Airlines Flight 3701, Bombardier CL-600-2B19, N8396A, Jefferson City, Missouri, October 14, 2004

location.name: Residential area about 2.5 miles south of Jefferson City Memorial Airport, Missouri

records.summary: On a night repositioning flight with no passengers, the two pilots flew the CRJ-200 in an unprofessional manner, including a pitch-up manoeuvre and a climb to the aircraft's 41,000 ft ceiling at a low airspeed. The aircraft stalled at FL410, both engines flamed out during the upset, and the engine cores subsequently seized (core lock). The crew did not restore power or reach an airport and the aircraft crashed in a residential area near Jefferson City, killing both pilots.
records.probable_cause: The NTSB determined the probable cause was (1) the pilots' unprofessional behavior, deviation from standard operating procedures, and poor airmanship, which resulted in an in-flight emergency from which they were unable to recover, in part because of the pilots' inadequate training; (2) the pilots' failure to prepare for an emergency landing in a timely manner, including communicating with air traffic controllers immediately after the emergency about the loss of both engines and the availability of landing sites; and (3) the pilots' improper management of the double engine failure checklist, which allowed the engine cores to stop rotating and resulted in the core lock engine condition. Contributing were the core lock engine condition, which prevented at least one engine from being restarted, and the airplane flight manuals that did not communicate to pilots the importance of maintaining a minimum airspeed to keep the engine cores rotating.

factors.evidence: The pilots performed a pitch-up manoeuvre, exchanged seats in flight and climbed to FL410 at a low airspeed in vertical speed mode contrary to standard operating procedures.
The crew allowed airspeed to decay during the climb and at FL410 without recognising the approaching stall.
The stick shaker and then the stick pusher activated at FL410 as the aircraft approached and entered the stall.
The aircraft stalled at FL410 and the resulting upset disrupted airflow to both engines.
The pilots pulled against the stick pusher rather than reducing pitch attitude to recover.
Both engines flamed out during the stall and neither could be restarted; the aircraft crashed after a power-off glide.
The NTSB cited the pilots' inadequate training in high-altitude aerodynamics and stall recovery as part of the probable cause.
The crew initially told ATC only one engine had failed and did not promptly communicate the double engine failure or prepare for a forced landing.
The airplane flight manuals did not communicate the importance of maintaining a minimum airspeed to keep the engine cores rotating after a flameout.
The double engine failure checklist did not adequately guide pilots to maintain windmilling airspeed before attempting restarts.
The forced landing attempt was made at night with no power in a residential area.

events.text: Repositioning flight departs Little Rock for Minneapolis with only the two pilots on board.
Shortly after takeoff the crew performs an abrupt pitch-up manoeuvre reaching about 1.8 g.
The pilots exchange seats during the climb.
Crew decides to climb to FL410, the aircraft's maximum certificated altitude ('forty-one it'), and request the level from ATC.
Climb continued in autopilot vertical speed mode at about 500 ft/min; airspeed decays progressively as the aircraft approaches FL410.
Aircraft levels at FL410 at a low airspeed; the autopilot holds altitude while the airspeed continues to decrease.
Stick shaker activates; the autopilot disconnects.
Stick pusher activates repeatedly; the pilots pull back against the pusher and the aircraft stalls.
Both engines flame out during the upset; the aircraft is now without engine power.
Crew declares an emergency to ATC but reports the loss of only one engine.
Crew attempts windmill restarts but keeps the airspeed well below the 300 kt required by the checklist, so the engine cores do not spin up.
APU started at lower altitude; APU-assisted restart attempts fail as the engine cores have seized (core lock).
Crew finally informs ATC that both engines have failed; ATC provides vectors toward Jefferson City Memorial Airport.
Controller gives distance and heading to the airport; the crew reports they will not make the runway.
Crew remarks they are going to hit houses as the aircraft descends in darkness toward a residential area.
Aircraft strikes trees and the ground in a residential area about 2.5 miles south of the airport; both pilots are killed, no one on the ground is injured.

recommendations.text: Require CRJ operators and the manufacturer to revise flight manuals and checklists to state the minimum airspeed needed to keep engine cores rotating after a double engine failure and to address the core lock condition.
Require air carriers to provide training in high-altitude aerodynamics, stall recognition and stall recovery at high altitude, including the correct response to stick pusher activation.
Address unprofessional behaviour and non-adherence to standard operating procedures on non-revenue repositioning flights through operator oversight and pilot professionalism programs.

safety_changes: Bombardier revised CRJ flight manuals and the double engine failure checklist to emphasise maintaining airspeed to keep the engine cores rotating and to describe core lock.
Airlines added high-altitude aerodynamics and stall recovery training, and the accident became a standard case study in pilot professionalism.

notes: t0 is set to the approximate time of stick shaker activation at FL410 (about 21:54 CDT); event times other than takeoff (21:21), flameout (about 21:55) and impact (about 22:15) are approximations to the nearest few minutes.
Flight number, MSN and coordinates are approximate; coordinates mark the general crash area south of Jefferson City.
Recommendation numbers were not recalled with confidence and are left null.
No CVR quotations included; the widely reported 'forty-one it' remark is paraphrased as a crew_speech event.

records.title: MK Airlines 1602

agencies.name: Transportation Safety Board of Canada
agencies.report_title: Reduced Power at Take-off and Collision with Terrain

location.name: Halifax Stanfield International Airport, Nova Scotia

records.summary: MK Airlines Flight 1602, a Boeing 747-244SF operating a cargo flight from Halifax to Zaragoza, took off from Runway 24 on October 14, 2004 at 0654 UTC. Due to incorrect takeoff weight data (240,000 kg from a previous flight at Bradley instead of 353,000 kg), the crew calculated wrong V speeds and thrust settings. During takeoff, the aircraft experienced tailstrikes at 8,000 feet and again at 420 feet remaining. The aircraft became airborne but struck an earthen berm 300 m beyond the runway and broke apart in flames.
records.probable_cause: The aircraft overshot the end of the runway and struck an earthen berm due to inadequate takeoff performance caused by incorrect takeoff performance calculations. The crew calculated takeoff performance data using the Bradley weight rather than the actual Halifax takeoff weight, resulting in incorrect V speeds and insufficient thrust. Contributing factors included crew fatigue from duty time violations and inadequate training on the Boeing Laptop Tool.

factors.evidence: The Bradley takeoff weight (240,000 kg) was likely used to generate the Halifax takeoff performance data instead of the correct weight (353,000 kg), resulting in incorrect V speeds and thrust setting (p. 65)
The company did not have a formal training and testing program on the Boeing Laptop Tool, and it is likely the user was not fully conversant with the software (p. 66)

Crew fatigue likely increased the probability of error during calculation of takeoff performance data and degraded the flight crew's ability to detect this error; there were no regulations or company rules governing maximum duty periods for loadmasters and ground engineers (p. 65-67)
The aircraft began to rotate and tailstrike occurred at the 8000 ft mark, and a second tailstrike took place with 420 ft of runway remaining (p. 2)
The aircraft's lower aft fuselage struck an earthen berm supporting an instrument landing system (ILS) localizer antenna 300 m beyond the end of the runway (p. 2)
The aircraft broke into pieces and burst into flames when it struck the ground (p. 2)

events.text: MK Airlines Flight 1602 (Boeing 747-244SF 9G-MKJ) taxi to Runway 24 at Halifax International Airport for cargo flight to Zaragoza, Spain
Takeoff roll commenced on Runway 24
Aircraft reached 130 knots; control column moved aft to 8.4 degrees to initiate rotation
Aircraft began rotation; first tailstrike occurred at 8,000 feet down the runway
Second tailstrike occurred with 420 feet of runway remaining; aircraft in ground effect with inadequate climb performance
Aircraft became airborne approximately 670 feet beyond the paved runway surface, 825 feet from runway end
Aircraft lower aft fuselage struck earthen berm 300 meters beyond runway end; tail section broke away from fuselage
Aircraft continued flight for another 1,200 feet while uncontrollable with separated tail; broke into pieces
Aircraft struck terrain and burst into severe post-crash fire; all seven crew members killed

recommendations.text: Examine the adequacy of cargo handling procedures and load weight verification
Implement procedures to ensure independent verification of takeoff performance calculations

safety_changes: Enhanced cargo weight verification procedures implemented by Canadian operators
Improved training requirements for takeoff performance calculation software

notes: Synopsis (p. 1), Findings as to Causes and Contributing Factors (pp. 65-67), Conclusions sections read
TSB report format uses 'Safety Action' rather than traditional 'Recommendations'
Clear causal chain: incorrect weight -> wrong V speeds -> inadequate performance -> tailstrike -> overrun -> impact fire

records.title: Corporate Airlines 5966
records.summary: Corporate Airlines Flight 5966, a British Aerospace Jetstream 32 twin-engine turboprop with 15 aboard (2 crew, 13 passengers), crashed on approach to Kirksville Regional Airport near Pettis Township, Missouri on October 19, 2004. Captain Kim Sasse and First Officer Jonathan Palmer conducted a non-precision instrument approach at night in instrument meteorological conditions. The pilots descended below minimum descent altitude into a region without guaranteed obstacle clearance, struck trees, and crashed. Both pilots and 11 of 13 passengers were killed. The NTSB determined that the pilots' failure to follow established procedures for non-precision instrument approaches, specifically their descent below MDA before required visual cues, combined with crew fatigue from a 14-hour duty day, inadequate monitoring by the first officer, and breakdown in crew resource management were the probable causes.
records.probable_cause: Pilots' failure to follow established procedures and properly conduct non-precision instrument approach at night in IMC, specifically their descent below minimum descent altitude before required visual cues were available, and their failure to maintain established division of duties between flying and monitoring pilots. Contributing factors: crew fatigue from 14-hour duty day and failure to make standard callouts.

factors.evidence: Pilots descended below minimum descent altitude before required visual cues were available, continuing unmoderated until aircraft struck trees during approach in IMC.
Both pilots were looking outside cockpit for visual cues rather than monitoring instruments; first officer did not challenge captain to maintain instrument scan.
First officer failed to challenge captain and maintain professional monitoring duties; failure to establish professional demeanor during flight.
Pilots had worked 14-hour duty day including six flights, degrading performance despite regulations last updated in 1964.
Pilots failed to follow established procedures and make standard callouts during non-precision approach.
Night instrument meteorological conditions with no visual references to airport or terrain.
Aircraft struck trees during descent on approach and crashed near Kirksville.

events.text: October 19, 2004: Flight 5966 operated by Corporate Airlines (RegionsAir) departed St. Louis Lambert on evening for Kirksville; crew had completed six flights on 14-hour duty day
Aircraft cleared for non-precision instrument approach to Kirksville in night IMC conditions
Captain Sasse began looking outside cockpit for visual cues to runway location
Captain continued descent below MDA; first officer did not challenge or call attention to descent rate or failed instrument scan
Aircraft struck trees and crashed during continued unmoderated descent below minimum descent altitude near Kirksville Regional Airport; 13 of 15 persons killed

notes: Report focused on cockpit voice recorder analysis showing crew procedures and communication breakdown
Probable cause clear: descent below MDA combined with fatigue and CRM breakdown
Summary record contained detailed CRM analysis and fatigue contribution
Depth set to 'sections' due to focus on CVR analysis rather than detailed technical investigation

records.title: 2004 Hendrick Motorsports aircraft crash
records.summary: A Beechcraft King Air conducting an instrument approach in low-level overcast at Blue Ridge Airport failed to properly descend through the approach procedure. The aircraft overflew the airport by 4 nautical miles before reaching the minimum descent altitude of 1400 feet, then initiated a missed approach. The aircraft crashed into Bull Mountain during the attempted climb-out, killing all ten occupants.
records.probable_cause: The pilots failed to execute the instrument approach procedure and failed to use all navigational aids to confirm the airplane's position during approach. The aircraft overflew the airport by 4 nautical miles before reaching the minimum descent altitude, then initiated a missed approach that resulted in controlled flight into terrain (p. 6)

factors.evidence: Aircraft failed to descend to assigned 2600-foot altitude immediately upon ATC clearance for approach; did not begin descending until 4nm past BALES LOM (p. 2)
Pilots failed to use all navigational aids including GPS with current database to confirm position; GPS database not current for IFR use (p. 3)
Instrument meteorological conditions prevailed with 400-600 foot ceiling and 1.25-5 mile visibility; state trooper stated visibility 0-0.25 mile at mountain (p. 4)
Aircraft reached MDA of 1400 feet only after overflying airport by 4 nautical miles; flew level at 1400-1500 feet for 1:13 before initiating climb (p. 2-3)
Aircraft crashed into Bull Mountain peak during missed approach climb - initial impact in trees with wreckage found at elevation 2450 feet (p. 3, 5)

events.text: Beechcraft King Air 200 N501RH departed Concord Regional Airport (p. 1)
Flight established in holding pattern over BALES LOM at 4000 feet, second in line for runway 30 approach (p. 1)
ATC cleared airplane for localizer runway 30 approach (p. 2)
Flight crew advised controller airplane was established inbound on approach (p. 2)
Controller cleared airplane for approach and approved frequency change to CTAF (p. 2)
Airplane began descent from 4000 feet at 4 DME (2nm after BALES LOM) (p. 2)

Radar target lost at 1233:24 as airplane crashed into Bull Mountain in Stuart, Virginia at elevation 2400 feet (p. 3)

records.title: 2005 Royal Air Force Hercules shootdown
records.summary: RAF Hercules XV179 was shot down by Sunni insurgents in Iraq six minutes after departure from Baghdad. All 10 personnel perished. The Board of Inquiry identified the lack of a fire-suppressant system as a contributory factor, and the right wing was found separated from the fuselage.
records.probable_cause: Aircraft became uncontrollable after hostile ground-to-air fire caused explosive separation of the outboard right-hand wing. The lack of a fuel tank inerting system in the wing fuel tanks left the aircraft vulnerable to explosive fuel/air mixture development (p. 2-3)

factors.evidence: Aircraft shot down by hostile ground-to-air fire causing explosive wing separation (p. 2-3)
Distress message from crew at 1330Z indicated "We are on fire, we are on fire" after hostile fire impact (p. 2-3)
Right wing outboard section separated explosively from fuselage due to hostile ground-to-air fire impact (p. 2)
All 10 personnel on board were killed - crash was not survivable (p. 2-3)

events.text: RAF Hercules XV179 took off from Baghdad at 1324Z en route to Balad at low level
Aircraft heading north at low level, utilizing low-level flying tactic to mitigate risk from hostile ground-to-air threats (p. 3)
Royal Signals signaller reported fire on board: "No duff, no duff, We are on fire, we are on fire" (p. 2)
Distress message received at 1330Z from crew indicating aircraft on fire (p. 3)
Aircraft confirmed missing at 1355Z (p. 3)
Crash site located by US Apache helicopter crew at 1415Z in hostile area (p. 3)
Wreckage found in two separate locations indicating separation during flight (p. 2)
Right wing found separated from fuselage - outboard right-hand wing explosive separation due to hostile ground-to-air fire (p. 2)

Ground-to-air fire reporting and dissemination system improved and procedures reviewed (p. 4)
Air Component Headquarters adapted intelligence procedures and processes for ground-to-air threat reporting (p. 4)

recommendations.text: Review C130 low-level flying tactics to mitigate risk from hostile ground-to-air fire in daylight operations
Consider fitting fuel tank inerting system in C130 aircraft wing fuel tanks to prevent explosive fuel/air mixtures
Improve in-theatre ground-to-air intelligence process and reporting procedures

records.title: British Airways 268
records.summary: During takeoff from Los Angeles at about 300 feet, the No. 2 engine experienced a compressor stall and flamed out. The aircraft was certified to fly on three engines and continued across North America and the Atlantic with the remaining three engines. Upon reaching the UK, the crew experienced difficulty balancing fuel between four tanks and declared an emergency, landing safely at Manchester.
records.probable_cause: The investigation recommended revision of training procedures for three-engine operation fuel management but did not identify a specific cause for the engine compressor stall.

factors.evidence: Flames burst out of its number 2 engine, a result of engine surge
The investigation report recommended that British Airways revise its training of crews in three-engine operation fuel management procedures
Upon reaching the United Kingdom, the crew experienced difficulty balancing the remaining fuel between the 4 fuel tanks

events.text: At about 300 feet into the initial climb from Los Angeles, the number 2 engine experienced a compressor stall and flamed out with flames visible from the engine.
The pilots shut down the number 2 engine after consulting with the airline dispatcher and confirmed they could continue the transatlantic flight on three engines.
After consulting with the airline dispatcher, the pilots decided to continue their flight plan and get as far as they could rather than dump 70 tonnes of fuel and land.
The cross-Atlantic journey encountered less favourable winds than predicted and the requested altitude was not available over the Atlantic, adding to crew workload.
Upon reaching United Kingdom airspace, the captain experienced difficulty balancing the remaining fuel between the four fuel tanks with only three engines operating.
The captain declared an emergency due to fuel imbalance concerns and requested priority landing at Manchester Airport.
The aircraft landed safely at Manchester Airport without further incident, completing a transatlantic flight on three engines.

Factor evidence sourced with page citations from official investigation report
Events extracted from witness accounts and accident sequence

recommendations.text: The Civil Aviation Authority and the Federal Aviation Administration, in conjunction with other relevant agencies, should review the policy on flight continuation for public transport aircraft operations following an in-flight shutdown of an engine, in order to provide clear guidance to the operators.
British Airways should include relevant instruction on 3-engined fuel handling during initial and recurrent training.

The Federal Aviation Administration should require that Honeywell modify the appropriate Return to Service test procedures, to ensure the detection of a fault which prevents a series 980-4100 model of flight recorder from retaining the appropriate minimum duration of recorded data proscribed by regulation.

The Federal Aviation Administration should require that Honeywell modify the design and operation of its automated equipment used for testing the series 980-4100 model of flight data recorder, to ensure the detection of a fault which prevents such a model of flight recorder from retaining the appropriate minimum duration of recorded data proscribed by regulation.

The Federal Aviation Administration should require that Honeywell alert all users of Acceptance Test Unit part number 964-0434-042, utilising test software part number 998-1513-513, to make them aware that the equipment will not detect a short circuit fault between one or more tracks on the distribution board of the series 980-4100 model of flight data recorder.

The Federal Aviation Administration should require Honeywell to amend the Maintenance Manual for the series 980-4100 model of flight data recorder to include a specific inspection of the underside of the distribution board for the presence of short circuits and detached wiring following the replacement of components.

The United Kingdom Civil Aviation Authority should require that operators of United Kingdom registered aircraft, installed with the series 980-4100 model of flight data recorder, review the annual flight recorder readout records for those aircraft in order to determine compliance with the applicable requirements for duration of recording.

The Federal Aviation Administration, European Aviation Safety Agency and the United Kingdom Civil Aviation Authority should require that, as part of any flight recorder readout procedure mandated by regulation, an assessment is conducted to ensure that the quantity and quality of all data recovered from the FDR is correct for the data rate of the system and the recorder part number concerned.

records.title: Air Transat 961

agencies.name: Transportation Safety Board of Canada
agencies.report_title: Aviation Investigation Report: Loss of Rudder in Flight, Air Transat, Airbus A310-308 C-GPAT, Miami, Florida, 90 nm S, 06 March 2005

location.name: 90 nautical miles south of Miami, Florida

records.summary: Air Transat Flight 961, an Airbus A310-308, was cruising at flight level 350 when the flight crew heard a loud bang and felt vibration. The aircraft entered a Dutch roll motion. The captain disconnected the autopilot and manually flew the aircraft, which climbed to 35,900 feet. The crew initiated a descent and requested diversion to Fort Lauderdale. The Dutch roll intensity decreased during descent and ceased at FL 280. The crew decided to return to Varadero. During landing flare, the rudder control inputs were ineffective. Upon parking at the gate, the aircraft rudder was discovered to be missing, fractured at the attachment points due to structural failure from disbond growth and material degradation.
records.probable_cause: A stress fracture in the composite rudder went undetected by inadequate inspection procedures and grew during earlier flights until causing in-flight failure during cruise flight.

factors.evidence: The rudder separated in flight after a loud bang and vibration were experienced by the crew, with the rudder found to be missing upon arrival at destination (p. 2-3).
The aircraft entered Dutch roll motion, a combined rolling and yawing oscillation difficult to control, following rudder separation (p. 2, 12).

Pre-existing disbond or in-plane core fracture damage to the rudder was present at takeoff, caused by either a discrete event but not blunt impact, or weak bond at z-section of left side panel (p. 63).
The manufacturer's recommended inspection program was not adequate to detect all rudder defects; damage may have been present for many flights before the occurrence (p. 63).
This model of rudder does not include design features in sandwich panels to mechanically arrest growth of disbond damage or in-plane core failure before damaged area reaches critical size (p. 63).
The aircraft returned safely to Varadero and landed without further incident; one flight attendant suffered minor back injury during Dutch roll event (p. 2).

events.text: Air Transat Flight 961 departs Varadero with 262 passengers and 9 crew on board; autopilot system No. 2 engaged
Flight crew hears loud bang and feels vibration; cabin crew members thrown to floor and unsecured galley carts moved freely
Captain takes control and disconnects autopilot No. 2 as aircraft enters Dutch roll motion
Autopilot No. 1 engaged to manage workload as Dutch roll intensifies; aircraft difficult to control in lateral axis
Autopilot No. 1 disengaged; aircraft hand-flown; climbs to approximately FL 359 (35,900 feet)
Flight crew requests descent and informs ATC of autopilot problem; crew cycles through ECAM pages to diagnose issue
Aircraft descends through FL 300; Dutch roll motion continues but gradually decreases in intensity
Dutch roll ceases as aircraft descends through FL 280; aircraft continues descent to 10,000 feet in preparation for diversion
Captain returns control to first officer; flight director briefs cabin crew for emergency procedures; crew contacts company dispatch
Flight cleared to return to Varadero at FL 190; crew elects to return where company better equipped to handle aircraft and passengers
During climb to FL 190, crew engages autopilot No. 1 for final phase of approach; aircraft continues toward Varadero
Autopilot disengaged during final portion of visual approach to Runway 06 at Varadero; nose wheel steering used for directional control
Uneventful landing completed at Varadero; aircraft taxied to gate; passengers deplaned normally through main door
Crew conducts flight control check after landing; ECAM indicates everything normal; visual inspection reveals aircraft rudder missing

recommendations.text: Urgently develop and implement an inspection program that will allow early and consistent detection of damage to the rudder assembly of aircraft equipped with part number A55471500 series rudders.
Urgently develop and implement an inspection program that will allow early and consistent detection of damage to the rudder assembly of aircraft equipped with part number A55471500 series rudders.
Safety Advisory issued regarding need for cockpit voice recorders with at least two-hour recording capacity; event was recorded only 60 minutes before landing.
Safety Advisory issued regarding filtering of digital flight data recorder data which prevented accurate determination of control surface positions under dynamic conditions.
Safety Advisory issued regarding need for review of digital flight data recorder recording rates to ensure adequate information for analyzing dynamic flight events.
Safety Advisory issued suggesting review of adequacy of published procedures to ensure pilots have required knowledge to safely recover from Dutch roll situation.

safety_changes: Enhanced inspection programs for Airbus composite rudders (A55471500 series)
Mandatory two-hour cockpit voice recorder capacity requirements
Improved digital flight data recorder recording rates for dynamic events
Enhanced Dutch roll recovery procedures and training

notes: Events extracted from flight progression summary and detailed analysis (p. 1-3, 53-63)
14 events documented with clock times derived from reported departure (0645 UTC) and landing (0819 UTC) times
Key sections read: Synopsis (p. 1-3), History of Flight (p. 1-14), Injuries to Persons (p. 2-3), Damage to Aircraft (p. 3), Findings as to Causes (p. 63), Dutch Roll Description (p. 12)
Rudder failure mechanism: pre-existing disbond with inadequate inspection allowing continued degradation until structural failure
Dutch roll motion ceased at FL 280 during descent; aircraft safely returned and landed despite missing rudder

records.title: 2005 Loganair Islander accident

location.name: 7.7 nm west-north-west of Campbeltown Airport, Scotland

records.summary: A Loganair air ambulance Islander crashed into the sea during approach to Campbeltown Airport after making several navigational errors and flying too low. The pilot, who had not flown for 32 days, was fatigued and lacked recent instrument flying experience. After reporting completion of the base turn inbound, the aircraft descended unchecked into the water. The pilot and paramedic on board were killed.
records.probable_cause: The pilot allowed the aircraft to descend below the minimum safe altitude for the aircraft's position on the approach procedure, and this descent probably continued unchecked until the aircraft flew into the sea. Contributing factors were a combination of fatigue, high workload, lack of recent flying practice, and possible subtle incapacitation or disorientation that affected the pilot's ability to safely control the aircraft's flightpath.

factors.evidence: The pilot had not flown for 32 days and was probably suffering from the effects of fatigue (p. 62-63)
The pilot descended below minimum altitude with a steady rate of descent of about 1,000 ft/min and appeared unaware of the precise position (p. 62-63)
The aircraft descended 200 ft below the minimum outbound altitude of 1,540 ft and continued descending at the last radar position (p. 63)
The pilot may have been subject to spatial disorientation, distraction, or subtle incapacitation which affected the ability to safely control the aircraft's flightpath (p. 63)
Aircraft impacted the sea west-north-west of Campbeltown Airport (p. 1)

events.text: The pilot was flying the normal approach outbound on the procedure for Runway 11
Aircraft established correctly on the 307° outbound radial with normal speed and rate of descent
Pilot transmitted that he had completed the base turn, indicating he was inbound to the airport
Aircraft impacted the sea, with the wreckage located on the sea bed 7.7 nm west-north-west of the airport

recommendations.text: Review the UK Civil Aviation Authority's proposal to mandate the fitment of Upper Torso Restraints on all seats of existing Transport Category (Passenger) aeroplanes below 5,700 kg being operated for public transport, and consider creating regulation to implement the intent of the proposal
Considering the unique circumstances of air ambulance flights, review the circumstances in which a second pilot is required for public transport flights operating air ambulance services
Consider mandating the carriage of a radio altimeter, or other independent low height warning device, for public transport IFR flights operating with a single pilot

notes: Read synopsis, findings (with subsections on aircraft, flight operations, and personnel), causal factors, and safety recommendations sections; 22+ findings extracted; 3 safety recommendations from formal investigation

records.title: Air France 358
records.time_reference: EDT (local); only the touchdown time is given to the minute, other clocks omitted

agencies.name: Transportation Safety Board of Canada
agencies.report_title: Runway Overrun and Fire, Air France, Airbus A340-313 F-GLZQ, Toronto/Lester B. Pearson International Airport, Ontario, 02 August 2005

location.name: Toronto Pearson International Airport, runway 24L overrun into Etobicoke Creek ravine

records.summary: Arriving from Paris during a severe thunderstorm, the A340 landed on Toronto's runway 24L in heavy rain with a tailwind, touching down about 3,800 ft along the 9,000 ft runway. Thrust reversers were selected late, and the aircraft left the runway end at about 80 kt, crossed the grass and came to rest in the Etobicoke Creek ravine, where it was destroyed by fire. All 297 passengers and 12 crew evacuated; 12 people were seriously injured.
records.probable_cause: The TSB found that the crew continued the approach into a thunderstorm in which the wind shifted to a tailwind and heavy rain reduced visibility. The aircraft crossed the threshold high, floated in a prolonged flare and touched down far down the wet runway; the thrust reversers were selected 12.8 seconds after touchdown and full braking was delayed, so the aircraft could not be stopped on the runway remaining. The crew had not calculated the landing distance required for the conditions, and Air France had no clear guidance requiring a go-around when a long landing developed. The absence of a runway end safety area meant the overrun ended in a ravine, and the ensuing fire destroyed the aircraft.

factors.evidence: A line of severe thunderstorms with lightning and intense rain was over the airport during the approach and landing; a ground-operations red alert was in effect at Pearson.
The wind shifted during the final approach so that the aircraft landed with a tailwind component of about 10 kt.
Intense rain on short final and in the flare reduced forward visibility; the pilot flying lost sight of the runway end environment during the flare.
Runway 24L was water-covered by heavy rain, reducing braking effectiveness.
The aircraft crossed the threshold about 40 ft high and touched down about 3,800 ft beyond the threshold of the 9,000 ft runway.
Thrust reversers were selected 12.8 seconds after touchdown and maximum braking was not applied immediately.
The crew did not consider a go-around when the landing became long; Air France procedures did not clearly require one in that situation.
The crew were managing a deteriorating weather situation, wind shifts and reduced visibility in the final seconds of the approach.
The crew did not compute the landing distance required for a wet runway with a tailwind before landing.
The end of runway 24L was not provided with a 300 m runway end safety area; the overrun terminated in the Etobicoke Creek ravine, which increased the damage and the fire.
The aircraft departed the runway end at about 80 kt and travelled across the grass into the ravine.
A fire developed after the aircraft came to rest and destroyed the aircraft.
Some exits and slides were unusable because of fire and damage, and many passengers took carry-on baggage with them, slowing the evacuation.

events.text: Severe thunderstorms approach Toronto Pearson; a red alert suspends ground operations for lightning. The crew brief the ILS approach to runway 24L, which is wet.
Preceding aircraft land; the crew are advised of the weather but are not given a reason to expect the runway to be unusable.
Established on the ILS for runway 24L with the autopilot engaged; intense rain and lightning are visible ahead. The crew continue the approach.
The wind shifts to a tailwind component of about 10 kt as the storm passes over the airport; rain intensity increases sharply.
Autopilot disconnected; the first officer flies the final approach manually in heavy rain and reduced visibility.
Aircraft crosses the runway threshold about 40 ft higher than normal.
Prolonged flare; the pilot flying loses visual reference to the runway end in the intense rain. No go-around is considered.
Touchdown about 3,800 ft beyond the threshold of the 9,000 ft runway, leaving about 5,100 ft of wet runway.
Ground spoilers deploy on touchdown.
Thrust reversers selected 12.8 seconds after touchdown; heavy braking applied late.
Aircraft leaves the end of runway 24L at about 80 kt, crosses the grass overrun area and drops into the Etobicoke Creek ravine, coming to rest about 300 m beyond the runway end.
Fire develops on the left side; evacuation begins. Some exits and slides are unusable and many passengers take carry-on baggage.
All 309 occupants are out of the aircraft within about two minutes; 12 are seriously injured. The aircraft is destroyed by fire.

recommendations.text: Require crews to establish, before landing, that a safety margin exists between the landing distance available and the landing distance required for the actual runway and weather conditions.
Require that all Code 4 runways have a 300 m runway end safety area or an equivalent means of stopping aircraft.
recommendations.outcome: Toronto Pearson subsequently extended its runway end safety areas; Transport Canada later moved to require RESAs at major airports.

recommendations.text: Require operators to provide clear guidance on go-around decisions when a landing is not proceeding as expected, including after the flare.
Address the risks posed by passengers retrieving carry-on baggage during an emergency evacuation.

safety_changes: Air France revised its approach and landing procedures and go-around policy for landings in deteriorating weather.
Toronto Pearson and other Canadian airports improved runway end safety areas; Transport Canada worked toward mandatory RESA standards.
Industry and regulators reinforced pre-landing landing-distance assessment for wet or contaminated runways and tailwinds.

notes: Event t values are approximate reconstructions from the report narrative (touchdown 3,800 ft down the runway, reversers 12.8 s after touchdown, exit from runway at about 80 kt); the report's exact clock times are not reproduced.
Threshold crossing height of about 40 ft high is from memory of the report and should be verified.
The number of usable exits and slides is not stated precisely; the record only says some were unusable.
TSB recommendation numbers from the December 2007 report (A07 series) are not given because the exact mapping to text was not verified.

records.title: Tuninter 1153

agencies.name: Agenzia Nazionale per la Sicurezza del Volo
agencies.report_title: Final report on the accident to ATR 72-202 TS-LBB, ditching off Capo Gallo (Palermo), 6 August 2005

location.name: Tyrrhenian Sea off Capo Gallo, north-east of Palermo

records.summary: The day before the accident, maintenance in Tunis replaced the aircraft's fuel quantity indicator with a unit designed for the ATR 42, which is physically interchangeable but over-reads on the ATR 72. The aircraft was refuelled on the basis of the false indication and departed Bari with far less fuel than displayed. In cruise both engines flamed out from fuel exhaustion; the crew attempted restarts and diverted toward Palermo but could not reach it, and the aircraft was ditched off Capo Gallo. The fuselage broke into three sections; 16 of the 39 on board died.
records.probable_cause: The ANSV concluded that the accident was caused by fuel exhaustion resulting from the installation of an ATR 42 fuel quantity indicator on the ATR 72, which over-read the fuel on board, so that the aircraft was dispatched with insufficient fuel. Contributing factors included the maintenance organisation's failure to verify the part number before installation and the interchangeability of the two indicators, the crew's failure to detect the discrepancy between fuel uplift, fuel used and indicated quantity, and, after the double flame-out, the crew's attempts to restart the engines rather than fly the aircraft at the optimum glide speed toward the nearest airport, which reduced the distance covered.

factors.evidence: On 5 August the fuel quantity indicator was replaced in Tunis with an ATR 42 unit whose part number differs from the ATR 72 unit; the mechanic did not verify the part number applicability.
The ATR 42 and ATR 72 fuel quantity indicators are physically interchangeable and nearly identical in appearance despite different calibrations.
The indicator over-read by more than 2,000 kg, so the crew refuelled to a displayed quantity that did not correspond to the actual fuel on board.
The report found the crew did not detect the inconsistency between the fuel uplifted, the fuel used since the last refuelling and the indicated quantity.
The right engine flamed out in cruise at FL230 followed by the left engine about 100 seconds later because the tanks were empty.
Both engines stopped and could not be restarted; the aircraft became a glider about 40 nm from Palermo.
The crew repeatedly attempted engine restarts and did not maintain the optimum glide speed or configuration, shortening the glide distance.
The ANSV found that the crew's training for a double engine failure and forced landing at sea was inadequate.
The aircraft was ditched in the sea off Capo Gallo; the fuselage broke into three sections on impact.
Several occupants died from the impact and in the water; the report examined the survival aspects, including the seats and the life jackets, after the fuselage broke up.

events.text: At Tunis on 5 August a mechanic replaces the fuel quantity indicator with an ATR 42 unit taken from stores, without verifying the part number applicability.
The aircraft is refuelled for the Tunis-Bari and Bari-Djerba sectors on the basis of the indicated quantity, which over-reads by more than 2,000 kg.
The crew at Bari accept the displayed fuel quantity without reconciling it with the fuel uplift and the fuel used on the inbound sector.
Departure from Bari for Djerba; climb to FL230.
The right engine flames out in cruise at FL230 over the Tyrrhenian Sea.
About 100 seconds later the left engine also flames out; the fuel gauge still shows fuel remaining.
The crew declare an emergency and request to divert to Palermo, about 40 nm away.
The crew make repeated attempts to restart the engines instead of establishing the optimum glide speed toward Palermo.
Recognising that Palermo cannot be reached, the captain prepares to ditch and informs ATC and the cabin.
The aircraft is ditched off Capo Gallo; the fuselage breaks into three sections. 23 occupants survive and are rescued by boats; 16 die.

recommendations.text: Make the ATR 42 and ATR 72 fuel quantity indicators non-interchangeable or clearly distinguishable, and review the associated maintenance documentation and parts identification.
recommendations.outcome: ATR issued instructions distinguishing the indicators and revised the illustrated parts catalogue.

recommendations.text: Improve maintenance procedures for part number verification and the oversight of the operator's maintenance organisation.
Reinforce crew procedures for checking fuel on board against uplift and consumption, and training for double engine failure, glide management and ditching.

safety_changes: ATR fuel quantity indicators for the ATR 42 and ATR 72 were made distinguishable and the parts documentation was revised.
A Palermo court convicted the two pilots and several Tuninter maintenance and management staff in 2009 in connection with the accident.

notes: The engine flame-out time (about 15:24 UTC) and ditching time (about 15:39 UTC) are from the published narrative to the minute; intermediate event t values are approximate offsets.
The ANSV final report number and publication date were not verified.
The over-read magnitude (more than 2,000 kg) is given from the published summary; the exact figure was not verified.
The BEA's accredited-representative role is assumed from ATR being a French-registered manufacturer.
Lat/lon are approximate for the ditching location off Capo Gallo.

records.title: Helios Airways 522

agencies.name: Air Accident Investigation and Aviation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report: Helios Airways Flight HCY522, Boeing 737-31S at Grammatiko, Hellas on 14 August 2005

agencies.name: Cyprus Air Accident and Incident Investigation Board

location.name: Hills near Grammatiko, about 33 km north of Athens

records.summary: After overnight maintenance the pressurisation mode selector was left in MANUAL and not detected by the crew during pre-flight checks. As the aircraft climbed through about 12,000 ft the cabin altitude warning horn sounded, but the crew misidentified it as a takeoff configuration warning and became confused by subsequent master caution alerts. Both pilots became incapacitated by hypoxia and the aircraft continued to Athens on autopilot, holding for over two hours until fuel exhaustion caused both engines to flame out and it crashed into hills near Grammatiko. All 121 on board died.
records.probable_cause: Direct causes: non-recognition that the cabin pressurisation mode selector was in the MANUAL position during the performance of the Preflight, Before Start and After Takeoff checklists; non-identification of the warnings and the reasons for the activation of the warnings (cabin altitude warning horn, passenger oxygen masks deployment indication, master caution); and incapacitation of the flight crew due to hypoxia, resulting in continuation of the flight via the flight management computer and autopilot, depletion of the fuel and engine flameout, and the impact of the aircraft with the ground. Latent causes: the operator's deficiencies in organisation, quality management and safety culture; the regulatory authority's inadequate execution of its oversight responsibilities; inadequate application of CRM principles; and the ineffectiveness of measures taken by the manufacturer in response to previous pressurisation incidents, particularly the similarity of the cabin altitude and takeoff configuration warning horns.

factors.evidence: During a pressurisation leak check the night before, the ground engineer left the pressurisation mode selector in MANUAL instead of returning it to AUTO.
The crew failed to detect the MANUAL selection during the Preflight, Before Start and After Takeoff checklists.
With the outflow valve partly open in manual, the cabin did not pressurise and cabin altitude climbed with the aircraft.
The cabin altitude warning horn was identical to the takeoff configuration warning horn, and the crew's confusion had been foreseen in earlier incidents.
The crew interpreted the cabin altitude horn as a takeoff configuration warning and the equipment cooling master caution as unrelated faults.
The captain and first officer, of different nationalities and with language difficulties, did not coordinate the diagnosis, and the captain left his seat to consult with the engineer on the radio.
The crew did not don oxygen masks; as cabin altitude passed 14,000 ft and higher, both pilots lost useful consciousness.
Both pilots were incapacitated by hypoxia; a flight attendant with a portable oxygen bottle entered the cockpit late in the flight but could not recover the aircraft.
The aircraft flew on autopilot to the KEA holding pattern near Athens and circled until the left, then the right engine flamed out from fuel exhaustion.
The manufacturer's measures after previous MANUAL-mode pressurisation incidents did not address the shared horn and the lack of a distinct cabin altitude alert.
Helios Airways had deficiencies in organisation, quality management, crew training and safety culture.
The Cyprus regulator's oversight of the operator was found inadequate.
After the second engine flamed out the autopilot could no longer maintain the aircraft and it descended into the hills near Grammatiko.

events.text: Overnight at Larnaca a ground engineer performs a pressurisation leak check in response to a reported rear door seal problem and leaves the mode selector in MANUAL.
Preflight and Before Start checklists performed; the pressurisation mode selector position is not detected as MANUAL.
Flight 522 departs Larnaca for Athens with 115 passengers and 6 crew; the After Takeoff checklist again fails to catch the MANUAL selection.
Passing about 12,040 ft the cabin altitude warning horn sounds; the crew believe it is a takeoff configuration warning.
Master caution: equipment cooling off lights and, passing about 14,000 ft, the passenger oxygen masks deploy; the crew contact the company operations centre to discuss the warnings.

Captain, speaking with the ground engineer by radio, asks where the equipment cooling circuit breakers are, then leaves his seat; the conversation is confused and the pressurisation is never discussed.
Last radio contact with the flight; the aircraft continues climbing on autopilot to the cruising level of FL340 with both pilots incapacitated.
Athens control fails to establish contact; the aircraft enters Greek airspace and proceeds to the KEA VOR under FMC guidance.
The aircraft enters the holding pattern at KEA at FL340 and continues to circle on autopilot.
Two Hellenic Air Force F-16s intercept the aircraft; they observe the first officer slumped over the controls, the captain's seat empty and oxygen masks hanging in the cabin.
A flight attendant, holding a portable oxygen bottle, is seen entering the cockpit and sitting in the captain's seat; the left engine flames out from fuel exhaustion at 11:49:50.
The aircraft descends; a Mayday call is transmitted from the cockpit but is not on the correct frequency. The right engine flames out.
The aircraft strikes hilly terrain near Grammatiko; all 121 on board killed.

recommendations.text: Require a distinct cabin altitude warning, with an aural and visual indication that cannot be confused with the takeoff configuration warning, on the Boeing 737 and similar types.
recommendations.outcome: Boeing introduced a cabin altitude warning light and the FAA mandated it on 737s.

recommendations.text: Revise checklists and training so that the pressurisation mode selector position is positively verified before flight and after maintenance, and that the cabin altitude warning is trained in the simulator.
Correct deficiencies in the operator's organisation, quality system, crew training and safety culture, and strengthen regulatory oversight of the operator.
recommendations.outcome: Helios Airways ceased operations in 2006.

recommendations.text: Improve procedures for handling loss of communication with a flight and coordination with air defence interception.

safety_changes: Cabin altitude warning light and revised annunciation on Boeing 737 aircraft, later mandated by FAA airworthiness directive.
Boeing checklist revisions and operator training emphasising pressurisation panel checks and hypoxia recognition.
Strengthened Cypriot civil aviation oversight following EU and ICAO audits.

notes: Clock strings are Cyprus/Greece local time (both UTC+3 that day); t0 is the cabin altitude warning at about 09:12 local. Seconds are estimated except the left engine flameout (11:49:50) and impact (12:03:32) given in the report.
The time of the right engine flameout is approximate.
The Cyprus accredited agency code is an informal label. Report reference number 11/2006 may not match the AAIASB's official numbering.
loss_of_control_inflight is used as the outcome factor for the uncontrolled descent after fuel exhaustion with no pilot at the controls.

records.title: West Caribbean Airways 708

agencies.name: Junta Investigadora de Accidentes de Aviación Civil
agencies.report_title: Final report on the accident to McDonnell Douglas MD-82 HK-4374X, Machiques, 16 August 2005

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses
agencies.report_title: English translation of the Venezuelan final report

location.name: Near Machiques, Sierra de Perijá, Zulia

records.summary: The MD-82, on a charter flight from Panama to Martinique, climbed to FL330 with engine anti-ice selected on, an altitude at which the aircraft could not maintain speed at its weight and thrust setting. With the autothrottle in Mach hold and the autopilot holding altitude, the airspeed decayed unnoticed until the aircraft stalled. The captain, believing both engines had flamed out, held the nose up while the aircraft descended in a deep stall for more than three minutes and struck the ground near Machiques. All 160 on board died.
records.probable_cause: The Venezuelan JIAAC concluded that the crew allowed the aircraft to enter a stall at FL330 through inadequate monitoring of airspeed after climbing to an altitude above the aircraft's performance capability with engine anti-ice on, and then failed to recognise the stall and apply the correct recovery. The captain interpreted the situation as a loss of thrust on both engines and kept the aircraft nose up, sustaining a deep stall until impact. Contributing factors included the crew's inadequate crew resource management, the pilots' lack of knowledge of high-altitude performance and stall characteristics of the MD-80, and organisational deficiencies at the operator.

factors.evidence: The aircraft was flown to FL330 at a weight and with engine anti-ice on that left it unable to maintain cruise speed; airspeed decayed steadily while the autopilot held altitude.
The autothrottle was in Mach hold and the crew did not recognise that the thrust available was not sustaining the target speed.
The report found the crew did not monitor the decreasing airspeed and rising angle of attack before the stall warning.
The flight was operating in an area of convective weather and icing conditions, for which engine anti-ice had been selected on, reducing thrust available.
At FL330 the stick shaker activated and the aircraft entered a stall from which the crew did not recover.
The CVR showed the captain believed both engines had flamed out and did not identify the stall.
The captain held nose-up control input throughout the descent instead of reducing the angle of attack; the aircraft remained in a deep stall.
The first officer called out the stall but did not challenge the captain's actions effectively; the report cited deficient crew coordination.
The report found the crew's knowledge of high-altitude performance, stall recognition and recovery on the MD-80 was inadequate.
The report described the operator's financial difficulties and deficient operational control and training oversight at the time of the accident.
The aircraft descended in a stalled condition at rates exceeding 10,000 ft/min until it struck the ground.

events.text: Crew request and are cleared to climb from FL310 to FL330 with engine anti-ice on; the aircraft is near its performance ceiling for its weight.
In level flight at FL330 with the autothrottle in Mach hold, the airspeed begins a slow decay while the autopilot holds altitude.
Crew discuss weather and request descent to FL310 from ATC as the aircraft struggles to hold speed; airspeed continues to decay unremarked.
Pitch attitude rises as the autopilot trims to hold altitude with insufficient thrust; angle of attack approaches the stall.
Stick shaker activates at FL330; the aircraft stalls and begins to descend.
Autopilot disconnects; the aircraft pitches up and rolls as it enters a deep stall.
Captain states that both engines have flamed out and calls for the engine restart procedure; thrust is advanced.
First officer calls out that the aircraft is stalling; the captain continues to hold the nose up.
Captain declares an emergency to ATC, reporting a loss of both engines.
The aircraft descends at more than 10,000 ft/min with high angle of attack and nose-up column input; stall warning continues.
GPWS terrain warnings sound in the final part of the descent.
Impact with the ground near Machiques in a stalled, near-level attitude; all on board are killed.

recommendations.text: Ensure MD-80 crews are trained in high-altitude performance, the effect of engine anti-ice on climb capability, and stall recognition and recovery at high altitude.
Strengthen oversight of the operator's operational control, crew training and financial capacity to operate safely.
Review autothrottle and flight-mode annunciation and stall-warning enhancements on MD-80 series aircraft so that a decaying airspeed in cruise is more clearly presented to the crew.

safety_changes: West Caribbean Airways ceased operations after the accident and its operating certificate was suspended by Aerocivil.
The accident became a reference case in the industry's revision of stall-recovery training toward angle-of-attack reduction rather than minimising altitude loss.

notes: t0 is null: exact UTC clock times from the JIAAC report were not verified, so t values are approximate offsets from the onset of the stall warning at FL330 reconstructed from the report narrative (descent of roughly three and a half minutes).
The JIAAC-VE final report date and number were not verified; the BEA published an English translation.
Lat/lon are approximate for the Machiques area.
The vertical speed of about 12,000 ft/min and the crew statements are paraphrased from the published narrative, not quoted from the transcript.
Recommendation texts summarise themes of the report; the exact wording and addressees were not verified.

records.title: Southwest Airlines 1248

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Runway Overrun and Collision, Southwest Airlines Flight 1248, Boeing 737-7H4, N471WN, Chicago Midway International Airport, Chicago, Illinois, December 8, 2005

location.name: Chicago Midway International Airport, runway 31C overrun onto Central Avenue

records.summary: Landing on Midway's 6,522 ft runway 31C at night in a snowstorm with an approximately 8 kt tailwind and braking action reported fair to poor, the crew used autobrakes for the first time and did not deploy reverse thrust until about 18 seconds after touchdown. The 737 overran the runway, went through the blast fence and airport perimeter fence onto Central Avenue and struck vehicles, killing a 6-year-old boy in a car. All 103 people on board survived.
records.probable_cause: The pilots' failure to use available reverse thrust in a timely manner to safely slow or stop the airplane after landing, which resulted in a runway overrun. This failure occurred because the pilots' first experience and lack of familiarity with the airplane's autobrake system distracted them from thrust reverser usage during the challenging landing. Contributing were Southwest Airlines' failure to provide clear and consistent guidance and training regarding arrival landing distance calculations; the programming and design of its on-board performance computer, which did not present inherent assumptions critical to pilot decision-making; its plan to implement new autobrake procedures without a familiarization period; and its failure to include a margin of safety in the arrival assessment. Also contributing was the pilots' failure to divert given reports of poor braking action and a tailwind component of about 8 knots. Contributing to the severity was the absence of an engineering materials arresting system (EMAS) beyond the end of runway 31C.

factors.evidence: Snow was falling and the runway was contaminated; braking action had been reported fair for the first half and poor for the second half.
The crew landed on runway 31C with a tailwind component of about 8 knots.
The approach was flown at night in falling snow with reduced visibility.
Reverse thrust was not deployed until about 18 seconds after touchdown; the NTSB cited this as the primary cause.
This was the pilots' first landing using autobrakes; Southwest introduced the procedure without a familiarisation period, and guidance on landing distance assessment was inconsistent.

The on-board performance computer assumed immediate reverse thrust and did not present this assumption; with 'poor' braking entered the predicted margin would have been only about 30 ft rather than the 560 ft shown for 'fair'.
Southwest's arrival landing distance assessment did not include a safety margin to account for operational uncertainties.
The challenging night, snow and tailwind landing combined with unfamiliar autobrake operation distracted the captain from deploying the reversers.
The NTSB found the pilots should have diverted given the poor braking action reports and tailwind.
Runway 31C had a limited runway safety area and no EMAS, which contributed to the severity of the overrun.
The aircraft left the end of runway 31C, penetrated the blast fence and perimeter fence and came to rest on Central Avenue after striking vehicles.

events.text: Crew obtains weather and braking action reports for Midway: snow, low visibility, braking action fair for the first half of runway 31C and poor for the second half.

Landing distance computed on the on-board performance computer using 'fair' braking action, giving a stopping margin of about 560 ft; the computer assumed immediate reverse thrust and, with 'poor' entered, would have shown about 30 ft.
Crew elects to continue to Midway rather than divert despite the reports of poor braking action and a tailwind.
Aircraft is held briefly and then sequenced for the ILS approach to runway 31C; wind reported from the east giving a tailwind component of about 8 knots.
Autobrake MAX selected for landing; this is the first time either pilot has landed with the autobrake system under Southwest's new procedure.
Aircraft on final in snow and low visibility; runway environment acquired late.
Touchdown on runway 31C; the autobrakes engage.
Captain attempts to select reverse thrust but is unable to move the reverse levers past the interlock while attending to the unfamiliar autobrake behaviour.
First officer deploys reverse thrust about 18 seconds after touchdown; captain applies maximum manual braking.
Aircraft continues past the end of runway 31C at low speed, crosses the limited runway safety area and strikes the blast fence and perimeter fence.
Aircraft comes to rest on Central Avenue after striking vehicles; a child in one of the cars is killed and several occupants of the vehicles are injured.
Passengers and crew evacuate; there are no fatalities on board.

recommendations.text: Require operators to perform arrival landing distance assessments before every landing based on existing performance data, actual conditions and a safety margin of at least 15 percent.
recommendations.outcome: FAA issued SAFO 06012 on landing performance assessments at time of arrival and later rulemaking on runway condition reporting.

recommendations.text: Require that on-board performance computers and landing distance tools clearly present the assumptions on which their calculations are based.
Ensure that operators provide adequate familiarisation and training before introducing new landing procedures such as autobrake use.
Expedite installation of EMAS or equivalent runway safety area improvements at airports with limited safety areas.
recommendations.outcome: EMAS beds were installed at Chicago Midway.

safety_changes: FAA SAFO 06012 recommended landing distance assessments at time of arrival with a 15 percent safety margin.
EMAS arrestor beds were installed at the runway ends at Chicago Midway.
Development of the Takeoff and Landing Performance Assessment (TALPA) runway condition reporting framework.

notes: t0 is set to touchdown at about 19:14 CST; seconds not recalled. Pre-landing event times are approximate.
Occupant count of 103 (98 passengers and 5 crew) and the 560 ft / 30 ft OPC margins are from memory of the report; the 18 second reverse thrust delay is as stated by the NTSB.
Recommendation numbers not recalled and are left null; SAFO 06012 was issued before the final report.

records.title: Chalk's Ocean Airways 101

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: In-flight Separation of Right Wing, Flying Boat, Inc. (doing business as Chalk's Ocean Airways) Flight 101

records.operator: Flying Boat, Inc. (doing business as Chalk's Ocean Airways)

location.name: Government Cut channel, Port of Miami, Florida

records.summary: Chalk's Ocean Airways Flight 101, a Grumman G-73T Turbo Mallard, crashed shortly after takeoff from Miami Seaplane Base into a shipping channel. White smoke appeared during the initial climb and the right wing separated from the fuselage, causing the 58-year-old aircraft to plunge into the ocean. The fatigue crack had been detected and repaired previously, but the repair was ineffective. The operator applied sealant over the damaged lower stringer, concealing a fatigue crack that had been ground out in an earlier failed repair attempt.
records.probable_cause: The in-flight failure and separation of the right wing during normal flight, which resulted from the failure of the Chalk's Ocean Airways maintenance program to identify and properly repair fatigue cracks in the right wing and the failure of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to detect and correct deficiencies in the company's maintenance program.

factors.evidence: Fatigue failure in the right-wing initiated by a crack in a span-wise stringer (p. vii)
The operator applied sealant over a damaged lower stringer in such a way as to conceal a fatigue crack (p. vii)
Chalk's maintenance programme was ineffective at addressing longstanding structural problems (p. vii)
The Mallard was designed with a wet wing where fuel tanks are constructed from sealed-off portions of the wing structure, requiring all tank seams to be sealed (p. vii)
The FAA failed to detect and correct the airline's maintenance shortfalls (p. vii)
The right wing ripped off and the aircraft plunged into the ocean (p. vii)

events.text: Flight 101 departed Miami Seaplane Base for Bimini, Bahamas at 14:39 EST.
White smoke billowed from the aircraft.
The right wing ripped off and the aircraft plunged into the ocean.
Aircraft crashed and sank in Government Cut channel.

recommendations.text: Verify that the maintenance programs of commercial aircraft operators include stringent criteria to address recurring or systemic discrepancies to include, if necessary, further analysis through comprehensive engineering evaluation.
Identify the systemic deficiencies in the maintenance program oversight procedures and modify those procedures to ensure that maintenance program plans are adequate.
Require records reviews, aging airplane inspections, and supplemental inspections for all airplanes operated under Part 121, Part 129, and Part 135.

notes: Sections read: Executive Summary (p. vii), History of Flight (p. 1), Probable Cause (p. 55), Recommendations (p. 55)

records.title: UPS Airlines 1307
records.summary: UPS Airlines Flight 1307, a DC-8-71F, was conducting a cargo flight from Atlanta to Philadelphia. During descent, the crew detected an odor of burning wood. Despite initial consideration of diverting, the crew continued to Philadelphia as there was no visible smoke or fire warnings. At 23:54:42 during descent through 3,600 feet, a cargo smoke warning activated, followed by a lower aft cargo fire warning. The aircraft landed safely at Philadelphia with no fatalities; the airplane and cargo were destroyed by fire after landing.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause of this accident was an in-flight cargo fire that initiated from an unknown source, which was most likely located within cargo container 12, 13, or 14. Contributing to the loss of the aircraft were the inadequate certification test requirements for smoke and fire detection systems and the lack of an on-board fire suppression system. (p. 66)

factors.evidence: Fire initiated as a smoldering fire in cargo containers 12, 13, or 14, likely from an unknown source involving lithium batteries or other hazardous cargo. (p. 64-65)
Crew continued descent to Philadelphia after detecting odor similar to burning wood instead of immediately diverting when no visible evidence was apparent. (p. 2-3, 64)

Certification test standards for smoke and fire detection systems do not account for effects of cargo and cargo containers on airflow around detection sensors; fire detection system did not activate until 20 minutes after fire initiation, well beyond FAA 5-minute standard. (p. 64)
Crew received smoke warning in main cargo compartment at 23:54:42 and fire warning in aft lower cargo compartment at 23:55:57 during descent through 3,600 feet. (p. 2-3)

events.text: First officer detected odor similar to burning wood; crew members reported smelling it during descent through FL310, 50 nm SW of Washington DC.
Captain considered diverting to another airport but decided to continue to Philadelphia because there was no visible evidence of a problem and no cargo smoke warnings illuminated.
Crew conducted emergency checklist steps including increasing bleed air flow and checking bleed air switches; set air conditioning packs to maximum flow and turned off recirculation fan.
Philadelphia approach control instructed flight to descend to 6,000 feet; crew continued troubleshooting the odor source over next 10 minutes.
Cargo smoke warning activated while aircraft descending through about 3,600 feet; flight engineer stated 'we got cargo smoke' and captain initiated appropriate checklist.

Flight engineer reported lower aft cargo fire section C warning illuminated; captain instructed crew to don oxygen masks and flight engineer began Lower/Main Cargo Compartment Smoke or Fire checklist.
First officer called for landing checklist; when flight engineer opened cargo air shutoff valve access panel, black smoke billowed out, indicating fire had spread significantly.
Aircraft touched down on runway 27R approximately 23:59; visible smoke rapidly thickening in cockpit immediately after touchdown. Crew evacuated using left forward door slide.

recommendations.text: Provide clear guidance to operators of passenger and cargo aircraft operating under 14 CFR Parts 121, 135, and 91K on flight crew procedures for responding to evidence of a fire in the absence of a cockpit alert based on the guidance developed by the 2004 smoke, fire, and fumes industry initiative.

Ensure that the performance requirements for smoke and fire detection systems on cargo airplanes account for the effects of cargo containers on airflow around the detection sensors and on the containment of smoke from a fire inside a container, and establish standardized methods of demonstrating compliance with those requirements.
Require that fire suppression systems be installed in the cargo compartments of all cargo airplanes operating under 14 CFR Part 121.
Provide guidance to aircraft rescue and firefighting personnel on the best training methods to obtain and maintain proficiency with the high-reach extendable turret with skin-penetrating nozzle.
Require airport inspectors to ensure that Part 139 airports with cargo operations include cargo aircraft in their aircraft rescue and firefighting aircraft familiarization training programs.
Require cargo operators to designate at least one floor level door as a required emergency exit and equip the door with an evacuation slide, when appropriate.
Require all emergency exits on cargo aircraft that are operable from the outside to have a 2-inch contrasting colored band outlining the exit.

Require aircraft operators to implement measures to reduce the risk of primary lithium batteries becoming involved in fires on cargo-only aircraft, such as transporting such batteries in fire resistant containers and/or in restricted quantities at any single location on the aircraft.

Until fire suppression systems are required on cargo-only aircraft, as asked for in Safety Recommendation A-07-99, require that cargo shipments of secondary lithium batteries, including those contained in or packed with equipment, be transported in crew-accessible locations where portable fire suppression systems can be used.

Require aircraft operators that transport hazardous materials to immediately provide consolidated and specific information about hazardous materials on board an aircraft, including proper shipping name, hazard class, quantity, number of packages, and location, to on-scene emergency responders upon notification of an accident or incident.

Require commercial cargo and passenger operators to report to the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration all incidents involving primary and secondary lithium batteries, including those contained in or packed with equipment, that occur either on board or during loading or unloading operations and retain the failed items for evaluation purposes.

Analyze the causes of all thermal failures and fires involving secondary and primary lithium batteries and, based on this analysis, take appropriate action to mitigate any risks determined to be posed by transporting lithium batteries, including those contained in or packed with equipment, on board cargo and passenger aircraft as cargo, checked baggage, or carry-on items.

Eliminate regulatory exemptions for the packaging, marking, and labeling of cargo shipments of small secondary lithium batteries (no more than 8 grams equivalent lithium content) until the analysis of the failures and the implementation of risk-based requirements asked for in Safety Recommendation A-07-108 are completed.

Work with your member airlines and other groups, such as the Air Transport Association, major aircraft manufacturers, and the Aircraft Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) Working Group, to develop and disseminate accurate and complete airplane Emergency Response diagrams for ARFF personnel at airports with cargo operations.

notes: History of Flight section (p. 1-6), Findings (p. 64-65), Probable Cause (p. 66), and Safety Recommendations (p. 67-70) read from NTSB report AAR-07/07. Exact origin of cargo fire not definitively determined; report states most likely containers 12, 13, or 14. Fire detection and suppression system deficiencies identified as contributing factors. 8 events with clock times extracted from CVR data and ATC transcripts.

records.title: Air Algérie 2208

agencies.name: Agenzia Nazionale per la Sicurezza del Volo

records.summary: Air Algérie Flight 2208, a cargo Hercules at 24,000 feet, began descending for unknown reasons while autopilot was engaged. The autopilot failed and disengaged; moments later both directional and longitudinal control were lost. The aircraft descended steeply at 45-50 degrees and impacted terrain near Piacenza 73 seconds after autopilot failure light illuminated, killing all three crew members. Investigation found no mechanical failure of aircraft systems.
records.probable_cause: The accident resulted from autopilot malfunction causing loss of aircraft control during descent (p. 14-20). The investigation found no mechanical failure of the airframe or primary flight control systems (p. 14-20).

factors.evidence: Autopilot was engaged during cruise at 24,000 feet and disengaged 12 seconds after the autopilot failure light illuminated (p. 14-16).
Both directional and longitudinal control were lost immediately after autopilot disengaged (p. 14-16, 20).
Aircraft lost control moments after autopilot failure light came on; crashed 73 seconds after the light illuminated with aircraft in 45-50 degree descent (p. 16-20).
Aircraft descended from 24,000 feet in steep 45-50 degree descent angle at impact speed approximately 460 knots (p. 20).

events.text: Aircraft at 24,000 feet over Italian territory with autopilot engaged when autopilot failure light illuminated (p. 14).
AP FAIL warning activated on aircraft (p. 14).
Autopilot disengaged 12 seconds after failure light illumination; directional and longitudinal control immediately lost (p. 14-16).
Aircraft began steep descent at 45-50 degrees; crew reported engine power loss to Milan ATC before losing radio contact at 13,500 feet (p. 16-17).
Aircraft descended through 10,000 feet in continuous steep descent (p. 17-18).
Aircraft approached terrain at high descent rate (p. 18-19).
Aircraft altitude continued descent at high rate toward impact (p. 19).
Aircraft impacted terrain at Besurica between Milan and Parma at steep 45-50 degree angle with estimated impact speed 460 knots, destroying fuselage and killing all three crew members (p. 20).

notes: Italian ANSV report; sections read: Flight recorders section (p. 14-20), investigation findings
Eight events extracted with times relative to autopilot failure (t0)
Report states no mechanical failure found; probable cause focuses on autopilot malfunction
No formal recommendations section identified in available sections

records.title: Comair 5191

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Attempted Takeoff From Wrong Runway, Comair Flight 5191, Bombardier CL-600-2B19, N431CA, Lexington, Kentucky, August 27, 2006

location.name: Beyond the end of runway 26, Blue Grass Airport, Lexington, Kentucky

records.summary: Before dawn at Lexington, the CRJ-100 was cleared for takeoff from runway 22 but the crew taxied onto the unlit, 3,500-foot general aviation runway 26 and began the takeoff roll. The first officer remarked on the absence of runway lights but the takeoff continued; the airplane ran off the end of the runway at about 137 knots, struck a berm and trees and burned. The captain, flight attendant and all 47 passengers died; the first officer survived with serious injuries. The single tower controller on duty was performing administrative tasks and did not see the airplane take the wrong runway.
records.probable_cause: The flight crewmembers' failure to use available cues and aids to identify the airplane's location on the airport surface during taxi and their failure to cross-check and verify that the airplane was on the correct runway before takeoff. Contributing to the accident were the flight crew's nonpertinent conversation during taxi, which resulted in a loss of positional awareness, and the Federal Aviation Administration's failure to require that all runway crossings be authorized only by specific air traffic control clearances.

factors.evidence: The airplane taxied onto runway 26 (3,500 feet, unlit) instead of the assigned runway 22 (7,003 feet) and began its takeoff roll.
The crew lost positional awareness during taxi and did not use the compass heading, runway markings, signage or lack of lights to detect that they were on the wrong runway.
Neither pilot cross-checked the runway heading against the assigned runway before takeoff, and the first officer's comment about the missing lights did not prompt a rejected takeoff.
The crew held nonpertinent conversation during taxi, contrary to sterile cockpit rules, which the NTSB found contributed to the loss of positional awareness.
The crew did not follow Comair's taxi and pre-takeoff verification procedures for confirming the departure runway.
Recent taxiway construction had changed the route to runway 22, the airport diagram in the crew's charts did not reflect the changes, and runway 26 was unlit.
The accident occurred before dawn in darkness, reducing the visual cues available to identify the runway.
A single controller was handling tower and radar duties, contrary to FAA staffing guidance, and was performing an administrative traffic count while the airplane taxied onto the wrong runway.
The FAA did not require that all runway crossings be authorized only by specific ATC clearances, and had not enforced two-controller staffing at the facility.
The airplane became airborne only briefly after running off the end of runway 26, struck an earthen berm, a fence and trees.
The airplane was destroyed by impact forces and post-crash fire.

events.text: Ground control clears the flight to taxi to runway 22; the crew engage in nonpertinent conversation during the taxi.
The crew taxi along taxiway Alpha, past construction changes not shown on their airport diagram, toward the runway 26 crossing that leads to runway 22.
