Tower controller clears 'Comair 191' to fly runway heading and take off; he then turns away to perform an administrative traffic count.
The captain turns the airplane onto runway 26 instead of continuing across it to runway 22, and transfers control to the first officer for the takeoff.
Takeoff thrust is set and the takeoff roll begins on the unlit 3,500-foot runway 26; the heading indicator shows about 260 degrees rather than 220.
First officer remarks 'that is weird with no lights'; the captain replies 'yeah' and the takeoff continues.
'One hundred knots' callout.
Captain calls 'V one, rotate' and then 'whoa' as the runway end approaches.
The airplane runs off the end of runway 26 at about 137 knots, strikes an earthen berm and briefly becomes airborne.
The airplane strikes the airport perimeter fence and trees, breaks apart and catches fire; the recording ends.
Airport police and rescue personnel reach the wreckage and pull the first officer, the only survivor, from the cockpit.

cvr.speaker: FO
cvr.text: that is weird with no lights.

recommendations.text: Require that all runway crossings be authorized only by a specific air traffic control clearance and prohibit taxi clearances that cross a runway without explicit instruction.
recommendations.outcome: FAA revised ATC procedures in 2010 so that explicit clearance is required for every runway crossing.

recommendations.text: Require operators to establish procedures for flight crews to confirm the assigned runway, including verification of runway heading and identification, before starting the takeoff roll.
recommendations.outcome: Operators added a line-up check of runway identification and heading to before-takeoff procedures; FAA issued guidance on wrong-runway takeoffs.

recommendations.text: Require cockpit moving map displays or automatic runway awareness systems that alert crews when they are not on the intended runway.
recommendations.outcome: Runway awareness and advisory systems were widely but voluntarily adopted.

recommendations.text: Ensure that runway and taxiway construction changes are promptly reflected in airport diagrams and NOTAMs and that closed or unlit runways are clearly marked.
Ensure air traffic control facilities are staffed so that a controller is not required to handle both tower and radar positions alone during periods of activity.
recommendations.outcome: FAA revised staffing at Lexington and similar facilities to provide two controllers during overnight and early morning hours.

safety_changes: FAA required explicit ATC clearance for every runway crossing from June 2010, ending taxi clearances that implied crossing authority.
Airlines added runway verification ('line-up check') steps to before-takeoff procedures, confirming runway identification and heading.
Runway awareness and advisory systems and electronic moving map displays were adopted across much of the U.S. airline fleet.

The FAA revised controller staffing guidance to ensure two controllers are on duty when tower and radar positions are both active, and reinforced sterile cockpit compliance through Safety Alerts for Operators.

notes: The clock for the start of the takeoff roll (t0) is estimated at about 06:06:05 EDT; the report's CVR times for 'that is weird with no lights' (06:06:24), 'one hundred knots' (06:06:31), 'V one, rotate' (06:06:33) and the end of recording (about 06:06:36) are used to place later events. t0 may be off by up to 10 seconds.
The takeoff clearance time 06:05:15 is as recalled from the report and may be off by a few seconds.
Speed at the runway end (about 137 knots) is from the report's performance study.
Aircraft MSN not given because it is not recalled with confidence.

records.title: Royal Air Force Nimrod XV230

agencies.name: Ministry of Defence
agencies.report_title: The Nimrod Review: An independent review into the broader issues surrounding the loss of the RAF Nimrod MR2 Aircraft XV230 in Afghanistan in 2006

records.summary: RAF Hawker Siddeley Nimrod MR2 XV230 suffered a catastrophic in-flight fire on September 2, 2006 during a routine mission over Kandahar Province, Afghanistan, while returning from Air-to-Air Refueling. Fuel accumulated in an aft compartment near the starboard wing root and auto-ignited when contacting a hot air duct at 400 degrees Celsius. The crew immediately descended from 23,000 feet but the fire spread rapidly. The aircraft exploded at approximately 3,000 feet above ground level near Kandahar. All 14 personnel on board, including 12 RAF crew and two mission specialists, perished.
records.probable_cause: Escaped fuel from the tank blow-off valve during Air-to-Air Refueling accumulated in the No. 7 Tank Dry Bay, saturating the Refrasil insulation around the Supplementary Cooling Pack air duct. The fuel auto-ignited upon contact with the 400-degree-Celsius hot air duct element. The catastrophic fire overwhelmed the crew's emergency procedures during the emergency descent to Kandahar.

factors.evidence: Fuel escaped during Air-to-Air Refueling at 11:11 hours, likely from tank blow-off valve overflow (p. 6).
Design flaw in location of fuel tank blow-off valve and lack of fire detection/suppression in fuel tank dry bays, identified by Haddon-Cave Review (p. 8).
Fuel-saturated insulation in SCP muff reached auto-ignition temperature when contacting 400-degree-Celsius air duct (p. 6).
Aircraft aged, having been in service since 1969, first Nimrod to enter RAF service (p. 7).
Nimrod Safety Case failed to identify catastrophic fire risk despite hazard analysis requirements (p. 10).
Harrier GR7 pilot observed starboard wing exploding followed by fuselage explosion at 3,000 feet (p. 6).

events.text: RAF Nimrod XV230 took off from Deployed Operational Base in early morning with full crew of 12 plus two mission specialists.
Fuel escape during Air-to-Air Refueling from Tristar tanker; approximately 1.5 minutes after AAR completion.
Fire warning in bomb bay and smoke/hydraulic mist warning in elevator bay alert crew to emergency.
Aircraft depressurized.
Camera operator reported 'we have flames coming from the rear of the engines on the starboard side.'
Crew transmitted MAYDAY and diverted to Kandahar airfield; emergency descent initiated.
Harrier GR7 pilot observed Nimrod in descent with flames from starboard wing root and aft fuselage.
Harrier pilot reported aircraft explosion at approximately 3,000 feet above ground; wreckage struck ground near Chalaghor village.

recommendations.text: Establish systematic airworthiness audit and independent safety advisor regime
Implement proper Safety Case methodology per Defence Standard 00-56

safety_changes: RAF implemented comprehensive review of Nimrod fleet airworthiness post-2006
MOD reformed safety case procedures for military aircraft
Enhanced focus on independent safety advisor oversight in aircraft modification programs

notes: Haddon-Cave Review (The Nimrod Review, 2009) analyzed loss of XV230
Board of Inquiry findings confirmed by AAIB and US Air Force Safety Center
No survivors; all 14 personnel killed in flight

records.title: Gol Transportes Aéreos 1907

agencies.name: Centro de Investigação e Prevenção de Acidentes Aeronáuticos
agencies.report_title: Final Report A-022/CENIPA/2008, PR-GTD and N600XL, 29 September 2006

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: NTSB comments appended to the CENIPA final report

location.name: Amazon rainforest near Peixoto de Azevedo, Mato Grosso

records.summary: An Embraer Legacy 600 business jet on its delivery flight from São José dos Campos to Manaus was cleared by ATC to FL370 and was not descended to FL360 at Brasília as its flight plan required. Its transponder inadvertently went to standby, disabling both its TCAS and the 737's ability to detect it, and Brasília ACC lost radio contact without acting on the loss of Mode C. The Legacy's winglet struck the left wing of Gol 1907, a 737-800 cruising at FL370 in the opposite direction on the same airway. The 737 broke up and crashed into the jungle with 154 dead; the Legacy landed at Cachimbo air base.
records.probable_cause: CENIPA concluded that the collision resulted from a combination of errors in the air traffic control system and by the Legacy crew: ATC issued a clearance to FL370 to Manaus that conflicted with the flight plan, failed to recognise the loss of the Legacy's transponder and its non-compliance with the planned level, did not re-establish communication or advise the Legacy to change level, and was affected by workload, staffing and training deficiencies; the Legacy crew inadvertently switched the transponder to standby, did not notice its loss for almost an hour, and did not manage the loss of communication adequately. The NTSB's appended comments placed greater weight on the ATC system.

factors.evidence: São José tower cleared the Legacy to FL370 to Manaus, contrary to the flight plan's FL360 segment after Brasília, and Brasília ACC never instructed a level change or re-established contact after the transponder and radio contact were lost.

CENIPA found deficiencies in controller training, staffing, supervision and sector handover procedures at Brasília ACC, including failure to act on the loss of the Legacy's Mode C for about 50 minutes.
The Legacy's transponder went to standby, most likely through inadvertent crew input on the radio management unit, and the crew did not notice the TCAS OFF indication for nearly an hour.
The Legacy crew remained at FL370 past Brasília instead of the planned FL360 and did not apply the loss-of-communication procedure after failing to reach Brasília ACC.
The Legacy's avionics presented the transponder standby status and TCAS OFF as small annunciations that did not attract the crew's attention.
CENIPA identified systemic deficiencies in the Brazilian ATC system's procedures, training and supervision at the time of the accident.
The Legacy crew were on their first flight in the aircraft type in Brazil with limited familiarity with the avionics and with Brazilian procedures.
The Legacy's left winglet struck the 737's left wing at FL370 at 19:56:54 UTC; the 737 lost part of its wing, broke up and crashed.

events.text: Legacy N600XL departs São José dos Campos for Manaus, cleared to FL370 by the tower; its flight plan calls for FL370 to Brasília, FL360 to TERES and FL380 thereafter.
Gol 1907 departs Manaus for Brasília and climbs to FL370 on airway UZ6, the reciprocal of the Legacy's route.
Last two-way radio contact between Brasília ACC and the Legacy; the controller gives no instruction to descend to FL360 at Brasília.
The Legacy passes over Brasília VOR and continues at FL370 rather than the planned FL360.
The Legacy's transponder goes to standby; Mode C and TCAS are lost. Brasília ACC's radar label changes to show the planned level rather than a measured altitude.
Brasília ACC controllers do not recognise or act on the loss of the Legacy's Mode C return; the sector is handed over without the discrepancy being resolved.

Brasília ACC begins attempts to contact the Legacy, without success; over the following half hour the controller makes several calls and the Legacy crew make many calls on the wrong or unresponsive frequencies.
The Legacy crew, unaware of the transponder status, continue at FL370 in radio blind; Gol 1907 at FL370 has no TCAS target to detect.
Head-on collision at FL370: the Legacy's left winglet cuts through the left wing of the 737. The 737 rolls, breaks up and falls into the jungle; all 154 aboard die.
The damaged Legacy lands at Cachimbo air base (Serra do Cachimbo); its seven occupants are uninjured.

recommendations.text: Revise ATC procedures so that clearances are consistent with filed flight plans, and that loss of transponder or radio contact with an aircraft under control triggers immediate coordinated action.
Improve controller training, staffing, supervision and the display of aircraft with lost Mode C so that predicted levels are not confused with measured altitude.
Improve the annunciation of transponder standby and TCAS OFF status on the Legacy 600 avionics so the condition is unmistakable to the crew.
Reinforce crew training on loss-of-communication procedures and on transponder and TCAS monitoring in cruise.

dissent.position: In its comments appended to the final report, the NTSB agreed that the loss of the transponder and the crew's failure to notice it were factors, but stated that the air traffic control system's errors, in particular the clearance to FL370 to Manaus, the failure to recognise the loss of Mode C and the lack of level instructions or communication, were the primary cause of the collision, and that the report placed undue weight on the Legacy crew's actions.
dissent.topic: relative weight of ATC versus Legacy crew errors

safety_changes: Brazil restructured airspace control procedures, controller training and staffing at Brasília ACC and reviewed the display of planned versus measured levels on ATC radar.
The FAA and Honeywell reviewed transponder-standby and TCAS-off annunciations on the Legacy 600 avionics.
The accident led to increased emphasis on strategic lateral offset procedures and TCAS monitoring on Brazilian airways.

notes: The collision time 19:56:54 UTC and the Legacy departure (17:51 UTC) are from the report; the transponder loss time (about 19:02 UTC) and the 18:51 last-contact time are given to the minute from the published narrative and t0 is set to the transponder loss.
Crash-site lat/lon left null: the wreckage lay in remote forest near Peixoto de Azevedo and exact coordinates were not verified.
The report number A-022/CENIPA/2008 and date 10 December 2008 are given from memory.
Recommendation ids and exact addressees were not verified.

records.title: 2006 Morecambe Bay helicopter crash

agencies.name: Air Accidents Investigation Branch
agencies.report_title: AAIB Special Bulletin: 1/2007 - Aerospatiale SA365N Dauphin 2, G-BLUN, 27 December 2006

location.name: Approximately 0.25 nautical miles south of North Morecambe platform, Morecambe Bay, Irish Sea

records.summary: A Eurocopter AS365 Dauphin helicopter operating a scheduled transit between gas platforms in Morecambe Bay crashed into the sea during an approach to North Morecambe platform on the night of 27 December 2006. During a dark night with poor weather, the co-pilot handling the helicopter became disoriented and misjudged the approach path. The co-pilot's request for assistance was not clearly articulated, and the commander's takeover was delayed approximately 4 seconds and not smooth. All seven occupants, including both flight crew, perished.
records.probable_cause: The co-pilot became disoriented in dark night and poor weather conditions, misjudging the approach path. The transfer of control to the commander was delayed and not smooth because the co-pilot did not articulate his need clearly and the commander was not mentally primed to assume control.

factors.evidence: The accident occurred during dark night conditions on 27 December 2006 at 1834 hrs, removing external visual references (p. 1).
Poor weather conditions with visibility between 3 to 5 nautical miles and rain reported at the time of approach (p. 1).
The co-pilot handling the helicopter became disoriented in dark night and poor weather conditions, misjudging the approach path during approach to North Morecambe platform (p. 1, 2).
The co-pilot did not articulate clearly his need for assistance; the request for help was not sufficiently explicit, hindering the commander's recognition of the need to take control (p. 1).
The commander was not mentally primed to take control of the helicopter, resulting in delayed and not smooth transfer of control approximately 4 seconds after co-pilot indicated difficulty (p. 1).
The helicopter crashed into the sea approximately 0.25 nautical miles south of North Morecambe platform with all seven occupants killed; fuselage disintegrated on impact (p. 1).

events.text: Helicopter departs Millom West platform at 1826 hrs, commencing transit to North Morecambe platform at height of 500 feet; co-pilot is handling pilot
Helicopter makes initial approach to North Morecambe platform on heading of 120°(M); approach appears normal to helideck team
During later stages of approach, helicopter slowly pitches nose down and commences slow roll to right; collective lever raised increasing power
Crew becomes unhappy with approach; co-pilot asks for assistance from commander
Commander takes control of helicopter as go-around is commenced; helicopter continues to roll to right and pitch nose down

One second after commander assumes control, helicopter attains maximum nose-down pitch attitude of 38° coincident with 38° bank angle to right; indicated airspeed 80 knots, radio altitude 300 feet, rate of descent 1,400 feet per minute

Over next 2.5 seconds, helicopter rolls level and pitch attitude reduces to 13° nose down; radio altitude 170 feet, indicated airspeed over 100 knots, rate of descent approximately 1,400 feet per minute
Over next 5.5 seconds, helicopter commences slow roll to right; pitch attitude remains relatively unchanged; indicated airspeed continues to increase
Last recorded parameters indicate radio altitude of 30 feet, 12° nose-down pitch attitude, indicated airspeed 126 knots, and angle of bank 20° to right
Helicopter crashes into the sea approximately 0.25 nautical miles south of North Morecambe platform; fuselage disintegrates on impact
Helideck team hears crash into sea; alarm raised and coastguard contacted at 1835 hrs; six bodies recovered that evening; seventh occupant remains missing

notes: Events extracted from flight progression and recorded data analysis (p. 1-2)
11 events documented with derived clock times from departure at 1826 hrs and crash at 1834 hrs (8 minutes elapsed)
Key sections read: History of Flight (p. 1), Recorded Data (p. 1-2), Engineering (p. 1), Weather (p. 1)
This is a Special Bulletin; detailed final investigation report not yet completed at time of publication
Spatial disorientation in dark night with poor weather contributed to crew coordination failure
No evidence of pre-impact mechanical malfunction; human factors were primary cause

records.title: Air France 7775
records.summary: Régional Flight 7775, a Fokker 100, crashed shortly after takeoff with heavy ice contamination on the wings. The aircraft lifted off with 144 knots airspeed and 11.9° angle of attack but experienced immediate loss of control due to aerodynamic degradation from ice accumulation. After several roll oscillations reaching 67° of bank, the aircraft touched down on its landing gear near the runway, bounced, overran 340 meters through the airport perimeter, crossed a road and struck a truck, killing the driver. All 54 aircraft occupants evacuated safely.
records.probable_cause: The accident resulted from a loss of control during takeoff caused by ice contamination on the wing surfaces combined with rapid pitch rotation in response to birds. The crew did not de-ice the aircraft despite meteorological conditions meeting the criteria for frost accumulation, insufficient awareness within the French aviation community of ground icing risks and their effects on aircraft performance, and the particular sensitivity of the Fokker 100 (without slats) to ground contamination.

factors.evidence: Heavy ice accumulated on wing surfaces due to meteorological conditions (air temperature 0°C, dew point -1°C, humidity >90%), reducing aerodynamic lift and increasing drag. Ice on the wings created contamination of the upper surface particularly on the leading edge (p. 70-71).

The captain did not initiate de-icing procedures despite meteorological conditions meeting the AFM criteria for frost risk. The aircraft was not equipped with ground edge heaters and no de-icing was performed before takeoff (p. 73-74).

The angle of attack increased to 12° at liftoff but reached 17° during the bank angle oscillations. With contaminated wings, the stall margin was reduced significantly below certification minimums (p. 65-66).
The left wing stalled at approximately 11-12° angle of attack, below the stall warning threshold of 17°, due to the aerodynamic effects of ice contamination (p. 62-65).
Uncontrolled roll oscillations followed the stall, with maximum bank angles of 35° left, 67° right, and 59° left. The control inputs could not suppress these oscillations (p. 66-67).
The aircraft touched down at 160 knots with the right main landing gear, bounced, and the captain attempted a belly landing (p. 61).

After touchdown and bounce, the aircraft rolled 340 meters through grass and collided with the airport perimeter fence, crossed a public road, struck a truck, and came to rest in a field. The landing gear was sheared off during the road crossing (p. 61).

events.text: Takeoff clearance granted for runway 13
TOGA power selected; crew observes birds in vicinity of runway
Aircraft lifts off runway 13 at 128 knots, immediately banks left with 35° maximum bank angle; bank angle alarm activates
Aircraft banks right to 67° maximum bank angle, then left again to 59°; don't sink alarm sounds at 107 feet altitude with right main landing gear touching ground at 160 knots
Captain reduces engine power and decides to abort takeoff; aircraft touches ground near end of runway 13

Aircraft slides 340 meters through grass, collides with airport perimeter fence, crosses departmental road RD289 striking truck cabin and killing driver, then slides into field as landing gear is sheared off
Engine two fail
Captain orders emergency evacuation

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: Le sol air france roméo tango mayday mayday mayday
cvr.translation: Ground air france roméo tango mayday mayday mayday

recommendations.text: Ensure that information regarding aircraft aerodynamic behavior when subjected to ground icing and accidents related to this phenomenon is provided to pilots during type qualifications and periodic training.
Ensure that operators in cooperation with manufacturers provide navigants with information about known accidents concerning their aircraft types, operating context, and their airline.
Ensure that operators have established organization and means including training to enable effective implementation of surface condition verification procedures when ground icing risk exists.

While maintaining operational requirements for de-icing checks before flight, evolve certification specifications to require analysis of aircraft behavior when wing surfaces are contaminated on the ground and ensure acceptable safety margins in case of light contamination.
Mandate installation of ground edge heating devices on the Fokker 28 fleet to reduce contamination risk on the critical leading edge area.
Ensure emergency evacuation procedures conform to those described in the AFM and can be executed rapidly even if a pilot is unavailable or incapacitated.
Study in cooperation with manufacturers and operators the opportunity to impose sufficient information and training for passengers seated near emergency exits.

notes: Extracted from BEA Final Report synopsis, findings, causes, recommendations, and CVR transcript sections
All factor evidence includes page citations from report
8 events extracted from detailed chronology with exact UTC times from CVR
Aircraft state values from FDR data at key moments

records.title: Blue Angels airshow crash
records.summary: During the final minutes of an airshow at Marine Corps Air Station Beaufort, Blue Angels aircraft number 6 crashed in a residential neighborhood. LCDR Kevin Davis, attempting to catch up to the lead aircraft with a faster and tighter turn than usual while performing a rendezvous maneuver, experienced a high-G turn (6.8 G) that subjected him to forces exceeding six times normal gravity. The rapid onset G forces and high turn rate caused spatial disorientation and tunnel vision, resulting in loss of altitude awareness. The aircraft struck terrain while in a steep right-wing-down bank at only 54 degrees, killing the pilot and injuring eight people on the ground.
records.probable_cause: LCDR Davis executed an excessively aggressive turn while attempting to catch up to the other aircraft during a rendezvous maneuver, subjecting himself to high-G forces (6.8 G) at rapid onset rate that caused spatial disorientation and loss of altitude awareness, resulting in loss of control and impact with terrain. (Command Investigation findings)

factors.evidence: LCDR Davis executed a sharper-than-usual right-hand 270-degree turn estimated at 6-7 G's out of the Loop Break Cross maneuver to cross above other aircraft; then performed a 'squatting' turn with rapid onset rate of at least 6.8 G in attempt to rendezvous with the lead aircraft (Delta); witnesses stated #6 was faster than usual and 'really squatted' the jet with a high G turn (Finding 75, 78, 81)

High-G maneuver with rapid onset (6.8 G) resulted in loss of blood flow to brain causing tunnel vision and disorientation; pilot failed to perform proper anti-G straining maneuver (AGSM) throughout the maneuver; pilot did not check in on radio at rendezvous point, indicating loss of situational awareness (Finding 78, 81-84)

After 'squatting the jet,' pilot maintained right-wing-down, slightly nose-low attitude until disappearing below tree line; pilot failed to monitor altitude during high-G turn and did not recover from spatial disorientation before impact (Finding 79)

Aircraft impacted in sparse residential area approximately 3 miles west of MCAS Beaufort; at impact, aircraft was in 6.8G, 54-degree right-wing-down roll, -1.4 degrees nose-down, at 320 knots with both engines at max afterburner; debris field approximately 2,000 feet long; pilot found without pulse strapped in ejection seat at far end of debris field (Finding 93, 94, 100, 107)

events.text: All six McDonnell Douglas F/A-18 Hornets of the Blue Angels are making final turns into landing pattern during airshow at Marine Corps Air Station Beaufort; weather clear with few clouds at 5,000 feet, visibility unlimited, temperature 74°F, winds variable 3 knots (Finding 70)

Blue Angel #6 (LCDR Kevin Davis) executes sharper-than-usual right-hand 270-degree high-G turn estimated at 6-7 G's out of Loop Break Cross maneuver, crossing above #'s 4 and 5 to set up rendezvous (Finding 75)
LCDR Davis goes somewhat wings-level after high-G turn, maintaining level flight path while accelerating toward Delta (lead formation) for rendezvous (Finding 76-77)

LCDR Davis executes 'squatting of the jet' with rapid onset rate turn of at least 6.8 G in attempt to rendezvous with Delta formation; witnesses report #6 faster than normal and 'really squats' the jet with high G turn (Finding 78, 81)
LCDR Davis should check in on radio with callsign per SOP but only a mike click is heard; other pilots, unsure where #6 is, assume minor problem and continue performance (Finding 82-84)

Aircraft maintains right-wing-down, slightly nose-low attitude until disappearing below tree line; aircraft in 6.8G, 54-degree right-wing-down roll, -1.4 degrees nose-down pitch, 320 knots, both engines at maximum afterburner (Finding 79, 94)

Aircraft impacts terrain in sparse residential area approximately 3 miles west of MCAS Beaufort at coordinates N 32 26 89, W080 46 31; aircraft completely destroyed; debris field extends approximately 2,000 feet from first tree impact to final resting position (Finding 93, 100)

LCDR Davis found without pulse, face down, still strapped into ejection seat at far end of debris field; rescue personnel from MCAS Beaufort arrive within 3-4 minutes but pilot does not survive; multiple blunt force injuries determined as cause of death (Finding 107, 110, 115, 117)
Blue Angels #1 and #3 wave off their landings and head to crash site; #1 assumes on-scene commander duties; eight civilians on ground sustain injuries from debris impact (Finding 88-89)

recommendations.text: Implement focused research to develop appropriate G-suit for use by Naval Flight Demonstration Squadron pilots to enhance physiological tolerance to high-G maneuvers

records.title: TAM Linhas Aéreas 3054

agencies.name: Centro de Investigação e Prevenção de Acidentes Aeronáuticos
agencies.report_title: Final Report A-67/CENIPA/2009, PR-MBK, 17 July 2007

location.name: São Paulo Congonhas airport, runway 35L overrun into TAM Express building on Avenida Washington Luís

records.summary: The A320 landed on the wet, recently resurfaced and ungrooved runway 35L at Congonhas with its right thrust reverser deactivated under the MEL. At touchdown the left thrust lever was moved to reverse but the right lever remained in the CLIMB detent. Because one lever was above idle, the ground spoilers did not deploy and the autobrake did not engage, and the right engine continued to deliver climb thrust. The aircraft veered left, ran off the end of the runway, crossed a major avenue and struck a TAM Express warehouse and a fuel station, killing all 187 on board and 12 people on the ground.
records.probable_cause: CENIPA concluded that the accident resulted from the right thrust lever remaining in the CLIMB position during the landing roll while the left was in reverse, which prevented ground spoiler extension and autobrake operation and produced forward thrust on the right engine, so that the aircraft could not be stopped on the runway. Contributing factors included the crew's failure to recognise the thrust lever position, the absence of a specific alert for a thrust lever asymmetry on landing, the deactivated reverser and the procedure in use for landing with a reverser inoperative, deficiencies in crew training and CRM, the wet, ungrooved runway with poor drainage at the time, the absence of a runway end safety area, and inadequacies in the oversight of operations at Congonhas.

factors.evidence: The right engine thrust reverser had been deactivated four days earlier and the aircraft was operating under the MEL with the reverser inoperative.
The FDR showed that at touchdown the left thrust lever was moved to idle and reverse while the right thrust lever remained in the CLIMB detent.
The crew did not move the right thrust lever to idle despite the RETARD callout and the aircraft's failure to decelerate.
The reverser-inoperative landing procedure required both thrust levers to be retarded to idle; the report found the crew's actions did not comply with the procedure in force.
The ground spoiler and autobrake logic inhibited deployment with one thrust lever above idle, and no dedicated warning drew attention to a thrust lever asymmetry on the ground.
Apart from the RETARD callout, the aircraft provided no alert that the spoilers had not deployed or that one engine was producing forward thrust during the landing roll.
CENIPA found deficiencies in the operator's training on landing with a reverser inoperative and on thrust lever handling.
Neither pilot identified the cause of the failure to decelerate in the seconds available; the report cited inadequate crew coordination.
Runway 35L was wet, had recently been resurfaced without grooves, and had poor drainage at the time of the accident.
Congonhas runway 35L had no runway end safety area and ended at a busy avenue and buildings; the runway had been reopened without grooving.
The report cited deficiencies in the oversight of the runway condition and of operations at Congonhas by the regulator and the airport operator.
The aircraft left the end of the runway at high speed, crossed Avenida Washington Luís and struck the TAM Express building.
The aircraft exploded and burned on striking the building and an adjacent fuel station; all on board and 12 on the ground died.

events.text: Four days before the accident the right engine thrust reverser is deactivated and the aircraft continues in service under the MEL.
Congonhas reports runway 35L wet and slippery; the runway has recently been resurfaced and has not yet been grooved.
Crew brief the landing with the right reverser inoperative and continue the approach to runway 35L.
In the flare the RETARD callout sounds; the left thrust lever is retarded to idle but the right thrust lever stays in the CLIMB detent.
Touchdown on runway 35L about 250 m past the threshold; the ground spoilers do not deploy and the autobrake does not engage because one thrust lever is above idle.
Left thrust lever moved to reverse; the right engine, with its lever in CLIMB, spools toward climb thrust as the autothrust disengages.
First officer calls out that the spoilers have not deployed; the captain calls 'decelerate, decelerate'.
Manual braking is applied but the aircraft, with forward thrust on the right engine and no spoilers, barely decelerates and begins to veer left.
The captain calls that the aircraft cannot be stopped and tries to steer; the first officer urges him to turn.
The aircraft leaves the end of runway 35L at about 90 kt, crosses Avenida Washington Luís and strikes the TAM Express building and a fuel station.
The aircraft explodes and burns; all 187 on board and 12 people on the ground die.

recommendations.text: Develop a flight-deck warning for a thrust lever not at idle during landing when the aircraft is on the ground with the other lever in reverse, and review the ground spoiler and autobrake activation logic.
recommendations.outcome: Airbus introduced an ECAM 'ENG x THR LEVER ABV IDLE' style alert and revised procedures; the FAA and EASA issued airworthiness directives for the software update.

recommendations.text: Groove runway 35L at Congonhas, improve drainage, and establish runway end safety areas or equivalent protection.
recommendations.outcome: Runway 35L was grooved and operational restrictions on wet-runway landings at Congonhas were introduced.

recommendations.text: Revise training on landing with a thrust reverser inoperative, thrust lever handling during landing and crew monitoring of the landing roll.
Strengthen regulatory oversight of the operational conditions at Congonhas, including runway condition reporting and wet-runway operations.

safety_changes: Airbus revised the A320 family procedures for landing with a thrust reverser inoperative (both levers to idle, then reverse on the operative engine) and added an alert for a thrust lever above idle on the ground during landing.

records.title: 2007 Phoenix news helicopter collision
records.summary: Two AS-350 AStar helicopters operating news coverage of a Phoenix police pursuit collided at 12:46 p.m. MST on 27 July 2007 over Steele Indian School Park. Both pilots were performing concurrent reporting and visual tracking duties while flying and failed to see and avoid the other helicopter. Contributing factors included high workload from dual reporting duties, lack of formal procedures for coordinating air operations among Phoenix news helicopters, and the failure of both pilots to maintain situational awareness. All four occupants were killed in the collision and subsequent crashes.

records.title: Air Moorea 1121

agencies.name: Bureau of Enquiry and Analysis for Civil Aviation Safety

records.summary: A 28-year-old DHC-6-300 Twin Otter crashed into the sea shortly after takeoff from Moorea when its elevator pitch-up cable failed at 350 feet altitude, causing an uncontrollable nose-down dive. The cable failure resulted from accelerated wear on stainless steel cables from abrasion and the high-frequency takeoff-landing cycle (40 times daily on the 7-minute Moorea-Tahiti route), which was not accounted for in the maintenance inspection intervals.
records.probable_cause: The accident was caused by loss of airplane pitch control following failure of the elevator pitch-up control cable at low altitude. The cable failure resulted from wear and abrasion accelerated by the unusual number of operating cycles, combined with the maintenance schedule not being modified to account for stainless steel cable wear characteristics and high-frequency operations.

the failing cable snapped completely, and the elevator fell into a permanent, full nose-down deflection

There were no modifications made to the maintenance schedule to account for this added wear, nor the higher than usual number of cycles

records.title: China Airlines 120
records.summary: China Airlines Boeing 737-800 caught fire at gate shortly after landing at Naha Airport. During slat retraction, a downstop assembly that had detached during maintenance punctured the wing fuel tank. factors.evidence: During maintenance on the downstop assembly, the washer fell off the nut side of the assembly; maintenance procedure did not include verification that washer remained properly secured (p. 22-25).

Maintenance procedure did not include inspection or verification that critical washer remained properly secured after assembly (p. 22-25).

records.title: British Airways 38

agencies.name: Air Accidents Investigation Branch
agencies.report_title: Report on the accident to Boeing 777-236ER, G-YMMM, at London Heathrow Airport on 17 January 2008

location.name: Undershoot area of runway 27L, London Heathrow Airport

records.summary: On final approach to Heathrow runway 27L, at about 720 ft, the right engine and then the left engine failed to respond to autothrottle commands for increased thrust, their fuel flows falling to little more than idle. The aircraft landed on the grass some 330 m short of the runway threshold; the landing gear collapsed and the aircraft was written off. There were no fatalities.
records.probable_cause: The reduction in thrust on both engines was the result of restricted fuel flow to the engine fuel-oil heat exchangers (FOHE). Ice had accreted in the fuel system during a flight through unusually cold ambient conditions, released as the aircraft approached, and accumulated on the face of the FOHE, restricting fuel flow. The FOHE was found susceptible to restriction when presented with soft ice in a fuel flow of high water concentration; certification requirements did not take account of this phenomenon.

factors.evidence: Ice formed from water in the fuel during the long cold-soaked cruise and was released as fuel flow increased on approach, restricting flow at the FOHE face on both engines.
Both engines rolled back to a fuel flow just above idle and failed to respond to commanded thrust increases at about 720 ft and 620 ft respectively.
Both engines suffered a simultaneous loss of thrust response on short final, leaving insufficient energy to reach the runway.
The fuel-oil heat exchanger design was susceptible to blockage by soft ice in fuel with high water concentration.
Certification requirements did not address the risk of ice accretion and release in fuel systems restricting flow at the FOHE.
With thrust stuck near idle the aircraft could not maintain the approach path and speed decayed toward stick shaker before touchdown.
The aircraft touched down on grass 330 m short of runway 27L; all occupants survived and evacuated.

events.text: Departure from Beijing with 79,000 kg of fuel at a fuel temperature of about -2 C.
Cruise over Siberia and Mongolia in unusually cold air; fuel temperature falls to a minimum of -34 C, remaining above the freezing point of the fuel.
Aircraft is held at Lambourne before being radar vectored for an ILS approach to runway 27L.
Aircraft established on the ILS with autopilot and autothrottle engaged; landing gear down and flap 30 selected.
Autothrottle commands a thrust increase during the approach; both engines initially respond.
At about 720 ft the right engine fails to respond to the autothrottle command; its fuel flow falls to about 6,000 pph.
About seven seconds later, at about 620 ft, the left engine also fails to respond; its fuel flow falls to about 5,000 pph.
First officer, as pilot flying, notices the reduced thrust; airspeed begins to decay below the approach speed.
Captain retracts the flaps from 30 to 25 to reduce drag and extend the glide toward the runway.
Stick shaker activates as the aircraft descends toward the ground short of the runway.
Aircraft touches down on the grass about 330 m short of the runway 27L threshold; landing gear collapses and the aircraft slides to a stop.
Emergency evacuation via the slides; one passenger seriously injured, all 152 occupants survive.

recommendations.text: Introduce interim measures for the Boeing 777 with Rolls-Royce Trent 800 engines to reduce the risk of ice formed from water in the fuel restricting fuel flow at the fuel-oil heat exchanger.
recommendations.outcome: Boeing issued revised operational procedures and Rolls-Royce redesigned the FOHE; a mandatory retrofit followed.

recommendations.text: Review the certification requirements for fuel systems to ensure that aircraft and engine fuel systems are tolerant to the potential build-up and sudden release of ice in the fuel feed system.
Review the design of the Rolls-Royce Trent 800 fuel-oil heat exchanger so that it is not susceptible to blockage by ice released from the fuel system.
recommendations.outcome: Modified FOHE with redesigned inlet introduced and mandated by airworthiness directive.

safety_changes: Redesign of the Rolls-Royce Trent 800 fuel-oil heat exchanger and mandatory retrofit across the 777 fleet.
Interim operational procedures for cold-soaked fuel on 777/Trent aircraft (periodic thrust increases, fuel temperature management).
Research into ice accretion in aircraft fuel systems and review of fuel system certification requirements.

records.title: Belavia 1834
records.summary: During takeoff from Zvartnots International Airport in icing conditions, the aircraft's wings became contaminated with frost and ice. As the CRJ100ER climbed through approximately 5 meters altitude at low airspeed, the left wing stalled due to ice-induced aerodynamic degradation. The aircraft rolled left uncontrollably and crashed, splitting into two pieces and catching fire, but all 21 occupants survived with seven seriously injured.
records.probable_cause: Asymmetric loss of wing lift during takeoff resulting in left wing stall at insufficient altitude for recovery, caused by wing surface contamination with frost that formed from fuel icing during ground handling in cold ambient temperatures. Wing contamination was not detected during the pre-flight inspection despite proper tactile inspection technique being available in the Flight Crew Operating Manual requirements, and was not removed with de-icing fluid application prior to takeoff. (p. 67-68)

factors.evidence: Frost and ice contamination of wing surfaces caused by fuel icing (fuel system icing) during aircraft ground time and taxi before takeoff, resulting from temperature differential between ambient air (-3°C) and cold fuel in tanks (-0°C or colder) following flight at altitude; frost layer 'contaminated' wing surface affecting aerodynamic lift (p. 67, 9)

CRJ-100 airframe aerodynamic characteristics highly sensitive to even minor leading edge contamination; left wing stalled during takeoff as aircraft climbed through ~5 meters altitude at low airspeed; asymmetric stall led to uncontrollable left bank roll (p. 67-68)

Aircraft rolled progressively left-wing-down; left wing tip struck runway surface during takeoff; aircraft departed runway onto ground, rotated inverted through right wing rotation, crossed runway again and came to rest; aircraft split into two pieces and caught fire (p. 10)

records.title: 2008 Biggin Hill Cessna Citation crash
records.summary: Cessna Citation VP-BGE crashed on 30 March 2008 near Farnborough while returning to Biggin Hill after reporting engine vibration shortly after takeoff. The pilot reported engine vibration and requested immediate return one minute after becoming airborne. The aircraft manoeuvred overhead and initiated descent when the crew reported a major power problem. The aircraft crashed into a house in Romsey Close after flying extremely low over a built-up area. All 5 occupants were killed.
records.probable_cause: The pilot reported engine vibration shortly after takeoff and decided to return to the airport. The reported vibration most likely came from a faulty air cycle machine rather than engine malfunction. Both engines were subsequently shut down either intentionally or inadvertently during the short flight. Relight attempts failed because the second engine was attempted to be relit before the first had reached sufficient speed, resulting in dual engine failure and loss of control.

records.title: East Coast Jets 81
records.summary: East Coast Jets Flight 81, a Hawker 800, touched down on runway 30 at Owatonna Degner Regional Airport then the crew initiated a go-around after noticing insufficient runway length remained. The aircraft overran the runway end at high speed, struck the approach lighting system antenna at 5 feet altitude, and crashed into a cornfield 2,136 feet from the runway end, killing all eight occupants. The captain had decided to go around too late with insufficient runway remaining and pilots failed to properly configure the aircraft for deceleration.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause of this accident was the captain's decision to attempt a go-around late in the landing roll with insufficient runway remaining. Contributing to the accident were the pilots' poor crew coordination and lack of cockpit discipline, fatigue which likely impaired both pilots' performance, and the failure of the Federal Aviation Administration to require crew resource management training and standard operating procedures for Part 135 operators.

factors.evidence: Captain decided to go around after aircraft had already touched down and crew noticed insufficient runway length remained (p. 19).

Pilots moved airbrake handle to OPEN position instead of DUMP position, causing only partial airbrake extension (p. 5). First officer stated at 0945:08 we're not dumped, indicating confusion about the system configuration (p. 19).
Pilots did not first select flaps 45 degrees then proper airbrake DUMP position as procedure required (p. 5).
NTSB cited poor crew coordination and lack of cockpit discipline; captain and first officer had conflicting intentions and communication (p. 14).
Fatigue likely impaired both pilots' performance; accident occurred on second leg of five-leg trip sequence (p. 14).
Aircraft overran the end of runway 30, lifting off at 978 feet from runway end and striking approach lighting antenna (p. 20).
Aircraft crashed into cornfield 2,136 feet from runway end after impacting ILS antenna, rolling to 90-degree right bank (p. 20).

Captain approved approach briefing stating it's gonna be the ILS to three zero

First officer stated airbrakes were not deployed properly, captain moved airbrake handle to DUMP position after touchdown

Aircraft overran runway 30 end at high speed, began nose-down pitch toward terrain
Aircraft lifted off ground approximately 978 feet from runway end, approximately 5 feet altitude
Aircraft struck approach lighting system antenna support structure about 1000 feet from runway end, rolled to 90-degree right bank with bank angle warning activated
Aircraft crashed into cornfield approximately 2136 feet from runway end, all eight occupants killed on impact

records.title: Spanair 5022

agencies.name: Comisión de Investigación de Accidentes e Incidentes de Aviación Civil
agencies.report_title: Report A-032/2008: Accident involving a McDonnell Douglas DC-9-82 (MD-82) aircraft, registration EC-HFP, operated by Spanair, at Madrid-Barajas Airport, on 20 August 2008

location.name: Beyond the end of runway 36L, Madrid Barajas Airport

records.summary: After returning to the stand because of an overheating ram air temperature probe, which maintenance addressed by pulling its heater circuit breaker, the MD-82 taxied out again for a second departure. The crew did not extend the flaps and slats for takeoff and the takeoff warning system did not sound. The aircraft rotated, stalled immediately after lift-off, rolled and struck the ground beside the runway, breaking up and burning. 154 of the 172 occupants died.
records.probable_cause: The crew lost control of the aircraft as a consequence of entering a stall immediately after takeoff due to an improper aircraft configuration, with the flaps and slats retracted, following a series of mistakes and omissions, together with the absence of the takeoff configuration warning. The crew did not identify the configuration error because they did not properly use the checklists that contain the items to select and verify the position of the flaps and slats, omitting the flaps/slats item in the After Start checklist, cross-checking of it in the Takeoff Briefing, and the visual check of the flaps/slats when performing the Takeoff Imminent checklist. The TOWS did not function because of a failure whose origin could not be determined, but which was associated with the R2-5 relay and the RAT probe heating problem.

factors.evidence: The flaps and slats were not extended for takeoff; the flap handle was found in the retracted position and the FDR shows flaps at zero.
The crew omitted the flaps/slats item of the After Start checklist, did not cross-check it in the takeoff briefing and did not carry out the visual check in the Takeoff Imminent checklist.
The takeoff warning system (TOWS) did not sound when the throttles were advanced with the flaps retracted.

Maintenance action on the RAT probe overheating consisted of pulling the Z-29 circuit breaker for the probe heater without investigating the cause, which was associated with the R2-5 ground-sensing relay that also feeds the TOWS.
The RAT probe heating on the ground had been reported on earlier flights and was deferred rather than diagnosed.
The TOWS was not designed to be fail-safe and was not monitored for its own failure; the same relay affected both the RAT heater and the TOWS ground logic.
The return to the stand, delay and rushed second departure disrupted the normal flow of the crew's preparation and checklists.
The CVR recorded non-essential conversation and interruptions during the second taxi-out that disrupted checklist execution.
The operator's checklists and the way they were executed did not ensure independent verification of the takeoff configuration.
The stall warning sounded immediately after rotation; the aircraft pitched up, rolled and stalled at low height with flaps retracted.
The crew did not identify the configuration cause and their responses did not recover the aircraft in the few seconds available.
The aircraft rolled alternately right and left with a very high angle of attack and struck the ground beside the runway.
The aircraft broke up and a fuel-fed fire destroyed the fuselage; most fatalities were due to impact and fire.
The report found deficiencies in the oversight of the operator's maintenance and MEL handling and in the harmonisation of TOWS airworthiness requirements.

events.text: During the first taxi to runway 36L the crew note the RAT probe temperature indicating an excessive value on the ground and return to the stand.
Maintenance technicians pull the Z-29 circuit breaker for the RAT probe heater in accordance with the MEL and release the aircraft, without investigating the R2-5 relay.
Engines restarted; the After Start checklist is read but the flaps/slats item is skipped and the flaps remain retracted.
Second taxi to runway 36L; the takeoff briefing does not cross-check the flap setting and there is non-essential conversation in the cockpit.
Takeoff Imminent checklist read; the flaps/slats response is given without a visual check of the handle or indicators.
Throttles advanced for takeoff; the takeoff warning system does not sound although flaps and slats are retracted.
Rotation at about 154 kt; the aircraft lifts off with flaps and slats retracted.
Stall warning and stick shaker activate immediately after lift-off; a synthetic voice calls stall.
The aircraft reaches about 40 ft with a high pitch attitude, then rolls right and left with bank angles of over 30 degrees; the crew apply inputs but do not identify the configuration.
The right wing and tail strike the ground beside the runway; the aircraft skids across the terrain, breaks up and catches fire near a stream.
Fuel-fed fire destroys the fuselage; 154 of the 172 occupants die and 18 survive with injuries.

recommendations.text: Require that takeoff warning systems on transport aircraft be designed so that a failure of the system is detected and indicated to the crew, and that the TOWS is checked before every flight.
recommendations.outcome: Boeing revised MD-80 procedures to include a TOWS check before each takeoff.

recommendations.text: Reinforce checklist discipline, in particular the independent verification of flaps and slats before takeoff, and the application of sterile cockpit rules during taxi.
Improve maintenance troubleshooting and MEL application so that defects with potential links to safety systems are diagnosed rather than deferred.
Investigate the R2-5 relay and RAT probe heating faults on MD-80 series aircraft and their relationship with TOWS operation.

safety_changes: Boeing MD-80 checklist revision requiring a TOWS functional check before every takeoff.
Spanish and European emphasis on sterile cockpit discipline and takeoff configuration verification.
Review of MEL procedures and maintenance troubleshooting for the RAT probe heater circuit on MD-80s.

notes: Clock strings are local time (CEST); the accident occurred at about 14:24 local. Seconds and the earlier taxi/maintenance times are approximate.
Rotation speed (about 154 kt) and the roughly 40 ft maximum height are from the report's FDR analysis; other values approximate.
Sterile cockpit violation is included on the basis of the report's discussion of interruptions and non-essential conversation during taxi; the report did not name it as a cause.
Recommendation ids not reproduced.

records.title: 2008 South Carolina Learjet 60 crash

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report: Runway Overrun During Rejected Takeoff, Global Exec Aviation, Bombardier Learjet 60, N999LJ, Columbia, South Carolina, September 19, 2008

records.summary: Bombardier Learjet 60 N999LJ overran runway 11 during a rejected takeoff at Columbia Metropolitan Airport on 19 September 2008 at 23:55 EDT. Multiple main landing gear tires failed during takeoff roll due to severe underinflation from inadequate maintenance. The captain executed a rejected takeoff after V1 decision speed, which was inconsistent with training. Tire debris damaged the hydraulic system and air-ground sensor, causing reverse thrust to fail. The aircraft overran the runway, struck terrain and roadway, and was destroyed by impact and fire. The captain, first officer, and two passengers were killed; two passengers seriously injured.
records.probable_cause: The operator's inadequate maintenance of the airplane's tires, which resulted in multiple tire failures during takeoff roll due to severe underinflation, and the captain's execution of a rejected takeoff after V1, which was inconsistent with her training and standard operating procedures. Contributing factors included deficiencies in the Learjet 60 thrust reverser system design and FAA certification, inadequate industry training standards for tire failure scenarios, and poor crew resource management.

factors.evidence: Global Exec Aviation's tire pressure inspections were inadequate; all four main landing gear tires were severely underinflated during takeoff roll (p. 3-4, findings 12)

Learjet 60 tires lose approximately 2% of pressure per day and require replacement after 8 days if not properly maintained; the company did not maintain adequate tire pressure check intervals (p. 3, findings 13)

Multiple main landing gear tires failed during takeoff roll at around 144 knots ground speed due to severe underinflation; loud rumbling sound recorded at 2355:12 and tire fragments found on runway (p. 2, history of flight)

Tire debris damaged the plane's hydraulic system causing failure of the air-ground sensing system; the air-ground sensor damage caused it to remain in air mode, preventing reverse thrust engagement (p. 2)
The captain executed a rejected takeoff at 144 knots, which exceeded V1 decision speed of 136 knots; Learjet 60 procedures call for never aborting above V1 (p. 2, findings 9)
Captain had accumulated only about 35 hours total in the Learjet 60 (8 hours as PIC); this was only her second flight of the day with the first officer (p. 4, findings 20-22)

Flight crew demonstrated poor crew resource management; the captain's indecision in responding to the anomaly and failure to follow standard operating procedures resulted from limited CRM skills and limited Learjet 60 experience (p. 72, findings 22)

The Learjet 60 thrust reverser system had design flaws that permitted failure of critical systems in the wheel well area to result in uncommanded forward thrust; FAA certification of the aircraft as a changed aeronautical product failed to detect this deficiency (p. 2, findings 17-19)

After tire debris damaged the hydraulic system and air-ground sensor, the aircraft experienced uncommanded forward thrust instead of reverse thrust; this accelerated the aircraft when full reverse thrust was commanded, increasing runway excursion speed (p. 2, findings 10)
Tire fragments damaged the plane's hydraulic system, causing the plane's brakes to fail; the aircraft could not decelerate (p. 2, findings 10)

Aircraft overran the runway end at Columbia Metropolitan Airport, passed through the 1,000-foot runway safety area, struck airport infrastructure and lighting, descended a steep downhill slope, crossed South Carolina Highway 302, and came to rest on an embankment before striking a lighting pole and perimeter fence (p. 2-3)

events.text: Ground controller provided taxi clearance to runway 11; captain initially turned left onto taxiway U instead of following amended clearance (p. 2)
Captain briefed rejected takeoff procedure; stated would abort for anything below 80 knots after V1, and after V2 would treat as in-flight emergency (p. 2)
Captain initiated takeoff roll from runway 11 at Columbia Metropolitan Airport (p. 2)
First officer reported V1 decision speed of 136 knots reached (p. 2)
Loud rumbling sound began; aircraft at position corresponding to first main landing gear tire fragment location; multiple tires failed during takeoff roll (p. 2)
Ground controller observed sparks from right main landing gear area (p. 2-3)
Aircraft ground speed reached peak of approximately 144 knots; captain stated 'go?' indicating uncertainty; aircraft had exceeded V1 speed (p. 2)
Captain stated 'I don't know. We're not goin' though.' - decision to execute rejected takeoff after V1 (p. 2)
Captain commanded 'full out' (full reverse thrust) (p. 2)
Tire debris damaged hydraulic system and air-ground sensor; air-ground sensor went to air mode, preventing reverse thrust engagement; uncommanded forward thrust occurred instead (p. 2)
Aircraft brakes failed due to hydraulic system damage; aircraft began accelerating despite reverse thrust commands (p. 2)

Aircraft overran runway 11, passed through runway safety area, struck airport lighting and navigation antennas, descended steep downhill slope, crossed South Carolina Highway 302, and came to rest on embankment with aircraft destroyed by impact and fire; captain, first officer, and two passengers killed; two passengers seriously injured (p. 3)
