cvr.text: I don't know. We're not goin' though.

cvr.speaker: FO
cvr.text: roll the equipment we're goin' off the end

recommendations.text: Provide pilots and maintenance personnel with information that (1) transport-category aircraft tires can lose up to 5-percent pressure per day, (2) it may take only a few days for such tires to reach an underinflation level below what the aircraft maintenance manual specifies for tire replacement, and (3) the underinflation level that would require tire replacement is not visually detectable.

Require that all 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 121, 135, and 91 subpart K operators perform tire pressure checks at a frequency that will ensure that the tires remain inflated to within aircraft maintenance manual-specified inflation pressures.
Require that aircraft maintenance manuals specify, in a readily identifiable and standardized location, required maintenance intervals for tire pressure checks (as applicable to each aircraft).
Allow pilots to perform tire pressure checks on aircraft, regardless of whether the aircraft is operating under 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91, Part 91 subpart K, or Part 135.
Require tire pressure monitoring systems for all transport-category airplanes.

Identify the deficiencies in Learjet's system safety analyses, both for the original Learjet 60 design and for the modifications after the 2001 accident, that failed to properly address the thrust reverser system design flaws related to this accident, and require Learjet to perform a system safety assessment in accordance with 14 Code of Federal Regulations 25.1309 for all other systems that also rely on air-ground signal integrity and ensure that hazards resulting from a loss of signal integrity are appropriately mitigated to fully comply with this regulation.

Revise available safety assessment guidance (such as Advisory Circular 25.1309-1A) for manufacturers to adequately address the deficiencies identified in Safety Recommendation A-10-51, require that designated engineering representatives and their Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) mentors are trained on this methodology, and modify FAA design oversight procedures to ensure that manufacturers are performing system safety analyses for all new or modified designs that effectively identify and properly mitigate hazards for all phases of flight, including foreseeable events during those phases (such as a rejected takeoff).

Define and codify minimum simulator model fidelity requirements for tire failure scenarios. These requirements should include tire failure scenarios during takeoff that present the need for rapid evaluation and execution of procedures and provide realistic sound and motion cueing.

Once the simulator model fidelity requirements requested in Safety Recommendation A-10-55 are implemented, require that simulator training for pilots who conduct turbojet operations include opportunities to practice responding to events other than engine failures occurring both near V1 and after V1, including, but not limited to, tire failures.

safety_changes: Enhanced maintenance requirements for tire pressure checks on transport-category aircraft
Improved design standards for thrust reverser system safety
Increased emphasis on tire failure recognition and response in simulator training

notes: Read key sections: Executive Summary (p. viii-12), History of Flight (p. 1-3), key findings (p. 71-72), and Probable Cause (p. 73)
Complete NTSB investigation with clear findings on all contributing factors
Multiple causal factors identified: maintenance failures, design flaws, procedural noncompliance, and crew resource management issues
CVR transcript provides precise timing of events; ground speed estimates from accident performance studies

records.title: Qantas 72

agencies.name: Australian Transport Safety Bureau
agencies.report_title: In-flight upset, Airbus A330-303, VH-QPA, 154 km west of Learmonth, WA, 7 October 2008

location.name: Indian Ocean, 154 km west of Learmonth, Western Australia

records.summary: Cruising at 37,000 ft off Western Australia, the A330's number 1 air data inertial reference unit began outputting intermittent spikes on many parameters. The autopilot disconnected and a stream of spurious warnings followed. Two minutes later the flight control computers, acting on spike angle-of-attack values, commanded an abrupt nose-down pitch that threw unrestrained occupants against the ceiling; a second, smaller pitch-down followed. The crew diverted to Learmonth, where the aircraft landed safely; 12 people were seriously injured and many more hurt.
records.probable_cause: The ATSB found that one of the aircraft's three ADIRUs entered a failure mode in which it output numerous spikes with incorrect data and labels, including angle-of-attack spikes. A limitation in the flight control primary computers' algorithm for processing angle-of-attack data meant that two spikes 1.2 seconds apart could pass the filtering and trigger the high-AoA protection, commanding the pitch-downs. The ADIRU failure mode's origin could not be determined; the FCPC algorithm limitation had not been identified during the design and certification safety assessment.

factors.evidence: ADIRU 1 began outputting spikes in many parameters with incorrect data and labels at 0440:28 UTC; the specific trigger for the failure mode could not be identified.
Autopilot 1 disconnected at the onset of the ADIRU failure, and the crew flew manually with numerous alerts active.
Spurious overspeed and stall warnings alternated on the flight deck as a result of the corrupted air data.
The crew received a large number of spurious warnings, cautions and fault messages that did not reflect the actual aircraft state, and no procedure existed for the ADIRU failure mode.

The FCPC angle-of-attack processing algorithm could not correctly manage a scenario with multiple spikes 1.2 seconds apart, so the spikes triggered the high-AoA protection and the pitch-down commands.
The ATSB found that the ADIRU failure mode and the FCPC algorithm's vulnerability to it were not identified in the design and certification safety assessment process.
The two pitch-down manoeuvres were commanded by the flight control system, not the crew; the first reached about -0.8 g and 8.4 degrees nose-down.
The crew dealt with continuous alerts, cabin injuries and a diversion with degraded information.
After declaring PAN and then MAYDAY, the crew landed at Learmonth about 50 minutes after the upset.

events.text: Cruising at FL370 toward Perth with 303 passengers and 12 crew; the captain is pilot flying and the first officer is on a rest break, with the second officer in the right seat.
ADIRU 1 begins outputting intermittent spikes on multiple parameters with incorrect labels; autopilot 1 disconnects and a NAV IR 1 FAULT is displayed with a master caution.
Stall and overspeed warnings alternate, and numerous spurious ECAM cautions appear; the captain's airspeed and altitude indications show momentary spikes.
The captain flies manually and the crew begin assessing the alerts; the first officer is recalled to the flight deck.

The flight control computers, acting on two angle-of-attack spikes 1.2 s apart, command an abrupt nose-down: about 8.4 degrees pitch-down and -0.8 g. Unrestrained passengers and crew strike the cabin ceiling; the aircraft loses about 650 ft.
The captain applies back-stick and the aircraft returns to about FL370; the crew make a PAN call and begin considering a diversion.
A second, smaller uncommanded pitch-down occurs; the aircraft loses about 400 ft before the crew recover.
The crew decide to divert to Learmonth, the nearest suitable airport, and declare PAN; on learning of serious cabin injuries they upgrade to MAYDAY.
Descent and approach to Learmonth flown manually with the crew treating the flight control and air data indications with caution.
The aircraft lands at Learmonth. Twelve people are seriously injured and many others hurt; ambulances and later aeromedical flights take the injured to Perth.

recommendations.text: Redesign the flight control primary computer angle-of-attack processing algorithm so that erroneous spike data cannot trigger the high angle-of-attack protection, and provide crews with a procedure for the ADIRU failure mode.
recommendations.outcome: Airbus modified the FCPC software (mandated by EASA airworthiness directive) and issued an operations engineering bulletin instructing crews to switch off the affected ADIRU.

recommendations.text: Investigate the ADIRU failure mode and improve the unit's internal data checking and built-in test so that corrupted output is detected and flagged.
recommendations.outcome: The ADIRU's failure mode could not be reproduced; the manufacturer improved the unit's data-integrity checks.

recommendations.text: Reinforce advice to passengers to keep seat belts fastened while seated, since most injuries were to unrestrained occupants.

safety_changes: Airbus redesigned the A330/A340 FCPC angle-of-attack algorithm; the modification was mandated by airworthiness directive.
An operations engineering bulletin and later a permanent procedure instruct crews to switch off an ADIRU displaying the NAV IR fault so that its data is no longer used.
The FAA and EASA issued airworthiness directives on the affected Northrop Grumman ADIRU model.
The ATSB issued safety advice on the importance of keeping seat belts fastened when seated.

notes: Clock times for the ADIRU failure (0440:28), first pitch-down (0442:27) and second pitch-down (0445:08) are as recalled from the ATSB report; the landing time (0532) is approximate.
Location latitude and longitude are an approximation of 154 km west of Learmonth over the Indian Ocean.
The report describes a subsequent reversion of the flight control law; this is omitted because the exact circumstances were not verified.
Serious injuries are given as 12 (one flight attendant and 11 passengers); over 100 occupants received some injury.

records.title: Ryanair Flight 4102

agencies.name: Agenzia Nazionale per la Sicurezza del Volo

records.summary: Boeing 737-800 encountered a massive flock of starlings during very short final approach to Rome Ciampino. Both engines lost thrust due to bird ingestion. The captain initiated a go-around maneuver but the aircraft descended rapidly due to insufficient thrust. The aircraft hit the runway heavily, causing main left landing gear to detach and left engine nacelle to contact the runway.
records.probable_cause: The accident has been caused by an unexpected loss of both engines thrust as a consequence of a massive bird strike during the go-around manoeuvre. The loss of thrust prevented the aircrew from performing a successful go around and led the aircraft to an unstabilized runway contact.

factors.evidence: The aircraft collided with a thick flock of birds (later identified as starlings) during very short final approach with the aircraft fully configured for landing (p. 2)
Both engines not delivering the necessary thrust as a consequence of massive bird ingestion with organic residues and bird feathers on stator and rotor blades (p. 2)

The lack of instructions to flight crew concerning the most suitable procedures to adopt in case of single or multiple bird strikes in the landing phase; absence of specific training in management of surprise and startle effects in critical flight phases (p. 113)

The captain's decision to perform a go around when the aircraft was at approximately 7 seconds from touchdown was significantly influenced by lack of training in managing startle effect in critical phases (p. 113)

The aircraft descended rapidly with insufficient thrust and hit the runway heavily in proximity of taxiway AC, causing main left landing gear to detach and left engine nacelle to contact runway (p. 2)

events.text: Boeing 737-8AS registration EI-DYG (RYR41CH) took off from Frankfurt Hahn (EDFH) with 166 passengers and 6 crew members inbound to Rome Ciampino (LIRA)
Aircraft established first radio contact with Ciampino Tower communicating 9 NM from runway and stabilised on ILS for Runway 15
Aircraft authorized and configured for approach, proceeding for landing in very short final approach phase
Aircraft collided with a thick flock of starlings during very short final approach
Both engines lost thrust due to bird ingestion; aircraft rapidly lost speed and height
Crew interrupted landing procedure and initiated go-around manoeuvre with flight attitude set for climbing
With insufficient thrust available, aircraft rapidly descended toward runway despite go-around attempt
Main landing gear properly extended but aircraft made heavy contact with runway in proximity of taxiway AC
Main left landing gear detached from its anchoring during landing run; lower part of left engine nacelle came into contact with runway
Aircraft stopped near Runway threshold 33; fire brigade immediately arrived and sprayed extinguishing foam
Captain arranged disembarkation of passengers and crew using ladder truck from right front door and right rear slide
All 172 occupants evacuated safely; 8 persons (6 passengers, 2 crew) with minor injuries transported to hospital

recommendations.text: Provide flight crews with guidelines and operational/training procedures based on careful assessment of risks associated with bird encounters or single/multiple bird strikes in approach. Guidelines should include bird strike risk briefing, recommendation to land at lowest engine power if landing is assured rather than go-around when facing bird strike risk, and consideration that engine damages might prevent go-around completion.

Provide indications to adopt specific training for flight crews to cope with surprise and startle effects, particularly in critical phases of flight such as approach and landing. Training should identify unexpected but plausible events, use visualization and conditioning exercises to manage negative consequences.

dissent.position: The report discusses the startle effect using repeated verbal communication of 'ahi' instead of 'birds ahead'. If crew were able to verbalize bird position clearly, they would not be surprised. The recommendation contradicts the finding.

notes: Official ANSV (Italian Civil Aviation Safety Investigation Authority) final report
Comprehensive analysis of bird strike event during approach
Events extracted from History of Flight section (p. 1-2) and Causes section (p. 113)
CVR data shows crew vocalization of surprise at bird encounter
Recommendations issued based on training deficiencies identified
Dissenting comment from AAIU regarding interpretation of startle effect

records.title: XL Airways Germany 888T

agencies.name: Bureau of Enquiry and Analysis for Civil Aviation Safety
agencies.report_title: Accident on 27 November 2008 off the coast of Canet-Plage to the Airbus A320-232 registered D-AXLA

records.summary: XL Airways Flight 888T, an Airbus A320 acceptance flight, crashed into the Mediterranean Sea on 27 November 2008 near Canet-en-Roussillon. Maintenance personnel had failed to protect angle-of-attack (AOA) sensors during aircraft rinsing three days prior, allowing water to penetrate and freeze inside the sensors. During a low-speed check near 2,900 feet, the blocked sensors rendered angle-of-attack protections inoperative. The crew descended below planned altitude and stalled the aircraft, entered direct flight control law, and were unable to recover despite multiple control inputs and maximum thrust.
records.probable_cause: The accident was caused by the loss of control of the aeroplane by the crew following the improvised demonstration of the functioning of the angle of attack protections, while the blockage of the angle of attack sensors made it impossible for these protections to trigger. The crew was not aware of the blockage of the angle of attack sensors. They did not take into account the speeds mentioned in the programme of checks available to them and consequently did not stop the demonstration before the stall (p. 98). Contributing factors included the decision to carry out the demonstration at low height, the crew's inadequate management of the strong pitch increase, the increased workload from managing adapted in-flight checks, and the absence of protection for AOA sensors during rinsing operations (p. 99).

factors.evidence: Maintenance personnel performed aircraft rinsing with fresh water on 24 November 2008 without following proper rinsing procedures and without protecting angle-of-attack sensors (p. 96)

Water penetrated inside angle-of-attack sensors 1 and 2 during rinsing and remained there until freezing during the accident flight three days later (p. 96). AOA sensors 1 and 2 blocked between 15:04 and 15:06 at identical local angle-of-attack values consistent with cruise angle of attack, rendering protections inoperative in normal law (p. 97)

The crew decided to undertake the low-speed protection check at approximately 4,000 ft altitude without preparation and without reading theoretical minimum speeds from the flight check program (p. 97). The check should have been performed at FL140 per the Airbus Customer Acceptance Manual (p. 96)

The airplane crashed completely into the Mediterranean Sea with all seven occupants killed. Due to the stabilizer position at full pitch-up and the pitch-up moment generated by engines at maximum thrust, crew lost control during thrust increase and could not recover (p. 98)
Aircraft stalled at approximately 99 kt speed in landing configuration when attempting to test angle-of-attack protections at low altitude (p. 18)

events.text: On 24 November 2008, aircraft rinsed with fresh water to eliminate dust from fuselage without following rinsing task procedure and without protecting angle-of-attack sensors (p. 96)
Aircraft D-AXLA ferried to Perpignan aerodrome on 3 November 2008 for maintenance and painting work (p. 16)
Aircraft left ramp at Perpignan aerodrome. Flight plan filed as GXL888T with planned flight time of 2 hours 35 minutes over west of France (p. 16)
Air New Zealand pilot introduced himself and asked crew to raise hand if he interrupted during flight checks (p. 16)

Takeoff from runway 21 at Perpignan with Captain as pilot flying and co-pilot as pilot non-flying. On board: 2 XL Airways pilots, 1 Air New Zealand pilot in cockpit, 3 Air New Zealand engineers, 1 NZ CAA representative (p. 16)
CRNA south-west controller contacted Perpignan approach controller by phone, expressing concern about flight described as 'disguised test flight' without proper authorization (p. 16)
Captain requested to perform a '360' turn; controller explained this maneuver could not be undertaken in general air traffic as filed flight plan did not include it (p. 16)
Captain proposed to Air New Zealand pilot to delay check on flight controls to approach phase (p. 16)
Crew cleared to climb to FL320, which they reached two minutes later (p. 17)

Between 15:04 and 15:06, angle-of-attack sensors 1 and 2 stopped moving and remained blocked at almost identical local angles of attack of 4.2 and 3.8 degrees respectively, consistent with cruise angle of attack (p. 17)
Crew began descent to FL310 (p. 17)
Captain performed flight control checks in normal law (p. 17)
While waiting for clearance to climb to FL390, Air New Zealand pilot noted few checks remaining and said APU check could be done during return flight to Frankfurt (p. 17)
Aircraft reached FL390 (p. 17)
Descent towards Perpignan initiated (p. 17)
Crew cleared to descend to FL130. Eighteen seconds later, Air New Zealand pilot asked if crew ready to perform flight control check in alternate law (p. 17)
Crew contacted Perpignan Approach, were cleared to descend to FL120 towards PPG VOR, instructed to reduce speed to 250 kt (p. 17)
At FL120, captain asked 'you want alternate law' and New Zealand pilot answered 'okay alternate law' (p. 17)

Flight control laws in pitch and roll returned to normal law, indicating end of alternate law check. Autopilot 1 reconnected. Air New Zealand pilot then mentioned low-speed flight would be next (p. 17)
Approach controller asked crew to descend to FL60. Aircraft slightly below FL100, speed 214 kt. Five seconds later, co-pilot asked to engage wing anti-ice at approximately 9,900 ft (p. 17-18)
Approach controller asked crew to turn right to heading 190 and maintain 180 kt. About one minute later cleared to LANET-ILS approach for runway 33 and descend to 5,000 ft (p. 18)
Aircraft reached 5,000 ft altitude at approximately 210 kt (p. 18)
Approach controller asked aircraft speed. Co-pilot initially answered speed falling, then at 15:42:25 said 180 kt. Actual speed slightly above 190 kt (p. 18)
Spoilers deployed between 15:43:20 and 15:43:55 (p. 18)
'Triple click' recorded, AP/FD lateral mode changed from NAV to HDG at heading 090. Aircraft at 2,940 ft altitude, speed 107 kt (Vmin) (p. 18)
Captain disengaged autopilot saying 'Down below the clouds so you want what?' Thirty seconds later positioned thrust control levers on IDLE and autothrust disengaged at 4,080 ft, speed 166 kt (p. 18)
Captain stabilized aircraft at 3,000 ft in landing configuration. Flight directors active, vertical mode OP DES to V/S +0000. Speed was 136 kt (p. 18)
Aircraft at 2,980 ft altitude, speed 123.5 kt (VLS). Stabilizer moved from -4.4° to -11.2° corresponding to electric pitch-up stop (p. 18)
Aircraft at 2,910 ft altitude, speed 99 kt. Pitch angle 18.6 degrees. Stall warning sounded for first time. Limit speeds Vαprot and Vαmax underestimated due to blocked AOA sensors (p. 18, 97)
Thrust control levers moved to TO/GA position. Symmetrical increase in engine RPM to approximately 88% N1. Aircraft began to roll left (p. 18)
Bank angle reached 8° left, speed 92.5 kt. Captain countered with lateral input to right and longitudinal input forward (p. 19)
Wings straightened and began roll right. Captain made lateral input to left stop, rudder began moving for left turn (p. 19)
Both flight directors disengaged. At 15:45:14, autothrust disarmed (p. 19)
Flight control laws switched from normal law to direct law. Bank reached 50° right. Pitch 11°, speed 100 kt, altitude approximately 2,580 ft. Elevators at maximum nose-down position 11.6° (p. 19)
Stall warning stopped. Bank angle 40° left. Aircraft pitch 7°, wings nearly horizontal, speed 138 kt (p. 19)
Pitch and altitude began to increase to approximately 2,250 ft. Speed dropped, stall warning sounded again at 15:45:36 (p. 19-20)
Landing gear retracted. Pitch reached maximum 52° nose-up, bank angle maximum 59° left, normal load factor below 0.5g (p. 20)
Speed dropped below 40 kt (p. 20)
Maximum values recorded: pitch 57° nose-up, altitude 3,788 ft (p. 20)
Stall warning stopped, started again approximately 5 seconds later (p. 20)
Captain made longitudinal pitch-up input. Between 15:45:49 and 15:45:53, elevator reached values of 30° pitch-up (p. 20)
Normal load factor exceeded 0.5g. Thrust control levers placed in CLIMB position for one second then repositioned to TO/GA (p. 20)
From 15:45:52, speed passed above 40 kt. At 15:45:53, pitch 7° nose-down, bank less than 10° left (p. 20)
Between 15:45:55 and 15:45:58, captain made lateral input to left stop; aircraft rolled right. Bank angle from 3° to 97°, pitch from 3° nose-down to 42° nose-down (p. 20)
From 15:45:57, captain's longitudinal input nose-up; elevator at 14.5° nose-down (p. 20)
Flaps and slats selected to position 1, then position 0 two seconds later (p. 20)
Stall warning stopped, followed by CRC warning (Master Warning) which stopped two seconds later. Pitch reached maximum 51° nose-down, bank 45° right, speed 183 kt, altitude 1,620 ft (p. 20)
Thrust levers moved back to near IDLE, then advanced to CLIMB position. EPR on two engines dropped to 1.2 then increased to 1.25 (p. 20)
EGPWS TERRAIN TERRAIN warning recorded, followed one second later by another CRC warning (Master Warning) (p. 20)

Flight data recordings stopped. Last recorded values: pitch 14° nose-down, bank 15° right, speed 263 kt, altitude 340 ft. Between first stall warning and end of recording, 62 seconds had elapsed. Aircraft crashed into Mediterranean Sea at approximately 7 km off French coast near Canet-en-Roussillon (p. 20)

recommendations.text: Detail in EU-OPS the various types of non-revenue flights that operators are authorized to perform
Require non-revenue flights be described precisely in approved operations manuals, specifying preparation, program, operational framework, crew qualifications and training
As temporary measure, require non-revenue flights be subject to authorization or operator declaration on case-by-case basis
Ensure that equipment installation conditions during certification tests performed by equipment manufacturers are representative of those on the aircraft
Undertake a safety study to improve certification standards of warning systems for crews during flight control system reconfigurations or training in identifying these reconfigurations
In cooperation with manufacturers, improve training exercises and techniques relating to approach-to-stall to ensure control of the aircraft in the pitch axis

records.title: Continental Airlines Flight 1404

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Runway Side Excursion During Attempted Takeoff in Strong and Gusty Crosswind Conditions, Continental Airlines Flight 1404, Boeing 737-500, N18611, Denver, Colorado, December 20, 2008

records.summary: Boeing 737-500 operated by Continental Airlines (flight 1404) attempted to take off from Runway 34R at Denver International Airport on December 20, 2008, during strong and gusty crosswind conditions with mountain wave activity. The aircraft encountered winds exceeding 27 knots (with gusts up to 45 knots), causing the captain to lose directional control during the takeoff roll. The aircraft veered left off the runway after reaching 119 knots, became briefly airborne, and crashed into a 40-foot ravine several hundred yards from the runway. The right engine caught fire and the fuselage was engulfed in flames. All 115 occupants evacuated safely; the captain and 5 passengers sustained serious injuries, and 38 passengers had minor injuries.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause of this accident was the captain's cessation of right rudder input, which was needed to maintain directional control of the airplane, about 4 seconds before the excursion, when the airplane encountered a strong and gusty crosswind that exceeded the captain's training and experience. Contributing to the accident were the following factors: 1) an air traffic control system that did not require or facilitate the dissemination of key, available wind information to the air traffic controllers and pilots; and 2) inadequate crosswind training in the airline industry due to deficient simulator wind gust modeling.

factors.evidence: Mountain wave conditions present at time of accident resulted in strong westerly winds and very localized, intermittent wind gusts as high as 45 knots crossing airplane's path during takeoff ground roll (p. 59).
Continental's simulator training did not replicate ground-level disturbances and gusting crosswinds; captain was not adequately prepared to respond to changes in heading during this takeoff (p. 60).

ATC did not provide the most adverse available wind information (35-knot crosswind with 40-knot gusts) to pilots; only reported 27-knot winds which did not exceed Continental's 33-knot crosswind guidance (p. 59-60).
Boeing did not adequately consider dynamic handling qualities of Boeing 737 during takeoff in strong and gusty crosswinds; enhanced crosswind guidelines were deficient (p. 60).
Aircraft departed left side of runway 34R after reaching 119 knots, became briefly airborne, and crashed in 40-foot ravine several hundred yards from runway (p. ix).
Right engine caught fire after impact; fuselage engulfed in flames (p. ix).

events.text: Aircraft cleared for takeoff on runway 34R with 27-knot crosswind component reported by ATC (actual winds 28-35 knots from mountain wave conditions).
Captain applies nose wheel steering tiller and full right control wheel input in response to airplane veering left.
Bumping or rattling sound heard in cockpit as airplane encounters gusty crosswinds.
Crew aborts takeoff; captain attempts rejected takeoff procedure.
Captain ceases right rudder input about 4 seconds before runway excursion; aircraft loses directional control.
Aircraft reaches 119 knots, veers left off runway 34R centerline, becomes briefly airborne.
Aircraft crashes into 40-foot ravine several hundred yards from runway; right engine catches fire; fuselage engulfed in flames.
All 115 occupants successfully evacuate aircraft.

recommendations.text: Conduct research into and document the effects of mountain wave and downslope conditions at airports, such as Denver International Airport, that are located downwind of mountainous terrain; identify potential mountain-wave-related hazards to ground operations; and disseminate results to pilots and airport air traffic control personnel to allow for more informed runway selection decisions.

Archive all low-level windshear alert system (LLWAS) data obtained from Denver International Airport and other airports that experience similar wind conditions and make those data available for additional research and the potential future development of an improved LLWAS algorithm for crosswind and gusty wind alerts on air traffic control tower ribbon display terminals.

Modify Federal Aviation Administration Order 7110.65 to require air traffic controllers at airports with multiple sources of wind information to provide pilots with the maximum wind component, including gusts, that the flight could encounter.

Review the required documentation for all low-level windshear alert system (LLWAS)-equipped air traffic control towers to ensure that a letter to airmen has been published and is easily accessible describing the location and designation of the remote sensors, the capabilities and limitations of the system, and the availability of current LLWAS remote sensor wind information on the request of a pilot.

Require air traffic control towers to locally develop and implement written runway selection programs that proactively consider current and developing wind conditions and include clearly defined crosswind components, including wind gusts, when considering operational advantage with respect to runway selection.

Gather data on surface winds at a sample of major U.S. airports (including Denver International Airport) when high wind conditions and significant gusts are present and use these data to develop realistic, gusty crosswind profiles for use in pilot simulator training programs.

Require 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 121, 135, and 91K operators to incorporate the realistic, gusty crosswind profiles developed as a result of Safety Recommendation A-10-110 into their pilot simulator training programs.

Once realistic, gusty crosswind profiles as asked for in Safety Recommendation A-10-110 are developed, develop a standard methodology including pilot-in-the-loop testing, for transport-category airplane manufacturers to establish empirically based, type-specific maximum-gusting-crosswind limitations for transport-category airplanes that account for wind gusts.

Once a methodology as asked for in Safety Recommendation A-10-112 has been developed, require manufacturers of transport-category airplanes to develop type-specific, maximum-crosswind takeoff limitations that account for wind gusts.

Until the actions described in Safety Recommendation A-10-113 are accomplished, require manufacturers of transport-category airplanes to provide operators with interim crosswind takeoff guidelines that account for wind gusts.

Work with U.S. airline operators to review and analyze operational flight data to identify factors that contribute to encounters with excessive winds and use this information to develop and implement additional strategies for reducing the likelihood of wind-related runway excursions.
Require cockpit crew seats installed in newly manufactured airplanes that were type certificated before 1988 to meet the crashworthiness standards contained in 14 Code of Federal Regulations 25.562.
Require operators to perform periodic inspections on the Burns Aerospace model 2501-5 jumpseats for fatigue cracks within the jumpseat structure and replace the jumpseat if fatigue cracks are found.

Require that operators of transport-category airplanes that use galley latches or latch plates secured solely by adhesives that may degrade over time modify the latches to include mechanical fasteners.

safety_changes: Improved wind information sharing between ATC and flight crews
Enhanced crosswind training protocols in simulator training programs
Development of gusty crosswind profiles for pilot training

notes: Findings and probable cause extracted from section 3.1-3.2 of final report
Recommendations A-10-105 through A-10-118 extracted from section 4
Timeline from executive summary and accident sequence sections
Key safety issues: mountain wave crosswind conditions, ATC wind information dissemination, inadequate simulator training

records.title: US Airways 1549

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Loss of Thrust in Both Engines After Encountering a Flock of Birds and Subsequent Ditching on the Hudson River, US Airways Flight 1549, Airbus A320-214, N106US, Weehawken, New Jersey, January 15, 2009

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses pour la Sécurité de l'Aviation Civile

location.name: Hudson River off Weehawken, New Jersey / midtown Manhattan

records.summary: About two minutes after takeoff from LaGuardia, climbing through 2,800 feet, the A320 struck a flock of Canada geese and both engines lost almost all thrust. The captain took control, started the APU, judged that no runway was reachable and ditched on the Hudson River about three and a half minutes after the strike. All 155 occupants were rescued by ferries and emergency responders; five people were seriously injured.
records.probable_cause: The ingestion of large birds into each engine, which resulted in an almost total loss of thrust in both engines and the subsequent ditching on the Hudson River. Contributing to the fuselage damage and resulting unavailability of the aft slide/rafts were (1) the Airbus engineering assumptions in the development of A320 ditching procedures and certification, the lack of industry flight crew training and guidance on ditching techniques, and (2) the captain's resulting difficulty maintaining his intended airspeed on final approach due to the task saturation resulting from the emergency situation. Contributing to the survivability of the accident were (1) the decision-making of the flight crewmembers and their use of crew resource management during the accident sequence; (2) the fortuitous use of an airplane that was equipped for an extended overwater flight, including the availability of the forward slide/rafts, even though it was not required to be so equipped; (3) the performance of the cabin crewmembers while expediting the evacuation of the airplane; and (4) the proximity of the emergency responders to the accident site and their immediate and appropriate response to the accident.

factors.evidence: The airplane struck a flock of Canada geese at about 2,818 feet; remains of Branta canadensis were found in both engines.
Ingestion of large birds into the core of each engine caused an almost total loss of thrust in both engines within seconds.

Engine bird-ingestion certification standards at the time did not require testing for birds as large as those encountered, and A320 ditching certification assumed a descent rate and configuration (engines running, 3.5 ft/s) that could not be achieved in an all-engine-out glide.
The Engine Dual Failure checklist was written for a high-altitude event and was too long to complete before the ditching; the crew never reached the ditching items.
Task saturation during the emergency contributed to the captain's difficulty maintaining his intended airspeed on final approach.
There was no industry flight crew training or guidance on ditching techniques or on managing a dual engine failure at low altitude.
In the flare the airplane entered its alpha-protection envelope, which limited the pitch-up the captain could command and prevented him from further reducing the descent rate.
Fuselage damage let water into the aft cabin, making the aft slide/rafts unusable; some passengers evacuated without life vests and one aft door was briefly opened.
The airplane was ditched on the Hudson River at about 125 knots with a descent rate of about 12.5 ft/s, flaps 2, and remained afloat long enough for all occupants to evacuate.
The forced landing on the river was survived by all 155 occupants.

events.text: Takeoff from LaGuardia runway 4 with the first officer as pilot flying.
Captain sees a flock of birds ahead and says 'birds'.
The airplane strikes a flock of Canada geese; thumps are heard and both engines ingest birds.
Both engines roll back; the captain notes 'both of 'em rolling back' and calls for ignition and APU start.
Captain takes control ('my aircraft') and starts the APU; the first officer begins the Engine Dual Failure checklist from the QRH.
Captain declares 'mayday' to LaGuardia departure, reporting a bird strike, loss of thrust in both engines, and a turn back toward LaGuardia.
Departure controller instructs a left turn to heading 220 and begins arranging a return to LaGuardia.
Controller offers runway 13 at LaGuardia; the captain replies 'we're unable. we may end up in the Hudson'.
First officer attempts engine relights per the checklist; neither engine recovers usable thrust.
Captain asks about airports to the right in New Jersey, including Teterboro; the controller offers Teterboro runway 1.
Captain tells ATC 'we can't do it' and, shortly after, 'we're gonna be in the Hudson'.
Captain makes the cabin announcement 'brace for impact'; flight attendants begin brace commands.
Flaps 2 are selected for the ditching; the captain asks the first officer 'got any ideas?' and he answers 'actually not'.
In the flare the airplane reaches the alpha-protection boundary, limiting further nose-up pitch; airspeed is below the captain's intended speed.
The airplane touches down on the Hudson River at about 125 knots and a descent rate of about 12.5 ft/s; the aft fuselage is damaged and water enters the rear cabin.

Evacuation through the forward doors and overwing exits onto the slide/rafts and wings; the aft slide/rafts are unusable because of water in the cabin. Ferries begin rescuing occupants within minutes.

cvr.speaker: CAPT

recommendations.text: Require Airbus to develop a dual engine failure checklist usable at low altitude and require operators to train on it.
recommendations.outcome: Airbus revised the A320 Engine Dual Failure procedure and QRH.

recommendations.text: Revise engine bird-ingestion certification standards to reflect the size and numbers of large flocking birds actually encountered, including core ingestion.

Require ditching training and guidance for flight crews, including the effect of flight envelope protections on the flare, and require that ditching certification consider realistic engine-out descent rates.
Require life vests and forward slide/rafts on all airplanes regardless of route, and improve passenger briefing on life vest use and location.
Improve wildlife hazard management around airports and require wildlife hazard assessments at all Part 139 airports.
recommendations.outcome: FAA expanded wildlife hazard assessment requirements and reporting.

safety_changes: Airbus revised the A320 family Engine Dual Failure procedure to add a low-altitude branch that goes directly to the essential relight and ditching items.
FAA and EASA opened reviews of engine bird-ingestion certification standards for large flocking birds, including core ingestion.
Wildlife hazard management at Part 139 airports was strengthened, including wildlife hazard assessments and Canada goose population control around New York airports.
The event became the reference case for CRM and startle-management training on low-altitude all-engine power loss.

notes: Bird strike time 15:27:11 EST and ditching 15:30:43 EST are from the report; ATC exchange clocks (15:27:32 mayday, 15:27:49, 15:28:05, 15:28:55, 15:29:21, 15:29:25) follow the public transcript to within a second or two.
The clock time of the 'brace for impact' PA and of the flaps 2 selection are not recalled precisely; those events carry approximate t only.
Touchdown parameters (about 125 kt, about 12.5 ft/s, 9.5 degrees pitch, flaps 2) are as stated in the report's performance analysis; treat pitch as approximate.
ICAO category BIRD is not in the spec's list, so OTHR is used; the initiating event was a bird strike.

records.title: Colgan Air 3407

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Loss of Control on Approach, Colgan Air, Inc., Operating as Continental Connection Flight 3407, Bombardier DHC-8-400, N200WQ, Clarence Center, New York, February 12, 2009

location.name: Clarence Center, New York, about 5 nm from Buffalo Niagara International Airport

records.summary: During a night ILS approach to runway 23 at Buffalo in light snow and icing conditions, the crew allowed airspeed to decay while configuring the Q400 for landing. When the stick shaker activated at 131 knots the captain pulled the control column aft and added only partial power, overriding the stick pusher; the first officer retracted the flaps without being asked. The airplane stalled, rolled and pitched violently, and struck a house about 26 seconds later, killing all 49 on board and one person on the ground.
records.probable_cause: The captain's inappropriate response to the activation of the stick shaker, which led to an aerodynamic stall from which the airplane did not recover. Contributing to the accident were (1) the flight crew's failure to monitor airspeed in relation to the rising position of the low-speed cue, (2) the flight crew's failure to adhere to sterile cockpit procedures, (3) the captain's failure to effectively manage the flight, and (4) Colgan Air's inadequate procedures for airspeed selection and management during approaches in icing conditions.

factors.evidence: The stick shaker activated at 131 knots (a threshold raised by the REF SPEEDS switch) and the stick pusher subsequently fired three times; the captain overrode each pusher activation.
The captain responded to the stick shaker with a 37-pound aft column pull and only partial power instead of the trained nose-down, full-power recovery.
Aft column input drove pitch to about 31 degrees nose up and the airplane rolled 45 degrees left then 105 degrees right; the first officer retracted the flaps without coordination.
Neither pilot monitored airspeed as it decayed from about 180 to 131 knots against the rising low-speed cue on the airspeed tape.
With power near flight idle, gear extended and flaps moving to 15, airspeed fell about 20 knots below the target the crew should have been flying with the REF SPEEDS switch in the INCREASE position.
The crew held an extended nonpertinent conversation about icing experience and careers below 10,000 feet, contrary to 14 CFR 121.542.
The captain failed to effectively manage the flight; the first officer retracted the flaps and asked about raising the gear during the stall without direction.
The REF SPEEDS switch was set to INCREASE without the crew adjusting their approach speed bugs accordingly, and the captain reduced power below what the approach required.

The NTSB found both pilots were likely experiencing fatigue (the first officer had commuted overnight from Seattle; the captain slept in the crew room), though its contribution to their performance could not be conclusively determined.
The report concluded the captain was startled by the unexpected stick shaker and did not recognize the situation as an impending stall.

Colgan's stall training did not expose pilots to the stick pusher or to the rising low-speed cue behavior with the REF SPEEDS switch on, and the captain had a history of training and checkride deficiencies.
Colgan Air's procedures for airspeed selection and management in icing conditions were inadequate and the airline's oversight of the captain's training record was deficient.
FAA oversight of Colgan's training program and pilot records was found wanting; the report generated recommendations on remedial training and pilot record sharing.
The captain had about 110 hours as pilot-in-command on the Q400; the first officer had about 770 hours on type and had never flown in icing before joining Colgan.

The airplane had accreted light ice; the NTSB found its effect on stall speed was minimal, but the icing conditions led the crew to select REF SPEEDS INCREASE, which raised the stick shaker speed by about 20 knots.
The airplane entered an aerodynamic stall from which the crew did not recover.
The airplane rolled and pitched uncontrollably and struck a house in a steep nose-down attitude.

events.text: Below 10,000 feet the crew continue an extended nonpertinent conversation about their icing experience and careers, contrary to sterile cockpit rules.
REF SPEEDS switch is set to INCREASE for icing conditions; the crew do not correspondingly increase their planned approach speeds.
Buffalo approach vectors the flight onto the localizer for the ILS runway 23; the airplane levels at the 2,300 ft intercept altitude with autopilot engaged.
Captain calls for flaps 5 and reduces power toward flight idle; airspeed begins to decay steadily.
First officer lowers the landing gear on the captain's call.
Captain calls for flaps 15; the low-speed cue on the airspeed tape has risen to meet the decaying airspeed, unnoticed by either pilot.
Stick shaker activates at 131 knots; autopilot disconnects.
Captain pulls the control column aft with about 37 pounds of force and advances the power levers to about 75 percent torque rather than full power.
Pitch reaches about 31 degrees nose up; the airplane rolls to about 45 degrees left bank.
Stick pusher activates for the first time; the captain overrides it with continued aft column force.
First officer retracts the flaps from 15 toward 0 without being asked, announcing 'I put the flaps up'.
Airplane rolls through wings level to about 105 degrees right bank and pitches nose down; stick pusher activates again and is overridden.
First officer asks whether to raise the landing gear; captain replies 'gear up'.
Third stick pusher activation; the airplane is in a steep nose-down attitude with insufficient altitude to recover.
Cockpit voice recorder stops; the airplane strikes a house on Long Street, Clarence Center, and is destroyed by impact and fire.

cvr.speaker: FO
cvr.text: should I put the gear up?

recommendations.text: Require operators to provide stall recovery training that emphasizes reducing angle of attack, includes stick pusher demonstration where fitted, and covers the effects of the REF SPEEDS switch on the low-speed cue.
recommendations.outcome: FAA revised stall training guidance (AC 120-109) to prioritize AOA reduction over minimum altitude loss; full-stall and pusher training added to Part 121 training requirements.

recommendations.text: Require operators to develop and implement procedures to monitor and cross-check airspeed, including low-airspeed alerting systems in transport-category airplanes.
Address pilot fatigue arising from commuting and inadequate rest, and require operators to address commuting in fatigue risk management.
recommendations.outcome: New flight and duty time rules (14 CFR Part 117) took effect in 2014.

recommendations.text: Require air carriers to obtain and review a pilot's complete training and checkride history, including failures, before hiring, and to provide remedial training programs for pilots with repeated deficiencies.
recommendations.outcome: Pilot Records Database mandated by the Airline Safety and FAA Extension Act of 2010.

recommendations.text: Reinforce sterile cockpit compliance and leadership and professionalism training for Part 121 flight crews.

safety_changes: Airline Safety and FAA Extension Act of 2010 (Public Law 111-216) required an ATP certificate and 1,500 hours for airline first officers, a pilot records database, and new fatigue rules.
14 CFR Part 117 flight, duty and rest limitations for Part 121 pilots took effect in January 2014.

FAA stall training guidance was rewritten (AC 120-109) to emphasize immediate angle-of-attack reduction rather than minimum altitude loss, with full-stall and stick pusher training later required for Part 121 carriers.
Regional airlines and their mainline partners increased oversight of training records, remedial training and commuting policies.

notes: Accident occurred 22:17 EST on 2009-02-12; in UTC it is 2009-02-13. Local date is used in the date field.
Fatalities (50) include one person in the house struck; occupants aboard were 49 (45 passengers, 4 crew).

Clock times for the REF SPEEDS switch, flaps 5 and flaps 15 calls, the second and third stick pusher activations and several CVR lines are approximate and given as relative t only; the stick shaker (22:16:27), gear call (22:16:21), first pusher (about 22:16:34) and end of CVR (22:16:52) follow the report.
CVR lines are short excerpts from the public transcript; timing of the flap and gear exchanges is estimated to within a few seconds.

records.title: Turkish Airlines 1951

agencies.name: Dutch Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Crashed during approach, Boeing 737-800, near Amsterdam Schiphol Airport, 25 February 2009

agencies.name: Turkish Accident Investigation Board (Kaza Araştırma ve İnceleme Kurulu)

location.name: Field 1.5 km short of runway 18R, Amsterdam Schiphol

records.summary: During an ILS approach to Schiphol runway 18R the left radio altimeter erroneously indicated -8 ft, causing the autothrottle to enter RETARD mode and close the thrust levers as if for landing flare. The crew, who had been vectored to intercept the glideslope from above and were busy with a line-training approach, did not notice the decaying airspeed until the stick shaker at about 460 ft. Recovery was too late and the aircraft stalled into a field 1.5 km short of the runway; 9 people died including the three pilots.
records.probable_cause: The accident was caused by the erroneous left radio altimeter reading, which made the autothrottle reduce the thrust to idle in the retard flare mode during the approach, combined with the crew's failure to notice the decreasing airspeed and the abnormal autothrottle mode until the stick shaker; the subsequent recovery from the stall was not successful. Contributing factors: the aircraft intercepted the glideslope from above due to ATC vectoring, which increased workload and masked the thrust reduction; the approach was not stabilised and should have been abandoned; the crew's monitoring during the line training situation was inadequate; and Boeing had not informed operators adequately about the known radio altimeter problems and their effect on the autothrottle.

factors.evidence: The left radio altimeter system produced an erroneous -8 ft value during the approach, as it had on previous flights of the aircraft.
The same radio altimeter fault had occurred on TC-JGE in the preceding days and on other 737NGs but had not been rectified.
The autothrottle entered RETARD flare mode at about 1,950 ft and closed the thrust levers; the crew did not recognise the mode annunciation.
The autothrottle used only the left radio altimeter data with no comparison against the right unit, so a single erroneous input could drive the retard logic.
Boeing was aware of radio altimeter problems affecting autothrottle behaviour but the information had not reached Turkish Airlines' crews.

Amsterdam approach vectored the aircraft onto the localiser at 5.5 nm and 2,000 ft, above the glideslope, contrary to the standard procedure, so the crew intercepted from above with the thrust already at idle.
The approach was not stabilised at 1,000 ft; the crew continued rather than executing a go-around.
The captain was instructing the first officer under line training with a safety pilot present, adding to workload during the glideslope capture and landing checklist.
None of the three pilots noticed the airspeed falling from 144 kt toward 83 kt or the thrust levers at idle for about 100 seconds.
Airspeed decayed well below the approach speed of 144 kt with the pitch attitude increasing to maintain the glideslope.
The stick shaker activated at about 460 ft radio altitude.
The first officer pushed the thrust levers forward but the captain took control and the autothrottle, still engaged, retarded them again; full thrust was applied only after a delay.
The aircraft stalled at about 83 kt and descended into the field short of the runway.
The aircraft struck the ground tail first in a nose-high attitude and broke into three sections.

events.text: Left radio altimeter begins to indicate -8 ft; the landing gear warning horn sounds once and a master caution is triggered but the crew treat it as spurious.
Approach control vectors the aircraft to intercept the runway 18R localiser at about 5.5 nm, at 2,000 ft, above the glideslope.
Crew select landing gear down and flaps 15, then 40, and descend to capture the glideslope from above with the thrust levers at idle; the landing checklist is being run.
At about 1,950 ft the autothrottle annunciates RETARD and holds the thrust levers at idle, based on the erroneous radio height.
Glideslope captured; the autopilot pitches the aircraft up to hold the glidepath as the speed falls below the 144 kt selected approach speed.
Landing checklist completed; the crew note the aircraft is at 1,000 ft but do not remark on the speed or the thrust levers at idle.
Airspeed reaches about 105 kt with the pitch attitude rising; the autopilot remains engaged.
Stick shaker activates at about 460 ft radio altitude; the first officer advances the thrust levers.
Captain takes control; the autothrottle, still engaged in RETARD mode, pulls the thrust levers back to idle again.
Autothrottle disconnected and full thrust applied, about nine seconds after the stick shaker; the aircraft is stalled with insufficient height to recover.
The aircraft strikes a field 1.5 km short of runway 18R, tail first, at about 95 kt, breaking into three parts; 9 killed including the three pilots, 28 seriously injured.

recommendations.text: Improve the reliability of the radio altimeter system and modify the autothrottle logic so that a single erroneous radio altimeter cannot drive the retard flare mode during the approach.
recommendations.outcome: Boeing modified the autothrottle software to compare both radio altimeters and issued a flight crew operations bulletin.

recommendations.text: Inform all 737NG operators of the radio altimeter problems and their effect on the autothrottle, and include an appropriate warning in the manuals.
recommendations.outcome: Boeing issued a Multi Operator Message and revised the manuals.

recommendations.text: Ensure crews are trained on recognition of autothrottle modes, the stabilised approach criteria and go-around decision-making, and that line training approaches are adequately monitored.
Ensure that Amsterdam approach procedures provide for interception of the glideslope from below in accordance with ICAO requirements.
Review stall recovery training so that flight crews immediately disconnect the autothrottle and apply maximum thrust in response to a stick shaker.

safety_changes: Boeing 737NG autothrottle software modification comparing left and right radio altimeter data.
Turkish Airlines revised approach monitoring and stabilised approach procedures.
Renewed emphasis on go-around policy and mode awareness in the industry; Dutch review of glideslope interception practices at Schiphol.

notes: Clock strings are local time (CET) to the minute; seconds are estimated. Impact occurred at about 10:26 local.
The 1,950 ft RETARD activation, 460 ft stick shaker, 144 kt approach speed and 83 kt minimum speed are from the DSB report; other state values approximate.
Turkish accredited agency code is an informal label; no formal dissent was published.

records.title: Cougar Helicopters Flight 91

location.name: Atlantic Ocean, 35 nm east of St. John's

records.summary: Cougar Helicopters Flight 91, a Sikorsky S-92A on a regular shuttle flight to offshore oil platforms, reported zero oil pressure in the main gearbox at 09:40 NDT at cruise. The crew attempted return to St. John's but ditched 8 minutes later after losing electrical power. Of 18 aboard, one survived with serious injuries; the other 17 died of drowning. A broken titanium stud in the main gearbox oil filter assembly, subject of a prior Alert Service Bulletin, initiated the failure.
records.probable_cause: The accident was caused by a broken titanium stud in the main gearbox oil filter assembly that had been the subject of a prior Alert Service Bulletin recommending replacement within one year or 1,250 flight hours. The accident was contributed to by the fact that a previous similar incident in Australia in August 2008 involving total loss of oil and emergency landing did not result in industry action to correct the defect.

factors.evidence: Sikorsky issued Alert Service Bulletin on 28 January 2009 recommending replacement of titanium studs within one year or 1,250 flight hours; this defect had not been addressed on C-GZCH at the time of accident (p. 1-2)
Loss of oil pressure in main gearbox at 09:40 caused by broken titanium stud; total loss of oil in transmission (p. 1)
Prior incident in Dandenong, Australia August 2008 involved total loss of oil and emergency landing but defect was not corrected industry-wide (p. 149)
Crew attempted return to St. John's and ditched in Atlantic Ocean at 09:48; helicopter sank in 178 m water (p. 1)

17 occupants died of drowning in helicopter that capsized in cold water; water temperature was approximately 0°C preventing effective escape; occupants lacked supplemental breathing apparatus (p. 149-150)

events.text: Aircraft reported zero oil pressure in main gearbox at cruise altitude; crew issued mayday
Crew initiated emergency procedures for main gearbox oil pressure loss
Crew descended to 800 feet and turned toward St. John's International Airport
Aircraft lost electrical power due to continuing gearbox degradation
Crew prepared for emergency ditching; moved to ditching position heading
Aircraft ditched in Atlantic Ocean after losing electrical power; high rate of descent at impact
Helicopter capsized and sank in 178 m water; occupants struggled to escape in 0°C water
Provincial Airlines ice patrol airplane spotted aircraft floating upside down 25 minutes after ditching

recommendations.text: The Federal Aviation Administration assess the adequacy of the 30 minute main gearbox run dry requirement for Category A transport helicopters.
Transport Canada prohibit commercial operation of Category A transport helicopters over water when the sea state will not permit safe ditching and successful evacuation.
Transport Canada require that supplemental underwater breathing apparatus be mandatory for all occupants of helicopters involved in overwater flights who are required to wear a PTSS.
Rotorcraft manufacturers include run dry time information in rotorcraft flight manuals to assist pilots during MGB abnormal or emergency situations.

safety_changes: S-92A gearbox malfunctions section amended to include statement advising pilots that total loss of MGB oil pressure may result in MGB failure in less than 10 minutes
Increased focus on emergency underwater breathing apparatus (EUBA) requirements for offshore helicopter operations
Enhanced sea state criteria for helicopter ditching capability assessments

notes: TSB Aviation Investigation Report A09A0016 read in full
Sections read: Occurrence Summary, Safety Issues, Findings, Causal Factors, Safety Action
Four formal recommendations identified: A11-01 through A11-04
Defect causation clearly documented with prior Alert Service Bulletin SB 329-77-1004
Drowning was immediate cause of death due to cold water and helicopter orientation after impact
One survivor recovered; this was one of TSB's most significant offshore aviation accidents

records.title: Emirates 407
records.time_reference: AEDT (local); exact clock times not reproduced, t is relative to the first rotation attempt at about 22:30

agencies.name: Australian Transport Safety Bureau
agencies.report_title: Tailstrike and runway overrun, Airbus A340-541, A6-ERG, Melbourne Airport, Victoria, 20 March 2009

records.summary: During pre-flight preparation the first officer entered the A340's take-off weight into the laptop performance tool as 262.9 tonnes instead of 362.9 tonnes. The resulting reduced thrust and low reference speeds went undetected through the crew's checks. On take-off from Melbourne's runway 16 the aircraft failed to lift off at the computed rotation speed, struck its tail on the runway, and became airborne only after the captain applied full thrust, beyond the end of the runway, hitting the localiser antenna and lights. The crew dumped fuel and returned safely; nobody was injured.
records.probable_cause: The ATSB found that the take-off weight was inadvertently entered 100 tonnes low in the electronic flight bag performance application, producing take-off speeds and a flex thrust setting that were too low for the actual weight, and that the crew's cross-checks did not detect the error. The design of the performance and flight management systems provided no effective gross-error check, and the operator's procedures for checking take-off performance data were vulnerable to a single undetected error. Distraction and time pressure during pre-flight contributed to the error not being caught.

factors.evidence: The take-off weight was entered as 262.9 t instead of 362.9 t, giving V speeds well below those required and a flex temperature that reduced thrust.
The captain's check of the first officer's performance calculation and the subsequent FMGS entry checks did not detect the 100 t discrepancy.
The ATSB found that the operator's take-off data verification procedure was not fully carried out as intended, and that the procedure itself was not robust against the error.
The crew were subject to distractions and time pressure during the pre-flight period when the data were calculated and checked.

Neither the EFB performance software nor the aircraft's flight management system contained a reasonableness or gross-error check that would flag take-off speeds inconsistent with the aircraft's weight.
When the aircraft did not lift off at the computed rotation speed and pitch was increased, the tail contacted the runway, causing substantial damage to the rear fuselage.
The aircraft became airborne beyond the end of runway 16 and struck the localiser antenna array and a strobe light.
After declaring PAN, holding and dumping fuel, the crew returned to Melbourne and landed safely.

events.text: During pre-flight the first officer enters the take-off weight into the laptop performance application as 262.9 t instead of 362.9 t; the resulting V speeds and flex temperature (74 degrees C) are calculated for an aircraft 100 t lighter.
The captain checks the first officer's figures and the crew enter the speeds into the FMGS; the checks compare values derived from the same wrong input and the error is not detected.
The loadsheet confirms a take-off weight of about 362.9 t, but the comparison against the performance data does not reveal the discrepancy.
Take-off roll on runway 16 (3,657 m) with the reduced flex thrust setting; acceleration is lower than normal but not recognised as abnormal.
At the computed rotation speed the first officer rotates; the aircraft does not lift off. As pitch is increased the tail strikes the runway.
The captain selects TOGA thrust.
The aircraft becomes airborne beyond the end of the runway, striking the localiser antenna array and a strobe light in the overrun area, then climbs away.
Cabin crew report a loud bang and smell during the take-off; the flight crew suspect a tail strike and stop the climb at a safe altitude.
Crew declare PAN, review the aircraft's condition with the cabin crew and decide to return after dumping fuel to reduce landing weight.
Fuel dumping carried out in a holding pattern; approach briefing for the return to Melbourne.
The aircraft lands back at Melbourne about an hour after departure; substantial damage to the rear lower fuselage is found. No injuries.

recommendations.text: Incorporate independent gross-error or reasonableness checks in take-off performance calculation tools and flight management systems so that speeds inconsistent with aircraft weight are flagged.
recommendations.outcome: Airbus developed a take-off securing function in the FMS that checks entered speeds against the aircraft's weight.

recommendations.text: Revise take-off performance procedures so that the calculation is independently performed and cross-checked by both pilots, and manage pre-flight distractions.
recommendations.outcome: Emirates changed its procedures to require independent calculations by each pilot and a comparison of results.

recommendations.text: Pursue the development of take-off performance monitoring systems capable of warning crews of inadequate acceleration during the take-off roll.

safety_changes: Emirates revised its take-off performance calculation and cross-check procedures.
Airbus introduced a take-off securing (TOS) function in the flight management system to detect inconsistent take-off speeds and weights.
The event added impetus to regulatory and industry work on take-off performance monitoring systems and on the design of EFB performance tools.

notes: All event times are approximate offsets; the report's exact clock times are not reproduced.
The distance beyond the runway end at which the aircraft became airborne (reported as about 115 m) is omitted from the events because it was not verified.
The ATSB discussed possible crew fatigue; it is not listed as a factor because the report's conclusion on it was not verified.
Occupant count of 275 (257 passengers, 18 crew) is from memory of the report.

records.title: FedEx Express 80

agencies.name: Japan Transport Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Investigation Report - Crash During Landing Federal Express Corporation McDonnell Douglas MD-11F, N526FE

records.summary: FedEx Express Flight 80 touched down on Runway 34L at Narita in gusty winds of 26 to 40 knots. The first officer executed a delayed flare with a high sink rate; when the aircraft bounced, he applied excessive nose-down pitch input. Repeated bounces caused severe pitch oscillations until the left wing struck the ground, the landing gear collapsed, and the aircraft inverted and burned. Both pilots survived impact but died from injuries before reaching the hospital.
records.probable_cause: The JTSB determined the accident was caused by porpoising oscillations that developed during touchdown following the first officer's delayed flare and high sink rate, compounded by his large nose-down inputs after the first bounce that deviated from approved MD-11 procedures of maintaining a 7.5-degree pitch angle and using thrust to control descent.

factors.evidence: surface winds 320° at 26 knots gusting to 40 knots reported at time of accident (p. 3)
high sink rate during final approach not suppressed until aircraft was nearly on runway (p. 88-90)
first bounce resulting from high touchdown sink rate (7 fps) coupled with large nose-up inputs, much higher than average of 60 previous landings (p. 91-92)

large nose-down input (-4.9°) applied just before first touchdown and continuing after first bounce (-6.7°), causing touchdown on nose gear and deviating from approved procedures requiring 7.5° pitch and thrust control (p. 92-93)
left wing transferred force into left main landing gear exceeding its design limit of 1200 ft/min touchdown (p. 3)
left wing struck the ground as left main gear collapsed during third touchdown, causing aircraft to veer to the left, burst into flames and invert (p. 8-9)
fire broke out near the rear of left engine at 06:48:29; aircraft engulfed in flames as it rolled inverted (p. 21)

events.text: Narita Tower informed wind 320° at 28 knots gusting to 40 knots
Narita Tower reported windshear plus/minus 15 knots on final approach below 2,000 feet
Narita Tower informed surface wind 320° at 26 knots with maximum 38 knots
Narita Tower issued landing clearance for Runway 34L, wind 320° at 29 knots with maximum 36 knots
100 feet callout; aircraft with CAS 154 knots and pitch angle 3.5°
Autopilot disconnected at 198 feet radio altitude; aircraft flying with unstable approach parameters
Large nose-down control column input (-3.0°) initiated at 20 feet radio altitude
First touchdown on right main landing gear with high sink rate of 7 feet per second; vertical acceleration 1.63 G
Aircraft bounced off runway; auto ground spoilers deployed at 25°
Second touchdown on nose landing gear in nose-low attitude (-1.8°) with pitch angle decreased 6.4° in 1.75 seconds; vertical acceleration 2.21 G
Second bounce initiated; large nose-down control inputs continued (-7.7° to -7.4°)
Third touchdown on nose landing gear followed by main landing gears; maximum vertical acceleration 3.06 G
Fire broke out near rear of left engine at pitch 10° and roll -15°; aircraft engulfed in flames
Aircraft rolled over to left and inverted off runway; came to rest in grass area with fuselage destroyed by fire except cockpit

recommendations.text: Enhance bounce recovery training for MD-11 pilots with emphasis on proper pitch attitude control (7.5°) and thrust application procedures
Conduct proficiency training on approaches in gusty wind conditions, including early recognition of unstable approach conditions requiring go-around
Ensure pilot monitoring performance during landing phase, including requirement for pilot monitoring to call out deviation from glide slope and prompt go-around recommendations
Review AGS (auto ground spoiler) deployment timing and effectiveness in preventing bounce-induced pitch oscillations during landing

notes: Sections read: synopsis (pages 3-4), flight history (pages 16-22), analysis including causes (pages 74-93)
Full depth reading performed due to complex porpoising sequence with multiple bounces and pitch oscillations
Detailed CVR and DFDR reconstruction provided in report showing second-by-second aircraft behavior
All major factors and contributing causes identified through comprehensive technical analysis

records.title: 2009 Bond Helicopters Eurocopter AS332 crash

location.name: North Sea, 11 nm northeast of Peterhead

records.summary: Bond Offshore Helicopters Flight 85N crashed in the North Sea on 1 April 2009 while returning from a BP oil platform to Aberdeen Airport. The main rotor separated following catastrophic failure of the main rotor gearbox. A fatigue fracture of a second stage planet gear in the epicyclic module caused the gearbox failure. Metallic debris had been detected on the gearbox chip detector 36 flying hours before the accident but was not recognized as indicating degradation requiring action.
records.probable_cause: Catastrophic failure of the main rotor gearbox resulting from fatigue fracture of a second stage planet gear in the epicyclic module. The detection of metallic particles on the chip detector on 25 March 2009 was not recognized as an indication of gear degradation requiring immediate action before the next flight.

factors.evidence: Fatigue fracture of second stage planet gear in epicyclic module caused gearbox failure (p. 1)
Magnetic particle on chip detector not recognized as gear degradation indicator (p. 1)
Main rotor gearbox failure and rotor separation; helicopter crashed with all 16 killed (p. 1)

events.text: 36 flying hours before accident: magnetic particle detected on epicyclic module chip detector during routine inspection (p. 1)
Catastrophic failure of main rotor gearbox during cruise flight from BP Miller platform to Aberdeen (p. 1)
Helicopter crashed 11 nautical miles northeast of Peterhead in North Sea (p. 1)
Investigation confirmed fatigue fracture of second stage planet gear as root cause; metallic debris detection systems inadequate for early warning (p. 1)
All 16 occupants (2 flight crew, 14 passengers/crew) killed in crash and North Sea waters (p. 1)

notes: AAIB Final Report 2/2011; 5 key events extracted
History of flight section reviewed; fatigue failure in gearbox identified as root cause
Chip detector metallic particle detection discussed as contributing factor

records.title: Air France 447

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses pour la sécurité de l'aviation civile
agencies.report_title: Final Report on the accident on 1st June 2009 to the Airbus A330-203 registered F-GZCP operated by Air France flight AF 447 Rio de Janeiro - Paris

agencies.name: Centro de Investigação e Prevenção de Acidentes Aeronáuticos

location.name: Atlantic Ocean, about 570 nm north-east of Natal, Brazil

records.summary: In cruise at FL350 near the intertropical convergence zone the Pitot probes were obstructed by ice crystals, the airspeed indications became inconsistent and the autopilot and autothrust disconnected, with the flight control law reverting to alternate. The pilot flying applied nose-up inputs and the aircraft climbed to about 38,000 ft, where the stall warning sounded and the aircraft stalled. The stall was never recognised and the aircraft descended for 3 minutes 30 seconds, striking the ocean at 02:14:28 with all 228 occupants killed.
records.probable_cause: The accident resulted from the temporary inconsistency between the measured airspeeds, likely as a result of the obstruction of the Pitot probes by ice crystals, which led to autopilot disconnection and reconfiguration to alternate law; inappropriate control inputs that destabilised the flight path; the crew not making the connection between the loss of airspeed indications and the appropriate procedure; the late identification by the PNF of the deviation from the flight path and insufficient correction by the PF; the crew not identifying the approach to stall, the lack of an immediate response and exit from the flight envelope; and the crew's failure to diagnose the stall situation and consequently the lack of inputs that would have made recovery possible. Contributing factors included the absence of training in manual aircraft handling at high altitude and in the approach to stall procedure, the ergonomics of the stall warning and the absence of an angle of attack display, the lack of a clear display of airspeed inconsistency, the crew task-sharing and CRM weaknesses after the captain left the cockpit, and the known Pitot icing issue that had not yet led to replacement of the probes.

factors.evidence: The aircraft entered a region of ice crystals at the top of convective cloud in the ITCZ; the crew had made only a small deviation around the weather.
The Thales C16195AA Pitot probes were obstructed by ice crystals, producing a sudden fall in indicated airspeed on the left and standby instruments.
Inconsistency between the three airspeed sources caused rejection of the ADR data; airspeed indications were lost for up to about a minute.
The autopilot and autothrust disconnected at 02:10:05 as a consequence of the airspeed inconsistency.
Flight controls reverted to alternate 2 law, removing angle-of-attack protection and leaving the aircraft in a mode with which the crew were unfamiliar.
Pitot icing events on the A330/A340 with Thales AA probes were known to Airbus, Air France and the authorities; the replacement programme was in progress but F-GZCP had not yet received new probes.
The sudden autopilot disconnection, warnings and unusual conditions surprised the crew and degraded their response.
The PF made abrupt, predominantly nose-up sidestick inputs that took the aircraft into a steep climb to about 38,000 ft at over 6,000 ft/min.
Numerous ECAM messages, warnings and the need to hand-fly at altitude saturated both pilots; neither called the unreliable airspeed procedure.
The captain had left for rest without a clear designation of relief responsibilities; task sharing and communication between the two co-pilots broke down.
The PNF noticed the climb late and did not effectively challenge the PF's inputs or take control.
Stall warning sounded continuously from 02:10:51; angle of attack exceeded 40 degrees and the aircraft descended at about 10,000 ft/min in a stalled condition.
Neither pilot referred to the stall warning or identified the stall; the aircraft's behaviour was not understood.
The PF held the sidestick back and applied TOGA thrust; nose-down inputs were never sustained and the trimmable stabiliser reached 13 degrees nose-up.
The PNF and captain intervened with sidestick inputs without a clear takeover, producing dual inputs in the final minute.
The stall warning stopped when indicated airspeed fell below 60 kt and resumed when the nose was lowered, giving misleading feedback; no angle of attack was displayed.
Air France crews received no training in manual handling at high altitude or in approach-to-stall in alternate law.
The report noted the erosion of manual handling skills in highly automated operations as a contributor to the crew's inability to control the aircraft.
The crew lost awareness of the aircraft's energy state and attitude, and the captain on his return could not diagnose the situation from the available indications.
The aircraft remained stalled until impact with the ocean at 02:14:28.

events.text: Captain leaves the cockpit for rest; the junior co-pilot in the right seat is PF, the more experienced co-pilot takes the left seat as PNF.
PNF suggests turning a little to the left; the crew alter heading about 12 degrees left to avoid returns on the weather radar and reduce speed to Mach 0.80 with engine anti-ice on.
Turbulence increases slightly and a noise of ice crystals is heard on the windshield; the aircraft is in ice crystals at the top of convective cloud.
Autopilot and autothrust disconnect; the left PFD speed falls from 274 kt to 52 kt in a few seconds. Flight control law reverts to alternate.
PF takes control and applies a nose-up, left-roll sidestick input; the aircraft rolls right then left and pitches up.
Stall warning sounds twice briefly as angle of attack momentarily exceeds the alternate-law threshold; the vertical speed reaches about 7,000 ft/min.
PNF announces that the speeds have been lost and that they are in alternate law; ECAM actions begin but the unreliable airspeed procedure is not called.
PNF says several times to go back down, noting the climb; pitch reaches about 11 degrees nose-up as the aircraft passes FL360.
Left PFD airspeed indication becomes valid again, showing 223 kt; the standby (ISIS) speed follows later; no comment is made by the crew.
Stall warning sounds continuously; the aircraft is at about 37,500 ft with angle of attack increasing beyond 6 degrees.
PF advances the thrust levers to TOGA and maintains nose-up sidestick; the trimmable horizontal stabiliser begins to move nose-up from 3 to 13 degrees over the following minute.
Aircraft reaches its maximum altitude of about 37,924 ft with pitch about 16 degrees nose-up; it then begins to descend while still pitched up as the stall develops.
