Captain returns to the cockpit; the aircraft is descending through about 35,000 ft with angle of attack above 40 degrees and vertical speed near -10,000 ft/min, and rolls of up to 40 degrees.
As indicated airspeed falls below 60 kt the angle of attack values are considered invalid and the stall warning stops; it sounds again whenever the nose is lowered and speed increases.
PF says he no longer has any indication; PNF says they have no valid indications. Thrust levers are briefly reduced to idle and speedbrakes momentarily extended.
PF reveals he has been holding the sidestick fully back for some time; the captain and PNF respond that he must not climb. PNF takes over briefly, with dual inputs.
PF resumes nose-up inputs; the aircraft descends through about 4,000 ft; GPWS 'pull up' and sink rate warnings sound.
PF calls that they are going to hit; last recorded values show pitch about 16 degrees nose-up, roll 5 degrees left, ground speed 107 kt, vertical speed about -10,900 ft/min.
Aircraft strikes the ocean surface in a stalled condition; recordings stop. All 228 occupants killed.

cvr.speaker: PF
cvr.translation: I don't have any more indications.

cvr.speaker: PF
cvr.text: Mais je suis à fond à cabrer depuis tout à l'heure.
cvr.translation: But I've been at full nose-up for a while.

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: Non non non ne remonte pas.

recommendations.text: Review the certification criteria for Pitot probes in icing conditions, including high-altitude ice crystals, and require probe replacement where standards are not met.
recommendations.outcome: Thales AA probes were replaced fleet-wide by airworthiness directive; ice crystal icing certification requirements were revised.

recommendations.text: Make mandatory the triggering of the flight data recorder ULB with extended transmission time and study deployable recorders and regular position transmission for aircraft over remote areas.
recommendations.outcome: ICAO standards on flight recorder locating, 90-day ULBs and autonomous distress tracking followed.

recommendations.text: Require training in manual aircraft handling at high altitude, approach-to-stall recognition and recovery in degraded flight control laws, and startle effect, for airline pilots.
recommendations.outcome: Upset prevention and recovery training (UPRT) became mandatory; stall recovery procedures were revised to prioritise reducing angle of attack.

recommendations.text: Study the inclusion of an angle of attack indicator on transport aircraft and improve the stall warning logic so that it remains consistent with the aircraft state at very low airspeed.
Review the ergonomics and the logic of the flight director bars during unreliable airspeed and stall warning, and the display of dual sidestick inputs.
Define criteria for relief crew composition and the handover of command when the captain leaves the cockpit, and reinforce CRM in a two-co-pilot configuration.

safety_changes: Fleet-wide replacement of Thales AA Pitot probes on A330/A340 and revised ice crystal icing certification criteria for probes.
Revised stall recovery procedures from Airbus, Boeing and regulators emphasising reduction of angle of attack over thrust application.
Mandatory upset prevention and recovery training and high-altitude manual handling training.
Extended 90-day underwater locator beacons, low-frequency airframe beacons and ICAO autonomous distress tracking requirements.
Air France changes to relief crew designation and captain handover procedures.

notes: CVR clock times are those given in the BEA final report to within a second or two; wording of the French lines follows the report transcript and translations are the BEA's or close paraphrases.
Recommendation ids left null: BEA issued FRAN-2009, FRAN-2011 and FRAN-2012 series recommendations, but individual numbers are not reproduced to avoid mis-attribution.
Some intermediate altitudes (e.g. 35,000 ft at the captain's return) are approximate readings from the FDR plots.
The fdr field refers to a separate FDR keyframe file to be supplied.

records.title: Yemenia 626

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses
agencies.report_title: Final Report

records.summary: Yemenia Flight 626, an Airbus A310-324 flying from Sanaa to Moroni, crashed into the Indian Ocean on 30 June 2009 after a botched go-around. While climbing away from a failed approach, the crew's control inputs caused the autopilot to set thrust to idle; saturated by workload and lacking training, the crew made repeated nose-up inputs and failed to recover from the resulting aerodynamic stall, ignoring the aircraft's warnings. All but one of the 153 aboard were killed; a 12-year-old girl survived by clinging to wreckage.
records.probable_cause: The accident was caused by inappropriate crew actions on flight controls leading to an aerodynamic stall that was not recovered. The crew, saturated by workload during an unstabilized visual approach and lacking training, failed to properly respond to multiple alarms and recover from the stall.

factors.evidence: The crew executed an unstabilized visual approach which they then abandoned for a go-around (p. 36).
During the go-around climb, crew control inputs caused the autopilot to set thrust to idle, decreasing airspeed (p. 73).
The crew was saturated by workload managing the aircraft trajectory and locating the runway while multiple alarms were triggered (p. 73).
The crew lacked adequate training and briefing for the Moroni MVI procedure and for handling emergency situations (p. 73).
The crew's control inputs and thrust reduction led to an aerodynamic stall that developed during the climb (p. 72-73).
The crew failed to properly recover from the stall, continuing to make nose-up inputs (p. 73).
The crew did not properly respond to multiple GPWS SINK RATE and PULL UP warnings (p. 38-39).
The aircraft entered an unrecoverable stall and impacted the Indian Ocean at 65 ft altitude with 185 kt airspeed and 15° nose-up pitch (p. 40-41).

events.text: The crew decided to abandon the unstabilized approach and execute a go-around.
Autopilot 2 disconnected; first officer initiates right turn at 1000 ft altitude.
GPWS SINK RATE alarm triggered; aircraft at 548 ft radio altitude with -2000 ft/min descent and 27° right bank.
Crew levels wings to 0° and increases pitch to 12° in response to GPWS warnings.
GPWS TOO LOW TERRAIN alarm at 230 ft altitude with -1000 ft/min descent and 29° right bank.
Crew levels wings and increases pitch to 17°; aircraft reaches minimum altitude of 161 ft radio altitude.
Landing gear retracted; gear not down warning triggers for 16 seconds.
LVL/CH mode engaged at 700 ft with 2000 ft altitude selected; autothrottle commands TOGA power.
Stall alarm recorded in FDR at 13° angle of attack; airspeed rapidly decreasing from 185 kt while climbing.
Alpha Floor protection triggered at 12.1° angle of attack and 191 kt; thrust lever speed increases to 8°/s.
Autopilot disconnected; altitude 653 ft; pitch and angle of attack continue to increase; stall alarm continues.
Pilot applies full nose-down pitch input at 698 ft altitude (only occurrence after stall began); airspeed is 170 kt.
Crew applies go-lever thrust command at 1034 ft altitude while in high-altitude stall condition with 15-23° angle of attack.
AP instinctive disconnect alarm ends; continuous stall warning continues until impact.
Aircraft strikes Indian Ocean at pitch angle 15° nose-up, 21° right bank, 185 kt, 65 ft altitude.

recommendations.text: Establish permanent dedicated search and rescue means adapted to the search for and rescue of aircraft accident survivors at sea near aerodromes.
Ensure that all crews performing flights to Moroni are properly trained in execution of the MVI procedure.
Review pilot training conditions for Yemenia, particularly their ability to react to emergency situations.

notes: Full BEA final report read; sections 2.1 (scenario), 3.2 (causes), and 4 (recommendations) extensively reviewed
Detailed flight data timeline from FDR analysis with specific altitudes, airspeeds, pitch angles and angles of attack
CVR content not explicitly transcribed in sections read but event times precisely match FDR timestamps
Report clearly identifies inappropriate crew actions leading to stall and inadequate recovery despite multiple warnings

records.title: Sudan Airways 2241

location.name: 1.6 km from end of Runway 30, Sharjah International Airport

records.summary: A Boeing 707 cargo aircraft crashed 1.6 km from the runway at Sharjah after takeoff when the No. 4 engine core cowls separated during initial climb. The crew misinterpreted the resulting erroneous engine pressure ratio indication as engine failure, initiated a turn, and the aircraft exceeded the maximum bank angle causing an aerodynamic stall. All six crew members were killed.
records.probable_cause: The aircraft exceeded the maximum bank angle during attempted recovery from a perceived No. 4 engine power loss, resulting in an aerodynamic stall and uncontrollable loss of altitude that was not recoverable. The No. 4 engine cowling had separated and damaged the engine's pressure ratio flex line.

factors.evidence: No. 4 engine core cowls departed from engine at takeoff approximately 15 seconds after liftoff (p. 1); cowls had gone through multiple skin repairs not up to aviation standards
Crew response to perceived engine failure was inappropriate, exceeding published maximum bank angle of 15 degrees for single-engine emergency (p. 62)
Aircraft entered into a stall after the published maximum bank angle was exceeded (p. 62)
Aircraft loss of control that was not recoverable (p. 62)

Aircraft was not properly maintained; No. 4 engine cowls had been through multiple skin repairs not up to aviation standards; operator's maintenance system failed to correctly address cowl latch issues (p. 62-63)
SCAA safety oversight system deficiency to adequately identify operator's chronic maintenance, operations and quality management deficiencies (p. 63)

events.text: Tower cleared SUD 2241 for takeoff from Runway 30
Approximately 15 seconds after liftoff at 300 feet AGL, No. 4 engine core cowls detached and collapsed onto departure runway
Crew responded to perceived engine failure but response was inappropriate, exceeding maximum bank angle (p. 62)
Aircraft at approximately 380 feet AGL with aircraft stalled after exceeding maximum bank angle
Aircraft in extreme right wing down attitude impacted ground 1.6 km from runway end with approximately 90 degree right wing down attitude

recommendations.text: Enhance its safety oversight system to assure the operations and airworthiness of Sudan operators and Sudan registered aircraft are in compliance with current applicable Air Navigation Regulations and in conformity with Annexes to ICAO Convention

Ensure that all operators' maintenance management systems are in compliance with applicable current Air Navigation Regulations including proper maintenance of aircraft records, inspection systems, and flight recorders

Ensure that all operators' operations management systems are in compliance with applicable current Air Navigation Regulations including maintenance of company and aircraft manuals, crew training programs and records
Ensure that all operators have a quality system to assure that operations and maintenance functions are performed in accordance with applicable regulations

Assure that inspection, maintenance and quality functions are improved including proper troubleshooting and corrective repair actions according to Aircraft Maintenance Manual and reporting of unairworthy conditions to local Civil Aviation Authority

recommendations.to: General Civil Aviation Authority of United Arab Emirates
recommendations.text: Take necessary measures to facilitate adequate aviation pathology testings on deceased crew bodies and remains

recommendations.to: General Civil Aviation Authority of United Arab Emirates
recommendations.text: Improve Civil Aviation Regulations to contain provisions for more proactive approach to safety regarding foreign operators

safety_changes: Enhanced maintenance oversight for aging aircraft
Improved standards for engine cowling repairs and inspections
Enhanced crew training for single-engine emergencies

notes: Read sections: aircraft accident brief, synopsis, history of flight, findings, causes, contributing factors, safety recommendations

records.title: Divi Divi Air 014

location.name: Caribbean Sea south of Klein Bonaire

records.summary: A Britten-Norman BN-2A Islander departed Curacao with 1 pilot and 9 passengers bound for Bonaire. At approximately 3500 feet during climb, the starboard engine failed. The pilot elected to continue to Bonaire on one engine despite the aircraft's inability to maintain altitude. The aircraft was overloaded by approximately 9% of maximum structural weight. During descent to Bonaire, the pilot did not deploy flaps and made minimal effort to brief passengers on the emergency. The aircraft ditched in shallow water south of Klein Bonaire. All 9 passengers survived the impact but the pilot, who struck his head during landing and lost consciousness, drowned when the aircraft sank.
records.probable_cause: The accident was caused by the failure of the starboard engine in cruise, combined with the pilot's decision to continue to the destination airport despite the aircraft being unable to maintain altitude due to structural overloading. Contributing factors included the pilot's inadequate preparation of passengers for the emergency landing, landing without flaps selected, insufficient company safety management and oversight of weight control procedures, and inadequate regulatory oversight of the airline's operations.

factors.evidence: Starboard engine ceased running at altitude approximately 3500 feet during initial climb phase (p. 16)
Aircraft departed with overload of 9% above maximum structural take-off weight of 6600 lb (p. 25, 3467-3471)
With one engine inoperative, aircraft could not maintain altitude and descended at approximately 140 feet per minute average (p. 19)
Pilot undertook insufficient attempts to inform passengers about approaching emergency landing at sea after engine failure; safety briefing not properly understood by all passengers (p. 3484-3485)
Pilot did not brief cabin crew or passengers effectively on emergency procedures, and landing was executed without proper configuration (flaps up)
Pilot lost consciousness upon impact with water and drowned when aircraft sank (p. 26-27, 1322-1328)
Aircraft touched down on water at position 0.7 nautical miles south of Klein Bonaire at 10:17 local time (p. 800-801)

events.text: Aircraft takes off from Hato International Airport, Curacao with 1 pilot and 9 passengers
Aircraft climbs to flight level 035 (3500 feet) and pilot reduces power from climb to cruise power (p. 16)
Starboard engine fails during cruise at FL035. Pilot increases left engine power, feathers right propeller, and attempts restart (p. 16)
Pilot reports to Hato Tower: 'Divi 014 requesting switch to Flamingo, priority landing with Flamingo, have lost one of the engines' (p. 16)
Pilot contacts Flamingo Tower, reports one engine out, maintaining 3000 feet, 24 miles out from destination (p. 16)
Pilot reports 10 nautical miles from airport, flying at 1000 feet altitude, expecting to land in 10 minutes (p. 18)
Pilot reports 8 nautical miles away, 600 feet altitude, having trouble maintaining altitude (p. 18)
Pilot reports 6 nautical miles away, flying at 300 feet altitude (p. 18)
Last radio contact: Pilot reports 5 nautical miles away, flying at 200 feet, still losing altitude, planning emergency landing (p. 18)
Aircraft impacts water approximately 0.7 nautical miles south of Klein Bonaire with left wing slightly down; left front door breaks off on impact (p. 18-19)
Pilot strikes head on vertical door/window frame or instrument panel during impact and loses consciousness (p. 18-19)
All 9 passengers exit aircraft through emergency exits; some sit on wings briefly; passengers form circle in water to support those without life jackets (p. 19)
Aircraft sinks with pilot still on board as cabin fills rapidly with water following loss of left front door and shattered windscreen (p. 19)
Two boats with recreational divers arrive at scene approximately 5 minutes after ditching; passengers rescued and transferred to second boat (p. 19)
Passengers arrive at Kralendijk at approximately 10:37 local time; 6 transported to hospital for examination, 3 others depart on own (p. 19)

recommendations.text: Demonstrate that the load and balance programme, the pilot training, the safety equipment and instructions of the Britten-Norman Islander aircraft in use are brought up to standard and comply with legal requirements and limitations specified by the aircraft manufacturer, and that risks of the load and balance programme are assessed and structurally controlled in the safety management system (p. 3604-3609)

recommendations.to: Minister of Traffic, Transport and Division of Urban Planning and Housing of Curacao
recommendations.text: Ensure that CARNA is correctly applied and user specifications by manufacturer of Britten-Norman Islander being used at airlines fall under supervision of Curacao Civil Aviation Authority in light of findings in conclusion 6 (p. 3613-3615)

recommendations.to: Minister of Traffic, Transport and Division of Urban Planning and Housing of Curacao
recommendations.text: Provide Dutch secretary of State of Infrastructure and Environment with follow-up status of ICAO audit 2008 findings in relation to findings in this report (p. 3616-3618)

Ensure that alerting process and emergency supporting services are improved by regularly practicing with deployment of multiple disciplines, assessment of practice and taking measures for arising shortcomings (p. 3620-3624)

notes: Sections read: Description of events (2.3), personal injury (2.4), aircraft info (2.8), survival aspects (2.17), conclusions (6), recommendations (7)
Engine model and specific failure cause not determined by investigation
Flaps position at impact could not be confirmed due to aircraft damage during recovery
Standard passenger weight discrepancy (160 lb on papers vs 187 lb actual) contributed to overloading calculation

records.title: Pel-Air Westwind VH-NGA
records.time_reference: UTC; clock times not reproduced, t is relative to the ditching (t=0) with earlier events negative

agencies.name: Australian Transport Safety Bureau
agencies.report_title: Ditching of Israel Aircraft Industries Westwind 1124A, VH-NGA, 6 km SW of Norfolk Island Airport, 18 November 2009 (re-opened investigation, final report 2017)

records.operator: Pel-Air Aviation (air ambulance flight for CareFlight)

location.name: Pacific Ocean about 6 km south-west of Norfolk Island

records.summary: An air ambulance Westwind carrying a patient from Apia to Melbourne via a refuelling stop at Norfolk Island departed at night with fuel for the island but no alternate. Weather at Norfolk Island deteriorated below the landing minima after departure and the crew did not obtain the updates in time to divert. After four unsuccessful instrument approaches in cloud and rain, with fuel critical, the pilot in command ditched the aircraft in the sea near the island. All six on board escaped the sinking aircraft and were rescued about 90 minutes later.
records.probable_cause: The ATSB's re-opened investigation found that the pilot in command's pre-flight planning did not adequately consider the possibility of weather deterioration at Norfolk Island and that the flight departed without an alternate or additional fuel to cope with it, which the operator's procedures and the regulations then in force permitted. Updated forecasts and reports showing conditions below the minima were not obtained by the crew until the aircraft had passed the point at which a diversion was possible. Contributing were deficiencies in Pel-Air's operational risk controls and fuel planning guidance for its air ambulance operations, and shortcomings in CASA's oversight of the operator.

factors.evidence: The re-opened investigation found Pel-Air's risk controls for long over-water air ambulance flights, including fuel planning and in-flight decision guidance, were inadequate.
The ATSB found that CASA's surveillance of Pel-Air's operations had not identified the operator's deficiencies, and that the regulations did not require an alternate for the flight.
The pilot in command's flight planning did not make adequate provision for weather deterioration at an isolated aerodrome; the flight departed without an alternate or fuel to reach one.
The crew did not obtain the updated Norfolk Island weather in time and did not recognise the deteriorating situation until diversion was no longer possible.
Cloud and rain at Norfolk Island were below the landing minima on arrival; the crew could not see the runway on four instrument approaches.
The approaches and the ditching took place at night.
With fuel critical and no landing possible, the pilot in command elected to ditch while engine power remained available.
The aircraft was ditched in the sea about 6 km south-west of the airport, broke up on impact and sank; all six occupants escaped.

events.text: Pre-flight planning at Apia: the forecast then available indicates Norfolk Island conditions above the alternate minima, so no alternate is planned and no extra fuel is carried beyond the operator's requirement.
Departs Apia at night for Norfolk Island with the patient, a doctor, a nurse, the patient's partner and two pilots on board.
After departure, updated Norfolk Island observations and forecast amendments show deteriorating cloud and visibility; the crew do not obtain them at this stage.
The crew obtain the Norfolk Island weather en route; conditions are now below the landing minima but the aircraft has passed the point from which a diversion to another aerodrome is possible.
First instrument approach to Norfolk Island; no visual reference at the minima; missed approach.
Second approach, also unsuccessful; the crew consider options as fuel decreases.
Third approach unsuccessful in cloud and rain.
Fourth approach unsuccessful; fuel is now critical.
The pilot in command decides to ditch while fuel and engine power remain; a MAYDAY is transmitted and the cabin is prepared.
The aircraft is ditched at night in the sea about 6 km south-west of the airport; the fuselage is damaged on impact and the aircraft sinks. All six occupants escape.
After about 90 minutes in the water the survivors are located and rescued by a local vessel.

recommendations.text: Strengthen fuel, alternate and in-flight re-planning requirements for flights to isolated aerodromes, particularly for air ambulance and passenger-carrying charter operations.
recommendations.outcome: CASA revised the fuel and alternate requirements applying to such operations and to remote island destinations.

recommendations.text: Improve operational risk controls, fuel planning guidance and crew decision-support for long over-water air ambulance flights.
Improve the effectiveness of regulatory surveillance so that operator deficiencies of this kind are identified.

safety_changes: CASA introduced stricter fuel and alternate requirements for air ambulance and passenger charter flights to isolated aerodromes.

The original 2012 ATSB report was criticised by a Senate inquiry and an independent review; the ATSB re-opened the investigation and published a revised report in 2017 with broader organisational findings.
Pel-Air revised its long-range over-water operating procedures.

notes: All event times are approximate offsets relative to the ditching; the report's clock times and the sequence of the four approaches (types and exact timing) were not verified.

The re-opened report also discussed possible fatigue of the pilot in command and the handling of weather information by air traffic services; these are not listed as factors because their exact findings were not verified.
Injury details for the occupants are not given (injuries_serious null).

records.title: Lufthansa Cargo 8460
records.summary: A Lufthansa Cargo MD-11 touched down with excessive force at Riyadh and bounced repeatedly on the runway. The crew failed to recognize the bouncing condition and applied control inputs that worsened the bouncing. On the third and final impact, the aft fuselage ruptured, causing the aircraft to break up and veer off the runway. Post-impact fire consumed the midsection before being controlled by emergency services. Both crew members evacuated with injuries.
records.probable_cause: The aircraft touched down with excessive vertical speed and bounced. The flight crew did not recognize the bouncing condition. Their control inputs, particularly a large nose-down input by the Captain during the first bounce, worsened the bouncing. Successive hard landings with increasing load factors (2.1g, 3.0g, 4.4g) culminated in the third touchdown rupturing the aft fuselage at Fuselage Station 1441. (p. 3, 52-53)

factors.evidence: Main gear touched down at 945 feet with descent rate of -780 ft/min (13 ft/sec), achieving 2.1g normal load factor (p. 9)
Flare was delayed and initiated between 1.7-2.0 seconds before touchdown at 23-31 feet above runway (p. 9)
Flight crew did not recognize the bounce condition after initial touchdown (p. 9, Finding 3)
Captain made large nose-down control column input during first bounce, unloading aircraft and causing second hard landing (p. 9, 52)
Aft fuselage ruptured at Fuselage Station 1441 due to 4.4g vertical load on third touchdown (p. 10, 51)
Fuel spilled from severed lines ignited in left wheel well and traveled to upper cargo area (p. 10)

events.text: Auto Pilot and Auto Throttle turned OFF by First Officer during approach
Aircraft centered on glide slope and localizer; dipped half dot below 25 seconds before touchdown
First Officer initiated flare 1.7-2.0 seconds before touchdown at 23-31 feet above runway
Main gear touched down 945 feet from runway threshold at -13 ft/sec descent rate, normal load factor 2.1g
Spoilers deployed to 30 degrees; aircraft bounced to 4 feet maximum height
Captain pushed forward on control column during first bounce, unloading aircraft
Second touchdown with main and nose gear at -11 ft/sec descent rate, normal load factor 3.0g
Both pilots pulled back creating 14 degree pitch angle during second bounce
Main gear reached 12 feet during second bounce; spoilers reached full 60 degree extension
Third and final touchdown at -17 ft/sec descent rate, normal load factor 4.4g
Aft fuselage ruptured behind wing trailing edge at Fuselage Station 1441; fuel lines severed
Captain deployed thrust reversers; engines 1 and 3 responded; requested Mayday declaration
First Officer declared Mayday while aircraft departing runway
Nose gear collapsed; aircraft stopped 8800 feet from threshold, 300 feet left of centerline
Fire ignited from spilled fuel and traveled to upper cargo area
Both pilots evacuated aircraft using left forward door slide

recommendations.text: Require Boeing to revise MD-11 Flight Crew Operating Manual to reemphasize high sink rate awareness during landing, importance of maintaining landing pitch attitude after touchdown, and proper go-around procedures for bounced landings
recommendations.outcome: MD-11 Flight Crew Operating Manual revised by Boeing 15 February 2011

recommendations.text: Require all MD-11 operators to incorporate Boeing-recommended bounce recognition and recovery procedure in operating manuals and recurrent simulator training
Should consider installing Head-Up Displays (HUDs) on MD-11F aircraft
Shall ensure all Departments using recording devices at airports synchronize time with ATC time
Shall ensure Airport Security Services properly cordon-off accident sites
Shall ensure all fire fighting personnel wear appropriate Personal Protection Equipment (PPE)
Should consider installing cameras with recording capability at all airports within KSA

notes: Deep read from BFU final report: synopsis, history of flight, findings, recommendations sections (p. 3-10, 52-59)
15 events extracted with descent rates and load factors
All factors include page citations

records.title: 2010 Alaska Turbo Otter crash
records.summary: A de Havilland DHC-3T floatplane on a scenic/fishing trip crashed into mountainous terrain in the Muklung Hills about 10 nautical miles northeast of Aleknagik, Alaska. The aircraft was climbing and turning left when it struck terrain at approximately 950 feet elevation. The airline transport pilot and four passengers were killed; four passengers were seriously injured. The investigation could not establish the probable cause with certainty due to the lack of flight data or cockpit voice recorders, but concluded the pilot's temporary unresponsiveness was the likely cause.
records.probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Board determines that the probable cause of this accident was the pilot's temporary unresponsiveness for reasons that could not be established from the available information. Contributing to the investigation's inability to determine exactly what occurred in the final minutes of the flight was the lack of a cockpit recorder system with the ability to capture audio, images, and parametric data.

factors.evidence: Pilot's temporary unresponsiveness; possible medical event such as stroke recurrence or other incapacitation (p. 70)
Aircraft departed from expected route and turned toward rising terrain in a manner inconsistent with the pilot's reported proficiency level (p. 47-49)
Although precursors for fatigue were present, insufficient evidence to determine if fatigue-related performance impairments played a role (p. 68)
Ceilings and visibility likely reduced pilot's ability to see terrain; visibility estimated between 2-5 miles with 500-1000 foot overcast (p. 48-49)
Aircraft in climbing left turn when it impacted terrain at approximately 950 feet msl elevation (p. 47)

events.text: Aircraft departed Lake Nerka lodge for Nushagak River fishing camp with 9 occupants
Aircraft at approximately 1,080 feet msl with changing altitudes indicating pilot maneuvering to remain below clouds
Last recorded Sky Connect position at approximately 920 feet msl altitude on east-northeast heading toward Muklung Hills
Aircraft radar altimeter provided visual and aural altitude alerts approximately 4-6 seconds before impact, likely prompting control input
Aircraft in climbing left turn with nose-up pitch and left bank angles impacted terrain at approximately 950 feet msl elevation in Muklung Hills, about 500 meters short of planned landing site

recommendations.text: Consult with appropriate specialists and revise the current internal Federal Aviation Administration guidance on issuance of medical certification subsequent to ischemic stroke or intracerebral hemorrhage to ensure that it is clear and includes specific requirements for a neuropsychological evaluation and assessment of risk of recurrence

Correct the deficiencies with the in-service automated weather sensor system (AWSS) stations, specifically the known problems with present weather sensors and ceilometers, to ensure that the AWSS stations provide accurate information as soon as practical

Implement a collaborative test program in Alaska between the Federal Aviation Administration, the National Weather Service (NWS), the local academic community, and private entities to establish the viability of relaying weather information collected from airborne aircraft equipped with existing data-link technology

If the Federal Aviation Administration's test program recommended in Safety Recommendation A-11-50 establishes that the use of existing data-link technology is a viable means of relaying collected information in real-time from an airborne platform, encourage and provide incentives to data link-equipped aircraft operators in Alaska to outfit their aircraft with weather-sensing equipment for real-time data relay

Educate pilots of 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 flight operations about the benefits of notifying passengers about the location and operation of survival and emergency communication equipment on board their airplanes

Require a detailed inspection, during annual inspections, of all emergency locator transmitters installed in general aviation aircraft to ensure that the emergency locator transmitters are mounted and retained in accordance with the manufacturer's specifications

Determine if the emergency locator transmitter (ELT) mounting requirements and retention tests specified by Technical Standard Order (TSO) C91a and TSO C126 are adequate to assess retention capabilities in ELT designs. Based on the results of this determination, revise, as necessary, TSO requirements to ensure proper retention of ELTs during airplane accidents

Require all existing turbine-powered, nonexperimental, nonrestricted-category aircraft that are not equipped with a cockpit voice recorder and are operating under 14 Code of Federal Regulations Parts 91, 121, or 135 to be retrofitted with a crash-resistant flight recorder system

Require all existing turbine-powered, nonexperimental, nonrestricted-category aircraft that are not equipped with a flight data recorder and are operating under 14 Code of Federal Regulations Parts 91, 121, or 135 to be retrofitted with a crash-resistant flight recorder system

notes: Read accident history, accident sequence, human performance analysis, findings, probable cause, and all recommendations sections (both new and reiterated); 20 findings extracted; 9 recommendations from formal NTSB issuance; depth=full due to extensive detail from analysis sections

records.title: UPS Airlines 6

agencies.name: General Civil Aviation Authority
agencies.report_title: Air Accident Investigation Sector final report, Uncontained cargo fire leading to loss of control inflight and uncontrolled descent into terrain, Boeing 747-44AF N571UP, Dubai, 3 September 2010

location.name: Nad Al Sheba military area, about 10 km south of Dubai International

records.summary: About 22 minutes after departure from Dubai, climbing through the Bahrain FIR, a fire warning sounded for the main deck cargo compartment, where a shipment including lithium batteries had ignited. The crew turned back toward Dubai. Smoke filled the cockpit and the captain's oxygen supply failed; he left his seat and was incapacitated. The first officer flew alone, unable to see the instruments or tune the radios, communicating through relay aircraft, and with degraded pitch control from fire-damaged cables. The aircraft overflew Dubai, could not be positioned for a landing, and struck the ground south of the airport. Both pilots died.
records.probable_cause: The GCAA concluded that a large fire developed in the palletised cargo on the main deck, most probably originating in a shipment containing lithium batteries, and that the resulting smoke entered the flight deck. The fire damaged the control cables, limiting pitch control, and the captain's oxygen supply was interrupted, leading to his incapacitation. The first officer, with severely reduced visibility of the instruments, no direct communication with Dubai and limited control authority, was unable to land the aircraft. Contributing factors included the lack of a requirement to declare lithium batteries as hazardous in cargo, the class E cargo compartment's lack of fire suppression, the inadequate smoke barrier between the main deck and the flight deck, and the absence of a supplementary oxygen supply that could be used without leaving the seat.

factors.evidence: A fire developed in palletised cargo on the main deck containing lithium batteries and other flammable material; the fire warning sounded about 22 minutes after takeoff.
The shipment contained lithium batteries in quantities that did not require declaration as hazardous goods, in proximity to combustible packaging.
The fire spread rapidly through the main deck; the class E compartment had no active fire suppression.
The smoke barrier between the main deck and the flight deck did not prevent smoke ingress, and the crew oxygen system did not provide a portable supply usable without leaving the seat.
The regulations in force did not require lithium batteries in the quantities carried to be declared, packaged or segregated as dangerous goods.
The captain's oxygen supply ceased; he left his seat to find a portable bottle and was incapacitated by smoke and fumes.
The fire damaged the control cables on the main deck, degrading pitch control; the first officer relied on the autopilot for control.
With fire-damaged cables and unreliable elevator response the first officer had limited ability to control pitch during the final descent.
The first officer alone flew the aircraft, managed the emergency, and relayed communications through other aircraft because he could not tune the radios.
Unable to see the instruments through the smoke, the first officer overflew the airport and could not establish the aircraft's position for an approach.
The aircraft descended into the ground south of Dubai while the first officer attempted to return to the airport.
The aircraft was destroyed by impact forces and fire.

events.text: Takeoff from Dubai runway 30R for Cologne with a main-deck cargo load that includes lithium batteries.
Fire warning for the main deck cargo compartment while climbing through about FL320 in the Bahrain FIR.
The crew declare an emergency to Bahrain ACC and elect to return to Dubai rather than divert to Doha, which is closer.
Crew run the fire checklist; the main deck is depressurised and the aircraft turns back toward Dubai.
Smoke enters the flight deck and rapidly reduces visibility of the instruments and the outside.
The autopilot is used for control; pitch control through the column becomes limited as the fire damages the control cables.
The captain's oxygen supply fails; he leaves his seat to find a portable oxygen bottle and is overcome by smoke and fumes.
The first officer, flying alone, cannot see the radio panel to tune Dubai frequencies and communicates with Bahrain ACC through relay aircraft.
The aircraft descends toward Dubai; the first officer, unable to read the instruments, passes over the airport at about 4,000 ft without seeing the runway.
Relayed instructions to turn toward Sharjah are received; the aircraft turns but continues to descend with limited pitch authority.
GPWS warnings sound as the aircraft descends toward the ground.
The aircraft strikes the ground at the Nad Al Sheba military area about 10 km south of Dubai International and is destroyed by impact and fire.

recommendations.text: Review the classification, packaging, quantity limits and declaration requirements for lithium batteries carried as cargo, and prohibit or restrict their carriage in bulk on aircraft without suppression.
recommendations.outcome: ICAO prohibited lithium metal batteries as cargo on passenger aircraft in 2015 and lithium-ion batteries in 2016, with state-of-charge limits on cargo aircraft.

recommendations.text: Improve fire detection and suppression for class E main-deck cargo compartments, and the smoke barrier between cargo compartment and flight deck.
recommendations.outcome: Industry development of fire-resistant containers and fire containment covers; FAA fire-safety research on class E compartments.

recommendations.text: Provide flight crews with full-face oxygen masks and smoke-vision systems or equivalent means to see the instruments in dense smoke, and a portable oxygen supply usable without leaving the seat.
recommendations.outcome: UPS installed full-face oxygen masks and Emergency Vision Assurance Systems on its fleet.

recommendations.text: Train crews to divert to the nearest suitable airport in the event of an uncontrolled cargo fire.

safety_changes: ICAO banned the carriage of lithium metal batteries as cargo on passenger aircraft (2015) and lithium-ion batteries as cargo on passenger aircraft (2016), with a 30 percent state-of-charge limit on cargo flights.
UPS fitted its fleet with full-face oxygen masks, Emergency Vision Assurance Systems and fire-resistant cargo containers and fire containment covers.
The FAA issued guidance on lithium battery transport and accelerated research on class E cargo compartment fire protection.

notes: Times are given to the minute from the GCAA report narrative (takeoff 14:51, fire warning about 15:12, impact about 15:41 UTC); intermediate event t values are approximate offsets.
The report number is not given because the GCAA case reference was not verified.
The cfit outcome factor is used as instructed; the GCAA described the impact as an uncontrolled descent into terrain after loss of control, so loss_of_pilot_control_authority is also listed.
Crash-site lat/lon are approximate for Nad Al Sheba.

records.title: 2010 Fox Glacier FU-24 crash

agencies.name: Transport Accident Investigation Commission
agencies.report_title: Report 10-009: Walter Fletcher FU24, ZK-EUF, loss of control on take-off and impact with terrain

records.summary: A modified Fletcher FU-24 operated by Skydive New Zealand crashed shortly after takeoff on a skydiving flight from Fox Glacier aerodrome. The aircraft's centre of gravity was located beyond its rear limit due to the seating arrangement of unrestrained passengers and weight calculation errors. The aircraft became airborne at too low an airspeed, pitched nose-up until nearly vertical, rolled left, and impacted the ground at a near-vertical angle, killing all 9 occupants.
records.probable_cause: The aircraft's weight and balance configuration resulted in the centre of gravity being located beyond its rear limit. The aircraft became airborne at too low an airspeed to be controllable, resulting in uncontrollable nose-up pitch. Contributing factors included passengers not individually weighed with estimates used instead, documentation errors not detected by the Civil Aviation Authority, and the aircraft being modified for parachuting without adequate weight and balance controls.

factors.evidence: Centre of gravity at least 0.122m rear of maximum permissible limit created a tendency for nose to pitch up (p. 29)
Each passenger had not been individually weighed, estimates of total weight were used instead, and documentation errors had not been noticed by the CAA (p. 29, 30)
Aircraft was modified for parachuting with no adequate weight and balance controls (p. 29)
Aircraft became airborne early at too low airspeed, pitched upwards until almost vertical, rolled left, and dived toward ground (p. 29, 4)

events.text: Eight passengers from tour group arrived at Fox Glacier aerodrome facilities for tandem skydive jump, divided into 2 groups of 4 (p. 4)
Pilot flew 9 flights in morning totalling 3.6 hours before stopping for 45-minute lunch break; engine shutdown and refueled to 160 litres standard fuel load (p. 4)

Pilot re-boarded aircraft and started engine; each tandem master led passenger to aircraft and boarded; passengers seated on floor in rear of aircraft, tandem masters attached via 4-point harnesses (p. 4)
Last tandem pair loaded and door closed; pilot taxied forward few metres onto runway and increased power to commence takeoff roll, witnessed by about 10 people (p. 4)
Aircraft accelerated normally down airstrip and got airborne at about usual position, possibly earlier than normal (p. 4)
Aircraft continued pitching upward until it appeared almost vertical, reaching extreme pitch-up attitude (p. 4, 29)

At about 100 metres altitude aircraft entered wing-over to the left to point almost vertically downwards; some witnesses recounted aircraft appeared to maneuver out of dive before left wing lowered further (p. 4)

Aircraft struck ground in near-vertical attitude 100 metres south of runway about 200 metres past end of bitumen section; fine mist or vapour shrouded aircraft on impact then erupted into flames; emergency services notified at 13:27 (p. 4, 5)

recommendations.text: Alert all pilots and operators using Fletcher FU24-954 aircraft for parachuting operations that when loaded with 6 or more passengers it is possible for the aircraft CG to be aft of allowable limit, that this could result in control difficulties, and that parachutists should be seated in forward cabin area, preferably restrained to prevent moving rearward
recommendations.outcome: Emergency Airworthiness Directive DCA/FU24/179 issued 11 September 2010 restricting maximum occupancy and requiring weight and balance calculations for each flight

recommendations.text: As a matter of urgency review the approvals granted for the FU24-954 aircraft with view to amending Flight Manual to allow more accurate determinations of aircraft centre of gravity, and extend review to other conversions of Fletcher and Cresco aircraft
recommendations.outcome: Emergency Airworthiness Directive DCA/FU24/180 issued to address CG limit issues in parachute configurations and review all AFM parachute operation supplements

recommendations.text: Ensure that high engineering standards are maintained by the aircraft maintenance organisations that performed ZK-EUF modification and other similar organisations
recommendations.outcome: Newly introduced risk-based surveillance processes improved effectiveness of CAA audits through better targeting and focus on risk issues

recommendations.text: Take necessary action to ensure thorough and coordinated oversight when accepting aircraft modifications and approving changes in category, especially for specialised operations like parachuting
recommendations.outcome: CAA amended conditions of all design delegation holders effective 24 August 2010 to enable closer oversight of major design changes

recommendations.text: Monitor outcome of joint FAA/USPA study on seat restraints and determine if any findings are applicable for New Zealand parachuting industry
recommendations.outcome: Director committed to monitor the study and consider applicability to New Zealand aviation environment

recommendations.text: Ensure coordinated and proactive approach by relevant departments within CAA to ensure safety efforts are best directed to promote coordinated safe management of flying activities
recommendations.outcome: CAA undergoing major change programme to target resources more effectively; Civil Aviation Rule Part 115 enables closer oversight of commercial parachute operations

recommendations.text: Promote introduction of drug and alcohol detection and deterrence regime for persons employed in safety critical transport roles
recommendations.outcome: Ministry monitoring international experience; Civil Aviation Rule Part 115 provides incentive through safety certification risks

safety_changes: Emergency Airworthiness Directive DCA/FU24/179 restricting maximum occupancy and requiring weight and balance calculations for parachuting operations
Emergency Airworthiness Directive DCA/FU24/180 addressing CG limit issues and reviewing all AFM parachute operation supplements
Civil Aviation Rule Part 115 requiring tandem parachute operators to be certificated with CAA oversight
CAA design delegation holder amendments effective 24 August 2010 enabling closer oversight of major design changes

notes: Read sections: Title, Executive Summary (p. 1), Narrative (p. 3-9), Site and impact information (p. 5-6), Aircraft information (p. 8), Findings (p. 29-33), Recommendations (p. 40-43)
Events extracted from detailed witness accounts and investigation findings with specific page citations
All 9 recommendations extracted from report with official recommendation numbers from TAIC
Probable cause wording synthesized from report findings section

records.title: Qantas 32

agencies.name: Australian Transport Safety Bureau
agencies.report_title: In-flight uncontained engine failure, Airbus A380-842, VH-OQA, overhead Batam Island, Indonesia, 4 November 2010

agencies.name: Air Accident Investigation Bureau of Singapore

location.name: Over Batam Island, Indonesia, shortly after departure from Singapore

records.summary: About four minutes after take-off from Singapore, the number 2 Trent 900 engine of the A380 suffered an uncontained failure of its intermediate-pressure turbine disc. Disc fragments punctured the wing and fuel tanks and severed wiring and hydraulic lines, degrading many aircraft systems. The five-pilot crew spent about 50 minutes working through the ECAM messages, assessed landing performance and returned to Changi for an overweight landing, stopping with about 150 m of runway remaining. Nobody was injured.
records.probable_cause: The ATSB found that an oil feed stub pipe in the engine's HP/IP bearing structure had been manufactured with a misaligned counter-bore, leaving a thin wall that cracked by fatigue. Oil released through the crack ignited in the buffer space, and the fire heated the IP turbine drive arm until the disc separated from the shaft, overspeed and burst. Rolls-Royce's manufacturing quality processes had not detected the non-conforming pipes, and when the non-conformance was identified in service the company's risk assessment did not lead to the affected engines being removed.

factors.evidence: An oil feed stub pipe was manufactured with a misaligned counter-bore, a non-conformance that produced a thin wall section susceptible to fatigue cracking.
Rolls-Royce's manufacturing inspection and quality processes did not detect the misaligned counter-bore before the pipe entered service.

Non-conforming stub pipes had been identified in other engines before the accident, but the retrospective risk assessment did not recognise the fatigue-cracking hazard, so engines with the defect remained in service.
A fatigue crack developed through the thin wall of the stub pipe, releasing oil into the HP/IP bearing chamber buffer space.
The leaking oil ignited and the resulting internal fire heated the IP turbine drive arm, leading to the separation of the disc from the shaft.
The IP turbine disc overspeed and burst into three main fragments that penetrated the engine casing, the wing and the fuselage.
Disc fragments punctured left-wing fuel tanks, causing a large fuel leak and preventing fuel transfer, which produced a lateral imbalance.
The green hydraulic system was lost, along with parts of the electrical system, degrading brakes, spoilers, flaps, gear and other services.
The crew processed dozens of ECAM messages over about 50 minutes while holding, and had to assess landing performance with degraded systems.
The aircraft landed overweight at Changi at about 166 kt with a computed stopping margin of about 100 m, stopping with about 150 m of runway remaining.

events.text: Departs Singapore Changi runway 20C for Sydney with 440 passengers and 29 crew, including five pilots (the operating crew plus a check captain and a supervising check captain).
Climbing through about 7,000 ft over Batam Island, the engine 2 IP turbine disc fails; fragments penetrate the left wing, fuel tanks and fuselage.

Multiple ECAM warnings begin, including engine 2 failure and fire indications, fuel leak and transfer faults, green hydraulic system loss, electrical bus losses, and degradations of brakes, spoilers and flight controls.
Crew declare PAN, level off and request a holding area east of Singapore to process the ECAM actions.
Engine 2 fire warning: the crew discharge both fire extinguisher bottles into engine 2, without confirmation of discharge.
The crew work through the ECAM procedures; fuel cannot be transferred or jettisoned, fuel is leaking from the left wing and a lateral imbalance develops.
Landing performance is computed with the landing distance performance application for the degraded configuration, giving a stopping margin of about 100 m on runway 20C.
Crew perform a controllability check in the landing configuration at low speed, then commence the approach to Changi.

Overweight landing on runway 20C at about 166 kt with limited braking and spoilers; the aircraft stops with about 150 m of runway remaining. Brake temperatures reach about 900 degrees C and four tyres deflate.
Fuel leaks from the left wing near the hot brakes; airport fire services apply foam. The crew keep passengers on board while the area is made safe, then disembark them by stairs.
Engine 1 cannot be shut down from the cockpit because its control wiring was severed; it is finally stopped about two hours after landing by drowning it with fire-fighting foam.

recommendations.text: Address the manufacturing quality-control deficiencies that allowed non-conforming oil feed stub pipes to enter service, and improve the process for assessing the risk of identified non-conformances.
recommendations.outcome: Rolls-Royce revised its quality management and non-conformance risk assessment processes; affected engines were removed or modified.

recommendations.text: Mandate inspection and, where necessary, replacement of Trent 900 HP/IP bearing structure oil feed stub pipes, and require IP turbine overspeed protection.
recommendations.outcome: EASA emergency airworthiness directives required repetitive inspections and engine changes; Rolls-Royce introduced an IP turbine overspeed protection software modification.

safety_changes: EASA emergency airworthiness directives required inspection and replacement of affected Trent 900 oil feed stub pipes across the fleet.
Rolls-Royce introduced an IP turbine overspeed protection system that shuts the engine down if the turbine begins to overspeed.
Rolls-Royce revised its manufacturing quality and non-conformance risk assessment processes.
Airbus and operators reviewed ECAM presentation and crew procedures for managing multiple system failures on the A380.

notes: Take-off (0156), failure (0201) and landing (0346) times are to the minute; intermediate event times are approximate offsets.
The time engine 1 was finally shut down (about two hours after landing) is approximate.
ATSB safety recommendation numbers for this investigation were not verified, so ids are null.

records.title: Southwest Airlines 812

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Rapid Depressurization and Structural Failure

records.summary: Southwest Airlines Flight 812 experienced rapid depressurization while climbing through 34,400 feet on April 1, 2011. A 60-inch section of fuselage skin fractured and flapped open due to metal fatigue at a manufacturing lap joint. The crew conducted an emergency descent to 11,000 feet and diverted safely to Yuma.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause was the improper installation of the fuselage crown skin panel at the S-4L lap joint during the manufacturing process, which resulted in multiple site damage fatigue cracking and eventual failure of the lower skin panel. Contributing to the injuries was flight attendant A's incorrect assessment of his time of useful consciousness, which led to his failure to follow procedures requiring immediate donning of an oxygen mask when cabin pressure is lost.

factors.evidence: Improper installation of fuselage crown skin panel at S-4L lap joint; misaligned panels caused misdrilled holes (p. 14).
Multiple site damage fatigue cracking initiated at rivet hole 85 almost immediately after manufacture; longest fatigue crack grew over 38,261 cycles (p. 9, 14).
Cumulative fatigue cracking reached critical length; panel residual strength insufficient to carry pressurization loads, hole flapped open (p. 14).
Rapid depressurization when fuselage skin fractured and separated (p. 1).

events.text: Unidentified sound recorded on cockpit microphone at FL340 during climb to FL360 (p. 1).
Captain announced cabin pressurization lost and called for oxygen masks (p. 1).
Captain declared emergency with ATC and requested lower altitude (p. 1).
Cabin oxygen masks deployed; aircraft descended to 11,000 feet within 5 minutes (p. 1).
About 16:05, cabin crew relayed reports of 2-foot fuselage hole and broken-nose injury (p. 1).
Airplane cleared to descend to 9,000 feet; captain requested radar vectors to Yuma (p. 1).
Aircraft landed at runway 21R at Yuma International Airport without incident (p. 1).
Passengers deplaned via airstairs; flight attendant A struck nose on forward partition (p. 2).

notes: Sections: History of Flight (p. 1), Analysis (p. 13-14), Probable Cause (p. 15)

Manufacturing fatigue analysis from materials examination

records.title: Omega Aerial Refueling Services 70

location.name: Naval Base Ventura County, Naval Air Station Point Mugu

records.summary: On 18 May 2011, Omega Aerial Refueling Services Flight 70, a Boeing 707 tanker, experienced engine pylon separation shortly after takeoff from Naval Air Station Point Mugu, California. The No. 2 engine separated from the wing and struck the No. 1 engine inlet, reducing thrust. Despite full control inputs, the aircraft descended and made multiple runway contacts before departing the runway into a saltwater marsh. All three crew members survived with injuries.
records.probable_cause: The NTSB determines that the probable cause of this accident was the failure of a midspar fitting, which was susceptible to fatigue cracking and should have been replaced with a newer, more fatigue-resistant version of the fitting as required by an airworthiness directive. Also causal was an erroneous maintenance entry made by a previous aircraft owner, which incorrectly reflected that the newer fitting had been installed. (p. 17)

factors.evidence: The No. 2 engine pylon midspar fitting had a preexisting fatigue crack that had propagated to critical length. The No. 2 engine nacelle and pylon assembly struck the No. 1 engine nacelle, causing the No. 1 engine inlet cowl to separate and resulting in significant loss of thrust on the left side. (p. 17, 659-661)

The fatigue crack initiated at the upper inboard corner of the reduced section between the lug where the drag support fitting is normally attached and the chromium-coated radius. The reduced section radius was measured at nominal 0.38 inch, an older fitting design subject to fatigue cracking. (p. 17, 667-676)

Erroneous maintenance entry made by previous aircraft owner in 1983 incorrectly reflected that the newer fitting had been installed. Omega records review in 2003 based on the erroneous entries led to deletion of the repetitive inspection requirement from its maintenance plan. (p. 17, 677-688)

AD 93-11-02 and Boeing SBs required either repetitive visual inspections or replacement with more fatigue-resistant design incorporating 1.0-inch radius. The replacement was a terminating action, but erroneous records showed falsely that it was completed. (p. 17, 673-676)
Even with full right aileron and rudder inputs, the plane started to descend and drift to the left after engine separation, reducing pilot's ability to maintain control. (p. 7, 401-403)
The plane made multiple contacts with the runway and departed the runway, crossing a taxiway before coming to rest in a saltwater marsh. (p. 7, 405-407, 458)

events.text: Flight cleared for takeoff from runway 21 at Naval Air Station Point Mugu. Takeoff roll was normal. (p. 7, 427)

Shortly after liftoff, approximately 20 feet above ground and 7,000 feet down the runway, the No. 2 engine pylon midspar fitting failed due to fatigue crack propagation. The No. 2 engine separated from the wing. (p. 17, 659-661)

The No. 2 engine nacelle and pylon assembly struck the No. 1 engine's inlet cowling, causing the No. 1 engine inlet cowl to separate and degrading No. 1 engine's ability to produce thrust. Significant loss of thrust occurred on left side of airplane. (p. 17, 660-661)
Captain made appropriate decision to reject takeoff and attempt to land on remaining runway. He lowered the nose and leveled the wings, applying full right aileron and rudder. (p. 17, 662-665)

Despite full control inputs, the plane started to descend and drift to the left due to loss of thrust from both left engines. The loss of thrust made continued takeoff highly unlikely. (p. 7, 401-403, 447)
Aircraft made first contact with runway, followed by multiple contacts as it descended with unequal thrust condition. (p. 458)
Aircraft drifted left off the runway, crossed a taxiway, and departed the runway area. (p. 458)
Aircraft came to rest in saltwater marsh. All three crew members survived but sustained serious injuries. Aircraft substantially damaged. (p. 7, 389, 458)

Sections read: Analysis (p. 17), Probable Cause (p. 17)

No CVR transcript in public report
Maintenance history revealed erroneous compliance entry that caused inspection termination
Part of series of fatigue crack failures in 707 midspar fittings (1992, 1998, 2011)

records.title: 2011 Dalamot helicopter crash
records.summary: An Airlift Eurocopter AS350 helicopter crashed at Dalamot in Ullensvang municipality, Norway on July 4, 2011. During descent for approach in mountainous terrain, the helicopter entered a tight right turn, lost control, and descended steeply. The aircraft impacted the ground about 500 meters short of the planned landing site and immediately caught fire, killing all five persons on board.
records.probable_cause: The investigation concluded that abrupt maneuvering initiated a sequence where control of the helicopter was partly lost, and the altitude was insufficient for recovery. The Accident Investigation Board Norway determined the hydraulic system likely reached its limitation during the maneuvering, resulting in servo transparency (jack stall) occurring.

factors.evidence: Abrupt maneuvering resulted in servo transparency (jack stall) causing control of the helicopter to be lost with high bank and steep descent
Height was insufficient for the commander to recover in time after loss of control
Helicopter hit the ground about 500 metres short of the planned landing site

events.text: Helicopter started descent for approach in mountainous terrain
Helicopter observed turning tightly to the right, with loss of control and high bank and steep descent
Helicopter impacted ground about 500 metres short of planned landing site and immediately caught fire

recommendations.text: Establish an industry standard for maneuvering limitations for passenger transport, with limits such as 30 degrees roll and 15 degrees pitch at heights below 500 feet
Require the type certificate holder Eurocopter to issue a warning of the hazard when encountering servo transparency in a right turn, preferably as a permanent note in the Flight Manual
Consider introducing requirements for flight recorders on more aircraft including light helicopters, beyond those covered by current regulations

notes: Report text was web-scraped summary rather than full investigation document; extracted investigation findings, causal factors, and 3 formal safety recommendations; minimal event details available from source document

records.title: Angara Airlines 9007

agencies.name: Interstate Aviation Committee
agencies.report_title: Final Report on the Investigation of the Accident with An-24RV RA-47302

records.summary: An Antonov An-24RV encountered an engine fire in the left engine during cruise descent on July 11, 2011. The crew, after noticing a chip warning and burning smell, eventually shut down the engine following severe vibration. Unable to extinguish the fire using onboard systems, the captain ditched the aircraft into the Ob River. The aircraft was destroyed by collision with underwater obstacles, killing 7 people on board.
records.probable_cause: The engine fire originated from failure of the compressor rotor rear support bearing, likely due to improper installation during maintenance or manufacturing defect. The captain's reluctance to shut down the engine despite initial warnings allowed the fire to develop. The aircraft was destroyed when it struck underwater obstacles during the water landing.

factors.evidence: Failure of the compressor rotor rear bearing of the left engine, possibly due to incorrect bearing installation or assembly defect during maintenance.
The left engine was overhauled on 29.10.2009 at Aramil Repair Plant with violations of repair technology and inadequate quality control.
Engine fire developed in the left engine at 04:52:12, confirmed visually by the captain at 04:52:59.

The captain's apparent reluctance to shut down the affected engine despite chip warning, burning smell, fire alarm activation, and oil pressure drops. Engine was not shut down until severe vibration forced the decision.
Crew ditched into the Ob River at 04:56:08 when the fire could not be extinguished and the aircraft became too damaged to continue to an airport.
Aircraft made emergency water landing into the Ob River.

events.text: Magnetic chip detector signaled presence of particles in the left engine oil system.
Aircraft entered Nizhnevartovsk ATC zone and reported navigation estimates.
Captain smelled burning odor in the cockpit.
Crew reported chip warning and oil pressure drop to ATC, requested descent to alternate airport Nizhnevartovsk.
Reduced left engine to idle and closed air bleed from left engine.
Captain decided not to shut down the engine despite flight engineer's question about feathering.
Aircraft entered clouds and crew activated engine inlet heating systems.
Began descent preparation, completed pre-landing checklist.
Severe vibration detected in left engine.
Captain ordered to feather (shut down) the left engine. Flight engineer executed engine shutdown and reported completion.
Captain reported engine fire detected visually. Crew attempted to extinguish using fire suppression systems; efforts unsuccessful.
Aircraft ditched into the Ob River at 04:56:08 UTC (11:56 local time) near Strezhevoy after the fire could not be controlled.

recommendations.text: Issue directives to all operators requiring immediate action upon identification of engine failure signs (chip warning, oil pressure drop, burning smell) including engine shutdown procedures.
Conduct author oversight of repair quality for AI-24 engines at Aramil Repair Plant.
Coordinate with engine manufacturer on repair scope for failed engines when repair instructions are not available.
Review and update An-24 Flight Manual Section 7.1.6 regarding crew procedures when chip warning, oil parameter changes, and burning smell are detected.

safety_changes: Angara Airlines developed and implemented action plan addressing inspection findings from post-accident regulatory inspection.

Events derived from detailed timeline in History of Flight section with precise UTC times from report
Factors identified from causal analysis and maintenance records in report
