records.title: First Air 6560
records.time_reference: CDT (local); intermediate clock times are not reproduced, so t is relative to impact (t=0) with earlier events negative

agencies.name: Transportation Safety Board of Canada
agencies.report_title: Controlled Flight into Terrain, Bradley Air Services Limited (First Air), Boeing 737-210C C-GNWN, Resolute Bay, Nunavut, 20 August 2011

location.name: Hill about 1 nm east of runway 35T, Resolute Bay, Nunavut

records.summary: The chartered 737 combi was flying an ILS approach to runway 35T at Resolute Bay in low cloud when it struck a hill about 1 nm east of the runway. The autopilot had not captured the localizer and the aircraft flew a track diverging to the right of the approach course; the first officer repeatedly voiced concern and called for a go-around, but the captain continued the approach until seconds before impact. Twelve of the 15 people on board were killed.
records.probable_cause: The TSB found that the autopilot did not transition to localizer-capture mode and the aircraft diverged to the right of the localizer while the crew tried to reconcile conflicting heading, localizer and GPS indications; the captain believed the localizer indication might be erroneous. The approach was unstable and below the required standard, and the crew's coordination broke down: the first officer's concerns and go-around calls were not acted on until it was too late. Contributing factors included the crew's high workload, the compass and mode indications that were not understood, low cloud at the approach minima, and First Air's standard operating procedures and crew resource management training, which did not provide effective defences.

factors.evidence: The autopilot remained in a heading/roll mode instead of capturing the localizer, which the crew did not recognise in time.
The aircraft flew a track diverging to the right of the localizer course; heading and compass indications available to the crew were not reconciled with the localizer and GPS information.
The captain believed the localizer indication might be erroneous and did not appreciate that the aircraft was off course and heading toward rising terrain east of the runway.
The crew were dealing with an unresolved navigation discrepancy, approach configuration and communications during the final approach.
The first officer expressed concern several times and called for a go-around; the captain did not respond effectively and the two pilots did not share a common understanding of the situation.
The aircraft was not established on the localizer and did not meet the operator's stabilized-approach criteria.
The approach was continued although the criteria for a go-around had been met.
A go-around was not initiated until about two seconds before impact, too late to avoid the terrain.
Low cloud and reduced visibility at Resolute Bay prevented the crew from seeing the terrain or the runway in time.
First Air's crew resource management training was of the older, less effective type; the TSB recommended contemporary CRM training for all commercial operators.
The aircraft struck a hill about 1 nm east of the runway threshold in controlled flight.

events.text: Crew brief the ILS approach to runway 35T at Resolute Bay; weather is low cloud with reduced visibility near the approach minima. A military exercise is under way at the airport and a temporary military control unit is in operation.

The aircraft turns toward the final approach course with the autopilot engaged, but the autopilot does not transition to localizer-capture mode and the aircraft continues on a heading-based track that diverges to the right of the localizer.
The first officer notes that the localizer indication is not centred and points out the discrepancy between the heading and the GPS track.
The captain, recalling earlier experiences of erroneous ILS indications, doubts the localizer and continues descending on the glideslope while offset right of the course.
The captain disconnects the autopilot and attempts to correct toward the localizer while continuing the approach; workload is high and the crew's understanding of the situation diverges.
The first officer suggests a go-around; the captain does not act on the suggestion.
The first officer again calls for a go-around as the aircraft continues below cloud toward terrain east of the runway.
The captain calls for a go-around and advances the thrust levers about two seconds before impact.
The aircraft strikes a hill about 1 nm east of the runway 35T threshold and breaks up; 12 of the 15 occupants are killed, 3 are seriously injured.

recommendations.text: Require commercial air operators to provide contemporary crew resource management training for pilots of air taxi and commuter operations (CAR 703 and 704).
recommendations.outcome: Transport Canada introduced a contemporary CRM training standard applying to all Canadian commercial air operators in 2019.

recommendations.text: Require operators to implement measures that ensure unstable approaches are recognised and result in a go-around.

safety_changes: Transport Canada mandated contemporary CRM training for all Canadian commercial air operators.
First Air revised its standard operating procedures, stabilized-approach criteria and go-around policy, and updated its CRM training.
The TSB placed unstable approaches that are continued to a landing on its Watchlist of key safety issues.

notes: Only the impact time (about 1641 CDT) is given; all other event times are approximate offsets reconstructed from the report narrative.
The precise nature of the compass/heading discrepancy described in the TSB report (its magnitude and origin) is not reproduced; the record describes it generically.
GPWS alerts in the final seconds are not itemised because their exact timing was not verified.
Recommendation A14-01 text is paraphrased; a second TSB recommendation from this investigation exists but its number and exact wording were not verified.

records.title: 2011 Reno Air Races crash
records.summary: During the third lap of the National Championship Air Races unlimited class gold race at Reno/Stead Airport, a modified North American P-51D (Race 177, The Galloping Ghost) experienced a left roll upset and high-G pitch-up at 445 knots near pylon 8. The upset exceeded the structural limits of the elevator trim tab system, which had been weakened by loosened attachment screws and a fatigue crack. The left elevator trim tab separated in flight, causing loss of control. The pilot became incapacitated from high G-forces, and the aircraft descended onto the airport ramp in the spectator box seating area, killing the pilot and 10 spectators.
records.probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Board determines that the probable cause of this accident was the reduced stiffness of the elevator trim tab system that allowed aerodynamic flutter to occur at racing speeds. The reduced stiffness was a result of deteriorated locknut inserts that allowed the trim tab attachment screws to become loose and to initiate fatigue cracking in one screw sometime before the accident flight. Aerodynamic flutter of the trim tabs resulted in a failure of the left trim tab link assembly, elevator movement, high flight loads, and a loss of control. Contributing to the accident were the undocumented and untested major modifications to the airplane and the pilot's operation of the airplane in the unique air racing environment without adequate flight testing.

factors.evidence: Aerodynamic flutter of elevator trim tabs occurred at racing speed of 445 knots, caused by reduced structural stiffness (p. 2, 30-31). Loosened attachment screws and deteriorated locknut inserts allowed flutter to develop.

Elevator trim tab attachment screws had loose connections and a fatigue crack developed in one screw. Deteriorated locknut inserts rendered them ineffective at providing clamping pressure to keep hinge surfaces tight (p. 1, 43).

Undocumented and untested major modifications to aircraft, including single controllable elevator trim tab (increased aerodynamic load), filler material on trim tabs (increased weight and moved CG aft), and elevator counterweight modifications (p. 2). No engineering evaluations or flight testing for modifications (p. 1).

Failure of left elevator trim tab link assembly due to dynamic compressive loads exceeding buckling strength, caused by flutter excitation (p. 1). Right elevator trim tab also showed failure of its fixed link assembly (p. 1).

During upset, vertical acceleration peaked at 17.3 G, airplane rolled from 73° left bank to 93° left bank in less than 1 second, then entered right-rolling climb (p. 2). Pilot likely experienced G-induced loss of consciousness within 1 second (p. 2).

Aircraft descended in helical flightpath and collided with airport ramp in spectator box seating area at approximately 1625 PDT, killing 1 pilot and 10 spectators, injuring at least 64 people on ground (p. 2).

events.text: National Championship Air Races unlimited class gold race underway at Reno/Stead Airport. Aircraft in third place, about 4.5 seconds behind Voodoo, 8.8 seconds behind Strega.
Aircraft approaching pylon 8 during third lap of six-lap race
Aircraft rounding pylon 8 at 445 knots in established left-bank turn
LEFT ROLL UPSET BEGINS: Aircraft rapidly rolls from 73° left bank toward 93° left bank; vertical acceleration reaches 11 G during upset
Aircraft rolling right and pitching up; reaches maximum vertical load factor; elevator trim tab link assembly experiencing peak dynamic compressive loads
Aircraft pitching up with left elevator trim tab at trailing edge down position, right trim tab trailing edge up, full right-wing-down aileron deflection
LEFT ELEVATOR TRIM TAB SEPARATES IN FLIGHT; inboard piece detached from hinges
COLLISION: Aircraft descends in helical flightpath and strikes airport ramp in spectator box seating area; fragments upon impact

recommendations.text: Require engineering evaluations and flutter analysis for aircraft with major modifications before race eligibility
Require flight testing and certification of modified racing aircraft flight characteristics
Issue guidance on spectator safety distances and safety areas for air races
Provide high-G training requirements for air race pilots and evaluate G-suit feasibility

safety_changes: NTSB issued 10 safety recommendations on April 10, 2012 to RARA, NAG, and FAA addressing air race safety
Focus on engineering evaluations for aircraft with major modifications, spectator safety, course design guidance, and high-G training

notes: Final NTSB Aircraft Accident Brief with detailed narrative and analysis sections
8 events with approximate timestamps derived from video study and telemetry data (pages 1-2, 14-20)
Comprehensive evidence citations from pages 1-2, 30-31, 43 including flutter analysis, structural failures, and G-force data
Probable cause and contributing factors taken directly from section 3
Recommendations not formally numbered in brief; represented as text descriptions
No CVR data available; aircraft not equipped with flight recorders

records.title: Air Tindi 200

agencies.name: Transportation Safety Board of Canada
agencies.report_title: Aviation Investigation Report - Controlled Flight into Terrain

location.name: Pehtei Peninsula, 26 nautical miles west of Lutsel K'e

records.summary: A Cessna 208B operated by Air Tindi Ltd. departed Yellowknife for Lutsel K'e on 4 October 2011, conducting a visual flight rules flight at low altitude to maintain visual contact with the ground. The aircraft encountered low forward visibility and fog as it approached Pehtei Peninsula. The aircraft struck rising terrain at cruise speed in a wings-level attitude. The pilot and one passenger were fatally injured; two passengers were seriously injured. The investigation found that the pilot was impaired by cannabinoids, and combined with low visibility, this prevented the detection and avoidance of terrain.
records.probable_cause: The aircraft was flown at low altitude into an area of low forward visibility during a day VFR flight, which prevented the pilot from seeing and avoiding terrain. The pilot was impaired by concentrations of cannabinoids that were sufficient to cause impairment in pilot performance and decision-making.

factors.evidence: Low cloud persisted for the entire flight, flown at low level so the pilot could maintain visual contact with the ground; in the last minutes of flight, visibility had become reduced, with forecast showing temporary lower broken cloud height of 500 feet agl (p. 4, 13).

Toxicology analysis revealed concentrations of cannabinoids in the pilot's system that were sufficient to have caused impairment in pilot performance and decision-making on the accident flight (p. 4, 13).

The aircraft was flying on a direct track at low level in marginal VFR conditions; due to low visibility and the obscured terrain crest, the pilot did not see or detect the terrain and made no effective evasive maneuvers before impact (p. 4, 13).

The pilot elected to conduct VFR flight in marginal weather conditions suitable for IFR operations; the aircraft and company were qualified for IFR, and safe IFR altitude would have provided 2000 feet of terrain clearance (p. 4, 13).

Aircraft struck rising terrain on Pehtei Peninsula at 1013 feet above sea level in a wings-level attitude at cruise speed, with landing gear striking terrain first, followed by continuation down an eastern slope where it came to rest inverted (p. 3).

events.text: Aircraft departed Yellowknife under visual flight rules clearance with visibility at VFR minimums of 3 statute miles in rain and mist; altitude varied between 850 and 1470 feet above sea level during flight (p. 3).
Aircraft established direct track to Lutsel K'e while maintaining low level flight below low ragged cloud base; ground speed varied with slight variations in track (p. 3-4).
Aircraft continued on low-level direct track in marginal VFR conditions; forward visibility was reduced due to low forward visibility during the descent phase (p. 4, 13-14).

Pilot transmitted position report stating aircraft was 20 nautical miles from Lutsel K'e, though actual position was 26 nautical miles away; report did not include usual information such as arrival intentions and estimated time of arrival (p. 3).
One minute before impact, aircraft was at 1325 feet above sea level, 500 feet above ground level, 136 knots ground speed, on track 091 degrees true (p. 3).
Aircraft descended further; immediately before impact altitude was 1060 feet above sea level, ground speed 141 knots, track 098 degrees true (p. 3).
Crest of Pehtei Peninsula became visible; pilot applied increased engine power in response to suddenly visible terrain (p. 4, 13).

Aircraft struck rising terrain on the west side of Pehtei Peninsula at 1013 feet above sea level in a wings-level attitude; first impact was by landing gear, followed by belly cargo pod and propeller (p. 3).
Aircraft continued over crest of hill and became airborne again before coming to rest inverted 477 feet down the eastern slope; cockpit was crushed and forward cabin distorted (p. 3).
When aircraft failed to arrive at scheduled time of 11:45, Air Tindi representative at Lutsel K'e alerted the company at 12:23; company emergency response plan activated at 12:45 (p. 3).
SkyTrac GPS tracking system showed last transmission at 11:40 indicating aircraft at rest, marking time of accident; device data recorded at 5-second intervals had recorded entire flight path (p. 3).

safety_changes: Air Tindi initiated dispatch policy requiring all scheduled flights to be dispatched under IFR with VFR only with management authorization
Air Tindi no longer dispatches scheduled passenger flights when observed weather is at or forecast to be lower than alternate minimums
Air Tindi revised drug and alcohol policy to include random testing of employees in safety-sensitive positions
Air Tindi commenced installation of Appareo Vision 1000 Systems cockpit imaging and flight data monitoring devices
Transportation Safety Board issued Safety Advisory 825-A11W0151-D1-A1 regarding loose ELT attachment
FAA issued Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin HQ-12-32 regarding hook and loop style ELT fasteners
Kannad Aviation developed new Integra ELT with internal antenna and automatic fallback capability
Transport Canada committed to publish article in Aviation Safety Letter highlighting ELT installation requirements

notes: Sections read: History of Flight (p. 2-3), Meteorological Conditions (p. 3-4), Analysis (p. 13-15), Findings (p. 14-15)
All clock times in Mountain Daylight Time (UTC-6) per report
Aircraft registration verified as C-GATV (not C-GATH as in batch summary)
Pilot impairment from cannabinoids documented via toxicology

records.title: JetBlue Airways 191
records.summary: Captain Clayton Osbon suffered an acute mental breakdown en route from New York to Las Vegas, making incoherent statements about terrorists and behaving erratically on the flight deck. First Officer Jason Dowd locked the cockpit door and with assistance from an off-duty captain and flight attendants restrained Osbon. The aircraft diverted safely to Amarillo, Texas with no injuries to anyone on board.
records.probable_cause: Cause of captain's mental breakdown remains undetermined; Osbon later claimed complex partial brain seizure, though possibilities included psychotic disorder or intoxication from medication.

factors.evidence: Captain Osbon started acting erratically and ranting about terrorists, apparently suffering from an unspecified mental breakdown (p. 2-3)
First Officer Dowd grew concerned when Osbon made comments such as We need to take a leap of faith and yelling at air traffic controllers on frequency ordering them to be quiet (p. 3-4)
dimming his primary flight display, engine instruments and navigation display to the point they were almost totally switched off and unusable (p. 3)
First Officer Dowd locked the cockpit and diverted safely to Amarillo with the assistance of crew and off-duty captain (p. 4)

events.text: Captain Osbon began making incoherent statements such as "We need to take a leap of faith," "We're not going to Vegas," and "I can't be held responsible when this plane crashes" (p. 2-3)

Osbon dimmed his primary flight display, engine instruments, and navigation display to the point they were almost totally switched off and began yelling at air traffic controllers on frequency, ordering them to be quiet (p. 3)
Osbon leapt from his seat, opened the cockpit door, and ran into the forward lavatory (p. 3)

First Officer Jason Dowd locked the cockpit door completely, preventing Osbon from regaining access even with the emergency door code, with assistance from an off-duty captain and flight attendants (p. 3)
Aircraft diverted safely to Amarillo International Airport where Osbon was met by law enforcement; all 150 occupants survived with no injuries (p. 4)

records.title: UTair Flight 120
records.summary: UTair Flight 120, an ATR 72-201, crashed during takeoff from Roshchino on April 2, 2012, in snow and rain with ice and snow accumulated on the aircraft. Despite visible contamination, the flight crew decided not to de-ice the aircraft before takeoff. After takeoff at low airspeed, flaps were retracted at 139 knots in conditions requiring 160 knots minimum, triggering an aerodynamic stall. The crew failed to recognize the stall and apply appropriate recovery procedures, resulting in loss of control and impact with an open field near the runway.
records.probable_cause: The aircraft departed without de-icing treatment despite visible ice and snow contamination on the surfaces. The flap retraction at 139 knots instead of the required 160 knots in icing conditions caused an aerodynamic stall. The crew failed to recognize the stall and apply appropriate recovery procedures, instead pulling back on the control column until impact. Contributing factors included shortcomings in ground handling, inadequate crew training on stall recognition, and deficiencies in the airline's safety management system.

factors.evidence: Ice and snow accumulated on the aircraft surfaces; the aircraft had been parked for hours in snowy conditions without being de-iced (p. 1).
The crew of the flight were aware that ice and snow had accumulated on the aircraft but decided not to de-ice it despite para. 2.14 of FAP-128 and AFM requirements (p. 193).
Aircraft stall occurred at operational angles of attack right after flaps retraction with engaged autopilot, caused by loss of wing lift effectiveness (p. 193).
The crew seemed to have trouble identifying the problem with increasing stress as the situation developed; stall warning appeared but crew became confused (p. 1).
Crew applied ailerons and rudder but were unable to counteract subsequent left roll; pilots were pulling back on the control column until impact (p. 193).
The first officer's tone suggested high levels of stress during the emergency; crew preoccupation with banking and buffeting (p. 1).
Aircraft began uncommanded roll and eventually crashed at a left bank of 55 degrees and nose-down angle of 11 degrees (p. 1).

events.text: Flight 120 crew arrives at aircraft in snowy conditions; visible snow and ice on surfaces.
Crew decides not to de-ice despite visible contamination and crew awareness of ice/snow accumulation.
Aircraft departs from gate and begins taxi to runway for takeoff.
Flight 120 takes off from Roshchino at 07:33 local time with visible ice/snow on aircraft.
Aircraft reaches about 600 feet altitude; autopilot engaged; flaps retracted at 139 knots.
Stall warning sounds as aircraft loses lift due to wing contamination.
Aircraft begins uncommanded roll to the right; first officer asks 'what is this buffeting'; crew disengages autopilot.
Crew applies ailerons and rudder but cannot counteract left roll at 40-55 degree bank angles.
Aircraft crashes into open field near runway at 55 degree left bank and 11 degree nose-down angle.

recommendations.text: Develop Federal Aviation Regulations for aircraft maintenance and ground handling.
Develop guidance on aircraft ground icing protection and training for de-icing personnel.
Assure compliance with de-icing/anti-icing procedures and personnel training requirements.
Organize conferences to share experience of ATR 42/72 aircraft operation and safety issues.
Improve simulator training programs for stall prevention and recovery procedures.

safety_changes: Enhanced de-icing procedures and regulatory framework in Russia (State Standard GOST R 54264-2010 effective July 2012)
Improved crew training on stall recognition and recovery
Mandatory compliance with Clean Aircraft Concept

Safety Recommendations section reviewed (lines 9029-9122)

records.title: Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky Air 251 (2012)

agencies.name: Interstate Aviation Committee
agencies.report_title: Final Report on Investigation of Aircraft Accident - Antonov An-28 RA-28715

records.summary: An Antonov An-28 descended below approach minimums in instrument meteorological conditions and collided with a forested slope near Palana airport. Both pilots were intoxicated with alcohol present in their blood. The crew deviated from the standard approach procedure and descended prematurely without visual contact with terrain. Ten persons were killed in the accident.
records.probable_cause: The accident was caused by the crew's violation of the established approach procedure to Palana airport, including flight outside the approach route and premature descent below minimum safe altitude in mountainous terrain with weather conditions that excluded stable visual contact with ground references, resulting in aircraft collision with a mountain slope. Contributing factors included pilot incapacitation due to alcohol intoxication and inadequate pre-flight medical screening. (p. 47)

factors.evidence: Weather conditions excluded stable visual contact with ground references during approach to Palana (p. 47)
Crew conducted premature descent below minimum safe altitude for mountainous terrain (p. 47)
Alcohol was detected in blood of both flight crew members; both pilots were intoxicated during flight (p. 47)
Crew inaction when radio altimeter warning signal activated indicating dangerous altitude (p. 47)
Crew violated established approach scheme by flying outside approach route and providing false position information to dispatcher (p. 48)
Aircraft collided with slope of Pyatibrarka mountain and was destroyed on impact (p. 45-46)

events.text: Aircraft established approach to Palana Airport in instrument meteorological conditions; dispatcher expected crew report on third turn waypoint at 00:23
Crew begins descent from cleared altitude, deviating from standard approach procedure and flying outside designated approach route (p. 48)
Radio altimeter warning signal activated indicating dangerous altitude; crew did not respond to warning (p. 47)
In attempt to avoid terrain collision, crew abruptly pulled control column with elevator deflected to maximum 30°; both engine throttles moved to takeoff mode (p. 45)
Pitch angle increased sharply by 24° in 0.9 seconds; both engines shut down during pitch increase; power loss prevented thrust recovery (p. 45)
Aircraft speed dropped sharply to 130-135 km/h and aircraft stalled; continued flight for approximately 500 meters in steep nose-up attitude (p. 45)
Aircraft struck trees and terrain on slope of Pyatibraska mountain with severe right bank; aircraft was destroyed on impact (p. 45-46)
Dispatcher expected crew report did not arrive; dispatcher initiated call to aircraft; declared 'alarm' at 00:24:30; at 00:27 filed initial report of flight loss of radio contact (p. 46)

recommendations.text: Disseminate information about this accident to flight and command personnel of civil aviation operators and AON (5.1.1)

Review feasibility and initiate action with Ministry of Transport to modify FAP-128 paragraph 5.7 to require mandatory flight data analysis program as part of flight safety management system for aircraft with data recording systems regardless of maximum takeoff weight (5.1.2)
Review feasibility of adding limiting and control bearing values needed for aircraft flight monitoring to Palana Airport Flight Operations Instructions (5.2.1)
Supplement Palana Airport Flight Operations Instructions section 7.8.5 regarding interaction with meteorological personnel on 'Alarm' signal (5.2.2)
Conduct additional training for Palana dispatch personnel on radio communication procedures with aircraft conducting instrument approaches in mountainous terrain without radar control (5.2.3)
Organize effective pre-flight crew control in accordance with FAP regulations to prevent crew members from performing duties while intoxicated (5.3.1)
Consider adding responsibility for quality control of pre-flight preparation to job descriptions of flight safety inspection and duty navigator personnel (5.3.2)
Develop and implement flight data analysis program with special attention to crew adherence to approach procedures (5.3.3)
Develop and incorporate into Flight Operations Manual recommended procedure for approaches using visual reference points in mountainous terrain (5.3.4)
Conduct additional training for flight crew on instrument approaches in areas without radar control in mountainous terrain (5.3.5)

safety_changes: Enhanced pre-flight medical screening and alcohol testing protocols for Russian aviation
Improved flight data monitoring and analysis procedures for regional operators
Enhanced approach procedure adherence monitoring and enforcement

records.title: FlyMontserrat 107
records.summary: FlyMontserrat 107 crashed during takeoff from Antigua on 7 October 2012 at 1610 local time (2010 UTC). The Britten-Norman Islander's right engine lost power due to water contamination of the fuel system. The improper fuel filler cap allowed water ingress during heavy rain. With asymmetric thrust and unfeathered propeller, the aircraft yawed right, rolled right, descended rapidly and out of control, impacting the ground within the airport perimeter with its right wingtip first. The aircraft cartwheeled destroying the forward fuselage and killing the pilot and two forward-cabin passengers.
records.probable_cause: Water contamination of the right-hand engine fuel system resulting from incompatible fuel filler caps (p. 3). The right-hand engine lost power during takeoff due to fuel system contamination, and without propeller feathering, the aircraft became uncontrollable with asymmetric thrust and crashed (p. 1-2, 3).

factors.evidence: Right-hand fuel filler cap was of design incompatible with filler neck. Tests showed cap, installed in neck, could allow water to pass into fuel tank if aircraft parked during rain (p. 3). Aircraft Construction Number 082 had not been modified with improved fuel suction filter assembly despite availability since 1968 (p. 3).

Right-hand engine was not producing power at impact; fuel system feeding engine contained significant quantities of water (p. 1, 3). Water in fuel tank sumps probably entered engine fuel supply lines when aircraft rotated into takeoff attitude (p. 3).

Following loss of power on one engine, propeller should be feathered to reduce drag. Right-hand propeller was not in feathered position; bench test of propeller control unit functioned satisfactorily, suggesting no attempt was made to feather propeller (p. 3).

Shortly after takeoff, aircraft yawed and rolled to right, descending rapidly and apparently out of control (p. 1-2). Ground marks and damage indicated aircraft cartwheeled after right wingtip impact (p. 2).
Fuselage forward of wings destroyed; fuselage forward of wings destroyed by impact forces and subsequent fire (p. 2).

events.text: FlyMontserrat 107 cleared for takeoff from runway 07 at V.C. Bird International Airport, Antigua (p. 1)
Aircraft begins takeoff roll after rain showers had passed and approximately 40 mm of rain had fallen; no evidence water drain check was conducted following rainfall (p. 1-2)
Right-hand engine fails due to water contamination in fuel system caused by incompatible fuel filler cap (p. 1, 3)
Aircraft starts to yaw to right and stops climbing as asymmetric thrust develops from failed right engine (p. 1-2)
Aircraft rolls to right and descends rapidly, apparently out of control (p. 1-2)
Aircraft impacts ground within airport perimeter right wingtip first, steeply banked to right, at low forward speed; aircraft cartwheels before coming to rest erect (p. 1-2)
Fuselage forward of wings destroyed; pilot and two passengers seated in forward cabin fatally injured; rear passenger severely injured (p. 2)
Survivor evacuated to hospital for treatment; aircraft remains destroyed (p. 2)

recommendations.text: It is recommended that the European Aviation Safety Agency takes action to require that Britten-Norman Islander aircraft are equipped with fuel suction filter assemblies which minimise the likelihood of any water present in the fuel tank sumps being fed to the engines. (p. 6)

records.title: Red Wings Airlines 9268
records.summary: A Tupolev Tu-204-100B operating a repositioning flight from Pardubice touched down on runway 19 at Vnukovo between 900 and 1000 m along the runway at 230 km/h in crosswind gusts reaching 11.5 m/s. The right landing gear strut failed to compress on touchdown, preventing reverse thrust deployment and disabling the wheel brakes through a safety interlock that required simultaneous compression of both landing gear sets. Without deceleration systems available, the aircraft accelerated back to 240 km/h and skidded off the runway 32 seconds after landing, striking ground structures.
records.probable_cause: The accident was caused by failure of the right landing gear to compress on touchdown, which disabled the automatic reverse thrust and brake systems through a safety interlock, combined with high crosswind conditions of 11.5 m/s on runway 19 at Vnukovo. The investigation identified that the landing gear compression signal was not sensed, preventing both reversers and wheel brakes from functioning. (p. 178)

factors.evidence: At the moment of touchdown only the left side gear was in contact with the runway. The right gear strut compression signal had not yet been sensed, preventing activation of safety systems dependent on simultaneous compression of both landing gear sets. (p. 72-78)

It had been snowing prior to the accident and there was a significant cross wind with gusts of up to 29 knots (11.5 m/s). During the landing the right side wind gusts reached up to 11.5 m/s on runway 19. (p. 56-60)

Because there was no compression of the right landing gear strut, the reversers were never deployed. The wheel brakes were also ineffective, as they also required compression of the gear strut to function correctly through the interlock system. Aircraft reached minimum airspeed of 200-205 km/h then accelerated back to 240 km/h. (p. 140-155)

The aircraft skidded off the runway 32 seconds after landing at an air speed of about 215 km/h, striking the ditch and highway structures (Kyiv Highway), resulting in destruction of the aircraft. (p. 11)

events.text: Aircraft touched down on runway 19 at Vnukovo between 900 and 1000 m from the runway threshold at an airspeed of 230 km/h in crosswind gusts reaching 11.5 m/s. Right landing gear strut failed to compress on initial touchdown.
Almost simultaneously with nose gear compression, crew moved engines into reverse thrust position and applied mechanical brakes per standard landing procedure.
Nose gear compression detected and signals received; however right main landing gear strut compression signal remained absent.

Reverse thrust did not deploy because right landing gear compression signal was absent, violating the safety interlock requiring simultaneous compression of both main landing gear sets to enable reversers and brakes.
Aircraft reached minimum airspeed of 200-205 km/h approximately 1400 m along the runway, then began accelerating again due to ineffective braking with reversers inoperative.
Aircraft airspeed increased to 240 km/h as it approached the runway end, accelerating due to unavailable wheel brakes and reverse thrust.
Aircraft main fuselage struck ground structures after 1600 m of skidding at high speed without reverse thrust or effective braking.

Aircraft skidded off runway at approximately 215 km/h after 1800 m ground run, struck ditch and Kyiv Highway structures, resulting in destruction of aircraft and fire. Flight crew (3 members) and 2 cabin crew killed; 1 driver on highway seriously injured.

recommendations.text: Review the safety interlock system that prevents reverse thrust and brake operation when landing gear compression is not sensed on all main gear units, to evaluate whether alternative deceleration methods should be available in single-gear failure scenarios.
Develop procedures for high crosswind landing operations with landing gear anomalies, including go-around options and crew training.

safety_changes: Enhanced landing gear monitoring systems
Review of interlock systems for landing gear related safety systems

records.title: SCAT Airlines 760

location.name: Kyzyltu, 1.6 km short of Almaty runway 23R

records.summary: SCAT Airlines Flight 760 crashed on 29 January 2013 during go-around to Almaty. At 07:03:24 UTC, the CRJ200 was at 1,600 m altitude on final approach in thick freezing fog with runway visibility of 175-200 m when the crew initiated a go-around due to inability to see the runway. Fourteen seconds after initiating the go-around, the aircraft entered an uncontrolled nose-down dive at approximately 20 degrees pitch-down. The aircraft impacted the ground 1.6 km short of the runway near Kyzyltu, killing all 21 occupants.
records.probable_cause: The nose-down elevator deflection during go-around maneuvering was the result of pilot input, though the investigation could not determine why the pilot made these control inputs (p. 3278-3315). Possible scenarios included: spatial disorientation from instrument meteorological conditions and turbulence; pilot incapacitation from sudden medical event (autopsy revealed Captain had coronary artery disease with significant stenosis); or somatogravitational illusion causing inversion of pilot's pitch perception during dynamic flight in poor visibility (p. 2048-2050, 3300-3315).

factors.evidence: Approach in freezing fog with runway visibility 175-200 m, below operator's meteorological minimums for crew's CAT I certification (p. 2362-2368)
Go-around initiated at 07:03:24 UTC when visibility remained below operating minimums (p. 2367-2369)
Autopsy revealed Captain Evdokimov had coronary artery disease with significant stenosis; sudden medical incapacitation scenario would cause uncontrolled input to control yoke (p. 3300-3310)
Aircraft descended from 1,600 m in uncontrolled dive with pitch 20-25 degrees nose-down, speed 360+ kt, impacting ground 1.6 km short of runway at 07:03:38 UTC, killing all occupants (p. 1675, 3278)

Reached cruise altitude 10,650 m, cruise speed 460 km/h in automatic mode (p. 2236)
Captain took control; Second Officer moved to radio duties without formal handover (p. 2236)
Captain reported: ETA 06:55, weather min CAT II 30x300, alternates Chymkent/Karaganda, fuel 2.5 hrs (p. 2236)

At 7,000 m, 540 km/h: Captain commanded 'Cowl on' - engine anti-ice system activated (p. 2236)
Approach clearance obtained, descending toward Almaty with visibility 175 m reported (p. 2237)
Captain confirmed decision to descend to runway visual range (VPR) despite below-minimums visibility (p. 2237)
Aircraft level at 1,600 m altitude in automatic mode - altitude hold active, navigation mode in lateral channel (p. 2237)
Flaps extended to 8 degrees during right turn to heading 230; aircraft positioning for landing approach (p. 2237)
ATIS Sierra: visibility improved to 300 m midpoint. Captain satisfied: 'OK, 3 hundred, that's fine, we need the start' (p. 2238)
Flaps to 8 degrees during turn to heading 140; speed 345 km/h at 1,600 m altitude (p. 2238)
Go-around initiated: runway not visible at descent minimum altitude, visual contact lost (p. 3278)
Fourteen seconds into go-around: elevator deflection commanded uncontrolled nose-down dive, pitch changed to -20 degrees (p. 3278, 2048-2050)
Aircraft crashed 1.6 km short of runway 23R near Kyzyltu at pitch 20 degrees nose-down, 360+ kt speed, landing gear down, flaps 10-15 degrees. All 21 killed (p. 1675, 3278)

records.summary: Boeing 747 cargo flight crashed shortly after takeoff when improperly secured heavy vehicles shifted aft during climb, damaging hydraulic systems and the horizontal stabilizer, causing pitch-up, stall, and impact.
records.probable_cause: National Airlines' inadequate procedures for restraining special cargo loads resulted in the loadmaster's improper restraint of the cargo, which moved aft and damaged hydraulic systems Nos. 1 and 2 and horizontal stabilizer drive mechanism components, rendering the airplane uncontrollable.

records.title: 2013 Polar Airlines Mil Mi-8 crash
records.summary: A Mil Mi-8T helicopter crashed into elevated terrain at 00:13 UTC on July 2, 2013, during the initial climb phase in darkness. The crew deviated from the filed flight plan route and altitude, descended below minimum safe altitude while attempting to maintain visual flight rules in deteriorating weather conditions including rain, snow, and icing, and struck a mountainside at 660 meters elevation during a turn to return to the departure airport. Weather forecasting deficiencies, crew resource management failures, inadequate terrain awareness systems training, and lack of guidance documentation contributed to the accident.
records.probable_cause: The pilot lost control of the helicopter due to flight in instrument meteorological conditions while not approved for instrument flight rules, compounded by descent below minimum safe altitude, deviation from flight plan, lack of terrain awareness system activation, and deficient weather briefing practices.

factors.evidence: Forecast and actual weather showed strong winds (40 km/h at altitude, 5 m/s near surface) perpendicular to the mountainous terrain, which could have contributed to control difficulties during the low-altitude flight near ridges.
Flight took off at 23:51 local time and crashed at 00:13 UTC in complete darkness without external visual references, reducing crew's ability to detect terrain.
Meteorological data indicated freezing level at 1000 meters; report describes crew encountering precipitation including rain, snow, and weak icing during descent.
Crew descended below minimum safe altitude (1164 m for the route) to 600-800 meters and deviated from filed route while trying to maintain visual flight in clouds.
Crew made uncoordinated route changes and descended without coordinating with air traffic control; the pilot received conflicting altitude instructions and made independent navigation decisions.
Crew lacked approval for instrument flight rules operations; training program did not emphasize decision-making for go-around procedures when weather conditions deteriorated.
Terrain awareness and warning system (SRPBZ) was not activated and crew lacked sufficient training for its operation; regulatory oversight was insufficient in enforcing SRPBZ activation procedures.
Helicopter struck mountainside at magnetic heading 15 degrees, pitch angle 32-40 degrees nose-up, indicating loss of control during terrain avoidance attempt.
Aircraft impacted elevated terrain (660 m elevation) at the base of a 772-meter mountain while attempting to return to departure airport.
Post-impact fire destroyed the aircraft after impact due to fuel system rupture in suspended fuel tanks.

events.text: Flight mechanic refueled the helicopter with 2800 liters of ice-resistant fuel.
Pilots received and signed meteorological forecast for the route with no concerns noted.
Pilot in command requested takeoff clearance using visual flight rules and confirmation to start engines.
Flight 9949 received takeoff clearance and lifted off with right-hand turn.
Flight crew reported altitude 1300 m, minimum pressure 748 mm, estimated exit time from zone 20 minutes, and arrival time 00:00 UTC.

Captain reported onboard weather conditions: westerly winds 280 degrees, 15-20 km/h; visibility more than 10 km; cloud tops at 1400 m, 1700 m respectively; temperature +8 degrees C; flight normal, no dangerous phenomena.
Final radio transmission: pilot reports 'Until zone exit' then radio contact terminated.
Helicopter struck mountainside at 660 meters elevation during return-to-base turn in darkness, completely destroying the aircraft.

recommendations.text: Develop and enforce standardized procedures for activation and use of terrain awareness and warning systems (SRPBZ) on all Mi-8 helicopters during night and instrument weather operations.

Establish mandatory go-around procedures and decision gates for pilots when meteorological conditions deteriorate below minimums for visual flight rules, with emphasis on returning to departure airfield rather than attempting alternate landing areas.

Improve meteorological forecasting coordination with aviation companies; provide specific area forecasts for mountainous regions showing cloud height and visibility at planned flight altitudes, not just route forecasts.
Ensure flight crews receive briefing on planned route, intended altitude, and minimum safe altitude before departure; document this briefing in flight plan and crew records.
Audit aviation companies operating in remote mountainous areas for compliance with instrument flight rules training requirements and enforcement of visual flight rules limitations.

safety_changes: Russian aviation authorities reviewed requirements for terrain awareness system training and activation procedures on regional helicopter operations
Increased regulatory focus on meteorological briefing procedures for routes with terrain obstacles
Enhanced crew resource management training requirements for helicopter operators in remote mountainous regions

notes: Report in Russian; History of Flight (section 1.1) and Analysis sections read comprehensively
Key findings: crew exceeded weather minimums for VFR, descended below minimum safe altitude, terrain awareness system not activated, meteorological briefing deficiencies
Four survivors: three crew and one passenger with serious injuries
Descent trajectory analysis indicates pilot attempted terrain avoidance during low-altitude return maneuver
Report includes detailed crew interviews, meteorological analysis, and SRPBZ system simulation showing that system would have provided 26-second warning if activated

records.title: Asiana Airlines 214

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Descent Below Visual Glidepath and Impact With Seawall, Asiana Airlines Flight 214, Boeing 777-200ER, HL7742, San Francisco, California, July 6, 2013

agencies.name: Aviation and Railway Accident Investigation Board

location.name: Runway 28L seawall, San Francisco International Airport, California

records.summary: On a daytime visual approach to runway 28L at San Francisco (glideslope out of service), the 777 was high and fast. The pilot flying selected flight level change, then disconnected the autopilot and pulled the thrust levers to idle, which placed the autothrottle in HOLD so that it no longer protected speed. The crew did not notice the decaying airspeed until the airplane was below 200 feet and initiated a go-around only seconds before the main gear and tail struck the seawall. Three passengers died and 49 people were seriously injured.
records.probable_cause: The flight crew's mismanagement of the airplane's descent during the visual approach, the pilot flying's unintended deactivation of automatic airspeed control, the flight crew's inadequate monitoring of airspeed, and the flight crew's delayed execution of a go-around after they became aware that the airplane was below acceptable glidepath and airspeed tolerances. Contributing were (1) the complexities of the autothrottle and autopilot flight director systems that were inadequately described in Boeing's documentation and Asiana's pilot training, which increased the likelihood of mode error; (2) the flight crew's nonstandard communication and coordination regarding the use of the autothrottle and autopilot flight director systems; (3) the pilot flying's inadequate training on the planning and executing of visual approaches; (4) the pilot monitoring/instructor pilot's inadequate supervision of the pilot flying; and (5) flight crew fatigue, which likely degraded their performance.

factors.evidence: Moving the thrust levers to idle after selecting FLCH SPD transitioned the autothrottle to HOLD; the pilot flying believed the autothrottle would still maintain the selected speed.
The crew did not recognize that the autoflight system's mode combination left neither autopilot nor autothrottle managing airspeed.
The pilot flying relied on the autothrottle to protect airspeed and was uncomfortable hand-flying a visual approach without the ILS glideslope.
None of the three pilots monitored airspeed, which fell about 30 knots below the 137-knot approach speed before anyone called it out.
The airplane reached a minimum airspeed of 103 knots with idle thrust and a high sink rate, well below the glidepath.
The airplane was above the glidepath and fast at 1,600 feet, then below it and slow below 500 feet; the approach never met stabilized criteria.
The go-around was delayed until about three seconds before impact, when the airplane was below 100 feet with thrust only just advancing.
Communication and coordination about autoflight mode use were nonstandard, and the instructor pilot did not adequately supervise the pilot flying.
The pilot flying's training on planning and executing visual approaches was inadequate, and Asiana's training did not adequately explain the autothrottle HOLD behaviour.
The NTSB concluded that fatigue from the overnight trans-Pacific flight and circadian disruption likely degraded the crew's performance.
The complexity of the 777 autothrottle and autopilot flight director system interactions increased the likelihood of mode error.
Boeing's documentation inadequately described the autothrottle HOLD mode and the conditions under which speed protection is not available.
The pilot flying was transitioning to the 777 with about 35 hours on type and the instructor pilot was on his first flight as an instructor.
The low-airspeed alerting available did not provide timely enough warning; the NTSB recommended improved low-energy alerting for transport airplanes.
Evacuation was delayed about 90 seconds while the cabin manager consulted the cockpit, two slides inflated inside the cabin, and one ejected passenger was struck by a rescue vehicle.
The main landing gear and then the aft fuselage struck the seawall; the tail section separated.
A fire developed in the fuselage after the airplane came to rest, destroying the cabin.

events.text: Approach control vectors the flight for a visual approach to runway 28L; the ILS glideslope is out of service and the crew are asked to maintain 180 knots to 5 nm.
The airplane is above the desired glidepath and fast; the pilot flying uses vertical speed mode and then increases the descent rate to regain the path.
At about 1,600 feet the pilot flying selects FLCH SPD with the MCP altitude set at 3,000 feet; the autopilot begins to command a climb.
Pilot flying disconnects the autopilot and moves the thrust levers to idle; the autothrottle transitions to HOLD and no longer controls airspeed.
Autothrottle mode annunciation changes to HOLD on the flight mode annunciator; the change is not called out by either pilot.
The pilot flying hand-flies the descent using the PAPI as reference; thrust remains at idle and airspeed decays through the 137-knot approach speed.
The airplane passes 500 feet slightly below glidepath at about 134 knots with sink rate increasing; the PAPI shows three red lights shortly afterwards.
Passing about 200 feet the instructor pilot notices the four-red PAPI indication and low airspeed and calls for more speed; airspeed is about 118 knots.
Instructor pilot calls 'sink rate' as the airplane passes about 100 feet; the pilot flying pulls the nose up without adding thrust.
Thrust levers are advanced toward full thrust about seven seconds before impact; engines begin to spool up from idle.
Stick shaker activates about four seconds before impact.
Airspeed reaches its minimum of 103 knots about three seconds before impact; the instructor pilot calls for a go-around.
Main landing gear and aft fuselage strike the seawall short of the runway 28L threshold; the tail separates and the airplane slides and spins before coming to rest.
After a delay of about 90 seconds while the cabin manager checks with the cockpit, an evacuation is ordered when fire is seen outside; two slides have inflated inside the cabin.

recommendations.text: Require Boeing to revise 777 flight crew documentation and training to clearly describe the autothrottle HOLD mode and the conditions under which the autothrottle will not maintain the selected airspeed.
recommendations.outcome: Boeing revised 777 Flight Crew Training Manual and Operations Manual material on autothrottle modes.

recommendations.text: Convene a panel of human factors, aviation operations and design experts to evaluate the current Boeing autoflight design philosophy and recommend changes that would minimize mode confusion.
Develop a standard for low-energy alerting on transport-category airplanes so that crews receive timely warning of a low airspeed, high sink rate condition.
Revise training to require pilots to hand-fly visual approaches and to reinforce standard callouts, monitoring and go-around decision-making, including for instructor pilots.
recommendations.outcome: Asiana revised its training program and increased manual flying practice.

recommendations.text: Improve aircraft rescue and firefighting training and procedures for vehicle operation near an accident site and for interior firefighting of large aircraft.

dissent.position: In its formal comments on the draft report the Korean ARAIB argued that the autothrottle and autopilot flight director system design and Boeing's documentation should carry greater weight in the probable cause rather than being listed only as contributing factors.
dissent.topic: probable cause weighting of autoflight design

safety_changes: Boeing clarified 777 documentation and training material on autothrottle HOLD mode and speed protection.
Asiana Airlines revised its pilot training program, adding manual flying and visual approach practice and stronger instructor pilot standards.
FAA renewed emphasis on manual flight skills and monitoring (SAFO 13002 and Operational Use of Flight Path Management Systems working group follow-up).
San Francisco International Airport and other ARFF services revised procedures for vehicle movement and passenger accounting at accident sites.
