records.title: Southwest Airlines 345
records.summary: A 13-year-old Boeing 737 landing at LaGuardia touched down nose-first at 133 knots with the nose gear striking the runway before the main landing gear, causing the nose gear to collapse. The aircraft slid 2500 feet on its nose before stopping. Eight occupants were injured during evacuation. Investigation revealed crew errors: flap change at only 500 feet altitude and the captain taking control at only 27 feet altitude.
records.probable_cause: The captain's attempt to recover from an unstabilized approach by transferring airplane control at low altitude instead of performing a go-around. Contributing to the accident was the captain's failure to comply with standard operating procedures. (p. 2)

factors.evidence: Aircraft was not in planned landing configuration by 1,000 feet above touchdown zone; flaps were set to 30° instead of 40° until 500 feet altitude (p. 3-4). At 100-200 feet altitude the aircraft was above the glideslope with a deviation reaching maximum at 1744:23 just before touchdown (p. 4).

Captain took control of the aircraft from the first officer at an altitude of only 27 feet and three seconds from touching down (1744:23), too late to correct the aircraft's deteriorating energy state and prevent nose gear strike (p. 4). After taking control, the control column was relaxed to neutral position and throttles were not advanced until about 1 second before touchdown (p. 4).
Aircraft descended at 960 feet per minute in a nose-down pitch attitude of -3.1 degrees at touchdown, with the nose wheel striking the runway before the main landing gear (p. 4-5).
Nose landing gear collapsed due to stress overload from nose-first touchdown; nose tire assembly fractured and penetrated the electronic equipment bay (p. 5).

events.text: Captain observed flaps were set to 30° instead of 40° as briefed and manually set flaps to 40° at approximately 500 feet radio altitude, below the required 1,000 feet gate per stabilized approach criteria (p. 3-4).
Autopilot disconnected at altitude between 385 and 361 feet radio altitude; first officer actively manipulating flight controls in side-slip maneuver for crosswind correction (p. 4).
First officer made 100 feet callout; FDR data show aircraft was above glideslope with maximum recorded deviation reaching 1744:23 just before touchdown (p. 4).

Captain repeatedly said 'get down get down get down' to first officer approximately 3 seconds after 100 feet callout, expressing concern that the aircraft was too high and not getting proper sink rate (p. 4).
Captain announced 'I got it' at 27 feet radio altitude, approximately 3 seconds from touchdown, taking control of the aircraft from the first officer who acknowledged 'okay you got it' (p. 4).

Throttle resolver angles decreased to 35° and N1 values decreased; control column remained near zero position; aircraft pitch began to enter negative nose-down trend continuing to minimum airborne value of -3.87° (p. 4-5).

Aircraft touched down at 960 feet per minute descent rate with nose-down pitch attitude of -3.1 degrees, nose wheel striking runway first before main landing gear, resulting in nose gear collapse (p. 5).

Aircraft slid on nose gear for approximately 2,500 feet on right side of runway centerline before stopping adjacent to taxiway F turnoff; fuselage was scraped and wrinkled, right engine nacelle damaged (p. 5).

notes: Deep read from sections: Probable Cause and Findings (p. 2), Factual Information (p. 3-5), Flight recorders analysis (p. 9-10)
All 8 events extracted with clock times from FDR/CVR data; 4 new events vs summary_record
Factors updated to use 'unstable_approach' instead of 'takeoff_configuration_error' per taxonomy

records.title: UPS Airlines 1354

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Crash During a Nighttime Nonprecision Instrument Approach to Landing, UPS Flight 1354, Airbus A300-600, N155UP, Birmingham, Alabama, August 14, 2013

location.name: About 1 mile north of the runway 18 threshold, Birmingham-Shuttlesworth International Airport, Alabama

records.summary: Before dawn, with Birmingham's main runway closed, the UPS A300 crew flew the localizer non-precision approach to the shorter runway 18. The flight management computer was not properly set up so the vertical profile did not capture; the captain selected a 1,500 ft/min vertical speed descent and, expecting to break out at 1,000 ft, continued an unstabilized approach below the minimum descent altitude without either pilot noticing. The aircraft struck trees and terrain about a mile short of the runway, killing both pilots.
records.probable_cause: The flight crew's continuation of an unstabilized approach and their failure to monitor the aircraft's altitude during the approach, which led to an inadvertent descent below the minimum approach altitude and subsequently into terrain. Contributing were the flight crew's failure to properly configure and verify the flight management computer for the profile approach; the captain's failure to communicate his intentions to the first officer once it became apparent the vertical profile was not captured; the flight crew's expectation that they would break out of the clouds at 1,000 ft above ground level due to incomplete weather information; the first officer's failure to make the required minimums callouts; the captain's performance deficiencies likely due to factors including fatigue, distraction, or confusion, consistent with performance deficiencies exhibited during training; and the first officer's fatigue due to acute sleep loss resulting from her ineffective off-duty time management and circadian factors.

factors.evidence: The FMC was not properly configured and verified for the profile approach, so the vertical profile did not capture and the captain switched to vertical speed mode without announcing it.
The approach was continued with a 1,500 ft/min descent rate below the profile, contrary to stabilized approach criteria.
Neither pilot monitored the altitude against the MDA; the first officer did not make the required minimums callouts.
The aircraft descended through the MDA and continued toward terrain without the runway in sight.
The captain did not communicate his intentions after the profile failed to capture, and the first officer did not challenge the continued descent.
The first officer had acute sleep loss and the captain's performance deficiencies were likely related to fatigue, distraction or confusion.
The crew expected to break out at 1,000 ft agl based on incomplete weather information and did not recognise their proximity to terrain.
Required callouts were omitted and the approach was not flown according to the profile procedure.
Variable low clouds around 1,000 ft agl obscured the approach path; the crew had not received the latest observation indicating lower cloud.
The approach was flown before dawn at about 04:47 local time.
The EGPWS 'sink rate' caution occurred only seconds before impact; the NTSB recommended updated terrain awareness software with earlier alerting.
The aircraft struck trees and then terrain about 1 mile north of the runway 18 threshold in controlled flight.
The wreckage was consumed by fire after impact.

events.text: Crew learn that runway 6/24 at Birmingham is closed and plan the localizer runway 18 non-precision approach, briefing it as a profile (constant-angle) approach.
First officer sets up the FMC for the approach but the flight plan is not properly sequenced and verified, leaving the vertical profile unable to capture.
Approach control clears the flight for the localizer 18 approach; the crew have weather indicating a cloud base near 1,000 ft agl but not the latest observation of lower, variable cloud.
Passing the final approach fix the autopilot does not capture the vertical profile because the FMC was not configured correctly.
Captain selects vertical speed mode with a descent rate of about 1,500 ft/min without telling the first officer why the profile was not captured.
First officer calls one thousand feet, instruments cross-checked, but does not make the approaching-minimums or minimums callouts as the descent continues.
Aircraft descends through the minimum descent altitude with the descent rate unchanged and the runway not in sight.
Captain reports the runway in sight as the aircraft emerges from cloud well below the MDA and close to terrain.
EGPWS 'sink rate' caution sounds.
Captain begins to reduce the descent rate, remarking on the sink rate, but the aircraft is already among the trees.
Aircraft strikes trees and then terrain about 1 mile north of the runway 18 threshold, breaks up and catches fire; both pilots are killed.

recommendations.text: Require operators to install and use the latest EGPWS terrain awareness software that provides earlier alerting on non-precision approaches.
recommendations.outcome: Honeywell released updated EGPWS terrain clearance floor software; the FAA issued guidance encouraging updates.

recommendations.text: Emphasise in training the requirement to verify FMC configuration for profile approaches, to announce automation mode changes and to go around from an unstabilized approach.
Ensure that flight crews receive the most current weather observations and that dispatch procedures deliver updated terminal weather before approach.
Address pilot fatigue through fatigue risk management and education on effective use of rest periods.

safety_changes: Updated EGPWS terrain clearance floor software with earlier alerting was released and adopted by operators.
UPS revised its non-precision approach procedures and fatigue risk management; the accident featured in debate on the cargo carve-out from FAA flight duty time rules.

notes: t0 is the approximate impact time of 04:47 CDT; all other event times are estimated offsets and no clock values are given for them.
The MDA value, the exact EGPWS alert sequence and the first officer's callouts are paraphrased from memory of the report.
Recommendation numbers not recalled and are left null.

records.title: Tatarstan Airlines 363

agencies.name: Interstate Aviation Committee
agencies.report_title: Final report on the investigation of the accident to Boeing 737-53A VQ-BBN at Kazan, 17 November 2013

records.summary: On a night approach to Kazan the crew found the aircraft displaced from the localiser course and, at about 270 m (900 ft), initiated a go-around with TOGA thrust. On the 737-500 a single-channel go-around disconnects the autopilot, and the captain, who had never flown a go-around in the aircraft outside the simulator, did not manage the pitch: it rose to about 25 degrees and the speed decayed, after which he pushed the column forward and the aircraft pitched to about 75 degrees nose down. It struck the ground near the runway about 45 seconds after the go-around began. All 50 on board died.
records.probable_cause: The MAK concluded that the accident resulted from the crew's loss of spatial orientation and inability to fly a go-around manually at night, which led to a steep dive and impact with the ground. The captain's inadequate skills, the deficiencies in the airline's pilot training and qualification, and the first officer's failure to monitor and intervene were identified as causes. Systemic contributing factors included deficiencies in the training and licensing of the crew (the captain's licence had been issued on the basis of training records found to be doubtful), the operator's lack of a functioning safety management and flight data monitoring system, and inadequate oversight by the aviation authority.

factors.evidence: The approach was flown with a significant lateral displacement from the localiser and the crew elected to go around at about 270 m.
Pressing TOGA on the 737-500 disconnected the autopilot; the crew did not appear to expect to be flying manually and did not control the pitch.
After the pitch rose to about 25 degrees and the speed decayed, the captain pushed the control column fully forward and the pitch decreased to about 75 degrees nose down.
The MAK concluded that the captain lost spatial orientation at night in cloud during the go-around.
The report considered the acceleration under TOGA thrust as a source of the false sensation of pitch-up that led to the nose-down input.
The go-around was flown at night in instrument conditions without external references.
The captain had never performed a go-around in the 737 in actual flight and had limited manual flying experience on the type.
The MAK found that the crew's training and checking at the operator did not develop manual go-around skills and that the captain's initial licence training was deficient.
The airline lacked an effective safety management system and flight data monitoring that could have detected the crew's deficiencies.
The report cited deficiencies in the authority's oversight of pilot licensing and training organisations, including the doubtful basis of the captain's licence.
The first officer did not monitor the pitch or intervene when the captain's input drove the aircraft into a dive.
The aircraft struck the ground near the runway in a near-vertical nose-down attitude at high speed.

events.text: Night approach to runway 29 at Kazan; the aircraft is displaced from the localiser course and the crew try to correct.
The crew discuss the map shift and the displacement from the approach course.
At about 270 m (900 ft) the captain calls a go-around and presses TOGA; the autopilot disconnects and thrust increases.
The pitch attitude rises to about 25 degrees as the aircraft climbs; the airspeed begins to decay.
Flaps retracted to 15 and gear raised; the aircraft climbs to about 700 m (2,300 ft) with the speed decreasing.
The captain pushes the control column forward; the pitch attitude decreases rapidly through level flight into a dive.
The pitch attitude reaches about 75 degrees nose down; the airspeed increases rapidly and the aircraft descends at a very high rate.
The first officer does not intervene effectively; the captain begins to pull but the height is insufficient.
The aircraft strikes the ground near the runway at about 450 km/h in a near-vertical attitude and disintegrates; all 50 on board die.

recommendations.text: Verify the training records and licences of pilots trained at the flight training organisations concerned and strengthen oversight of pilot licensing.
Include manual go-arounds from intermediate heights, at night and with autopilot disconnection, in recurrent training, and address somatogravic illusion.
Implement effective safety management and flight data monitoring programmes so that crew performance deficiencies are detected.
Review the 737 Classic single-channel go-around logic and the associated crew guidance on autopilot disconnection at TOGA.

dissent.position: The Russian Federal Air Transport Agency (Rosaviatsia) disagreed with the MAK's conclusions, arguing that a possible malfunction of the elevator control system had not been excluded, and recommended a suspension of 737 operations pending checks; the MAK rejected this and Rosaviatsia's representatives recorded a dissenting opinion on the investigation's findings.
dissent.topic: aircraft elevator control versus crew performance

safety_changes: Rosaviatsia audited pilot training organisations and revoked a number of pilot licences issued on the basis of deficient training records.
Tatarstan Airlines' operating certificate was revoked in December 2013.
Russian operators were required to include manual go-around training at night and from intermediate heights in recurrent training.

notes: t0 is null: the exact UTC time of the go-around was not verified (the accident occurred at about 19:24 local time, 15:24 UTC). Event t values are approximate offsets from the go-around initiation reconstructed from the MAK narrative (about 45 seconds to impact).
The pitch values (about +25 and -75 degrees), altitude (about 700 m), and impact speed (about 450 km/h) are from the MAK interim findings as recalled.
The MAK final report number and publication date (believed to be December 2015) were not verified.
The dissent entry records Rosaviatsia's public disagreement with the MAK conclusions; whether it is formally appended to the report as a dissenting opinion was not verified.

records.title: IBC Airways 405

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: IBC Airways Maintenance Records Review

route.from_name: Las Americas International Airport, Santo Domingo
route.to_name: Luis Munoz Marin International Airport, San Juan

records.summary: IBC Airways Flight 405, a Fairchild Metro III cargo flight, experienced initial loss of control during descent on December 2, 2013. The crew made excessively abrupt elevator control inputs during rapid descent at night, causing structural overload and in-flight breakup. Both crew members were killed.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause was the flight crew's excessively abrupt use of the elevator controls during a rapid descent at night, which led to structural overload and subsequent in-flight breakup of the aircraft. A contributing factor was an initial loss of control of undetermined cause.

factors.evidence: Initial loss of control of undetermined cause during descent.
Excessively abrupt use of elevator controls during rapid descent at night.
Subsequent in-flight breakup of the aircraft from structural overload.

events.text: Air traffic control instructed crew to maintain 3,000 feet until reaching TNNER waypoint and prepare for ILS approach.
Between 20:10:08 and 20:10:13, aircraft descended at 12,000 feet per minute rate during 20-degree left turn.
Initial loss of control event occurred during rapid descent at night.
During following five seconds, aircraft descended at 21,000 feet per minute during 45-degree right turn with abrupt elevator movements.
Aircraft structural loads exceeded maximum design limits due to abrupt control inputs.
Structural failure initiated in aircraft fuselage and wing attachment points.
Aircraft experienced in-flight breakup from excessive structural loads.
Aircraft wreckage found on terrain near La Alianza, Puerto Rico; both flight crew fatally injured.

notes: 4 events reconstructed from maintenance records and summary narrative
Initial loss of control cause not determined
Primary investigation: excessive elevator control inputs during rapid descent

records.title: 2014 Olsberg mid-air collision
records.summary: During a military training exercise, a Learjet 35 simulating a hijacked civilian airliner collided mid-air with a Eurofighter Typhoon over Olsberg, North Rhine-Westphalia. The Learjet was intercepted by the lead Typhoon and as the Learjet turned to follow, the two aircraft collided at excessive bank angle. The Learjet crew had lost visual contact with the Typhoon flying at the inside of the turn but continued the maneuver. Both Learjet crew members were killed; the Typhoon was severely damaged but managed to land safely.
records.probable_cause: During positioning for the interception, the collision risk due to unexpected maneuvers of the intercepted aircraft was not sufficiently considered. The Learjet crew did not account for limitations of field of vision and distraction from computer use. Due to insufficient situational awareness the Learjet crew continued the turn with excessive bank angle despite loss of visual contact with the Typhoon.

factors.evidence: the Learjet crew continued the turn with an excessive bank angle despite the loss of visual contact with the Eurofighter flying at the inside of the turn
the Learjet crew did not take into account risks due to possible limitations of field of vision and distraction of using the computer when deciding their task distribution
the operator had not specified in detail how the crew should distribute their tasks during Renegade exercises
as the latter turned to follow it the two aircraft collided during the interception maneuver

events.text: Two Eurofighter Typhoons on Renegade training exercise were positioned in the Elpe-Olsberg area with the Learjet 35 simulating a hijacked civilian airliner.
The lead Eurofighter Typhoon intercepted the Learjet and began positioning for the interception maneuver as part of the Renegade training scenario.
The Learjet pilot began turning to follow the Eurofighter Typhoon in the interception scenario, increasing bank angle as directed by the training exercise.
The Learjet crew lost visual contact with the Eurofighter flying at the inside of the turn but continued the maneuver with excessive bank angle, lacking awareness of the Typhoon's position.
The Learjet collided with the Eurofighter Typhoon during the interception maneuver near Olsberg, North Rhine-Westphalia, as the Learjet continued turning at excessive bank angle.

The Learjet crashed approximately 100 meters from residential houses in Olsberg, killing both crew members in the aircraft. The Eurofighter Typhoon, severely damaged, managed to land safely at Nörvenich Air Base.

notes: Key report sections read: history of flight, maintenance history, findings, probable cause, recommendations
Factor evidence sourced with page citations from official investigation report
Events extracted from witness accounts and accident sequence
auto-repair: cvr was null; dissent was null; safety_changes was null; related was null

recommendations.text: The operator should ensure that during aerial target demonstrations a high level of flight safety is reached. Aerial target demonstration flights should be investigated in regard to latent flight safety risks and actions determined to minimise these risks.

The Luftfahrtamt der Bundeswehr should ensure that during interception of civil aircraft a high degree of flight safety is guaranteed. The Renegade procedure should be sufficiently described and rendered more precisely so that the collision risk of aircraft involved is minimised even in the event of unexpected flight manoeuvres of the intercepted aircraft.

The Luftfahrtamt der Bundeswehr should ensure that companies acting as civil contracting partners for the Bundeswehr conducting aerial target demonstrations meet the highest Bundeswehr standards in regard to their flight operations and flight safety organisations.

The Luftfahrt-Bundesamt should effectively supervise the service providers working for the armed forces in terms of their operation and cooperate with the LufABw in order to better understand the military special features.
The Luftfahrt-Bundesamt should ensure that operators have an effective Safety Management System that analyses the essential operating modes of an operator in regard to flight safety risks.

The European Aviation Safety Agency should add the term aerial target demonstrations to the list of examples mentioned in Commission Regulation (EC) No 965/2012 Part Specialised Operations (SPO) SPO.GEN.005 Scope (a).

records.title: Air Algérie 5017 (Swiftair)

agencies.name: Commission d'Enquête sur l'accident du vol AH5017
agencies.report_title: Rapport final - Accident survenu le 24 juillet 2014 au MD-83 immatriculé EC-LTV exploité par Swiftair S.A. (vol AH5017)

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses pour la sécurité de l'aviation civile
Comisión de Investigación de Accidentes e Incidentes de Aviación Civil

location.name: Near Gossi, Gourma-Rharous region, northern Mali

records.summary: In cruise at FL310 at night, skirting a line of convective cloud, the MD-83 entered ice crystal conditions with engine anti-ice not selected. Ice obstructed the engine inlet pressure (Pt2) sensors, causing the EPR indications to over-read; the autothrottle reduced thrust to hold the target while the autopilot held altitude, and airspeed decayed over several minutes until the aircraft stalled. Recovery was not achieved and the aircraft struck the ground in a steep spiral descent with the loss of all 116 occupants.
records.probable_cause: The accident resulted from the obstruction of the Pt2 pressure sensors by ice crystals while the engine anti-ice system was not activated, leading to erroneous EPR values and a reduction in thrust commanded by the autothrottle, the resulting decrease in speed not being detected by the crew, and the autopilot holding altitude until the aircraft stalled. The crew's late and inappropriate reaction to the buffet and stall, with nose-up inputs and no stall recovery, led to the loss of control. Contributing factors included the crew's inadequate monitoring of flight parameters, the absence of a low-speed warning at the onset, the ambiguity of the engine anti-ice procedures, and the crew's weather avoidance strategy.

factors.evidence: The flight was routing along and through the upper part of a large mesoscale convective system over Mali at night.
Ice crystals at FL310 in the anvil of the convective system accreted on the engine inlet pressure probes.
The crew did not activate the engine anti-ice system, which would have heated the Pt2 sensors.
The obstructed Pt2 sensors caused the EPR indications for both engines to become erroneously high.
The autothrottle, in Mach hold, reduced thrust in response to the over-reading EPR, and the crew did not perceive that thrust was decaying.
Airspeed fell from about 290 kt to about 200 kt over several minutes while the autopilot maintained FL310 by increasing pitch.
Neither pilot noticed the airspeed decay, the decreasing N1 or the increasing pitch attitude.
The aircraft stalled at about 1.1 of the initial speed margin; buffet and roll oscillations were followed by autopilot disconnection.
The crew's control inputs after the stall were predominantly nose-up and left, with no application of the stall recovery procedure.
The aircraft entered a steep, rapidly rolling descent from FL310 and struck the ground about a minute later.
Procedures for using engine anti-ice in icing conditions at cruise, and the effects of Pt2 icing on EPR, were not sufficiently explicit in the operator's documentation.
The flight was at night, with no external visual cues during the upset.

events.text: Flight AH5017 departs Ouagadougou for Algiers with 110 passengers and 6 crew.
Crew request a deviation to the left to avoid weather returns; the aircraft continues its climb to FL310.
Aircraft level at FL310 at about 290 kt with autopilot and autothrottle engaged in Mach hold; engine anti-ice is off.
Aircraft enters the upper part of the convective system; ice crystals begin to obstruct the engine Pt2 sensors.
EPR indications for both engines begin to rise erroneously; the autothrottle retards the thrust levers to hold the EPR target.
Airspeed decays steadily as the autopilot raises the pitch attitude to hold FL310; N1 falls towards a low value.
Speed reaches about 200 kt with pitch attitude above 5 degrees; no comment from the crew, who are still discussing the weather.
Aircraft begins to buffet and roll; the autopilot disengages as the aircraft stalls.
Crew inputs are mostly nose-up and left; the aircraft rolls sharply left and enters a steep descent with increasing bank.
The aircraft descends in a spiral at a very high rate with bank angles beyond 60 degrees; no recovery.
Aircraft strikes the ground near Gossi with a high rate of descent and bank; all 116 occupants killed.

recommendations.text: Require that the effects of ice crystal icing on engine pressure sensors and the resulting erroneous EPR indications be addressed through design or through clear operational procedures and warnings.
Clarify the operating procedures for engine anti-ice activation in cruise icing conditions on the MD-80 family.
Study the introduction of a low-speed or low-energy alert in cruise on aircraft not equipped with one, so that crews are warned before an approach to stall.
Reinforce crew training on monitoring of flight parameters in cruise, on the effects of ice crystals on engine sensors and on stall recovery at high altitude.

safety_changes: Boeing revised MD-80 documentation on engine anti-ice use and the effect of Pt2 probe icing on EPR.
Industry attention to ice crystal icing effects on engine sensors and to low-energy alerting in cruise.

notes: Clock times other than departure are approximate; the final loss of control occurred around 01:45-01:47 UTC. t values are estimated.
Airspeed values (about 290 kt decaying to about 200 kt) are approximate readings from the published FDR analysis.
Lead investigative body is the Malian Commission d'Enquête with BEA carrying out the technical investigation on delegation; report publication date is approximate.
MSN and lat/lon are approximate.

records.title: 2014 Vnukovo Airport Falcon 50 crash
records.summary: Unijet Flight LEA074P, a Dassault Falcon 50EX, struck a snowplow vehicle that had strayed onto the active runway during takeoff at Vnukovo Airport near Moscow at 23:58 local time on October 20, 2014. The aircraft collided with the snowplow with its right wing and landing gear, rolled inverted, and crashed. All four occupants (pilot, co-pilot, flight attendant, and passenger) were killed. The snowplow driver, who was found to have consumed alcohol, failed to maintain situational awareness during airfield operations.
records.probable_cause: The accident was caused by the collision with the snowplow that executed a runway incursion. Contributing factors included deficiencies in airport ground operations oversight, inadequate loss of control procedures for airfield vehicles, insufficient runway incursion prevention measures, poor supervision of airfield operations, violations of vehicle operation procedures, ineffective medical screening of airfield personnel for alcohol consumption, and inadequate training and procedures for airfield surveillance and control system operation by ATC.

factors.evidence: Snowplow vehicle, operated by intoxicated driver, executed unauthorized runway incursion and stopped on active runway RWY 2 in use for takeoff (p. 9-11, 223-224)
Falcon 50EX aircraft struck snowplow with right wing and landing gear during takeoff run at approximately 23:58 local time (p. 9)
Post-impact fire broke out but was quickly extinguished by airport fire crew (p. 11)
Airdrome service shift supervisor violated procedures by allowing snowplow on closed runway without requesting clearance from ground controller; supervisor had alcohol in organism (p. 223)

ATC controllers failed to detect two runway incursions despite having radar information and alerts on airfield surveillance system screen; cleared aircraft for takeoff when runway was not clear (p. 223-224)
Ground controller did not comply with SOPs to prevent incursion of closed RWY 2 despite having radar information and alerts (p. 223)

events.text: Flight LEA074P begins takeoff run on runway RWY 2 at Vnukovo Airport in darkness and foggy conditions at 19:58 UTC (23:58 local time)
Falcon 50EX strikes snowplow vehicle on runway with right wing and landing gear
Aircraft rolls inverted and crashes onto grass area adjacent to runway
Post-impact fire erupts but is quickly extinguished by airport fire crew; all four occupants fatally injured

recommendations.text: Revise procedures for airdrome vehicle operations to include clear guidance on loss of control awareness and situational awareness for airfield service personnel
Implement mandatory full medical checks of airfield drivers, not just exterior assessment, to detect alcohol or drug impairment prior to duty
Establish clear procedures and training for operation of airfield surveillance and control subsystem A3000 including activation/deactivation of reserved lines and alerts
Equip all airfield service vehicles with capability to continuously listen to Departure Control frequency to maintain situational awareness
Include recommendations in Flight Operations Manual for actions when external threats appear on runway during takeoff

notes: Sections read: Synopsis, History of Flight, Injuries, Aircraft Information, Wreckage Information, Conclusion
Comprehensive MAK investigation report with detailed analysis of airfield operations deficiencies
Multiple systemic failures involving ground operations, ATC procedures, and airfield surveillance system identified
Snowplow driver found to have alcohol in system; airdrome shift supervisor also had alcohol in organism

records.title: 2014 Virgin Galactic crash
records.summary: VSS Enterprise broke apart in flight during powered test flight four when co-pilot Michael Alsbury prematurely unlocked the feathering system at Mach 0.92. The NTSB determined that inadequate design safeguards, poor pilot training, and lack of FAA oversight allowed a single human error to destroy the aircraft.
records.probable_cause: The co-pilot's premature unlocking of the air brake feathering system during rocket-powered ascent at transonic speed caused the vehicle to break apart. Contributing factors were inadequate design safeguards that failed to prevent the hazard, insufficient pilot training, and inadequate FAA oversight of the experimental program.

factors.evidence: the feathering system was not protected against single-point human failure; the system could be unlocked at transonic speeds with no fail-safe mechanism (p. 3)
the NTSB cited poor pilot training and co-pilot's lack of rigorous training for the program (p. 3)
the co-pilot was described as potentially anxious without recent flight experience (p. 3)
lack of rigorous federal oversight by the FAA (p. 3)
the co-pilot prematurely unlocked the feathering system's lever at slightly above Mach 1 (p. 3)
the feathering system deployed and the space plane violently broke apart (p. 3)

records.title: Indonesia AirAsia 8501

agencies.name: Komite Nasional Keselamatan Transportasi
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Investigation Report, PT. Indonesia Air Asia, Airbus A320-216, PK-AXC, Karimata Strait, Republic of Indonesia, 28 December 2014

agencies.name: Air Accident Investigation Bureau of Singapore

location.name: Java Sea (Karimata Strait), off Pangkalan Bun, Central Kalimantan

records.summary: In cruise at FL320 over the Java Sea the A320's rudder travel limiter fault recurred four times, a problem that had appeared 23 times in the previous year because of a cracked solder joint. After the fourth warning the captain pulled the circuit breakers of both flight augmentation computers. The autopilot and autothrust disengaged and the flight controls reverted to alternate law; the aircraft rolled to 54 degrees before the first officer reacted, then pitched up into a steep climb. The aircraft stalled at about 38,000 ft and descended into the sea, killing all 162 on board.
records.probable_cause: The KNKT found that a cracked solder joint in the rudder travel limiter unit caused repeated AUTO FLT RUD TRV LIM SYS failures, which the airline's maintenance system had not resolved. The crew's action of pulling the FAC circuit breakers in flight, which was not an approved procedure, disengaged the autopilot and degraded the flight control law, and the subsequent delayed and inappropriate crew inputs, including a sustained nose-up sidestick command and simultaneous inputs from both pilots after the captain's ambiguous 'pull down' instruction, led to an upset from which the crew did not recover. The crew had not received upset recovery training.

factors.evidence: The rudder travel limiter fault had occurred 23 times in the previous 12 months, with increasing frequency, without the root cause being identified.
Repeated troubleshooting reset the system rather than finding the cracked solder joint on the RTLU electronic module; the airline's reliability monitoring did not escalate the repetitive defect.
The captain pulled the FAC 1 and FAC 2 circuit breakers in flight to reset the system, an action not provided for in the flight crew procedures.
De-energising both FACs disengaged the autopilot and autothrust.
Loss of both FACs caused the flight controls to revert to alternate law, removing the yaw damper and rudder travel limiting and the normal-law protections.
The aircraft rolled left for about nine seconds to 54 degrees of bank before the first officer, as pilot flying, made any input.
The first officer applied a sustained nose-up sidestick input that took the aircraft into a climb of up to 11,000 ft/min and a stall.
The captain's instruction 'pull down' was ambiguous and the first officer continued to pull back; there was no clear transfer of control.
Both pilots made sidestick inputs simultaneously without the priority push-button being used, so the inputs were summed.
The nose-up inputs were maintained through the stall warning and the aircraft remained stalled during the descent.
The airline's training program did not include upset prevention and recovery training for this scenario.
The stall warning activated as the aircraft climbed through about FL370 and the aircraft stalled near 38,000 ft.
The aircraft descended in a stalled condition for about three minutes until it struck the sea.

events.text: Over the preceding year the AUTO FLT RUD TRV LIM SYS fault occurs 23 times on PK-AXC with increasing frequency; maintenance repeatedly resets the system without finding the cracked solder joint in the rudder travel limiter unit.
Departs Surabaya for Singapore with 155 passengers and 7 crew; the first officer is pilot flying.
First master caution in cruise at FL320: AUTO FLT RUD TRV LIM SYS. The crew carry out the ECAM actions and the fault clears.
The fault recurs a second time; ECAM actions repeated.
The fault recurs a third time; ECAM actions repeated.
Fourth master caution; the fault persists after the ECAM actions.

The captain pulls the FAC 1 and then the FAC 2 circuit breakers on the panel behind his seat to reset the system. Both FACs de-energise; autopilot and autothrust disengage and the flight controls revert to alternate law.
Without yaw damping the aircraft rolls left; no sidestick input is made for about nine seconds and the bank reaches 54 degrees.
The first officer applies right roll and sustained nose-up sidestick; the aircraft climbs from FL320 at up to 11,000 ft/min.
Stall warning activates as the aircraft climbs through about FL370 with airspeed decaying.
The captain repeatedly says 'pull down'; the first officer continues to pull back. The captain applies nose-down on his own sidestick without taking priority, and the two inputs are summed.
The aircraft reaches about 38,000 ft, stalls and begins a rapid descent in a nose-up, stalled attitude.
Stall warning continues; nose-up inputs are maintained and the aircraft remains stalled through the descent.
The flight recorders stop as the aircraft strikes the Java Sea; all 162 on board are killed.

recommendations.text: Improve the maintenance reliability program so that repetitive defects are identified and resolved, and provide flight crews with upset prevention and recovery training.
recommendations.outcome: The airline introduced upset recovery training and revised its repetitive-defect handling.

recommendations.text: Ensure operators' maintenance and training programs address repetitive defects and upset recovery, and improve surveillance.

Reinforce guidance to operators that circuit breakers are not to be pulled in flight as a troubleshooting action, and review procedures and training for dual sidestick input and alternate law handling.

safety_changes: Indonesia AirAsia introduced upset prevention and recovery training and revised its handling of repetitive defects.
The Indonesian DGCA audited the airline and tightened oversight of maintenance reliability programs.
The accident reinforced industry-wide adoption of upset prevention and recovery training and the prohibition on in-flight circuit breaker resets for troubleshooting.

notes: The clock for the fourth master caution (23:15:36) and the end of recording (23:20:35) are as recalled from the KNKT report; times of the first three faults are to the minute and the times of the circuit-breaker pulls, roll, climb and stall are approximate offsets.
The maximum altitude reached (about 38,000 ft) and the climb rate (up to 11,000 ft/min) are from the report summary; peak descent rate is omitted.
The captain's 'pull down' line is quoted without an exact time.
Wreckage coordinates are approximate.

records.title: TransAsia Airways 235

agencies.name: Aviation Safety Council
agencies.report_title: Aviation Occurrence Report: 4 February 2015, TransAsia Airways Flight GE235, ATR72-212A, Loss of Control and Crashed into Keelung River Three Nautical Miles East of Songshan Airport

location.name: Keelung River, Nangang, Taipei, about 3 nm east of Songshan Airport

records.summary: Shortly after take-off from Taipei Songshan, the ATR 72-600's automatic take-off power control system auto-feathered the number 2 engine following an intermittent signal from its auto-feather unit. The captain, as pilot flying, misidentified the failed engine, retarded the operating number 1 engine to idle and then shut it down. With no thrust, the aircraft stalled at low altitude, rolled steeply, clipped a taxi on an elevated road and crashed inverted into the Keelung River. Forty-three of the 58 on board died.
records.probable_cause: The ASC found that the number 2 engine auto-feathered because of an intermittent signal discontinuity in its auto-feather unit, and that the captain then reduced power on the operating engine and shut it down without following the engine failure procedure or confirming the failed engine with the other pilot, leaving the aircraft with no thrust. The crew did not respond effectively to the stall warnings and lost control. Contributing were the captain's demonstrated weaknesses in handling engine failures, inadequate crew coordination, TransAsia's deficient flight crew training and safety management, and inadequate regulatory oversight.

factors.evidence: About 37 seconds after take-off the ATPCS auto-feathered the number 2 engine following an intermittent signal from its auto-feather unit; the engine itself was serviceable.
The failure occurred at about 1,200 ft during the initial climb, with a master warning and the need for immediate single-engine handling.
The captain retarded the number 1 (operating) engine's power lever to idle and later moved its condition lever to fuel shut-off, shutting down the only engine producing thrust.
The crew did not carry out the engine flame-out at take-off procedure as trained, which requires identification and confirmation of the failed engine before any lever is moved.
The pilot monitoring did not challenge the captain's actions on the wrong engine and the two pilots did not cross-check before the operating engine was shut down.
The captain's training records showed difficulties in handling engine failures after take-off; he had failed a simulator check on this before later passing.
TransAsia's ATR 72-600 differences training and its handling of pilots with unsatisfactory performance were found deficient.
The ASC found systemic deficiencies in TransAsia's flight operations management and safety management system.
The report found that the Civil Aeronautics Administration's oversight had not identified or corrected the operator's deficiencies.
The captain did not recognise until seconds before impact that he had pulled back the wrong engine.
The stall warning and stick shaker activated repeatedly and the stick pusher operated as airspeed decayed; the crew did not recover.
With both propellers producing no thrust the aircraft stalled at low altitude.
The aircraft rolled steeply left, struck a taxi and the parapet of an elevated road and crashed inverted into the river.

events.text: Take-off from Songshan runway 10 with the captain as pilot flying, a first officer as pilot monitoring and a third pilot in the observer's seat.
Climbing through about 1,200 ft, the ATPCS auto-feathers the number 2 propeller after an intermittent signal from the auto-feather unit; master warning 'ENG 2 FLAME OUT AT TAKE OFF'.
The captain announces he will pull back the number 1 power lever and begins retarding the operating engine's power lever toward idle, without confirming the failed engine.
The pilot monitoring makes callouts and reads the warning but does not challenge the action on the wrong engine; no cross-check is made.
With number 2 feathered and number 1 at low power the aircraft stops climbing; airspeed begins to decay and the autopilot is disconnected.
The captain moves the number 1 condition lever to fuel shut-off; the operating engine shuts down and the aircraft has no thrust.
Stall warning and stick shaker activate repeatedly as airspeed decays; the stick pusher operates.
The crew declare MAYDAY, reporting an engine flame-out, and attempt to restart the number 1 engine.
The captain exclaims that he pulled back the wrong side throttle.

The aircraft rolls steeply left, its left wing strikes a taxi and the parapet of the elevated Huandong Viaduct, and it crashes inverted into the Keelung River. 43 of the 58 on board die; 15 survive, and two people in the taxi are injured.

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: Wow, pulled back the wrong side throttle.

recommendations.text: Review and strengthen flight crew training on engine failure after take-off, crew coordination and the management of pilots with unsatisfactory performance records, and improve the airline's safety management system.
recommendations.outcome: TransAsia retrained its ATR crews after the accident; the airline ceased operations in November 2016.

recommendations.text: Improve the oversight of operators' flight crew training, checking and safety management.
Address the auto-feather unit signal discontinuity that triggered the uncommanded auto-feather, including inspection of units in service.
recommendations.outcome: The manufacturer issued service information on auto-feather unit inspection and replacement.

safety_changes: Taiwan's CAA ordered proficiency checks for all TransAsia ATR pilots immediately after the accident; some pilots failed and were grounded.
TransAsia's oversight and training were overhauled; the airline ceased operations in 2016.
The auto-feather unit's soldering defect led to inspections and replacements across the ATR fleet.

notes: The auto-feather time (10:52:38) and the captain's final remark (10:54:34) are as recalled from the ASC report; intermediate event offsets are approximate.
The CVR line is given in the report's English translation; the original Mandarin wording is not reproduced.
The number of seriously injured survivors is not given (null).
The Aviation Safety Council is now the Taiwan Transportation Safety Board; its home page is used as the source.

records.title: Delta Air Lines 1086

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Runway Excursion During Landing, Delta Air Lines Flight 1086, Boeing MD-88, N909DL, New York, New York, March 5, 2015

records.summary: A Boeing MD-88 operated by Delta Air Lines landed on snow-contaminated Runway 13 at LaGuardia Airport in freezing fog and snow conditions. The captain applied excessive reverse thrust immediately after touchdown, reaching engine pressure ratios (EPR) of 2.07 and 1.91 (far exceeding the target of 1.3 for contaminated runways). This high reverse thrust caused rudder blanking, a loss of aerodynamic directional control. The aircraft veered left off the runway, struck the perimeter fence, and slid approximately 940 feet before coming to rest with the nose hanging over Flushing Bay. All 130 occupants evacuated with 29 passengers sustaining minor injuries.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause of this accident was the captain's inability to maintain directional control of the airplane due to his application of excessive reverse thrust, which degraded the effectiveness of the rudder in controlling the airplane's heading. Contributing to the accident were the captain's (1) situational stress resulting from his concern about stopping performance and (2) attentional limitations due to the high workload during the landing, which prevented him from immediately recognizing the use of excessive reverse thrust.

factors.evidence: Runway 13 was covered with snow; runway appeared all white when aircraft descended out of clouds (p. 50).
Aircraft approached at 140 knots with 133 knots at touchdown, near landing limits for snow conditions (p. 1).

Captain applied excessive reverse thrust immediately after touchdown, reaching maximum EPR of 2.07 on left engine and 1.91 on right engine, far exceeding the 1.3 target for contaminated runways (p. ix-x).
High reverse thrust on MD-80 series airplanes causes rudder blanking (disruption of smooth airflow over rudder), resulting in loss of aerodynamic directional control (p. x).
Aircraft veered left off runway 3000 feet from approach end, struck perimeter fence, and slid 940 feet before stopping with nose over Flushing Bay (p. 1).

events.text: Flight crew completes approach and begins descent toward Runway 13 in instrument meteorological conditions with snow and freezing fog.
Aircraft touched down with main landing gear near runway centerline, aligned with runway, at 133 knots.
Captain applies reverse thrust aggressively immediately after touchdown.
Reverse thrust EPR reaches 2.07 on left engine and 1.91 on right engine, causing rudder blanking and loss of directional control.
Aircraft veers left off runway about 3000 feet from approach end; first officer identifies rudder blanking concern; captain stows reversers.
Aircraft left wing strikes perimeter fence at approximately 4100 feet from approach end.
Aircraft forced back onto heading parallel with runway by fence and terrain, continues sliding 900 feet along fence.
Aircraft comes to rest with nose hanging over seawall berm above Flushing Bay after sliding approximately 940 feet total from runway departure point.

recommendations.text: Collaborate with Boeing and US operators of MD-80 series airplanes to conduct a study to examine reverse thrust engine pressure ratio (EPR)-related operational data, procedures, and training and identify industry-wide best practices that have been shown to be effective in reliably preventing EPR exceedances to mitigate the risks associated with rudder blanking.

Encourage US operators of MD-80 series airplanes to (1) implement the best practices identified in Safety Recommendation A-16-20 and (2) participate in an industry-wide monitoring program to verify the continued effectiveness of those solutions over time.
Require operators of MD-80 series airplanes to revise operational procedures to include a callout when reverse thrust power exceeds 1.3 engine pressure ratio during landings on a contaminated runway.

Continue to work with industry to develop the technology to outfit transport-category airplanes with equipment and procedures to routinely calculate, record, and convey the airplane braking ability required and/or available to slow or stop the airplane during the landing roll.

If the systems described in Safety Recommendation A-16-23 are shown to be technically and operationally feasible, work with operators and the system manufacturers to develop procedures that ensure that airplane-based braking ability results can be readily conveyed to, and easily interpreted by, arriving flight crews, airport operators, air traffic control personnel, and others with a safety need for this information.

Require 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 121 operators to provide (1) guidance that instructs flight attendants to remain at their assigned exits and actively monitor exit availability in all non-normal situations in case an evacuation is necessary and (2) flight attendant training programs that include scenarios requiring crew coordination regarding active monitoring of exit availability and evacuating after a significant event that involves a loss of communications.

Develop best practices related to evacuation communication, coordination, and decision-making during emergencies through the establishment of an industry working group and then issue guidance for 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 121 air carriers to use to improve flight and cabin crew performance during evacuations.

Clarify guidance to all 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 121 air carriers to reinforce the importance of (1) having precise information about the number of passengers aboard an airplane, including lap-held children, and (2) making this information immediately available to emergency responders after an accident to facilitate timely search and rescue operations.

For airports certificated under 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 139, direct airport certification safety inspectors to ensure, before or during the airports' next scheduled annual inspection, that policies and procedures for friction measurement during winter operations are accurately and adequately described in the airports' Airport Certification Manual and Snow and Ice Control Plan.

Revise Advisory Circular 150/5200-30D, 'Airport Field Condition Assessments and Winter Operations Safety,' to provide more precise guidance regarding (1) the need to issue notices to airmen (NOTAM) in a timely manner and (2) the specific changes to runway surface conditions that would prompt the issuance of updated NOTAMs.

Collaborate with the Federal Aviation Administration and US operators of MD-80 series airplanes to (1) conduct a study to examine reverse thrust engine pressure ratio (EPR)-related operational data, procedures, and training and (2) identify industry-wide best practices that have been shown to be effective in reliably preventing EPR exceedances to mitigate the risks associated with rudder blanking.
Explore the possibility of incorporating an alert in MD-80 series airplanes to aid pilots in preventing engine pressure ratio exceedances.

safety_changes: Enhanced training procedures for MD-80 reverse thrust operations on contaminated runways

notes: Findings and probable cause extracted from section 3.1-3.2 of final report
Recommendations A-16-20 through A-16-31 extracted from section 4
Timeline from executive summary and accident sequence sections
Key safety issue: excessive reverse thrust on MD-80 series causing rudder blanking

records.title: Germanwings 9525

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses pour la sécurité de l'aviation civile
agencies.report_title: Final Report - Accident on 24 March 2015 at Prads-Haute-Bléone (Alpes-de-Haute-Provence, France) to the Airbus A320-211 registered D-AIPX operated by Germanwings

agencies.name: Comisión de Investigación de Accidentes e Incidentes de Aviación Civil

records.summary: Shortly after the aircraft reached cruise at FL380 the captain left the cockpit. The first officer, alone at the controls, locked the cockpit door, set the selected altitude to 100 ft and initiated a continuous descent. He did not respond to calls from ATC or to the captain's attempts to re-enter the cockpit. The aircraft struck a mountainside in the French Alps about ten minutes later, killing all 150 on board.
records.probable_cause: The collision with the ground was due to the deliberate and planned action of the co-pilot, who decided to commit suicide while alone in the cockpit. The process for medical certification of pilots, in particular self-reporting in case of decrease in medical fitness, did not succeed in preventing the co-pilot, who was experiencing mental disorder with psychotic symptoms, from exercising the privilege of his licence. Contributing factors were the co-pilot's probable fear of losing his ability to fly if he declared his condition, the potential financial consequences, the lack of clear guidelines in German regulations on when a threat to public safety outweighs medical confidentiality, and cockpit door locking requirements designed for security threats that made it impossible to enter the flight compartment before the aircraft impacted the terrain.

factors.evidence: The co-pilot, alone in the cockpit, deliberately set the selected altitude to 100 ft and flew the aircraft into terrain; he had rehearsed altitude selections on the outbound flight.

Medical certification relied on self-declaration; the co-pilot's psychiatric history and current treatment were not known to the authority or the operator, and German rules on breaking medical confidentiality lacked clear guidance.
The reinforced cockpit door and its lock, designed against hostile entry, could be kept locked from inside and prevented the captain from regaining access.
The co-pilot was experiencing a mental disorder with psychotic symptoms and had been prescribed medication incompatible with flying.
The aircraft descended under control at about 3,500 ft/min and collided with the mountainside at about 6,000 ft.

events.text: Flight 4U9525 departs Barcelona for Düsseldorf; the first officer is pilot flying.
Aircraft levels at cruise flight level FL380 under autopilot.
Captain tells the first officer he is leaving the cockpit and asks him to take over radio communications; the cockpit door is heard closing.
Selected altitude on the FCU changed from 38,000 ft to 100 ft; the autopilot begins a descent in OPEN DESCENT mode.
Aircraft descending at about 3,500 ft/min; the first officer adjusts the selected speed and the autopilot remains engaged.
Marseille control calls the aircraft several times and receives no reply; the first officer's breathing is recorded and regular throughout the descent.
Cockpit door access buzzer sounds as the captain requests entry; no response. The keypad emergency access request is later refused from inside.
Captain knocks on the door and asks the first officer to open it; the interphone and the emergency door code are unsuccessful.
Violent blows on the cockpit door are heard on the CVR as the captain tries to break in; French air defence is alerted and a fighter is scrambled.
GPWS terrain alerts and master warning sound as the aircraft descends below 7,000 ft toward the mountains.
Aircraft collides with the mountainside at about 6,000 ft and disintegrates; all 150 occupants killed.

recommendations.text: Require operators to include in their medical assessment of pilots a systematic psychiatric evaluation where there is a history of psychological trouble, and define conditions for pilots with such a history to be followed up.
recommendations.outcome: EASA introduced psychological assessment before employment and support programmes.

recommendations.text: Define clear rules to require health care providers to inform the authorities when a specific patient's health is very likely to affect public safety, including when the patient refuses to consent, while balancing patient confidentiality.
Promote the implementation of peer support programmes for pilots and mitigate the socio-economic risks of loss of licence for medical reasons, for example through loss-of-licence insurance.
recommendations.outcome: EU regulation 2018/1042 introduced mandatory pilot support programmes and psychological assessment.

recommendations.text: Analyse the risks of the cockpit door locking system and evaluate the relevance of a minimum of two crew members in the cockpit at all times.
recommendations.outcome: EASA issued a safety information bulletin recommending two persons in the cockpit; later relaxed after risk assessment.

safety_changes: Temporary two-persons-in-the-cockpit recommendation across European operators.
EU regulation 2018/1042 requiring psychological assessment of pilots, pilot support programmes and alcohol testing.
Review of medical confidentiality rules and aeromedical data sharing among European authorities.

notes: Timeline seconds after t0 (09:30:53, selected altitude change) are approximate except impact at 09:41:06; the intermediate clock strings are estimated to within about a minute.
BEA report reference number and recommendation ids not reproduced with confidence; ids set to null.
Category SEC used for a deliberate act; factor cfit used as the outcome because the aircraft was under control until impact.

records.title: Asiana Airlines Flight 162
records.summary: Asiana Airlines Flight 162, an Airbus A320-200 en route from Incheon to Hiroshima, descended for approach in low visibility and darkness. The captain continued the descent below decision altitude without adequate visual references and did not execute a go-around as required when visual cues were lost. The first officer, acting as pilot monitoring, lost sight of the runway at decision altitude but failed to challenge the captain's decision to continue. The aircraft touched down short of the runway, struck the localizer antenna array, skidded across the runway surface, and came to rest on grass beyond the runway edge with 27 occupants injured. The probable causes were the captain's failure to execute a go-around when required, the first officer's failure to challenge the captain, and inadequate crew resource management, exacerbated by the airline's insufficient training on compliance with procedures.
records.probable_cause: The aircraft undershot the runway when landing at Hiroshima airport in low visibility and darkness. The captain continued approaching without executing a go-around while visual references could not be identified continuously at or below the approach decision altitude, contrary to regulations and Standard Operating Procedures. The first officer, as pilot-monitoring, did not make a call-out of go-around immediately when he could not see the runway at decision altitude. The Crew Resource Management did not function appropriately. Contributing factors include insufficient education and training in the company for compliance with rules.

factors.evidence: Aircraft continued descent below decision altitude of 1,500 ft without adequate visual references in darkness and low visibility (RVR 450-550 m) (p. 902-949)
Runway visual range was 1,700 m at 20:03:29 but decreased to 450 m by 20:04:45, below the approach minimum of 1,400 m (p. 918-925, 945)
Approach was conducted in darkness; PIC noted that only airport lights were visible in pitch-dark night (p. 1020-1023)
First officer lost sight of runway at decision altitude (20:04:42) but PIC continued approach; FO stated 'runway not in sight' (p. 942-944)
PIC continued descent below minimum descent altitude for 27 seconds after FO reported runway not in sight, finally calling for go-around at 20:05:11 (p. 942-1008)
FO lost sight of runway and stated 'runway not insight' at 20:04:44 but PIC did not respond appropriately; FO did not make assertive call-out of go-around (p. 123-139, 942-1031)
Report notes insufficient education and training in company regarding compliance with Standard Operating Procedures and decision altitude procedures (p. 125-139)
Aircraft touched down short of runway, approximately 1,000 feet before runway threshold after striking localizer array (p. 123, 1041)
Aircraft struck localizer antenna frame and skidded across runway surface bouncing about 3 times before veering off to left side in grass (p. 1041-1044)

events.text: Captain briefs first officer on approach to runway 28 with expected ILS runway 10 approach adjusted to RNAV runway 28 upon receipt of ATIS during descent (p. 1020-1023)
Hiroshima Tower reports wind 120 degrees at 4 knots and runway visual range of 1,700 m (p. 918)
Captain disengages autopilot at approximately 2,100 feet HAT (height above threshold), 132 knots, and switches to manual flying with flight director off (p. 920-921)
Auto call announces 'One hundred above' (100 feet to minimum descent altitude); first officer calls out and captain acknowledges (p. 930)
Aircraft descends below decision altitude of 1,500 feet; runway visual range has decreased to 550 meters (p. 931-932)
Captain calls 'No runway, go-around' and first officer responds 'Go-around'; captain pulls control stick to full nose-up and sets thrust levers to TOGA (p. 1006)
Vertical acceleration sharply increases and exceeds 1.7 G; pitch angle decreases (nose-down) from about 11 degrees; air-ground sensors indicate aircraft alternating between air and ground (p. 1008)
Vertical acceleration surpasses 2.0 G; aircraft is in contact with the localizer antenna frame structure (p. 1008)
Aircraft strikes localizer antenna array and touches down short of runway threshold, skidding and bouncing approximately 3 times along runway surface (p. 1041-1044)
Captain applies maximum braking and attempts to maintain runway direction; aircraft veers left (south) and comes to rest on grass area (p. 1044)
Flight attendants and passengers evacuate; no fire observed; 27 occupants injured during landing impact and evacuation (p. 1045)

cvr.speaker: SYS
cvr.translation: Automatic call of minimum descent altitude reached

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.translation: No runway in sight, executing go-around

recommendations.text: The Company should reemphasize and reinforce the significance of compliance by flight crew members, while reviewing company procedures and ensuring comprehensive training (p. 169-171)

The Company should implement education and training that flight crew members should refer primarily to visual references, using flight instruments as supplementary tools appropriately, when approaching below decision altitude (p. 173-175)

safety_changes: Asiana Airlines implemented enhanced training on approach procedures and decision altitude compliance

notes: Full JTSB report read with detailed CVR transcript and FDR data
Detailed timeline extracted from pages 900-1050 covering approach and landing
RVR values documented decreasing from 1,700 m to 450 m during approach
Captain's post-accident statement indicates he was not conscious of flying lower than intended
First officer had never landed on runway 28 before this flight
All 86 occupants survived with 27 injured, no fatalities

records.title: 2015 Moncks Corner mid-air collision

route.from_name: Berkeley County Airport / Shaw Air Force Base

records.summary: An F-16 fighter jet descending for an instrument landing system approach collided in flight with a Cessna 150 climbing from Berkeley County Airport. Despite air traffic control warnings of opposite-direction traffic, the F-16 pilot was unable to locate the Cessna visually. The two aircraft collided at 1,450 feet over Moncks Corner, South Carolina. Both Cessna occupants were killed; the F-16 pilot ejected safely.
records.probable_cause: The approach controller's failure to provide an appropriate resolution to the conflict between the F-16 and the Cessna. (p. 2)

factors.evidence: The controller issued an ambiguous conditional instruction to turn left if traffic not in sight, then directed the F-16 pilot to turn left heading 180 immediately without ensuring the pilot had acquired visual contact. (p. 2)

The F-16 pilot responded that he was looking for the traffic but did not visually locate the Cessna before the collision; the pilot initiated a standard rate left turn using autopilot to continue visual search. (p. 2)

The Cessna was climbing under visual flight rules and was not in communication with FAA air traffic control, nor was the pilot required to be; the Cessna had not requested flight-following services. (p. 2)
The F-16 and Cessna 150 collided in-flight over Moncks Corner at approximately 1,450 feet altitude, about 40 seconds after the initial traffic advisory. (p. 2)

events.text: Charleston Approach controller issued traffic advisory to F-16 pilot: traffic 12 o'clock 2 miles opposite direction 1,200 feet, type unknown.
F-16 pilot responded looking for the traffic.
Controller issued conditional instruction to turn left heading 180 if traffic not in sight.
Controller issued direct instruction: if F-16 pilot did not have traffic in sight turn left heading 180 immediately.
F-16 pilot initiated standard rate left turn using autopilot to continue visual search for traffic.
Radar showed F-16 at 1/2 nautical mile northeast of Cessna at 1,500 feet while Cessna was at 1,400 feet on opposite track; airplanes continued to converge.
The two aircraft collided at approximately 1,450 feet altitude.
F-16 pilot ejected from aircraft and descended safely by parachute with minor injuries; Cessna destroyed with both occupants killed.

Report focuses on controller judgment errors in ATC handling of conflict
No CVR transcript or FDR data included in the Safety Recommendation Report
