records.title: Shoreham Airshow Hawker Hunter

agencies.name: Air Accidents Investigation Branch
agencies.report_title: Report on the accident to Hawker Hunter T7, G-BXFI near Shoreham Airport on 22 August 2015

location.name: A27 road near Shoreham Airport, West Sussex

records.summary: During a display at the Shoreham Airshow the Hunter entered a loop-type manoeuvre from too low a height and at too low an airspeed. At the apex the aircraft was at 2,700 ft, below the minimum required to complete the manoeuvre, and the pilot did not fly an escape manoeuvre. The aircraft descended into traffic on the A27 dual carriageway, killing 11 people on the ground; the pilot survived.
records.probable_cause: The aircraft did not achieve sufficient height at the apex of the accident manoeuvre to complete it before impacting the ground, because the combination of low entry speed and low engine thrust in the upward half of the manoeuvre was insufficient. An escape manoeuvre was not carried out, despite the aircraft not achieving the required minimum apex height. The pilot either did not perceive that an escape manoeuvre was necessary or did not realise one was possible at the speed achieved at the apex. Contributing: the display sequence had been planned for a different aircraft type, the pilot had not practised the sequence in the Hunter, and the regulatory and organisational oversight of displays did not ensure adequate risk management for the public outside the display site.

factors.evidence: The loop was entered at about 185 kt and 200 ft, lower and slower than required, with the throttle not advanced to full power during the pull-up.
The pilot did not recognise at the apex that the aircraft was 800 ft below the required gate height and that an escape manoeuvre was needed.
The pilot had not practised the display sequence in the Hunter, and the escape manoeuvre had not been practised or trained.
The CAA's oversight of flying displays did not require adequate risk assessment for areas outside the display site, and display authorisation evaluation was limited.
The display organiser's and operator's risk assessments did not adequately consider third parties outside the airfield boundary or enforce the gate heights in the pilot's display plan.
The pilot's recent display experience was predominantly on the Jet Provost, with limited recent flying on the Hunter.
The aircraft struck the A27 road in a nose-up attitude at about 100 kt below the speed at which recovery was possible, colliding with vehicles.
A fireball followed the impact, contributing to the deaths of persons on the road.

events.text: G-BXFI departs North Weald for the Shoreham display.
Pilot commences the display with a run-in and a series of aerobatic manoeuvres over the display line.
Following a turn to the north, the pilot positions for a bent loop with a quarter clover at the top, entering from the east of the display line.
Pull-up into the loop starts at about 185 kt and about 200 ft agl, below the 350 kt / 500 ft entry parameters in the pilot's plan; throttle not advanced to full.
Aircraft climbs inverted; engine at less than full power throughout the upward half of the manoeuvre.
Apex of the manoeuvre reached at about 2,700 ft, 800 ft below the 3,500 ft minimum gate height, at about 105 kt.
No escape manoeuvre (rolling upright and recovering) is flown; the pilot continues the downward half of the loop.
Recognising the aircraft is low, the pilot applies increasing back stick; the aircraft reaches maximum g but is unable to arrest the descent.
Aircraft strikes the A27 westbound carriageway in a nose-high attitude, colliding with vehicles and breaking up; a fireball follows.
Eleven people on the road are killed; the pilot is thrown clear of the wreckage and seriously injured.

recommendations.text: Introduce measures to ensure that flying displays are not conducted over areas where members of the public may be present unless the risk is acceptable; a review of the risk to third parties outside display sites.
recommendations.outcome: CAA introduced restrictions on aerobatics by vintage jets over land and enhanced display risk assessment requirements.

recommendations.text: Require that display pilots' authorisations are evaluated for the specific aircraft type and manoeuvres they intend to fly, and that escape manoeuvres are trained and practised.
Require the recording of flight data on ex-military jets used for displays and improve the maintenance standards oversight for such aircraft.

safety_changes: CAA restricted vintage jet displays over land to flypasts pending review, and later introduced new display risk assessment requirements (CAP 403 revisions).
Enhanced oversight of display authorisation evaluations and requirements for display sequences to be practised on type.
Increased separation distances between display lines and the public, including areas outside the airfield boundary.

notes: Entry and apex speeds/heights are the AAIB's derived values (approximately 185 kt / 200 ft entry, 2,700 ft / 105 kt apex, 3,500 ft required gate).
Event clock times are approximate relative to the 12:22 impact; the seconds are estimated.
Only one recommendation number (2015-039) is given; others left null. MSN is uncertain.

records.title: Dynamic Airways 405
records.operator: Eastern Airlines, LLC (operating as Dynamic International Airways)
records.summary: On 29 October 2015, a Boeing 767 caught fire while taxiing for departure at Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport. The main fuel supply line coupling assembly disconnected in the wing-to-engine strut, causing fuel leakage. Fire developed during taxi. All 101 passengers and crew were evacuated using emergency slides with 22 people injured. The aircraft was destroyed by fire.
records.probable_cause: The separation of the flexible fuel line coupling and subsequent fuel leak due to the failure of maintenance personnel to install the required safety lockwire. Contributing to the severity of the accident was the initiation of the evacuation before the right engine was shut down which led to a passenger's injury. (p. 2)

factors.evidence: A significant fuel leak developed in the left engine strut and nacelle during taxi due to a Wiggins coupling (flexible fuel line coupling) loosening and disengaging from the main fuel supply line (p. 1-2, 5). The leak was caused by the lack of a required safety lockwire on the coupling assembly per Boeing maintenance manual requirements (p. 2, 5).

Maintenance personnel failed to install the required safety lockwire on the fuel line coupling assembly during maintenance performed in October 2012 at the 4C check prior to aircraft storage (p. 1-2). No broken lockwire was recovered in the strut compartments, confirming it was never installed (p. 5).
The leaking fuel contacted hot engine case surfaces with exhaust gas temperatures of at least 452°C (845.6°F), igniting a fire in the left engine strut and nacelle during taxi (p. 2, 7).

events.text: Aircraft pushes back from Gate E9 for taxi to Runway 28 right (p. 3).
Another aircraft taxiing behind accident aircraft advised ATC they observed a large amount of fluid leaking from the left engine of the accident airplane (p. 3).
Flight crew heard the transmissions about fluid leak, advised they would return to ramp, and were instructed by ATC to stop on taxiway B just east of taxiway T1 (p. 3).
The trailing aircraft advised that the engine was on fire (p. 3).
Captain shut down the left engine using the fire handle; fire handle found actuated and rotated to bottle 1 discharge position in post-accident inspection (p. 3, 5).
Flight crew requested fire equipment from ATC (p. 3).

Flight attendant activated emergency signaling system to notify flight deck; CVR recorded the chime but flight crew did not respond via interphone (p. 7). Cabin crew initiated evacuation without coordination with flight crew; passengers saw fire and insisted on evacuation (p. 1, 3).

Flight attendants opened forward left (1L), forward right (1R), and aft right (2R) cabin doors; slide rafts deployed though 2R slide did not inflate quickly or symmetrically (p. 3). A passenger opened the right overwing exit but the slide did not deploy (p. 3).
After evacuation had already begun, flight crew advised over PA to evacuate out the right side of the airplane (p. 3).

Number 2 (right) engine still running as passengers evacuated through 2R door; one passenger who evacuated through 2R passed behind the running engine, was blown to the pavement by exhaust, and received serious injuries (p. 3).
Number 2 engine shut down approximately 35 seconds after the initial passenger injury (p. 3).
Airport authority official arrived and repositioned the 2R slide; airport firefighting vehicles arrived approximately 1 minute later and began extinguishing the fire (p. 3).

safety_changes: Dynamic International Airways issued a Fleet Campaign Directive to inspect remainder of their aircraft to ensure proper installation of fuel line coupling assemblies (p. 4)

notes: Deep read from sections: Analysis (p. 1-2), Probable Cause and Findings (p. 2), Factual Information History of Flight (p. 3), Examination of fuel coupling (p. 5)
12 events extracted with clock times and detailed sequence from taxi to fire suppression; 9 new events vs summary_record
Maintenance error factor emphasized per probable cause; Boeing maintenance manual requirement for lockwire documented (p. 5)

records.title: Execuflight 1526

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Crash During Nonprecision Instrument Approach to Landing - Execuflight Flight 1526

records.summary: Execuflight Flight 1526 crashed into a four-unit apartment building in Akron, Ohio during a nonprecision localizer approach on November 10, 2015, killing the captain, first officer, and seven passengers. The flight crew mismanaged the approach, flew significantly below minimum descent altitude, and descended below prescribed minimums without visual contact with the runway. The aircraft entered an aerodynamic stall and impacted the apartment building.
records.probable_cause: The flight crew's mismanagement of the approach and multiple deviations from company standard operating procedures, which placed the airplane in an unsafe situation and led to an unstabilized approach, a descent below minimum descent altitude without visual contact with the runway environment, and an aerodynamic stall. Contributing factors included Execuflight's casual attitude toward compliance with standards, inadequate hiring, training and operational oversight, lack of formal safety program, and the FAA's insufficient oversight.

factors.evidence: flight crew performed an unstabilized approach with the aircraft significantly below Vref speed (p. 72)
captain voiced concerns about approach conditions but did not take corrective action (p. 72)
airspeed had decayed substantially below normal approach speed during descent (p. 2)
flight crew deviated from standard operating procedures multiple times (p. 72)
aircraft entered aerodynamic stall during nonprecision approach (p. 72)
aircraft impacted apartment building from uncontrolled descent (p. 2)

events.text: Flight 1526 departed Dayton-Wright Brothers Airport at 14:13 EST
Flight contacted Indianapolis ARTCC and received IFR clearance to climb to 17,000 ft
Flight crew began preparing for approach to Akron, attempting to obtain weather
ATC instructed aircraft to slow down and remain at 3,000 ft due to traffic on same runway
First officer increased descent rate to 2,000 fpm and reduced airspeed to approximately 98 knots, well below normal
Captain expressed concerns about descent rate and airspeed but did not take corrective action
Aircraft descended below minimum descent altitude of 1,540 ft without visual contact with runway
Aircraft entered aerodynamic stall approximately 14 seconds after reaching MDA
Aircraft impacted four-unit apartment building approximately 2 miles from runway threshold

recommendations.text: Require 14 CFR Part 135 operators to equip their aircraft with flight data recording devices capable of supporting a flight data monitoring program
Require all 14 CFR Part 135 operators to establish a structured flight data monitoring program that reviews all available data sources to identify deviations from established norms and procedures
Require all 14 CFR Part 135 operators to establish safety management system programs
Develop and incorporate into Hawker 700- and 800-series pilot training programs a nonprecision approach procedure aligned with stabilized approach criteria
Develop and incorporate into Hawker 700- and 800-series pilot training programs a definition of 'landing assured' aligned with 14 CFR 91.175(c)(1)
Train flight crews in continuous descent final approach technique as primary means for conducting nonprecision approaches
Issue safety alert for operators describing this accident and reminding to ensure current accurate information in weight-and-balance software
Review Safety Assurance System to identify 14 CFR Part 135 operators not complying with standard operating procedures
Review problems with CVR data quality to determine why problems were not detected and corrected before accident; revise AC 20-186 if needed

notes: Read history of flight, probable cause, and recommendations sections
9 occupants killed - captain, first officer, 7 passengers
Aircraft impacted apartment building with no ground casualties
Both pilots had been rejected by previous employers per investigation

records.title: 2015 Fox Glacier helicopter crash

agencies.name: Transport Accident Investigation Commission
agencies.report_title: Final Report: Airbus Helicopters AS350BA, ZK-HKU, collision with terrain, Fox Glacier, 21 November 2015

records.operator: Alpine Adventures (Fox and Franz Heli Services)

location.name: Fox Glacier, 2500 meters up glacier near Chancellor Shelf

records.summary: Airbus Helicopters AS350D crashed into crevasse at Fox Glacier shortly after takeoff from glacier landing zone in heavy rain and overcast conditions. Aircraft weight exceeded maximum permitted and weather was unsuitable for operations. Operator's pilot training was inadequate and regulatory oversight was deficient. All seven occupants perished.
records.probable_cause: The helicopter struck the glacier surface with high forward speed and high rate of descent. The all-up weight of the helicopter almost certainly exceeded the maximum permitted weight throughout the flight. Weather conditions on the day were unstable and unsuitable for conducting a scenic flight, with the pilot's perception of height affected by cloud, precipitation, flat light and condensation. The pilot had not been properly trained and did not have appropriate experience for the role, and the operator's training system was ill-defined and lacked proper oversight.

factors.evidence: Weather conditions were unstable and unsuitable; localised conditions very likely frequently below minimum criteria. Cloud, precipitation, flat light conditions and condensation on windscreen affected pilot's height perception (p. 2598-2607)
Throughout the flight, the all-up weight of the helicopter almost certainly exceeded the maximum permitted weight (p. 2583-2584)

The pilot had not been properly trained and did not have the appropriate level of experience expected under the operator's categorisation scheme for a senior pilot in this type of operation (p. 2609-2611)

The Civil Aviation Authority had identified significant and repetitive non-compliance issues with the operator's training system and managerial oversight that warranted intervention long before this accident occurred (p. 2620-2622)
The helicopter crashed into a crevasse on Fox Glacier approximately 600 m south and 800 ft below Chancellor Shelf with the engine delivering power (p. 2580-2581)

events.text: Helicopter departed on scenic flight from Chancellor Shelf with pilot and six passengers on board
Weather was cloudy and changeable with heavy rain and cloud conditions
Helicopter observed overhead terminal face of Fox Glacier at 3,200 ft (975 m), heading east
Other pilot saw helicopter climbing towards Chancellor Shelf. This was last sighting of helicopter.
Helicopter was reported overdue. Search revealed wreckage had crashed near right edge of upper Fox Glacier, about 600 m south and 800 ft (244 m) below Chancellor Shelf

recommendations.to: Director of Civil Aviation, New Zealand
recommendations.text: Initiate an independent review of CAA surveillance reports and any findings raised for Part 135 operators since 2014 to measure the effectiveness of the surveillance policies and procedures that the CAA has put in place, including the effectiveness of their implementation. If the independent review finds unidentified or unresolved safety issues with specific operators, take the appropriate urgent action to resolve those issues.

safety_changes: CAA published article on helicopter weather decision making (March/April 2016)
CAA issued letter to all Part 135 operators on pilot training programmes (18 July 2016)
CAA issued revision 9 to advisory circular 61-18 clarifying Category D flight instructor privileges (3 August 2016)
Operator's air operator certificate suspended and revoked (27 May 2016 and 9 June 2016)
CAA prosecution and penalties imposed against operator senior persons

notes: Full report read: executive summary (lines 595-679), narrative (lines 817-872), analysis (lines 1800-2577), findings (lines 2578-2623), safety issues (lines 2629-2638), recommendations (lines 2698-2808)
Weight and balance exceeded maximum permitted weight - key contributing factor
Pilot training inadequate and regulatory oversight deficient
All seven occupants perished in crash

records.title: Daallo Airlines 159

agencies.name: Ministry of Transport and Civil Aviation of Federal Republic of Somalia
agencies.report_title: Final Report - Accident to the AIRBUS A321 registered SX-BHS

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses pour la sécurité de l'aviation civile

records.summary: Daallo Airlines Flight 159, an Airbus A321, departed Mogadishu with 74 passengers and 7 crew en route to Djibouti. At 14,000 feet altitude, 20 minutes after takeoff, an explosion occurred in the cabin creating a fuselage hole near seats 15/16F at the forward wing root. Investigators confirmed explosive residue and concluded the bomb was likely concealed in a laptop and carried aboard by a person in a wheelchair. Only the suicide bomber died; the aircraft successfully returned to Mogadishu for emergency landing.
records.probable_cause: The explosion was caused by a bomb detonated in a suicide attack, hidden within a laptop. The Islamist militant group Al-Shabaab claimed responsibility. The flight was delayed 20 minutes awaiting additional passengers, which prevented the aircraft from reaching cruising altitude where the explosion could have been catastrophic.

factors.evidence: an explosion occurred on board the aircraft at 10,400 feet, 20 minutes after takeoff. The investigation indicated that the explosion was caused by a bomb detonated in a suicide attack. The Islamist militant group Al-Shabaab claimed responsibility (p. 4)
The explosion created a hole in the fuselage behind the R2 door at approximately 1 square meter at the level of row 16 around frame 35.8 (p. 8)
The aircraft returned to Aden Adde International Airport and performed an emergency landing safely at 08:53 UTC, 12 minutes after the explosion. There were three injuries on board (p. 5)
A bomb hidden within a laptop was carried onto the aircraft by a passenger in a wheelchair, suggesting airport security screening procedures failed to detect it (p. 4)

events.text: Flight delayed 20 minutes awaiting additional passengers to board
Flight DAO159 cleared for takeoff from runway 05, wind 090 degrees at 17 knots
ATC cleared flight to climb to FL 300; aircraft passing 9,000 feet
Explosion in cabin at 10,400 feet altitude; sound heard on CVR
Master Warning and CAB PR EXCESS CAB ALT message triggered on ECAM
Captain takes control of aircraft; applies nose down inputs and left turn orders
First Officer requests ATC clearance for emergency return to Mogadishu
Flight attendant reports explosion in cabin; Captain confirms safe return
Cabin pressure warning turns off at 8,100 feet altitude
Aircraft lands safely at Mogadishu airport in full configuration

recommendations.text: Search all passenger baggage and employees at Mogadishu airport
Have all laptops switched on before checking in
Perform random questioning of passengers based on profiles
Implement Somalian Police Force (SPF) watchers in uniform at each access point
Install random swabs with disposable explosive detection kits
Reinforce the separation between the passengers terminals and cargo areas

notes: Sections read: synopsis (page 4-5), flight history (pages 6-7), injuries/damage (pages 8), analysis and conclusions (pages 25-26), safety recommendations (page 26)
This is a security/terrorism incident; aircraft was not damaged by mechanical failure but by deliberate hostile act
Limited CVR transcript provided; critical communications reconstructed from report text

records.title: Flydubai 981

agencies.name: Interstate Aviation Committee
agencies.report_title: Final report on the investigation of the accident to Boeing 737-8KN A6-FDN at Rostov-on-Don, 19 March 2016

records.summary: After a first go-around from an approach to Rostov-on-Don in strong gusting wind and windshear, the crew held for about two hours and made a second approach at night. At about 220 m (720 ft) the captain initiated a second go-around; with TOGA thrust at light weight the aircraft pitched up steeply. The captain, subject to a somatogravic illusion and without outside references, pushed the control column forward and applied nose-down stabilizer trim for about 12 seconds. The aircraft pitched to a steep dive and struck the runway at high speed about 40 seconds after the go-around began. All 62 on board died.
records.probable_cause: The MAK concluded that the accident was caused by an incorrect aircraft configuration and crew piloting during the go-around, leading to the captain's loss of situational awareness under the effect of a somatogravic illusion at night in instrument conditions, an inappropriate nose-down control input and prolonged nose-down stabilizer trim, and a dive from which recovery was not possible. Contributing factors included the presence of turbulence and windshear, the crew's fatigue after a long night duty, the lack of specific training for go-arounds from intermediate heights with high thrust and light weight, inconsistencies in the flight director cues during the go-around, and deficiencies in the crew's resource management and in the captain's psychological state during the second approach.

factors.evidence: Strong gusting wind and windshear warnings led to the first go-around and were present during the second approach.
The second approach and go-around were flown at night in cloud with no external visual references.
The crew had been on duty since the evening and the accident occurred at about 03:40 local time after two hours of holding; the MAK cited fatigue as contributing.
The second approach was flown in turbulent conditions with speed and path deviations before the go-around decision at about 220 m.
The report found that the flight director pitch command during the go-around did not correspond to the crew's expectation and contributed to the captain's confusion.
The MAK concluded that the acceleration under TOGA thrust produced a false sensation of excessive pitch-up which led the captain to push the nose down.
The captain lost awareness of the aircraft's attitude and did not use the attitude indicator to recover from the dive.
The captain pushed the control column forward and applied nose-down stabilizer trim for about 12 seconds, pitching the aircraft into a steep dive.
The first officer did not intervene effectively when the captain applied the nose-down input and the aircraft entered the dive.
The MAK found that go-arounds from intermediate heights with full thrust at light weight, and somatogravic illusion, were not adequately addressed in the operator's training.
The report identified loss of situational awareness by the captain as the central element of the sequence.
The aircraft struck the runway in a steep nose-down attitude at high speed about 40 seconds after the go-around was initiated.

events.text: First approach to runway 22 abandoned at about 1,100 ft after a windshear warning; the aircraft climbs away and enters a holding pattern.
The crew hold for about two hours awaiting improvement in the wind, discussing whether to divert; the captain decides on a second approach.
Second ILS approach to runway 22 at night in gusting wind and turbulence with the autopilot disengaged.
At about 220 m (720 ft) the captain calls a go-around and presses TOGA; the thrust increases toward full and the aircraft pitches up.
With full thrust at light weight the pitch attitude rises to about 18 degrees and the aircraft accelerates and climbs rapidly; the flight director pitch cue differs from the crew's expectation.
Flaps retracted to 15 and landing gear raised; the pitch and climb rate remain high.
Under a somatogravic illusion the captain pushes the control column forward; the pitch attitude decreases and passes through level flight.
The captain applies nose-down stabilizer trim for about 12 seconds; the pitch attitude continues to decrease into a dive.
The first officer calls out and pulls back on the column; the captain's input and the nose-down trim dominate.
The aircraft is in a steep nose-down dive with airspeed increasing; GPWS warnings sound.
The aircraft strikes runway 22 at high speed in a steep nose-down attitude about 40 seconds after the go-around began; all 62 on board die.

recommendations.text: Include in training the recognition of and recovery from somatogravic illusion during go-arounds with high thrust and light weight, and go-arounds from intermediate heights.
Review the flight director go-around pitch guidance and its transitions on the 737 so that the cues are consistent during a go-around initiated above the normal decision height.
Review crew rostering and fatigue risk management for long night duties with extended holding, and the decision-making guidance for diversion in adverse weather.
Reinforce crew resource management training on monitoring and intervention by the pilot monitoring during go-arounds.

safety_changes: Flydubai revised its go-around training, fatigue management and diversion decision-making guidance after the accident.
The accident reinforced industry attention (including the Flight Safety Foundation and EASA) on go-around safety and somatogravic illusion at night.

notes: t0 (about 00:40:50 UTC, the start of the second go-around) and the first go-around time (about 22:42 UTC) are given from the MAK narrative as recalled; the exact seconds were not verified. Event offsets within the final 40 seconds are approximate.
The final pitch attitude and impact speed are deliberately not given as numbers because the exact figures were not verified.
The MAK final report was published in November 2019; the exact report number was not verified.
The accredited representative list (GCAA, NTSB) is based on the states of registry and manufacture.

records.title: Batik Air 7703
records.summary: Batik Air Flight 7703, a Boeing 737-800, collided with a TransNusa Air Services ATR 42 during its takeoff roll on 4 April 2016 at Halim Perdanakusuma Airport in Jakarta. The ATR 42 was being towed across the active runway when the 737 was cleared for takeoff, resulting in a runway collision. The 737's left wing caught fire but all occupants evacuated safely with no fatalities, though 3 people were injured.
records.probable_cause: Weak coordination between Air Traffic Control, the tow crew, and the flight crew allowed the TransNusa ATR 42 to remain on the active runway while Batik Air Flight 7703 was cleared for takeoff, resulting in a collision during the takeoff roll. The collision occurred because ATC cleared the 737 for takeoff while the ATR 42 was being towed across the runway. (p. 1-2)

factors.evidence: Batik Air cleared for takeoff while TransNusa ATR 42 was still on the runway being towed to hangar (p. 1)
TransNusa ATR-42 was being towed to hangar on active runway when Flight 7703 was taking off (p. 1)
Weak coordination between ATC, tow crew, and Flight 7703 crew; pilots were aware collision was inevitable (p. 1-2)
Left wing of Flight 7703 sliced off vertical stabilizer and left outer wing of ATR 42, severely damaged Flight 7703's left wing (p. 1-2)
Left wing caught fire; survivors felt bump like hitting pothole, others heard loud bang (p. 1)

Flight 7703 left wing ignited; fire developed on 737
Pilot attempted emergency landing at Halim; aircraft veered left due to damage
Aircraft came to stop on ground; fire brigade responded
All 132 passengers and 3 crew evacuated safely; 3 minor injuries reported

records.title: 2016 Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations Il-76 crash
records.operator: Ministry of Emergency Situations of Russia

location.name: Near Lake Baikal, northeast of Irkutsk, Siberia

records.summary: An Ilyushin Il-76 aerial firefighting aircraft crashed near Lake Baikal while operating at minimum altitude over a wildfire area. The hot air from the wildfires reduced engine thrust, causing loss of altitude. The tail struck a hillock, then the aircraft collided with the hillside. All ten crew members were killed.
records.probable_cause: Loss of engine thrust caused by hot air from the wildfires resulted in loss of altitude; tail struck terrain leading to collision with hillside. (p. 11-13)

factors.evidence: Wildfires in Siberia created hot air conditions in the area (p. 11)
Hot air from wildfires caused loss of engine thrust, resulting in loss of altitude (p. 13)
SRPBZ warnings 'PULL UP' and 'TERRAIN AHEAD' registered repeatedly for 7 minutes (p. 12)

Aircraft at 3,300m altitude on course 45 degrees, speed 450 km/h (p. 11)

records.title: 2016 Lockhart hot air balloon crash

aircraft.type: Balóny Kubíček BB85Z hot air balloon

records.summary: A Balóny Kubíček BB85Z hot air balloon operated by Heart of Texas Balloon Ride struck power lines, caught fire and crashed near Lockhart Texas on July 30 2016 killing all 16 aboard. The NTSB determined the accident was caused by the pilot's pattern of poor decision-making including launching despite weather forecasts indicating cloud layers as low as 1100 feet when other balloon operators cancelled flights. The pilot continued into fog and clouds while impaired by diazepam, oxycodone, and diphenhydramine equivalent to drunken driving.
records.probable_cause: Pilot's pattern of poor decision-making in launching and continuing flight into unsuitable weather, complicated by medical conditions and medications that impaired judgment. Pilot made decisions to launch despite deteriorating weather forecasts, continued flight into fog and clouds, and descended in conditions that decreased ability to see and avoid obstacles (p. 10)

factors.evidence: Weather observations 1 hour 50 minutes before launch indicated clouds as low as 1100 ft AGL; fog reported near launch site; deteriorating conditions available but not rechecked (p. 10)

Toxicology detected diazepam, oxycodone, methylphenidate, and diphenhydramine at levels equivalent to blood alcohol content of a drunken driver; pilot had untreated depression, ADHD, and bipolar disorder (p. 15-16, 17)
Balloon pilots do not require medical certification unlike other commercial pilots; no requirement for flight review documentation found in records (p. 14-15)
Aircraft struck power lines and crashed into field during descent through clouds that obstructed ground view (p. 12)
Balloon caught fire after power line impact (p. 12)

events.text: Balloon launched from Fentress Airpark on northerly course after pibal checks (p. 11)
Passenger photograph 2 minutes after launch showed low clouds and fog visible along route of flight (p. 11)
Balloon much closer to fog and clouds; ground crew saw balloon enter fog that became thicker (p. 11)
Passenger photograph at 19 minutes after launch showed reduced visibility in mist/fog/clouds (p. 11)
First photograph showing balloon above thin clouds at 24 minutes after launch; ground visible through clouds (p. 11)
Pilot sent position signal to ground crew via navigation app at 28 minutes after launch, then no further communication (p. 11)
Passenger photograph at 40 minutes after launch showed balloon flying above overcast cloud layer extending to horizon, obstructing ground view (p. 11)
Passenger photograph at 42 minutes after launch showed balloon shadow near hole in clouds with visible power line tower (p. 11-12)
Balloon struck power lines during descent through cloud layers; power operator reported power trip at 0742 CDT (p. 12)
Balloon caught fire; basket located beneath power lines, burner and envelope found 0.5 mile downwind; crash destroyed aircraft (p. 12)

All major decision points and environmental factors extracted

recommendations.text: Require commercial hot air balloon pilots to obtain and maintain a medical certificate to ensure medical fitness to fly
Conduct targeted FAA oversight of commercial balloon operations to mitigate risk before accidents occur rather than focusing oversight primarily on balloon gatherings

safety_changes: Identified critical safety gaps in medical oversight for commercial balloon pilots
Highlighted need for improved FAA risk-based oversight of balloon operations outside gatherings

records.title: Emirates 521

agencies.name: General Civil Aviation Authority
agencies.report_title: Air Accident Investigation Sector final report, Runway impact during attempted go-around, Boeing 777-31H A6-EMW, Dubai International Airport, 3 August 2016

records.summary: Landing on runway 12L at Dubai in hot conditions with a reported windshear, the 777 experienced a shift to a tailwind in the flare and floated well beyond the touchdown zone. After the main gear touched down the crew initiated a go-around, but because the aircraft was on the ground the TOGA switches were inhibited and the autothrottle left the thrust levers at idle, which the crew did not notice. The aircraft became airborne on pitch alone, the gear was retracted, and it sank back onto the runway with the engines still at idle. The fuselage slid to a stop and caught fire; all 300 occupants evacuated, but a firefighter was killed when the centre fuel tank exploded.
records.probable_cause: The GCAA concluded that the aircraft impacted the runway during an attempted go-around because the flight crew did not realise that the autothrottle had not responded to the TOGA switch presses, which were inhibited by the on-ground logic, so that the thrust levers remained at idle and the aircraft could not sustain flight after it became airborne. Contributing factors included the crew's reliance on automation and lack of awareness of the TOGA inhibit logic, the absence of a flight-deck alert or procedural guidance for a go-around after touchdown, the crew's ineffective monitoring of the flight mode annunciations and engine thrust during the go-around, the long landing resulting from a headwind-to-tailwind shift, and the decision to retract the landing gear before a positive rate of climb was established with thrust.

factors.evidence: A windshear warning had been broadcast; in the flare the wind shifted from a headwind to a tailwind of about 16 kt, extending the float.
The tailwind component in the flare increased the groundspeed and the landing distance.
The aircraft floated and the main gear touched down about 1,100 m beyond the threshold, well past the touchdown zone; the RAAS 'LONG LANDING' aural alert sounded.
The crew pressed the TOGA switches after touchdown, when they were inhibited by the weight-on-wheels logic, and did not recognise that the go-around mode had not engaged.
The autothrottle remained in its landing idle mode and the thrust levers stayed at idle for about 12 seconds after the go-around was called; the crew expected the autothrottle to advance them.
Neither pilot monitored the flight mode annunciations or engine indications; the thrust levers were advanced manually only about 3 seconds before impact.
The TOGA switch inhibit after touchdown and the absence of an alert when a go-around is attempted with the switches inhibited were identified as contributing to the crew's lack of awareness.
No flight-deck alert indicated that TOGA had not engaged or that thrust remained at idle during the attempted go-around.
The crew had not been trained for a go-around after touchdown and the operator's procedures did not address the TOGA inhibit logic.
After the aircraft came to rest, fire from the separated right engine spread to the fuselage; the centre tank exploded about nine minutes later, killing a firefighter.
Several slides were unusable in the wind, and passengers retrieving cabin baggage slowed the evacuation.
The aircraft sank back onto the runway with the gear retracting, struck the runway on its underside, and slid about 800 m before stopping.

events.text: Dubai ATIS and tower report windshear on approach to runway 12L; the aircraft is on a stabilised approach in hot conditions.
Below about 100 ft the wind shifts from a headwind to a tailwind of about 16 kt.
The aircraft floats in the flare along the runway with the thrust levers at idle under autothrottle control.
Right main gear touches down about 1,100 m beyond the threshold, followed by the left main gear; the aircraft is on the ground with idle thrust.
RAAS 'LONG LANDING, LONG LANDING' aural alert sounds.
The commander decides to go around and presses the TOGA switches; they are inhibited by the on-ground logic and the autothrottle does not advance the thrust levers.
The commander pitches the aircraft up and it becomes airborne on residual speed alone; the pilot monitoring calls a positive rate of climb.
Landing gear selected up on the commander's command; the flaps are set to 20.
The tower clears the aircraft to climb straight ahead to 4,000 ft, adding to the crew's workload during the go-around.
The aircraft reaches a maximum height of about 85 ft with the thrust levers still at idle and the airspeed decaying; it begins to sink.
The thrust levers are advanced manually about 3 seconds before impact; the engines have not yet accelerated.
The aircraft strikes the runway on its underside with the gear in transit; the right engine separates and the aircraft slides about 800 m before stopping.
Fire spreads from the separated engine along the right side; evacuation is ordered; some slides are unusable in the wind and some passengers take cabin baggage.
About nine minutes after the aircraft stopped, the centre wing fuel tank explodes; a firefighter is killed.

recommendations.text: Review the go-around logic so that a TOGA request after touchdown is either honoured or clearly annunciated to the crew, and provide guidance and alerting for a go-around initiated after touchdown.
recommendations.outcome: Boeing issued operator communications and flight crew training material on go-arounds after touchdown and TOGA inhibit logic.

recommendations.text: Include go-around after touchdown scenarios in training and emphasise the flight crew's responsibility to verify thrust lever position and flight mode annunciations during every go-around.
Reinforce guidance on the retraction of the landing gear only after a positive rate of climb has been established with thrust.
Review airport rescue and firefighting procedures for aircraft with fuel tank fire exposure and the guidance to firefighters on the risk of tank explosion.
Address the retrieval of cabin baggage during evacuations through passenger briefing and cabin crew procedures.

safety_changes: Boeing issued a flight operations bulletin and training material to 777 operators on go-arounds initiated after touchdown and the TOGA inhibit logic.
Emirates revised its go-around training and procedures, including scenarios with a bounced or long landing and a go-around after touchdown.
The accident became a reference case for the industry's guidance on cabin baggage retrieval during evacuations.

notes: t0 (first main gear touchdown at 08:37:19 UTC) and the impact time (08:37:38) are given from memory of the GCAA report timeline and may be off by a few seconds; intermediate offsets follow the report narrative (about 85 ft maximum height, thrust levers advanced about 3 s before impact).
The emergency_landing outcome factor is used as instructed to represent the aircraft settling back onto the runway; the ICAO category ARC (abnormal runway contact) is used.
The tailwind value (16 kt) and touchdown distance (about 1,100 m) are from the report narrative as recalled; the exact figures were not verified.
Recommendation ids were not verified; the GCAA report contains numbered safety recommendations to Boeing, the FAA, Emirates and the airport.

records.title: FedEx Express Flight 910
records.summary: FedEx Express Flight 910, an MD-10-10F cargo aircraft, experienced a left main landing gear collapse after landing at Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport on October 28, 2016. The left MLG failed during rollout, causing the left wing to strike the runway and catch fire. Both crew members evacuated safely. The aircraft sustained substantial damage.
records.probable_cause: The failure of the left main landing gear (MLG) due to fatigue cracking that initiated at a corrosion pit. The pit formed in the absence of a required protective cadmium coating the cause of which could not be determined from available evidence. Contributing to the failure of the left MLG was the operator's overhaul limit, which exceeded that recommended by the airplane manufacturer without sufficient data and analysis to ensure crack detection before it progressed to failure. (p. 5)

factors.evidence: A thumbnail crack was observed on both mating fracture surfaces of the MLG, which exhibited features consistent with a pre-existing crack that progressed to fracture of the MLG. Fatigue striations were observed during microscopic examination indicating fatigue cracking had initiated at a corrosion pit at the air filler valve bore radius and propagated through mixed mode fatigue, overstress, and intergranular fracture. The corrosion pit measured 0.004 inch wide with a depth of 0.002 inch and formed in the absence of a required protective cadmium coating. (p. 1-3)

Although the ASB inspection found no cracks and corrosion repair was completed with brush cadmium plating during the last overhaul in February 2008, there is no routine procedure to effectively inspect the air filler valve bore area during on-wing maintenance activities since the last overhaul. It was not possible to determine whether the cadmium plating properly bonded to the bore surface, was removed during later maintenance, or wore off over time. (p. 3-4)

FedEx adopted a 9-year MLG overhaul limit used by the previous owner/operator of the first DC10s purchased by FedEx, exceeding the manufacturer-recommended 8-year interval, without producing documentation or data analysis supporting the longer overhaul interval. The company produced no documentation or data analysis supporting the longer overhaul interval. (p. 4)

The left main landing gear collapsed during rollout at approximately 17:50:41, after the left MLG touched down on runway 10L at 17:50:31. The outer cylinder of the left MLG shock strut fractured around its entire circumference at the air filler valve bore. (p. 1, 5-6)

The left engine and left wing scraped the runway as the aircraft veered left, with the left wing catching fire. The nearly empty left main fuel tank exploded after the exterior surfaces were heated by burning fuel, which flowed from a broken fuel supply tube in the left engine pylon. (p. 1)

events.text: ATC cleared the flight for final approach to the instrument landing system (ILS) approach to runway 10L at KFLL.
First officer set the flaps at 35 degrees when the airplane was 3,000 ft above ground level.
First officer disconnected the autopilot when the airplane was 1,000 ft above ground level.
First officer disconnected the autothrottles at 100 ft above ground level, as briefed.
Left main landing gear touched down in the touchdown zone left of runway centerline.
First officer deployed the spoilers.
Nose gear touched down, 3 seconds after left MLG touchdown.
Captain instructed the first officer to begin braking. CVR recorded sound of multiple thuds consistent with gear collapse.
Thrust reversers were deployed.
Left main landing gear collapsed. FDR data indicate increase in brake pedal position angle and longitudinal deceleration. Aircraft yawed to the left.
Captain stated 'I have the airplane' and applied full right rudder without effect as first officer continued braking.
Captain instructed the first officer to call the tower and inform about the emergency.

No. 1 engine initially supporting the airplane after the left MLG collapse when fire began near left-wing tip. Airplane eventually stopped off the left side of runway 10L, about 30 to 40 degrees off the runway heading.
Flight crew began executing the evacuation checklist.
An explosion occurred, with a fireball erupting at the No. 1 engine. Airport video showed debris above the fireball at more than twice the height of the 75-ft-tall airplane tail.
Pilots evacuated the airplane through the right cockpit window using an escape rope. Captain sustained minor injuries during evacuation; first officer was not injured.

recommendations.text: Implement improvements in the plating method for air filler valve bores in MLG cylinders, including moving to tank dip methods that provide improved uniformity, adherence, and coverage over brush plating methods.

Establish requirements for periodic borescope inspection of air filler valve bores on main landing gear during on-wing maintenance to detect corrosion, plating defects, or cracks before they lead to fatigue failure.

safety_changes: FedEx reverted to the 8-year overhaul limit for MLG cylinders as recommended by the manufacturer, following the accident.
FedEx inspected all MLGs in its MD-10-10F fleet and permanently removed 16 cylinders identified as 'concerns' from service.
Hawker Pacific Aerospace introduced tank dip method for plating air filler valve bores, providing improved uniformity and adherence over brush plating.

notes: Sections read: History of Flight (p. 1-4), Analysis (p. 1), Probable Cause and Findings (p. 5), Wreckage and Impact Information (p. 6-9), Tests and Research (p. 10-13). Full metallurgical analysis of fatigue crack initiation and propagation documented.
At least 14 events with precise clock times extracted from report and flight data recorder analysis.
Factor evidence includes page citations to corrosion pit analysis, fatigue striation counts, and maintenance history documentation.

records.title: American Airlines 383

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Uncontained Engine Failure and Subsequent Fire

records.summary: American Airlines Flight 383 suffered an uncontained right engine failure during takeoff roll at O'Hare on October 28, 2016. The HPT stage 2 disk ruptured, penetrating the wing fuel tank and causing a severe fire. Captain rejected takeoff and crew evacuated all 170 occupants; 21 sustained injuries.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause was the failure of the high-pressure turbine stage 2 disk, which severed the main engine fuel feed line and breached the right main wing fuel tank, releasing fuel that resulted in a fire during the takeoff roll. The HPT stage 2 disk failed because of low-cycle fatigue cracks that initiated from an internal subsurface manufacturing anomaly that was most likely not detectable during production and in-service inspections. Contributing factors included lack of a separate engine fire checklist for ground operations and lack of communication between flight and cabin crews.

factors.evidence: HPT stage 2 disk rupture during takeoff power at 1431:43.4 when airspeed was 128 knots; sudden engine imbalance detected (p. 2, 16).
Right engine suffered uncontained failure with disk fragment penetrating inboard section of right wing, severing fuel feed line and breaching fuel tank (p. 1, 2).
HPT stage 2 disk had discrete dirty white spot manufacturing anomaly undetectable by production inspection methods; fatigue cracks not detectable at last in-service inspection (p. 75).
Severe fire on right side of airplane following engine failure and fuel tank breach (p. 1, 2).

events.text: Tower controller cleared airplane for takeoff; first officer acknowledged (p. 1).
At 14:31:19, CVR recorded sound of increasing engine RPM; at 14:31:24 engines achieved takeoff power (p. 1-2).
At 14:31:32, first officer made routine callout of 80 knots airspeed; crew described spool-up as normal (p. 2).
At 14:31:43.4, with 128 knots indicated, longitudinal acceleration decreased suddenly from 0.23 to 0.13 G; CVR recorded 'bang' sound (p. 2).
Captain initiated rejected takeoff maneuver; throttles moved to idle at 14:31:45.6 (p. 2).
Autobrakes activated at rejected takeoff airspeed of 134 knots (V1); speedbrakes activated about 2 seconds later (p. 2).
At 14:31:50, first officer contacted ATC stating airplane stopping on runway; controller responded with fire warning (p. 2).
At 14:32:00, CVR recorded engine fire warning; FDR showed 'ENG FIRE R' annunciated; airplane decelerated to 35 knots (p. 2-3).
At 14:32:04.1, captain called for engine fire checklist (20.6 seconds after engine failure); fuel switch shut off (p. 3).
FDR showed airplane came to stop at 14:32:09.8, 26.4 seconds after engine failure; captain could smell smoke (p. 3).

recommendations.text: Establish and lead an industry group to evaluate current and enhanced inspection technologies for nickel alloys and issue guidance for nickel alloy rotating engine components.
Require subsurface in-service inspection techniques such as ultrasonic inspections for critical high-energy, life-limited rotating parts for all engines.
Revise Advisory Circular 20-128A to minimize hazards from uncontained engine failures based on analysis of recent uncontained engine failure data.
Require operators to develop emergency checklist procedures for engine fire on the ground to expeditiously address fire hazard.
Develop guidance for flight attendant training regarding assessing exits during emergencies and identifying conditions that preclude opening exits.
Review training programs to ensure flight attendants and crews receive training on different interphone systems.
Conduct research on effects of carry-on baggage on evacuation times and identify countermeasures.
Work with operators to develop engine fire checklist procedures for ground operations.
Review engine fire checklists and ensure procedures expeditiously address ground engine fires without delaying evacuation.

notes: Sections: History of Flight (p. 1-4), Findings (p. 75-76), Probable Cause (p. 75-76), Recommendations (p. 77-78)

9 formal safety recommendations extracted with IDs

records.title: Ameristar Charters 9363

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Runway Overrun During Rejected Takeoff, Ameristar Air Cargo, Inc., dba Ameristar Charters, flight 9363, Boeing MD-83, N786TW

records.operator: Ameristar Air Cargo, Inc. (dba Ameristar Charters)

location.name: Willow Run Airport (YIP), Ypsilanti, Michigan, runway 23L departure end

records.summary: Boeing MD-83 experienced jammed right elevator due to wind exposure while parked at Willow Run Airport, rendering it unable to rotate during takeoff. Captain rejected takeoff 12 seconds after reaching V1 when aircraft did not respond to control column input. Aircraft overran departure end of runway but all 116 occupants evacuated safely with only one minor injury.
records.probable_cause: The jammed condition of the airplane's right elevator, which resulted from exposure to localized, dynamic wind while the airplane was parked and rendered the airplane unable to rotate during takeoff. Contributing factors: (1) effect of a large hangar structure on gusting surface wind at parked location, which generated localized turbulence with vertical component causing dynamic loads sufficient to jam elevator despite wind speed being below certification design limits, and (2) lack of means to enable flight crew to detect jammed elevator during preflight checks for Boeing MD-83.

factors.evidence: Right elevator was positioned full trailing-edge-down (TED) and remained locked in overcenter position throughout accident sequence, rendering airplane incapable of rotation during takeoff (p. 467-468, 478)
MD-83 was not equipped with a gust lock to prevent elevator motion from wind loads while parked (p. 475)

Flight crew's preflight inspection and control check could not detect overcenter position of elevator geared tab linkage; elevators cannot be inspected during typical preflight walk-around for free-floating condition (p. 3124-3127)
Airplane overran departure end of runway 23L at 100 knots, traveled 950 ft across grassy runway safety area before striking airport perimeter fence and paved road (p. 577-579)

events.text: Airplane parked on ramp east of large hangar at Willow Run Airport for 2 days
Flight crew first powered up the airplane following company procedures for nontowered airports
Captain (pilot flying) performed preflight walkaround inspection and noticed no anomalies
High wind from west resulted in power outage at airport affecting weather observing equipment and prompted air traffic control tower evacuation
Takeoff roll began at 14:51:12 EST and was normal until rotation speed at 150 knots
At VR, captain pulled back on control column to rotate the aircraft, but aircraft failed to respond even after captain applied additional back force
Captain executed rejected takeoff 12 seconds after V1 because aircraft did not respond to rotation input
Airplane overran runway 23L at approximately 100 knots, traveled 950 ft across grassy runway safety area before striking airport perimeter fence and raised paved road

recommendations.text: Complete the development of a modification for Boeing DC-9/MD-80 series and 717 model airplanes that will prevent the possibility of elevator jamming due to ground wind exposure.
Develop new preflight procedures or other mitigations for Boeing DC-9/MD-80 series and 717 model airplanes that will enable a flight crew to verify before takeoff that the elevators are not jammed.

Until the actions in Safety Recommendations A-19-1 and -2 are completed, revise the Aircraft Operating Manual and Aircraft Maintenance Manual for Boeing DC-9/MD-80 series and 717 model airplanes to lower the ground gust criteria that will require physical inspections and operational checks of the elevators by maintenance personnel.

Determine if the ground gust limit loads contained in Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations 25.415 adequately ensure that critical flight control systems are protected from hazards introduced by ground gusts that contain dynamic, vertical wind components.

Ensure the operators of Boeing DC-9/MD-80 series and 717 model airplanes have procedures that define who is responsible for monitoring the wind that affects parked airplanes and for notifying maintenance personnel when conditions could meet or exceed the ground gust criteria specified in the Aircraft Maintenance Manual.

Revise Order JO 7900.5D, Surface Weather Observing, Change 1, to specify sign-off procedures and backup augmentation responsibilities for all types of weather-observing personnel when they are unable to perform their prescribed duties from their normal duty station during normal duty hours.

Require all 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 139 certificated airports to upgrade all runway safety areas that could, with feasible improvements, be made to meet the minimum standards established by Advisory Circular 150/5300-13.

Require all 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 139 certificated airports to install engineered materials arresting systems in each runway safety area available for air carrier use that could not, with feasible improvements, be made to meet the minimum standards established by Advisory Circular 150/5300-13.

safety_changes: Ameristar implemented procedures for monitoring wind affecting parked airplanes
FAA runway safety area (RSA) upgrade program led to improvements
Evacuation slide manufacturer issued revised maintenance procedures to prevent improper cable installation

notes: Full report read: executive summary (lines 448-611), history of flight (lines 619-650), findings and probable cause (lines 3114-3193), safety recommendations (lines 3200-3251)
Right elevator jammed due to dynamic wind loads from large hangar nearby generating localized turbulence
Captain's timely rejected takeoff and crew's disciplined procedures contributed to survivability
All 116 occupants evacuated safely with only one minor injury despite substantial aircraft damage

records.title: 2017 Teterboro Learjet crash
records.summary: A Learjet 35A on approach to Teterboro Airport stalled and crashed during a circle-to-land maneuver when the captain allowed an under-qualified first officer to act as pilot flying contrary to company policy. The crew conducted no approach briefing, failed to stabilize the approach, and continued maneuvering below minimum descent altitude with inadequate airspeed. Both pilots were killed in the crash into a commercial building.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause of this accident was the pilot-in-command's attempt to salvage an unstabilized visual approach, which resulted in an aerodynamic stall at low altitude. Contributing to the accident were the PIC's decision to allow an unapproved SIC to act as pilot flying, the PIC's inadequate and incomplete preflight planning, and the flight crew's lack of an approach briefing. Also contributing were Trans-Pacific's lack of safety programs to identify poor performance patterns and the FAA's ineffective oversight procedures which failed to identify these company deficiencies (p. 55).

factors.evidence: The first officer (SIC) was rated for single-pilot operations (SIC-0 rated) and was under-qualified as pilot flying; the company's own check airman noted he was 'Not Yet Proficient' with deficiencies in takeoff checks, engine starting, and landing procedures (p. 37, 55).
The captain allowed the unqualified SIC to act as pilot flying in violation of Trans-Pacific's standard operating procedures that restricted SIC-0 pilots to pilot monitoring duties only (p. 37, 55).

No approach briefing was conducted by either crew member, failing to establish situational awareness and clear communication. The crew did not verify the approach procedure or discuss the circle-to-land maneuver (p. 37, 50).

Airspeed decayed during the circle-to-land approach from 127 knots to 111 knots (slowest recorded by radar) while the pilot flying focused on runway alignment rather than monitoring speed indicators. Target airspeed was 139 knots (p. 37-38, 50-51).

The circle-to-land approach was not properly stabilized, with the aircraft descending to the MDA from 1 nm away from runway threshold and continuing inbound rather than beginning the circling maneuver at the final approach fix (TORBY) as directed by ATC (p. 50-51).

The captain focused on coaching the SIC and aligning the aircraft with the runway rather than on cockpit indications showing airspeed decay and descent rate warnings. The captain disregarded EGPWS '500-foot' and 'sink rate, pull up' alerts (p. 37-38, 51).
Aircraft stalled during circle-to-land approach at 35 degree left bank angle with airspeed at 111 knots (versus stall speed of 102 knots). The pilot announced 'stall' in a strained voice (p. 51-52).

After stall, aircraft impacted commercial building at Carlstadt, New Jersey with both pilots killed. Wreckage trail was 315 feet long. Both engines were operating at impact with flaps and landing gear extended (p. 20-21, 34).

events.text: Captain filed instrument flight rules flight plan from Philadelphia to Teterboro; no weather briefing conducted and no approach briefing prepared
Aircraft crosses TORBY (final approach fix) at 1,550 feet altitude; captain did not initiate circle-to-land maneuver at this point as instructed by ATC
First officer acting as pilot flying begins right turn toward runway 1; aircraft at 650 feet altitude and begins descending
EGPWS '500-foot' aural alert sounds; captain disregards alert and tells SIC to disregard it. Aircraft continues descent and right turn
EGPWS 'sink rate, pull up' alert sounds. Aircraft at 350 feet altitude in 28-degree right bank. No go-around initiated
Captain takes control from SIC, stating 'my controls'; instructs SIC to monitor airspeed. Aircraft makes rapid left turn toward runway 1
Captain announces 'stall' in strained voice at 35-degree left bank; SIC responds 'yup'
Aircraft right wing tip impacts roof of office building at Carlstadt, New Jersey; aircraft fragments and catches fire; both pilots killed in impact

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: follow the glideslope. do not go below fifteen

recommendations.text: Require all Title 14 CFR Part 135 operators to establish programs for flight crewmembers who have demonstrated performance deficiencies or experienced failures during training and administer additional oversight and training to address and correct performance deficiencies
Develop guidance for Title 14 CFR Part 135 operators to help them create and implement effective crew resource management training programs

Review operators' Learjet 35A operations manuals to determine whether they contain manufacturer-recommended approach speed wind additives and encourage those operators without that information to add it to their operations documents

Issue an advisory circular with guidance on leadership training for upgrading captains at 14 CFR Part 121, 135, and 91K operators, including methods and techniques for effective leadership and professional standards
Require all 14 CFR Part 121, 135, and 91K operators to provide a specific course on leadership training to their upgrading captains
Require all 14 CFR Part 135 operators to install flight data recording devices capable of supporting a flight data monitoring program
After the action in Safety Recommendation A-16-34 is completed, require all 14 CFR Part 135 operators to establish a structured flight data monitoring program that reviews all available data sources
Require all 14 CFR Part 135 operators to establish safety management system programs
Review the Safety Assurance System and develop and implement procedures needed to identify 14 CFR Part 135 operators that do not comply with standard operating procedures
