records.title: Thomson Airways 1526

agencies.name: Air Accidents Investigation Branch
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report: 2/2018

records.summary: A Boeing 737-86J (C-FWGH) operated by Sunwing Airlines departed Belfast International Airport for Corfu on 21 July 2017. During pre-flight setup, the crew incorrectly entered -52°C (instead of the actual 16°C) as the outside air temperature in the Flight Management Computer. This caused the FMC to calculate an N1 setting of only 81.5%, approximately 60% of the required thrust. During takeoff, the aircraft accelerated abnormally slowly and reached rotation speed near the runway end. After liftoff, the landing gear struck a runway approach light. The aircraft climbed away at a very low rate but continued without further incident. There was no damage and no injuries.
records.probable_cause: An incorrect outside air temperature (-52°C instead of 16°C) was entered into the flight management computer, causing the FMC to calculate a significantly reduced N1 setting for takeoff. The crew did not detect this error, and the abnormally slow acceleration was not recognized until the aircraft was rapidly approaching the runway end. The aircraft's systems lacked automated safeguards to alert the crew to the data entry error or the abnormal takeoff performance.

factors.evidence: An incorrect outside air temperature of -52°C was entered into the flight management computer instead of the actual OAT of 16°C, causing the FMC to calculate an N1 setting for takeoff of only 81.5%, significantly below the required 92.7% (p. 2).

The aircraft's FMC software (revision U10.8A) did not include an automated crosscheck of manually-entered OAT against the actual ambient temperature sensed by the aircraft; a later software standard (U12.0) included this capability (p. 2-3).

The Electronic Flight Bags used by the crew did not display the calculated N1 value, preventing the crew from comparing the FMC-calculated N1 against an independently-calculated value to detect the discrepancy (p. 3).
Although both pilot and manufacturer required crews to crosscheck FMC entries, neither pilot detected the incorrect -52°C OAT entry during pre-flight checks (p. 6).

events.text: Flight crew reported for duty at Belfast International Airport for scheduled departure at 14:15 hrs (p. 5).
During pre-flight FMC programming, the commander entered an incorrect OAT of -47°C into the n1 limit page instead of the actual value (p. 5-6).
Aircraft began to push back from the parking stand; ground crew noticed worn nose landing gear tyre and aircraft returned for tyre change (p. 6).
Co-pilot updated weather from ATIS and recalculated takeoff performance; commander entered a second incorrect OAT of -52°C into the FMC along with a corrected assumed temperature of 48°C (p. 6).
Aircraft cleared for takeoff from Runway 07; takeoff roll began with FMC set to 81.5% N1, only 60% of maximum thrust (p. 7).
At approximately 120-130 knots, crew realized aircraft was not accelerating normally; rotation speed (V1) reached with approximately 900 meters of runway remaining (p. 7).
Aircraft rotated and lifted off the runway, taking a significant time to lift off and climbing at a very low rate (p. 7).
Aircraft's landing gear tire struck a 36-cm tall runway approach light located 29 meters beyond the end of the runway (p. 7).
Crew checked FMC and noted N1 of 81.5% had been used; this figure was significantly below the required N1 setting of 92.7% (p. 7).
Full thrust was applied when aircraft was approximately 4 km from the end of the runway at 800 feet above airfield level (p. 7).
Aircraft continued to Corfu without further incident; no damage found on inspection (p. 8).

recommendations.text: Mandate the use of Flight Management Computer OPS software revision U12.0, or later, and the Common Display System Block Point 15 update where this is required, to enable the automated outside air temperature crosscheck on all applicable Boeing 737 aircraft.
Give guidance to operators of Boeing 737 aircraft on how they might verify the FMC-calculated value of N1 against an independently-calculated value.

In conjunction with the Federal Aviation Administration, sponsor the development of technical specifications and, subsequently, develop certification standards for a Takeoff Acceleration Monitoring System which will alert the crew of an aircraft to abnormally low acceleration during takeoff.
Note the conclusions of this report and introduce provisions addressing Takeoff Acceleration Monitoring Systems.

safety_changes: Sunwing Airlines upgraded their Boeing 737 fleet to FMC Update 13 and CDU BP15 to enable OAT alerting
Sunwing Airlines updated EFB software to display N1 and added N1 crosscheck to standard operating procedures
UK CAA amended MATS Part 1 to require senior controllers to notify the AAIB by telephone following aircraft accidents or serious incidents

notes: Sections read: History of Flight (lines 666-750), Findings (lines 3757-3940), Conclusions (lines 3748-4040)
All clock times in UTC per report
N1 setting 81.5% vs required 92.7% sourced from page 7
Four numbered safety recommendations from final report

records.title: Air France 66

agencies.name: Bureau of Enquiry and Analysis for Civil Aviation Safety
agencies.report_title: Uncontained failure of Engine No 4 of Airbus A380-861 N°087 registered F-HPJE

records.summary: Air France Flight 66, an Airbus A380 with 521 passengers and crew, experienced an uncontained failure of its number 4 (right-side) Engine Alliance GP7200 engine while in cruise climb over Greenland at 13:49 UTC on September 30, 2017. The engine fan hub fractured and separated along with the air intake and fan case. The failure resulted from cold dwell fatigue cracking in the titanium alloy fan hub, a phenomenon previously unknown for this alloy. The aircraft diverted safely to Goose Bay Airport in Canada and landed without further incident.
records.probable_cause: The fan hub of engine No 4 failed due to cold dwell fatigue cracking in the titanium alloy (Ti-6-4) fan hub. The crack initiated in a macro-zone (large colony of similarly oriented crystal grains) in the subsurface of a blade slot bottom and progressed over approximately 1,650 cycles until catastrophic failure. Contributing factors included the engine designer's and manufacturer's lack of knowledge of the cold dwell fatigue phenomenon in Ti-6-4; absence of certification body instructions on accounting for macro-zones and cold dwell fatigue in engine critical parts; absence of non-destructive means to detect unusual macro-zones in titanium parts; and increased risk of large macro-zones in larger Ti-6-4 forgings required for bigger engines (p. 72-74).

factors.evidence: Cold dwell fatigue crack initiated in a macro-zone in the subsurface of a blade slot bottom of the fan hub and progressed over 1,650 cycles before failure (p. 74). The macro-zone where the crack initiated was approximately one order of magnitude larger and more intense than average observed in other engine hubs.
The engine manufacturer and certification authorities had not anticipated the cold dwell fatigue phenomenon in Ti-6-4 during engine design and certification (p. 74).
The fan hub separated, causing detachment of the fan, air inlet, and fan case from engine No 4 (p. 73).

events.text: Air France Flight 66 departed Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport for Los Angeles with 497 passengers and 24 crew members (p. 9).
During cruise climb over Greenland, strong vibrations appeared with the aircraft simultaneously yawing to the right (p. 73).
Engine Alliance GP7200 engine No 4 failure messages displayed on ECAM: 'ENG 4 STALL' and 'ENG 4 FAIL' nearly simultaneously (p. 73).
Front part of engine No 4, including fan hub, air inlet and associated fairings separated from engine (p. 73).
Engine debris struck wing, airframe and trimmable horizontal stabilizer; aircraft speed started to decrease and began descent (p. 73).
Captain took the controls and became pilot flying; began processing failure in accordance with FOR-DEC decision making method (p. 73).
Relief pilot from crew rest station entered cockpit to assist flight crew with emergency procedures (p. 73).
Crew chose to divert to Goose Bay aerodrome in Canada in agreement with Air France Operations Control Centre (p. 73).
Aircraft landed at Goose Bay Airport without any further incident or anomalies; all 521 passengers and crew members evacuated safely (p. 9).

recommendations.text: Ensure that the design and sizing criteria and methods along with the manufacturing processes and in-production checks of engine rotor-grade critical parts made of α/β titanium alloy, and in particular the titanium alloy Ti-6-4, are such that the risk of failure of these parts due to the cold dwell fatigue phenomenon is controlled.

Ensure that the design and sizing criteria and methods along with the manufacturing processes and in-production checks of engine rotor-grade critical parts made of α/β titanium alloy, and in particular the titanium alloy Ti-6-4, are such that the risk of failure of these parts due to the cold dwell fatigue phenomenon is controlled.

Carry out a review of engine rotor-grade critical parts made of α/β titanium alloy, and in particular the titanium alloy Ti-6-4, which undergo a manufacturing process likely to lead to the presence of intense macro-zones and for which the risk of failure due to cold dwell fatigue phenomenon has not been sufficiently taken into account during certification. Subsequently ensure that an adapted in-service inspection programme is implemented to detect possible incipient cracks which might lead to the failure of the part.

Carry out a review of engine rotor-grade critical parts made of α/β titanium alloy, and in particular the titanium alloy Ti-6-4, which undergo a manufacturing process likely to lead to the presence of intense macro-zones and for which the risk of failure due to cold dwell fatigue phenomenon has not been sufficiently taken into account during certification. Subsequently ensure that an adapted in-service inspection programme is implemented to detect possible incipient cracks which might lead to the failure of the part.

safety_changes: Design and certification criteria for titanium rotor-grade critical parts revised to account for cold dwell fatigue phenomenon
Service bulletins published requiring in-service inspections of fan hubs for high-cycle engines
Development of new fan blade lock ring with improved design to reduce maintenance-induced damage risk
Implementation of regular ultrasonic inspections for early crack detection in fan hubs

notes: Read Synopsis, Findings, Contributing Factors, Measures Taken, and Safety Recommendations from BEA report BEA2017-0568
Nine events with clock times extracted from narrative (converted to UTC format)
All factor ids verified against taxonomy
Four safety recommendations (FRAN-2020-006 through FRAN-2020-009) issued to EASA and FAA
BEA format uses 'Contributing factors' rather than 'probable cause' terminology
Successful emergency landing with no injuries or fatalities

records.title: West Wind Aviation Flight 282
records.summary: An ATR 42-320 registered C-GWEA departed Fond-du-Lac Airport on 13 December 2017 at 18:15 CST in cloudy weather with temperature of minus 19 degrees Celsius. During the initial climb stage, the aircraft lost altitude and struck the ground 600 metres away from the runway, leaving an 800 foot trail of debris. All 25 occupants initially survived the crash, but one 19-year-old passenger died on 25 December 2017 from injuries. Ice contamination on critical surfaces during takeoff resulted in increased drag (58%) and decreased lift (25%), causing uncontrolled roll and loss of control.
records.probable_cause: Ice contamination on the aircraft's critical surfaces during takeoff. The aircraft's departure from Fond-du-Lac Airport was made despite awareness of icing conditions and residual ice on the aircraft. Weather conditions on the ground were conducive to additional ice formation. The flight crew's decision to depart was influenced by continuation bias and the normalization of unsafe practices at remote airports with inadequate de-icing facilities. During takeoff, the increased drag and decreased lift from ice contamination, combined with asymmetric ice distribution causing asymmetric lift, resulted in an uncommanded left roll. The captain's control inputs, based on expectation of normal handling characteristics, were insufficient to counteract the roll due to diminished roll damping caused by the ice contamination. This loss of control in the roll axis led to collision with terrain.

factors.evidence: residual ice accumulated on the aircraft during the approach due to activated ice protection systems not being designed to shed all ice, and additional ice formed on the ground during the 36-minute stop (p. 7656-7680)
Fond-du-Lac Airport had inadequate de-icing equipment and services, and the flight crew decided to continue with the planned departure route despite knowing of forecast ground icing (p. 7656-7665)

During takeoff, the aircraft experienced uncommanded left roll due to asymmetric lift from uneven ice contamination. The control inputs were insufficient due to diminished roll damping, resulting in loss of control and collision with terrain (p. 7700-7715)
The flight crew inspection was conducted in darkness on a dimly lit apron without a flashlight, limiting visibility of the full extent of ice contamination on critical surfaces (p. 7676-7681)

events.text: Aircraft began takeoff roll from Fond-du-Lac Airport runway 10 in cloudy weather with temperature minus 19 degrees Celsius
During initial climb, aircraft experienced uncommanded left roll; roll damping was diminished due to ice contamination on critical surfaces
Aircraft impacted terrain 600 metres east-northeast of the runway in level pitch with 30 degrees left bank angle; aircraft wreckage trail extended 800 feet
All aircraft occupants were rescued and evacuated within hours; one 19-year-old passenger died on 25 December 2017 from impact injuries

recommendations.text: The Department of Transport collaborate with air operators and airport authorities to identify locations where there is inadequate de-icing and anti-icing equipment and take urgent action to ensure that the proper equipment is available to reduce the likelihood of aircraft taking off with contaminated critical surfaces

The Department of Transport and air operators take action to increase compliance with Canadian Aviation Regulations subsection 602.11(2) and reduce the likelihood of aircraft taking off with contaminated critical surfaces

safety_changes: West Wind implemented new risk assessment requirements for new procedures, managerial changes, and all airports where the company operates
West Wind established Safety, Operations and Customer Experience (SOCE) Committee for corporate oversight of safety culture
Increased emphasis on compliance with clean aircraft concept and de-icing procedures

notes: Sections read: Executive Summary (p. 283-300), History of Flight (p. 528-727), Findings as to Causes (p. 7656-7750)
Flight number in report is WEW282, not WEW280 as listed in batch title
Aircraft departed despite forecast ground icing and visible ice on critical surfaces; crew decision influenced by continuation bias and normalization of unsafe practices
Flight crew inspection inadequate: conducted at night on dimly lit apron without flashlight

records.title: Nature Air Flight 9916
records.summary: Nature Air Flight 9916, a Cessna 208B Caravan, crashed into terrain shortly after takeoff from Punta Islita Airport on December 31, 2017. The aircraft reached a maximum bank angle of 75 degrees and an airspeed below the airplane's published aerodynamic stall speed before impacting rising terrain near the airport. The wreckage was destroyed by impact forces and post-impact fire.
records.probable_cause: The flight crew's failure to maintain airspeed while maneuvering to exit an area of rising terrain, which resulted in an exceedance of the airplane's critical angle of attack and an aerodynamic stall. Contributing to the accident was the flight crew's decision to continue the takeoff toward rising terrain that likely exceeded the airplane's climb capability, the lack of adequate weather reporting available for wind determination, and the lack of documented training for an airport requiring a non-standard departure.

factors.evidence: Witness at airport estimated wind magnitude between 10 and 15 knots; wind models indicated 5 knots from northeast at time of accident (p. 2)
Aircraft swayed to the left seconds after departure and rolled during initial climb; video analysis showed bank angle reached approximately 75 degrees (p. 1, 14)

Aircraft reached airspeed below the published aerodynamic stall speed before impacting terrain; video determined airplane reached maximum bank angle of about 75° and descended at 1,510 ft/minute (p. 1, 14)
Aircraft exploded and burst into flames on impact; extensive post-crash fire damage observed at wreckage site (p. 2, 12)

events.text: Cessna 208B Caravan departed from runway 3 at Punta Islita Airport carrying 10 passengers and 2 pilots.
Aircraft climbs at approximately 715 feet per minute with groundspeed of 68±3 knots.
Seconds after departure the aircraft swayed to the left and entered a left turn.
Aircraft bank angle steepened, airspeed fell below stall speed at 60° bank (98-110 knots), descent rate increased to approximately 1,510 feet per minute.
Aircraft impacted terrain on northwest side of valley approximately 0.4 statute miles from departure end of runway 3 at elevation of 238 feet msl.
Aircraft wreckage consumed by post-impact fire and explosion.

notes: Key sections read: summary, analysis, probable cause, findings, factual information including history of flight, aircraft systems, weather, and airport information
Video analysis section provided precise details of bank angle and descent rate
No CVR transcript or FDR data in public report
Report demonstrates flight crew error in terrain navigation resulting in stall

records.title: Saratov Airlines 703

agencies.name: Interstate Aviation Committee
agencies.report_title: Final report on the investigation of the accident to An-148-100B RA-61704

location.name: Near Stepanovskoye, Ramensky district, Moscow region

records.summary: The crew took off from Domodedovo without switching on the pitot probe heaters. About two and a half minutes after takeoff, in the climb through about 1,300 m, the pitot probes iced and the captain's and first officer's airspeed indications began to disagree. The autopilot was disconnected at about 2,000 m and the crew, acting on the erroneous decreasing airspeed indication, pushed the aircraft into a steep descent; it struck the ground near Stepanovskoye about six minutes after takeoff. All 71 on board died.
records.probable_cause: The MAK concluded that the accident was caused by the crew's erroneous actions in the climb after the pitot heaters had not been switched on before takeoff, which led to icing of all three pitot probes, disagreement of the airspeed indications, disconnection of the autopilot and loss of spatial/situational awareness. The crew pushed the aircraft into a steep descent in reaction to the erroneous airspeed indications and did not recover. Contributing factors included deficiencies in the crew's training and CRM, non-compliance with the checklist that included the pitot heating item, and the crew's failure to recognise and apply the unreliable airspeed procedure.

factors.evidence: The flight data showed the pitot probe heating was not switched on before takeoff, contrary to the checklist.
With the heaters off, all three pitot probes iced in the climb through cloud.
About 2.5 minutes after takeoff, at about 1,300 m, the captain's and first officer's airspeed indications began to diverge; the captain's indication fell toward zero.
The autopilot was disconnected at about 2,000 m when the airspeed disagreement developed.
The crew interpreted the falling airspeed indication as a real loss of speed and did not recognise the indications as erroneous.
The crew pushed the aircraft into a descent of 30 to 35 degrees nose down in response to the low airspeed indication.
The MAK found the crew did not coordinate their actions or clearly identify the failure, and neither pilot called for the unreliable airspeed procedure.
The report concluded the crew lost situational awareness as to the aircraft's true speed and attitude during the descent.
The MAK cited deficiencies in the crew's training for unreliable airspeed and in the operator's crew training and monitoring.
The report noted that the aircraft did not provide a clear alert that the pitot heating was off before takeoff and that the disagree indication was not sufficiently attention-getting.
The aircraft struck the ground at high speed in a steep nose-down attitude.

events.text: Before-takeoff checks completed without the pitot probe heaters being switched on.
Takeoff from Domodedovo in snow conditions; pitot heating remains off.
About 2.5 minutes after takeoff at about 1,300 m and 465 to 470 km/h, the captain's and first officer's airspeed indications begin to disagree as the pitot probes ice.
Airspeed disagree alerting is presented to the crew; the indications continue to diverge.
At about 2,000 m the autopilot is disconnected and the crew fly manually.
Believing the aircraft is losing speed, the pilot flying pushes the nose down; the aircraft transitions from climb to descent.
The captain's airspeed indication drops to zero while the first officer's shows a different, also erroneous, value.
The pilots exchange confused remarks about the speed and the aircraft's behaviour; no unreliable airspeed procedure is called for.
The aircraft is descending with 30 to 35 degrees nose down pitch; ground proximity warnings sound.
The crew pull back in the final seconds but the aircraft does not recover.
Impact with the ground near Stepanovskoye at a speed in excess of 800 km/h in a steep nose-down attitude.

recommendations.text: Reinforce flight crew training on unreliable airspeed recognition and the memory items for the procedure, including in simulator training.
Review the An-148 pitot heating switching logic and crew alerting so that takeoff with pitot heating off is prevented or clearly annunciated.
Improve checklist discipline, crew resource management and flight operations quality monitoring at the operator.

safety_changes: Russian operators of the An-148 issued additional guidance on pitot heating checks and unreliable airspeed procedures after the MAK preliminary findings.
Saratov Airlines' operating certificate was revoked by Rosaviatsia in May 2018.

notes: Times are from the MAK preliminary information (takeoff about 14:21 Moscow time, disagreement about 2.5 minutes after takeoff, autopilot disconnected at about 2,000 m); event t values between those anchors are approximate offsets and clock strings are omitted where not stated.
The MAK final report publication date and report number were not verified and are left null.
The warning_system_deficiency factor reflects the report's discussion of the absence of a clear pitot-heat-off alert; its exact wording was not verified.
Altitudes in state objects are converted from the metric values in the report (1,300 m, 2,000 m).

records.title: Southwest Airlines 1380

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses pour la Sécurité de l'Aviation Civile

records.summary: Southwest Airlines Boeing 737-700 experienced catastrophic left engine failure at 32,000 feet 30 minutes after departure from LaGuardia. A latent fatigue crack in fan blade No. 13 caused the blade to detach and strike the engine case at a critical location, causing fan cowl latch failure and separation. Engine debris damaged the leading edge of the wing and broke a cabin window at row 14, causing explosive decompression. The aircraft descended and diverted to Philadelphia International Airport. One passenger was partially ejected and died; eight others sustained minor injuries.
records.probable_cause: A low-cycle fatigue crack in the dovetail of fan blade No. 13 resulted in the fan blade separating in flight and impacting the engine fan case at a location critical to the structural integrity of the fan cowl structure. This impact led to the in-flight separation of fan cowl components, including the inboard fan cowl aft latch keeper, which struck the fuselage near a cabin window and caused the window to depart from the airplane, the cabin to rapidly depressurize, and the passenger fatality.

factors.evidence: a low-cycle fatigue crack in the dovetail of fan blade No. 13 caused the blade to detach from the fan disk (p. 462)

the detached blade fragment struck the fan case at the six o'clock position; although it did not penetrate the case, the impact caused the cowling latch to fail and engine cowling to detach (p. 462-463)

the impact of the separated fan blade with the fan case imparted significant loads into the fan cowl through the radial restraint fitting, causing cracks that propagated forward and aft, severing three latch assemblies (p. 462)
the inboard fan cowl aft latch keeper struck the fuselage near the cabin window at row 14, breaking the window and causing rapid depressurization (p. 462)
the aircraft rolled to the left by 41.3° as a result of the engine failure and structural damage (p. 690-691)

events.text: Fan blade No. 13 in left CFM56-7B engine fractured due to low-cycle fatigue crack at the dovetail
Cabin altitude warning horn activated; cabin altitude exceeded 10,000 ft due to window breach
Aircraft uncommanded left roll reached maximum of 41.3°
Pilot flying (first officer) began emergency descent; right engine power reduced to idle
Left engine fuel cutoff; engine began windmilling
Aircraft landed successfully at Philadelphia International Airport runway 27L

cvr.speaker: SYS
cvr.text: Loud bang and increased background noise; flight crew felt significant airplane vibration

cvr.speaker: CAP
cvr.text: Southwest thirteen eighty has an engine fire descending

cvr.speaker: CAP
cvr.text: we're single engine descending have fire in number one

recommendations.text: Require Boeing to determine the critical fan blade impact location(s) on the CFM56-7B engine fan case and redesign the fan cowl structure on all Boeing 737 next-generation-series airplanes to ensure the structural integrity of the fan cowl after a fan-blade-out event
Once the actions requested in Safety Recommendation A-19-17 are completed, require Boeing to install the redesigned fan cowl structure on new-production 737 next-generation-series airplanes

Once the actions requested in Safety Recommendation A-19-17 are completed, require operators of Boeing 737 next-generation-series airplanes to retrofit their airplanes with the redesigned fan cowl structure

Expand the Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 25 and 33 certification requirements to mandate that airplane and engine manufacturers work collaboratively to analyze all critical fan blade impact locations for all engine operating conditions, the resulting fan blade fragmentation, and the effects of the fan-blade-out-generated loads on the nacelle structure
Develop and issue guidance on ways that air carriers can mitigate hazards to passengers affected by an in-flight loss of seating capacity

Include the lessons learned from the accident involving Southwest Airlines flight 1380 in initial and recurrent flight attendant training, emphasizing the importance of being secured in a jumpseat during emergency landings

Expand your certification requirements for transport-category airplanes and aircraft engines to mandate that airplane and engine manufacturers work collaboratively to analyze all critical fan blade impact locations for all engine operating conditions, the resulting fan blade fragmentation, and the effects of the fan-blade-out-generated loads on the nacelle structure

safety_changes: CFM developed eddy current inspection (ECI) procedure for fan blades at overhaul to detect subsurface cracks
CFM developed on-wing ultrasonic inspection technique for fan blade relubrication to detect cracks before critical failure
FAA and EASA issued multiple airworthiness directives requiring enhanced fan blade inspections on CFM56-7B engines

notes: Sections read: Executive Summary (p. viii), History of Flight (p. 644-843), Findings (p. 4406-4464), Probable Cause (p. 4465-4472), Recommendations (p. 4479-4511)
Fan blade impact at six o'clock position was critical to fan cowl failure; certification tests used twelve o'clock position
Fatigue crack likely initiated before October 2012 overhaul but not detected by fluorescent penetrant inspection

records.title: Lion Air 610

agencies.name: Komite Nasional Keselamatan Transportasi
agencies.report_title: Final Aircraft Accident Investigation Report, PT. Lion Mentari Airlines Boeing 737-8 (MAX) PK-LQP

location.name: Java Sea off Karawang, West Java

records.summary: A replacement angle-of-attack sensor fitted the previous day had been miscalibrated by about 21 degrees during repair, and the same fault had produced a stick shaker and repeated automatic nose-down trim on the previous flight, which the crew countered with the trim cutout switches but did not fully record. On flight 610 the stick shaker activated at rotation and, after flap retraction, MCAS repeatedly trimmed the stabilizer nose down. The captain countered with electric trim for several minutes, then handed control to the first officer, whose shorter trim inputs did not keep up; the aircraft dived into the Java Sea about 12 minutes after takeoff.
records.probable_cause: The KNKT identified nine contributing factors: the MCAS design's reliance on a single AOA sensor and the assumptions made about pilot response during development; the AOA sensor that had been miscalibrated during repair by Xtra Aerospace; the installation test that failed to detect the miscalibration; the AOA DISAGREE alert that was not functional on the aircraft; the absence of MCAS information in the flight manuals and pilot training; the incomplete documentation of the previous flight's defects, which meant the aircraft was dispatched with an unresolved problem; the multiple alerts, repetitive MCAS activations and distractions which were not effectively managed; and the crew's ineffective communication and coordination, in the context of the first officer's demonstrated difficulty in handling the aircraft.

factors.evidence: The left AOA sensor installed at Denpasar on 28 October had been miscalibrated by about 21 degrees during repair at Xtra Aerospace, and the post-installation test did not detect the bias.
From rotation the FDR recorded a left-right AOA difference of about 20 degrees that persisted to the end of the recording.

The previous flight (Denpasar to Jakarta) had experienced the same stick shaker and automatic trim; the crew wrote up IAS and ALT disagree and the feel differential pressure light but not the stick shaker or trim runaway, so the aircraft was dispatched.
The left stick shaker activated during rotation and continued for most of the flight.
The erroneous AOA corrupted the left-side airspeed and altitude, producing IAS DISAGREE and ALT DISAGREE indications.
After flap retraction the FDR recorded repeated automatic nose-down stabilizer trim, more than 20 activations, which stopped only while the flaps were re-extended.
MCAS relied on a single AOA input and could repeatedly command stabilizer motion; the report cited the design and development assumptions about pilot reaction as contributing.
The report found that the assumptions used in MCAS's functional hazard assessment about pilot recognition and response were not consistent with the accident crew's actual response.
The AOA DISAGREE alert was not functional on the aircraft because the optional AOA indicator had not been purchased, a fact Boeing had not communicated to operators.
MCAS was not described in the flight crew operations manual or training and the non-functional AOA DISAGREE alert had not been disclosed.
The flight crew had received no information or training on MCAS and were expected to treat its effects as a runaway stabilizer.
The report found ineffective communication and coordination between the pilots, including when control was transferred to the first officer without a clear briefing of the trim problem.
Multiple alerts, repetitive MCAS activations, ATC communication and checklist reading distracted the crew and were not effectively managed.
The first officer's shorter nose-up trim inputs did not fully counter the automatic nose-down trim and the stabilizer moved toward full nose down; aft column force could not stop the dive.
The aircraft entered a steep dive and struck the sea at high speed about 12 minutes after takeoff.

events.text: At Denpasar on 28 October the left AOA sensor is replaced with a unit repaired by Xtra Aerospace; the installation test does not reveal a 21-degree calibration bias.

On the previous flight (Denpasar to Jakarta) the stick shaker activates at rotation and automatic nose-down trim occurs after flap retraction; the crew set the stabilizer trim cutout switches and continue to Jakarta, recording IAS/ALT DISAGREE and the feel differential pressure light but not the stick shaker or trim.
Takeoff from runway 25L; during rotation the left stick shaker activates and the FDR records a left-right AOA difference of about 20 degrees.
First officer asks ATC to confirm the aircraft's altitude, then at 23:21:28 reports a flight control problem.
Flaps retracted; shortly afterwards the FDR records automatic nose-down trim for about 10 seconds followed by crew nose-up electric trim.
Flaps re-extended to 5; the automatic nose-down trim stops.
First officer asks ATC for the aircraft's speed as displayed on radar and requests a holding point; ATC assigns altitudes and headings while the crew work the problem.
Flaps retracted to 0 again; automatic nose-down trim resumes and the captain repeatedly counters each activation with nose-up electric trim, more than 20 cycles.
Captain asks the first officer to run the non-normal checklist for airspeed unreliable; the checklist reading is interrupted by ATC communications.
Captain hands control to the first officer without describing the trim problem, and takes over the radio and checklist.
The first officer's nose-up trim inputs are shorter than the automatic nose-down inputs; the stabilizer moves progressively nose down and the aircraft begins to descend.
First officer reports he cannot hold the aircraft up; both pilots pull on the control columns.
End of FDR recording; the aircraft strikes the Java Sea at high speed in a steep nose-down attitude.

recommendations.text: Redesign MCAS so that it is not vulnerable to a single erroneous AOA input and consider the effect of all flight-deck alerts and indications on flight-crew recognition and response.
recommendations.outcome: MCAS was redesigned to compare both AOA sensors and to limit activation and authority; FAA AD 2020-24-02.

recommendations.text: Review the assumptions used in the aircraft certification process about pilot recognition and reaction time to flight control system failures.
Improve the reporting of technical defects by flight crews and the hazard identification and risk assessment of reported problems so that aircraft are not dispatched with unresolved defects.
Ensure that AOA sensor repair and calibration procedures and their oversight prevent the release of miscalibrated units.
recommendations.outcome: The FAA revoked Xtra Aerospace's repair station certificate in October 2019.

recommendations.text: Improve crew resource management training, including the handover of control and the management of multiple simultaneous alerts.

safety_changes: FAA Emergency Airworthiness Directive 2018-23-51 (November 2018) reminded 737 MAX crews of the runaway stabilizer procedure for erroneous AOA conditions.
After the Ethiopian Airlines 302 accident the 737 MAX was grounded worldwide until MCAS was redesigned and recertified in November 2020.
The FAA revoked the repair station certificate of Xtra Aerospace, which had repaired the accident AOA sensor.

notes: The accident date is 29 October 2018 local time (WIB); in UTC the flight departed at 23:20 on 28 October, which is why t0 is on 2018-10-28.
t0 is the departure time to the minute as stated in the report; events without a clock string are placed by approximate offset from the report narrative.
The count of MCAS activations (more than 20) is from the report narrative; individual activation times are not listed.
Recommendation ids are not given because the KNKT numbering was not verified.
The report contains a CVR transcript, but no lines are quoted here because exact wording was not verified.

records.title: Atlas Air 3591

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Rapid Descent and Crash into Water, Atlas Air Inc. Flight 3591, Boeing 767-375BCF, N1217A, Trinity Bay, Texas, February 23, 2019

records.operator: Atlas Air (operating for Amazon Prime Air)
records.summary: Descending toward Houston through turbulence and cloud around a line of weather, the 767 freighter's go-around mode was inadvertently triggered, most likely when the first officer's wrist bumped the go-around switch while he was manipulating the speedbrake lever. The autopilot pitched up and thrust increased; the first officer, experiencing a somatogravic illusion that the airplane was pitching up steeply and stalling, pushed the nose down to nearly 50 degrees. The captain did not take control in time and the airplane struck Trinity Bay about 30 seconds later, killing the two pilots and a jumpseat passenger.
records.probable_cause: The inappropriate response by the first officer as the pilot flying to an inadvertent activation of the go-around mode, which led to his spatial disorientation and nose-down control inputs that placed the airplane in a steep descent from which the crew did not recover. Contributing to the accident was the captain's failure to adequately monitor the airplane's flightpath and assume positive control of the airplane to effectively intervene. Also contributing were systemic deficiencies in the aviation industry's selection and performance measurement practices, which failed to address the first officer's aptitude-related deficiencies and maladaptive stress response. Also contributing to the accident was the Federal Aviation Administration's failure to implement the pilot records database in a sufficiently robust and timely manner.

factors.evidence: The go-around mode was most likely activated inadvertently when the first officer's wrist or watch contacted the go-around switch on the thrust lever while he was moving the speedbrake lever in turbulence.
Neither pilot recognized that go-around mode had engaged; the resulting pitch-up and thrust increase were not understood as an automation mode change.
The unexpected pitch-up and acceleration startled the first officer, triggering a maladaptive stress response.
The forward acceleration from go-around thrust in cloud produced a false sensation of steep pitch-up; the first officer believed the airplane was pitching up excessively and stalling.
The first officer became spatially disoriented and did not use the attitude indicator to correct his perception of the airplane's attitude.
The first officer called out that the airplane was stalling although airspeed was increasing and angle of attack was low.
The first officer pushed the control column forward, driving pitch to about 49 degrees nose down with thrust still high.
The airplane was deviating around a line of convective weather in instrument conditions with light to moderate turbulence, removing outside visual references.
The captain did not adequately monitor the flightpath as the airplane pitched down and did not recognize the developing upset for several seconds.
The captain did not assume positive control of the airplane in time; his eventual aft column inputs were too late to recover.
Atlas Air's hiring process did not obtain the first officer's full training history, which included repeated training failures at previous employers that he had not disclosed.
The FAA had not implemented the pilot records database required by the 2010 Airline Safety Act in a sufficiently robust and timely manner, so his record was not available to Atlas.
Industry pilot selection and performance measurement practices did not identify or address the first officer's aptitude-related deficiencies during training.
The airplane entered a steep dive at high speed and struck the water about 32 seconds after go-around mode activation.

events.text: Houston approach clears the flight to descend and coordinates deviations west around a line of thunderstorms; the airplane is in cloud with turbulence.
The first officer, as pilot flying with the autopilot engaged, calls for flaps 1 as the airplane descends through about 6,300 feet and prepares for a turn toward the approach.
The first officer moves the speedbrake lever with his left hand; turbulence jostles the airplane.
Go-around mode activates, most likely from inadvertent contact with the go-around switch on the thrust lever; the autothrottle advances thrust and the autopilot commands a pitch-up.
Thrust increases toward go-around power; the airplane accelerates and begins to pitch up about 4 degrees.
Feeling a strong sensation of pitching up, the first officer pushes the control column forward, overriding the autopilot; he says something to the effect that the airplane is stalling.
The autopilot disconnects; pitch passes through nose-down and continues toward 49 degrees nose down with thrust near maximum; airspeed rises rapidly.
The captain, who had been handling the radios and the flap selection, expresses confusion about what is happening; he does not take control.
The airplane breaks out of cloud in a steep dive over the bay; the ground proximity warning sounds.
Both pilots pull aft on the control columns; pitch begins to recover toward about 20 degrees nose down but the airplane is too low and too fast.
The airplane strikes the shallow water of Trinity Bay at high speed and is destroyed; all three occupants die.

recommendations.text: Complete implementation of the pilot records database so that air carriers can obtain a pilot's complete training and employment history, including records from previous employers, before hiring.
recommendations.outcome: The Pilot Records Database final rule was issued in 2021 and became mandatory for carriers.

recommendations.text: Require air carriers to include in pilot training a scenario-based understanding of inadvertent go-around mode activation and of somatogravic illusion, with practice in recognizing and recovering from resulting unusual attitudes.
Develop pilot selection and performance measurement methods that identify aptitude-related deficiencies and maladaptive stress responses during training and before pilots enter line operations.
Evaluate the location and activation force of go-around switches on the 767 and similar types to reduce the likelihood of inadvertent activation.

safety_changes: The FAA published the Pilot Records Database final rule in 2021, requiring carriers to report and check pilot training and employment records.
Atlas Air and other carriers revised hiring practices to obtain complete training histories and strengthened monitoring of pilots with repeated training failures.
Operators added training on inadvertent go-around mode activation, somatogravic illusion and upset recovery in instrument conditions.
The report reinforced pilot monitoring and intervention guidance for captains when the first officer is pilot flying.

notes: Go-around mode activation is placed at about 12:38:31 CST and impact about 32 seconds later; both are as recalled from the report and could be off by several seconds.
Altitude at go-around activation (about 6,200 feet) and the maximum nose-down pitch (about 49 degrees) are as stated in the report; intermediate pitch values are approximate.

records.title: Ethiopian Airlines 302

agencies.name: Ethiopian Civil Aviation Authority Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau Investigation Report on Accident to the B737-MAX8 Reg. ET-AVJ operated by Ethiopian Airlines

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: NTSB comments on the AIB-ET final report

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses
agencies.report_title: BEA comments on the AIB-ET final report

location.name: Near Bishoftu (Ejere), Oromia, about 28 nm south-east of Addis Ababa

records.summary: Shortly after lift-off from Addis Ababa the left angle-of-attack sensor failed and recorded about 74.5 degrees, triggering the left stick shaker and erroneous left-side airspeed and altitude. With flaps up and autopilot disengaged, MCAS repeatedly trimmed the stabilizer nose down. The crew cut out the electric stabilizer trim but, at high speed with takeoff thrust still set, could not trim manually, re-engaged electric trim, and a final MCAS activation drove the aircraft into a dive from which it did not recover. All 157 on board died.
records.probable_cause: The AIB-ET concluded that repetitive and uncommanded airplane-nose-down inputs from MCAS, due to erroneous AOA input, and its unrecoverable activation system made the airplane dive close to the ground and was the most probable cause. Contributing factors included MCAS's reliance on a single AOA sensor and its unlimited repetitive authority, the absence of MCAS information and training for flight crews, the lack of an AOA DISAGREE alert on the aircraft, and the multiple simultaneous warnings and high workload the design imposed on the crew.

factors.evidence: Seconds after lift-off the left AOA value deviated from the right and reached 74.5 degrees while the right AOA stayed near 15 degrees; the left value stayed erroneous to the end of the recording.
The left stick shaker activated at the AOA failure and remained active until near the end of the recording.
Left-side airspeed, altitude and flight director pitch bar deviated from the right side; the left overspeed clacker later sounded while the left IAS read lower than the right.

After flap retraction and autopilot disconnect the FDR recorded automatic nose-down stabilizer trim at 05:40:00 (9 s), 05:40:20, 05:40:41 (no motion, cutout) and a final activation at 05:43:20 that moved the stabilizer from 2.3 to 1.0 units.
The autopilot disengaged at 05:39:55; MCAS operates only with the autopilot off and flaps up, and the first automatic nose-down trim followed five seconds later.
MCAS took input from a single AOA sensor and could re-activate repeatedly with full authority; the report identified the design as a contributing factor.
The report found that the MCAS safety assessment and certification did not adequately account for a single erroneous AOA input and for pilot reaction assumptions.
The AOA DISAGREE alert was not functional on this aircraft and multiple simultaneous alerts (stick shaker, master caution, overspeed, GPWS) did not identify the failure.
The report found that MCAS was not described in the flight crew operations manual and that information provided to operators after the Lion Air accident was insufficient.
The report cited shortcomings in FAA oversight of the MCAS certification and in the post-Lion Air continued airworthiness decisions.
The crew had received no simulator training on MCAS or on runaway stabilizer at high speed; the report cited the lack of MCAS training as contributing.

Engine thrust remained at the takeoff setting of about 94 percent N1 throughout; indicated airspeed rose to and beyond VMO (340 kt), making manual trim impossible and finally exceeding 458 kt (left) and 500 kt (right).
With the stabilizer trim cut out, the first officer reported the manual trim wheel was not working at high speed; aft column force on both columns could not overcome the mistrimmed stabilizer.
The crew handled stick shaker, unreliable airspeed, GPWS DON'T SINK, master caution, overspeed warning and ATC communications simultaneously during the first minutes after takeoff.
After the final MCAS activation the pitch reached about 40 degrees nose down and the aircraft struck the ground at very high speed.

events.text: Takeoff roll on runway 07R; engines stabilise at about 94 percent N1, which they hold for the rest of the flight.
Shortly after lift-off the left AOA value deviates from the right, reaching 74.5 degrees; left stick shaker activates and stays on; left airspeed and altitude begin to read low.
Left autopilot engaged at about 1,000 ft radio altitude; it disengages about 33 seconds later.
Captain requests flaps up; flap lever moved from 5 to 0.
Autopilot disengages.
First automatic nose-down stabilizer trim (MCAS) for 9 seconds; trim moves from 4.60 to 2.1 units; the climb is arrested and the aircraft descends slightly.
GPWS 'DON'T SINK' sounds for 3 seconds.
Manual electric trim nose up recorded; stabilizer moves to 2.4 units. Pitch about 2 degrees nose down.
Second automatic nose-down trim; stabilizer reaches 0.4 units. Three more GPWS 'DON'T SINK' warnings follow.
Manual electric trim nose up; stabilizer reverses and reaches 2.3 units.
First officer calls 'stab trim cut-out' twice; captain agrees and the stabilizer trim cutout switches are set to cutout.
Third automatic nose-down trim command with no stabilizer motion, consistent with the cutout switches being in cutout.
First officer asks ATC to maintain 14,000 ft and reports a flight control problem; ATC approves.
Right overspeed clacker sounds and remains active to the end. Left IAS has risen from about 305 kt toward 340 kt with aft force held on both columns.
Captain asks whether the trim is functional; the first officer says it is not working and tries the manual trim wheel, then reports at 05:41:54 that it is not working.
Both pilots call out 'left alpha vane' after a master caution.

Two momentary manual electric nose-up trim inputs are recorded at about 13,400 ft pressure altitude, indicating the trim cutout switches had been returned to normal; stabilizer moves from 2.1 to 2.3 units.
Final automatic nose-down trim moves the stabilizer from 2.3 to 1.0 units in about 5 seconds; the aircraft pitches nose down despite aft force on both columns, reaching about 40 degrees nose down.
End of recording; impact near Bishoftu. Left IAS about 458 kt and right IAS about 500 kt; last recorded pressure altitude 5,419 ft (left).

recommendations.text: Ensure that the 737 MAX flight control system (MCAS) is redesigned so that it does not rely on a single AOA input and cannot repeatedly command stabilizer motion with full authority, and that the redesign is certified and validated before return to service.
recommendations.outcome: FAA AD 2020-24-02 (November 2020) mandated flight control software using both AOA sensors, single MCAS activation per event and limited authority, plus an AOA DISAGREE alert.

recommendations.text: Provide flight crews with full system information and simulator training on MCAS and on runaway stabilizer and high-speed manual trim before the aircraft returns to service.
recommendations.outcome: Simulator training on MCAS-related scenarios became mandatory for 737 MAX pilots before return to service.

recommendations.text: Review the certification process for the MCAS system and for flight-crew reaction assumptions in the aircraft safety assessment.
recommendations.outcome: US Aircraft Certification, Safety, and Accountability Act (December 2020) reformed delegated certification.

recommendations.text: Improve flight-deck alerting so that a single AOA failure and the resulting cascade of warnings can be quickly recognised by the crew.

dissent.position: In comments published after the final report, the NTSB stated that the report did not adequately address the flight crew's performance, in particular that thrust was left at takeoff power for the entire flight, that the crew did not perform the runaway stabilizer procedure completely or promptly, and that the crew had been trained on the MCAS-related emergency AD after the Lion Air accident. The NTSB also stated that the left AOA sensor was most likely damaged by a bird or foreign object rather than by a production quality or electrical defect as the report suggested.

The BEA published comments stating that the report should have given weight to the crew's handling of the situation: thrust remaining at takeoff setting leading to an overspeed, the incomplete application of the runaway stabilizer procedure, the re-engagement of electric trim, and crew resource management; the BEA also considered the AOA vane most likely separated after a bird strike.

safety_changes: Worldwide grounding of the Boeing 737 MAX fleet from March 2019 until the redesigned flight control software was certified (FAA return-to-service November 2020).
MCAS redesigned to use both AOA sensors, activate only once per high-AOA event, and never command more stabilizer movement than the crew can counter with the control column.
AOA DISAGREE alert made standard on all 737 MAX aircraft and mandatory simulator training on MCAS scenarios for MAX pilots.
US Aircraft Certification, Safety, and Accountability Act (2020) reformed FAA delegation of certification work to manufacturers.

notes: Timeline clock times and stabilizer units are taken from the AIB-ET preliminary and final report narrative; the takeoff-roll event time (t=-70) is approximate.
Recommendation ids are not given because the exact AIB-ET numbering was not verified; the text reflects the report's key recommendations.
The NTSB docket URL is given from memory (DCA19RA101); the AIB-ET report URL is the agency home page.
CVR lines are the short callouts quoted in the report narrative, not a verbatim transcript.

records.title: Miami Air Flight 293
records.summary: Miami Air Flight 293, a Boeing 737-800 military charter, landed on runway 10 at Jacksonville Naval Air Station during heavy rain and thunderstorms. The aircraft touched down approximately 1,600 feet beyond the displaced threshold, reducing available landing distance to 7,800 feet. Hydroplaning on the wet ungrooved runway prevented effective braking. The left thrust reverser was inoperative. The aircraft overran the runway, struck a rock embankment, and came to rest in the St. Johns River in shallow water. All 143 occupants were rescued with 21 injured but no fatalities.
records.probable_cause: Hydroplaning caused by heavy rainfall on the ungrooved runway prevented effective braking. Pilot errors during approach and landing, including a long touchdown, had little effect on the final outcome as the aircraft would have been unable to stop regardless due to hydroplaning conditions.

factors.evidence: Heavy rainfall on ungrooved runway 10 caused hydroplaning which precluded effective braking action (p. 4-6)
Weather observation at 2122 reported 5 miles visibility with heavy rain, thunderstorms, and mist; visibility reduced to 3 miles by 2145 (p. 20-31)
Heavy thunderstorms with frequent lightning overhead at time of landing; cumulus clouds at 800-1,500 feet AGL (p. 20-31)

Aircraft landed on runway 10 with wind from 240 degrees at 10 knots, creating tailwind component; using runway 10 reduced available landing distance to 7,800 feet due to displaced threshold (p. 79-80, 111-112)
Aircraft touched down approximately 1,600 feet beyond the displaced threshold, reducing available runway distance for landing (p. 85-86, 111-116)
Aircraft overran runway 10, crossed overrun area, struck rock embankment, and came to rest in St. Johns River approximately 1,200 feet from end of runway (p. 85-92)

events.text: Jacksonville approach control advises pilot to expect RNAV runway 28 approach with moderate-to-heavy precipitation on final approach (p. 42-48)
Pilot requests runway 10 due to better weather appearance; controller advises moderate-to-heavy precipitation building over runway 10; pilot acknowledges and remains with runway 28 (p. 50-54)
Controller reports both runways 'pretty rough' and 'socked in'; pilot vectored for RNAV runway 28 approach (p. 56-62)
Controller advises pilot that runway 10 might be better as precipitation moving eastbound; pilot agrees 'yeah go ahead, let's do it' and is vectored for runway 10 approach (p. 70-74)
Controller clears flight for RNAV runway 10 approach; flight transferred to radar controller (p. 75-77)
Radar controller reports winds from 240 degrees at 10 knots and clears aircraft to land on runway 10 approximately 5 nautical miles from threshold (p. 78-81)
Pilot reports field in sight to radar controller; no further communications before landing (p. 81-84)
Aircraft touches down approximately 1,600 feet beyond runway 10 displaced threshold; tire marks show touchdown point (p. 85-86, 111-116)
Aircraft hydroplanes on wet ungrooved runway, unable to maintain braking control; veers right of centerline and departs runway surface onto grass (p. 118-123)

Aircraft strikes rock embankment at end of runway 10 overrun area; both main landing gears separate and aircraft comes to rest in shallow water of St. Johns River approximately 1,200 feet from runway end (p. 85-92)
All 143 occupants evacuated using forward and overwing exits and deployed life rafts; 21 injured but no fatalities reported (p. 99-104)

notes: NTSB investigative update read (not final report)
Heavy rain with 0.63 inches precipitation since 2053 local time
Wind shifted from 350 degrees at landing to 240 degrees, creating tailwind
Left thrust reverser was inoperative
First officer had only 18 hours experience in Boeing 737
All occupants rescued with 21 injuries, zero fatalities
Probable cause from summary_record: hydroplaning on ungrooved runway

records.title: Aeroflot 1492
records.summary: Aeroflot Flight 1492, a Sukhoi Superjet 100 scheduled passenger flight from Moscow Sheremetyevo to Murmansk, was struck by lightning during climb-out at flight level 8,900 meters. The lightning strike caused failure of primary radio and autopilot systems, forcing the aircraft to revert to DIRECT mode flight control. The crew returned to Sheremetyevo for an emergency landing. During approach, the aircraft encountered crosswind conditions and bounced on landing. After bouncing, the aircraft touched down hard, the landing gear collapsed, and fuel spilled from the wings. A post-impact fire erupted in the rear fuselage, killing 41 of 78 occupants. The accident was precipitated by lightning-induced systems failure combined with challenging approach conditions and non-optimal landing technique.
records.probable_cause: The accident was caused by a combination of factors: (1) Lightning strike at FL89 causing primary radio and autopilot inoperative conditions, resulting in flight control mode degradation to DIRECT mode; (2) Crew attempt to land with excessive crosswind component; (3) Aircraft bounce on landing with subsequent hard touchdown causing landing gear collapse; (4) Fuel system structural damage resulting in fuel spillage from wings; (5) Post-impact fire in rear fuselage section. The investigation determined the crew encountered challenging approach conditions including crosswind and executed landing procedures while aircraft was in degraded DIRECT control mode without standard flight control system protections.

factors.evidence: Aircraft struck by lightning at flight level 8,900 meters at 15:08 UTC. Primary radio and autopilot became inoperative due to electrical failures from lightning strike (p. 15)

Flight control mode degraded from normal to DIRECT mode following lightning strike. DIRECT mode represents degraded, more challenging aircraft operation without normal flight control law protections and automatic trim functions (p. 15-16)
Aircraft bounced on landing, then touched down hard. FDR data and physical evidence confirmed hard landing resulting in landing gear structure failure and fuselage damage (p. 16-17)
Landing gear collapsed under impact forces from hard landing. Aircraft fuselage contacted runway surface during gear collapse sequence (p. 17)
Fuel system structural integrity compromised during hard landing and gear collapse. Fuel spilled from wing fuel tanks following impact (p. 17)

Post-impact fire erupted in rear fuselage section. Fire propagated rapidly due to fuel spillage and aircraft interior materials. Fire caused fatalities and forced evacuation from rear exits (p. 17-18)

Fire in rear section of fuselage prevented evacuation from rear doors. Passengers and crew evacuated primarily from forward doors using slides. 41 of 78 occupants perished, primarily those unable to evacuate from rear sections (p. 18)

events.text: Aeroflot Flight SU-1492 (AFL1492) departed Moscow Sheremetyevo Airport on runway 24C bound for Murmansk. Aircraft carried 2 flight crew, 3 cabin crew, and 73 passengers (78 total occupants). Aircraft configured for scheduled passenger operation.
Six minutes into flight at flight level 8,900 meters (FL89), aircraft was struck by lightning. Lightning strike caused immediate electrical system failures affecting critical aircraft systems.

Following lightning strike: Primary radio systems became inoperative. Autopilot systems became inoperative. Flight control mode automatically reverted to DIRECT mode as a consequence of system failures. DIRECT mode is a degraded control law without normal protections and automatic trim.

Captain assumed manual control of aircraft in DIRECT mode. Transponder code changed to 7700 (emergency). Crew initiated return to Moscow Sheremetyevo Airport for emergency landing due to loss of primary radio and autopilot capabilities.
Aircraft established communications via secondary radio. ATC coordinated emergency descent and approach to Sheremetyevo. Weather conditions reported with crosswind component relative to runway 24L.

Aircraft on final approach to runway 24L in DIRECT control mode. Crew configured aircraft for landing with flaps at 25 degrees in preparation for overweight landing. Crosswind component present but crew did not initiate go-around.

Aircraft bounced on landing. After bounce, aircraft touched down hard at runway surface. Landing gear shock struts exceeded design load limits. Fuselage contacted runway surface during landing sequence.

Landing gear structural failure and collapse. Main landing gear legs separated from fuselage. Fuel system structural damage sustained during hard impact and gear collapse. Fuel spilled rapidly from wing fuel tanks. Post-impact fire erupted in rear fuselage section, propagated by fuel and interior materials. Fire rapidly consumed rear section of aircraft, preventing evacuation from rear doors. Passengers and crew evacuated from forward doors using emergency slides. 41 of 78 occupants died; majority from fire exposure or evacuation barrier created by fire.

recommendations.text: Develop and implement enhanced crew training procedures for emergency operations in degraded flight control modes including DIRECT mode

recommendations.recipient: Sukhoi Civil Aircraft and aircraft manufacturers
recommendations.text: Review and enhance lightning strike protection systems for critical avionics and flight control computers
Implement procedures ensuring crew executes go-around when crosswind limits are approached or exceeded during approach
Enhance emergency evacuation procedures and training for incidents involving post-impact fire in rear fuselage sections
Review structural integrity of landing gear attachment points and fuel system components to withstand hard landing scenarios
Establish mandatory go-around procedures when aircraft control systems are degraded and approach conditions are marginal
Review redundancy of primary flight control systems to reduce likelihood of complete mode reversion to DIRECT control
Enhance weather reporting and crosswind forecasting for Moscow Sheremetyevo operations

records.title: 2019 Alaska mid-air collision

aircraft.type: de Havilland DHC-2 Beaver / DHC-3 Turbine Otter

records.summary: On May 13, 2019, a DHC-2 Beaver floatplane (N952DB) operated by Mountain Air Service and a DHC-3 Otter floatplane (N959PA) operated by Taquan Air collided in mid-air about 8 miles northeast of Ketchikan, Alaska. Both aircraft were conducting sightseeing flights under visual flight rules. The DHC-2 broke up in mid-air with 5 occupants killed. The DHC-3 sustained damage but was landed by the pilot with 1 passenger killed and 9 serious injuries.
records.probable_cause: The inherent limitations of the see-and-avoid concept, which prevented the two pilots from seeing the other airplane before the collision, and the absence of visual and aural alerts from both airplanes' traffic display systems, while operating in a geographic area with a high concentration of air tour activity. Contributing to the accident were (1) the Federal Aviation Administration's provision of new transceivers that lacked alerting capability to Capstone Program operators without adequately mitigating the increased risk associated with the consequent loss of the previously available alerting capability and (2) the absence of a requirement for airborne traffic advisory systems with aural alerting among operators who carry passengers for hire. (p. 1-2)

factors.evidence: Both aircraft were conducting sightseeing flights under visual flight rules where the pilot of each aircraft is responsible for visually ensuring adequate separation from other air traffic in Class G airspace. (p. 1)

The DHC-3 automatic alert feature had been disabled by an equipment change, while the DHC-2 system's alert did not trigger because avionics in the DHC-3 were not broadcasting the aircraft's altitude. (p. 2)
The DHC-2 pilot's view was obscured by aircraft structure and a passenger in the right-hand seat; the DHC-2 was blocked from the DHC-3 pilot's view by the left front window post. (p. 2)
The two aircraft collided at approximately 12:21 local time at an altitude of about 3,350 feet MSL. (p. 1)

events.text: DHC-3 (N959PA) departed Rudyerd Bay for Ketchikan under company VFR flight plan as Part 135 sightseeing flight. (p. 3)
Both aircraft were returning to Ketchikan Harbor Seaplane Base approximately 7 miles southwest in visual meteorological conditions at approximately 3,350 feet. (p. 1)
DHC-3 pilot did not perceive any ADS-B collision warnings before seeing a flash to his left as aircraft began collision sequence. (p. 1)
One of the passengers in the DHC-3 reportedly saw the other aircraft before collision and yelled 'pull up' before impact. (p. 1)
The two aircraft collided at 12:21 local time at altitude of approximately 3,350 feet MSL about 8 miles northeast of Ketchikan. DHC-2 broke up in mid-air. (p. 1)

DHC-2 created debris field approximately 2,000 by 1,000 feet about 1.75 miles southwest of DHC-3 crash site. DHC-3 sustained substantial damage but was landed by pilot at Ketchikan Harbor Seaplane Base. (p. 1)
Search and rescue teams located survivors and fatalities. Five occupants killed in DHC-2; one passenger and one crew fatality in DHC-3 with nine passengers seriously injured. (p. 3-4)

records.title: Ural Airlines 178
records.summary: During takeoff rotation at 03:13:44 UTC+3, the aircraft struck a flock of large gulls at approximately 2 meters altitude, causing damage to both CFM56-5B engines. The damage reduced total available thrust below single-engine thrust requirements. The crew did not retract the landing gear after takeoff due to a missed callout of positive climb by the first officer, preventing the aircraft from climbing effectively. After reaching a maximum altitude of approximately 315 feet, the aircraft was unable to maintain altitude and speed, resulting in a belly landing in a corn field with landing gear partially extended and flaps in takeoff configuration.
records.probable_cause: The accident resulted from a bird strike during takeoff that damaged both engines, reducing available thrust below the minimum required for single-engine climb. The inability to continue the flight was compounded by the crew's failure to retract the landing gear after takeoff due to a missed callout of positive climb, which resulted from a breakdown in crew coordination and contributed to the aircraft's inability to maintain minimum climb performance.

factors.evidence: Multiple seagulls with individual masses exceeding 1.13 kg struck the aircraft shortly after liftoff at approximately 2-4 feet altitude, as confirmed by CVR sound effects, eyewitness accounts, bird remains found on the aircraft and runway, and bird feather fragments located in the wing leading edge devices (p. 178-179).

Both CFM56-5B engines sustained damage from bird ingestion, with vibration levels reaching maximum recordable values (9.8 units) within one second of impact. The left engine thrust decreased to approximately idle, and the right engine thrust decreased by approximately 20%, resulting in total available thrust below the single-engine thrust available at FLEX 49 takeoff mode (p. 177-178).

The first officer did not properly call out 'positive climb' after liftoff, contrary to standard operating procedures. The CVR recording does not capture the word 'POSITIVE' in the FO's call, indicating a missed call that resulted in the failure to retract the landing gear as required by procedures (p. 177, 179, 219).

The landing gear was not retracted after takeoff, remaining in the extended position throughout the flight. Standard operating procedures for engine failure after V1 require landing gear retraction, which would have reduced drag significantly and improved climb performance. The crew did not acknowledge the positive climb callout requirement due to the FO's missed callout (p. 177, 219).

Unable to maintain altitude or climb performance with the damaged engines and extended landing gear, the aircraft descended at 3-4 m/s and executed a belly landing in a corn field at 03:15:17.7, touching down with landing gear partially retracted (unarmed), flaps in takeoff configuration (CONF 1+F), and pitch angle of approximately 8 degrees nose-up (p. 190-192).

events.text: Takeoff roll begins on runway 12
First officer calls V1 and rotate
Aircraft rotates and lifts off runway at airspeed 181 kt

Bird strike: flock of seagulls strikes aircraft at 2-4 feet altitude; rotor vibration increases to maximum levels on both engines (9.8 units); left engine thrust drops to near idle; right engine thrust decreases by approximately 20%

ECAM alert: 'ENG 1 REVERSE UNLOCKED' with amber caution level; Master Caution light and audio warning (single chime) activated (caused by bird strike damage to reverser position sensor, not actual reverser malfunction)
First officer: 'Climb' call (word POSITIVE not audible on CVR); Captain does not respond
Captain deflects right rudder pedal (offset 8 units); landing gear not retracted due to missed positive climb callout
Captain engages Autopilot No. 1 (left); aircraft at 230 feet altitude, 171 kt airspeed
Aircraft reaches maximum altitude of approximately 315 feet (300 feet above runway); autothrottle maintains SRS (Speed Reference System) mode attempting to hold V2+10 kt
Autopilot disengages automatically due to pilot rudder pedal deflection exceeding trimmed position; AP OFF warning generated (red on ECAM); continuous Master Warning and audio alert (continuous tone)
EGPWS 'DON'T SINK' warning activated
Captain attempts to declare emergency: 'PAN-PAN, PAN-PAN, PAN-PAN, Свердловск...' (phrase not completed)
ECAM warning: 'ENG 1 EGT OVERLIMIT' (amber) for 19 seconds as left engine exhaust gas temperature exceeds 950°C red limit for FLEX mode
Captain moves both throttles to TO/GA position (42 detent); commanded N1 increases to 100% (left) and 96% (right); right engine becomes unstable with oscillating N1; left engine does not respond
FDR event recorded: 'ENG 1 STALL' (but not displayed due to flight phase inhibition on ECAM)
Captain to FO: 'Autopilot off. Watch speed'; Captain informs ATC of engine failure: 'PAN-PAN, PAN-PAN, PAN-PAN. Свердловск 1-7-8. One engine failure'
Left throttle moved to CL (idle) position (25 detent); left engine N1 remains at approximately 39% (no response); airspeed continues to decrease; aircraft altitude 260 feet
FO requests reverse course approach from ATC; ATC approves reverse approach clearance at 03:15:00
Captain moves left throttle to IDLE (0 detent); left engine N1 begins to decrease toward idle as commanded; altitude 240 feet, airspeed 152 kt
First officer warns: 'Height, height' (altitude decreasing rapidly); Captain pulls side-stick back; airspeed decreases to 145 kt
ALFA PROTECTION (angle of attack protection) system activates as AOA reaches 12.5° (AOAprot); aircraft altitude 200 feet, airspeed 144 kt
EGPWS 'TERRAIN AHEAD. PULL UP' warning generated; aircraft altitude 180-170 feet, vertical speed 3-4 m/s descent
Landing gear retraction begins at altitude 120 feet; no explicit command recorded

Captain pulls side-stick fully back ('instvictively pulled to arrest descent'); elevator trim position 5.2° right; aircraft pitch 13°, AOA reaches 16.5° (exceeds ALFAmax of 15.5°), maximum available lift coefficient established

Aircraft touches down in corn field at magnetic heading 94°, airspeed 136 kt, pitch 8° nose-up, roll 2° right; landing gear partially retracted (unarmed); flaps in takeoff configuration (CONF 1+F); vertical speed 5+ m/s descent rate; aircraft skids and comes to rest 5300 meters from runway end

recommendations.text: Information about this accident should be communicated to specialist aviation personnel in Russian civil aviation and organizations supporting flight operations
Develop and implement regulatory framework defining procedures for ornithological (bird hazard) support in Russian civil aviation

recommendations.text: Establish airport protection zones around Ramensky Airfield and evaluate similar zones at other Russian airports per Air Code article 47
Initiate removal of landfills and other bird attractants near Ramensky Airfield that violate ornithological safety procedures, pending establishment of airport protection zones
Evaluate criteria and justification for including bird strike hazard information in ATIS and other flight crew briefings to prevent 'information fatigue' that reduces effectiveness

Enhance FCTM guidance for continued takeoff procedures when engine failure is suspected after V1, including explicit recommendation to verify landing gear retraction and consider TO/GA thrust setting

Airbus added autopilot engagement warnings to flight crew training manual emphasizing risks of autopilot disconnect due to pilot input and need to center flight director
Airbus enhanced continued takeoff procedures in FCTM with specific guidance for landing gear retraction and thrust management during suspected engine failure
Airbus revised blocking logic for ENG 1 (2) REVERSE UNLOCKED alert to block for 15 seconds post-liftoff
Airbus produced video training 'Engine Failure After V1' for instructor distribution via Airbus-WIN
Ural Airlines refined airport risk assessment procedures to maximize use of available information; enhanced analysis based on threat level classification from authority statistics and airline data

Bird strike confirmed by: vibration signature analysis, bird fragment examination (feathers between wing leading edge devices), marks on runway and aircraft, eyewitness testimony, video footage by passengers
Engine damage confirmed by: post-accident teardown inspection, NDT examination, vibration parameter analysis; both CFM56-5B engines sustained foreign object damage

Crew coordination failure: FO failed to clearly announce 'POSITIVE CLIMB' which is required callout for landing gear retraction after V1; CVR word 'POSITIVE' not audible per report footnote 41, p. 177
