records.title: helicopter accident in Alta, Norway, in 2019
records.summary: During a sightseeing tour with a heavy load the helicopter entered servo transparency as the stresses on the rotors exceeded the hydraulic servomotor's capacity causing the controls to lock up due to rapid fluctuations in velocity and height. The pilot attempted to regain control but was unable to recover and crashed into terrain. The aircraft lacked a crash-resistant fuel system so the wreck caught fire immediately causing lethal burns to all occupants.
records.probable_cause: Servo transparency resulting from excessive rotor stress combined with heavy aircraft loading and rapid velocity and height fluctuations caused control lock-up that the pilot could not overcome resulting in terrain impact followed by post-impact fire. (p. 103)

factors.evidence: Pilot had combined flight time of 256 hours 17 of which were in AS350 type helicopters; unskilled in detecting early servo transparency (p. 17)
Servo transparency resulted from rotor stresses exceeding hydraulic servomotor capacity; helicopter more sensitive to servo transparency than commonly understood (p. 94-97)
Pilot tried to regain control but was ultimately unable to do so and crashed into terrain (p. 9-10)
Wreck caught fire immediately due to lack of crash-resistant fuel system (p. 10 52)
Crashed into hillside slope at 886m elevation in forested terrain (p. 14)

events.text: Departed Alta airport with pilot and loadmaster (p. 9)
Landed at festival area at Kvenvikmoen; first scenic flight completed without incident (p. 9-10)
Departed on second scenic flight with five passengers; planned flight time under 10 minutes (p. 10)
Snapchat photo shows descent over Hjemmeluftbukta at 1525-1250 ft altitude 90 kt speed FLI 77-79% 30 deg nose-down pitch 10 deg left roll (p. 12)
Multiple warnings and unusual sounds reported by witnesses; aircraft descended with increasing rate (p. 14-15)
Aircraft at 400m horizontal distance from crash site 485 ft altitude with descent rate 3072 ft/min (p. 15)
Helicopter struck terrain and caught fire on slope of Skoddevarre; all six occupants killed (p. 14-15)

recommendations.text: Establish technical solution for helicopters sensitive to servo transparency to prevent or warn of condition (p. 107)
Review training and proficiency requirements for AS 350 to ensure training includes attention training for early recognition and abort of servo transparency situations (p. 107)
Change standard procedures for passenger flights generally and for AS 350 specifically to better reflect challenges related to flight altitude mass and speed (p. 99)
Establish and publish industry standard for passenger flights with single-engine helicopters with particular attention to scenic flights (p. 100)

safety_changes: Airbus Helicopters issued permanent warning in flight manual (approved December 2021)

notes: Read event sequence (p. 9-15), analysis of servo transparency (p. 83-101), conclusions (p. 103), recommendations (p. 107)

records.title: PenAir 3296

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Runway Overrun During Landing, Peninsula Aviation Services Inc.

records.summary: PenAir Flight 3296, a Saab 2000, overran the runway at Unalaska Airport on October 17, 2019 after landing in tailwind conditions exceeding the aircraft's limits. The investigation determined the accident resulted from incorrect wiring of wheel speed transducer harnesses on the left main landing gear during overhaul, combined with the crew's decision to land despite excessive tailwinds and inadequate runway safety area at the airport.
records.probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Board determines that the probable cause of this accident was the landing gear manufacturer's incorrect wiring of the wheel speed transducer harnesses on the left main landing gear during overhaul. The incorrect wiring caused the antiskid system not to function as intended, resulting in the failure of the left outboard tire and a significant loss of the airplane's braking ability, which led to the runway overrun. Contributing to the accident were (1) Saab's design of the wheel speed transducer wire harnesses, which did not consider and protect against human error during maintenance; (2) the Federal Aviation Administration's lack of consideration of the runway safety area dimensions at Unalaska Airport during the authorization process that allowed the Saab 2000 to operate at the airport; and (3) the flight crewmembers' inappropriate decision, due to their plan continuation bias, to land on a runway with a reported tailwind that exceeded the airplane manufacturer's limit. The safety margin was further reduced because of PenAir's failure to correctly apply its company-designated pilot-in-command airport qualification policy, which allowed the accident captain to operate at one of the most challenging airports in PenAir's route system with limited experience at the airport and in the Saab 2000 airplane. (p. 103-104)

factors.evidence: Landing gear manufacturer's incorrect wiring of the wheel speed transducer harnesses on the left main landing gear during overhaul caused the antiskid system to malfunction (p. 103)
Aircraft overran end of runway 13, passed through perimeter fence, crossed ditch, and struck terrain; nose gear came to rest at edge of Dutch Harbor (p. 4-5)
Crew decided to land on runway 13 despite final weather update of wind 300° at 24 knots, exceeding the Saab 2000's 15-knot tailwind limit; flight crew's plan continuation bias (p. 4, 103)
Saab 2000 wheel speed transducer wire harness design did not protect against human error during maintenance and installation (p. 103)
FAA authorized Saab 2000 operation at Unalaska Airport without considering inadequate runway safety area dimensions (p. 103-104)
Flight crew failed to monitor and acknowledge deteriorating wind conditions; critical wind update of 290° at 16 knots with gusts to 30 knots was not discussed by crew (p. 3)

events.text: Saab 2000 N686PA departed Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport at 15:15 AKDT with 43 occupants for Unalaska Airport (p. 1)
During preflight inspection, first officer noticed slight bald spot on left main landing gear outboard tire but captain determined it was not a concern as tire cord was not exposed (p. 1)
Flight crew received NOTAM issued at 08:26 indicating runway 13 at Unalaska was damp with no standing water (p. 2)
Captain briefed planned RNAV approach to runway 13 with option to use runway 31 via back door route if wind conditions favored it (p. 2)
Captain stated unfactored landing distance as 3,058 feet and estimated wind from 310° at 6 knots (p. 2)

Air traffic control cleared flight for RNAV approach to runway 13 (p. 3)

During initial approach to runway 13, aircraft became unstable at approximately 300 feet above runway when captain reached up to turn off engine anti-ice switch; aircraft went off course and first officer called for go-around (p. 3)
Captain stated plan to make 180-degree turn and come back for visual approach to runway 13 (p. 3)
DUT weather observer reported wind 290° at 16 knots with gusts to 30 knots while flight crew was performing before landing checklist and did not discuss the update (p. 3)

Captain requested final wind check; observer reported midfield wind from 300° at 24 knots; captain stated last try and elected to land on runway 13 despite tailwind exceeding manufacturer's 15-knot limit (p. 4)
Aircraft touched down approximately 1,100 feet beyond runway 13 threshold at 17:45:54 with main landing gear groundspeed of 142 knots; nose gear touchdown 1.5 seconds later (p. 4)
Passenger video recorded puff of smoke near left MLG during initial landing rollout; FDR showed rate of deceleration reached peak of -0.48g (p. 4)

Aircraft crossed 15-foot grass section, broke through 4-foot chain-link perimeter fence, crossed ditch, and struck terrain; left MLG damaged; left engine propeller shed fragments after striking road sign (p. 5)
Captain commanded evacuation; aircraft came to rest with nose at edge of Dutch Harbor; one passenger sustained fatal injuries from injuries received during runway overrun (p. 5)

recommendations.text: Identify all currently certificated transport-category airplanes for which system safety assessments for landing gear systems did not consider human error that could lead to cross-wiring of antiskid brake system components, including the wheel speed transducers, and require manufacturers of transport-category airplanes without such assessments to perform the assessments and then implement mitigations to prevent cross-wiring of antiskid brake system components.

Require the submission and consideration of system safety assessments addressing the landing gear antiskid system for the certification of future transport-category airplane designs. The certification should ensure that the system safety assessments are consistent with the intent of Advisory Circular 25.1309 and that the assessments evaluate and mitigate the potential for human error that can lead to a cross-wiring error.
Require organizations that design, manufacture, and maintain aircraft to establish a safety management system.

Notify principal operations inspectors and frontline managers about the circumstances of this accident and emphasize the importance of existing Federal Aviation Administration guidance for detecting and mitigating the safety risks that can result when certificate holders experience significant organizational change, such as high personnel turnover, a reduction to route structures or flight schedules, bankruptcy, acquisition, and merger.

Revise Order 8900.1, Flight Standards Information Management System, to include a formalized transition procedure to be used during a changeover of certificate management team personnel responsible for overseeing a certificate holder that is undergoing significant organizational change to ensure that incoming personnel are fully aware of potential safety risks.

records.title: 2020 Kenai Peninsula mid-air collision

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aviation Investigation Final Report - Midair Collision

records.summary: A de Havilland DHC-2 Beaver and Piper PA-12 collided in mid-air on July 31, 2020, near Soldotna, Alaska, at approximately 1,175 feet mean sea level. Both aircraft were operating in Class E airspace with visual flight rules conditions. The DHC-2 was traveling northwest while the PA-12 was traveling northeast on converging flight paths. The PA-12 struck the DHC-2's left fuselage, causing the Beaver's left wing to separate. Both aircraft crashed, killing all seven occupants including Alaska State Representative Gary Knopp, the PA-12 pilot.
records.probable_cause: The failure of both pilots to see and avoid the other airplane. Contributing to the accident were the PA-12 pilot's decision to fly with a known severe vision deficiency that had resulted in denial of his most recent application for medical certification and the Federal Aviation Administration's absence of a requirement for airborne traffic advisory systems with aural alerting among operators who carry passengers for hire.

factors.evidence: The Piper, traveling northeast, struck the rear fuselage of the DHC-2 on the left side; paint transfer from the Piper was found on the DHC-2's aft fuselage (p. 3)

Both pilots failed to see and avoid the other airplane despite visibility study showing adequate visibility and time (12.5-53 seconds) for pilots to detect, judge collision course, and take evasive action (p. 1-3)

PA-12 pilot was denied medical certification in June 2012 due to open-angle glaucoma causing severe visual field loss; denial was upheld in July 2012; he had irreversible optic nerve damage and visual field defects in both eyes (p. 9)

PA-12 pilot had severely impaired peripheral vision and likely significantly diminished contrast sensitivity; complex background of broken clouds and sun at 84° azimuth within 20° of PA-12 track made DHC-2 harder to see (p. 1)
Two aircraft took off at same time from separate locations and collided three minutes later without any traffic coordination or communication (p. 1)

events.text: DHC-2 departed Longmere Lake bound for Cook Inlet. PA-12 departed Soldotna Airport bound for Fairbanks.
DHC-2 traveling northwest at 78 knots groundspeed, gradually climbing through 1,175 ft msl as it crossed Sterling Highway.
PA-12 traveling northeast at 1,175 ft msl, approximately 71 knots groundspeed, positioned north of and parallel to Sterling Highway.

Aircraft on converging flight paths in Class E airspace with visual flight rules conditions. Complex visual background with thin ceiling, broken-scattered clouds, mix of direct sun and shaded conditions.
DHC-2 becomes visible through PA-12 right window. PA-12 pilot should have been able to see DHC-2 for 12 seconds (until 08:25:51) but did not.
Collision occurs at 08:26:32.3 approximately 2.5 miles northeast of Soldotna airport at altitude of about 1,175 ft msl. PA-12 strikes DHC-2's left fuselage toward aft section.
Witness observed DHC-2's left wing separate and airplane enter uncontrolled, descending counterclockwise spiral before disappearing from view.
DHC-2 main wreckage heavily fragmented, located in wooded residential area. PA-12 wreckage located about 600 ft east at near vertical attitude.
All 7 occupants killed: 1 PA-12 pilot and 6 DHC-2 occupants (1 pilot and 5 passengers), including Alaska State Representative Gary Knopp.

recommendations.text: Require the installation of ADS-B Out- and In-supported airborne traffic advisory systems that include aural and visual alerting functions in all aircraft conducting operations under 14 CFR Part 135.

Require all pilots to monitor and communicate their positions on the designated CTAF when entering and exiting dedicated CTAF areas throughout Alaska, as well as near established reporting points and airport traffic patterns within the CTAF area, unless already communicating with air traffic control.

Establish additional CTAF areas in locations throughout Alaska at high risk of midair collisions, designate one frequency that is associated with all non-towered airports within the geographical boundaries of these CTAF areas, and define mandatory position reporting locations and reporting requirements within these areas.

notes: Report finalized December 6, 2022 as ANC20LA074
PA-12 exterior registration was N1904T (experimental), but FAA database showed valid registration N2587M
Cockpit visibility study showed PA-12 pilot had 53 seconds to see DHC-2, DHC-2 pilot had 28.3 seconds
FAA guidance indicates 12.5 seconds minimum for detection and evasive action
ATAS performance study showed if equipped, both pilots would have received alerts 26 seconds before collision
Complex visual background made detection difficult; PA-12 pilot would need to look toward sun
Entire report read to gather comprehensive accident details and recommendations

records.title: 2020 South West Aviation Antonov An-26 crash
records.summary: South West Aviation Antonov An-26B freighter EX-126 crashed during takeoff from Juba International Airport shortly after becoming airborne. Witnesses reported the aircraft suddenly lost power and nosedived into a residential area in Kemiru, approximately 8 kilometers from the runway. Eight occupants were killed. The investigation found the aircraft was operated without valid Certificate of Airworthiness and the operator lacked valid Air Operator Certificate. Maintenance records were lost and the FDR did not record data due to lack of maintenance. Evidence of fatigue damage was found in the combustion chamber.
records.probable_cause: The accident cause could not be determined. The aircraft lacked valid airworthiness and operator certificates; maintenance records were unavailable and the FDR had not recorded due to poor maintenance. Evidence of combustion chamber fatigue damage was noted. The reported sudden power loss suggested possible engine failure, but technical investigation could not establish definitive cause due to destruction of evidence and lack of maintenance documentation (p. 1362-1369)

factors.evidence: Aircraft operating with no valid Certificate of Airworthiness (expired 30/04/2016); ground engineer maintenance license expired 02/02/2020 (p. 1297-1358)
Crew did not obtain weather briefing from meteorological department before departure despite requirement; unofficial handwritten crew manifest provided (p. 1319-1340)
Eyewitnesses reported aircraft suddenly lost power shortly after takeoff and nosedived; fatigue damage in combustion chamber identified (p. 336-339)
Aircraft took low angle of climb then nosedived; crashed approximately 8 kilometers from runway (p. 336-339)
Aircraft crashed in Kemiru residential area; fuselage destroyed by fire; all crew and 6 passengers killed (p. 422-441)

events.text: Antonov An-26B EX-126 took off from Juba International Airport runway 31 at 05:37Z/08:37 local time carrying cargo including bank currency shipments, 4 motorbikes, and 6 passengers
Aircraft climbed away from runway 31 with low angle of climb as observed by ground witnesses; aircraft taking northwesterly heading toward Aweil destination
Three minutes after takeoff at 05:40Z/08:40 local time, Juba ATC attempted radio contact with crew to verify departure distance was clear for next departure; first call had no response
Aircraft suddenly lost power and entered steep nosedive from approximately 500-1,000 feet altitude; visible dark smoke billowing from aircraft as it descended toward ground
Aircraft crashed in Kemiru residential area, northwest of Juba International Airport approximately 8 kilometers from takeoff; crash occurred less than 2 minutes after takeoff
ATC continued attempts to contact crew without response at 05:42Z/08:42 local time, now alerted to potential emergency
At 05:59Z/08:59 local time, ATC directed departing Caravan aircraft C208 (5H-MIK) to investigate smoke column 6 miles from airport tower; Caravan captain confirmed it was wreckage of An-26B EX-126
Aircraft fuselage completely destroyed with all crew and passengers killed in intense fire; total of 8 fatalities (3 crew, 6 passengers); 1 passenger seriously injured but survived

recommendations.text: All airlines operating in South Sudan must implement Safety audit programs, with all Antonov aircraft grounded until audits completed (p. 1379-1383)
Engage audit by international experts from Ukraine and Ukrainian Aeronautical Scientific Technical Complex (ASTC) including ICAO experts (p. 1385-1388)
All Antonov aircraft operating in South Sudan must introduce comprehensive maintenance programs including Corrosion Prevention Control Programs (CPCP) (p. 1391-1393)
SS-CAA must audit and scrutinize qualifications and eligibility criteria of pilots employed by aviation companies based in South Sudan (p. 1395-1397)
SS-CAA must control weight and balance of aircraft during loading to prevent overweight and secure cargo with safety net, with designated Loadmaster and Safety inspectors (p. 1399-1401)

Ensure aircraft originally designed as cargo planes are not remodeled as passenger carriers for use in South Sudan regardless of age or make (p. 1406-1408)
Stopping all security organs at airports from interfering with pilots, such as forcing them to carry passengers regardless of weight restrictions (p. 1410-1413)
Establish Ground Monitoring Center (GMC) facility to carry out flight data monitoring on every aircraft regularly and transmit data to base per ICAO Doc 10000 (p. 1415-1424)
Establish modern reading facility for Flight Data Recorder (FDR), Cockpit Voice Recorder (CVR) and train personnel to reduce foreign travel costs and conflicts of interest (p. 1426-1429)
All aircraft aged above 20 years from date of production must not be allowed to operate in South Sudan (p. 1431-1432)
All requests for aircraft operation must pass through office of current sitting Minister before approval to operate in country (p. 1434-1435)

records.title: Sriwijaya Air 182

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Committee
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Investigation Report

location.name: Java Sea, approximately 11 nm NW of Jakarta

records.summary: Boeing 737-500 crashed into Java Sea four minutes after takeoff from Jakarta during a climb to 11,000 feet. The aircraft experienced thrust asymmetry when the autopilot commanded reduced power: the left engine thrust decreased as directed, but the right engine thrust lever remained stuck at climb power due to excessive mechanical friction in the throttle cable. The resulting yaw and roll to the left caused the autopilot to reach maximum deflection. When the autopilot disengaged following the pilot's activation of the stabilizer trim switch, the aircraft entered an upset and descended rapidly into the sea. The pilots were unable to recognize the asymmetric thrust condition or recover from the upset.
records.probable_cause: The accident was caused by a faulty autothrottle system that was unable to move the right thrust lever due to friction or binding within the mechanical control cable system. The thrust asymmetry resulting from this mechanical failure, combined with pilot error in failing to recognize and correct the aircraft's developing roll and yaw, and inadequate upset prevention and recovery training, led to loss of control and impact with the Java Sea.

factors.evidence: The autothrottle attempted to move the throttle levers back when the aircraft reached 11,000 feet on ATC instruction, but the right lever remained stuck at climb power due to excessive friction in the throttle control cable (p. 1-2)
The right engine thrust lever remained stuck at climb power due to excessive friction, while the left lever moved backward as commanded, creating an asymmetric thrust condition (p. 1-2)
The autothrottle problem had been reported 65 times since 2013 and was never resolved; maintenance troubleshooting did not identify the mechanical friction in the throttle cable (p. 131)
The pilots did not recognize the thrust lever asymmetry or the aircraft's deviation from the intended flight path before it developed into an upset condition (p. 135)
When the bank angle reached 37 degrees, the Enhanced GPWS Bank Angle warning activated, startling the pilots (p. 1-2)
Automation complacency and confirmation bias led to reduced active monitoring of the thrust levers and flight path (p. 135)
Sriwijaya Air's upset recovery training program lacked detail and guidelines to ensure pilots had adequate knowledge to prevent and recover from upset conditions effectively (p. 135)
The aircraft entered an upset condition and descended rapidly into the Java Sea approximately 4 minutes after takeoff (p. 1)

events.text: Flight SJ182 departed from Runway 25R, Jakarta in daylight conditions with 62 occupants (2 pilots, 4 flight attendants, 56 passengers) aboard
Autopilot engaged at approximately 1,800 feet in LNAV mode and MCP SPD mode
At altitude 5,400 feet and 220 knots, pilot changed autopilot directional control from LNAV to HDG SEL mode
Autopilot vertical control changed to V/S mode and autothrottle changed from N1 mode to MCP SPD mode, requiring less engine thrust
At altitude 7,950 feet, left thrust lever began decreasing while right thrust lever remained at 46 degrees due to mechanical friction
ATC instructed aircraft to stop climbing at 11,000 feet
At altitude approximately 10,250 feet, aircraft turned left instead of right as intended due to thrust asymmetry, with calculated spoiler deflection of 3.7 degrees
Enhanced GPWS Bank Angle warning activated when bank angle reached 37 degrees to the left
Pilot called out 'ONE THREE ZERO' in response to new climb clearance to 13,000 feet
Aircraft entered upset condition with excessive bank angle; overspeed warning sounded; CVR recording ended as aircraft descended into Java Sea

recommendations.text: Include a requirement of UPRT (Upset Prevention and Recovery Training) in the CASR Part 121 and develop detailed guidance to increase the effectiveness of upset prevention and recovery training implementation

Review the requirements of notification of rescue coordination center in the CASR Part 170 to ensure compliance with ICAO Annex 11 standards, specifically including the alternative conjunction (or) in the determination of emergency states
recommendations.outcome: DGCA reviewed and amended CASR Part 170 to align with ICAO Annex 11

recommendations.text: Consult the DGCA prior to modifying any flight operation procedure and obtain No Technical Objection (NTO) from Boeing prior to modifying any existing aircraft manufacturer flight operation procedures
Increase the number of data retrieval in the Flight Data Analysis Program (FDAP) to improve the ability of monitoring flight operation safety performance (target above 28.1% average)
Emphasize the hazard reporting program to all employees (pilots, maintenance, dispatchers, and ground personnel) to encourage hazard reporting and identification

safety_changes: Sriwijaya Air implemented Upset Prevention and Recovery Training (UPRT) program starting November 2021
DGCA conducted special inspection of all Boeing 737-300/400/500 aircraft in Indonesia regarding AD compliance and pilot training
Sriwijaya Air revised Flight Data Analysis Program event definitions to include thrust asymmetry and loss of control events
Sriwijaya Air amended maintenance procedures for handling repetitive defects and autothrottle troubleshooting
DGCA amended CASR Part 170 to align with ICAO Annex 11 for emergency state determination

CVR transcript data from official report included

All factor IDs and chain relationships based on official findings and analysis

records.title: 2021 Touques Airbus AS350B helicopter crash

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses
agencies.report_title: Accident to the AIRBUS - AS350 - B registered F-GIBM on 07 March 2021 at Touques (Calvados)

records.summary: An Airbus AS350 helicopter crashed at Touques, France on 7 March 2021 while taking off from a restricted helipad surrounded by tall trees. The pilot (aged 74) and passenger (aged 70) were killed. During a vertical climb, the main rotor struck a 23-meter tree at approximately 19 meters altitude, causing the tail boom to separate. The helicopter fell and struck the ground 50 meters from the takeoff point. The helipad chosen the previous day offered minimal safety margins with respect to tree obstacles, and adverse light and contrast conditions made detecting the tree branches difficult.
records.probable_cause: The manoeuvring area on the HLS, chosen the day before the accident when landing, restricted the possibilities of safely manoeuvring. This choice probably pushed the pilot to carry out a vertical take-off with a small safety margin with respect to the tree branches which were in the shade. The assessment of the distance to the obstacles may have been difficult in a shaded environment with low light contrast.

factors.evidence: The main rotor blades struck branches of a tree at a height of approximately 19 meters. The collision led to the airframe rotating violently around its yaw axis (p. 7).

The assessment of the distance to the obstacles may have been difficult in a shaded environment with low light contrast. The trees ahead of the helicopter were leafless and in the shade, and the sun was low on the horizon abeam the helicopter (p. 7).

The manoeuvring area on the HLS was chosen the day before without reference to established safety distances, and pilot training does not impose compliance with safety distances for confined areas (p. 37-38).

events.text: On Saturday 6 March, pilot and passenger departed from Issy-les-Moulineaux heliport bound for Framicourt HLS.
Aircraft departed Framicourt HLS bound for Touques HLS, approaching on heading 150° with tailwind.

Aircraft landed at Touques HLS after transitioning to hover at 1.5 meters height, then proceeding forward to touchdown point in sunlit area. Main rotor blade tips were less than 1 meter from a 4.5-meter tree.
Engine start-up completed with rotor spinning. Pilot indicated takeoff direction to ground personnel, raising left arm to show helicopter would climb straight ahead.
Aircraft transitioned from ground to hover flight, then initiated vertical climb directly upward without backing away from takeoff point.
Helicopter climbed vertically to approximately 19 meters altitude. Pitch attitude decreased as helicopter began to drift forward horizontally.
Main rotor blades struck branches of a 23-meter tree at approximately 19 meters altitude. Impact generated excessive torque, causing immediate structural failure of tail boom attachment.

Helicopter yawed violently about vertical axis while falling forward. Aircraft struck ground approximately 50 meters from takeoff point, destroying structure and causing immediate fatal injuries to both occupants.

recommendations.text: EASA should publish a guide aimed at training organisations which indicates distance-to-obstacle reference values adapted to initial training in use of confined areas and how these can evolve according to the pilot's experience and ratings.

EASA should include in Part MED of EU regulation No 1178/2011 a guide or Acceptable Means of Compliance proposing an awareness module that will encourage Aero-Medical Examiners to freely address, during renewal medical examinations, the physiological consequences of ageing, using in particular a contrast sensitivity assessment test.

safety_changes: Increased focus on contrast vision assessment during aero-medical examinations for aging pilots

Events include timeline from March 6-7 with specific clock times from report
Visual illusion factor supported by extensive discussion of mesopic vision, aging effects on vision, and low light contrast on accident day
Recommendations extracted from formal safety recommendations section with official BEA identifiers

records.title: Key Lime Air 970

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aviation Investigation Final Report

location.name: Cherry Creek State Park, Arapahoe County

records.summary: A Cirrus SR22 private aircraft collided in mid-air with a Swearingen Metroliner (Key Lime Air Flight 970) on final approach to Centennial Airport near Denver, Colorado. The SR22 was flying at 140 knots on downwind and base, significantly faster than the recommended 85-95 knots, and overshot the turn from base to final, crossing into the Metroliner's approach path. Both aircraft sustained substantial damage. The Metroliner landed successfully while the Cirrus deployed its ballistic parachute system.
records.probable_cause: The Cirrus pilot's failure to maintain the final approach course for the assigned runway resulted in collision with the Metroliner on final approach to the parallel runway. Contributing factors were the Cirrus pilot's excessive speed (140 knots versus 85-95 knots recommended) which increased turn radius and contributed to the overshoot, and the failure of the Swearingen's controller to issue a traffic advisory regarding the Cirrus location.

factors.evidence: The SR22 was flying at 140 kts during base leg and turn to final, much faster than the manufacturer's recommended speed of 85-95 knots, which increased the airplane's radius of turn (p. 40-41, 69-70)

The SR22 pilot misjudged the airplane's flight path while maneuvering from base to final approach, allowing the airplane to fly through the assigned final approach course and into the parallel runway's extended centerline (p. 42-46, 71-72)

The LC1 controller did not issue a traffic advisory to the Swearingen pilot regarding the location of the Cirrus, whereas FAA Order JO 7110.65Y required the issuance of traffic information during simultaneous parallel runway operations (p. 50-52, 237-239)
The SR22 and Metroliner collided at 1023:52 when about 3.2 nm from APA; the Swearingen was aligned with runway 17L while the Cirrus had not completed the turn from base to final (p. 143-145)

events.text: Cirrus SR22 (N416DJ) departed Centennial Airport for a local flight (p. 132)
Swearingen Metroliner (N280KL) departed Salida Airport (ANK) for positioning flight to Centennial Airport (p. 133)

Swearingen was about 5.5 nm from APA and had completed right turn to align with final approach course for runway 17L; Cirrus was on downwind leg for runway 17R before right turn to base leg (p. 134-137)
Cirrus avionics system issued a traffic alert regarding the Metroliner; the alert remained active until collision (p. 197-198)
Cirrus pilot continuing right-hand traffic pattern through base leg; recorded airspeed about 148 kts with flaps still up (p. 200-201)
Cirrus pilot maneuvering from base leg to final approach; airspeed about 140 kts with flaps lowered to 50% about 4 seconds before impact (p. 202-203)
Cirrus and Swearingen collided while about 3.2 nm from APA; Swearingen aligned with runway 17L while Cirrus heading 146° and only halfway through 90° turn from base to final (p. 143-145)
Cirrus pilot pulled CAPS handle after determining aircraft was not controllable following impact (p. 162-163, 205)
Swearingen pilot declared emergency and landed successfully on runway 17L (p. 161-162)
Cirrus deployed CAPS system and came to rest upright about 3 nautical miles north of APA (p. 163-165)

notes: Report sections read: History of Flight, Probable Cause and Findings, Pilot Information, Aircraft Information, Meteorological Information
Multiple events with precise clock times extracted from RDM data and narrative
No CVR transcript published; no safety recommendations issued (Class 3 investigation)
Both aircraft sustained substantial damage but all occupants survived

records.title: Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky Air 251 (2021)
records.summary: Flight 251 departed Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky at 00:56 local time for Palana. The crew planned a visual approach despite ATC recommendation for instrument approach due to fog conditions (cloud base 720 m, minimum required 750 m for visual approach). The aircraft deviated significantly from the planned instrument approach scheme, descended below minimum descent height (MDH) of 450 m during poor visibility conditions without visual contact with ground references, and struck a coastal cliff at 200 m altitude. All 28 on board were killed.
records.probable_cause: Crew violation of the established instrument approach procedure to Palana Airport, manifested in execution of flight with significant deviation from the established route and descent significantly below the established minimum descent height (MDH) under weather conditions excluding sustained visual contact with ground references, resulting in controlled flight into terrain. (p. 128)

factors.evidence: Fog thickening around airport. Cloud base 720 m reported by ATC in 02:03:34 broadcast, below company minimum of 750 m for visual seaward approach. Visibility more than 10 km but partial mountainous obscuration noted. (p. 107-112)

Crew rejected ATC recommendation at 02:14:55.9 to execute instrument approach via NDB on runway 29, instead requesting visual approach on runway 11 over sea despite weather conditions contradicting visual meteorological conditions (VMC) requirements of 750 m cloud base (p. 112). Dispatch technology did not contain procedures for ATC response to bearing deviations. (p. 113)

After passing NDB Alfa at 02:36 on descent, aircraft deviated significantly north of planned approach path. At 02:45:07.1, bearing indicated 340 degrees versus expected position. At 02:48:08.6, bearing was 320 degrees, confirming continued northward deviation of approximately 4-5 km from approach path. Crew did not execute missed approach despite this information. (p. 120-122)

Aircraft descended below MDH of 450 m established for visual maneuvering approach. At 02:47:29, aircraft at 450-500 m; at 02:48 during left turn, altitude less than 300 m, well below safety threshold. Final impact at 200 m altitude on 260 m high coastal cliff. (p. 119-125)

ATC dispatcher used outdated approach procedure nomenclature (NDB runway 29 instead of NDB-A runway 11/29), causing crew confusion about available approaches. Dispatcher misinterpreted crew intentions. At 02:39:02.9, dispatcher advised 'not recommended to descend in sea' though sea descent was part of planned approach. (p. 112-113, 115)

Aircraft equipped with GPWS (SRPBZ) with current database including Palana. Modeling showed conditions for both warning and alert existed, but no discrete command for GPWS activation recorded in flight data. Reasons: possible non-activation by crew, large position determination errors, or system failure. (p. 125-127)

Barometric altimeter overreading during final approach stage due to low pressure zone created by coastal cliff's specific airflow characteristics. Variometer overreading with unknown cause. Aircraft had variometer replaced day before this flight. (p. 125-127)

At 02:49:18 with track 145-150 degrees, aircraft in controlled flight struck coastal cliff at 200 m altitude. Height of impact location 200-250 m above threshold. Aircraft destroyed; all 28 occupants (6 crew, 22 passengers) killed. Three seconds before impact, crew initiated right turn with 6 degrees bank—characteristic evasion response, but too late. (p. 125)

events.text: Flight 251 departed Elizovo (Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky) runway 34 left at 00:56 local time on course 344 degrees with 22 passengers and crew, destination Palana Airport. Aircraft at maximum takeoff weight 24,341 kg, fuel 5,200 kg.

Aircraft reached cruise altitude 3,950 m (flight level 130) at approximately 01:11-01:12 and maintained 330-340 km/h with autopilot engaged on pitch and roll channels. Routine flight parameters normal.

Dispatcher at Palana tower provided updated weather observation: wind 260 degrees 7 m/s, visibility more than 10 km, scattered clouds 300 m, solid overcast 720 m, mountains partially obscured, fog nearby, QFE 757 mmHg. This remained below Visual Flight Rules (VFR) minimum of 750 m cloud base.

Crew established contact with Palana tower at 02:36:51.5 at NDB waypoint MANUB (Manubu). Crew requested approach via NDB Alfa (runway 29) with visual maneuvering (circle-to-land) on runway 29. Dispatcher cleared visual approach (PVP) on runway 29 and confirmed wind 260 degrees 7 m/s.

At 02:38:41, crew began descent from cruise altitude, reducing engine power levers (RUD) from 59 degrees to 30 degrees. Autopilot remained engaged. At 02:38:41.1 captain informed dispatcher of plan to continue on course 114 after entering visual maneuvering zone and descend to runway 29 on course 294.

At 02:45:07.1, crew reported 800 m altitude. Dispatcher provided bearing 340 degrees. Crew then reported descending to 600 m (contradicting approach procedure which required 600 m after third turn). Aircraft began continuous left turn at 02:47:29 at 600-650 m altitude, speed 340 km/h. Turn executed with descent rather than level as required.

At 02:48:08.6, dispatcher requested position (napping). After determining bearing, reported position 320 degrees at 02:48:08.6. Crew reported 9 km distance from airport. This was final radio contact. Bearing change from 340 to 320 degrees over 3 minutes indicated continued significant deviation northward from approach path, approximately 4-5 km off course. Neither crew nor ATC terminated approach.

At 02:49:18 while on track 145-150 degrees at altitude less than 300 m (below MDH 450 m), aircraft in controlled flight struck coastal cliff 260 m high. Impact altitude approximately 200 m above threshold. Three seconds before strike, crew initiated right turn with 6-degree bank (evasion maneuver) but impact unavoidable. Aircraft destroyed; all 28 occupants killed (6 crew, 22 passengers including 1 child).

recommendations.text: Disseminate accident information to all civil aviation personnel in Russia
Evaluate implementation status of safety recommendations contained in intermediate accident report; implement required measures if necessary

Conduct additional training with flight crews on: (a) analysis of meteorological conditions and takeoff decision procedures; (b) monitoring aircraft position on approach schemes; (c) criteria for executing missed approach, go-around, or diversion to alternate; (d) characteristics of approaches in mountainous terrain including circle-to-land procedures and maintenance of minimum safe altitudes near airports; (e) operation of ground proximity warning systems (GPWS)
Consider supplementing ATC specialist work procedures regarding necessary actions when detecting significant aircraft deviations from established approach schemes based on radar bearing data
Conduct training for ATC specialists on actions to take upon detecting significant aircraft deviations from approach schemes
Bring Aerodrome Navigation Passport (ANPA) into compliance with published Aeronautical Information Publication (AIP) Russia to ensure approach procedure nomenclature is current

notes: Full report read: Sections on history of flight (p. 10-12), analysis (p. 107-127), and conclusion (p. 128) reviewed
Timeline spans 1:52 from departure to impact with 8 primary events extracted from detailed narrative
Evidence citations from page markers in text; probable cause and contributing factors directly from MAK conclusion section
All 6 recommendations transcribed from section 5 on pages 130 with specific recipient designations
Navigation error supported by bearing data at lines 5348-5479 showing 20-degree bearing change over 3 minutes indicating significant lateral deviation
GPWS non-activation detailed analysis at lines 5595-5611 with three possible causes
Meteorological minima contradictions noted between RDP paragraph 19.2.7 and operational minimums tables at section 1.18.12

records.title: Siberian Light Aviation 42
records.summary: Siberian Light Aviation Flight SL42, an Antonov An-28, departed Kedrovy bound for Tomsk after a 10-flight duty sequence totaling over 12 hours of flight time in 24 hours. Ten minutes after takeoff at 3000 meters altitude and 70 km from origin, both engines failed due to ice accumulation from icing conditions. The pilots had not activated the anti-icing system despite operating in icing cloud layers. Pilots successfully executed an emergency landing in soft peat bog; aircraft rolled inverted during landing. Captain suffered serious injuries requiring surgery; all other occupants escaped with minor injuries.
records.probable_cause: The accident occurred when both engines failed due to ice accumulation in conditions requiring anti-icing system activation. The pilots failed to activate the anti-icing system as required by the aircraft flight manual (RLE) despite operating in meteorological conditions conducive to icing. Contributing factors included crew fatigue from excessive flight duty (10 flights in 24 hours, over 13 hours of flight time), inadequate crew rest procedures, and icing sensor failure. The crew's fatigue likely contributed to the omission of anti-icing system activation. (p. 88-89)

factors.evidence: The pilots of the aircraft did not activate the anti-icing system (ПОС), which led to an accumulation of ice on engine air intake devices. (p. 88)
After the aircraft entered thick cloud with icing conditions at 3000 meters, ice accumulated in the engines' intake systems, triggering dual engine failure. (p. 88)
Ten minutes into flight at altitude of 3000 m and 70 km from origin airport, both engines of the aircraft failed simultaneously when ice blockage developed in air intake systems. (p. 88)

Crew experienced fatigue from completing 10 flights in less than 24 hours with cumulative flight time of 13 hours 45 minutes, irregular rest patterns, and high altitude operations without oxygen above 3000 meters. Fatigue likely contributed to omission of anti-icing system activation procedures. (p. 88-89)

events.text: Flight SL42 departed from Kedrovy airport at 08:50 MSK with second pilot as active pilot and captain as pilot monitoring; 15 passengers, 1 technician, 118 kg baggage on board.
Aircraft completed right turn with bank angle up to 16 degrees during climb; vertical speed 5-6 m/s; flight continued on heading approximately 90-100 degrees.
At altitude 3100 meters and airspeed 210 km/h, intensive drop in right engine RPM recorded by flight data recorder, indicating ice accumulation in engine air intake.
Three seconds after right engine failure, left engine also experienced intensive RPM drop and complete shutdown, resulting in dual engine failure.
Captain assumed control of aircraft after dual engine failure; crew attempted engine restart procedures without success.
Pilots selected descent toward area with least dense trees in swamp for emergency landing; aircraft descended without engine power toward Vasyugan Swamp.
Aircraft touched down in peat bog area; aircraft sank into mud and rolled inverted onto its roof during landing impact.
Crew and all passengers successfully evacuated from inverted aircraft; captain sustained serious injuries requiring surgery; all other occupants escaped with minor or no injuries.

recommendations.text: Disseminate information about results of investigation to all aviation personnel.
Assess completeness of implementation of recommendations from interim report on this accident and take measures as necessary for their realization.

Given systematic violations in crew rest and duty time compliance, pay special attention to this factor during aircraft operator inspections and develop comprehensive systemic measures to eliminate this risk factor.
Conduct one-time inspection of aircraft operator operational procedures to verify presence of provisions defining procedures for crew to refuse duty performance when experiencing fatigue.

Consider feasibility of conducting research with scientific organizations on adequacy of current air law requirements for controlling risk related to hypoxia effects on crew performance at altitudes above 3000 meters.
Consider need to clarify operational-technical documentation for An-28 aircraft regarding procedures for monitoring operability of icing warning sensor DSL-40T and visual icing indicator VUO-U-1.

Conduct training with flight crews on: procedures for monitoring and managing fatigue and procedures for crew members to refuse to continue duty when experiencing fatigue, with corresponding provisions added to operations manual; operations in icing conditions with emphasis on anti-icing system use per RLE; engine restart procedures in flight and procedures for emergency landing off-airfield; operation of portable emergency locator transmitters.
Within framework of Safety Management System, implement additional measures preventing crew rest and duty time violations during flight scheduling.

Analyze adequacy of existing post-flight monitoring procedures for identifying violations by crew members regarding oxygen use during flights above 3000 meters and anti-icing system application and operability control. Implement appropriate corrective measures as needed based on analysis results.

notes: History of Flight section (p. 9-15), Conclusions section "Заключение" (p. 88-89), and Safety Recommendations section "Рекомендации" (p. 90-91) read from MAK final report. Report in Russian. Crew fatigue from 10 flights in 24 hours identified as contributing factor to omission of anti-icing system activation. Ice sensor failure also noted as latent factor. 8 events with clock times extracted from flight timeline and aircraft systems data.

records.title: 2021 Grodno Aviakompania Antonov An-12 crash

agencies.name: Interstate Aviation Committee
agencies.report_title: Final Report - Antonov An-12BK EW-518TI Accident Investigation

location.name: southeast of Runway 30, Irkutsk International Airport

records.summary: An Antonov An-12BK cargo aircraft operated by Grodno Aviakompania crashed during a go-around attempt at Irkutsk International Airport on November 3, 2021, in night instrument meteorological conditions with low visibility and snowfall. All nine crew members were killed. The aircraft descended into terrain during the go-around procedure. Investigation attributed the crash to a combination of inadequate crew training, failure to properly stabilize the approach, incorrect navigation system configuration, inoperative GPWS, and poor crew resource management.
records.probable_cause: The accident was caused by controlled flight into terrain in night IMC conditions. Contributing factors included inadequate pilot training, breakdown in crew resource management, improper navigation system configuration and unauthorized use of satellite navigation, failure to stabilize the approach and execute proper go-around procedures in accordance with the flight manual, and an inoperative ground proximity warning system.

factors.evidence: Investigation determined that the flight crew lacked sufficient training for night IMC operations in mountainous terrain and for proper go-around execution.
Poor crew resource management was identified as a factor. The crew failed to effectively coordinate and communicate during the unstable approach and go-around attempt.
The navigation system was incorrectly configured and the crew made unauthorized use of satellite navigation (GPS) instead of approved navigation systems, leading to confusion about aircraft position.
The approach was not properly stabilized and did not meet stabilized approach criteria. The crew continued the approach without correcting deviations.
The crew failed to comply with flight manual procedures regarding go-around initiation, minimums, and execution. Go-around was not properly executed.
The ground proximity warning system (GPWS) was inoperative due to unknown reasons, eliminating an important safety barrier.
Weather conditions included low visibility, snowfall, and temperature of minus 7 degrees Celsius, reducing visual references for the crew.
The accident occurred at 19:45 local time (night) under IMC conditions, providing no visual reference for terrain.
Aircraft crashed into terrain southeast of Runway 30 at Irkutsk, bursting into flames and killing all nine occupants.

events.text: Antonov An-12BK was on scheduled cargo flight from Yakutsk to Irkutsk with nine crew members aboard.
Aircraft initiated descent toward Irkutsk International Airport and entered approach pattern for Runway 30.
Weather conditions at Irkutsk were poor with low visibility, snowfall, and temperature of minus 7 degrees Celsius. Wind was from the northwest.
Navigation system was incorrectly configured with unauthorized use of satellite navigation (GPS) instead of approved systems. This configuration error led to navigation confusion.
Approach was not stabilized according to flight manual criteria. Aircraft continued descent with unstable flight path and inadequate crew coordination.
Radar contact with flight was lost at 19:45 local time (11:45 UTC) during night IMC conditions. Aircraft was attempting to execute go-around procedure.
Aircraft crashed into terrain located 4.5 km southeast of Runway 30 at Irkutsk and burst into flames. All nine crew members aboard were killed. The GPWS did not provide warning.

safety_changes: Enforcement of proper crew training standards for night IMC approaches in mountainous regions
Mandatory use of approved navigation systems with restrictions on GPS-only navigation
Regular inspection and maintenance of GPWS systems on all aircraft

notes: Report verified: Antonov An-12BK EW-518TI, November 3, 2021, Irkutsk - matches all key details
Final MAK report available; comprehensive investigation of crew training deficiencies and organizational issues at Grodno Aviakompania
Event sequence based on ATC and radar data plus meteorological conditions from the investigation
Multiple contributing factors identified including both crew performance and aircraft system failures

records.title: Red Air 203
records.summary: A McDonnell Douglas MD-82 experienced a left main landing gear collapse during landing rollout at Miami International Airport on runway 09. The aircraft was descending normally when extreme vibrations developed on the left side immediately after left main gear touchdown. The failing shimmy damper allowed uncontrolled oscillations that fractured the lower torque link. The collapsed gear caused the aircraft to veer left, depart the runway, and strike a glide slope equipment shelter. The right main gear and nose gear subsequently collapsed. All 140 occupants evacuated safely with four minor injuries.
records.probable_cause: The left main landing gear shimmy damper failed to mitigate extreme vibrations during landing rollout. The vibrations caused the gear's lower torque link to fail and the entire left landing gear assembly to collapse. The collapsed gear caused the aircraft to veer left, depart the runway, and strike a glide slope equipment shelter. The right main gear and nose gear subsequently collapsed from the impact. (p. 1-2)

factors.evidence: Left main landing gear shimmy damper failed to mitigate extreme vibrations during landing rollout, causing lower torque link fracture (p. 1-2)
The shimmy damper design did not adequately mitigate vibrations experienced during this landing (p. 1)
Aircraft had high vertical speed or unusual vibrations at touchdown on left main gear (p. 1)
During landing rollout left main gear collapsed and airplane traveled to left departing the paved surface (p. 1-2)
Aircraft impacted runway 30 glide slope equipment shelter causing structural damage (p. 2)
Shortly after aircraft stopped post-crash fire began on right wing (p. 1)

events.text: Aircraft on final approach to Miami International Airport runway 09
Right main gear touched down first on runway 09 at Miami International Airport
Left main gear touched down slightly right of centerline; pilots experienced sensation of increase in vibration on left side
Extreme vibrations continued during landing rollout due to shimmy damper failure; aircraft vibrating violently (p. 1-2)
During landing rollout left main gear collapsed and airplane traveled to left departing paved surface (p. 1-2)
Airplane impacted runway 30 glide slope equipment shelter; right main gear and nosewheel also collapsed (p. 1-2)
Fuel tanks breached; shortly after airplane stopped post-crash fire began on right wing (p. 1)
All 140 occupants evacuated safely approximately 5 seconds after aircraft stopped
Emergency response personnel contained fire and secured scene

notes: Deep read from NTSB investigation summary (DCA22FA132)
9 events extracted from landing sequence
Probable cause and factors from investigation findings

records.title: 2022 Mutiny Bay DHC-3 crash

aircraft.type: de Havilland Canada DHC-3 Turbine Otter

location.name: Mutiny Bay, near Freeland, Whidbey Island

records.summary: A DHC-3 Turbine Otter floatplane operated by Friday Harbor Seaplanes departed Friday Harbor at 14:50 PDT on September 4, 2022, for Renton Municipal Airport. During cruise flight at 600-700 feet mean sea level, the aircraft entered a climb to about 1,000 feet then pitched down in a nose-low, near-vertical descent and impacted the water in Mutiny Bay. All 10 occupants (1 pilot and 9 passengers) were fatally injured and the aircraft was destroyed. The NTSB preliminary investigation found the horizontal stabilizer trim actuator lock ring was missing, allowing the clamp nut to unthread from the barrel and rendering pitch control uncontrollable.
records.probable_cause: Loss of control of the aircraft due to the unthreading of the clamp nut from the horizontal stabilizer trim actuator barrel due to a missing lock ring, which resulted in the horizontal stabilizer moving to an extreme trailing-edge-down position rendering the airplane's pitch uncontrollable. The actuator lock ring was the only mechanism designed to prevent unthreading of the clamp nut.

factors.evidence: horizontal stabilizer actuator lock ring was missing from the aircraft; the lock ring is designed to prevent the clamp nut from unscrewing from the actuator barrel (p. 56-57)
clamp nut unthreaded from horizontal stabilizer trim actuator barrel due to missing lock ring, allowing the actuator to move to an extreme trailing-edge-down position (p. 53-59)
with the actuator unthreaded, the horizontal stabilizer moved to an extreme trailing-edge-down position rendering the airplane's pitch uncontrollable (p. 118-119)
aircraft entered a nose-low, near-vertical descent and impacted the water in Mutiny Bay at high speed, disintegrating the aircraft (p. 34-35)

events.text: DHC-3 departed Friday Harbor Seaplane Base bound for Renton Municipal Airport
Aircraft in cruise flight at altitudes between 600 and 700 feet mean sea level, groundspeed between 115 and 125 knots
Aircraft began climb, reaching maximum altitude of about 1,000 feet mean sea level
Aircraft entered rapid nose-low, near-vertical descent and impacted water in Mutiny Bay; wreckage sank; all 10 occupants fatally injured

recommendations.text: Require all operators of De Havilland Canada DHC-3 airplanes to conduct an immediate one-time inspection of the horizontal stabilizer actuator lock ring in accordance with the instructions in Viking Air Limited Service Letter DHC3-SL-27-001 and report their findings to the Federal Aviation Administration

Require all operators of De Havilland Canada DHC-3 airplanes to conduct an immediate one-time inspection of the horizontal stabilizer actuator lock ring in accordance with the instructions in Viking Air Limited Service Letter DHC3-SL-27-001 and report their findings to Transport Canada

safety_changes: Viking Air Limited published Service Letter DHC3-SL-27-001 recommending visual inspection of stabilizer actuator lock ring presence and correct seating
Urgent recommendations issued by NTSB on October 26, 2022 for immediate inspection of lock rings on all DHC-3 aircraft

notes: This is a preliminary urgent safety recommendation report (AIR-22-08) issued on October 26, 2022, during an ongoing investigation
Report date is more than 7 weeks after the accident; final accident investigation report has not yet been issued
Primary finding: missing or improperly installed horizontal stabilizer actuator lock ring causing loss of pitch control
Aircraft wreckage recovered from sea floor (85% recovered); examination confirmed clamp nut unthreaded from barrel
Lock ring itself has not been found; investigation ongoing into failure modes and maintenance records

records.title: 2022 Dallas airshow crash

aircraft.type: Boeing B-17G Flying Fortress and Bell P-63F Kingcobra

records.summary: Two World War II-era restored aircraft, a Boeing B-17G Flying Fortress and a Bell P-63F Kingcobra, collided in midair at 1322 local time on November 12, 2022, during the Commemorative Air Force's Wings Over Dallas air show. The P-63F, performing a high-speed descending banked turn toward the runway approach, collided with the B-17G from above and slightly behind, severing the B-17G's fuselage just aft of the wing. Both aircraft were destroyed in the impact and subsequent fires. The accident resulted from inadequate prebriefing with no altitude deconfliction procedures, reliance on real-time air boss directives and see-and-avoid strategy, and diminished pilot visibility due to aircraft structures and attention demands of the air show performance.
records.probable_cause: The air boss's and air show event organizer's lack of an adequate, prebriefed aircraft separation plan for the air show performance, relying instead on the air boss's real-time deconfliction directives and the see-and-avoid strategy for collision avoidance, which allowed for the loss of separation between the two aircraft. Contributing cause: the lack of FAA guidance and oversight of air bosses and air show event organizers.

factors.evidence: Lack of FAA guidance for air bosses and air show event organizers on developing plans and performing risk assessments that ensure the separation of aircraft that are not part of an approved maneuvers package.

A pilot on the ground speculated that the P-63F pilot might have mistaken one of the trailing bombers for the leader, leading him to believe he had already cleared the bomber formation's flight path. The P-63F pilot was executing a descending banked turn targeting the bomber formation.

The P-63F pilot executed a high-speed descending banked turn onto the runway approach. The pilot tightened his trajectory and positioned the aircraft's belly toward the bomber line, which obscured the pilot's view of the approaching B-17G.
The P-63F collided with the B-17G on the rear port quarter from above at 1322 local time. The collision severed the B-17G's fuselage from a point just aft of the wings.
Both aircraft broke apart immediately after collision and fell to the ground, where both aircraft experienced in-flight and on-ground fires. The B-17G also experienced an explosion on the ground.

events.text: Boeing B-17G departed Dallas Executive Airport for local air show flight.
Bell P-63F departed Dallas Executive Airport for local air show flight, 5 minutes after B-17G departure.
Air boss directed bomber formation (B-17G and trailing bombers) to fly parallel to spectator viewing line at 1000 feet show line.
Fighters (including P-63F) instructed to enter trail formation and fly at 500 feet show line in front of bomber formation.

P-63F pilot performing high-speed descending banked turn toward runway approach, targeting the bomber line. Pilot tightens trajectory and positions aircraft belly toward bomber line, obscuring view of approaching B-17G.
P-63F collides with B-17G on rear port quarter from above. Impact severs B-17G's fuselage from point just aft of wings. B-17G pitch angle at impact approximately 10-15 degrees nose down.

Both aircraft break apart in midair and fall to ground. B-17G with 5 occupants (pilot, copilot, flight engineer, 2 scanners) destroyed in impact and in-flight fire. P-63F with 1 occupant (pilot) destroyed in impact. Both aircraft experience ground fires; B-17G experiences additional ground explosion. All 6 occupants killed. No ground injuries.

recommendations.text: Develop and publish standardized procedures and guidelines for air show directors and air bosses on aircraft separation planning, including altitude deconfliction procedures, required briefing content, and risk assessment methodology for air shows involving multiple aircraft.

Establish and implement requirements for regular recurrent training and evaluation of air bosses, including proficiency checks on separation procedures, communication protocols, and emergency procedures.
Implement direct FAA surveillance and oversight of air boss performance during air shows, including real-time monitoring of air boss decisions and separation management.

Recommend that all air show operators develop and implement pre-flight briefings that include specific altitude deconfliction procedures for all aircraft not part of formally approved maneuver packages, with emphasis on preventing unplanned altitude conflicts.

Implement enhanced crew briefings for all multi-aircraft air show performances that explicitly address separation procedures, altitude assignments, field geometry, and limitations of see-and-avoid procedures in high-performance maneuvering environments.

safety_changes: FAA increased focus on air show safety oversight and air boss qualification standards
Emphasis on pre-flight briefing requirements for altitude separation in multi-aircraft air show performances
Enhanced industry guidance on see-and-avoid limitations in high-speed maneuvering air show environments

notes: NTSB Final Report published December 13, 2024; complete factual information section and probable cause findings read
Pilots: B-17G commander age 66 with 28,000 hours; co-pilot age 67 with 25,300 hours; P-63F pilot age 63 with 34,500 hours - all experienced with recent medical certifications
Weather: Visual meteorological conditions, 10 mile visibility, clear skies, 14 knots wind
Key finding: inadequate separation planning and reliance on see-and-avoid strategy proved insufficient; pilot visibility obscured by aircraft structures
Air show operated under Part 91 with certificate of waiver; no flight plan filed for either aircraft
Investigation conducted by NTSB with FAA and Commemorative Air Force participation

records.title: Yeti Airlines 691
records.time_reference: Nepal time (UTC+5:45); clock strings approximate to the minute, t is relative to the movement of the condition levers at about 10:56

agencies.name: Aircraft Accident Investigation Commission
agencies.report_title: Final Report on the Accident Investigation of 9N-ANC ATR 72-212A (ATR 72-500), Yeti Airlines Flight 691, Pokhara, Nepal, 15 January 2023

location.name: Seti River gorge, about 1.5 km from the runway 12 threshold, Pokhara

records.summary: On a visual approach to runway 12 at the newly opened Pokhara International Airport, the pilot flying called for flaps 30. The pilot monitoring, an instructor captain, instead moved both condition levers to the feather position, feathering both propellers and removing all thrust. Neither pilot noticed; the aircraft decelerated in the turn onto final, the stick shaker activated and the aircraft stalled and rolled at low altitude, crashing into the Seti River gorge. All 72 on board died.
records.probable_cause: The AAIC concluded that the probable cause was the inadvertent movement of both condition levers to the feather position by the pilot monitoring, which resulted in the feathering of both propellers and a loss of thrust that led to an aerodynamic stall and collision with terrain. Contributing were high workload and stress during a non-standard visual approach to a newly opened airport, the failure of the crew to monitor and cross-check the aircraft's configuration and performance, inadequate crew coordination and non-compliance with standard operating procedures, and shortcomings in the operator's training and the validation of the visual approach procedure.

factors.evidence: When flaps 30 was called, the pilot monitoring moved the condition levers, located next to the flap lever on the centre pedestal, to FEATHER instead of moving the flap lever.
The crew were flying a visual approach at low altitude to a new airport with a non-standard circuit, in a supervised familiarisation flight.
The approach was not flown according to a briefed and validated procedure, and the before-landing checks were not completed as required by the SOPs.
Neither pilot detected that the flaps had remained at 15 and that both engines' torque had dropped to zero after the levers were moved.
There was no effective cross-check of the configuration change, and the exchange between the pilots did not identify the loss of thrust.
The crew did not understand why the aircraft was not responding to power lever movement until the stall warning activated.
The report identified deficiencies in the operator's training and in the preparation of crews for operations at the new airport.
The stick shaker activated twice at low altitude; the crew did not recover before the aircraft rolled.
With both propellers feathered the airspeed decayed in the turn to final and the aircraft stalled.
The aircraft rolled sharply left and struck the ground in the gorge.

events.text: Departs Kathmandu for Pokhara. The captain in the left seat is pilot flying on a familiarisation flight to the new airport; an instructor captain in the right seat is pilot monitoring.
The crew request and are cleared for a visual approach to runway 12 instead of runway 30; the approach is flown at low altitude on a non-standard path without a validated procedure.
Flaps 15 selected and landing gear extended on the downwind leg.

The pilot flying calls for flaps 30. The pilot monitoring moves both condition levers to FEATHER instead of the flap lever; both propellers feather and engine torque drops to zero. The flap lever remains at 15.
The pilot monitoring reads the flaps as set; neither pilot notices the feathered propellers or the zero torque, and the before-landing checklist is not completed.
Flaps 30 is subsequently selected; the aircraft continues the turn toward final with the propellers feathered and airspeed decreasing.
The pilot flying reports that the engines are not producing power; the power levers are advanced but, with the propellers feathered, no thrust results.
Stick shaker activates at low altitude in the turn to final.
Stick shaker activates a second time; the aircraft rolls sharply to the left.
The aircraft strikes the ground in the Seti River gorge about 1.5 km from the runway 12 threshold and catches fire; all 68 passengers and 4 crew are killed.

recommendations.text: Ensure that visual approach procedures for new airports are properly designed, validated and published, and that operators' crews are trained on them before operations begin.

Strengthen SOP compliance, crew coordination and monitoring, including cross-verification of configuration changes and completion of checklists, and review training and supervision on familiarisation flights.
Consider design or procedural measures to reduce the risk of confusing the condition levers with the flap lever on the ATR 72 pedestal.

safety_changes: The Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal revised its approach procedures and crew training requirements for Pokhara International Airport.
Yeti Airlines revised its SOPs on configuration changes and checklist discipline.

notes: Clock strings are given only to the minute; event offsets are approximate reconstructions of the roughly 50-second sequence from the lever movement to impact.
The pilot monitoring's exact words when the levers were moved are paraphrased.

The report's findings on regulatory oversight and on the airport's procedure validation are summarised in the probable cause but regulatory_oversight is not listed as a factor because the exact wording was not verified.
The Nepal AAIC report is published through the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation; its home page is used as the source.

records.title: Alaska Airlines 1282 on 5 January 2024
records.summary: Alaska Airlines Flight 1282 experienced in-flight separation of left mid-exit door plug at 14,830 feet during climb. Four securing bolts were never reinstalled after factory rework. Aircraft descended safely to Portland with all 177 occupants surviving.
records.probable_cause: The probable cause was Boeing's failure to provide adequate training, guidance, and oversight to ensure manufacturing personnel could consistently comply with its parts removal process. Contributing was the FAA's ineffective compliance enforcement and audit planning activities which failed to identify Boeing's repetitive systemic nonconformance issues.

factors.evidence: Four vertical movement arrestor bolts and upper guide track bolts were missing before the plug moved upward, indicating they were never reinstalled after being removed at the factory (p. 133)
Door plug had no fail-safe secondary retention mechanism to prevent separation if bolts were removed (p. 119)

FAA compliance enforcement surveillance, audit planning, and records systems were deficient and lacked functionality to identify repetitive and systemic discrepancies with Boeing's Business Process Instruction (p. 135)
Boeing's on-the-job training was unstructured and undocumented; neither door team manager nor personnel had experience opening an MED plug (p. 120)
No removal record was generated when left MED plug was opened, increasing risk that closure would not be performed properly (p. 119)
Left MED plug separated causing cabin pressure drop from 14.09 psi at 14,830 feet (p. 2)

events.text: Flight 1282 departed Portland International Airport runway
Cabin pressure dropped; left MED plug separated from fuselage causing rapid depressurization
Master caution alert activated; flight deck door opened striking flight attendant D; oxygen masks deployed
Captain and First Officer donned emergency oxygen masks; Captain initiated descent
Aircraft reached maximum altitude of 16,320 feet and began descent
Selected altitude changed from 23,000 ft to 10,000 ft
Aircraft descended below 10,000 ft; cabin altitude warning deactivated
Aircraft landed safely on runway 28L at Portland with all 177 occupants surviving

recommendations.text: Issue airworthiness directive requiring retrofit of all in-service MED plug-equipped airplanes with design enhancement
Revise compliance enforcement surveillance system to identify, record, track and resolve recurring systemic discrepancies
Revise audit planning activities to provide necessary functionality for oversight
Revise records systems to provide records for identifying and resolving systemic discrepancies
Continue certification process for design enhancement for mid exit door plugs
Apply safety risk management process to revise Business Process Instruction to ensure clear guidance
Develop recurrent training on Business Process Instruction for manufacturing personnel
Develop structured on-the-job training program for manufacturing personnel

records.title: 2024 Alaska Air Fuel Douglas C-54 crash
records.summary: A Douglas C-54D carrying fuel from Fairbanks to Kobuk experienced failure of the left outboard engine shortly after takeoff. When the crew attempted to feather the failed engine's propeller, a maintenance defect in the feathering system allowed pressurized oil to spray onto the hot exhaust, igniting a fire. Fuel that had leaked from a damaged tank behind the engine subsequently exploded, severing aileron controls and forcing an uncontrolled descent into terrain.
records.probable_cause: Maintenance error in improper installation of the feathering system nut and failure to adequately repair a fuel tank leak, leading to inflight fire and loss of control when the pilot attempted to feather the failed engine. (Preliminary NTSB Form 6120.1)

factors.evidence: A fuel leak had developed in the outboard fuel tank of the left wing near engine one with fuel dripping at between five and ten drops of fuel per minute (p. 2, summary record).

The AN bulkhead fitting had a B-nut installed, but it was not attached to the corresponding oil hose for the feathering system, a critical safety component (p. 1-2, narrative). Engine was a newly rebuilt engine from Anderson Aeromotive with approximately seven hours total time since installation (p. 8).
Engine one lost power shortly after takeoff at approximately 1000 local time (p. 4, form data; p. 1, summary record).

Fire developed in or behind engine #1 shortly after engine failure was indicated; fire appears to have penetrated the #1 rear firewall and reached the #2 (inboard) main wing fuel tank (p. 1, narrative). Bright explosion was captured on video coming from the engine area (p. 1, summary record).
Aircraft entered a sharp left turn and began an uncontrolled descent following the engine fire and fuel tank explosion (p. 1, summary record).
The failing engine separated from the aircraft approximately 100 feet above the ground; fuel tank explosion severed aileron controls (p. 1-2, summary record).

events.text: Aircraft departed from Fairbanks Airport (PAFA) bound for Kobuk at approximately 0955 local time with fuel cargo load of 7,400 gallons 100LL avgas (p. 4, form data).
Smoke observed from engine one which was no longer operating; engine failure indicated on tracking data approximately 8 minutes after takeoff (p. 1, narrative).

White smoke and fire developed behind the engine with bright explosion captured on video; fire originated from pressurized oil from the feathering system nut (improperly installed) spraying onto hot exhaust surfaces (p. 1-2, narrative and summary).
Fire penetrated the #1 rear firewall and reached the #2 (inboard) main wing fuel tank causing that wing tank to explode in flight (p. 1, narrative).
Aircraft entered a sharp left turn following the explosion and began an uncontrolled descent (p. 1, summary record).
The failing engine separated from the aircraft approximately 100 feet above the ground (p. 1, summary record).

Infrasound data recorded the aircraft impacting terrain near Tanana River approximately 8 minutes and 8 seconds after departure with two occupants aboard; aircraft destroyed on impact (p. 1, summary record).

recommendations.text: Safety recommendations to follow after investigation of the #1 engine and wing area.

notes: Deep read from NTSB Pilot/Operator Aircraft Accident/Incident Report Form 6120.1: Narrative History of Flight (p. 7), Mechanical Malfunction/Failure section (p. 9), and Operator Safety Recommendation section (p. 8)
7 events extracted with 2 clock times from available data; integrated with summary record details for comprehensive timeline from departure through impact
This is a preliminary accident report form; formal investigation report with detailed mechanical analysis and formal recommendations from NTSB pending

Maintenance defect clearly identified: improper installation of feathering system nut allowing pressurized oil spray onto hot exhaust; newly rebuilt engine from Anderson Aeromotive with only 7 hours time since installation

records.title: Gazpromavia 9608
records.summary: A Sukhoi Superjet 100-95LR crashed on July 12, 2024, during a ferry flight from Lukhovitsy to Vnukovo, approximately 80 kilometers southeast of Moscow. The aircraft climbed to only 900 meters before beginning an uncontrolled descent. The investigation found that two angle-of-attack sensors had been installed with a five-degree deviation during maintenance, causing incorrect activation of the stall warning and protection systems.
records.probable_cause: Incorrect installation of angle-of-attack sensors during maintenance with approximately five-degree deviation, causing erroneous stall warning and protection system activation, resulting in uncontrolled descent and terrain impact.

factors.evidence: Two of the four angle-of-attack sensors installed with a deviation of approximately five degrees
An engineer at the Lukhovitsy Aviation Plant installed two AOA sensors with the deviation
Incorrect AOA readings caused elevator to automatically lower the nose and the aircraft to descend
Aircraft impacted with terrain in uncontrolled dive at 365 knots

events.text: Aircraft took off from Lukhovitsy Aviation Plant
Four minutes after takeoff aircraft made last radio contact, reached maximum altitude about 900 meters
Aircraft cruising with nose pitch angle 5-6 degrees; AOA sensors showing conflicting readings (10-11.5 vs 11-13.5 degrees)
First officer pulled nose up to nearly 14 degrees, autopilot disconnected; captain accelerated to 270 knots to arrest descent
At 4500 feet aircraft initiating to climb; crew disabled autothrottle, airspeed reached 308 knots triggering overspeed warning
At 3000 feet crew attempted to arrest descent but elevators did not respond; aircraft impacted wooded terrain at 365 knots
