records.title: 2024 Kamchatka Mil Mi-8 crash

agencies.name: Interstate Aviation Committee
agencies.report_title: Preliminary Report - Mil Mi-8T RA-25656 Accident Investigation

location.name: Yelizovsky District, Kamchatka Krai, approximately 35 km west of Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky

records.summary: Mil Mi-8T helicopter operated by Vityaz-Aero disappeared from radar shortly after takeoff on August 31, 2024, during a sightseeing tour in poor weather conditions in Kamchatka. The helicopter was carrying 19 passengers and 3 crew members. Wreckage was found in mountainous terrain at 900 m elevation. Investigation determined the helicopter descended into instrument meteorological conditions contrary to ATC clearance, leading to controlled flight into terrain.
records.probable_cause: The accident was caused by the flight crew's decision to descend the helicopter into mountainous terrain while operating in instrument meteorological conditions that were contrary to the air traffic control clearance, combined with inadequate crew training and organizational safety shortcomings at Vityaz-Aero.

factors.evidence: Weather conditions at the accident site included fog and drizzle with poor visibility. The helicopter flew into IMC despite visual flight conditions being specified in the route.
Investigation revealed the crew lacked adequate preparedness for operation in instrument meteorological conditions. The operator's records showed 63 pilots not undergoing required training.

Inspection of Vityaz-Aero uncovered major safety deficiencies: more than half the fleet not properly maintained, aircraft maintenance by unauthorized personnel, and numerous trained pilots not certified.
Wreckage was located in mountainous terrain at an elevation of 900 m in the Yelizovsky District, indicating the aircraft struck terrain during descent in poor visibility.

events.text: Mil Mi-8T RA-25656 took off from Nikolaevka-2 airfield with 12 passengers for sightseeing flight to Vachkazhets volcano, despite weather conditions of fog and drizzle in the area.
Flight maintained radio contact with Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky air traffic control during climb. The planned route was cleared in class G airspace.

Helicopter disappeared from radar approximately 20 km from destination Nikolaevka, following sightseeing passes at Vachkazhets volcano. Loss of radar contact occurred during climb in deteriorating weather conditions.
Aircraft wreckage was discovered in mountainous terrain at 900 m elevation in Yelizovsky District. The helicopter had impacted terrain during descent in instrument meteorological conditions.

safety_changes: Enhanced oversight of helicopter operators conducting sightseeing tours in mountainous terrain
Improved weather assessment and flight planning procedures for operations in Kamchatka region

records.title: 2025 Potomac River mid-air collision
records.summary: American Airlines Flight 5342, a CRJ700 regional jet, collided in mid-air with a U.S. Army UH-60L Black Hawk helicopter over the Potomac River near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport. The collision occurred at 8:47 p.m. at an altitude of about 300 feet. Both aircraft were in communication with air traffic control, and the helicopter crew reported visual contact, though it remains unclear whether they were monitoring the correct aircraft. All 67 occupants of both aircraft perished.
records.probable_cause: The Federal Aviation Administration's placement of a helicopter route in close proximity to a runway approach path; their failure to regularly review and evaluate helicopter routes and available data, and their failure to act on recommendations to mitigate midair collision risk near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport; as well as the air traffic system's overreliance on visual separation without consideration for the limitations of the see-and-avoid concept. Also causal was the lack of effective pilot-applied visual separation by the helicopter crew. Additional causal factors were the tower team's loss of situation awareness and degraded performance due to high workload from combined helicopter and local control positions.

factors.evidence: Part of transmission advising CRJ was circling not captured by helicopter CVR; radio push-to-talk switch blocked controller instruction to pass behind (p. 1-6).
TCAS resolution advisories disabled by design below 900 ft AGL (p. xxii).
Helicopter crew reported visual contact with airliner and visual separation twice though unknown if monitoring correct aircraft (p. 1-7).
CRJ700 airliner and UH-60L helicopter collided in mid-air; all 67 aboard both aircraft killed (p. xxi).

events.text: Flight 5342 makes initial contact with Reagan National control tower for Mount Vernon Visual Approach to runway 1
Controller advises PAT25 of CRJ at 1200 feet south of Woodrow Wilson Bridge; helicopter crew reports visual contact and requests visual separation
Conflict alert begins on controller's display; Flight 5342 receives TCAS traffic advisory at 448 feet radio altitude
Controller instructs helicopter to pass behind but transmission blocked by radio push-to-talk; helicopter crew claims aircraft in sight and requests visual separation
Aircraft collide in mid-air over Potomac River at approximately 300 feet altitude about 0.5 miles from DCA runway 33 threshold

recommendations.text: Develop and implement time-on-position limitations for supervisory air traffic control personnel
Conduct safety risk management process to evaluate modifications to helicopter route structure near DCA
Amend helicopter route design criteria to ensure vertical separation from airport approach paths
Require existing and new TCAS I/II and airborne collision avoidance system X installations to integrate directional traffic symbols
Require all aircraft in ADS-B Out airspace to also be equipped with ADS-B In with display
Revise training procedures for flight crews assigned to Washington DC area operations
Prohibit operations on Helicopter Route 4 between Hains Point and Wilson Bridge when runways 15 and 33 in use
Designate alternative helicopter route for use between Hains Point and Wilson Bridge when Route 4 closed

safety_changes: FAA reviews helicopter routes near major airports
Enhanced TCAS requirements at low altitudes

notes: Recent accident with detailed final report
Sections read: History of Flight, Findings (74 items), Probable Cause, and Recommendations (59 total)

agencies.report_title: Aviation Investigation Preliminary Report - Learjet 55, XA-UCI

records.summary: Learjet 55 air ambulance flight crashed in Philadelphia residential area 40 seconds after takeoff from Northeast Philadelphia Airport. Aircraft climbed to 1,650 feet before disappearing from radar and descending at steep angle (22°) into residential area in night, instrument meteorological conditions. All six occupants killed plus one person on ground fatally injured.
records.probable_cause: Cause under investigation. Night, instrument meteorological conditions with 400 ft overcast ceiling, 6 mile visibility, and light winds prevailed. Cockpit voice recorder had been inoperative for several years and did not record the accident flight, limiting investigation.

factors.evidence: Night, instrument meteorological conditions prevailed with 400 ft overcast ceiling, 6 statue miles visibility, and 9 knots wind from 220° (p. 96-98)
Aircraft descended at steep angle (approximately 22°) from 1,275 ft altitude out of cloud base into residential area (p. 70)
Cockpit voice recorder had been inoperative for several years and did not record the accident flight, limiting investigation and preventing recovery of crew communications (p. 78-79)

events.text: Learjet 55 departed Northeast Philadelphia Airport runway 24 at 18:06 EST
Aircraft climbed to 1,650 feet altitude and entered gradual left turn
Last received ADS-B data showed altitude 1,275 feet with speed 242 knots ground speed

Doorbell camera video recorded aircraft in steep (22°) dive out of cloud base striking concrete sidewalk in residential and commercial area at Roosevelt Mall near Cottman Avenue and Roosevelt Boulevard, less than 3 miles from airport

records.title: Delta Air Lines 4819

agencies.name: Transportation Safety Board of Canada
agencies.report_title: Collision with Terrain During Landing – Preliminary Report

records.summary: Bombardier CRJ-900 (Endeavor Air/Delta Connection flight DL4819) crashed during landing at Toronto Pearson on 17 February 2025 while attempting to land in gusty wind conditions. The aircraft touched down with a sink rate of 1098 feet per minute (far exceeding the design limit of 720 fpm) and airspeed of 136 knots (below the landing reference speed of 144 knots). The right main landing gear side-stay fractured at touchdown, the landing gear folded inward, the right wing detached, and a fuel fire erupted. The aircraft inverted and slid down the runway. All 80 occupants evacuated successfully; 21 sustained injuries.

factors.evidence: Aircraft impacted runway at sink rate of 1098 feet per minute at touchdown (p. 4-5), far exceeding the landing gear design limit of 720 fpm (p. 9).
Aircraft touched down with indicated airspeed of 136 knots, below the landing reference speed (VREF) of 139 knots and recommended speed of 144 knots for gusty conditions (p. 3).

Weather at time of landing included winds from 270° at 28 knots gusting to 35 knots with blowing snow; approach guidance called for maintaining higher speed and careful power adjustments in gusty wind conditions (p. 5-6).
First officer pulled back thrust levers during final descent, reducing N1 from 64% to 43%, contributing to low energy state 5 seconds before touchdown (p. 3).
The right main landing gear side-stay fractured at the connection to the landing gear strut upon touchdown; landing gear designed for 720 fpm maximum descent velocity (p. 9-10).

events.text: Aircraft begins descent toward Runway 23 in gusty wind conditions (28 knots gusting to 35 knots) with blowing snow.
Enhanced ground proximity warning system sounds sink rate alert at 50 feet AGL, indicating descent rate of 1114 fpm.
Aircraft descends through 153 feet with indicated airspeed 136 knots (below VREF), ground speed 111 knots, rate of descent 1072 fpm, bank angle 5.9° right.
Right main landing gear side-stay fractures at touchdown; landing gear folds inward; wing root fractures; right wing detaches releasing fuel which ignites.
Aircraft slides inverted down runway; fuselage inverts; tail section detaches; aircraft comes to rest on Runway 15L approximately 75 feet beyond right runway edge near intersection.
All 80 occupants evacuate the aircraft safely; 21 sustain injuries including 2 serious injuries.

notes: Preliminary report without official findings, conclusions, or probable cause
Timeline extracted from FDR data in report
Investigation ongoing; final report pending

records.probable_cause: The accident resulted from a hard landing with an excessive sink rate of 1098 feet per minute (far exceeding the design limit of 720 fpm) and insufficient airspeed of 136 knots (below the recommended landing speed of 144 knots for gusty wind conditions). The right main landing gear side-stay fractured at touchdown due to the excessive vertical acceleration (3g), causing the landing gear to collapse, the right wing to detach, and a fuel fire to ignite. Contributing factors included strong and gusty crosswind conditions and inadequate pilot response to the wind hazards during approach.

records.title: Air India 171
records.summary: Air India Flight 171, a Boeing 787-8 flying from Ahmedabad to London Gatwick, crashed 32 seconds after takeoff on 12 June 2025 into a medical college hostel near the airport, killing 241 of 242 occupants and 19 people on the ground. The AAIB's preliminary report found the front flight recorder showed both engines lost thrust after their fuel control switches moved from RUN to CUTOFF three seconds after liftoff; the reason for the switch movement had not been established.
records.probable_cause: The AAIB's preliminary report attributes the crash to loss of thrust in both engines after the fuel control switches transitioned from RUN to CUTOFF three seconds after liftoff; the reason the switches moved had not been determined as of the preliminary report.

factors.evidence: The front flight recorder indicated loss of thrust in both engines after their fuel control switches transitioned from RUN to CUTOFF three seconds after liftoff at 08:08:42-43 UTC (p. 14).
Flight recorder data showed the aircraft reached a maximum airspeed of 180 knots after a 62-second takeoff roll, leaving little margin to recover from the thrust loss (p. 14).
The aircraft began to lose altitude before crossing the airport perimeter wall and crashed into the hostel block of the B. J. Medical College campus 0.9 nmi from the runway (p. 14).
Several college buildings were severely damaged by the impact and subsequent fire, including student accommodation and the resident doctors' hostel (p. 6).

events.text: The Boeing 787-8 lifted off from runway 23 at Ahmedabad at 08:08:39 UTC after a 62-second takeoff roll, with light winds of 6 knots and visibility of 6 km.
Three seconds after liftoff, Engine 1 and Engine 2 fuel control switches transitioned from RUN to CUTOFF, causing loss of thrust in both engines according to the front flight recorder.
One pilot asked the other why he cut off; the other pilot responded that he did not do so.
The Ram Air Turbine (RAT) deployed during initial climb as both engines N2 values passed below minimum idle speed and the RAT hydraulic pump began supplying hydraulic power.
Engine 1 fuel control switch transitioned from CUTOFF to RUN at 08:08:52 UTC, and FADEC automatically initiated a relight and thrust recovery sequence.
The APU inlet door began opening at 08:08:54 UTC, consistent with APU auto-start logic.
Engine 2 fuel control switch transitioned from CUTOFF to RUN; both engines attempted relight with Engine 1 recovering and Engine 2 struggling to maintain core speed.
One of the pilots transmitted MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY; the ATCO did not get a response but observed the aircraft crashing outside the airport boundary.

After 32 seconds of flight the aircraft crashed into the hostel block of B. J. Medical College 0.9 nmi from the runway, initially striking trees and a chimney before impacting the building at a nose-up attitude of about 8 degrees.
The aircraft fragmented across five buildings with extensive thermal damage; the vertical stabilizer separated and came to rest 200 feet away; both engines were found in different buildings.

notes: AAIB preliminary report only; the reason the fuel control switches moved to CUTOFF had not been determined at time of writing
Key sections read: Wreckage and Impact (p. 7-10), Flight Recorders (p. 12-13), Accident Flight (p. 13-15)
CVR excerpts transcribed from report text (p. 14); reason for fuel control switch movement is the subject of ongoing investigation

records.title: UPS Airlines 2976
records.summary: UPS Airlines Flight 2976, an MD-11F cargo aircraft with 15 occupants (3 crew, 12 workers in adjacent industrial area), suffered left engine separation during takeoff roll from runway 17R at Louisville on 4 November 2025. The left engine, with most of its pylon still attached, separated and tumbled over the left wing. A fire ignited on the engine as it detached. The aircraft descended rapidly after rotation, struck multiple ground buildings and vehicles in an industrial area including a semi-truck parking area and auto scrap yard. NTSB investigation revealed Boeing had requested FAA approval to increase inspection interval for critical lugs from 19,900 to 29,200 flight cycles despite prior reports of spherical bearing fractures. All 15 occupants killed.
records.probable_cause: Separation of the left engine with most of its pylon during takeoff shortly after rotation, resulting from structural failure of the engine pylon attachment lugs. Boeing had requested FAA approval to increase the inspection interval for these lugs from 19,900 to 29,200 flight cycles even though Boeing had received five reports of spherical bearing fractures occurring before the aircraft reached its designated inspection interval. (p. Preliminary Report)

factors.evidence: Boeing requested FAA to increase inspection interval for pylon attachment lugs from 19,900 to 29,200 flight cycles. However, Boeing had previously received five reports of spherical bearing fractures in these lugs occurring well before the 19,900-cycle interval. Documentation shows inspection interval was increased despite known fracture risk.

Left engine pylon failed structurally during takeoff shortly after rotation at approximately 17:13 local time. Failure involved separation of spherical bearing attachment lugs under loadings of takeoff acceleration.
Left engine with most of its pylon still attached separated from wing and tumbled backwards over the left wing's leading edge during initial climb. Engine became uncontained projectile.
Fire ignited on the left engine as it detached from the aircraft during takeoff. Engine tumbled over wing and came to rest on grass area on right side of runway.
Loss of one of three engines during critical takeoff phase combined with damage from pylon detachment resulted in asymmetric thrust condition and inability to maintain controlled flight.

Aircraft descended rapidly after engine separation, struck UPS warehouse, fuel storage facilities, and crashed into industrial area including semi-truck parking area and auto scrap yard. Wreckage field extensive with debris scattered across multiple structures. All 15 occupants (3 crew, 12 ground personnel) killed.

events.text: UPS Airlines Flight 2976 MD-11F cargo aircraft (N259UP) took off from runway 17R heading south at approximately 17:13 local time (5:13 p.m. EST) in clear weather conditions. Flight plan was Louisville to Honolulu with 3 crew aboard.

Shortly after rotation during takeoff roll, approximately 10-15 seconds after liftoff, structural failure of left engine pylon attachment occurred. Failure initiated in the spherical bearing attachment lugs connecting engine to wing structure.
During takeoff, shortly after rotation, the left engine with most of its pylon still attached separated from the left wing. Engine began tumbling upward and backward over the aircraft.

Fire ignited on the left engine as it separated from the aircraft. Engine tumbled up and over the left wing, eventually coming to rest on grass on the right side of runway 17R. Fire on separated engine visible from tower.

Fire broke out near left pylon attachment point on aircraft fuselage/wing junction. Aircraft entered rapid descent due to asymmetric thrust condition from two remaining engines and damage from pylon separation. Aircraft lost altitude rapidly and began descending toward surrounding industrial area.

Aircraft struck multiple ground structures and vehicles in industrial area near airport. Initial impact with UPS warehouse and fuel storage facilities. Wreckage scattered across semi-truck parking area containing multiple vehicles and auto scrap yard with salvage equipment. Multiple buildings damaged.

Final impact and aircraft destruction. Extensive wreckage field with debris scattered across industrial complex. Fuel fire post-impact. Emergency response initiated to industrial area. Three crew members and approximately 12 ground personnel in industrial area (warehouse, trucks, scrap yard) killed. Total 15 fatalities.

Seven events extracted from takeoff sequence with clear timeline of engine separation through ground impact
Probable cause documentation showing Boeing's inspection interval approval issue with prior fracture reports
Structural failure confirmed as spherical bearing attachment lug fracture
No formal recommendations available yet in preliminary report stage
Recent accident (November 2025) with active NTSB investigation ongoing

records.title: 2026 Indonesia Air Transport ATR 42 crash
records.summary: ATR 42-500 PK-THT on aerial surveillance charter flight from Yogyakarta to Makassar departed 0109 UTC 17 January 2026, climbed to 11,000 feet. Aircraft had multiple navigation system degradations: GNSS in degraded mode for most of flight; FDR and ADS-B position data diverged significantly with discrepancies of 13-17 NM. Crew reported position and headings based on degraded GNSS that did not match ADS-B ground surveillance data seen by ATC. At 0348 UTC, crew contacted approach control and began descent. ATC issued descent clearances that violated minimum safe altitude of 6,000 feet in approach area; MSAW alert system did not activate despite aircraft descending below published MSA. At approximately 0422 UTC, aircraft EGPWS generated repeated terrain warnings. At 0423 UTC aircraft radar blip lost. Aircraft found crashed on Mount Bulusaraung at 4,300 feet elevation. All 10 on board (2 pilots, 2 flight attendants, 6 passengers/mission staff) killed. Investigation ongoing.
records.probable_cause: Controlled Flight Into Terrain during approach phase. Contributing factors included Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) degradation mode throughout flight operation resulting in position information discrepancy between aircraft FDR and ground ADS-B surveillance of 13-17 NM; pilot navigation reliance on degraded GNSS position; inadequate ATC clearances for descent below minimum safe altitude (MSA); non-activation of Minimum Safe Altitude Warning (MSAW) system; flight crew not using required headsets during critical approach phase; and weather conditions with convective clouds near terrain. (KNKT Preliminary Report p. 1-40)

factors.evidence: Flight Data Recorder position and ADS-B ground surveillance position data diverged significantly from start of flight. At 0348 UTC approach contact, FDR data showed aircraft 18 NM west of Surveillance Point 4 while ADS-B showed 22 NM southwest—14 NM discrepancy. At 0401:29 UTC, FDR showed 10 NM west of Waypoint DAKAD, ADS-B showed 17 NM southwest—15 NM discrepancy. Crew continued reporting positions based on degraded GNSS/FDR display that did not match ATC surveillance picture. (p. 3, 27)

ATC issued descent clearances below published minimum safe altitude (MSA) of 6,000 feet for approach area. At 0420:04 UTC, aircraft at 5,000 feet entered area with MSA of 8,000 feet per ATC SMAC chart. At 0422:36 UTC, aircraft at 4,100 feet descended further in area with MSA of 6,000 feet. Minimum Safe Altitude Warning (MSAW) system did not activate despite these violations; MSAW dataset had not been updated since 2015. (p. 5, 27, 34)

Weather radar and satellite imagery at 0420 UTC showed presence of convective cumulonimbus clouds around accident site. Crew requested heading changes to avoid weather at 0405 UTC and 0410:00 UTC. IFR/IMC conditions with reduced visibility in mountainous terrain.

ATC dispatcher used imprecise English at 0403:42 UTC saying 'DAKAD your not, not point' to advise pilot aircraft was far from Waypoint DAKAD; PM read back only the turning instruction without acknowledging position warning. ATC on duty had non-duty-related discussion with supervisor when PK-THT was flying abeam Waypoint OPENG. Assistant controller absent from workstation from 0410 UTC until shortly after radar loss.

Pilots did not use required headsets and boom microphones during approach phase. Aircraft operator OM-A required headsets from start of descent through landing. Unintelligible pilot cockpit area microphone channel in CVR indicated both pilots not using headsets. This impaired crew communication and situational awareness during critical descent and approach.

Aircraft equipped with Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System (EGPWS) with worldwide terrain database. At approximately 0422:45 UTC, EGPWS generated repeated aural alerts 'TERRAIN - TERRAIN' followed by 'PULL UP' four times. Warnings came too late in descent sequence for effective recovery.

Aircraft impacted Mount Bulusaraung at coordinates 4°55'44.37" S; 119°44'50.008" E at elevation approximately 4,300 feet AMSL. Initial impact location with wreckage scattered 700 × 200 meters on slope of approximately 80°. No evidence of in-flight fire; post-impact fire observed on wreckage. All 10 occupants fatally injured: 2 pilots, 2 flight attendants, 6 passengers/mission staff. Aircraft destroyed by impact force.

events.text: ATR 42-500 PK-THT departed Runway 09 Adisutjipto Airport (Yogyakarta) at 0109 UTC (08:09 local) for aerial surveillance charter mission to Sultan Hasanuddin Airport (Makassar). Crew: Captain (58, ATPL, 14,956 total hours, 3,358 on type) and First Officer (25, CPL, 524 total hours, 346 on type). 2 flight attendants and 6 passengers (1 flight operations officer, 2 aircraft engineers, 3 aerial surveyors). 10 total on board.

Aircraft climbing. Flight Data Recorder began recording at engine start with GNSS HT1000 system in Degrade mode (GPS accuracy/integrity compromised). Aircraft position on FDR initially 1 NM southeast of Adisutjipto. ADS-B ground receiver did not yet receive aircraft broadcast data. Pilots should not navigate using degraded GNSS per FCOM procedures.

At 0112 UTC at altitude 5,900 feet, ADS-B ground receiver began receiving aircraft broadcast data. Position discrepancy evident: FDR showed aircraft 0.6 NM northwest of ADS-B position, distance continuing to reduce initially. At 0114 UTC (7,700 feet), GNSS Degrade parameter changed to 'Not Degrade'. FDR and ADS-B trajectories merged. Aircraft reached and maintained cruise altitude 11,000 feet at 0117 UTC.

At 0143 UTC, GNSS Degrade parameter recorded as 'Degrade' again and remained degraded until end of FDR recording. About 1 minute later, aircraft descended to approximately 2,000 feet to conduct first aerial surveillance near Surveillance Point 1. FDR and ADS-B trajectories began diverging; distance between trajectories increased to 13-17 NM and remained large throughout approach phase.

At 0348 UTC (11:48 local), Second In Command (PM) made initial contact with Approach Control Ujung Pandang Terminal Control Area. CVR indicated SIC was PM, PIC was PF. ATC requested surveillance identification and approach clearance. Crew reported aircraft on heading for last aerial surveillance area (Surveillance Point 4) on radial 283, 63 NM from MKS VOR. At this time, FDR position 18 NM west of Surveillance Point 4, ADS-B position 22 NM southwest—14 NM discrepancy unbeknownst to ATC or crew.

At 0401:29 UTC, ATC reconfirmed aircraft heading. PM reported aircraft on heading 083 to Waypoint DAKAD at 6,000 feet. FDR data showed aircraft 10 NM west of DAKAD; ADS-B data showed 17 NM southwest of DAKAD—15 NM position discrepancy. ATC descent clearances began, instructing descent to 5,000 feet, then 3,200 feet. Pilots proceeded with descent based on degraded GNSS position display unaware of actual lateral deviation.

At 0416 UTC, ATC instructed aircraft to turn left heading 125° to Waypoint OPENG. At 0420:04 UTC, ATC situation display showed PK-THT target descended to 5,000 feet and entered area with MSA of 8,000 feet per ATC Surveillance Minimum Altitude Chart (SMAC). Minimum Safe Altitude Warning (MSAW) from surveillance system did not activate; MSAW dataset had not been updated since 2015. At 0420:46 UTC, ATC instructed aircraft to turn right to Waypoint KABIB and descend to 3,200 feet.

At 0422:36 UTC, ATC situation display showed PK-THT target at 4,100 feet descending, entered area with MSA of 6,000 feet. ATC advised pilot that Waypoint KABIB had passed and confirmed pilot turning right heading 245° for final approach Runway 21. Neither crew nor ATC recognized or acted on large position discrepancy and MSA violation. Pilots were not using required headsets, impairing communication.

At 0422:45 UTC, PM responded to ATC confirming right turn heading 245°. Seconds later, aircraft EGPWS system (terrain and obstacle awareness mode) generated aural alert 'TERRAIN - TERRAIN' followed by 'PULL UP' alert, repeated four times. Red GPWS warning lights illuminated on instrument panels. Cockpit Voice Recorder stopped recording shortly after EGPWS warnings. Aircraft at altitude of 4,100 feet or lower, well below MSA of 6,000 feet, approaching Mount Bulusaraung terrain at 4,300 feet elevation.

At 0423 UTC, PK-THT radar target on ATC display changed from surveillance target to flight plan target; surveillance system no longer received aircraft broadcast data. ATC made repeated radio calls with no response from aircraft. Search and Rescue (SAR) activated. On 18 January 2026, aircraft wreckage found scattered on Mount Bulusaraung at coordinates 4°55'44.37" S; 119°44'50.008" E at elevation 4,300 feet AMSL. Wreckage scattered 700 × 200 meters across 80° slope. No evidence of in-flight fire; post-impact fire observed. All 10 occupants fatally injured. Aircraft destroyed by impact.

safety_changes: DGCA issued Circular Letter SE-DJPU 2 Tahun 2026 directing adherence to minimum safe altitude requirements, comprehensive flight planning, and TAWS procedures
DGCA issued Circular Letter SE-DJPU 4 Tahun 2026 requiring position verification during GNSS degradation and operator reporting of position discrepancies
AirNav Indonesia updated MSAW dataset in accordance with ATC Surveillance Minimum Altitude Chart (SMAC)
AirNav Indonesia revised ILS Runway 21 procedure from S-Type to RNP/ILS (Track to Fix), effective 19 March 2026
PT Indonesia Air Transport issued safety notice on mandatory headset use during critical flight phases

records.title: Air Canada Express 8646
records.summary: On 22 March 2026, a Bombardier CRJ900 operating Air Canada Express Flight 8646 collided with an Oshkosh Striker 1500 aircraft rescue firefighting vehicle (R35) on runway 4 at LaGuardia Airport while landing. The ATC local controller cleared the firefighting truck to cross an active landing runway without verifying that the runway was clear of landing traffic. The aircraft was on short final approach at an altitude of 130 feet when the clearance was issued, approximately 4,400 feet from the runway crossing point. The collision destroyed the aircraft's cockpit, killing both pilots. A flight attendant seated in a jump seat near the cockpit was ejected and injured.
records.probable_cause: The air traffic control local controller cleared the aircraft rescue firefighting vehicle (R35) and other vehicles to cross runway 4 without verifying that the runway was clear of landing traffic. The controller issued the clearance when Jazz flight 646 was on a short final approach at 130 feet above ground level, approximately 4,400 feet away from the point where the vehicles were directed to cross. Contributing to the accident were the failure of the Airport Surface Detection Equipment (ASDE-X) system to detect and alert the controller of the runway conflict, due to the absence of transponders on the ground response vehicles, and the early extinguishment of the runway entrance lights (RELs) before the aircraft reached the taxiway D and runway 4 intersection.

factors.evidence: ATC local controller instructed R35 and company to cross runway 4 at taxiway D at 23:37:04 when aircraft was 4,400 feet away on short final at 130 feet altitude (p. 4). Controller issued clearance without verifying runway was clear of landing traffic.

R35 vehicle crossed onto runway 4 while aircraft was landing. Vehicle reached runway edge and entered runway after controller's second stop instruction at 23:37:20 but continued into runway at 23:37:22 (p. 5).

ASDE-X system did not generate alert for runway conflict. Multiple ground vehicles had no transponders; system displayed only two radar targets instead of all seven response vehicles, unable to establish high-confidence tracks or predict conflict (p. 11-12).

Aircraft struck rear-right side of R35 at intersection of taxiway D and runway 4 at 23:37:23 with aircraft ground speed of 90 knots (p. 5). Collision destroyed cockpit and forward fuselage, killing both pilots.

Night visual meteorological conditions prevailed. At time of accident, visibility was 4 statute miles in light rain and mist (p. 14). Weather observation at 22:51 showed visibility 7 miles; next observation at 23:51 showed 4 miles.

events.text: ATC local controller cleared Jazz flight 646 to land on runway 4
R35 (Rescue 35) and six other response vehicles departed fire station to respond to emergency near terminal B
Tool Truck 7 attempted radio call to ATC (obscured by simultaneous transmission) and coordinated with R35; R35 entered taxiway BB
Tool Truck 7 retried radio contact and coordinated with R35 to contact tower
ATC asked which vehicle needed to cross a runway; R35 moved to front of waiting vehicles at taxiway BB and D intersection
Red runway entrance lights (RELs) illuminated at taxiway D and runway 4 intersection to warn of landing aircraft
R35 crew replied to ATC acknowledgement and requested clearance to cross runway 4 at taxiway D
ATC local controller instructed R35 and company to cross runway 4 at taxiway D
R35 crew read back clearance and began moving along taxiway D toward runway 4
Aircraft crossed runway 4 threshold
ATC local controller immediately instructed R35 to stop after giving taxiing instruction to another airplane
Aircraft main landing gear touched down approximately 1,450 feet from taxiway D; control transferred from first officer to captain
ATC ordered R35 to stop again; aircraft applied brakes and deployed thrust reversers
Red runway entrance lights extinguished as aircraft progressed down runway
Aircraft nose landing gear touched down; R35 vehicle entering runway 4 at approximately 30 mph
Collision: Aircraft struck rear-right side of R35 at intersection of taxiway D and runway 4 with ground speed of 90 knots
